In the Sub-commentaries, that word 'upaddutassa' is explained as 'oppressed by the affliction of livelihood (ājīva).'

He speaks thus: 'What use has a recluse for expensive robes? It is proper for a recluse to collect rags from a cemetery, or a rubbish heap, or a shop, and having made them into a double-layered robe, wear it. This is suitable and proper. What use has a recluse for expensive almsfood? It is proper for a recluse to maintain his life by scraps of food obtained through wandering for alms. This is suitable and proper. What use has a recluse for expensive lodgings? It is proper for a recluse to be one who dwells at the foot of a tree or in the open air. This is suitable and proper. What use has a recluse for expensive medicinal requisites? It is proper for a recluse to make medicine with fermented urine or pieces of yellow myrobalan. This is suitable and proper.'

Based on those words of his, he wears coarse robes, consumes coarse almsfood, uses coarse lodgings, and uses coarse medicinal requisites. Householders recognize him thus: 'This recluse has few desires, is contented, secluded, unmingled, energetic, and a proponent of ascetic practices.' They invite him more and more with robes... requisites. Then that monk speaks thus: 'Due to the presence of three things, a faithful son of good family produces much merit: (1) due to the presence of faith... (2) due to the presence of the gift... (3) due to the presence of those worthy of offerings, a faithful son of good family produces much merit. You householders have this faith, the gift is present, and I am the recipient. If I do not accept, you will be excluded from merit. I have no need for this requisite. However, I accept it only out of compassion for you.' Based on such speech, or from that time on, he accepts many robes, many almsfood... many medicines. [25] Such frowning, the state of frowning, causing wonderment, the manner of causing wonderment, the state of being one who causes wonderment—this causing of wonderment is called the ground for scheming consisting in the use of requisites.' This is the Niddesa Pali.

Furthermore, the causing of wonderment in various ways by a monk who has only evil desires, through speech that indicates the attainment of jhāna, path, and fruition, is to be known as the ground for scheming called indirect talk (sāmantajappana).
25:
As it is stated (in the Mahāniddesa Pāḷi):

“What is the ground of scheming known as indirect talk (sāmantajappana)? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, being of evil desires, overwhelmed by desire, and wishing for praise from others, speaks words based on the noble states (ariya-dhamma) of the Path and Fruition with the intention, ‘If I speak thus, people will praise me.’ He says (referring to himself), ‘A monk who wears such a robe is of great power.’ He says, ‘A monk who uses such an alms-bowl... a bronze bowl... a water-strainer... a cloth filter... a key... such a waist-band... or sandals is of great power.’ [He says,] ‘The preceptor of such a monk is of such a nature; his teacher is of such a nature. His fellow preceptor... fellow teacher... friend... acquaintance... or intimate companion is of such a nature; that monk is of great power.’ [He says,] ‘Such a monk dwells in such a monastery; in a lean-to... a mansion... a flat-roofed house... a cave... a mountain cleft... a hut... a gabled house... a watchtower... a hall... a storehouse... an assembly hall... a pavilion... or at the foot of such a tree; that monk is of great power.’ (Referring to himself in all these instances.)

Alternatively, [a monk in this Dispensation] excessively constrains and suppresses his body and speech with evil desires like loathsome dust (korajika). Being one who frowns much, one who acts wonderfully, one who talks much, and one who seeks praise through his own words, he speaks deep, hidden, subtle, concealed, supramundane words connected with emptiness (suññatā) and Nibbāna, [implying,] ‘This monk is an attainer of such peaceful and subtle dwellings and attainments (vihara-samāpatti).’ Such frowning, the state of frowning, scheming, the act of scheming, and the state of being a schemer—this bringing about of wonder in one's presence is called the ground of scheming known as indirect talk (sāmantajappana).

Furthermore, the act of causing wonder through a posture performed with evil desires by a monk who wishes to be praised is to be known as the ground of scheming based on posture (iriyāpatha-sannissita). As it is said:

“What is the ground of scheming known as posture? In this Dispensation, a certain monk, being of evil desires, overwhelmed by desire, and wishing for praise, composes his posture of walking with the intention, ‘If I act thus, people will praise me.’ [26] He composes his posture of standing, he composes his posture of sitting, and he composes his posture of lying down. He walks, stands, sits, and lies down with the aspiration [to be seen as an Arahant]. He walks, stands, sits, and lies down as if he possessed concentration (samādhi). He acts as if entering meditative absorption (jhāna) in places where people can see him. Such frowning, the state of frowning, scheming, the act of scheming, and the state of being a schemer, which is called ‘the prioritizing of posture, the manner of posture, and the well-composed posture,’ [is the ground of scheming based on posture].”
26:
This deliberate arrangement of postures is called the 'basis of scheming consisting of postures.'

In that explanation (niddesa): 'paccaya-paṭisevana-saṅkhātena' means by what is called the use of requisites (by way of creating wonder); alternatively, by what is spoken of as the use of requisites.

Note 1: In the previous translation of the Pali text, it was translated according to this first explanation.

'Sāmantajappitena' means by speaking nearby (as if to another, but intended for the donor). 'Iriyāpathassa vā' means of the four postures. 'Aṭṭhapanā' means setting up initially; alternatively, setting up with respect. 'Ṭhapanā' means the manner of setting up. 'Saṇṭhapanā' means preparation; it means 'making oneself appear inspiring' or 'arranging to be inspiring.' 'Bhākuṭikā' means making a frown by showing a state of being disturbed by meditation practice; it means a contraction of the face. One who has the habit of making a frown is 'bhākuṭika'; the state of such a person is 'bhākuṭiya.' 'Kuhana' means causing amazement. Causing amazement to arise is 'kuhāyanā.' The state of one who causes amazement is 'kuhitatta.'

In the explanation of the word 'lapana': 'ālapana' means, upon seeing lay devotees arriving at the monastery, speaking first (without being asked, to suggest offerings or invitations) such as, 'Friends, for what purpose have you come? Have you come to invite the monks? If so, go ahead; I will take the bowl and follow later.' Alternatively, 'ālapana' is speech involving self-promotion, such as, 'I am Elder Tissa; the King is devoted to me. Such and such a great royal minister is also devoted to me.'

'Lapana' means the aforementioned kind of talking when one is asked (e.g., 'Which elder is Venerable Tissa?'). 'Sallapana' means talking well and repeatedly, being afraid of the lay devotees' boredom, by giving them opportunities to speak. 'Ullapana' means exalting speech, such as, 'Great householder, great ship-owner (or great boat-owner), or great donor.' 'Samullapana' means exalting speech in every way or in all aspects.

'Unnahana' means 'binding' speech by tying [the donor] from behind repeatedly, such as, 'Lay followers, in the past at such a time you used to give the first-fruits; why do you not give now?' until they say, 'We will give, Bhante, but we have not yet found the opportunity.' It means 'entangling speech.' Alternatively, [Page 27] seeing someone with sugarcane in hand, one asks, 'Lay follower, where did you bring that from?' He replies, 'I brought it from the sugarcane field, Bhante.' One asks again, 'Is the sugarcane in that field sweet?' If he replies, 'You can know if you chew (suck) it, Bhante,' then one says, 'Lay follower, it is not proper for a monk to say, "Give me sugarcane."' Even if the lay follower tries to answer evasively, such speech that entangles him (so he cannot escape) is called 'unnahana.' Repeatedly binding in every way is 'samunnahana.'

'Ukkācanā' means exalting (the donor's qualities) such as, 'That family or that household knows only me; if any gift arises in this family or household, they give it only to me.' It means 'showing by exalting.' In this context, the story of Telakandari should be told. Repeatedly exalting in every way is 'samukkācanā.'

'Anuppiyabhāṇitā' means repeatedly saying only what is pleasant, without regarding what is true or what is in accordance with the Dhamma. 'Cāṭukamyatā' means the state of being lowly; speaking by placing oneself in a lower position. 'Muggasūpyatā' means the state of being like bean soup. To explain: when green grams (mung beans) are cooked, only one or two remain uncooked while the rest are well-cooked and soft; similarly, in the speech of such a person, only one or two words are true, while all the remaining words are...
27: 1. Two monks entered a village and sat in the refectory. Seeing a young girl, they called her. When she came, one of the two asked the other, "Whose daughter is this girl, Bhante?" "She is the daughter of our supporter named Telakandarikā. When I go to her mother's house and she offers ghee, she offers it with the whole jar. This girl also offers it with the whole jar just like her mother," he said, speaking in a flattering manner. Regarding this, it is said, "The Telakandarikā story should be told here." (Sub-commentary) This story is also found in the Sammohavinodanī, page 464. It is wrong; such a person is called one whose speech is like bean soup. The state of having such bean-soup-like speech, or the talk that causes it, is called muggasūpyatā. Pāribhaṭyatā refers to the state of acting as a nurse. To elaborate: a monk who carries and cares for the children of lay supporters on his hip or shoulder, like a nurse; "carrying and bearing" is the meaning. The work of one who carries and cares for those children is called pāribhaṭya. The state of performing such nursing work is called pāribhaṭyatā (Note 1). In the explanation of the term nemittikatā, nimitta (a sign) is any physical or verbal action that creates the perception of giving requisites in others. Nimittakamma (making a sign) is making a sign for a gift by seeing people carrying food and asking, "What kind of food did you get?" and so on (Note 2). Obhāsa (insinuation) is talk connected with requisites (Note 1). Obhāsakamma is making an insinuation, such as seeing boys herding calves and asking, "Are these calves milk-fed or buttermilk-fed?" When they answer, "They are milk-fed, Bhante," saying, "They cannot be milk-fed; if they were milk-fed, the monks would also get milk," and so on, thereby informing the parents of those boys and causing them to offer milk. Sāmantajappa (roundabout talk) is talking in the vicinity of the desired object or talking circuitously (Note 2). In this context, the story of the monk who frequents a family (kulūpaka) should be told. Note 1: The work of nursing (pāribhaṭya) itself is called pāribhaṭyatā. (Sub-commentary) In this sense, pāribhaṭya and pāribhaṭyatā should be understood as having the same meaning; this is clearer. Note 2: Nimittakamma is the knowledge or skill in making signs for the offering of requisites. Regarding this nimittakamma, the following is a story. It is heard that another alms-collecting monk went to the door of a blacksmith who was his supporter. When asked by the blacksmith, "What is it, Bhante?" he put his hand through the gap in his robe and made a gesture as if striking with a chopper. The blacksmith said, "I understand well, Bhante," and having made a chopper, he offered it. (Sammohavinodanī, p. 465)
28:
“...Then, I saw the saliva mixed with venom coming out of the mouth of the angry snake, just like the butter kept in the butter jar,” he said. That housewife, reflecting, “It is impossible to deceive this shaven-headed one,” offered the sugarcane, cooked the rice, and offered everything together with the butter, molasses, and dried fish. Thus, speaking by bringing [the desired object] close, or by ‘rubbing’ against it, is to be known as sāmantajappa (indirect talk). Parikathā (roundabout talk) means speaking repeatedly in a circuitous manner to obtain that desired object.

In the definition of the term nippesikatā (belittling/extorting): Akkosana (reviling) means reviling by way of the ten bases of abuse.1 Vambhanā (disparaging) means speaking with contempt. Garahaṇā (fault-finding) means attributing faults by saying one lacks faith (does not believe in kamma and its results) or lacks devotion (to the Triple Gem), and so on. Ukkhepanā (extolling/excluding) means excluding someone by words from being a donor, etc., saying, “Do not mention this person in this act of giving.” Thoroughly excluding someone with grounds and reasons is called samukkhepanā. Alternatively, seeing someone who does not give and saying, “Oh, what a great donor!” in a mocking, uplifting manner is called ukkhepanā. Saying, “What a great donor!” excessively is called samukkhepanā. Khipanā (mocking) means scoffing, such as saying, “What is the use of the life of this person who merely consumes the seeds?” Saṅkhipanā (thorough mocking) means scoffing even more intensely, saying, “Why do you say this person does not give? This person always gives the word ‘No’ to all seekers.” Pāpanā (bringing to dispraise) means causing one to reach the state of a non-giver or bringing them into disrepute. Thoroughly bringing one to such a state is called sampāpanā. Avaṇṇahāritā (carrying dispraise) means carrying dispraise and spreading bad reports from house to house, village to village, and district to district, hoping that, “When I speak of his faults in this way, he will give to me out of fear of a bad reputation.” Parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā (backbiting) means the state of speaking sweetly in one’s presence but speaking dispraise behind one’s back. Indeed, such speaking is like [29] consuming the flesh of the back of those who have turned away, done by one who does not dare to look them in the face. Therefore, it is called parapiṭṭhimaṃsikatā. All these acts, such as reviling, are called nippesikatā—meaning that just as one scrapes off the oil applied to the body with a bamboo splinter, one ‘scrapes off’ another’s virtues. Alternatively, just as one seeks perfume by grinding and crushing various aromatic substances, this is the seeking of gain by grinding and thoroughly crushing another’s virtues. Therefore, it is called nippesikatā.

In the definition of the term ‘seeking gain with gain’ (lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā): ‘The state of seeking’ means the act of searching. (The grammatical meanings of the terms ito laddhaṃ, amutra, eṭṭhi, gaveṭṭhi, and pariyeṭṭhi explained here are the same as previously translated; therefore, they are omitted here as repeating them would not be very beneficial). In this context, the story of the monk who gave away the alms-food he received from the first house to the children of various houses until he finally obtained only milk porridge should be told. This aforementioned explanation is the meaning of terms such as kuhana (scheming).

Now, regarding the phrase “of such evil practices,” the word “such” refers to the many evil practices taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta, such as: “Furthermore, some recluses and brahmins, having consumed the offerings given in faith (by the public), live by such wrong livelihoods and base arts (tiracchānavijjā) as: palmistry, interpreting omens, interpreting celestial portents, interpreting dreams, fortune-telling from body marks, interpreting marks made by rats, fire-oblations, and oblations made with a ladle.” This should be understood as including these practices. Thus, it is to be understood as the power of transgressing the six training rules (sikkhāpada) prescribed on account of livelihood, as well as the evil practices such as kuhana (scheming), lapana (persuading), nemittikatā (hinting), nippesikatā (belittling), and lābhena lābhaṃ nijigīsanatā (seeking gain with gain).

Footnotes:
1. The ten bases of abuse are: (1) birth/caste, (2) name, (3) lineage, (4) occupation, (5) craft, (6) disease, (7) physical appearance (height, complexion, etc.), (8) defilements (greed, anger, etc.), (9) offenses, (10) general insults such as calling one an ox, dog, or animal.
2. This refers to reviling with the ten bases of abuse, thinking that the person might give out of fear of being reviled. Disparaging and the others are to be understood similarly. (Ṭīkā)
29:
Note 1: It should be understood that the phrase 'beginning with' is connected to the inclusion of evil practices.
Note 2: The arts that are contrary to the practice leading to heaven and Nibbāna are called 'low arts' (tiracchānavijjā).

That wrong livelihood, known as micchājīva, which occurs through the power of the aforementioned [evil] practices, exists. Abstaining from all such various forms of wrong livelihood is called ājīvapārisuddhisīla (virtue of purification of livelihood).

In this regard, the following is the word-definition (vacanattha): They live depending on this effort (for seeking requisites); the effort which is the basis for that living is called ājīva (livelihood). What is that effort? It is the effort for seeking requisites. Purity in all respects is called pārisuddhi. The purity in all respects of livelihood, or the effort of seeking requisites for livelihood, is called ājīvapārisuddhisīla.

## Paccayasannissitasīla

Furthermore, regarding the paccayasannissitasīla mentioned immediately after ājīvapārisuddhisīla, or in the scriptural passage concerning paccayasannissitasīla, [the determination of the meaning should be understood as follows]: 'Paṭisaṅkhā yoniso' means knowing by proper means and right method, that is, 'reflecting wisely.'

Note 1: When the Burmese translation term is presented as the subject of explanation, if it is identical to the explanatory word, or in cases explaining the grammatical meaning, the Pali is presented as the subject of explanation. In cases where the Burmese translation term should be presented, the Burmese term is used. In some cases, both Pali and Burmese are presented.

[30] In this context, the reflection stated in the manner 'for the purpose of warding off cold,' and so forth, should be understood as 'reflecting by proper means.' In that passage, 'the robe' refers to any one of the robes, such as the inner robe (antaravāsaka). 'Uses' means partakes of; it means 'he wears it or he drapes it.' The word 'yāvadeva' (only for) is a term that limits the scope of the intended benefit. Indeed, whatever benefit is intended, such as 'for the purpose of warding off cold,' that much alone is the desired benefit for the yogi monk in using the robe; there is nothing beyond this. 'Cold' refers to any kind of cold that arises either through the disturbance of elements within the body or through the change of seasons externally. 'Paṭighātāya' means for the sake of warding off, meaning 'for the sake of warding off that cold so that it cannot cause affliction to the body.' Indeed, when the body is oppressed by cold, the mind becomes distracted and one is unable to practice the Dhamma properly. Therefore, the Blessed One allowed, 'A robe should be used for the sake of warding off cold.' The same method applies to all subsequent sections. What is unique in the following sections is that 'heat' refers to the heat of fire; the occurrence of such heat should be understood in cases like forest fires, etc. 

Note 1: Since encountering forest fires and the like is rare, the benefit of warding off the heat of fire by robes or dwellings is very limited in scope. Therefore, it is also appropriate to take 'heat' (uṇha) here as any heat other than sunlight. Indeed, in very hot regions, the heat caused by the climate must be protected against by clothing and buildings. Therefore, in the commentary to the Cūḷavagga Pali (p. 58) on the phrase 'sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti' (it wards off cold and heat), it is explained that 'the words cold and heat are spoken in accordance with the desire for a suitable climate.'

In the phrase 'ḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapa-samphassānaṃ': 'ḍaṃsa' refers to biting flies (gadflies); they are also called 'blind flies.' 'Makasa' refers to mosquitoes. 'Vāta' (wind) refers to various kinds of wind, such as wind with dust or wind without dust. 'Ātapa' refers to the heat of the sun. 'Sarīsapa' refers to all creeping creatures with long bodies that move by crawling, such as snakes. The contact of those creatures, such as snakes, is of two kinds: the contact of biting and the contact of touching. Neither of these two kinds of contact can afflict a monk who stays draped in his robe. Therefore, in places where such creatures (snakes, etc.) are abundant, a monk uses the robe for the sake of warding off the contact of those snakes and so forth. The repetition of the word 'yāvadeva' is for the purpose of showing the limit of the constant benefit. Indeed, covering the parts of the body that cause shame (hirikopīna) is a constant benefit; other benefits occur only occasionally.
30:
In that context, "hirikopīna" refers to those various private parts of the body. Indeed, if those parts of the body are left uncovered, the quality of shame (hiri) is destroyed; because they cause the destruction of shame, those parts of the body are called "hirikopīna." Because it is for the purpose of covering those parts of the body that cause the destruction of shame, it is called "hirikopīnapaticchādanatthaṃ." There is also a variant reading: "hirikopīnaṃ paticchādanatthaṃ."

"Piṇḍapāta" (almsfood) refers to any kind of food (that is eaten). Indeed, any kind of food is called "piṇḍapāta" because it is dropped into the bowl through the monk's alms-gathering. Alternatively, it is the collection of almsfood (from many houses). It means "the collection or group of almsfood obtained from various houses."

Note 1: Alternatively, it is called "kopīna" because it deserves covering; it is also called "hiri" because of the sense of shame. It is "kopīna" (deserving covering). Therefore, it is called "hirikopīna." (Sub-commentary) According to this view, it is translated as "for the purpose of covering the parts that are shameful and deserve covering." In the previous footnote, this meaning was shown as "or, the shameful parts that should be covered."

Note 2: Piṇḍolya (by alms-gathering) + pāta (dropped/poured) = piṇḍolyapāta = piṇḍapāta (almsfood dropped into the bowl through alms-gathering).

Note 3: Piṇḍa (morsels of food) + pāta (collection) = piṇḍapāta (a collection of morsels of food).

"Neva davāya" means not for the purpose of playing or sporting like village children; it means "not for the sake of playing" or "not in order to be able to play." "Na madāya" means not for the purpose of intoxication with physical strength or manly pride like boxers or wrestlers. It means "not for the sake of intoxication based on strength." "Na maṇḍanāya" [31] means not for the purpose of making the limbs and body parts plump like palace women or courtesans. It means "not for the sake of the plumpness of the limbs." "Na vibhūsanāya" means not for the purpose of making the complexion clear and bright like dancers or acrobats. It means "not for the sake of having a clear and bright complexion."

Note 4: "Na maṇḍanāya" means one does not eat for the sake of the clarity of the body. In this context, women who live by their physical appearance, such as palace women, drink things like ghee and molasses. These women and palace attendants eat fine food with the intention: "By consuming this food, our physical bodies will have a good shape (proportionate) and our complexion will be clear." This yogi monk does not eat with such intentions. (Atthasālinī, p. 430). In the previous footnote, the translation of the Pali was done in accordance with this explanation.

Among these four phrases, "neva davāya" is taught to abandon the playfulness that is a strong condition (upanissaya) for delusion (moha), or to abandon the consumption that is a strong condition for delusion. "Na madāya" is taught to abandon the intoxication of pride that is a strong condition for hatred (dosa), or to abandon the consumption that is a strong condition for hatred. The combination of these two phrases, "na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya," is taught to abandon the increase of flesh and blood and the brightness of complexion which are strong conditions for lust (rāga), or for the purpose of abandoning the consumption that is a strong condition for lust. Alternatively, the combination of "neva davāya na madāya" is taught to prevent the arising of fetters (saṃyojana) in oneself as the consumer; the combination of "na maṇḍanāya na vibhūsanāya" is taught for the purpose of preventing the arising of fetters in others. Alternatively, it should be understood that with all four phrases, the Buddha taught the abandonment of improper practice (consumption) and the enjoyment of consumption through craving attached to sensual pleasures (kāmasukhallikānuyoga).

"Yāvad eva" has the meaning already explained. "Imassa kāyassa" refers to this body, a collection of matter dependent on the four great elements. "Ṭhitiyā" means for the endurance of the continuity of matter through successive occurrences. "Yāpanāya" means for the purpose of the non-interruption of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) called life; or for the endurance of the body for a long time (as long as the lifespan lasts). To illustrate with a simile: just as the owner of an old house props up the house (so it does not fall or collapse), and just as a cart owner greases the cart (so it rolls smoothly), in the same way, this yogi monk consumes almsfood for the endurance of the body and for its continued existence and movement for a long time. "He does not consume it for the purpose of playing, intoxication, making the limbs plump, or making the complexion bright." Alternatively, the name "ṭhiti" is a name for the life faculty (jīvitindriya).
31:
Therefore, by the phrase 'for the support and maintenance of this body' (imassa kāyassa ṭhitiyā yāpanāya), it should be understood that it also means 'for the sake of the continuous occurrence of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) which is the cause of the persistence of this physical body (material group).'

Vihiṃsūparatiyā: Hunger is called 'affliction' (vihiṃsā) because of its nature to oppress. To end this affliction of hunger, which is like a disease, this yogi monk consumes almsfood. (For example) just as a person with an abscess applies ointment, or just as one uses heat or cold to counteract heat or cold, [so too this yogi monk consumes almsfood].

Brahmacariyānuggahāya: This means for the sake of supporting (practicing) the holy life of the entire Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya) and the holy life of the Noble Path (maggabrahmacariya).1 Indeed, this yogi monk, by means of consuming almsfood, relies on physical strength to constantly apply himself to the three trainings (sikkhā) in order to cross over the difficult journey of existence (bhava); thus, he consumes [almsfood] to support the two kinds of holy life. (How so?) Just as a couple desiring to cross a waterless desert consume their son's flesh (without greed),2 or as those desiring to cross a river use a raft (without greed),3 or as those desiring to cross the ocean use a ship (without greed).

Iti purāṇañca vedanaṃ paṭihaṅkhāmi navañca vedanaṃ na uppādessāmi: This means that by consuming almsfood in this way, [the monk reflects:] 'I shall remove the old feeling of hunger that existed before [eating], and I shall not produce a new feeling caused by immoderate eating, like one of those brahmins who eat until they must be pulled up by the hand, or eat until their bellies are so distended they cannot wear their loincloths, or eat until they roll on the ground unable to rise, or eat until crows can peck from their mouths, or eat until they vomit.'1 Thus reflecting, he consumes [almsfood]. (How so?) Just as a sick person takes medicine.

Notes:
1. The holy life of the Dispensation (sāsanabrahmacariya) refers to all practices of virtue, concentration, and wisdom, both mundane and supramundane, taught by the Buddha. The holy life of the Path (maggabrahmacariya) refers to the supramundane virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the three trainings, specifically the eightfold Noble Path. Thus, the distinction between the two kinds of brahmacariya should be noted.
2. See the Puttamansūpama Sutta, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Nidāna Vagga, p. 322.
3. See the Alagaddūpama Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya, Mūlapaṇṇāsa, p. 188.

Alternatively, that painful feeling which arises in the present life due to improper and immoderate eating, occurring by the power of past kamma, is called 'old feeling' (by way of metaphorical cause). By eating proper food and eating with moderation, he destroys the old kamma that is the cause of that old feeling (preventing it from yielding results), thus removing that old feeling.2 That painful feeling which will arise in the future (such as in the woeful states) due to the kamma of consuming without reflection in the present life,3 or due to the kamma accumulated through improper consumption (without reflection), is called 'new feeling.' By the power of proper consumption (consuming with reflection), he does not produce the kamma of unreflective consumption, which is the root cause of that new feeling, and thus he reflects, 'I shall not produce that new feeling.' In this way also, the meaning in this text should be understood. By these two phrases, 'I shall remove the old feeling and not produce a new feeling,' or by these four phrases starting from the stilling of hunger and thirst, it should be understood that 'the adoption of proper consumption, the abandonment of the practice of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga), and the non-abandonment of righteous happiness are shown.'

Notes:
1. Connect as: 'I shall remove... and I shall not produce a new feeling... thus reflecting.'
2. Connect as: 'I shall remove the old feeling... and I shall not produce that new feeling... thus reflecting.'
3. Connect as: 'The kamma... performed [in this life].'

Yātrā ca me bhavissati: This means reflecting, 'By consuming food in moderation, because of the absence of dangers that cut off the life faculty or destroy the postures, there will be for me a "going" or "maintenance," which is the ability of this physical body to proceed for its full lifespan in connection with its causes.' (For example) just as a person with a disease that prevents standing takes medicine that is the opposite of that disease, or medicine that cures that disease.

Anavajjatā ca phāsuvihāro ca: This means blamelessness by avoiding improper seeking, receiving, and consuming, and living at ease by consuming with moderation.1
32:
Alternatively, there is blamelessness due to the absence of faults such as lack of delight (in the secluded meditation monastery and the wholesome states of meditation), drowsiness, stretching of the limbs (due to being oppressed by sloth and torpor), and being censured by the wise, which arise from consuming unsuitable food or excessive consumption without moderation. And there is living at ease because of the physical strength that arises from consuming suitable food in moderation. 

Alternatively, he uses almsfood reflecting: 'Blamelessness will be mine through the abandonment of the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining on either side, and the pleasure of torpor, by avoiding eating to full satisfaction as much as one desires; and living at ease will be mine by achieving suitability for the four postures through eating four or five mouthfuls less than full.' Indeed, it has been said:

'One should drink water after refraining from four or five mouthfuls. This is sufficient for the living at ease of a monk who has directed his mind [toward Nibbāna].'

By this much, through the phrases starting with 'maintenance' (yātrā), it should be understood that the grasping of the intended purpose and the middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā) are shown.

Lodging (senāsana) means a bed (sena) and a seat (āsana). To explain: wherever one sleeps, whether in a dwelling or a lean-to, that is a bed (sena). Wherever one sits, that is a seat (āsana). Taken together, it is called lodging (senāsana). Regarding the phrase 'for the purpose of dispelling the dangers of the seasons and for the delight of seclusion': the season (utu) itself, such as cold or heat, is called the 'danger of the season' (utu-parissaya) because of its oppressive nature. 

[33] It means: for the purpose of dispelling the danger of the seasons and for the purpose of delighting in seclusion (which is the mind's adherence to the object of meditation, having withdrawn from various distracting objects). It means: 'One can dispel unsuitable weather, which oppresses the body and causes mental distraction, by using the dwelling. It is for the purpose of dispelling unsuitable weather and for the purpose of the bliss of seclusion resulting from living alone (without the company of attendants or the companion of defilements).' Just as in the case of using robes, although the purpose of dispelling cold, etc., is mentioned, the purpose of covering the parts of the body that destroy the quality of shame (hiri) is the constant benefit, while other benefits like dispelling cold and heat occur only occasionally; similarly, in using this dwelling, it should be understood that this term 'for the purpose of dispelling the danger of the seasons' (utu-parissaya-vinodanatthaṃ) is taught with reference to the constant benefit of dispelling the danger of the seasons. 

Alternatively, this 'season' (utu) mentioned as cold, heat, or unsuitable weather is called only 'season' (it is not called 'danger'). The danger (parissaya) is of two kinds: manifest danger and unmanifest danger. Among them, manifest dangers are lions, tigers, etc.; unmanifest dangers are lust (rāga), hatred (dosa), etc. These manifest and unmanifest dangers cannot oppress a monk living in a secure dwelling. A monk who uses the dwelling, reflecting and recognizing it in this way (that the two kinds of dangers cannot oppress him), should be understood as 'using the dwelling for the purpose of dispelling unsuitable weather and manifest and unmanifest dangers by reflecting on the proper cause.'

In the term 'medicinal requisites for the sick' (gilāna-paccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāraṃ), it is called 'requisite' (paccaya) because of its meaning as an 'opponent' (paṭi-ayana) to illness. 'Because of the meaning of being an opponent'—this is...
33:
The meaning of 'paṭi-ayanaṭṭhena': The name 'paccaya' (requisite) is the name of a certain medicine suitable for curing illness. Because it is a medicine allowed by the Blessed One, who is like a great physician, it is the work of the physician (bhisakka), the Blessed One; therefore, it is called 'bhesajja' (medicine). The medicine that cures the illness of the sick (gilāna) is itself called 'bhesajja'; thus, it is called 'gilānappaccaya-bhesajja'. It refers to any medicinal item such as oil, honey, molasses, etc., which is the work of a physician and suitable for the sick.

Note 1: Paṭi (opposite/against) + aya (to go/become) = paccaya (that which goes against illness, i.e., cures it). Gilāna (sick) + paccaya (cure) = gilānappaccaya (requisite for the sick). According to the Ṭīkā, the sense of 'paṭi-ayanaṭṭha' refers to being the opposite of the disease characterized by the disturbance of elements and the painful feelings resulting from it. Thus, it means 'in the sense of being a counter-agent' or 'having the nature of curing'.

Furthermore, in such Pali passages as 'Sattahi nagara-parikkhārehi suparikkhittaṃ hoti' (It is well-protected by the seven city requisites, such as moats, ditches, and walls), the term 'parikkhāra' refers to protection or surroundings. In passages like 'Ratho sīla-parikkhāro, jhānakkhō cakkavīriyo' (The chariot of the Noble Path has virtue as its ornament, jhāna as its axle, and energy as its wheels), 'parikkhāra' refers to ornament. In passages like 'Ye ca kho ime pabbajitena jīvita-parikkhārā samudānetabbā' (These requisites of life should be well-collected by a renunciant), 'parikkhāra' refers to equipment or causes.

Note 2: The seven city requisites (nagara-parikkhāra) refer to the defenses surrounding a city. Teachers state they are: (1) the open space or road around the city, (2) the moat, (3) the slope at the base of the wall, (4) the city wall, (5) the gateposts, (6) the crossbar or bolt of the gate, and (7) the hard ground beyond the wall (pākāra-patthaṇḍila). In the Nagaropama Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Vol. 2, p. 478), they are listed as: (1) deep-set gateposts, (2) a deep and wide moat, (3) a high and wide patrol path, (4) many weapons, (5) a large army, (6) a wise gatekeeper, and (7) a high and wide city wall.

In this term 'gilānappaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāraṃ', both the meaning of 'equipment/cause' and 'protection' are appropriate. The reason is: that medicine which cures the illness of the sick protects life by not allowing the opportunity for life-destroying diseases to arise; thus, it is a protection for life. Because it is the cause for life to continue and persist for a long time, it is also an equipment/cause for life. Therefore, it is called 'parikkhāra'. In this way, that medicine is both 'gilānappaccaya-bhesajja' (medicinal requisite for the sick) and 'parikkhāra' (protection/equipment); hence, it is called 'gilānappaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra'. It refers to any medicinal item such as oil, honey, molasses, etc., allowed by the physician-like Blessed One, which is a protection and equipment for the life of the sick.

Note 1 (re-explained): Although 'gilānappaccaya-bhesajja-parikkhāra' literally means 'the medicinal protection that cures the illness of the sick', it can be understood simply as 'medicine' or 'medicinal requisites'.

Note 2 (re-explained): This explanation follows the original Pali structure (vibhattyanta-saṃvaṇṇanā), which is highly beneficial in Pali study, though less so in Burmese translation; it is included here to maintain the completeness of the Visuddhimagga.

'Uppannānaṃ' means those that have already arisen (in the body). In the word 'veyyābādhikānaṃ', the disturbance of the elements and the diseases resulting from that disturbance, such as leprosy, abscesses, tumors, etc., are called 'byābādha' (affliction) because they oppress and harass the sufferer.
34:
They are called 'veyyābādhika' (afflictive) because they arise from diseases that oppress and torture in various ways. In the word 'vedanānaṃ', it refers to painful feelings (dukkha-vedanā) which are the result of unwholesome actions (akusala-vipāka). (One makes use of medicine for the sake of removing) those painful feelings arising from diseases that oppress the sufferer. 'Abyābajjhaparamatāya' means for the purpose of reaching the ultimate state of freedom from suffering. It means for as long as it takes until all that suffering is abandoned.

Note:
1. This is a combined translation of the three terms: 'jātānaṃ', 'bhūtānaṃ', and 'nibbattānaṃ'.
2. The disturbance of one, two, three, or all four elements is called 'disturbance of elements' (dhātukkhobha). This disturbance is called 'ābadha' (disease/affliction) because it oppresses. 
3. 'Vi' (in various ways) + 'ābadha' (oppressive disease) + 'ika' (arising from) = 'veyyābādhika' (painful feelings arising from diseases that oppress in various ways).

Thus, in brief, virtue characterized by the use of requisites through wise reflection should be understood as 'virtue dependent on requisites' (paccayasannissita-sīla). Regarding the etymology of this term: because beings go on, proceed, or live (until the end of their lifespan) depending on and relying on robes and so forth, these are called 'paccaya' (requisites). Because one relies well on these requisites by using them with reflection, it is called 'paccayasannissita'.

## The Method of Fulfilling the Fourfold Purification of Virtue

19. In this fourfold virtue described above, the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla) should be accomplished through faith (saddhā). Indeed, it is achieved through faith because the laying down of training rules (sikkhāpada-paññatti) is beyond the scope of disciples (sāvaka); that is, it is a matter beyond their wisdom.

Note:
1. 'Pati' (relying on/using) + 'aya' (reaching/proceeding until the end of life) = 'paccaya' (requisites used as a support to reach the end of life).

The refusal of the request to lay down training rules (by the Venerable Sāriputta) is evidence of this. Therefore, one should undertake the training rules exactly as laid down, without remainder, through faith, and fulfill them well without regard even for life. Indeed, the following verse has been spoken:

'As a kiki bird guards its egg, as a yak (camarī) guards its tail, as a mother guards her beloved only son, as a one-eyed man guards his remaining eye; so too, you should always guard your virtue with reverence and be of good character (throughout youth and old age).'

Furthermore, the Blessed One also spoke the following:

Note:
1. The Buddha lays down rules knowing what should be laid down. If one transgresses these rules, it leads to unwholesome states and suffering in lower realms. If one follows them respectfully, it leads to wholesome states, happy destinies, and Nibbāna. Believing firmly that virtue is the foundation for concentration and wisdom, one must practice every training rule respectfully without even regarding one's life.

'Pahārāda, (just as the ocean does not overstep its shore), so too my noble disciples do not overstep the training rules I have laid down, even for the sake of their lives.'

In this regard (regarding not overstepping training rules even for life), the stories of the elders bound by thieves in the forest should be understood as examples.

It is said that in the Mahāvaṭṭani forest, thieves bound an elder with black creepers and made him lie down. While lying there as he was bound, the elder developed insight (vipassanā) for seven days, attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), passed away there, and was reborn in the Brahma world.
35:
It is said that in the forest known as Mahāvattanī, thieves tied up an elder with creepers (so that he could not go elsewhere and inform others) and left him lying there. That elder, remaining in that lying position, developed insight (vipassanā) for seven days, attained the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala), passed away right there, and was reborn in the Brahma realm.

[35] Another elder in the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka) was likewise tied up by thieves with samana-creepers and left lying there. When a forest fire approached, that elder did not cut the creepers but developed insight, became an Arahant known as a samasīsī, and attained parinibbāna.

Note: A samasīsī Arahant (in this context) is an Arahant for whom the 'head of the round of rebirth' (the life faculty) and the 'head of defilements' (ignorance) cease and are cut off simultaneously. To explain further: for such a person, the four paths (magga) in succession, ending with the path of Arahantship, exhaust ignorance. Then, while established in the nineteenth reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), as the mind descends into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) exhausts the life faculty. Because these two stages (the path-process that exhausts defilements and the death-process that exhausts the life faculty) occur in close proximity, he is called a samasīsī. That elder attained parinibbāna in this manner. Therefore, it is said, 'He became a samasīsī Arahant and attained parinibbāna.' (Sub-commentary: The mention of the nineteenth reviewing knowledge here includes the fifteen reviewing knowledges that occur after the lower paths and fruits.)

When the elder Abhaya, the reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya, arrived with five hundred monks and saw the elder's body, he had it cremated and caused a stupa to be built. Therefore, another faithful son of a good family—

Desiring to purify the restraint of the Pātimokkha (pātimokkha-saṃvara),
Should even surrender his life;
He should not break the restraint of virtue (sīla-saṃvara),
Prescribed by the Lord of the World.

Just as the restraint of the Pātimokkha is accomplished through faith, so should the restraint of the faculties (indriya-saṃvara) be accomplished through mindfulness (sati). Indeed, that restraint of the faculties has mindfulness as its means of accomplishment, because the faculties such as the eye, when governed by mindfulness, cannot be flowed into by unwholesome states like covetousness (abhijjhā). Therefore—

'Monks, it would be better for the eye faculty to be rubbed and pierced with a red-hot iron spike, glowing, blazing, and radiant, than to grasp at the signs (nimitta) or secondary details (anubyañjana) of forms cognizable by the eye.'

Reflecting on the Fire Sermon (Ādittapariyāya) taught in this and other ways, one should properly accomplish this restraint of the faculties by preventing, through mindfulness, the grasping of signs and such that allow covetousness and other states to flow into the consciousness occurring at the eye-door and so on in the presence of objects like forms. If this is not accomplished, even the virtue of the restraint of the Pātimokkha will not be long-lasting or enduring, like a crop without a well-constructed fence of thorny branches. Furthermore, such a person is harassed by the thieves of defilements, like a village with open gates is harassed by plunderers. Lust pierces his mind, just as rain pierces a poorly roofed house. For it is said:

'Regarding forms, sounds, and also tastes,
Smells, and touches, guard the faculty;
For when these doors are open and unguarded,
They destroy, like plunderers attacking a village.'

'Just as rain pierces a poorly roofed house,
So lust pierces an undeveloped mind.' (Dhammapada 13)

However, when it is accomplished, the virtue of the restraint of the Pātimokkha is long-lasting and enduring, like a crop with a well-constructed fence of thorny branches. He is not harassed by the thieves of defilements, just as plunderers cannot harass a village with well-secured gates.
36:
Lust does not pierce and harass the mind of that person who guards the faculties, just as rain cannot pierce a well-roofed house. For it is said:

'Regarding forms, sounds, and also tastes,
Smells, and touches, guard the faculty;
For when these doors are closed and well-restrained,
They do not destroy, like plunderers unable to attack a village.'

'Just as rain does not pierce a well-roofed house,
So lust does not pierce a well-developed mind.' (Dhammapada 14)

This aforementioned teaching is a teaching of the highest standard (ati-ukkaṭṭha-desanā).

The mind is indeed fickle and quickly changing; therefore, one should accomplish the restraint of the faculties by dispelling arisen lust through the reflection on foulness (asubha-manasikāra), just as the elder Vaṅgīsa did when he was newly ordained.

It is said that while the newly ordained elder was wandering for alms, he saw a woman and lust arose in him. Then he said to the elder Ānanda:

'I am burning with sensual lust, my mind is on fire;
Please, O Gotama, out of compassion, tell me how to extinguish it.'

The elder Ānanda replied:

'Your mind is burning because of a perversion of perception;
Avoid the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta) which is associated with lust.
Develop the mind to be one-pointed and well-concentrated on foulness (asubha).'

'See formations (saṅkhāra) as alien, as suffering, and not as self;
Extinguish the great fire of lust; do not be burned again and again.'

The elder dispelled his lust and continued his alms round. Furthermore, a monk who fulfills the restraint of the faculties should be like the elder Cittagutta, who resided in the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave, or like the elder Mahāmitta, who resided in the Coraka Great Monastery. In the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave, it is said, there was a beautiful painting of the renunciation of the seven Buddhas. Many monks wandering through the lodgings saw the painting and remarked, 'How beautiful...'
37:
This mind is swift to turn; or, it is prone to changing rapidly. Therefore, one should abandon arising lust by reflecting on foulness and thus fulfill the restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara). [Like whom?] Just like the Venerable Vaṅgīsa, who was newly ordained.

It is said that while the newly ordained Venerable Vaṅgīsa was on his alms round, lust arose in him upon seeing a woman. At that time, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:

“Venerable Ānanda of the Gotama clan, I am burning with the fire of sensual lust; my mind is severely scorched. I beg you, out of compassion, tell me a good way to extinguish this fire of lust.”

Venerable Ānanda said:

“Friend Vaṅgīsa, your mind is severely scorched because of the perversion of perception (regarding foulness as beautiful). Avoid the sign of beauty (subha-nimitta), which is the cause of lust. With a single object of foulness, make the mind well-established; perfume and develop the mind with the meditation on foulness (asubha-bhāvanā).

Note 1: ‘Fulfill’ means to fulfill through the means of purification, which is the resolution: ‘I shall not do this again.’ (Sub-commentary)

View formations (saṅkhāra) as alien and external; view them as suffering and non-self. Extinguish the great fire of lust; do not let it burn you again and again.”

Having abandoned lust, Venerable Vaṅgīsa continued his alms round.

Alternatively, a monk who wishes to fulfill the virtue of sense restraint should be like the Elder Cittagutta who resided in the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave, or like the Elder Mahāmitta who resided in the Coraka Great Monastery.

It is said that in the Kuraṇḍaka Cave, there were paintings of the renunciation scenes of the seven Buddhas, beginning with Vipassī, which were delightful to the heart. When many monks were touring the monastery and saw the paintings, they said, “Venerable sir, these paintings are truly delightful to the heart.” The Elder Cittagutta replied, “Friends, I have lived in this cave for over sixty years, but I did not know whether there were paintings or not. Only today, through you friends who have good eyesight, do I know of them.” Although the Elder Cittagutta lived in the cave for over sixty years, he had never opened his eyes and looked up at the cave.

Note 1: Lust is called ‘great’ because it arises by overwhelming the three realms of existence: the sensual realm, the fine-material realm, and the immaterial realm. (Sub-commentary)

At the entrance of that Elder’s cave, there was also a great Nāga tree (Ironwood). The Elder Cittagutta had never looked up at that great Nāga tree either. Only when he saw the pollen fallen on the ground every year did he know that the tree had bloomed.

King Kākavaṇṇatissa, having heard of the Elder’s perfect qualities and wishing to pay homage, sent for him three times. When the Elder did not come, the King caused the breasts of women in Mahāgāma who had nursing infants to be bound [with wraps] and applied the royal seal. He issued an order: “As long as the Elder Cittagutta does not come [to the palace], let the infants have no opportunity to drink breast milk.” Out of compassion for the children, the Elder Cittagutta went to Mahāgāma. Hearing that the Elder had arrived, the King said, “O ministers, go and invite the Elder into the palace; we shall take the precepts.” After inviting him into the palace, paying homage, and offering a meal, the King said, “Venerable sir, today there is no opportunity to observe the precepts; we shall take and observe them tomorrow.” He then took the Elder’s bowl, followed him for a short distance, and returned after paying homage together with the Queen. Whether the King paid homage or the Queen paid homage, the Elder Cittagutta would only say, “May the Great King be happy.” In this manner, seven days passed. The monks asked, “Venerable sir, why do you only say ‘May the King be happy’ whether it is the King or the Queen who pays homage?” The Elder Cittagutta replied:

“Friends, I make no distinction between ‘King’ or ‘Queen’.” After seven days had passed, the King released him, and the Elder, thinking, “Residing in this Mahāgāma is difficult for an Elder,” returned to the Kuraṇḍaka Great Cave. During the night, he stepped onto the cloister path. The deity residing in the Nāga tree stood holding a torch. At that time, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) became exceedingly pure and manifest to the Elder Cittagutta.
38:
Elder Cittagutta, reflecting with joy, "Is not the meditation subject very clear to me today?" attained Arahatship at the end of the middle watch, making the whole mountain resound. Therefore, any other noble son who desires his own welfare, other than Elder Cittagutta, should also follow this:

One should not have wandering eyes, looking here and there, like a monkey in the great forest, or like a deer that does not stand still but wanders trembling in the woods, or like a frightened child (who has no parents or relatives to rely on). One should cast the eyes down and look only a yoke's length ahead. One should not follow the whims of a restless mind that is as unsteady as a forest monkey.

[38] Furthermore, a poisonous boil, or an abscess of the breast, developed on the mother of Elder Mahāmitta. The daughter of that lay devotee (upāsikā) was also ordained among the bhikkhunīs. The mother said to the bhikkhunī, "Go, lady. Go to your brother, inform him of my illness, and bring back some medicine."

The bhikkhunī went and informed her brother. Elder Mahāmitta said, "I do not know how to gather medicinal roots and the like to boil medicine. However, I will tell you a 'medicine': Since I was ordained, I have never looked at the form of the opposite sex by breaking the restraint of the senses with a mind accompanied by greed. By this word of truth, may my mother be well. Go, and after speaking this word of truth, rub the body of the upāsikā."

The sister bhikkhunī went to her mother, informed her of this matter, and performed the act of truth as instructed by the Elder. At that very moment, the upāsikā's boil dissolved and disappeared like a lump of foam. The mother upāsikā rose from her bed and uttered words of joy, saying, "If the Fully Enlightened Buddha were still alive, why would He not stroke the head of a good monk like my son with His golden hand, which is adorned with the webbed characteristic? (He surely would)."

Therefore:
Now, any other noble son who has been ordained in the Dispensation should also, like Elder Mahāmitta, abide in the noble restraint of the senses.

Note: In this verse, the reading 'kulaputtamāni aññopi' is incorrect; only the reading 'kulaputto dāni aññopi' is correct. The translation is based on that reading.

Furthermore, just as the restraint of the senses (indriya-saṃvara) is to be accomplished through mindfulness, so too should the purification of livelihood (ājīva-pārisuddhi) be accomplished through effort (viriya). Indeed, that purification of livelihood is achieved through effort, because for a monk with well-exerted effort, the abandoning of wrong livelihood is possible. Therefore, one should abandon improper search (anesanā), which is unsuitable for the Dispensation, and accomplish this purification of livelihood by using requisites that are purely obtained through proper searches such as the alms-round, while avoiding impurely obtained requisites as if they were venomous snakes.

Among those two types of requisites—purely obtained and impurely obtained—for a monk who does not observe the ascetic practices (dhutanga), requisites obtained from the Sangha, from a group, or from laypeople who are inspired by his qualities such as preaching the Dhamma, etc., are called purely obtained requisites. However, those obtained through the alms-round and the like are extremely purely obtained. For a monk who observes the ascetic practices, requisites obtained through the alms-round and the like, or from those who are inspired by his ascetic qualities in accordance with the regulations of the dhutanga, are called purely obtained requisites.

Specifically, for such a dhutanga-observing monk, if fermented gallnuts (pūti-harīṭakī) and the 'four sweets' (catumadhura) are offered for the purpose of curing an illness, it is appropriate for him to observe the dhutanga by thinking, 'Other fellow monks will consume the four sweets,' and consuming only the pieces of gallnuts. Indeed, such a monk is called 'one of the highest noble lineage' (uttama-ariyavaṃsika). Furthermore, among the requisites such as robes, for a monk who wishes to purify his livelihood [39] (regardless of whether he observes dhutanga or not), hints (nimitta), suggestions (obhāsa), roundabout talk (parikathā), and intimation (viññatti) are improper regarding robes and alms-food. However, regarding a dwelling, hints, suggestions, and roundabout talk are permissible for a monk who observes the ascetic practices.
39:
Among these, 'hinting' (nimitta) refers to a monk who, while preparing the ground for the sake of a lodging, is asked by laypeople, "Venerable sir, what are you doing? Who is having this done?" and he replies, "No one is having it done." This is known as nimitta, which makes one's desire known. Any other similar act of hinting to make one's desire known is also called nimitta. [Note 1: Nimitta means making a sign to make one's desire known regarding requisites such as robes. (Commentary)]

'Intimation' (obhāsa) refers to asking, "Lay followers, where do you live?" When they reply, "Venerable sir, we live in a mansion," saying, "Lay followers, is a mansion not suitable for monks?" or any other similar act of intimation is called obhāsa. [Note 1: Obhāsa means speaking by giving a sign or intimation to make one's desire clear without speaking directly. (Commentary)]

'Roundabout talk' (parikathā) refers to saying, "The lodging for the Community of Monks is cramped" (with the intention of having a lodging donated), or any other similar indirect speech. [Note 2: Parikathā means speaking in a roundabout or indirect manner.]

Regarding medicinal requisites, all such acts as hinting are permissible. If one asks, "Is it permissible or not to consume medicine obtained through the power of such hinting and so forth after the illness has been cured?" In that case, the Masters of the Vinaya say, "It is permissible because the Blessed One has given permission for its use." However, the Masters of the Suttas say, "Although there is no formal offense (āpatti), it is not permissible (for a monk established in the practice of effacement) because it impairs the virtue of purity of livelihood (ājīva-sīla)."

In particular, a monk who, even though the Blessed One has permitted hinting, intimation, roundabout talk, and intimation, does not employ them, but relying only on qualities such as fewness of wishes, makes use of requisites that have arisen purely without intimation and so forth, even when faced with the end of his life—such a monk is called "one of supreme effacement" (parama-sallekha-vuttī). Who is such a person? He is like the Venerable Sāriputta Thera.

It is said that at one time, that Venerable Sāriputta, desiring to cultivate the seclusion of the fruit of Arahantship (paṭippassaddhi-viveka), was dwelling in a certain forest together with the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna. Then one day, an affliction of wind in the stomach arose in the Venerable Sāriputta, causing him great pain. In the evening, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera went to attend to the Venerable Sāriputta, and seeing the Elder lying down, he asked about the situation: "Friend, what used to give you relief in the past?" The Elder replied, "Friend, when I was a layman, my mother used to prepare milk-rice (pāyāsa) unmixed with water, combined with ghee, honey, and sugar; that gave me relief." Venerable Moggallāna said, "Friend, let it be so. If you or I have merit, perhaps we shall receive such milk-rice tomorrow."

A deity dwelling in a tree at the end of the cloister walk heard this conversation of the two Elders and thought, "Tomorrow I will cause milk-rice to be produced for the Venerable One." Immediately, the deity went to the house of the Venerable Sāriputta's [40] supporter, possessed the eldest son, and caused him distress. Then, to the relatives who had gathered to treat the eldest son, the deity said, "If you offer such milk-rice to the Venerable Sāriputta Thera tomorrow, I will release the son." The relatives replied, "Even if you, deity, did not say so, we always offer alms-food to the Elders," and on the following day, they prepared such milk-rice.

The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera, having come early in the morning, said, "Friend Sāriputta, stay right here until I return from the alms-round," and entered the village. Those lay supporters also came out to meet him, took the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna's bowl, filled it with the aforementioned kind of milk-rice, and offered it. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera made a sign of departing, but the lay supporters said, "Venerable sir, please eat; we shall offer more milk-rice." Having thus made the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna eat, they again offered a bowl full of milk-rice. The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna Thera went to the Venerable Sāriputta and said, "Friend Sāriputta, here, take this and eat." When the Venerable Sāriputta Thera saw that milk-rice, he thought, "The milk-rice is very delightful (or, it is very good)."
40:
When he considered, "By what means did this come about?" and saw the origin of that milk-rice, he said, "Friend Moggallāna, this milk-rice is unfit for consumption." Even though a person like himself had brought the alms-food, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna did not allow even a slight resentment to arise. With just that single word, he took the bowl by the rim and overturned it in a suitable place. As soon as the milk-rice touched the ground, Venerable Sāriputta’s wind ailment vanished. From then on, it did not recur for forty years [Note 1]. Then he said to Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, "Friend Moggallāna, milk-rice that arises depending on verbal intimation (vaci-viññatti) is of such a nature that it is unfit to be consumed even if one's entrails were to come out and crawl on the ground [Note 2]." Having said this, he uttered this inspired utterance (udāna):

"If I were to eat this sweet milk-rice produced through the expansion of verbal intimation, my livelihood would be censured by the virtuous.

Note 1: This translation is based on the Sinhalese variant reading 'forty years' (cattāḷīsa-vassāni). Since Venerable Sāriputta's seniority as a monk was only 44 years, the reading 'forty-five years' (pañca-cattāḷīsa-vassāni) is not appropriate.

Note 2: The phrase "entrails come out and crawl on the ground to search for food" was a common worldly idiom of that time. Therefore, the Commentary explains the Pali 'bahi care' as follows: 'Bahi care' (would wander outside) means if they were to actually wander outside by way of coming out from their place to seek food. This is said using a worldly idiom for the purpose of showing extreme fewness of wishes. Indeed, in the world, when censuring a glutton who habitually eats unsuitable food, people say, 'Why do his intestines wander outside?' (Commentary).

Even if my entrails were to come out and crawl outside, I would never break my livelihood, even at the cost of my life.

I shall satisfy my own mind; I shall avoid improper search (anesana). I will not engage in improper search, which is loathed by the Buddha."
(These are the three verses of the inspired utterance).

The story of Mahātissa Thera, a resident of Ciragumba who did not eat mangoes [that were not properly offered], should also be told here [Note 1]. Thus, in every way—
41:
Regarding this matter, it is stated (in the Visuddhimagga): "The story of the Elder Mahā Tissa, who did not pick up and eat mangoes, should also be mentioned here." (Ṭīkā)

In that statement (regarding reflection), reflection is of two kinds: reflection at the time of receiving the requisites and reflection at the time of using them. Indeed, for a monk who has reflected on requisites such as robes at the time of receiving them, either by way of elements [1] or by way of repulsiveness [2], and then uses them later, that usage is blameless. The same applies to reflection at the time of use. In this regard (reflection at the time of use), here is the definitive judgment that resolves all doubts.

To elaborate, there are four kinds of usage (paribhoga):
(1) Usage as a thief (theyya-paribhoga)
(2) Usage as a debtor (iṇa-paribhoga)

Note:
1. By way of elements: This means considering that the requisites such as robes and the person using them are merely natural elements occurring continuously according to causes. (Ṭīkā)
2. By way of repulsiveness: This means, first, by way of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā) for food. For all other requisites like robes, it means reflecting: "All these requisites are not repulsive by nature; however, when they come into contact with this foul carcass of a body, they will become extremely repulsive." (Ṭīkā)

(3) Usage as an heir (dāyajja-paribhoga)
(4) Usage as a master (sāmi-paribhoga)

Among these four, the usage by an immoral monk (dussīla) who sits and consumes [requisites] even in the midst of the Saṅgha is called "usage as a thief" (theyya-paribhoga) [1]. The usage by a virtuous monk without reflection is called "usage as a debtor" (iṇa-paribhoga) [2]. Therefore, the robe should be reflected upon every time it is worn. Almsfood should be reflected upon mouthful by mouthful.

Note:
1. Usage as a thief: This refers to the usage by an immoral person who is unworthy. The Blessed One allowed requisites in His Dispensation only for virtuous persons, not for the immoral. The donors' act of giving is also intended only for the virtuous, not for the immoral, because they desire great fruit for their meritorious deeds. Since it is not allowed by the Buddha and not given by the donors, the usage by an immoral person is usage by way of theft, hence it is called "usage as a thief." (Ṭīkā)
2. Usage as a debtor: This is usage in the manner of a debt. It is like using something borrowed because the recipient lacks the factor of virtue which makes the gift pure. This is the meaning of the term "usage as a debtor." (Ṭīkā)

If one is unable to reflect at every mouthful, it should be reflected upon during the morning, the afternoon, the first watch, the middle watch, or the last watch of the night. If the dawn rises while that monk has not yet reflected, he stands in the position of "usage as a debtor." Lodging should also be reflected upon every time it is used. Regarding medicine, it is proper to have mindfulness both at the time of receiving and at the time of use. However, if one is mindful at the time of receiving but not at the time of use, an offense (āpatti) is incurred. If one is not mindful at the time of receiving but is mindful at the time of use, no offense is incurred.

There are four kinds of purification (suddhi):
(1) Purification by confession (desanā-suddhi) [1]
(2) Purification by restraint (saṃvara-suddhi)
(3) Purification by search (pariyeṭṭhi-suddhi)
(4) Purification by reflection (paccavekkhaṇa-suddhi)

Note:
1. It is called "suddhi" because it is the cause of purification. The act of confessing an offense (desanā) according to the Vinaya is itself the purification. In this context, rising from a Saṅghādisesa offense (vuṭṭhāna) is also counted under confession. For one who has committed a Pārājika offense, the admission of no longer being a monk is itself considered the confession. (Ṭīkā)

Among these four, the Pātimokkha-saṃvara-sīla is called "purification by confession" (desanā-suddhi). Indeed, it is called "purification by confession" because it is purified through confession. Indriya-saṃvara-sīla is called "purification by restraint" (saṃvara-suddhi). Indeed, it is called "purification by restraint" because it is purified through the restraint of mental resolve, thinking, "I shall not do this again." Ājīva-pārisuddhi-sīla is called "purification by search" (pariyeṭṭhi-suddhi). Indeed, for one who gives up improper search and obtains requisites through righteous conduct of body and speech (or,
42:
For a monk who acquires requisites righteously, it is called purity of seeking (pariyēṭṭhisuddhi) because of the purity in the way they are sought. Virtue dependent on requisites (paccayasannissitasīla) is called purity of reflection (paccavēkkhaṇasuddhi). Indeed, it is called purity of reflection because it is purified through the aforementioned modes of reflection (such as 'to ward off cold,' etc.). Therefore, I have said: "There is no offense for one who, though not mindful at the time of receiving, is mindful at the time of use."

The use of requisites by the seven types of noble disciples in training (sekha) is called usage as an inheritance (dāyajjaparibhōga). This is because they are the sons of the Blessed One; therefore, being heirs to the four requisites belonging to their Father, they use those requisites. If it is asked: "Do they use the requisites of the Blessed One, or do they use the requisites of the lay donors?" The answer is: Although they are given by lay donors, because they are permitted by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One. Therefore, it should be understood that "they use the requisites of the Blessed One." The Dhammadāyāda Sutta is the supporting evidence in this matter.

The use by those who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) is called usage as an owner (sāmiparibhōga). This is because they have transcended the slavery of craving and use the requisites as owners.

Among these four types of usage, usage as an owner and usage as an inheritance are proper for all noble ones and virtuous worldlings. Usage as a debt (iṇaparibhōga) is not proper. As for usage as a theft (thēyyaparibhōga), it is beyond discussion. Furthermore, the usage with reflection by a virtuous person, being the opposite of usage as a debt, is either usage as freedom from debt (ānaṇyaparibhōga) or is included within usage as an inheritance.

This is because a virtuous monk, being endowed with this training (higher virtue), is counted as a trainee (sekha). Therefore, the usage with reflection by a virtuous monk is counted only as usage as an inheritance. Specifically, among the four types of usage, usage as an owner is the highest. Therefore, a monk who aspires to that usage as an owner should fulfill the virtue dependent on requisites by using them while reflecting with the aforementioned modes of reflection. One who does so is one who performs his duty. Indeed, this collection of verses was spoken:

"Having heard the Dhamma taught by the Sugata,
A wise and noble disciple should use
Alms-food, a dwelling, a bed and seat,
Water, and the robe that wards off dust and stains, only after reflecting."

[Note 1: Regarding virtues that have purity as their cause, they are called purity through confession (dēsanāsuddhi) because they have confession as the means of purification. The same logic applies to the remaining virtues like restraint (saṃvarasuddhi), etc. (Ṭīkā)]

[Note 2: The first interpretation follows the commentaries and sub-commentaries for the phrase 'āpañca saṅghāṭirazūpavāhanaṃ'. In that sense, the robe is not the primary focus, but rather water for washing away dust and stains. Therefore, interpreting 'razūpavāhanaṃ' as 'razōpavāraṇaṃ', the second interpretation is given as 'water and the robe that wards off dust and stains.' In this translation, the robe is primary, and water as a medicinal requisite for the sick is also included.]
43:
(Dhammika Sutta, Sutta Nipāta) "Therefore, in alms-food, in a bed and seat, in water, and in the robe that wards off dust and stains—in these things, a monk should remain unsullied, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf."

"Having received gifts from others at the proper time, whether hard food, soft food, or savories, he should always be mindful and know the proper measure, just as one applies ointment to a wound to make the skin grow."

"Like a couple eating the flesh of their own son in the wilderness, or like greasing an axle; thus should one consume food without greed or infatuation, merely for the sake of sustaining the body."

In the context of one who fulfills this virtue dependent on requisites, the story of the novice Saṅgharakkhita (nephew of Mahā-Saṅgharakkhita) should be told. Indeed, that novice used requisites after reflecting properly. As he said:

"While I was consuming the well-prepared hill-paddy alms-food, my preceptor said to me: 'Novice, do not let your tongue burn through lack of restraint (lack of reflection).'

Having heard the words of my preceptor, I then felt a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvēga). Sitting right there in that single session, I attained Arahantship.

I, whose aspirations are fulfilled like the full moon on the fifteenth day, have destroyed all taints; now there is no more renewed existence."

Therefore, any other person who desires the destruction of suffering should also use requisites after reflecting with wise consideration (yōnisō paccavēkkhaṇā). This is the instruction.

[Note 1: In this context, a literal translation would be 'in the state of being one who habitually performs the complete fulfillment of this virtue dependent on requisites.' To make the Burmese phrasing smoother, it was translated as above.]

Thus, virtue is fourfold by way of the virtue of restraint by the Pātimokkha, etc.

## The First Pentad of Virtue
20. In the first pentad of the fivefold categories, the meaning should be understood by way of the virtue of those not yet fully ordained (laypeople and novices), etc. For it is said in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

"What is the virtue of limited purity (pariyantapārisuddhisīla)? It is the virtue of laypeople and novices who have a limited number of training rules."
44:
This virtue is called the virtue of limited purification (pariyantapārisuddhisīla). What is the virtue of unlimited purification (apariyantapārisuddhisīla)? It is the virtue of monks who have unlimited training rules (excluding those who are noble worldlings and noble ones who are insight practitioners). This virtue is called the virtue of unlimited purification. What is the virtue of fulfilled purification (paripuṇṇapārisuddhisīla)? It is the virtue of noble worldlings who are constantly engaged in the practice of insight meditation, who fully fulfill the wholesome states limited by the states of a learner (up to the stage of gotrabhū), and who have no regard for their body or life, having sacrificed their lives. This virtue is called the virtue of fulfilled purification. What is the virtue of untarnished purification (aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīla)? It is the virtue of the seven types of learners (sekha). This virtue is called the virtue of untarnished purification. What is the virtue of tranquilized purification (paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla)? It is the virtue of the Arahants who are disciples of the Buddha, of Private Buddhas (Paccekabuddhas), and of the Fully Enlightened Buddhas (Sammāsambuddhas) who are like the former Buddhas and worthy of special offerings. This virtue is called the virtue of tranquilized purification. Thus it was taught.

In that Pali text, or among those five types of virtue, the virtue of novices (sāmaṇeras) should be understood as virtue of limited purification because it is limited by number. Regarding the virtue of monks:

"The training rules called the discipline of restraint (saṃvara-vinaya) proclaimed by the Buddha are nine thousand one hundred and eighty crores, and further five million thirty-six thousand.
These training rules are shown in brief in the Vinaya Piṭaka by the elders who compiled the scriptures using the method of ellipsis (peyyāla)."

Thus, although it is limited by number, it is called virtue of unlimited purification with reference to its being undertaken without remainder, and its being unlimited in terms of gain, fame, relatives, limbs, and life—like the virtue of Mahātissa Thera of Ciragumba who did not eat mangoes he picked up. To elaborate, that venerable one:

"A man should sacrifice wealth for the sake of a noble limb; he should sacrifice a limb while protecting his life; but a man, reflecting on the Dhamma, should sacrifice limbs, wealth, and life—everything."

Not abandoning this reflection of the virtuous, even when his life was in doubt (due to hunger), he did not transgress the training rule (prohibiting eating what is not offered), and relying on that very virtue of unlimited purification, he attained Arahantship even while riding on the back of a lay devotee. As he said:

"Neither your father nor your mother, nor your relatives nor your friends, perform such a task for you as this (carrying on the shoulder) because of your possession of virtue."
45:
"Having aroused a sense of urgency (saṃvega) and having reflected wisely (yoniso manasikāra), while still on his [the layman's] back, he attained Arahantship."

The virtue of noble worldling monks, from the time of their higher ordination, is like a well-polished genuine gem or like well-refined pure gold; because of its extreme purity, being free from the stain of even a momentary arising of defiled thought, it becomes the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for Arahantship itself. Therefore, it is called virtue of fulfilled purification (paripuṇṇapārisuddhi). It is like the virtue of Mahā Saṅgharakkhita Thera and his nephew, Cūḷa Saṅgharakkhita Thera.

It is said that when Mahā Saṅgharakkhita Thera, who had passed sixty vassa (years of monkhood), was lying on his deathbed, the community of monks asked him about his attainment of supramundane states. The Elder said, "I have no supramundane state." Then his attendant, a young monk, said, "Venerable Sir, people from as far as twelve yojanas around have gathered, hearing that you are about to pass away. If you pass away as a worldling, there will be great remorse among the multitude." The Elder replied, "Friend, I lived without practicing insight meditation because I intended to see the Blessed Metteyya Buddha. If it is as you say, please help me sit up and give me an opportunity (to practice)." When he said this, the young monk helped the Elder sit up and went outside. As soon as the young monk stepped out, the Elder attained Arahantship and gave a signal by snapping his fingers. The community of monks assembled and said, "Venerable Sir, you have done a difficult thing by attaining the supramundane state at such a time of death." The Elder replied, "Friends, attaining the supramundane state quickly at the time of death is not the difficult thing. Rather, I will tell you what is truly difficult: Friends, from the time I was ordained, I do not see any action I have done wrongly through lack of mindfulness or ignorance." His nephew also attained Arahantship in the same way when he reached fifty vassa.

If one is of little learning and not well-established in virtues, the wise censure him for both—for his lack of virtue and his lack of learning.

If one is of little learning but well-established in virtues, they praise him for his virtue; his learning (though little) is fulfilled.
