Even if one has much learning but is not well-established in virtues, they censure him for his lack of virtue; the learning of such a person without virtue is not called fulfilled. If one has much learning and is well-established in virtues, the wise praise him for both—for his virtue and for his learning.

Who would dare to censure such a monk, a disciple of the Buddha, who is full of much learning and endowed with mundane and supramundane wisdom, the ground for qualities like virtue? He is like a coin of pure Jambu-river gold; even the gods praise him, and he is praised by Brahmā as well. Here ends one section.

Furthermore, the virtue of learners (sekha) should be understood as virtue of untarnished purification (aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīla) because it is not misapprehended by the power of wrong view. Alternatively, the virtue of worldlings that is not misapprehended by the power of craving for existence is known as virtue of untarnished purification. It is like the virtue of Tissa Thera, the son of a householder. To elaborate, that Venerable Tissa, relying on such virtue and wishing to stand in the fruit of Arahantship, said to the bandits...
46:
“Friends, I shall break my two legs to assure you (that I will not flee). I loathe and am ashamed of a death accompanied by lust.”

“Having reflected in this manner and contemplated wisely, I attained Arahantship at the rising of the dawn.” Thus, he uttered this inspired exclamation.

Another obscure Elder was also severely ill; unable even to take food with his own hands, he lay wallowing and rolling in his own excrement and urine. Seeing that Elder rolling about, a young monk lamented, “Alas, the formations associated with the life-faculty are indeed suffering!”

Note 1: Aparāmaṭṭhapārisuddhisīla—Virtue of complete purity that is not misapprehended as ‘I’ or ‘mine’.

The Great Elder said to that young monk, “Friend, if I were to die now, I would attain heavenly bliss; of this I have no doubt. However, heavenly bliss attained by breaking this monastic virtue is like returning to the state of a layman after renouncing the training. (Therefore, I do not desire it.)” Having said this, he added, “I shall die together with my virtue alone.” After saying so, while lying on that very bed, contemplating the painful and oppressive disease,¹ he reached Arahantship and declared it to the Saṅgha of monks with the following verses:

“Friends, afflicted by a certain malady, suffering intensely and in pain, this carcass of mine will soon wither away like a flower cast upon the dust in the heat of the sun.

Those beings who are heedless and infatuated (by lust) regarding this putrid body, which is the cause of reaching a happy rebirth, cause even their virtue to decline and perish.²

Note 1: Contemplating the disease—This means contemplating the feeling (vedanā) arising from the disease, or the feeling itself as the disease, and by making that feeling the primary object, one collects and practices insight (vipassanā) on the remaining mental and physical phenomena (Commentary). From these words of the Commentary and Sub-commentary, it should be firmly noted that by contemplating the painful feeling called disease, one can attain Arahantship.

Let there be for you loathing for this putrid body, or rather, let there be revulsion toward this putrid body—which, though unpleasant and loathsome, is called pleasant (by the ignorant); which, though impure, is designated as pure; which is filled with various impurities (such as excrement and urine); which is a deceptive form that appears pleasant to the foolish who cannot see (with the eye of wisdom); [47] which is painful (with various diseases), foul-smelling, devoid of purity and attractiveness, and subject to illness.”

Furthermore, the virtue of Arahants, Paccekabuddhas, and Fully Enlightened Buddhas should be known as Paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla,³ because of the tranquillization of all distress from defilements and because of its complete purity.

Note 1: Here, by the word “even,” it means that they cause even virtue to decline and perish; it goes without saying that they cause the decline and destruction of jhānas and so forth (Sub-commentary).
47:
Note 2: This sentence is the latter half of the third verse in the Visuddhimagga; however, because it is an indefinite sentence, it is brought forward and translated before the second verse.
Note 3: Paṭippassaddhipārisuddhisīla—Virtue of complete purity through the tranquillization of defilements.

As stated above, virtue should be known as fivefold by way of Pariyantapārisuddhisīla and so forth.

## The Second Fivefold Set of Virtue

In the second fivefold set, the meaning should be understood by way of the abandoning (pahāna) of killing and so forth. Indeed, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, the following words were taught:

“Virtues are five: the abandoning (pahāna) of killing is virtue,¹ or rather, the wholesome mental state that causes abandoning is virtue;² abstinence (veramaṇī) is virtue; volition (cetanā) is virtue; restraint (saṃvara) is virtue; non-transgression (avītikkama) is virtue. (Thus there are five.) The abandoning of taking what is not given... of sexual misconduct... of false speech... of malicious speech... of harsh speech... of gossip...

Note 1: This first meaning is translated in accordance with the explanation in the Commentary to be shown later.
Note 2: This second meaning is translated in accordance with the Sub-commentary, which explains: “Killing is abandoned by that wholesome mental state headed by shame (hiri), fear of wrongdoing (ottappa), compassion (karuṇā), non-greed (alobha), etc. That wholesome mental state which causes the abandoning of killing is called virtue because of its characteristic of being virtuous.”

...of covetousness... of ill-will... of wrong view... the abandoning of sensual desire by renunciation (nekkhamma),¹ or rather, by a wholesome mental state dominated by non-greed; the abandoning of ill-will by non-ill-will (abyāpāda) which is loving-kindness; the abandoning of sloth and torpor by the perception of light (ālokasaññā); the abandoning of doubt by the definition of phenomena (dhammavavatthāna), which is the determination of wholesome and other states; the abandoning of ignorance by knowledge (ñāṇa);² the abandoning of discontent by joy (pāmojja) regarding the meditative attainments; the abandoning of the hindrances by the first jhāna; the abandoning of initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) by the second jhāna; the abandoning of rapture (pīti) by the third jhāna; the abandoning of pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha) by the fourth jhāna; the abandoning of the perception of form, the perception of resistance, and the perception of diversity by the attainment of the base of infinite space...

Note 1: Nekkhamma—This means a wholesome mental state dominated by non-greed; indeed, wholesome states that are the opposite of sensuality are intended here as renunciation (Sub-commentary).
Note 2: Now, in order to show (the abandoning of virtue, etc.) by way of the eight attainments and so forth along with the means of attaining them, the words “by knowledge” and so forth are taught. Indeed, for a person established in full understanding of the known (ñātapariññā) by removing the delusion that interferes with the knowledge of defining mentality-materiality and the knowledge of discerning conditions, the perception of impermanence and so forth are accomplished. Furthermore, when discontent, called arati, is removed by joy (pāmojja) which is the cause for delighting in the meditative attainments, the achievement of those jhānas and so forth is completed. Therefore, the cause for attainments and insight is the removal of discontent called arati and the breaking and abandoning of ignorance (Sub-commentary). According to this Sub-commentary, “abandoning ignorance by knowledge” should be taken as the abandoning of ignorance, which is the opposite of the knowledge of defining mentality-materiality and the knowledge of discerning conditions, by those very knowledges.

...the abandoning of the perception of the base of infinite space by the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness; the abandoning of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness by the attainment of the base of nothingness; the abandoning of the perception of the base of nothingness by the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;¹ the abandoning of the perception of permanence by the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); the abandoning of the perception of pleasure by the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā); the abandoning of the perception of self by the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā); the abandoning of delight (nandī) by the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā); the abandoning of lust (rāga) by the contemplation of fading away (virāgānupassanā); the abandoning of origination by the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā); the abandoning of grasping by the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā); the abandoning of the perception of compactness (ghanasaññā) by the contemplation of destruction (khayānupassanā); the abandoning of accumulation by the contemplation of fall (vayānupassanā); the abandoning of the perception of lastingness (dhuvasaññā) by the contemplation of change (vipariṇāmānupassanā); the abandoning of the sign (nimitta) by the contemplation of the signless (animittānupassanā); the abandoning of desire (paṇidhi) by the contemplation of the desireless (appaṇihitānupassanā); the abandoning of the misinterpretation of self by the contemplation of emptiness (suññatānupassanā); the abandoning of the misinterpretation of having a core by the contemplation of the higher wisdom of phenomena (adhipaññādhammavipassanā); the abandoning of the misinterpretation of delusion by the knowledge and vision of things as they are (yathābhūtañāṇadassana); the abandoning of the misinterpretation of attachment to formations as a refuge by the contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā); the abandoning of non-reflection by the contemplation of reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā); the abandoning of the misinterpretation of bondage by the contemplation of turning away (vivaṭṭanānupassanā);² the misinterpretation of formations through attachment...

Notes:
1. These eight meditative attainments and the states abandoned by them will be explained in detail in the chapter on Jhana.
2. These eighteen great insights and the states abandoned by them will be explained in detail in the chapters on Insight-wisdom and Path-knowledge.

Abandoning [wrong] attention... Abandoning defilements co-arising with [wrong] view by the Path of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-magga); gross defilements by the Path of Once-return (Sakadāgāmi-magga); subtle defilements by the Path of Non-return (Anāgāmi-magga); and all defilements by the Path of Arahantship (Arahatta-magga) is called virtue (sīla). Abstinence is virtue, volition is virtue, restraint is virtue, and non-transgression is virtue. Such virtues lead to the mind's non-remorse (avippaṭisāra), to gladness (pāmojja), to rapture (pīti), to tranquility (passaddhi), to happiness (somanassa), to repetition (āsevanā), to development (bhāvanā), to frequent practice (bahulīkamma), to adornment (alaṅkāra—the arising of faculties like faith, etc., which are the ornaments of concentration), to equipment (parikkhāra—of concentration), to accompaniment (parivāra—the fulfillment of the group of states like mindfulness and energy, which are the retinue of concentration), to fulfillment (pāripūri—of concentration), to utter disenchantment (nibbidā), to dispassion (virāga), to cessation (nirodha), to peace (upasama), to direct knowledge (abhiññā), to enlightenment (sambodha), and to the realization of Nibbāna. (This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga).

In the above Paṭisambhidāmagga text, 'abandonment' (pahāna) is nothing other than the non-arising of killing and so forth; or rather, it is simply the non-arising of those things. However, because that abandonment serves as a foundation (upadhāraṇa) by being the support for the respective subsequent wholesome states, and as a firm undertaking (samādhāna) by making them unwavering, it is called virtue (sīla) in the sense of 'upholding' and 'composing' as previously mentioned. The other four states—abstinence (veramaṇī), volition (cetanā), restraint (saṃvara), and non-transgression (avītikkama)—are mentioned with reference to the occurrence of the mind by way of abstaining from killing etc., by way of restraining them, by way of the volition associated with both, and by way of the non-transgression of one who does not transgress. The nature of virtue for these four—abstinence and so on—has already been shown. Thus, there are five kinds by way of abandonment-virtue and so on.

With this much, the answers to these questions: '(a) What is virtue? (b) In what sense is it virtue? (c) What are its characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? (d) What are its benefits? (e) How many kinds of virtue are there?' are finished.

Note:
1. In translating the Pali, the term 'pahāna' was translated as 'abandoning' in accordance with this commentary's explanation.

## Defilement and Purification of Virtue

21. (f) What is its defilement?
(g) What is its purification?

In this regard, we say: the state of being broken and so on is the defilement of virtue; the state of being unbroken and so on is its purification. That state of being broken and so on is comprised of the breach caused by gain, fame (relatives, limbs, life), etc., and the seven kinds of sexual association.

For if a monk's training rule is broken at the beginning or at the end among the seven groups of offenses, his virtue is called 'broken' (khaṇḍa), like a cloth torn at the edge. Furthermore, if a training rule is broken in the middle, his virtue is called 'holed' (chidda), like a cloth with a hole in the middle. If two or three training rules are broken in succession, his virtue is called 'spotted' (sabala), like a cow with a body of a different color, such as black or red spots appearing on its back or belly.
49:
1. To distinguish these seven from the sexual intercourse known as *maggena maggapatipatti*, they are translated as 'minor sexual bonds' (methuna-ngal) with the adjective 'minor'.

It is called 'mottled'. If a monk's training rules are broken here and there, his virtue is called 'mottled', like a cow whose hide is variegated with spots and patches of a different color from its natural body color (such as black or red) appearing here and there. The state of being broken, etc., in virtue due to causes such as gain, occurs in the manner described above.

The state of being broken, etc., by way of association with the seven types of minor sexual bonds, occurs in the following manner. Indeed, the Blessed One said (in the *Methuna Sutta*):

"Brahmin Jāṇussoṇi, here in this world, some recluse or brahmin, while claiming to be one who practices the holy life (virtue) perfectly [Note 1], does not indeed engage in the major sexual intercourse [Note 2] of 'two-by-two' with a woman. However, he consents to a woman's anointing (with perfumes, etc.), rubbing, bathing, and massaging. That recluse or brahmin relishes that anointing and rubbing, etc.; he desires it and finds satisfaction in it. Brahmin, this too is a break, a hole, a spot, and a mottle in the holy life. Brahmin, such a recluse or brahmin is said to practice an impure holy life, being bound by the bond of sexual intercourse. I say he is not freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not freed from suffering. (1)

[Notes]
1. Connect: 'While claiming... does not engage in major sexual intercourse... however, he consents to massaging.'
2. Translated as 'major sexual intercourse' with the adjective 'major' to distinguish it from the seven minor sexual bonds.

Furthermore, Brahmin, here some recluse or brahmin, while claiming to be one who practices the holy life perfectly [Note 1], does not indeed engage in major sexual intercourse with a woman, nor does he consent to a woman's anointing... or massaging [Note 1]. However, he laughs loudly, plays, and sports (with bodily contact [Note 3]) with a woman. That recluse or brahmin relishes that loud laughter, etc.; he desires it and finds satisfaction in it... I say he is not freed from suffering. (2)

[Notes]
1. Connect: 'While claiming... does not engage... does not consent... however, he laughs loudly, plays, and sports.'
2. Translated as 'minor sexual bond' to distinguish it from the previously mentioned major sexual intercourse.
3. The phrase 'sports' in brackets is shown in accordance with the commentary: '*kāyasaṃsaggavasena kīḷati*—plays by way of bodily contact.' If so, this second minor sexual bond seems more coarse than the first, where one does not take initiative to touch but merely consents to the woman's touch. Therefore, it would be appropriate if the commentary said '*kāyavikāravasena*—plays with distorted bodily movements'.

Furthermore, Brahmin, here some recluse or brahmin... does not engage in major sexual intercourse, nor does he consent to a woman's anointing, rubbing, bathing, or massaging, nor does he laugh loudly, play, or sport with a woman. However, he gazes eye-to-eye into a woman's eyes, or looks at her askance. That recluse or brahmin relishes that gazing... I say he is not freed from suffering. (3)

[50] Furthermore, Brahmin, here some recluse or brahmin... does not engage in major sexual intercourse, nor does he consent to a woman's massaging, nor does he laugh loudly, play, or sport with a woman, nor does he gaze eye-to-eye into a woman's eyes or look at her askance. However, he listens to the sound of a woman laughing, talking, singing, or weeping from behind a wall or a fence. That recluse or brahmin relishes that sound... I say he is not freed from suffering. (4)

Furthermore, Brahmin, here some recluse or brahmin... does not engage in major sexual intercourse, nor does he consent to a woman's massaging, nor does he laugh loudly, play, or sport with a woman, nor does he gaze eye-to-eye into a woman's eyes, nor does he listen to the sound of weeping... However, he recalls the laughter, talk, and play (bodily contact) he had with a woman in the past (before undertaking the practice)."
50:
That ascetic or brahmin delights in and finds satisfaction in those past laughs, talks, and plays. ... I say he is not free from suffering. (5)

Again, O Brahmin, here some ascetic ... [as before] ... although he does not engage in sexual intercourse, nor does he enjoy being massaged by a woman, nor does he laugh, play, and dally with a woman, nor does he stare eye-to-eye or look askance at a woman, nor does he listen to the sound of a woman laughing, talking, singing, or weeping through a wall, nor does he remember past laughs, talks, and plays with a woman; yet he sees a householder or a householder's son endowed with and fully enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure, and he looks at them (with a delighted mind). That ascetic or brahmin delights in and finds satisfaction in that sensual pleasure. ... I say he is not free from suffering. (6)

Again, O Brahmin, here some ascetic or brahmin, while claiming to lead the holy life (sīla) well, although he does not engage in sexual intercourse reached by two people together, nor does he enjoy being massaged by a woman, nor does he laugh, play, and dally with a woman, nor does he listen to the sound of weeping through a wall, nor does he remember past laughs, talks, and plays with a woman, nor does he look at or see a person endowed with and fully enjoying the five cords of sensual pleasure (with a delighted mind); yet he leads the holy life aspiring to a certain heavenly realm, thinking: "By this virtue (sīla)¹, or this practice (vata), or this austerity (tapa), or this holy life (brahmacariya), I shall become a god (deva) or one among the gods." He delights in that, desires that, and finds satisfaction in that. O Brahmin, this is a breach, a hole, a stain, and a mottle in the holy life. O Brahmin, such an ascetic or brahmin is said to lead an impure holy life, being bound by the bonds of minor sexuality. I say he is not free from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; he is not free from suffering. (7)" (Methuna Sutta)

Note
1—In "by virtue" etc., virtue (sīla) is so called by the power of undertaking restraints, etc.; practice (vata) is so called by the power of non-transgression. (Meaning: undertaking is sīla; non-transgression as undertaken is vata). Alternatively, both undertaking and non-transgression are called sīla. A practice performed by virtue of being difficult to do is called vata. Alternatively, virtue (sīla) has the characteristic of receding and abstaining from various deeds designated as improper. Practice (vata) is a special practice such as assuming the appearance of one who has such undertakings, or performing deeds related to food (i.e., performing them with difficulty). In every way, a practice that is difficult to perform (dukkara-cariyā) is called austerity (tapa). Abstaining from sexual intercourse is called the holy life (brahmacariya). (Commentary)

Thus, it should be understood that the state of being breached, etc., is comprised of the destruction caused by gain, etc., and the sevenfold bonds of sexuality.

The state of being unbroken, etc., is comprised of the non-destruction of the training rules in every way, the restoration of those that are broken but remediable, and the absence of the sevenfold bonds of sexuality. [51] Furthermore, it is comprised of the non-arising of evil states such as "anger (kodha), malice (upanāha), hypocrisy (makkha), rivalry (paḷāsa), envy (issā), stinginess (macchariya), deceit (māyā), craftiness (sāṭheyya), stubbornness (thambha), impetuosity (sārambha), conceit (māna), arrogance (atimāna), intoxication (mada), and negligence (pamāda)"; and the arising of virtues such as fewness of wishes, contentment, and the thinning out of defilements.

Indeed, those virtues are not destroyed for the sake of gain, etc.; even if they are destroyed due to the fault of negligence, they are restored again. They are not oppressed or destroyed by the bonds of minor sexuality, nor by evil states such as anger and malice.
51:
Such virtues are called 'unbroken, unpierced, unspotted, and unsplattered.' These very virtues—unbroken, unpierced, unspotted, and unsplattered—are also called 'free' (bhujissa) because they bring about the state of being free [from the slavery of craving, being a support for liberation]; 'praised by the wise' (viññuppasattha) because they are commended by the wise; 'ungrasped' (aparāmaṭṭha) because they are not misapprehended by craving and views; and 'conducive to concentration' (samādhisamvattanika) because they give rise to access concentration or absorption concentration. Therefore, this state of being unbroken and so on should be understood as 'purification' (vodāna).

This purification of virtue is accomplished through two means: by seeing the danger in the failure of virtue and by seeing the benefit in the perfection of virtue. Among these two, the danger in the failure of virtue should be understood according to the method in such suttas as: 'Monks, there are these five dangers for an immoral person in the failure of virtue' [Note 1: This refers to the teaching previously cited on page 30: 'Householders, there are these five benefits for a virtuous person in the perfection of virtue...'].

Furthermore, an immoral person, due to the cause of immorality, is disagreeable to gods and humans; he is uninstructable by his fellow practitioners; he suffers greatly from the censure of immorality; and he is remorseful when the virtuous are praised [thinking, 'Alas, I have not practiced well']. Moreover, through that immorality, he is like hemp cloth—unattractive in appearance [lacking the beauty of virtue]. Furthermore, for those monks who follow his example, he is a 'bad touch' that brings suffering, as he leads them to the suffering of the states of deprivation for a long time. To those donors whose offerings he accepts, he is of little value because he does not make their gifts yield great fruit. Like a cesspool that has accumulated excrement for many years, he is difficult to clean. Like a brand from a funeral pyre [Note 2: A brand from a funeral pyre is useless for woodcraft in the village and useless in the forest; it is excluded from both human and monastic benefits], he is an outsider to both types of prosperity. Even though he claims the status of a monk, he is not a true monk; he is like a donkey following a herd of cattle. He is constantly trembling like a man who has enemies on all sides. He is unfit for association like a corpse. Even if he is possessed of qualities such as learning, he is unworthy of honor from his fellow practitioners, just as a cemetery fire is unworthy of honor from Brahmins. He is incapable of attaining distinction [jhāna, path, or fruit], like a blind man is incapable of seeing forms. He is hopeless regarding the True Dhamma of practice and realization, like a low-caste boy is hopeless regarding kingship. Even if he considers himself happy, he is only suffering because he shares the suffering described in the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta.

[52] To elaborate further: for immoral persons whose minds are greedy and delighted by the pleasure arising from the enjoyment of the five cords of sensual pleasure, and the pleasure arising from the salutations and reverence of others, the Blessed One—who sees the fruit of kamma in every way—taught [the following] to show the extremely terrible and hard-to-endure suffering that can cause the vomiting of hot blood and cause distress of heart even by merely reflecting on it [Note 3: The three types of association (saṃvāsa) are: (1) performing common legal acts (ekakamma), (2) common recitation of the Pātimokkha (ekuddesa), and (3) equality in training (samasikkhatā)].
52:
To show the extremely bitter suffering of the immoral persons [Note 1]—a suffering caused by [Note 2] the enjoyment of the five cords of sensual pleasure, homage, and honor, which is capable of causing the vomiting of hot blood by generating heart-burning even by mere recollection for those whose minds are attached to such pleasures—the Blessed One, to whom the results of kamma are manifest in every way, said:

“Bhikkhus, do you see that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing?”

“Yes, Venerable Sir,” they replied.

“Bhikkhus, what do you think? Which is better: that one should embrace that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing, and sit or lie down close to it; or that one should embrace a Khattiya maiden, a Brāhmaṇa maiden, or a Gahapati maiden, with soft and tender hands and feet, and sit or lie down close to her?”

“Venerable Sir, it is better to embrace a Khattiya maiden, a Brāhmaṇa maiden, or a Gahapati maiden, with soft and tender hands and feet, and sit or lie down close to her. For, Venerable Sir, it is painful to embrace that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing, and sit or lie down close to it.”

“Bhikkhus, I announce to you, I declare to you: for one who is immoral, of evil character, of impure and suspicious conduct, of secretive actions, who is not a recluse but claims to be one, who is not a celibate but claims to be one, who is rotten within, lustful, and full of filth—for such an immoral monk, it would be better to embrace that great mass of fire, burning, blazing, and glowing, and sit or lie down close to it. Why is that? Because on that account, bhikkhus, he might meet death or death-like suffering, but he would not, on that account, with the breakup of the body, after death, be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell.

(Bhikkhus, if that immoral monk, full of filth, were to embrace a Khattiya maiden, a Brāhmaṇa maiden, or a Gahapati maiden, and sit or lie down close to her—Bhikkhus, that act of embracing, sitting, or lying down with that maiden would be for his harm and suffering for a long time; and with the breakup of the body, after death, he would be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, in hell. [Note 3])”

Having thus shown, by the simile of the mass of fire, the suffering caused by the enjoyment of the five cords of sensual pleasure associated with women, the Buddha continued in the same manner:

“Bhikkhus, what do you think? Which is better: that a strong man should wrap both legs with a stout horsehair rope and rub them so that the rope cuts the outer skin, then the inner skin, then the flesh, then the sinews, then the bone, and stops only after reaching the marrow? [53] Or that he should delight in and accept the homage of wealthy Khattiyas, wealthy Brāhmaṇas, or wealthy householders [Note 4]? Which is better?”

“Monks, what do you think? Which is better: that a strong man should strike one's chest with a sharp spear, whetted with oil, or that [an immoral monk] should enjoy the salutation of great khattiya nobles, great brahmins, or great householders? Which of these two is better?”

Which of these two is better?”

“Monks, what do you think? Which is better: that a strong man, having seized one by the head or shoulders, should make one sit or lie down on a red-hot iron bed or iron chair, glowing, burning, and ablaze, or that [an immoral monk] should use a bed or chair given out of faith by great khattiya nobles, great brahmins, or great householders? Which of these two is better?”

“Monks, what do you think? Which is better: that a strong man, having seized one feet-upwards and head-downwards, should throw one into a red-hot iron cauldron [54], glowing, burning, and ablaze, where, being cooked and producing foam, he would go once up, once down, and once across, or that [an immoral monk] should use a monastery given out of faith by great khattiya nobles, great brahmins, or great householders? Which of these two is better?”—thus He asked.

By these metaphors of the horsehair rope, the sharp spear, the iron sheet, the iron ball, the iron bed and chair, and the iron cauldron, He showed the suffering caused by accepting salutations and añjali, and the use of robes, alms-food, beds, chairs, and monasteries. Therefore:¹

What happiness is there for a monk of broken virtue who does not renounce sensual pleasures, which result in bitter fruit and suffering more extreme than the pain of embracing a great mass of fire? (There is none).

What happiness is there for one of corrupted virtue in accepting salutations, which leads to a share of suffering greater than the pain of being rubbed with a coarse horsehair rope? (There is none). What happiness is there for the immoral in accepting the añjali-salutation of the faithful, which is the cause of suffering greater than being struck by a spear? 

What happiness is there for the unrestrained in the enjoyment of robes, through which the touch of a glowing iron sheet must be experienced for a long time in hell?

Note: ¹Therefore... this should be connected with: "through such reflection, one should understand the seeing of faults and the seeing of benefits."
54:
Or rather, it is the cause of suffering; it is not happiness, but only suffering.

Because of the alms-food consumed by an immoral monk, he must swallow red-hot iron balls for a long time. Even if that alms-food has a good flavor, it is like a deadly poison to that immoral monk.

Red-hot iron beds and chairs will oppress that immoral monk (in hell) for a long time. The use of such beds and chairs, though considered pleasant, is only the cause of suffering and is suffering itself.

That immoral monk must dwell in red-hot iron cauldrons. What kind of delight or benefit can there be in his dwelling and taking pleasure in a monastery given out of faith?

The Teacher, the Honored of the World, rebuking him, said: “One whose conduct is suspicious,” “one who is like rubbish,” “one who is damp (with defilements),” “one who is evil,” and “one who is rotten within.”

Woe to the life of that unrestrained one, who is not a true and good monk yet wears the garb of the community of good monks, carrying around a self that is destroyed (by the loss of virtue) and uprooted (by the destruction of the root of merit). How disgusting is his life!¹

Note: ¹The above meaning is translated by taking the words "upahataṃ khataṃ" in the verse as modifiers of "attānaṃ" (self). [55] Just as young men in this world who wish to adorn themselves avoid excrement and carcasses, so do the virtuous avoid the immoral monk. What benefit is there in such a life for that immoral monk?

The immoral monk is not free from all dangers such as self-reproach; he is deprived of all attainable qualities (such as access concentration, etc.).

Note: These terms mean that by uprooting virtue, which is the foundation of concentration and wisdom, the self or the existence of that immoral person is also uprooted. By destroying or killing virtue, the self of that immoral person is also destroyed or killed. The life of that immoral person, who looks after a body whose foundation is thus uprooted and destroyed, is said to be truly disgusting.

In the Pyay Visuddhimagga Nissaya, however, the words "upahataṃ khataṃ" are construed as modifiers of "jīvitaṃ" (life). According to that interpretation, it would be: "The life of that immoral one... which is destroyed (by the loss of virtue) and which uproots oneself (by destroying the root of merit)..."
55:
A livelihood obtained by destroying [the body of virtues] is loathsome; or, let there be loathing for such a livelihood. 

He is deprived of the happiness of the attainments of Jhāna, Path, and Fruition. The gates of heaven are closed to him. He has entered and is traveling upon the path leading to the four woeful states. 

Who else is an object of compassion for a compassionate person as much as an immoral man? There is none. In this way, there are many kinds of faults in immorality. 

Through such reflection, one should understand the seeing of danger in the failure of virtue, and by the opposite of what was stated [1], the seeing of benefits in the fulfillment of virtue. Furthermore—

For a monk whose virtue is perfectly pure, his bearing of the bowl and robes is graceful. His renunciation is fruitful. 

Just as darkness cannot enter the sunlight, the danger of self-reproach and so forth cannot enter the heart of a monk with pure virtue. 

Shining with the fulfillment of virtue, a monk in the forest of ascetic practice is as beautiful as the moon in the sky with its full radiance. 

Even the bodily scent of a virtuous monk brings joy and delight even to the gods; what then need be said of the scent of his virtue? 

The scent of virtue surpasses the excellence of all kinds of perfumes; without any hindrance, it wafts in all directions. 

Even small acts of service performed for a virtuous monk yield great fruits. Thus, a virtuous person is a worthy recipient of offerings and respect. 

The dangers known as 'āsavas' (such as killing or binding) that occur in the present life cannot oppress a virtuous monk. A virtuous person digs up the root of the sufferings of the future life, that is, he abandons the failure of virtue. 

Whatever prosperity exists among humans and whatever excellence exists among the gods, these two kinds of prosperity are not difficult to obtain for a virtuous monk if he so desires; rather, they are easily attained. 

That excellence of Nibbāna, which is exceedingly peaceful and limitless, the mind of a virtuous person naturally flows towards that very Nibbāna. 

[56] In this manner, a wise person should manifest the benefits of virtue, which is the root of all mundane and supramundane prosperity, in many ways [1].

Note
1. 'By the opposite of what was stated' means by the reverse of the manner described regarding the failure of virtue. For example, one should understand it as: 'A person endowed with virtue is cherished and loved, gladdening the hearts of gods and humans because of his fulfillment of virtue.' (Commentary)

Note
1. Regarding this, the commentary mentions that the verse beginning with 'Gandho isīnaṃ ciradikkhitānaṃ' should be cited. This verse is found in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka of the Cattālīsanipāta. In that Jātaka, when Sakka, the King of Gods, came to pay respects to the ascetics led by the Bodhisatta Sarabhaṅga, he stood downwind. An assistant disciple told him to move so as not to smell the foul odor from the ascetics' bodies. Sakka replied: 'Let the scent from the bodies of these ascetics, who have long practiced renunciation (and are endowed with virtue), come to us. We desire that scent as if it were the fragrance of flowers. The gods do not consider the bodily scent of virtuous ones to be loathsome.'
56:
Thus, a wise person should manifest the benefits [of virtue] in many ways, for virtue is the root of all prosperity.

This concludes one part of the discourse.

Note
1. Here, 'should manifest' (vibhāvaye) does not mean to show to others, but rather to make it clear within one's own mind and wisdom—to reflect and contemplate so that it becomes evident. Only by taking it this way can the result mentioned in the subsequent sentence arise.

The benefit of such manifestation is that the mind of a monk who manifests it in this way shrinks from the failure of virtue and leans toward the fulfillment of virtue. Therefore, seeing this danger of the failure of virtue and this benefit of the fulfillment of virtue as stated [1], one should purify virtue with all respect, or with absolute reverence. This is the instruction.

By this much, in this Visuddhimagga (Path of Purification), which is the path to Nibbāna taught by making virtue, concentration, and wisdom the main headings in the verse 'A man established in virtue...', virtue has first been fully described.

This is the first chapter called the 'Description of Virtue' (Sīlaniddesa) in the Visuddhimagga, composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## The Description of Virtue is finished.

Note
1. Connect 'as stated' with 'this danger' and 'this benefit'. It means that by seeing all the dangers of failing in virtue and the benefits of fulfilling virtue mentioned earlier, one must purify and cleanse one's virtue.

## 2. Dhutaṅganiddesa - Description of the Ascetic Practices
## Sādhāraṇakathā - General Talk

[57] 22. Now, the purification of virtue in the various ways already described (in the Sīlaniddesa) is accomplished by, or because of, those qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhitā), and so forth.
57:
## 2. Description of the Ascetic Practices (Dhutaṅganiddesa)

22. Now, in order to fulfill those qualities such as fewness of wishes and contentment, the yogi monk who has already undertaken virtue should undertake the ascetic practices. For when he does so, his virtue will be thoroughly purified, being washed of stains—or rather, having the stains washed away—by the waters of such qualities as fewness of wishes, contentment, effacement (sallekha), seclusion, the practice of destroying defilements, the arousal of energy, and being easy to support; and his ascetic vows will be fulfilled.

When this occurs, the yogi, whose conduct is entirely purified by the qualities of blameless virtue and ascetic vows, and who stands upon the three ancient lineages of the Noble Ones (ariyavaṃsa), will be worthy of attaining the fourth lineage of the Noble Ones, which is known as delight in meditation (bhāvanārāmatā). Therefore, we shall begin the discussion on the ascetic practices.

Indeed, the Blessed One allowed thirteen ascetic practices for those sons of good family who have abandoned worldly gains, who are indifferent to body and life, and who desire to achieve only the practice that is in accordance with the path to Nibbāna. These thirteen practices are:

(1) The refuse-rag-folder’s practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga)
(2) The triple-robe-wearer’s practice (tecīvarikaṅga)
(3) The alms-food-eater’s practice (piṇḍapātikaṅga)
(4) The house-to-house-walker’s practice (sapadānacārikaṅga)
(5) The one-session-eater’s practice (ekāsanikaṅga)
(6) The bowl-food-eater’s practice (pattapiṇḍikaṅga)
(7) The after-food-refuser’s practice (khalupacchābhattikaṅga)
(8) The forest-dweller’s practice (āraññikaṅga)
(9) The tree-root-dweller’s practice (rukkhamūlikaṅga)
(10) The open-air-dweller’s practice (abbhokāsikaṅga)
(11) The charnel-ground-dweller’s practice (sosānikaṅga)
(12) The any-bed-user’s practice (yathāsanthatikaṅga)
(13) The sitter’s practice (nesajjikaṅga)

Among these thirteen:

"The decision should be known by meaning, by characteristic and so on, by the method of undertaking and practice, by classification, by breach, and by the benefits of each; also by the triad of the wholesome, by the division of 'dhuta' and so on, and by brief and detailed explanation."

23. Therein, first, as to "by meaning": because they are found on top of the dust (paṃsu) in any place such as a high road, a charnel ground, or a rubbish heap, and because they have risen up [above the dust], they are like dust-heaps; thus they are "refuse-rags" (paṃsukūla). Alternatively, they are called "refuse-rags" because they go to a loathsome state like dust. The wearing of refuse-rags of such etymology is the "refuse-rag-wearing." One whose habit is that is a "refuse-rag-folder." The factor of the refuse-rag-folder is the "refuse-rag-folder’s practice." "Factor" (aṅga) means cause. Therefore, it should be understood that this is a name for that volition of undertaking by which one becomes a refuse-rag-folder.

By this same method, one who has the habit of wearing only the three robes—namely, the double-layered outer robe, the upper robe, and the inner robe—is a "triple-robe-wearer." The factor or volition of the triple-robe-wearer is the "triple-robe-wearer’s practice."
58:
2. Pāṃsukūlika—The factor of a monk who habitually wears rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) + aṅga (factor) = Pāṃsukūlikaṅga—the factor of a monk who habitually wears rag-robes. The essence of this factor will be shown later. Know the derivation of the terms in the subsequent ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) in the same way.

3. Tecīvara—wearing three robes + ika—habitual = Tecīvarika—a monk who habitually wears three robes. Tecīvarika + aṅga =

[58] The falling of morsels of material food known as alms-food is called piṇḍapāta. It means the falling into the bowl of morsels of food given by others. Because he seeks that falling of morsels by approaching various houses, he is called a piṇḍapātika. Alternatively, because he has the practice of wandering for the sake of alms-food, he is called a piṇḍapātī. Piṇḍapātī is the same as piṇḍapātika. The factor, which is the volition (cetanā) of that person (piṇḍapātika)—the monk who habitually seeks the falling of morsels or the monk who has the practice of wandering for alms—is called piṇḍapātikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the alms-food eater).

Cutting the sequence is called dāna. Because it is free from cutting the sequence, it is called apadāna, meaning without interruption. Because it occurs together with non-interruption, it is called sapadāna, meaning "house to house without interruption." Because he habitually wanders without interruption (i.e., house to house), he is called a sapadānacārī. Sapadānacārī is the same as sapadānacārika.

Note:
Tecīvarikaṅga—The factor of a monk who habitually wears three robes.
1. Piṇḍapāta—the falling of morsels of alms-food + ika—one who seeks = Piṇḍapātika—one who seeks the falling of morsels. Alternatively, piṇḍa—for the sake of alms + pāta—wandering + ī—one who has the practice = piṇḍapātī—one who has the practice of wandering for alms, or one who has the practice of alms-gathering. It is further shown that this term becomes piṇḍapātika with the letter 'ka'.

The factor, which is the volition of that monk (sapadānacārika) who habitually wanders for alms, is called sapadānacārikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the house-to-house alms-seeker).

Eating in one sitting is called ekāsana. Because he habitually eats in one sitting, he is called an ekāsanika. The factor, which is the volition of that monk (ekāsanika) who habitually eats in one sitting, is called ekāsanikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the one-sessioner).

Because of the rejection of a second vessel, the alms-food that stays only in a single bowl is called pattapiṇḍa. Now, by applying the name pattapiṇḍa to the taking of alms-food in a single bowl, he is called a pattapiṇḍika because he habitually takes and eats alms-food that stays in a single bowl. The factor, which is the volition of that monk (pattapiṇḍika) who habitually takes and eats alms-food in a single bowl, is called pattapiṇḍikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the bowl-food eater).

Note:
1. The phrase "eating in one sitting" should be taken as a general rule. This is because for a sick person who cannot sit, eating while lying or standing in one place should also be included.
2. Ekāsanika—one who habitually eats in one sitting + aṅga—factor = ekāsanikaṅga—the factor of one who habitually eats in one sitting.
3. Pattapiṇḍa—eating alms-food in a single bowl + ika—habitual = pattapiṇḍika—one who habitually eats in a single bowl. Pattapiṇḍika + aṅga = pattapiṇḍikaṅga—the factor of one who habitually eats in a single bowl.

The word "khalu" is a particle meaning prohibition. For a monk who has indicated satiety (pavārita), food obtained after that is called pacchābhatta. Eating that later food (by making it "leftover" through a Vinaya procedure) is called pacchābhattabhojana. By applying the name pacchābhatta to that eating of later food, a monk who habitually eats food obtained after indicating satiety is called a pacchābhattika. A monk who does not habitually eat food obtained after indicating satiety is called a khalupacchābhattika. This name "khalupacchābhattika" refers to a monk who rejects food that has been made "leftover" (according to the Vinaya rule for extra food) by the power of undertaking the ascetic practice. In the Mahā-Aṭṭhakathā, it is said: "Khalu is a type of bird. When that khalu bird takes a fruit in its beak and that fruit falls, it does not eat another fruit again. This monk who undertakes this ascetic practice is like that khalu bird (in that he does not eat food obtained after refusing it)." Therefore, he is called a khalupacchābhattika. The factor, which is the volition of that monk, is called khalupacchābhattikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the refuse-later-food eater).

Note:
1. If a monk, while eating any of the five types of food—(1) cooked rice, (2) barley meal, (3) flour/groats, (4) fish, (5) meat—refuses any food offered within arm's reach by another monk or layperson by saying "enough," he has "indicated satiety" (pavārita). This refers to such a monk.
2. Pacchā—after indicating satiety + bhatta—food obtained = pacchābhatta—food obtained after indicating satiety. Here, eating such food is called pacchābhatta. Pacchābhatta—eating food after indicating satiety + ika—habitual = pacchābhattika—one who habitually eats food after indicating satiety.
3. Khalu—not + pacchābhattika—one who habitually eats food after indicating satiety = khalupacchābhattika—not one who habitually eats food after indicating satiety, i.e., one who does not habitually eat later food, or one who does not eat later food.

Because he habitually lives in the forest, he is called an āraññika. The factor, which is the volition of that forest-dwelling monk, is called āraññikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the forest dweller).

Living at the foot of a tree (under a tree) is called rukkhamūla. Because he habitually lives at the foot of a tree, he is called a rukkhamūlika. The factor, which is the volition of the rukkhamūlika monk, is called rukkhamūlikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the tree-root dweller). The same method applies to the terms abbhokāsikaṅga and sosānikaṅga.

[59] Only that place which has been spread out or designated (is used). (Therefore, that place) is called yathāsanthata. This name yathāsanthata is the name of the lodging or seat that is first designated, such as "This place is for you." Because he habitually lives in that lodging or seat as it was spread or designated, he is called a yathāsanthatika. The factor, which is the volition of that yathāsanthatika monk, is called yathāsanthatikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the "as-laid-out" user).

Because he habitually lives by sitting, having given up lying down, he is called a nesajjika. The factor, which is the volition of that monk (nesajjika) who habitually lives by sitting, is called nesajjikaṅga (the ascetic practice of the sitter).

The meaning of the term "dhutaṅga" which applies to all is: all these factors such as pāṃsukūlikaṅga, etc., are the factors of a monk called "dhuta" (one who has shaken off), because he has shaken off defilements such as craving by means of undertaking those respective practices (through the abandonment by substitution of opposites, tadaṅgapahāna).
59:
Therefore, they are called dhutaṅga. Alternatively, knowledge called 'dhuta' because it is capable of shaking off (destroying) defilements is the factor (the antecedent cause) for these undertakings such as the refuse-rag-man's practice and so on.

Note 1: These [terms] should be connected as: "Therefore they are called dhutaṅga," etc.
Note 2: This is the meaning of the word 'samādānena'. In this context, the Pyay Nissaya also translates it with the sense of 'state' (bhāva) as 'by undertaking'; it does not translate it with the sense of 'instrument' (karaṇa) as 'by the volition which is the cause of undertaking'. This point should be especially noted.

Thus, they are called dhutaṅga. Alternatively, those undertakings such as the refuse-rag-man's practice are called 'dhuta' because they shake off (destroy) opposing defilements, and they are also 'aṅga' (factors) of the practice (paṭipatti) such as virtue and so on; therefore, they are also called dhutaṅga. In this way, the decision regarding the meaning of the words in these thirteen dhutaṅgas should first be understood.

Furthermore, all these dhutaṅgas have the characteristic of the volition of undertaking; or rather, these dhutaṅgas are to be understood as the volition of undertaking. Indeed, it has been said:

"He who undertakes is the person. Those [states] by which he undertakes are the mental states (consciousness and its concomitants). The volition of undertaking is the dhutaṅga. That which he rejects is the object (vatthu)."

Note 1: Dhuta (knowledge that shakes off/destroys defilements) + Aṅga (having an antecedent cause) = Dhutaṅga (an undertaking that has knowledge as its antecedent cause). In this regard, the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) explains as follows:
By this definition—"Knowledge is the factor/cause of these undertakings such as the refuse-rag-man's practice"—it clearly shows that the undertaking of the refuse-rag-man's practice and so on is preceded by knowledge. (Ṭīkā)
Note 2: Since 'paṭipattiyā' is explained in the Sub-commentary as the excellent practice of virtue and so on, it is translated with the addition of the qualifier "(such as virtue)."
Note 3: It is called 'samādāna' because it is the cause of undertaking; it refers to the volition occurring by the power of the cause of undertaking—in accordance with this explanation in the Sub-commentary, it is translated here as "the volition which is the cause of undertaking." However, it is still necessary to reconcile this with the following Commentary passage.

Note 1: In accordance with the explanation in the Sub-commentary mentioned in the previous note, here too it is translated as "the cause of undertaking." This translation seems to overlap with the statement that the associated states are the "instrumental cause of undertaking." Therefore, to avoid overlapping with the statements that the person is the "agent who undertakes" and the associated states are the "instrumental cause of undertaking," it seems appropriate to take the word 'samādāna' here as a 'verbal noun' (bhāva-sādhana) and understand it as the volition which is the act of undertaking. If 'samādāna' in this evidentiary text is taken as the act of undertaking, then in the phrase 'samādāna-cetanā-lakkhaṇāni', which is the thing to be proven, it should be translated as "having the volition of undertaking as their characteristic." Furthermore, although only the volition of undertaking is identified here as the dhutaṅga, the volition of practicing [the dhutaṅga] is also still called dhutaṅga. Therefore, it is stated in the Sub-commentary: "Taking only the volition of undertaking as the dhutaṅga is because that volition is the root; (however,) the volition of practicing according to what has been undertaken is also still called dhutaṅga."

This statement was made in the ancient Commentaries. All dhutaṅgas have the function of destroying greed (loluppa-taṇhā) (which excessively plunders wholesome assets). They are manifested to knowledge as the state of being free from greed. They have noble states such as fewness of wishes as their proximate cause. In the manner already stated, the decision regarding these thirteen dhutaṅgas should be understood by way of their characteristics and so on.

Furthermore, regarding the five headings such as "by way of undertaking and procedure," the decision should be understood as follows: While the Blessed One is alive, all dhutaṅgas should be undertaken only in the presence of the Blessed One.

Note 1: This statement (that they should be undertaken only in the presence of the Buddha) is made for the sake of non-interruption and non-failure in the intervening period. It is just like a person who makes a living depending on a king will certainly not fail in the duty he has promised to the king. The same principle applies to undertaking them in the presence of other persons. (Ṭīkā)
Note 2: "In the presence of a teacher of the Commentaries" means a teacher for whom the lineage of the Commentaries is thoroughly mastered. (Ṭīkā)

When the Blessed One has attained Parinibbāna, they should be undertaken in the presence of a Great Disciple. In his absence, in the presence of an Arahant... a Non-Returner... a Once-Returner... a Stream-Enterer... a bearer of the Tipitaka... a bearer of two Pitakas... a bearer of one Pitaka... a bearer of one of the five Nikāyas... a teacher (who is learned and proficient) in the Commentaries. In the absence of such a teacher of the Commentaries, in the presence of one who observes the dhutaṅgas. If such a dhutaṅga-observer is also absent, one should sweep the terrace of a shrine, sit in a crouching position, and undertake them as if speaking in the presence of the Fully Enlightened One. Alternatively, it is also proper to undertake them by oneself. In saying that it is good to undertake them by oneself, the story of the fewness of wishes regarding the dhutaṅga-observance of the elder of the two brother elders (residing) at Cetiyapabbata should be told. This is the general discussion concerning all dhutaṅgas.

## 1. Explanation of the Refuse-rag-man's Practice (Paṃsukūlikaṅga)

24. Now, I shall describe the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of each dhutaṅga. First, the refuse-rag-man's practice: "I reject robes given by householders..."

Note 1: The story of the fewness of wishes regarding the dhutaṅga-observance of the elder brother elder is as follows: That elder brother elder reportedly observed the sitter's practice (nesajjika-dhutaṅga). No one knew of his observance of that dhutaṅga. Then one day, during the night, the younger brother elder saw him sitting on his bed-bench by the light of a flash of lightning and asked, "Venerable Sir, are you observing the sitter's practice?"
60:
That elder, out of fewness of wishes regarding the virtue of ascetic practices (or because he did not want his practice to be known), lay down at that moment and re-undertook it later. This is the story mentioned. (Sub-commentary)

In the Commentaries to the Majjhima Nikāya (Vol. 2, p. 46) and Aṅguttara Nikāya (Vol. 1, p. 59), the story is found as follows:

Two brother elders were residing on Cetiya Mountain. One day, the younger elder brought pieces of sugarcane sent by a supporter and went to the elder brother, saying, 'Please partake of these, venerable sir.' The elder brother had finished his meal and was rinsing his mouth. He said, 'Enough, friend, I do not need them.' The younger asked, 'Why, venerable sir? Do you observe the ekāsanika (one-sessioner) practice?'

'Gahapatidānacīvaraṃ paṭikkhipāmi—I reject robes given by householders.'
'Paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmi—I undertake the refuse-rag-wearer's practice.'

[60] Between these two statements, the practice is undertaken by either one. This is the initial undertaking of this refuse-rag-wearer's practice.

Note:
(The story continues) The elder said, 'Bring the sugarcane, friend.' Although he had observed the ekāsanika practice for fifty years, because he wished to conceal his ascetic practice, he consumed the sugarcane, rinsed his mouth, and then re-undertook the practice before departing.

1. Gahapatidānacīvaraṃ: In this text, even monks who give robes are considered in the category of 'householders' for a person observing the strict refuse-rag practice. Cloth discarded with the intention that 'a monk will pick it up' can be a householder's robe (gahapaticīvara). However, it is not a robe 'given' by a householder (gahapatidānacīvara). Therefore, to exclude such cloth (from rejection), the word 'gift' (dāna) is included along with 'householder' (gahapati). (Sub-commentary)

2. It can be undertaken in pure Pali, pure Burmese [English], or both. If undertaking in Pali, it can be done with 'Gahapatidānacīvaraṃ paṭikkhipāmi' or 'Paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmi', or both. The same applies to Burmese [English]. Reciting once is sufficient, but for firmness, it should be recited three times. The same applies to undertaking subsequent ascetic practices.

Having thus undertaken the practice, that monk should take any of these twenty-three types of cloth: (1) (Sosānika) cloth from a cemetery, (2) (Pāpaṇika) cloth from a shop door, (3) (Rathiyacoḷa) cloth from a main road, (4) (Saṅkāracoḷa) cloth from a rubbish heap, (5) (Sotthiya) cloth used for cleaning after childbirth, (6) (Nhānacoḷa) cloth discarded after a ritual bath by exorcists, (7) (Titthacoḷa) cloth from a bathing place, (8) (Gatapaccāgata) cloth worn to a cemetery and discarded after returning, (9) (Aggidaḍḍha) burnt cloth, (10) (Gokhāyita) cattle-gnawed cloth, (11) (Upacikākhāyita) termite-gnawed cloth, (12) (Undurakhāyita) rat-gnawed cloth, (13) (Antacchinna) edge-cut cloth, (14) (Dasacchinna) fringe-cut cloth, (15) (Dhajāhaṭa) flag or banner cloth, (16) (Thūpacīvara) cloth wrapped around an anthill as an offering to deities, (17) (Samaṇacīvara) a monk's robe, (18) (Ābhisekika) cloth discarded at a king's consecration site, (19) (Iddhimaya) a robe created by psychic power through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' call,

Note:
(20) (Panthika) cloth dropped on a path, (21) (Vātāhaṭa) wind-blown cloth, (22) (Devadattiya) deity-given cloth, (23) (Sāmuddiya) ocean-washed cloth. Having picked up any of these twenty-three types of cloth, he should tear it, discard the weak parts, wash the strong parts, make a robe, and then discard the old householder-given robe and use the new one.

Among these twenty-three types: Sosānika is cloth dropped in a cemetery. Pāpaṇika is cloth dropped at a shop door. Rathiyacoḷa is cloth discarded on a main road through a window by those seeking merit. Saṅkāracoḷa is cloth discarded at a rubbish heap. Sotthiya is cloth discarded after wiping the impurities of childbirth. It is said that the mother of Minister Tissa had the impurities of childbirth wiped with a cloth worth a hundred [pieces] and had it discarded on the Tālaveḷi road, thinking, 'Refuse-rag-wearing monks will pick it up.' Monks took only small pieces for the purpose of patching worn-out parts. Nhānacoḷa is cloth discarded by those who have had a ritual head-wash by exorcists, considering it to be 'ill-luck cloth.'

Titthacoḷa is a rag discarded at a bathing place. Gatapaccāgata is cloth that people wore to a cemetery and then discarded after returning and bathing (considering it inauspicious). Aggidaḍḍha is cloth with holes or edges burnt by fire; people discard such burnt cloth (as inauspicious). Gokhāyita (cattle-gnawed cloth) and others are well-known; people discard such cloth as well. Dhajāhaṭa is cloth used as a flag when boarding a ship; it is allowable to take it once it is out of the sight of the sailors. Also, a victory banner set up on a battlefield is allowable to be taken when both armies have departed.

Thūpacīvara is cloth wrapped around an anthill as an offering to deities. Samaṇacīvara is a robe belonging to a monk. Ābhisekika is a robe discarded at a king's consecration site. Iddhimaya is a robe created by psychic power for 'Ehi Bhikkhu' monks. Panthika is cloth dropped on a path. Furthermore, if cloth is dropped due to the owner's forgetfulness, it should be picked up only after waiting for a short while. Vātāhaṭa is cloth blown by the wind and dropped far away. Furthermore, a monk who does not see the owners [61] should wait for a short while before picking up such wind-blown cloth.
61:
Devadattiya cloth refers to cloth given by deities, such as the cloth given to the Venerable Anuruddha by the deity Jālinī. Sāmuddiya cloth refers to cloth cast up onto the shore by the waves of the ocean.

Let us further examine what constitutes paṃsukūla (refuse-rag) and what does not. If a robe is given with the words, “We give this to the Saṅgha,” it is not paṃsukūla. If it is obtained by monks wandering for alms-cloth, it is also not paṃsukūla. (Note 1: Robes belonging to the Saṅgha or communal robes obtained through distribution are not paṃsukūla because they are neither the 17th type, known as samaṇacīvara, nor any of the other 22 types of paṃsukūla.) Regarding robes given by a monk, if the robe is given to be taken according to seniority (vassagga), it is not paṃsukūla (Note 2: This refers to robes given to be received by monks in order of their years of standing). If it is a robe intended for resident monks of a monastery, it is also not paṃsukūla (Note 3: This refers to a share of robes given to monks residing in a particular monastery).

A robe is considered paṃsukūla only if it is given without being taken according to seniority (Note 1: This refers to a robe given specifically to an individual rather than by seniority, or a robe left for the first person who arrives to take it. Note 2: The phrase “after taking it by one’s own seniority” indicates a robe that is one’s own share from the Saṅgha or a group; robes received as a personal gift are also included. If the owner monk places such a robe at the feet of a paṃsukūla-wearer or puts it into his hand, it becomes the 17th type of paṃsukūla called samaṇacīvara). 

In the case of such a robe (given by a monk without seniority), if the donors place it at the feet of a monk, and that monk then gives it into the hand of the paṃsukūla-wearer, it is called “pure on one side” (ekatosuddhika). If the donors give it into the hand of a monk, and that monk then places it at the feet of the paṃsukūla-wearer, it is also called “pure on one side.” However, if the donors place it at the feet of a monk, and that monk likewise places it at the feet of the paṃsukūla-wearer, it is called “pure on both sides” (ubhatosuddhika). If it is received after being placed in a monk's hand and is then given into the hand of the paṃsukūla-wearer, it is called “not superior” (anukkaṭṭha). Knowing these distinctions of paṃsukūla, the paṃsukūla-wearer should use the robe. This is the procedure for this practice.

Furthermore, there are three grades of paṃsukūla-wearers: (1) the strict (ukkaṭṭha), (2) the moderate (majjhima), and (3) the mild (mudu). Among them, the one who takes cloth only from a cemetery (Note 1: This is the literal translation. It implies that if one uses cloth from the other 22 sources and not the cemetery, one is not strict. Therefore, some suggest the text should imply “from cemeteries and such.”) is the strict practitioner. The one who takes cloth left with the thought, “Monks will take this,” is the moderate practitioner. The one who takes cloth given by being placed at his feet is the mild practitioner. These are the grades of the practitioners.

For any of these three types of practitioners, the ascetic practice is breached at the moment they take pleasure in accepting cloth given by laypeople, whether by their own wish or by consenting to a request (Note 1: Some editions of the Visuddhimagga lack the word ‘khantiya,’ but the commentary explains it as ‘nijjhanakkhantiya,’ so it must be included. The practice is broken if one accepts for personal use. If one accepts out of consideration for the donor to give it to another, the practice is not broken, according to the Cūḷa-ṭīkā).

The following are the benefits: (1) Having a practice in accordance with the dependence (nissaya) declared at ordination, based on the Buddha’s words: “The monkhood is dependent on refuse-rag robes”; (2) Being established in the first of the four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa); (3) Absence of the suffering of having to protect the robes; (4) Livelihood that is independent of others; (5) Freedom from the fear of thieves; (6) Absence of craving for use; (7) Having requisites suitable for a recluse; (8) Possessing requisites praised by the Blessed One as “cheap, easy to get, and blameless”; (9) Being inspiring or possessing an inspiring quality; (10) Fulfillment of the fruits of fewness of wishes, etc.; (11) Encouragement of right practice; and (12) Providing an example for future generations to follow. These are the benefits of the paṃsukūla practice.

To destroy the army of Māra,
The sage who wears the refuse-rags
Shines like a warrior-king in war,
Arrayed in armor for the fight.
62:
Having abandoned fine clothes such as those from Kāsī, the Teacher of the World wore refuse-rag robes. Who would not wear those refuse-rag robes? [1]

Therefore, a monk, well-remembering his own promise (made at the time of ordination), should delight in refuse-rag robes suitable for the practice of a yogi. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of the refuse-rag wearer’s practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga).

## 2. The Triple-Robe Wearer’s Practice (Tecīvarikaṅga)

25. Furthermore, following the refuse-rag wearer’s practice, the triple-robe wearer’s practice is undertaken by one of these two statements:

“I reject a fourth robe (suitable for wearing or wrapping).” [2]
“I undertake the triple-robe wearer’s practice.”

As for the procedure: When a monk who has undertaken the triple-robe wearer’s practice obtains cloth for a robe, he may store it as long as he is unable to sew it due to illness, or as long as he cannot find someone to help sew it, or as long as he lacks necessary tools such as needles. There is no fault in storing it for such reasons. However, from the time it is dyed, it is not proper to store it; if he does so, he is called a “thief of the ascetic practices” (dhutaṅgacora). This is his procedure.

Regarding classification, this practice is also of three types. Among them, the strict practitioner (ukkaṭṭha), at the time of dyeing, should first dye either the inner robe (antaravāsaka) or the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), and having worn that, dye the other. Having wrapped himself in that, he should dye the double-layered outer robe (saṅghāṭi). However, it is not proper to wear the double-layered outer robe as a lower garment. This is the rule for those living in the vicinity of a village. For a forest-dweller, it is proper to wash and dye two robes together. Nevertheless, he should sit in a nearby place so that if he sees someone, he can pull the robe over himself to cover his body. For the medium practitioner (majjhima), there is a so-called “dyeing-robe” in the dyeing hall; it is proper to perform the dyeing work while wearing or wrapping himself in that. For the mild practitioner (mudu), it is proper to perform the dyeing work while wearing or wrapping himself in the robes of fellow monks. [3] A bedspread (paccattharaṇa) belonging to that monastery (whether his own or another’s, which has been determined as such) is also permissible for the mild practitioner; however, it is not proper to carry it away when going elsewhere. It is also not proper to use the robes of fellow monks frequently. For a monk who observes the triple-robe wearer’s practice, if there is a fourth robe, only a shoulder cloth (aṃsa-kāsāva) is permissible. [4] That shoulder cloth is permissible only if it is one span in width and three cubits in length. [5]

For all three types of practitioners, the ascetic practice is breached at the very moment they consent to a fourth robe suitable for wearing or wrapping. This is the breach herein.

This refers to that robe.
[2] “A fourth robe” refers to a fourth robe suitable for wearing or wrapping. This is because the shoulder cloth (aṃsa-kāsāva) is not rejected. (Commentary)
[3] Although this is a single sentence in the Visuddhimagga, it is translated here as two sentences for clarity.
[4] The shoulder cloth is considered a minor accessory (parikkhāracola). Therefore, teachers say that these two items—the bedspread and the shoulder cloth—even if they exist in addition to the three robes, do not cause a breach of the ascetic practice. (Commentary)

(Cūḷaṭīkā as shown in the Pyay Edition Visuddhimagga-nissaya)

[63] These are the benefits: The monk who observes the triple-robe-eater's ascetic practice (tecīvarikaṅga) is content with robes that merely protect and sustain the body. Therefore, for that monk: (1) he can go wherever he wishes, taking only his requisites like a bird with its wings; (2) he has few concerns; (3) he avoids storing cloth; (4) he leads a light livelihood; (5) he abandons the greed of craving for more than three robes; (6) he leads a scrupulous life by limiting himself to the allowable measure of three robes; (7) the benefits such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā) are fulfilled—these and other such qualities are perfected. This is the benefit of the triple-robe-eater's practice.

The wise yogi who wears the triple robes, having abandoned the craving for extra cloth and avoiding storage, knows the flavor of the happiness of contentment.

Therefore, like a bird that can go wherever it wishes with its wings (or, whose wings are its only burden), the noble yogi, being with only the robes worn on his body, should take delight in the restriction of robes to only three, desiring to wander at ease. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classification, the breach, and the benefits of the triple-robe-eater's practice.

## 3. Explanation of the Alms-food-eater's Practice

26. The alms-food-eater's practice (piṇḍapātikaṅga) is undertaken with one of these two statements:

"I reject extra gains (atirekalābha—such as meals for the Saṅgha, etc., which are in excess of alms-food)."

"I undertake the alms-food-eater's practice (the volition which is the factor of a monk who has the habit of wandering for alms)."

Furthermore, that monk who practices the alms-food-eater's practice should not enjoy or accept these fourteen types of meals: (1) Saṅghabhatta—a meal offered to the entire Saṅgha; (2) Uddesabhatta—a meal offered to designated monks from the Saṅgha; (3) Nimantanabhatta—a meal offered by invitation; (4) Salākabhatta—a meal offered by drawing lots or tickets; (5) Pakkhika—a meal offered once a fortnight; (6) Uposathika—a meal offered on the Uposatha day; (7) Pāṭipadika—a meal offered on the first day of the fortnight; (8) Āgantukabhatta—a meal intended for guest monks; (9) Gamikabhatta—a meal intended for traveling monks; (10) Gilānabhatta—a meal intended for sick monks; (11) Gilānupaṭṭhākabhatta—a meal intended for those attending to the sick; (12) Vihārabhatta—a meal intended for the monastery; (13) Dhurabhatta—a meal provided regularly at a specific house (the first house on the alms round); (14) Vārakabhatta—a meal provided by rotation. 

However, if they do not say, "Please accept a Saṅgha meal," etc., but instead say, "The Saṅgha accepts alms at our house; please accept alms too," and thus offer it (using the term for alms-food), it is proper to enjoy and accept those meals. A ticket for things other than food (such as medicine) received from the Saṅgha, or food cooked and offered in the monastery, is also allowable. This is the procedure for the alms-food-eater's practice.

As for classification, this alms-food-eater's practice is also of three kinds. Among them, the strict (ukkaṭṭha) monk accepts alms-food brought from a house he has not yet reached (in front) or from a house he has already passed (behind). He gives his bowl to donors who stand at the door of the house he is currently at to take the bowl [to fill it]. He also accepts alms-food brought from a house to the refectory. However, he does not sit and wait for food on that day. The moderate (majjhima) monk also accepts food while sitting and waiting on that day, but he does not accept an invitation for the next day. The mild (mudu) monk accepts food for the sake of the next day or the day after. Both the moderate and the mild monks do not obtain the happiness of living as they please (serivihārasukha); only the strict monk obtains it.
64: Only the strict monk obtains (that happiness). [64] It is said that in a certain village, there was a Dhamma festival concerning the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta. The strict monk said to the medium and mild ones, 'Friends, let us go to hear the Dhamma.' Among them, one (the medium) monk said, 'Venerable sir, a donor has made me sit and wait (for a meal).' The other (mild) monk said, 'Venerable sir, I have accepted a donor's meal for tomorrow.' Thus, both of those monks were deprived (of the happiness of living as they please, or the joy of the Dhamma, etc.). Only the strict person, having wandered for alms early in the morning and gone (to the festival), experienced the joy of the Dhamma. (This is the classification of persons observing the alms-food-eater's practice). Furthermore, the ascetic practice of these three types of persons is breached at the very moment they enjoy or accept extra gains (such as Saṅghabhatta) beyond alms-food. This is the breach in this alms-food-eater's practice. These are the benefits: (1) Having a practice in accordance with the original dependence (nissaya) because of the Buddha's words: 'Going forth is dependent on the morsel-food of alms-gathering'; (2) standing in the second Ariyavaṃsa (Noble Lineage); (3) having a livelihood independent of others; (4) having requisites praised by the Blessed One as 'being of little value, easy to get, and blameless'; (5) being able to suppress laziness in going for alms; (6) having a pure livelihood; (7) fulfilling the Sekhiya training rules; (8) not having to support others; (9) helping others (by allowing them to offer alms); (10) abandoning pride; (11) being able to restrain and abandon craving for tastes; (12) not incurring offenses regarding group meals (gaṇabhojana), successive meals (paramparabhojana), and conduct (cāritta) rules; (13) having a livelihood in accordance with fewness of wishes, etc.; (14) developing right practice; (15) helping future generations (by setting an example). These are the benefits of the alms-food-eater's practice. The monk who is content with the morsel-food of alms, who has a livelihood independent of others, and who has abandoned greed for food, is free in all four directions and can go wherever he wishes. He can also dispel laziness; the livelihood of that alms-food-eater is pure. Therefore, a wise monk should not despise the practice of alms-gathering. Indeed, for such a monk— Who supports himself and supports no others, who is firm (tādi) (being equanimous towards the desirable and undesirable), who is habituated to alms-gathering—if he is not attached to gain and fame, even the gods envy him.
65:
