2. Connect these qualifying terms with the term 'to the monk'.
3. Connect with 'the monk... is still loved'.
If one does not rely on fame, even the gods (such as Sakka) still love him. This is the instruction.
This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classifications, the breach, and the benefits of the alms-food seeker's practice.

## 4. Explanation of the House-to-House Alms-Round Practice (Sapadānacārikaṅga)
27. The house-to-house alms-round practice is undertaken with one of these two statements:
"I reject greedy wandering (skipping houses out of greed)."
"I undertake the factor of the house-to-house alms-round."
(This is the method of undertaking.)

Furthermore, the monk who undertakes this house-to-house alms-round practice should stand at the village gate and observe if there are any dangers (such as elephants, horses, buffaloes, or cattle). If there is danger in a particular street or village, it is proper to avoid that street or village and go elsewhere. If he receives nothing at a particular house-door, street, or village, he should proceed, treating it as if it were not a village. If he receives something at a house-door, street, or village, it is not proper to skip it and go elsewhere. Moreover, this monk should enter for alms early; thus, if he encounters an unsuitable place (due to danger), he will be able to go elsewhere. Furthermore, if people who are giving alms at the monastery or people coming along the road take his bowl and give alms-food, it is proper to accept it. Also, while traveling, this monk should not skip a village he reaches at the time for alms-round. If he receives nothing or only a little there, he should wander through the village in order. This is his procedure.

As to classification, this practice is also of three kinds. Among them, the strict monk does not accept alms-food brought from a house ahead which he has not yet reached, nor food brought by someone following from a house he has already passed, nor food brought to the refectory. He simply hands over his bowl at the door of the house he has reached. Indeed, in this dhutaṅga, there is no one equal to the Elder Mahākassapa. Even for that Elder, only the instance of handing over the bowl (to Sakka disguised as a weaver) is known. The moderate monk accepts food brought from a house ahead or from a house behind, and also food brought to the refectory. He also hands over his bowl at the door of the house he has reached, but he does not sit waiting for food that has been invited for that day. By not waiting, this moderate monk conforms to the strict alms-food seeker. The mild monk sits and waits for food invited for that day. (This is the classification of persons undertaking the house-to-house alms-round practice.)

Furthermore, for all three types of persons, the dhutaṅga is breached as soon as greedy wandering (skipping houses for better food) occurs. This is the breach here.

These are the benefits: (1) being always a newcomer among families, (2) being like the moon, (3) abandoning stinginess regarding families, (4) having equal compassion for all families, (5) being free from the faults of associating with families, (6) not delighting in invitations, (7) not desiring food to be brought to him, and (8) living in conformity with fewness of wishes and so forth. These are the benefits of the house-to-house alms-round practice.
66:
In this Dispensation, the monk who wanders from house to house for alms is like the moon (in having a mind unattached and pure in all places); he is always a newcomer among families; he is free from stinginess regarding families; he has equal compassion for all families; and he is free from the faults that befall those monks who associate with families by sitting and eating in their houses.

Therefore, a wise man who desires to wander at will upon the earth should reject greedy wandering, keep his eyes downcast looking only a yoke's length ahead, and practice the duty of house-to-house alms-round. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classifications, the breach, and the benefits of the house-to-house alms-round practice.

## 5. Explanation of the One-Sessioner's Practice (Ekāsanikaṅga)
28. The one-sessioner's practice is undertaken with one of these two statements:
"I reject eating in several sessions."
"I undertake the factor of the one-sessioner."
(This is the method of undertaking.)

As for the procedure: when the monk who undertakes the one-sessioner's practice sits in the refectory, he should not sit in the seats of senior elders, but should sit in a suitable seat, estimating, "This seat will fall to me." If his teacher or preceptor arrives before his meal is finished, he should rise and perform his duty. However, the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya said: "One should protect either the seat or the food. Since this monk's meal is unfinished, let him perform the duty (by rising), but let him not eat again." This is the procedure for the one-sessioner.

As to classification, this one-sessioner's practice is also of three kinds. Among them, the strict person, whether the food be little or much, once he has lowered his hand to the food (to begin eating), he may not take any other food. If people bring ghee and so forth, thinking, "The Elder has not eaten anything yet," it is proper to accept them only for the purpose of medicine, not for the purpose of nourishment. The moderate person may take other food as long as the food in his bowl is not finished. Indeed, this moderate person is called 'one whose limit is the food'. The mild person may eat as long as he does not rise from his seat. Indeed, that mild person is either 'one whose limit is the water' because he eats until he takes the bowl-washing water, or 'one whose limit is the seat' because he eats as long as he does not rise from his seat. (This is the classification of persons undertaking the one-sessioner's practice.)

Note:
1. If a monk who is eating rises to perform duties for his teacher or preceptor, the food does not protect the dhutaṅga because he is in the act of eating, and the seat does not protect it because he has risen. Therefore, he must not eat again; if he does, the dhutaṅga is breached.
67:
Furthermore, for all three types of these persons, the ascetic practice is breached at the moment they eat in more than one place. This is the breach in this one-sessioner's practice.

The following are the benefits: (1) freedom from illness, (2) freedom from affliction, (3) lightness of body, (4) strength, (5) living in comfort, (6) freedom from offenses that may occur by eating food that is not 'leftover' (anatiritta), (7) dispelling greed for tastes, and (8) living in accordance with fewness of wishes and so forth. These are the benefits of this one-sessioner's practice.

Diseases that arise from [repeated] eating do not oppress the monk who delights in eating in one session. Being not greedy for tastes, he does not neglect his own duties as a monk but fulfills them.

Therefore, a monk with a pure mind should develop a delight in eating in one session, which is a cause for living in comfort, which thins out craving, and which is practiced by the noble ones who delight in pure effacement. This is the exhortation.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of the one-sessioner's practice.

## 6. The Bowl-food-eater's Practice (Pattapiṇḍikanga)

29. The bowl-food-eater's practice is also undertaken with one of these two statements:
“Dutiyakabhājanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi—I refuse a second vessel.”
“Pattapiṇḍikangaṃ samādiyāmi—I undertake the bowl-food-eater's practice.”
(This is the undertaking.)

Note: 
1. Connect with “...delight in eating in one session.”
2. Connect with “...in the practice [of effacement].”

Regarding the procedure: When the monk who carries the bowl-food-eater's practice is drinking rice gruel, if he receives side dishes such as meat or fish, he should either eat the side dish first or drink the gruel first. The reason is that if he puts it into the gruel, and if the side dish consists of things like pieces of putrid fish, the gruel would become repulsive. Indeed, one should eat only after making it not repulsive. Therefore, I have said this with reference to such repulsive side dishes. However, things that are not repulsive, such as honey or sugar, may be put into the gruel. When receiving food, one should take only a moderate amount sufficient for the stomach. Raw greens (such as young mango leaves) may be eaten by holding them with the hand, but it is better to put them into the bowl. Since a second vessel is refused, even a tree leaf is not allowed [as a second vessel]. This is the procedure for the bowl-food-eater's practice.

As for the classification, this bowl-food-eater's practice also has three grades. Among them, for the strict person, it is not allowed to discard even scraps (such as fish bones or husks) [into a second vessel] except when eating sugarcane.

Note:
1. This is the intended meaning of the word 'gaṇhantena'. In terms of grammatical meaning, it is 'by the one who is receiving', or 'when receiving', or 'while receiving'.
2. One should receive only as much as one bowlful, bearing in mind not to take a large amount and then discard or waste the excess. (Ṭīkā)

At other times, it is not allowed to discard scraps (such as fish bones or grain husks) [into a second vessel]. Even rice balls, fish, meat, and cakes [68] should not be broken into pieces [to eat]. For the medium person, it is allowed to break them with one hand. This medium person is called a 'hand-user' (hattha-yogī). The mild person is called a 'bowl-user' (patta-yogī). For the mild person, whatever food or snacks can be put into the bowl, all of it...

Note:
1. Here, the words in parentheses '(into a second vessel)' are from the Pyay version of the Visuddhimagga Nissaya. According to that meaning, it is not only a second eating vessel that is prohibited, but even an extra vessel for discarding scraps is not allowed.
68:
If that were the case, it would be as if a spittoon should not be kept at the place of eating. What is meant in the Commentary is this: even so, when eating sugarcane, one may peel the skin before chewing and discard it. Otherwise, it seems to mean that one should not pick out debris from the bowl beforehand, but should remove it only after it reaches the mouth. Eating without selection in this way has the benefit of abandoning craving for tastes (rasataṇhā) that arises for various delicacies; it seems to be explained for that benefit.

2. Here, the meaning of 'breaking' (into pieces) is the interpretation of the Pyay Sayadaw. If so, it would be as if one must eat large lumps of rice or pieces of meat without breaking them. Here too, what the Commentator seems to mean is that one should not separate lumps of rice, fish, meat, or cakes to eat them one by one to enjoy the taste, but should mix everything together and eat without distinction.

It is allowable to eat by breaking (into pieces) with the hands or teeth. (This is the distinction of the person practicing the Alms-bowl-eater's practice.)

Furthermore, the ascetic practice of these three types of persons is broken at the moment they take delight in and accept a second vessel. This is the breach in the Alms-bowl-eater's practice.

The following are the benefits: (1) Abandoning craving for various tastes; (2) Abandoning the state of desiring various tastes found in various separate vessels; (3) The state of habitually seeing only the purpose (permitted by the Buddha) in food; (4) The absence of weariness caused by carrying extra plates and dishes; (5) The state of eating without distraction (by other vessels); (6) The state of living in accordance with fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and so forth. These are the benefits of the Alms-bowl-eater's practice.

The practitioner of the Alms-bowl-eater's practice, who has good conduct and a good heart, having abandoned attachment to various vessels, with downcast eyes fixed only on the single bowl, as if digging up the roots of craving for tastes, should consume food while maintaining contentment as if it were his own body. Who else but the alms-bowl-eater could consume food in such a way? This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classification, the breach, and the benefits of the Alms-bowl-eater's practice.

## 7. Explanation of the Refuser-of-later-food Practice (Khalupacchābhattikanga)

30. The Refuser-of-later-food practice should be undertaken with one of these two statements:
“Atirittabhojanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi—I refuse food that is not leftover (i.e., food made allowable by the atiritta procedure).”
“Khalupacchābhattikangaṃ samādiyāmi—I undertake the factor of the refuser-of-later-food practice.”
(This is the method of undertaking.)

As for the procedure, that monk who observes the refuser-of-later-food practice, having refused (indicating he has had enough), must not eat food (obtained in another posture) by having it made allowable (through Vinaya procedures). This is the procedure for the practitioner of the refuser-of-later-food practice.

By way of classification, this practitioner of the refuser-of-later-food practice is also of three types. Among them, for the strict (ukkaṭṭha) person, there is no 'refusal' (pavāraṇā) yet at the first mouthful; however, once that first mouthful is swallowed, for the monk who refuses further food, 'refusal' occurs. Therefore, having thus refused and swallowed the first mouthful, he does not eat a second mouthful. The medium (majjhima) person eats only that food during which he was 'refused' (i.e., the food already in his bowl). The mild (mudu) person eats (food that is offered) as long as he has not yet risen from his seat. (This is the classification of the practitioners of the refuser-of-later-food practice.)

Note 1: If an ordinary monk who has refused wishes to eat food again in another posture, he must bring that food to a monk who knows the Vinaya and say, “Atirittaṃ karotha bhante—Venerable sir, please make this leftover.” That monk, after taking a little and eating, says, “Alametaṃ sabbaṃ—This is all enough,” and thus makes it leftover. The monk who had refused may then eat that food which has been made leftover. It means that this ascetic practitioner must not eat by having it made leftover in that way.

Note 2: Connect “The strict person... having refused and swallowed the first mouthful, does not eat a second mouthful.”

Furthermore, the ascetic practice of these three types of persons is broken at the moment they eat (food obtained in another posture) by having it made allowable, even though they have already refused.
69:
This is the breach of this khalupacchābhattika practice.

[69] The following are the benefits: (1) being far from the offense of eating food that has not been made 'allowable' (anati-ritta) through the Vinaya procedure; (2) the absence of gluttony; (3) the absence of storing material things; (4) the absence of seeking food again; (5) living in conformity with fewness of wishes and so on. These are the benefits of the khalupacchābhattika practice.

The wise practitioner who observes the khalupacchābhattika practice does not experience the fatigue of seeking food again, does not store food, and abandons gluttony.

Therefore, a practitioner who wishes to shake off faults such as great desire should resort to this khalupacchābhattika practice, which is praised by the Sugata and which produces growth in qualities such as contentment. This is the instruction.

This is the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classification, the breach, and the benefits of the khalupacchābhattika practice.

## 8. The Forest-Dweller’s Practice (Āraññikanga)

31. The forest-dweller’s practice is undertaken with one of these two statements:

"Gāmanta-senāsanaṃ paṭikkhipāmi—I reject village-border dwellings."

"Āraññikangaṃ samādiyāmi—I undertake the forest-dweller’s practice."

(This is the undertaking.)

As for the procedure: that forest-dwelling monk should leave the village-border dwelling and let the dawn rise in the forest.

In this context (regarding the terms 'village-border dwelling' and 'forest'): a village together with its precincts is called a village-border dwelling (gāmanta-senāsana).

A 'village' means any place of human habitation, whether it consists of one house or many houses, whether it is fenced or unfenced, whether it is inhabited or [temporarily] uninhabited, or even a caravan that has stayed for more than four months.

The 'precinct of a village' (gāmūpacāra) is defined as follows: in a fenced village like Anurādhapura, if there are two gateposts (indakhīla), it is the distance of a stone's throw by a man of average strength standing at the inner gatepost. Regarding the characteristic of that stone's throw, Vinaya experts say it is the area within the spot where a stone falls when thrown by young men who, wishing to show their strength, stretch their arms and throw it. Suttanta teachers, however, say it is within the spot where a stone falls when thrown to scare away crows. In an unfenced village, the 'precinct of a house' is the spot where the water falls when a woman standing at the door of the outermost house throws it from a vessel. From that house precinct, the distance of one stone's throw as mentioned before is the 'village' [limit]. A second stone's throw from there is the 'precinct of the village.'

As for 'forest' (arañña), according to the Vinaya method, it is said: "Except for the village and its precincts, all the rest is forest."

According to the Abhidhamma method, it is said: "Having gone out beyond the gatepost, [70] all this area is forest." But in the context of this forest-dweller’s practice, the standard to be noted is the one given in the Suttanta method: "A dwelling at least five hundred bow-lengths (dhanu) away (from a village) is a forest dwelling" (as taught in the Āraññika-sikkhāpada regarding a forest-dwelling monk).
70:
Regarding that forest monastery of five hundred bow-lengths: if it is a village with an enclosure, the distance should be measured and demarcated from the threshold of the gate; if it is without an enclosure, from the first stone's throw, up to the enclosure of the monastery.

If, however, the monastery has no enclosure, the measurement should be taken by defining the boundary at the very first building encountered (when coming from the village)—whether it be a dwelling, a refectory, a regular assembly place, a Bodhi tree, or a Cetiya—even if it is far from the main dwelling. This is stated in the Vinaya Commentaries. In the Majjhima Commentary, however, it is stated that the measurement should be taken between the two stone's throws, having determined the precinct (upacāra) of the monastery just as one does for a village. This statement from the Majjhima Commentary is the standard (pamāṇa) for measuring the distance of a forest monastery.

Even if a village is nearby and the voices of people can be heard by those staying in the monastery, if it is impossible to go directly because of intervening mountains, rivers, and so on, the five hundred bow-lengths should be calculated according to the regular path, even if one must travel by boat. However, if a monk blocks various paths here and there to fulfill the requirement of a forest-dwelling attribute for a nearby village, he is a 'thief of ascetic practices' (dhutanga-cora).

If the preceptor (upajjhāya) or teacher (ācariya) of a forest-dwelling monk is ill and does not receive suitable requisites in the forest, the monk should take him to a village monastery and attend to him. However, he should leave early and ensure that dawn rises while he is in a place that meets the forest-dwelling requirements. If the illness of the teacher or preceptor worsens at the time of dawn, he should only attend to their needs; he need not be concerned with the purity of the ascetic practice. This is the procedure for him.

As to its classification, this practice is also of three kinds. Therein, the strict (ukkaṭṭha) practitioner must always let dawn rise in the forest. The intermediate (majjhima) practitioner is allowed to live in a village monastery during the four months of the Rains. The mild (mudu) practitioner is allowed to live in a village monastery during the four months of Winter as well.

Furthermore, for these three types of practitioners, the ascetic practice is not broken if dawn rises while they are listening to a Dhamma discourse in a village monastery during the permitted times, having come from the forest. Nor is it broken if dawn rises while they are on the path back after listening to the Dhamma. However, if they fall asleep thinking, 'We will go after sleeping for a moment,' even after the Dhamma teacher has departed, and dawn rises, or if they let dawn rise in a village monastery of their own will, the ascetic practice is broken. This is the breach herein.

The following are the benefits (ānisaṃsa): A monk who undertakes the forest-dwelling practice, by attending to the perception of the forest, can attain concentration not yet attained and can protect concentration already attained.
71:
(2) The Blessed One is also pleased with that forest-dwelling monk. As it is said: “Nāgita, I am pleased with that monk's forest-dwelling” (A. Ni. 6.42, 8.86). (3) Unsuitable sights and so on do not distract the mind of that monk who dwells in remote lodgings. (4) He is free from fear. (5) He abandons the attachment (nikanti) to life. (6) He enjoys the taste of the bliss of seclusion. (7) The state of being a rag-robe-dweller and so on (the remaining twelve ascetic practices) is also suitable for that forest-dwelling monk. These are the benefits of the forest-dweller's practice.

Secluded and unattached,
Delighting in remote lodgings,
Satisfying the Master's heart
By living in the forest.

Note: These adjectives refer to the monk.

The bliss a sage finds
Living alone in the forest,
Even the gods with Indra
Do not experience that taste.

Wearing the rag-robe
Like a coat of armor,
Entering the forest battlefield
With the remaining ascetic practices as weapons,

He is able, before long,
To defeat Māra and his army. Therefore, a wise person should delight in forest-dwelling. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of the forest-dweller's practice.

Note: Here, a verse ends in the Visuddhimagga. For clarity for those comparing texts, it is separated here, though the sentence continues. Thus, "He is able..." in the next paragraph completes the sense.

## 9. The Tree-Root-Dweller's Practice (Rukkhamūlikanga)

32. The tree-root-dweller's practice is undertaken by one of these two statements:
“I reject a roof (lodgings covered by the five types of roofing).”
“I undertake the tree-root-dweller's practice.”
(This is the undertaking.)

As for the procedure, the tree-root-dweller should avoid these trees: (1) a tree on the boundary of two kingdoms, (2) a shrine tree (worshipped by people), (3) a resinous tree, (4) a fruit tree, (5) a tree where bats dwell, (6) a hollow tree (where snakes or scorpions might hide), and (7) a tree in the middle of a monastery. He should choose a tree standing at the edge of the monastery. This is the procedure for the tree-root-dweller.

By classification, this tree-root-dweller is also of three types. Among them, the strict (ukkaṭṭha) person, having chosen a tree to his liking, is not allowed to have it cleaned. He must live there after clearing away the fallen leaves with his feet. The medium (majjhima) person is allowed to have the area cleaned only by those who happen to arrive there. The mild (mudu) person may call monastery attendants or novices to have it cleaned, leveled, spread with sand, and have a fence or wall built [72] and a gate fitted. On festival days, the tree-root-dweller should not stay under that tree but should stay in some other concealed place (to hide his practice). (This is the classification of the tree-root-dweller.)

Note: The five types of roofing are: (1) tiles, (2) stone, (3) plaster, (4) grass, and (5) leaves (such as palm or sal leaves). (Vin. 4.301)

Furthermore, the ascetic practice of these three types of persons is breached at the moment they stay in a place covered by tiles, etc., with the desire for a roof. Even if they stay under a roof until dawn while knowing it...

Note: (In Vin. 1.264, Vin. 4.359) “Devadatta,”
72:
"I have allowed staying at the foot of a tree for eight months," because of this statement by the Buddha, and because it is explained (in the Samantapāsādikā, Vol. 2, p. 189), "For the four months of the rainy season, staying at the foot of a tree is indeed forbidden," and because of the regulations (in Vinaya Vol. 3, p. 212), "One should not enter the Vassa in the open air" and "One should not enter the Vassa without a dwelling," it appears that the Tree-root-dweller's practice and the Open-air-dweller's practice should not be undertaken during the four months of the rainy season. However, if there is a rain-proof dwelling with a door, one may enter the Vassa there. If one does not enter under the roof of that dwelling, there is no breach of the ascetic practice. This distinction should also be noted here.

The reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya say: [Staying under a roof] for the sake of listening to the Dhamma, etc., does not break the practice; therefore, they say, "only if one knowingly lets the dawn rise while under a roof." This is the breach in this Tree-root-dweller's practice.

The following are the benefits (ānisaṃsa): (1) In accordance with the statement of the Blessed One, "Going forth depends on the foot of a tree as a dwelling," it is a practice consistent with the (third) support (nissaya). (2) It is a requisite praised by the Blessed One, saying, "These are few, easy to find, and blameless." (3) It can arouse the perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) by constantly seeing the changes and alterations of tree leaves. (4) There is an absence of stinginess regarding dwellings and delight in new construction. (5) One lives together with tree deities. (6) It is a conduct in accordance with fewness of wishes (appicchatā), etc. These are the benefits of the Tree-root-dweller's practice.

Where else can there be a place for a yogi desiring seclusion equal to the foot of a tree, which was praised by the Best of Buddhas and spoken of as the support (nissaya) for the monkhood?

For, a well-behaved yogi living at the secluded foot of a tree, which is protected by tree deities and is a place for removing stinginess regarding dwellings,

Seeing the tree leaves—bright red (when budding), then green, and then turning yellow and falling from their stalks—he can dispel the perception of permanence.

Therefore, a wise monk should not despise but should highly respect the secluded foot of a tree, which is the heritage of the Buddha and the abode of those who delight in meditation. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of the Tree-root-dweller's practice.

## 10. The Open-air-dweller's Practice (Abbhokāsikaṅga)

33. The Open-air-dweller's practice is undertaken by one of these two statements:
"I refuse a roof and the foot of a tree."
"I undertake the Open-air-dweller's practice."

This is the method of undertaking. The procedure is as follows: It is permissible for that monk who is an open-air-dweller to enter the Uposatha hall for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma or for the Uposatha ceremony. If it rains after he has entered, he should not leave while it is raining but should leave when the rain stops. It is permissible to enter a refectory or a fire-room to perform duties, or to enter a refectory to ask senior monks about the meal. It is permissible for a teacher monk who is reciting or a student monk who is being taught to enter under a roof (during the lesson). It is also permissible to bring inside beds, stools, etc., that have been poorly placed outside. If a monk who is traveling [73] is carrying the requisites of senior monks and it rains, it is permissible to enter a rest house (sālā) located in the middle of the road. If he is not carrying any requisites (of senior monks), he should not walk fast with the intention of sheltering in a rest house. However, he may go at his normal pace and, having entered (the rest house), stay until the rain stops before proceeding. This is the procedure for the open-air-dweller.
73:
The procedure for the tree-root dweller should also be understood in the same manner as the procedure for the open-air dweller (such as for listening to the Dhamma, etc.).

By way of classification, this open-air dweller's practice is also of three kinds. Among them, for the strict person, it is not proper to stay leaning against a tree, a mountain, or a house. He should stay in the open air, having made a hut out of his robes. For the medium person, it is proper to stay leaning against a tree, a mountain, or a house, but without entering inside.1 For the mild person, an unbounded mountain cleft or valley (to prevent rain), a pavilion made of sparse branches, a cloth cover stiffened with paste, or a hut left behind by field-watchers and the like, are proper. This is the classification of the open-air dweller.

Note 1: 'Inside a tree' means the area at the foot or under the tree. 'Inside a mountain' means the area under a mountain peak or ledge that resembles a valley, cleft, or cave. (Commentary)

Furthermore, for all three types of persons, the ascetic practice is broken at the moment they enter under a roof or at the foot of a tree for the purpose of dwelling. The Aṅguttara-bhāṇakas (reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya) say that it is broken only if they stay there knowingly until dawn. This is the breach in this open-air dweller's practice.

The following are the benefits: (1) the cutting off of the impediment of a dwelling; (2) the dispelling of sloth and torpor; (3) suitability for the praise: "Like deer, the monks wander unattached and dwell without a home"; (4) being unattached to shade and shelter; (5) having unobstructed movement in the four directions; (6) living in accordance with fewness of wishes and so forth.

Note 2: Even at the foot of some trees, there is comfort and ease of living; therefore, the impediment of a dwelling preceded by attachment can still occur there. In the open air, however, it cannot. Thus, the benefit of cutting off the impediment of a dwelling is mentioned only for this ascetic practice. (Commentary)

Note 3: Because there is no dwelling to stay in at a particular place, there is no thought such as "I cannot go to that place." Thus, there is unobstructed movement in the four directions. (Commentary)

In the open air, which is like a jeweled canopy of stars illuminated by the great lamp of the moon, the monk who dispels sloth and torpor with a mind like a deer, and who is devoted to the delight of meditation, soon finds the taste of the bliss of seclusion, which is the happiness of the paths, fruits, and Nibbāna. Therefore, the wise should delight in the open air. This is the exhortation.

This is the description of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of the open-air dweller's practice.

## 11. The Cemetery Dweller's Practice

[74] 34. The cemetery dweller's practice should be undertaken with one of these two statements:

"I reject a non-cemetery."
"I undertake the cemetery dweller's practice."
74:
Regarding the procedure: The monk who undertakes the cemetery dweller's practice should not stay in a place that people have merely designated as a cemetery when establishing a new village, saying, "Let this place be the cemetery."

This is because as long as a corpse has not been cremated (or buried) there, that designated place is not yet called a cemetery. However, from the time a corpse has been cremated (or buried), even if it has been abandoned for twelve years without further cremations or burials, that place is indeed a cemetery.2

Note 1: The monk should not stay in a place that is merely designated.
Note 2: Because it has reached the characteristics of a cemetery by the mere lying of a corpse, it is indeed a cemetery. Indeed, 'chava-sayana' (the bed of a corpse) is called 'susāna' (cemetery). (Commentary)

A special point to note: The monk staying in that cemetery should not stay there building pavilions for walking, setting up beds or chairs, providing drinking and washing water, or teaching the Dhamma. This ascetic practice is heavy and difficult to maintain. Therefore, to dispel potential dangers, he should inform the Sangha elder or a royal official such as a village head (of his stay in the cemetery) and dwell diligently. When walking, he should walk with eyes half-open, looking toward the cremation (or burial) ground.

When going to the cemetery, he should leave the main road and go by a secret side path. He should mark the landmarks (such as stumps, trees, or anthills that might look dark and prominent at night) during the day. The benefit is that if he marks them thus, those objects like stumps will not appear frightening (like ghosts) to him at night. Even if non-humans (spirits) wander about crying out at night, he should not throw anything such as clods of earth or stones at them. It is not proper to fail to go to the cemetery for even a single day. The Aṅguttara-bhāṇakas say: "It is proper to spend the middle watch in the cemetery and depart from the cemetery in the last watch."

Note 1: Because a cemetery is a place where people can commit secret misdeeds, it is a place where thieves who have committed or are about to commit robbery may enter. If thieves, seeing the owners (or police), drop their stolen goods near the monk and flee, the monk might be mistaken for a thief and be captured or beaten. To dispel such dangers, he must inform the Sangha elder, village head, etc. (Commentary - slightly summarized).

He should not consume foods liked by non-humans, such as crushed sesame, bean rice, fish, meat, milk, oil, and molasses. He should not enter the houses of donors (on his way back from the cemetery). This is the procedure for the cemetery dweller.

By way of classification, this cemetery dweller's practice is also of three kinds. Among them, the strict person should stay only in a cemetery where there is constant cremation, the constant smell of corpses, and constant weeping. For the medium person, it is proper to stay if even one of these three—constant cremation, constant smell, or constant weeping—is present. For the mild person, it is proper to stay in a cemetery that has merely reached the characteristics of a cemetery as mentioned before.

Furthermore, for all three types of persons, the ascetic practice is broken by making a dwelling in a non-cemetery. The Aṅguttara-bhāṇakas say it is broken on the day one does not go to the cemetery. This is the breach in this cemetery dweller's practice.

The following are the benefits: (1) obtaining mindfulness of death; (2) living diligently; (3) obtaining the sign of foulness (asubha); (4) dispelling sensual lust; (5) constantly seeing the foul nature of the body; [75] (6) having an abundance of spiritual urgency (saṃvega).
75:
(7) The ability to abandon the intoxication (pride) based on health, youth, and life (by seeing those who are sick, aged, and dead); (8) the ability to endure great and small fears; (9) being worthy of respect and honor by non-human beings; (10) living in accordance with fewness of wishes and so forth. These are the benefits of the cemetery dweller’s practice.

Due to the power of the meditation on mindfulness of death, the faults of negligence do not affect or oppress the monk who dwells in a cemetery, even while he is asleep (in his dreams). Because he clearly sees many corpses, the mind of that monk who dwells in a cemetery does not fall under the influence of lust that repeatedly clings to sensual objects.

Note: The teachers of the Aṅguttara Nikāya say, "It is broken on the day one does not go to the cemetery," because it is intended that one should leave the cemetery at dawn. (Sub-commentary)

Because he attains great spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he no longer reaches a state of intoxication. Furthermore, desiring the peace of Nibbāna, he strives rightly. Since it brings about many such virtues in this manner, the yogi whose heart is inclined toward Nibbāna should constantly cultivate the cemetery dweller’s practice. This is the exhortation.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classifications, the breach, and the benefits of the cemetery dweller’s practice.

## 12. The Any-Bed-User’s Practice (Yathāsanthatikaṅga)

35. The any-bed-user’s practice is undertaken with one of these two statements:
“Seṇāsanaloluppaṃ paṭikkhipāmi—I refuse greed for lodgings.”
“Yathāsanthatikaṅgaṃ samādiyāmi—I undertake the any-bed-user’s practice.”
(This is the method of undertaking.)

As for the procedure: That monk who carries out the any-bed-user’s practice [Note 1: Connect with "should be satisfied"] should be satisfied with whatever lodging is assigned to him (by the person in charge), saying, “This falls to you.” He should not displace another junior monk (from a place already obtained). [Note 1: In a communal monastery, the person in charge assigns places according to seniority. If a senior monk wants a junior monk's place, the junior must move, causing distress. This practitioner stays only where assigned and does not ask for or take others' places; thus, it is said he should not displace junior monks.] This is the procedure for the monk who carries out the any-bed-user’s practice.

As for the classifications, this any-bed-user’s practice is also of three kinds. Among them, the strict practitioner (ukkaṭṭha) is not allowed to ask whether the lodging assigned to him is far or near, whether it is infested by non-human beings or snakes, etc., or whether it is hot or cold. The moderate practitioner (majjhima) is allowed to ask, but he is not allowed to go and inspect it (with greed). The mild practitioner (mudu) is allowed to go and inspect it, and if that assigned lodging is not pleasing or suitable for him (due to ill health or lack of health requirements) [Note 2: This is the meaning of the sub-commentary's addition ‘aphāsukabhāvena’. In the Pyay Visuddhimagga Nissaya, it is translated as ‘not being comfortable for attaining seclusion, etc.’ In the sub-commentary, regarding how greed arises for the mild practitioner, it should be compared with the explanation: ‘Taking another lodging when one is not sick is called greed.’], he is allowed to take another (suitable) lodging.

Furthermore, for all three types of practitioners, the practice is broken as soon as greed (loluppa) for lodgings arises. This is the breach of the any-bed-user’s practice.

The following are the benefits: (1) Following the instruction given (by the Buddha), “One should be satisfied with what is obtained”; (2) wishing for the welfare of fellow Dhamma-farers; (3) abandoning the discrimination between inferior and superior, or good and bad; (4) abandoning approval and disapproval; (5) closing the door to excessive desire; (6) living in accordance with fewness of wishes and so forth.

Note 1: For the mild practitioner, if he is not sick, rejecting an assigned lodging to take another is called greed. For the moderate practitioner, going to inspect is called greed. For the strict practitioner, inquiring is called greed. For all three types, there is no need to mention that greed occurs when displacing a junior monk from his place. (Sub-commentary)
76:
The quality of desiring the welfare of fellow monks by not asking junior monks to vacate their places [to give him a spot]. (Sub-commentary)
(5) Closing the door to the desire for a dwelling other than what one has received; (6) Having a practice consistent with fewness of wishes and so forth. These are the benefits of the Any-bed-user's Practice.

A monk who observes the Any-bed-user's Practice is content with whatever dwelling he receives, without deliberation; he dwells happily even on grass mats.

He does not lust after an excellent dwelling or bed; he is not displeased when receiving an inferior one. He looks after his fellow monks with compassion for their welfare.

Therefore, a wise monk should apply himself to the practice of being content with whatever dwelling is assigned—a practice constantly cultivated by the Noble Ones and praised by the Great Sages. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, procedure, classification, breach, and benefits of the Any-bed-user's Practice.

## 13. The Sitter's Practice (Nesajjikanga)

36. The Sitter's Practice is also undertaken with one of these two statements:
“I reject lying down.”
“I undertake the sitter's practice.”
(This is the undertaking.)

As for the procedure: The monk who observes the sitter's practice should get up and practice walking meditation for one watch out of the three watches of the night. Indeed, among the four postures, only lying down is not permitted. (The other three postures are permitted.) This is the procedure for the sitter.

By way of classification, this sitter's practice also has three grades. Among them, for the strict person, a backrest is not allowed, nor is a cloth wrap (dussapallaṭthikā), nor a binding strap (āyogapaṭṭa). For the medium person, any one of these three is allowed. For the mild person, a backrest, a cloth wrap, a binding strap, a bolster, a five-limbed chair, and a seven-limbed chair are allowed.

A “five-limbed” (pañcaṅga) chair is a chair made with a backrest. A “seven-limbed” (sattaṅga) chair is a chair made with a backrest and armrests on both sides.

It is said that such a seven-limbed chair was made for Elder Miḷābhaya. The Elder became a Non-returner (Anāgāmī) and attained Parinibbāna. (This is the classification of the sitter's practice.)

Furthermore, for all three grades, the practice is broken at the moment one lies down [with the head down] to sleep. This is the breach.

The following are the benefits: (1) Severing the mental bond mentioned as “He lives devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, the pleasure of sleep”; (2) Suitability for devotion to all meditation subjects; (3) Having an inspiring posture; (4) Favorability for the arousal of energy; (5) The development of right practice. These are the benefits of the Sitter's Practice.

Sitting cross-legged, with the body held erect, the monk makes the heart of Māra tremble.
77:
Giving up the pleasure of sleep and the pleasure of sloth, a monk who is possessed of strenuous energy and delights in sitting, beautifies the forest of asceticism (tapovana) which is the Dispensation.

He attains the joy and happiness that is free from worldly attachments (nirāmisa). Therefore, the wise yogi should devotedly practice the ascetic duty (vatta) pertaining to the sitting posture. This is the instruction.

This concludes the explanation of the undertaking, the procedure, the classification, the breach, and the benefits of the sitting-man's practice (nesajjika-dhutaṅga).

Note:
1. "Shaken off" (tuna) means making it fail to occur according to one's desire.
2. "Forest of asceticism" (tapovana)—this meaning follows the definition of the term 'tapovana'. Tapa (practice that burns away or dries up defilements) + vana (forest) = tapovana, the forest of practice that burns away defilements. This is indeed the Dispensation (Sāsana) consisting of virtue, concentration, and wisdom.

## Miscellaneous Discussion on the Ascetic Practices

37. Now:

The decision should be understood by way of the triad of the wholesome (kusalattika), by way of the division of 'dhuta' etc., and also by way of brevity and detail.

I shall explain according to the meaning of this verse.

Therein, "by way of the triad of the wholesome": (the decision should be understood thus) all ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) may be wholesome (kusala) or indeterminate (abyākata) according to the intention of learners (sekkha), worldlings (puthujjana), and those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava). It should be noted that there is no unwholesome (akusala) ascetic practice.

To clarify by raising a differing view: If someone should say, "Because of the words in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, 'One is a forest-dweller because of evil desires, being overcome by evil desires,' etc., there is also an unwholesome ascetic practice," that person should be answered thus: We do not say that one does not live in the forest with an unwholesome mind. Indeed, one who lives in the forest is a forest-dweller (āraññika). And that person living in the forest might have evil desires or fewness of wishes. However, these [practices] are the factors (aṅga) of a monk who has shaken off (dhuta) defilements through those respective undertakings. Or else, the knowledge which has acquired the name 'dhuta' because it shakes off defilements is the factor (aṅga) of these [undertakings]; thus they are 'dhutaṅga'. Alternatively, they are 'dhuta' because they shake off the opposition, and they are 'aṅga' (factors/parts) of the practice (paṭipatti); thus they are 'dhutaṅga'.

Note:
1. Refers to the dhutaṅga of worldlings and learners.
2. Refers to the dhutaṅga of Arahants.

(Continuing the etymology) These undertakings like the refuse-rag-wearer's practice are the factors (aṅga) of the monk who is 'dhuta' (one who has shaken off defilements). Thus they are called dhutaṅga.

Note:
1. This explanation shows the Tappurisa compound: dhutassa (of the one who shakes off) + aṅgāni (factors) = dhutaṅga. This is a matter for those proficient in Pali grammar.
2. This explanation shows the Bahubbīhi compound: dhutaṃ aṅgaṃ etesaṃ (those whose factor is the knowledge called 'dhuta'). This is also a matter for those proficient in Pali grammar.
3. This explanation shows the Kammadhāraya compound: dhutāni ca tāni aṅgāni ca (they are both 'dhuta' and 'aṅga').

I have already stated this. To explain further: there is no person at all who is called 'dhuta' by means of what is unwholesome (because unwholesome states do not shake off defilements).
78:
(If such a person existed, these undertakings would be the factors of that 'dhuta' person). Furthermore, what is unwholesome cannot shake off or destroy any defilement (as it is not the opposite). (If it could shake them off), that unwholesome state would be called 'dhuta' (like knowledge), and those undertakings would be called 'dhutaṅga' by way of being the factors of that unwholesome state.

Note:
This explains the Kammadhāraya compound meaning of dhutaṅga. This is a matter for those proficient in Pali grammar. Therefore, if these statements are not understood, one should consider them beyond one's scope.
1. The word 'bhaveyyuṃ' (might be) is used in the Pali instead of 'honti' (are), so it is translated accordingly. If translated starting from the indefinite clause: "These volitions of undertaking would be the factors of whichever person is called 'dhuta'; but there is no such person called 'dhuta' by means of what is unwholesome." This means unwholesome states do not make one 'dhuta', and thus cannot be dhutaṅga.

They would be called dhutaṅga (if unwholesome states could shake off defilements). Furthermore, unwholesome states do not shake off greed for robes (loluppa-taṇhā) and so on, nor are they factors (parts) of the practice (paṭipatti) such as virtue. Therefore, the statement "There is no unwholesome ascetic practice" is well-considered and correct.

Note:
1. If the indefinite clause is translated first: "That unwholesome state would be called 'dhuta' as the preceding cause that shakes off defilements for these volitions of undertaking, and thus those volitions would be called dhutaṅga. However, unwholesome states do not shake off anything."
2. Since unwholesome states do not shake off defilements like greed for robes, they are not 'dhuta'; and since they are not factors of practice like virtue, they are not 'aṅga'. Thus, they cannot be 'dhutaṅga'.

[78] Even in the view of the teachers residing at Abhayagiri (who say that dhutaṅga is merely a designation), the ascetic practice is exempt from the triad of the wholesome; in their view, in the ultimate sense (paramattha), the ascetic practice itself does not exist. How can a designation that does not exist in the ultimate sense be called 'dhutaṅga' because it shakes off defilements? Moreover, their view incurs the fault of contradicting the Pāḷi text: "He practices having undertaken the qualities of shaking off (dhuta-guṇa)." Therefore, the words of those Abhayagiri dwellers should not be accepted. This is the explanation by way of the triad of the wholesome.

In the phrase "by way of the division of dhuta etc.": 'dhuta' should be understood; 'dhutavāda' (one who speaks of shaking off) should be understood; 'dhutadhamma' (the states of shaking off) should be understood; 'dhutaṅga' (the ascetic factors) should be understood; and the answer to the question "For whom is the resort to ascetic practices suitable?" should be understood.

Therein, 'dhuta' is either a person who has shaken off defilements or a state (dhamma) that shakes off defilements.

As for 'dhutavāda': here, there is one who is 'dhuta' but not 'dhutavāda'; there is one who is not 'dhuta' but is 'dhutavāda'; there is one who is neither 'dhuta' nor 'dhutavāda'; and there is one who is both 'dhuta' and 'dhutavāda'.

Therein, one who has shaken off his own defilements through ascetic practices but does not advise or instruct others in ascetic practices, like the Elder Bākula—this one is 'dhuta' but not 'dhutavāda'. As it is said: "Thus this Venerable Bākula is dhuta but not dhutavāda." One who has not shaken off his own defilements through ascetic practices but merely advises and instructs others in ascetic practices, like the Elder Upananda—this one is not 'dhuta' but is 'dhutavāda'. As it is said: "Thus this Venerable Upananda, the son of the Sakyans, is not dhuta but is dhutavāda." One who is deficient in both, like Lāḷudāyī—this one is neither 'dhuta' nor 'dhutavāda'. As it is said: "Thus this Venerable Lāḷudāyī is neither dhuta nor dhutavāda." One who is perfect in both, like the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta)—this one is both 'dhuta' and 'dhutavāda'. As it is said: "Thus this Venerable Sāriputta is both dhuta and dhutavāda."

'Dhutadhamma' should be understood: These five states that surround the volition of the ascetic practices—fewness of wishes (appicchatā), contentment (santuṭṭhitā), effacement (sallekhatā), seclusion (pavivekatā), and specific worthiness (idamaṭṭhitā)—are called 'dhutadhamma' because of the words "depending on fewness of wishes itself," etc. Among them, fewness of wishes and contentment are non-greed (alobha). Effacement and seclusion fall within two states: non-greed and non-delusion (amoha). Specific worthiness (idamaṭṭhitā) is knowledge (ñāṇa) itself.
79:
In this context, 'dhuta' refers to either a person who has shaken off and destroyed the defilements [1], or the qualities (dhamma) that shake off and destroy the defilements [2].

Note:
1. All Arahants have already shaken off and destroyed the defilements and are thus called 'dhuta'. However, in this context, it refers to an Arahant who, having prioritized the practice of asceticism (dhutaṅga), remains after having shaken off and destroyed the defilements (dhuta-kilesa). (Ṭīkā)
2. All Noble Paths (ariya-magga) are essentially the qualities that shake off and destroy the defilements. Specifically, the Path of Arahantship is the quality that shakes off and destroys the defilements. In a figurative sense (upacāra-pariyāya), insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and so forth are also called qualities that shake off and destroy the defilements. At the minimum level, the knowledge (ñāṇa) associated with the volition of ascetic practice (dhutaṅga-cetanā) should be understood as the 'quality that shakes off and destroys the defilements'. (Ṭīkā)

Regarding the term 'dhutavāda' (one who preaches the ascetic practices), there is a person who is 'dhuta' but not 'dhutavāda'; there is a person who is not 'dhuta' but is 'dhutavāda'; there is a person who is neither 'dhuta' nor 'dhutavāda'; and there is a person who is both 'dhuta' and 'dhutavāda'.

Among these four, a person who has shaken off his own defilements through ascetic practices but does not admonish or instruct others in them is like the Elder Bākula. This person is called 'dhuta' only, not 'dhutavāda'. This is in accordance with the statement: "That Elder Bākula shook off defilements himself but did not admonish or preach to others regarding the ascetic practices."

A person who has not shaken off or destroyed his own defilements through ascetic practices but merely admonishes and instructs others in them is like the Elder Upananda. This person is not called 'dhuta' but is called 'dhutavāda'. This is in accordance with the statement: "That Elder Upananda, the son of the Sakyans, did not shake off defilements himself but admonished and preached to others regarding the ascetic practices."

A person who is deficient in both aspects, like the Elder Lāḷudāyī, is neither 'dhuta' nor 'dhutavāda'. This is in accordance with the statement: "That Elder Lāḷudāyī could not shake off defilements himself and did not admonish or preach to others regarding the ascetic practices."

A person who is endowed with both aspects, like the General of the Dhamma, the Elder Sāriputta, is both 'dhuta' and 'dhutavāda'. This is in accordance with the statement: "That Elder Sāriputta could shake off defilements himself and also admonished and preached to others regarding the ascetic practices."

Regarding the phrase "the dhuta-dhammas should be known," there are five qualities that are the attendants of the volition for ascetic practice: (1) fewness of wishes (appicchatā), (2) contentment (santuṭṭhitā), (3) effacement (sallekhatā), (4) seclusion (pavivekatā), and (5) the state of desiring [the practice] through this wholesome ascetic quality. These are called 'dhuta-dhammas' (qualities that shake off defilements) because they are taught starting with the phrase "relying only on fewness of wishes." Among these five, fewness of wishes and contentment are essentially non-greed (alobha). Effacement and seclusion fall under these two qualities: non-greed and non-delusion (amoha). The state of desiring [the practice] through this wholesome ascetic quality is simply knowledge (ñāṇa).

Among those qualities of non-greed and non-delusion: Through non-greed, one shakes off greed for objects such as robes donated by laypeople, which are rejected [by the respective ascetic practices]. Through non-delusion, one shakes off the delusion that conceals the faults (such as the suffering of maintenance, dependence on others, and the danger of thieves) in those very same rejected objects. Alternatively, through non-greed, one shakes off the pursuit of sensual happiness (kāmasukhallikānuyoga) that arises from the use of objects (such as soft rugs and blankets) permitted [by the Buddha] for use without craving. Through non-delusion, one shakes off the pursuit of self-mortification (attakilamathānuyoga) that arises from the practice of extreme effacement in the ascetic practices. Therefore, these aforementioned qualities (fewness of wishes, etc.) should be known as 'dhuta-dhammas'.

Regarding the phrase "the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) should be known," the thirteen ascetic practices should be known, starting from (1) the refuse-rag-robe wearer's practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga) ... to (13) the sitter's practice (nesajjikaṅga). These have already been explained in terms of meaning and characteristics.

Regarding the question "For whom is the practice of asceticism suitable?", it is suitable for those of greedy temperament (rāgacarita) and those of deluded temperament (mohacarita). Why? Because the practice of asceticism is both a painful progress (dukkhā paṭipadā) and a living in effacement (sallekha-vihāra). Relying on the painful progress, greed is subsided. Relying on the living in effacement, delusion is abandoned for one who is diligent.
80:
Alternatively, among these thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), the practice of the forest-dweller (āraññakaṅga) and the tree-root-dweller (rukkhamūlikaṅga) are suitable for a person of a hateful temperament. Indeed, for one who lives in the forest or at the root of a tree without being disturbed by others, anger is appeased. This concludes the explanation by way of classifying the ascetic practices.

Regarding the brief and detailed classification: in brief, there are only eight ascetic practices, consisting of three principal factors and five separate factors. Among them, the house-to-house seeker's practice (sapadānacārikaṅga), the one-sessioner's practice (ekāsanikaṅga), and the open-air-dweller's practice (abbhokāsikaṅga) are the principal factors. Indeed, if the house-to-house seeker's practice is maintained, the alms-food-eater's practice (piṇḍapātikaṅga) will also be maintained. Furthermore, one who maintains the one-sessioner's practice can easily maintain the bowl-food-eater's practice (pattapiṇḍikaṅga) and the later-food-refuser's practice (khalupacchābhattikaṅga). For one who maintains the open-air-dweller's practice, there is no further duty to maintain the tree-root-dweller's practice or the any-bed-user's practice (yathāsanthatikaṅga). Therefore, these three are called principal factors. Moreover, the forest-dweller's practice, the refuse-rag-wearer's practice (paṃsukūlikaṅga), the triple-robe-wearer's practice (tecīvarikaṅga), the sitter's practice (nesajjikaṅga), and the charnel-ground-dweller's practice (sosānikaṅga) are the five separate ascetic practices. Thus, there are only eight.

Again, they are fourfold: two practices connected with robes, five practices connected with alms-food, five practices connected with lodging, and one practice connected with energy. Among these four, the practice connected with energy is the sitter's practice. The other three categories are well-known.

Again, all ascetic practices are twofold by way of support: twelve practices depending on requisites and one practice depending on energy. They are also twofold by way of being practiced or not practiced. Indeed, if a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) increases when one practices an ascetic practice, that person should practice it. If the meditation subject decreases when practiced, that person should not practice it. If the meditation subject increases whether one practices it or not, and does not decrease, that person should also practice it for the sake of benefiting future generations. [80] Even for one whose meditation subject does not increase whether practicing or not, that person should still practice it for the sake of establishing a good habit and tendency for the future.

Although there are two kinds by way of being practiced or not practiced as mentioned, all are of one kind by way of volition (cetanā). Indeed, the ascetic practice is the single volition of undertaking. In the ancient Commentaries, it is also said: "The volition which is the undertaking, that they call the ascetic practice."

In detail, there are forty-two: thirteen for monks (bhikkhus), eight for nuns (bhikkhunīs), twelve for novices (sāmaṇeras), seven for female probationers (sikkhamānās) and female novices (sāmaṇerīs), and two for laymen (upāsakas) and laywomen (upāsikās). To explain: if there is a charnel ground in an open-air area endowed with the qualities of a forest, a single monk can practice all ascetic practices at once. For bhikkhunīs, however, the two practices of forest-dwelling and later-food-refusing are prohibited by the training rules themselves. The three practices of open-air-dwelling, tree-root-dwelling, and charnel-ground-dwelling are difficult for bhikkhunīs to maintain. Indeed, it is not proper for a bhikkhunī to live without a companion. In such places, it is difficult to find a companion with the same desire. Even if one is found, she would not be free from living in association. In that case, the very purpose of seclusion for which one would practice the ascetic practice would not be fulfilled. Because they are thus difficult to maintain, five practices are omitted, and it should be understood that there are only eight for bhikkhunīs. Apart from those mentioned, excluding the triple-robe-wearer's practice, the remaining

Note:
1. The forest-dweller's practice is prohibited by the Ohīyana training rule regarding staying behind from the group.
81:
the later-food-refuser's practice is prohibited for bhikkhunīs by the fourth Pavārita training rule in the Ārāma-vagga of the Bhikkhunī Pācittiya.
(In the Ṭīkā manuscript, it says 'by the Anatirittabhojana training rule'. That reading does not seem appropriate.)
2. For a bhikkhunī, although there are five robes including the vest and the bathing cloth, they are counted only as the 'triple robes' (tecīvarika); thus, it is considered that there are only eight practices (including the triple-robe practice). (Ṭīkā)

Twelve ascetic practices should be known as pertaining to novices (sāmaṇeras). Seven ascetic practices should be known as pertaining to female probationers (sikkhamānās) and female novices (sāmaṇerīs). For laymen (upāsakas) and laywomen (upāsikās), these two practices—the one-sessioner's and the bowl-food-eater's—are both suitable and possible to practice. Thus, in detail, there are forty-two. This is the explanation by way of brief and detail.

By this much, in this Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) taught by way of virtue, concentration, and wisdom in the verse "A man of wisdom, established in virtue," the purification of virtue of the kind described is accomplished through such qualities as fewness of wishes and contentment. The discourse on the ascetic practices to be undertaken for the sake of fulfilling those qualities has been concluded.

This concludes the Second Chapter, the Description of Ascetic Practices (Dhutaṅga-niddesa), in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.
