## 3. Kammaṭṭhānaggahana-niddesa
## Detailed Description of Taking a Meditation Subject

[81] 38. Now, when a monk is established in this virtue which is purified on all sides by such qualities as fewness of wishes, etc., which have been fulfilled by maintaining the ascetic practices (as shown in the description of ascetic practices), he should develop concentration, which is indicated by the heading of 'mind' (citta) in the teaching: "A man of wisdom, established in virtue, developing the mind and wisdom." Since that concentration was taught very briefly, it is not even easy to understand, let alone to develop. Therefore, in order to show its details and the method of its development, the following set of questions is presented:

## Explanation of the Nature of Concentration, etc.

(a) What is concentration?
(b) In what sense is it called concentration?
Note:
1. Connect 'Now' with 'the following set of questions is presented'.
2. Connect 'a monk' with 'should develop concentration'.
3. This refers to the two reasons: the necessity to develop concentration and the difficulty of developing it.

(c) What are its characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?
(d) How many kinds of concentration are there?
(e) What is its defilement?
(f) What is its purification?
(g) How should it be developed?
(h) What are the benefits of developing concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā)?

The answers to these questions are as follows:

(a) To the question "What is concentration?": Concentration is of many kinds and various aspects (such as wholesome concentration, etc., and by way of various objects).

If one were to attempt to show all those variations, the explanation would not achieve the desired purpose and would lead to further distraction. Therefore, we shall speak only of the concentration intended in this context: wholesome one-pointedness of mind (kusalacittekaggatā) is concentration.

(b) In what sense is it called concentration? It is concentration in the sense of concentrating (samādhāna). What is this 'concentrating'? It is the placing (ādhāna) of the mind and its mental factors evenly (samaṃ) and rightly (sammā) on a single object. Therefore, it should be understood that 'concentrating' is that state by the power of which the mind and mental factors remain on a single object evenly and rightly, without being distracted or scattered.

(c) Regarding its characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause: Here, concentration has non-distraction (avikkhepa) as its characteristic. Its function (rasa) is the destroying of distraction. It is manifested (paccupaṭṭhāna) as non-wavering. Because of the statement "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," happiness (sukha) is its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna).

39. (d) How many kinds of concentration are there? First, it is of one kind by way of the characteristic of non-distraction. It is of two kinds by way of access (upacāra) and absorption (appanā); likewise, by way of mundane and supramundane, by way of with-rapture and without-rapture, and by way of being accompanied by happiness and accompanied by equanimity. It is of three kinds...
82:
(b) To the question "In what sense is it concentration (samādhi)?"... It is called concentration in the sense of placing well (samādhāna). What is this "placing well"? It is the placing of the mind and mental factors evenly and rightly on a single object (so that they are not scattered or dispersed). It is the placing well (so that they do not wander or run away). "Placing" here means to cause them to stand still. Therefore, by the power of which state (samādhi) the mind and mental factors do not scatter but stand evenly and rightly on a single object, and do not wander but stand well (calmly)—this state should be understood as "placing well" (samādhāna).

(c) To the question "What are its characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause?"... Concentration has non-distraction as its characteristic. Its function is to eliminate distraction. It is manifested as non-wavering (in the meditator's knowledge). Because it is said, "The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated," happiness (sukha) is its proximate cause.

## Classification of Concentration

(d) To the question "How many kinds of concentration are there?"... Concentration is of one kind by way of its characteristic of non-distraction.

It is of two kinds as access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Similarly, as mundane concentration and supramundane concentration; as concentration with zest (sappītika) and concentration without zest (nippītika); as concentration accompanied by happiness (sukhasahagata) and concentration accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata).

It is of three kinds as inferior concentration (hīna), medium concentration (majjhima), and superior concentration (paṇīta). Similarly, as concentration with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra), etc.; as concentration accompanied by zest, etc.; and as limited concentration (paritta), great concentration (mahaggata), and immeasurable concentration (appamāṇa).

It is of four kinds as painful practice with slow intuition (dukkhapaṭipadā-dandhābhiññā), etc. Similarly, as limited concentration with a limited object, etc.; by way of the factors of the four jhānas; as diminishing concentration (hānabhāgiya), etc.; as sense-sphere concentration (kāmāvacara), etc.; and by way of the four predominants (adhipati).

It is of five kinds by way of the factors of the five jhānas in the fivefold method.

## Explanation of Onefold and Twofold Concentration

Among these, the onefold part has a clear meaning. In the twofold part, the concentration obtained by way of the ten meditation subjects—namely, the six recollections (recollection of the Buddha, Dhamma, Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and deities), mindfulness of death, recollection of peace, the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, and the definition of the four elements—and the concentration in the preliminary stage of absorption concentrations, is called access concentration (upacāra-samādhi).1 Because it is said, "The preliminary work (parikamma) of the first jhāna is a condition for the first jhāna by way of proximity-condition (anantara-paccaya)," the concentration that occurs immediately after the preliminary work (gotrabhū) is called absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Thus, it is of two kinds as access and absorption.

In the second dyad, the unification of the wholesome mind in the three planes (sense, fine-material, and immaterial) is mundane concentration. The unification associated with the Noble Path is supramundane concentration. Thus, it is of two kinds as mundane and supramundane.

In the third dyad, in the fourfold method, the unification in the first two jhānas, and in the fivefold method, the unification in the first three jhānas, is concentration with zest (sappītika). The unification in the remaining two jhānas is concentration without zest (nippītika). Access concentration, however, may be with zest or without zest. Thus, it is of two kinds as with zest and without zest.

Note: 1. Upacāra-samādhi = concentration occurring in the vicinity of absorption. Although the concentration in the 10 subjects from recollection of the Buddha to the definition of elements does not occur in the immediate vicinity of absorption, it is called access concentration because it is similar to it in terms of abandoning the hindrances (nīvaraṇa).
83:
(If evidence is needed, see Mahāṭီkā I, 436). Alternatively, while developing the recollection of the Buddha, etc., one can contemplate the zest, etc., that arises with insight (vipassanā) and reach the absorption concentration of the Noble Path. In that case, it can be said to occur in the vicinity of the absorption of the Path. Therefore, it should also be called access concentration.

In the fourth dyad, in the fourfold method, the unification in the first three jhānas, and in the fivefold method, the unification in the first four jhānas, is concentration accompanied by happiness (sukhasahagata). The unification in the remaining jhāna is concentration accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata). Access concentration, however, may be accompanied by happiness or accompanied by equanimity. Thus, it is of two kinds as accompanied by happiness and accompanied by equanimity.

## Explanation of Threefold Concentration

Among the triads, in the first triad, concentration that is merely obtained is inferior (hīna). Concentration that is not yet fully developed is medium (majjhima). Concentration that is well-developed and has reached mastery is superior (paṇīta). Thus, it is of three kinds as inferior, medium, and superior.

In the second triad, the first jhāna concentration together with access concentration is concentration with initial and sustained thought (savitakka-savicāra). In the fivefold method, the second jhāna concentration is concentration without initial thought and with only sustained thought (avitakka-vicāramatta). Indeed, when a person, seeing the disadvantage in initial thought alone and not seeing it in sustained thought, desires only the abandoning of initial thought and transcends the first jhāna, he obtains concentration without initial thought and with only sustained thought. It is with reference to such concentration that this statement is made. In the fourfold method, the unification in the three jhānas starting from the second, and in the fivefold method, the unification in the three jhānas starting from the third, is concentration without initial and sustained thought (avitakka-avicāra). Thus, it is of three kinds as with initial and sustained thought, etc.

In the third triad, in the fourfold method, the unification in the first two jhānas, and in the fivefold method, the unification in the first three jhānas, is concentration accompanied by zest (pītisahagata). In those same methods, the unification in the third jhāna (fourfold) and the fourth jhāna (fivefold) is concentration accompanied by happiness (sukhasahagata). In the final jhāna, it is concentration accompanied by equanimity (upekkhāsahagata). Access concentration, however, is either accompanied by zest and happiness or accompanied by equanimity. Thus, it is of three kinds as accompanied by zest, etc.

In the fourth triad, the unification on the plane of access is limited (paritta) concentration.1 The unification in the fine-material and immaterial wholesome states is great (mahaggata) concentration.2 The unification associated with the Noble Path is immeasurable (appamāṇa) concentration.3 Thus, it is of three kinds as limited, great, and immeasurable.

Note: 1. Paritta = small/limited due to having little power. 2. Mahaggata = reached greatness/exalted. 3. Appamāṇa = immeasurable/highly exalted.

## Explanation of Fourfold Concentration

Among the tetrads, in the first tetrad, there is concentration that is painful practice with slow intuition (dukkhapaṭipadā-dandhābhiññā). There is concentration that is painful practice with quick intuition (dukkhapaṭipadā-khippābhiññā). There is concentration that is pleasant practice with slow intuition (sukhapaṭipadā-dandhābhiññā). There is concentration that is pleasant practice with quick intuition (sukhapaṭipadā-khippābhiññā).

Therein, the development of concentration that occurs from the first attention until the access of each jhāna arises is called "practice" (paṭipadā). The wisdom that occurs from access until absorption is called "intuition" (abhiññā). That practice is painful for some because it is difficult and unpleasant to cultivate due to the frequent occurrence of opposing states such as the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). This is the meaning of the word "painful" (dukkha). For others, it is pleasant (easy) because of the absence of such difficulties. Intuition is also slow for some, being sluggish and not occurring rapidly.
84:
...is sluggish; it does not occur quickly. For some individuals, it is swift; it is not sluggish, occurring quickly.

Note: The words within these quotation marks are explanations of the preceding word 'painful' (dukkha). Therefore, it continues to point out 'this is...' and so forth.

Among those (modes of progress and direct knowledge), regarding the suitable and unsuitable factors to be explained later, the preliminary duties such as cutting off impediments (palibodha), and the skill in absorption (appanā-kosalla): [84] for one who resorts to what is unsuitable, there is painful progress (dukkha-paṭipadā) and sluggish direct knowledge (dandhābhiññā). For one who resorts to what is suitable, there is pleasant progress (sukha-paṭipadā) and swift direct knowledge (khippābhiññā). For one who resorts to what is unsuitable in the initial stage (before attaining access concentration) and resorts to what is suitable in the later stage (after attaining access concentration), or resorts to what is suitable in the initial stage and resorts to what is unsuitable in the later stage, the state of being mixed (vomiassakata) should be understood. Furthermore, for one who applies himself to meditation without having performed the preliminary duties such as cutting off impediments, there is painful progress. Conversely, there is pleasant progress. For one who is not accomplished in skill in absorption, there is sluggish direct knowledge. For one who is accomplished in them, there is swift direct knowledge.

Alternatively, the distinction between these modes of progress and direct knowledge should be understood by way of craving (taṇhā) and ignorance (avijjā), and by way of previous practice (adhikāra) in serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā).

Note: 'Among those (modes of progress and direct knowledge)... there is painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge'—connect it in this manner.

To explain in detail: for one overcome by craving, there is painful progress; for one not overcome, there is pleasant progress. For one overcome by ignorance, there is sluggish direct knowledge; for one not overcome, there is swift direct knowledge. Furthermore, for one who has not performed previous practice in serenity, there is painful progress. For one who has performed previous practice, there is pleasant progress. For one who has not performed previous practice in insight, there is sluggish direct knowledge. For one who has performed previous practice, there is swift direct knowledge.

Moreover, the distinction between these modes of progress and direct knowledge should also be understood by way of defilements (kilesa) and faculties (indriya). To explain in detail: for one with intense defilements and weak faculties, there is painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge; but for one with sharp faculties, there is swift direct knowledge. For one with mild defilements and weak faculties, there is pleasant progress and sluggish direct knowledge; but for one with sharp faculties, there is swift direct knowledge.

Among these aforementioned modes of progress and direct knowledge, when an individual reaches absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) through painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge, that person's concentration is called 'concentration of painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge.' This same method applies to the remaining three types of concentration. Thus, there are four types by way of painful progress and sluggish direct knowledge, etc.

In the second tetrad, there is limited concentration with a limited object (paritta parittārammaṇa), limited concentration with an immeasurable object (paritta appamāṇārammaṇa), immeasurable concentration with a limited object (appamāṇa parittārammaṇa), and immeasurable concentration with an immeasurable object (appamāṇa appamāṇārammaṇa). Thus, there are four types. Therein, the concentration that is not proficient and cannot serve as a condition for a higher jhāna is called 'limited' (paritta) concentration. The concentration that occurs with respect to an object that has not been expanded is called 'concentration with a limited object' (parittārammaṇa). The concentration that is well-developed and proficient, being able to serve as a condition for a higher jhāna, is called 'immeasurable' (appamāṇa) concentration. The concentration that occurs with respect to an expanded object is called 'concentration with an immeasurable object' (appamāṇārammaṇa). The mixed method (such as limited concentration with an immeasurable object, etc.) should be understood by the mixing of the aforementioned characteristics. Thus, there are four types by way of limited concentration with a limited object, etc.

Note: 'One who has not performed previous practice' refers to one who has not practiced in a previous life. Just as a text that was thoroughly mastered but then set aside can be well-recalled with only a little effort, similarly, the meditation of one who has practiced in a previous life is accomplished easily and without hardship. Therefore, it is said that for one who has performed previous practice, there is pleasant progress. (Commentary)
85:
[85] In the third tetrad, there is the first jhāna with five factors by way of initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), happiness (sukha), and concentration (samādhi) for those who have suppressed the hindrances. From that (higher up), there is the second jhāna with three factors (zest, happiness, and concentration) as initial and sustained application have subsided. From that (higher up), there is the third jhāna with two factors (happiness and concentration) as zest has faded. From that (higher up), there is the fourth jhāna with two factors by way of concentration accompanied by equanimous feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) as happiness has been abandoned. Thus, the concentrations that are factors of these four jhānas are four. In this way, there are four types by way of the factors of the four jhānas.

In the fourth tetrad, there is concentration partaking in diminution (hānabhāgiya), concentration partaking in stagnation (ṭhitibhāgiya), concentration partaking in distinction (visesabhāgiya), and concentration partaking in penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya). Among these, the state of partaking in diminution should be understood by way of the occurrence of opposing states. The state of partaking in stagnation should be understood by way of the persistence of mindfulness that is appropriate to that attained jhāna. [Note 1]

[Note 1: Regarding 'by way of the persistence of mindfulness,' the Sammohavinodanī Commentary states that this mindfulness is indeed 'wrong mindfulness' (micchā-sati), which is either the craving called delight (nikanti) in that attained jhāna or the mental aggregates associated with that craving. For a person who has a lingering attachment to that attained jhāna, since they are unable to produce a higher distinction because they are not free from delight and attachment, it is also appropriate to call it mindfulness that carries that particular jhāna. Therefore, regarding the word of the Commentary which definitely says 'of mindfulness,' the twofold explanation 'either of mindfulness or of attachment (nikanti)' is also suitable (Mahāṭīkā). The author of the Mūlaṭīkā on the Sammohavinodanī states that 'wrong mindfulness' refers to either attachment (nikanti) or the mental states (cittuppāda) occurring together with attachment.]

The state of partaking in distinction should be understood by way of the ability to attain a higher distinction. The state of partaking in penetration should be understood by way of the occurrence of perception and mental advertence accompanied by the wisdom of revulsion (nibbidā). As it is said:

'If perceptions and mental advertence accompanied by sensuality occur to a person who has attained the first jhāna, his wisdom partakes in diminution. If mindfulness appropriate to that (first jhāna) persists, his wisdom partakes in stagnation. If perceptions and mental advertence accompanied by the absence of initial application occur, his wisdom partakes in distinction. If perceptions and mental advertence accompanied by revulsion occur, his wisdom, being connected with dispassion, partakes in penetration.'

The concentrations associated with these four types of wisdom are also four. In this way, there are four types by way of concentration partaking in diminution, etc.

In the fifth tetrad, there are four types of concentration: sense-sphere concentration (kāmāvacara-samādhi), fine-material-sphere concentration (rūpāvacara-samādhi), immaterial-sphere concentration (arūpāvacara-samādhi), and the unincluded (apariyāpanna) concentration. Among these, all access one-pointedness (upacāra-ekaggatā) is called sense-sphere concentration. Similarly, the one-pointedness associated with fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousness, etc., are the other three types of concentration. In this way, there are four types by way of sense-sphere concentration, etc.

In the sixth tetrad, 'If a bhikkhu, having made desire (chanda) the predominant factor, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind, this is called concentration of desire... etc... If a bhikkhu, having made energy (viriya)... etc... If a bhikkhu, having made consciousness (citta)... etc... If a bhikkhu, having made investigation (vīmaṃsā) the predominant factor, attains concentration, attains one-pointedness of mind, this is called concentration of investigation.' In this way, there are four types by way of the four predominant factors (adhipati).

## Explanation of the Fivefold Concentration

[86] In the fivefold system (the group of five types of concentration), regarding the division of the fourfold system previously mentioned, the second jhāna is split into two: one as the second jhāna by surmounting only initial application (*vitakka*), and another as the third jhāna by surmounting both initial application and sustained application (*vicāra*). Thus, the five jhānas should be understood. The concentrations that are factors of these five jhānas are also five. In this way, concentration is of five kinds by way of the factors of the five jhānas.

Note: In the explanation of the fourfold concentration according to the third catukka, the second jhāna was shown as having three factors: rapture (*pīti*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), being free from both initial and sustained application. If that jhāna is divided into two—one as the second jhāna having four factors (sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness) by surmounting only initial application, and another as the third jhāna having three factors (rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness) by surmounting sustained application—then the third and fourth jhānas mentioned in the fourfold system become the fourth and fifth jhānas in this system. Thus, there are five jhānas.

40. (e-f) To the questions "What is its defilement? What is its purification?", the answer has already been given in the *Vibhaṅga*. For it is said there: "Defilement is the state partaking of diminution (*hānabhāgiya*). Purification is the state partaking of distinction (*visesabhāgiya*)." (Vibh. 828). In that context, the state partaking of diminution should be understood by the method beginning with: "If perceptions and intentions accompanied by sense-desire occur to one who has attained the first jhāna, his wisdom is partaking of diminution." (Vibh. 799). The state partaking of distinction should be understood by the method beginning with: "If perceptions and intentions accompanied by the absence of initial application (*avitakka*) occur, his wisdom is partaking of distinction." (Vibh. 799).

## Explanation of the Ten Impediments

41. (g) Regarding the question "How should it be developed?", among the divisions of concentration previously mentioned as being of two kinds—mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*)—the concentration associated with the Noble Path (*ariya-magga*) has its method of development included within the method of the development of wisdom. For when wisdom is developed, that concentration is also developed. Therefore, we shall say nothing separately about how it should be developed with reference to that Path concentration.

As for mundane concentration, one should first purify one's virtue according to the method described (in the *Sīlaniddesa*). Standing on well-purified virtue, if there is any of the ten impediments (*palibodha*), one should sever it. Then, one should approach a noble friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) who gives a meditation subject and take one of the forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) that is suitable to one's temperament (*carita*). After giving up a dwelling unsuitable for the development of concentration and residing in a suitable one, one should also sever minor impediments and develop it without neglecting any part of the meditation procedure. This is the summary here.

Note: The phrase "As for mundane concentration..." should be connected with "...should be developed without neglecting."

The following is the detailed explanation. In the words previously mentioned, "if there is any of the ten impediments, one should sever it":

Dwelling, family, gain, group, and work as the fifth,
Travel, kin, affliction, books, and psychic power—these are the ten.

[87] These ten are called impediments (*palibodha*). Among them, the dwelling itself is the impediment of dwelling (*āvāsa-palibodha*). The same method applies to family and so on.

## (1) The Impediment of Dwelling

(Regarding the statement "the dwelling itself is the impediment of dwelling"): In this context, a single room, a single precinct, or an entire monastery (*ārāma*) is called a dwelling. That dwelling is not an impediment for every yogi. It is an impediment only for those who are anxious about duties and work in the dwelling, or who have a mind of attachment because they have stored many possessions (such as alms-bowls and robes) for some reason. It is not an impediment for others.
87:
Regarding the phrase "for some reason"—it refers to reasons such as being endowed with shade, shelter, and water, or the ease of obtaining alms-food, and so forth (according to the Ṭīkā).

In the context of where there is no such impediment, the following story should be noted. Two sons of good family left the city of Anurādhapura and, traveling in due course,¹ were ordained at the Thūpārāma Monastery. Among those two monks, one mastered the two Mātikās (Codes of Discipline) and, upon reaching five years of seniority (Vassa), performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony and departed for a place called Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji.² The other monk remained at that very Thūpārāma Monastery. The monk who went to Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji lived there for a long time, and when he attained the status of an Elder (Thera),³ he thought: "This place is suitable for seclusion; indeed, I shall inform my friend about it." Having thought thus, he set out from that place and, traveling in due course, entered the Thūpārāma Monastery. Even as he was entering, the resident Elder of equal seniority saw him, went out to meet him, took his bowl and robes, and performed the duties. The visiting Elder entered the lodging and thought: "Now my friend will send ghee, or molasses, or a drink. For he has been a long-time resident in this city."

Notes:
1. Anupubbena—this term indicates that after leaving the city, one must travel a certain distance to reach the Thūpārāma Monastery.
2. Pācīna (East) + Khaṇḍa (Broken) + Rāji (Line/Range) = Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji: The broken forest range or mountain range of the East.
3. Thero hutvā—literally "having become an Elder"; translated as "when he attained the status of an Elder" for the smoothness of the sentence.

When the visiting Elder did not receive anything during the night as expected, he thought in the morning: "Now he will send the gruel and snacks brought by his supporters." Not seeing that gruel and snacks either, he thought: "There are no donors to send them. I suppose he will give them when we enter the village for alms." Thinking thus, he entered the village with the resident Elder early in the morning. While those two monks were wandering for alms along a street, they received only a ladleful of gruel, and having sat in the refectory, they drank it. Then the visiting Elder thought: "It seems there is no regular provision of gruel; now at mealtime, people will surely give choice alms-food." Later, at mealtime as well, they wandered for alms and ate only what they had received. Then the visiting Elder asked the resident Elder,¹ "Venerable sir, do you always subsist in this way?"

Notes:
1. In the Pali texts of the Visuddhimagga, the reading "itaro āha" is inappropriate. The reason is that the previous sentence stated "āgantuko cintesi" (the visitor thought). If this sentence says "itaro" (the other), it would mean the resident Elder spoke. In truth, it is the visiting Elder who asks the resident Elder. Therefore, the reading should be "itaramāha" (spoke to the other); based on this preferred reading, it is translated here as "asked the resident Elder."

"Yes, friend," the resident Elder replied. "Venerable sir, Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji is pleasant; let us go there," the visiting Elder suggested. The resident Elder left the city by the south gate and took the road toward the potters' village. The visiting Elder asked, "Venerable sir, why have you taken this road?" The resident Elder replied, "Friend, did you not speak in praise of Pācīnakhaṇḍarāji?" The visiting Elder then asked, "Venerable sir, do you have no extra requisites in the place where you have lived for so long?" The resident Elder said, "No, friend. The bed and chair belong to the Saṅgha; they have already been put away. There is nothing else."

The visiting Elder then said, "[88] Venerable sir, my walking staff, oil tube, and sandal bag are still at that Thūpārāma monastery." The resident Elder, in surprise, said, "Friend, you stayed for only a single day and yet you have left behind so many things!" "Yes, venerable sir," the visiting Elder admitted. With a heart full of faith, he prostrated to the resident Elder and said: "Venerable sir, for persons like you, living anywhere is truly living in the forest. The Thūpārāma Cetiya is the place where the personal relics and bodily relics of four Buddhas are enshrined. One also gets to hear suitable Dhamma at the Brazen Palace (Lohapāsāda), behold the Mahācetiya, and see the Elders. It is as if the Buddha were still alive. May you, venerable sirs, continue to reside right here." Having said this, he took his bowl and robes the next day and departed alone.
88:
This is the story. For a person such as this resident elder, the dwelling is not an impediment. (The discussion on the impediment of dwelling is concluded).

## (2) The Impediment of Families (Kula-palibodha)
'Family' (kula) refers to either a family of relatives or a family of supporters. Indeed, for a certain monk who lives in close association with them, in such a way as 'he is happy when they are happy' and so on, even a family of supporters becomes an impediment. Such a monk cannot even go to a nearby monastery to hear the Dhamma without his lay supporters. However, for some monks, even parents are not an impediment, as in the case of the young monk who was the nephew of the elder residing at Koraṇḍaka Monastery.

That young monk, it is said, went to the Rohaṇa region to study the Pali texts. The elder’s sister, a lay devotee (upāsikā), always asked the elder for news of him. One day, the elder set out for Rohaṇa, thinking, 'I will bring the young monk back.' The young monk also set out from Rohaṇa, thinking, 'I have lived here for a long time; now I will go to see my preceptor, find out news of the lay devotee, my mother, and then return.' Both of them met on the bank of the river Gaṅgā [Note 1]. The young monk performed his duties to the elder at the foot of a tree [Note 2]. When asked, 'Where are you going?', he explained the reason for his journey. The elder said, 'You have done well. The lay devotee always asks about you. I also came for this very purpose. You go on; I will spend the rains retreat right here,' and he sent the young monk away. The young monk arrived at that Koraṇḍaka Monastery on the very day of entering the rains retreat. It so happened that the dwelling he received was the one built by his father.

Then, his father, the lay devotee (upāsaka), came to the monastery the next day and asked, 'Venerable sirs, to which monk has our dwelling been assigned?' Hearing that it was assigned to a visiting young monk, he approached him, paid homage, and said, 'Venerable sir, there is a duty for the monk who spends the rains retreat in our dwelling.' When asked, 'What is the duty, lay devotee?', he replied, 'For the three months, you must take your alms-food only at our house, and after the invitation (pavāraṇā) ceremony, you must inform us before you leave.' The young monk consented by remaining silent. The lay devotee went home and said, 'A visiting venerable monk has arrived at our monastery; we must serve him respectfully.' The lay devotee (upāsikā) agreed and prepared excellent food. The young monk went to the house of his relatives at mealtime. However, no one recognized that young monk.

Note 1: This river is the one called Mahāveligangā in the island of Sri Lanka.
Note 2: Although it should be translated strictly as 'having performed the duties' according to the text 'vattaṃ katvā', it is translated here as a separate sentence to make the Burmese phrasing clearer and more distinct.

The young monk took his meals at that house for the entire three months. When the rains retreat was over, he informed them, 'I am going.' Then, the relatives said, 'Venerable sir, please leave tomorrow,' and on the next day, after offering alms-food at the house, they filled a tube with oil, gave him a lump of molasses and a piece of cloth nine cubits long, and said, 'Please go, venerable sirs [Note 1].' After giving a talk of appreciation (anumodanā), the young monk set out for the Rohaṇa region.

His preceptor, the elder, having also completed the pavāraṇā ceremony, met the young monk at the same place where they had met before. The young monk performed his duties to the elder at the foot of a tree. Then the elder asked, 'Friend of cheerful countenance, did you see the lay devotee?' The young monk replied, 'I saw her, venerable sir,' and after relating the whole story, he anointed the elder's feet with that oil, prepared a drink with the molasses, and offered the cloth to the elder. Then, having paid homage to the elder, he said, 'Venerable sir, only the Rohaṇa region is suitable for me,' and he departed. The elder also arrived at the monastery and entered Koraṇḍaka village the next day.

Note 1: This is a translation of 'Gacchatha bhante'; addressing a single person in the plural is a way of showing respect according to the Pali method.
89:
The laywoman also remained constantly watching the road, thinking, "My brother (the Elder) will now come bringing my son." When she saw the Elder arriving alone, she thought, "I suppose my son is dead; the Elder is coming alone," and falling at the Elder's feet, she wept and lamented. The Elder, thinking, "Surely the young monk, out of fewness of wishes (appicchatā), has gone without making himself known," comforted her, told her the whole story, and taking the piece of cloth (offered by the young monk) out of his bowl-bag, showed it to her.

The laywoman, filled with faith, prostrated herself facing the direction her son had gone and said: "It seems the Blessed One taught the practice found in the Rathavinīta Sutta, the Moneya practice taught to the monk Nālaka, the practice in the Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta, and the Great Noble Lineage practice (Mahā-ariyavaṃsa) which explains contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation, by making a monk like my son a living witness (kāya-sakkhī). Although he ate for three months in the house of the mother who gave birth to him, [90] he did not even say, 'I am the son of the laywoman, and the laywoman is my mother.' Oh, what an amazing man!"

For such a monk, even parents do not become an impediment (palibodha); what need is there to mention other supporting lay-devotees? The section on the impediment of family (kula-palibodha) is finished.

## (3) The Impediment of Gains (Lābha-palibodha)

The four requisites are called "gains" (lābha). How do these four requisites become an impediment? The answer is: for a monk of great merit, people in every place he goes offer him requisites with a large following. That monk has to give thanks and preach to those people, and thus finds no opportunity to practice the duties of a recluse (samaṇa-dhamma).

Notes:
1. In the Rathavinīta Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, the ten subjects of talk (kathā-vatthu) and the seven stages of purification (visuddhi) are explained using the simile of the seven relay-chariots (rathavinīta). The ten subjects of talk are: (1) talk on fewness of wishes, (2) talk on contentment, (3) talk on seclusion, (4) talk on aloofness from society, (5) talk on energy, (6-10) talk on virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. The seven purifications are well-known.
2. The Moneya practice is taught in the Sutta Nipāta (p. 388), starting with "I shall explain the sage's practice to you." Specifically, it states that a monk entering a village should not mix with laypeople; when seeking food, he should be like a mute and not speak to obtain alms. It includes many practices related to fewness of wishes. In brief, he must constantly practice meditation while standing or sitting under a tree in the forest. When entering a village for alms in the morning, he must go from house to house in order and accept what is given. He must not accept invitations to houses or food brought to him. He must not converse with laypeople. He should stay only one day at one tree in one forest, and collect alms only one day in one village, moving to another forest, tree, and village the next day. This is the summary of the Moneya practice.
1. The Tuvaṭṭaka practice is taught in the Sutta Nipāta (p. 421), starting with "Having understood the root of obsession (papañca)... let him completely suppress the conceit 'I am'." It specifically mentions not mixing with laypeople in the village and not speaking to people with the desire for gains like alms and robes.
2. In the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta (Aṅguttara Nikāya I, 336), four practices are shown: (1) contentment with any kind of robe, (2) contentment with any kind of alms-food, (3) contentment with any kind of lodging, and (4) delight in meditation. Contentment with alms-food includes contentment with medicine; therefore, the Visuddhimagga refers to it as contentment with the four requisites (catu-paccaya-santosa).
90:
From dawn until the first watch of the night, association with people does not cease. Again, in the very early morning before daybreak, monks who are practitioners of the alms-food dhutaṅga and who desire an abundance of requisites come and say, "Venerable sir, such-and-such a lay devotee (male or female), or a minister, or a minister's daughter, wishes to see you." That monk of great merit, [ordering his attendant monk], says, "Friend, take my bowl and robes," and prepares to go. In this way, [in favoring the donors], he is constantly occupied. For such a monk, these four requisites become an impediment. Therefore, that monk of great merit should leave the group and practice alone in a place where people do not know him. When he practices in this way, that impediment is severed. The discussion on the impediment of gain (lābha-palibodha) is finished.

## (4) The Impediment of the Group
A group is said to be either a Suttanta group or an Abhidhamma group. For a monk who, by teaching the Pāḷi or the Commentaries to that group, finds no opportunity for the practice of a recluse (samaṇadhamma), the group itself becomes an impediment. That monk should sever that impediment in the following way: If those [student] monks have already learned much and only a little remains, he should finish that remainder and then enter the forest. If they have learned only a little and much remains, he should not go beyond one league (yojana), but within the limit of one league, he should approach another teacher of the group and say, "Venerable sir, please favor these monks by teaching them the Pāḷi and so forth." If he does not find such a person, he should say, "Friends, I have a certain task; you may go to wherever you find comfortable," and having left the group, he should perform his own monastic duty. The discussion on the impediment of the group (gaṇa-palibodha) is finished.

## (5) The Impediment of Work
New construction (navakamma) is called "work" (kamma). For one performing such work, he must know whether the carpenters and others have received their wages or not, and he must be concerned with what has been done and what remains to be done. Therefore, it is an impediment at all times. This impediment of work should also be severed in the following way: If only a little remains, it should be completed. If much remains, and if it is the Saṅgha’s work, it should be handed over to the Saṅgha or to the monks who bear the Saṅgha’s burdens. If it is his own work, it should be handed over to his own stewards. If he does not find such a person, he should renounce it to the Saṅgha and depart. The discussion on the impediment of work (kamma-palibodha) is finished.

## (6) The Impediment of Travel
[91] Traveling is called "travel" (addhāna). If a monk has a candidate for whom he must perform an ordination in a certain place, or if there are certain requisites he is entitled to receive, and if he cannot bear not receiving that candidate or those requisites, then even if he enters the forest and strives in the recluse’s practice, it will be difficult for him to dispel the thought of traveling. Therefore, he should go and complete that task first, and only then should he apply himself and strive in the recluse’s practice. The discussion on the impediment of travel (addhāna-palibodha) is finished.

## (7) The Impediment of Relatives
"Relatives" in the monastery refers to the teacher (ācariya), the preceptor (upajjhāya), the co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika), the assistant pupil (antevāsika), fellow-pupils of the same preceptor, and fellow-pupils of the same teacher. In the house, it refers to the mother, father, brother, and so forth. When those teachers and others are unwell...
91:
(Sub-commentary) In Sri Lanka, the custom of choosing auspicious days and times still exists to this day.

2. A co-resident pupil (saddhivihārika) is a pupil who has taken a preceptor (upajjhāya).

3. A resident pupil (antevāsika) is a pupil of teachers other than the preceptor.

When [they are sick], they become impediments to this yogi monk. Therefore, one should cut off that impediment by attending to and caring for those persons, such as teachers, to restore them to their normal health.

Among those teachers and others, first: if the preceptor is sick and does not recover quickly from the illness, he should be cared for even for the rest of one's life. Likewise, the teacher who gave the novice ordination (pabbajjācariya), the teacher who gave the higher ordination (upasampadācariya), the co-resident pupil, the resident pupil whom one has ordained or given higher ordination, and fellow residents under the same preceptor should be cared for. As for the teacher from whom one takes dependence (nissayācariya), the teacher who gives instruction (uddesācariya), the resident pupil who takes dependence (nissayantevāsika), the resident pupil who receives instruction (uddesantevāsika), and fellow residents under the same teacher, they should be cared for as long as the dependence or instruction is not yet completed. If one is able, they should be cared for even beyond that.

One should act towards one's mother and father as towards a preceptor. Even if the parents are in a royal position, if they expect care from their son (the monk), it must be given. If the parents have no medicine, one should give one's own. If one has none, one must seek it through the practice of alms-gathering and give it. For brothers and sisters, one should prepare medicine using their own property. If they have none, one should give one's own medicine temporarily (as a loan) and take it back if they obtain some later. If they do not obtain any, one should not ask for it back. It is not proper to treat or give medicine to an unrelated brother-in-law. However, one may give it to one's sister, saying, "Give this to your husband." The same applies to a sister-in-law (the wife of an elder or younger brother). But since the children of that brother-in-law or sister-in-law are the monk's own relatives, it is proper to treat them. The discussion on the impediment of relatives is finished.

## (8) The Impediment of Sickness

Sickness means any kind of disease. When that sickness causes pain and oppression, it becomes an impediment. Therefore, it should be cut off by medical treatment. If it does not subside even after a few days [1] of treatment, one should disparage the body, thinking, "I am not your slave, nor your hireling; [92] by serving you alone, I have come to suffering in this beginningless round of rebirths (saṃsāra)," and should only strive in the monk's practice (samaṇadhamma). The discussion on the impediment of sickness is finished.

Note:
1. This is the meaning of the word katipāhaṃ. These "few days" could be 2 or 3 days, or 4, 5, or 6 days. Some diseases disappear in 2 or 3 days, while others take 4 or 5 days. Therefore, to allow for appropriate interpretation according to the disease, it is translated here as "a few days" according to the original meaning. In the Pyay edition Nissaya, it is translated as "2 or 3 days." That translation is also consistent with the teaching "Today itself the effort must be made" (ajjeva kiccamātappaṃ).

## (9) The Impediment of Scripture

Scripture (gantha) means the undertaking of the learning (pariyatti). For a monk who is constantly occupied with reciting and studying that scripture, it becomes an impediment. For a monk who is not constantly occupied, it is not an impediment. Regarding this state of not being an impediment, there are many stories.

The Elder Deva, a reciter of the Majjhima Nikāya, went to the Elder Deva of Malayavāsī (living in the Malaya region) to request a meditation subject. The Elder Deva of Malayavāsī asked, "Friend, what is your status in the learning?" "Venerable Sir, I have memorized the Majjhima Nikāya." "Friend, this Majjhima Nikāya is difficult to maintain. For one reciting the Mūlapaṇṇāsa, the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa comes to the mouth; for one reciting the Majjhimapaṇṇāsa, the Uparipaṇṇāsa comes to the mouth. How will you be able to practice meditation?" (The Elder Deva of Majjhima Nikāya replied,) "Venerable Sir, once I have received the meditation subject from you, I will not look back at the learning again." Having taken the meditation subject, he did not recite for 19 years, and in the twentieth year, he reached the fruit of Arahantship. At that time [1]...

Note:
1. Patvā - having reached.
92:
Or—regarding the word "having reached"—it has been translated as "He reached. At that time," splitting the sentence to make the Burmese phrasing clear and distinct.

To the monks who came for the purpose of recitation, he said, "Friends, it has been twenty years since I last looked at the scriptures (Pariyatti). However, I am proficient and well-versed in this Majjhima Nikāya; you may begin." From the beginning to the end, not even regarding a single syllable did that Elder (Deva, the bearer of the Majjhima Nikāya) have any doubt.

The Elder Nāga, who resided on Karuḷiya Mountain, also abandoned the scriptures for eighteen years and then taught the Dhātukathā to the monks. When those monks (who learned from Elder Nāga) compared it with the Elders residing in Anurādhapura, there was not even a single question that came out of order from their memory.

Also, in the Mahāvihāra monastery, an Elder named Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya, without having learned the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā)¹, had the golden drum beaten, announcing, "I will expound the Three Piṭakas in the assembly of those who have learned the five Nikāyas." The Saṅgha of monks said, "Whose lineage of teaching is this? Speak only according to your own teacher's lineage; otherwise, we will not allow you to speak." His preceptor (Upajjhāya) also asked him when he came to pay respects, "Friend, did you have the drum beaten?" "Yes, venerable sir." "For what reason?" "Venerable sir, with the intention of expounding the scriptures (Pariyatti)."

Note
1. Connect "without having learned" with "had the drum beaten."

"Friend Abhaya, how do the teachers expound this passage?" "They expound it in this way, venerable sir," he replied. The preceptor rejected it, saying "Hum." Again, that Elder Abhaya explained it in another way, saying "They expound it in this way, venerable sir," repeating it three times (with corrections). The preceptor rejected all of them by saying "Hum," and then said, "Friend, [93] only the first explanation you gave is the lineage of the teachers. However, because you did not learn it from the lips of the teachers, you are unable to stand firm and say, 'This is how the teachers expound it.' Go now, and learn from your own teachers." "Where should I go, venerable sir?" "In the Rohaṇa district, on the other side of the Gaṅgā River, at the Tūlādhārapabbata monastery, there lives an Elder named Mahādhammarakkhita who is thoroughly proficient in the entire scriptures (the Three Piṭakas)¹; go to that Elder."

Note
1. According to the Ṭīkā, "In this person, the scriptures known as the Three Piṭakas are well-determined; therefore, he is called 'Sabbapariyattika' (one who possesses the entire scriptures) or 'Tepiṭaka' (one who bears the Three Piṭakas)." This has been translated with slight modifications to make it easier for Burmese readers to understand.

(Elder Cūḷābhaya) said, "Very well, venerable sir," and after paying homage to his preceptor, he went to Elder Mahādhammarakkhita along with five hundred monks. After paying homage, he stayed there. Elder Mahādhammarakkhita asked, "Why have you come?" "I have come to listen to the Dhamma of the Commentaries, venerable sir," he replied. "Friend Abhaya, I am occasionally asked about the Dīgha Nikāya and Majjhima Nikāya. As for the remaining Nikāyas, I have not reviewed them for thirty years. However, you recite the Pāli text to me during the night. I will teach you the Commentary during the day." Elder Abhaya said, "Very well, venerable sir," and did exactly as the Elder said. Having a large pavilion built at the gate of the compound, the villagers came every day to listen to the Dhamma. Elder Abhaya recited the Pāli text at night. Expounding the Pāli text recited that night during the day, Elder Mahādhammarakkhita¹ gradually² completed the teaching. Then, (descending from the seat) and sitting on a mat, he requested, "Friend, please preach the meditation subject (Kammaṭṭhāna) to me." "Venerable sir, what are you saying? Did I not learn only from you? How can I preach a Dhamma that you do not yet know?" (Elder Abhaya replied). Then, the teacher, Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, said to his pupil, Elder Abhaya, "Friend Abhaya..."

Note
1. If the word "kathayanto" is translated literally as "the Elder who expounds," the Burmese phrasing is not smooth; therefore, it is translated as "expounding... Elder Mahādhammarakkhita."
93:
2. 'Successively' means by way of explaining in order.

'This path of practice of one who has gone and known through the going that is practice (paṭipatti) is distinct,' he said. At that time, Elder Abhaya was a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). [Therefore,] at that time, Elder Abhaya, having given the meditation subject to Elder Mahādhammarakkhita, returned and was explaining and teaching the Pāli of the Tipiṭaka at the Lohapāsāda. While he was thus teaching, he heard that 'Elder Mahādhammarakkhita has attained Parinibbāna.' Having heard this, he said, 'Friends, bring the robes,' and having donned the [clean] robes, he said, 'Friends, the Path of Arahatship is truly fitting for our teacher. Friends, our teacher was upright and a man of noble breeding (ājānīya). Our teacher sat on a mat in the presence of his own student and requested, "Please teach me a meditation subject." Friends, the Path of Arahatship is truly fitting for the Elder.' For monks of such nature as Elders Deva, Nāga, and Mahādhammarakkhita, scriptures are not an impediment. The discussion on the impediment of scriptures is finished.

## (10) The Impediment of Psychic Power (Iddhi-palibodha)

Psychic power refers to the psychic power of worldlings (puthujjana). Indeed, that psychic power of worldlings is difficult to maintain [without it perishing], like a young child lying on its back or like a young crop. It can be destroyed by even a slight disturbance. That psychic power is an impediment [only] to insight (vipassanā), not to concentration (samādhi), because it is attained only after reaching concentration. Therefore, one who desires insight should cut off the impediment of psychic power. One who desires concentration, however, [should cut off] only the remaining nine impediments. The discussion on the impediment of psychic power is finished. This which has been stated is the detailed explanation of the section on impediments [in their proper order].

## Explanation of the Giver of Meditation Subjects

[94] 42. In this heading, 'approaching a good friend who gives meditation subjects,' there are two types of meditation subjects: the universally useful meditation subject (sabbattha-kammaṭṭhāna), which is desirable in all circumstances, and the meditation subject to be constantly maintained (pārihāriya-kammaṭṭhāna). Among these two types: (1) the meditation subject of loving-kindness (mettā) [to be developed] towards the Saṅgha and others, and (2) the recollection of death (maraṇassati) are called universally useful meditation subjects. (3) Some say that the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā) is also [a universally useful meditation subject].

Note: In the Khuddasikkhā, these three universally useful meditation subjects along with the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) are presented as the 'Four Protections' (caturārakkhā). According to that view, the recollection of the Buddha should also be called a universally useful meditation subject.

To elaborate: a monk practicing meditation should first define [all the monks in this monastery] and develop loving-kindness towards the Saṅgha in the monastery precinct (upacārasīma), thinking, '[May all the monks in this monastery] be happy and free from mental suffering.' Then, he should develop it towards the deities within the monastery precinct; then towards the headman who rules the alms-resort village; then, starting with the people in that alms-resort village, towards all sentient beings. The benefit of such development is: through loving-kindness [developed] towards the Saṅgha, he softens the hearts of his fellow monks. Then, those fellow monks who live with him treat him with pleasant and smooth conduct. The deities whose hearts are softened by loving-kindness [developed] towards the deities in the monastery precinct protect [that meditating monk] well with righteous protection. Because the mental continuum of the ruling authorities is softened by loving-kindness [developed] towards the headman of the alms-resort village, those rulers protect [the monk's] requisites well with righteous protection. Because he can clear the hearts of the people in the alms-resort village with loving-kindness [developed] towards them, he can go about and reside there without their oppression or harassment. Through loving-kindness [developed] towards all sentient beings, he can travel in all directions without harm or hindrance.
94:
By repeatedly reflecting on death (maraṇassati), thinking "I will surely die," one abandons improper ways of seeking requisites, develops successive stages of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), and possesses a mind that does not shrink back (from right practice). For one whose mind is familiar with the perception of foulness (asubha-saññā), even celestial objects cannot overwhelm the mind through the power of greed.

Notes
1. "Surakkhitaparikkhāro"—If translated literally as "having well-guarded requisites," it is difficult for those unfamiliar with Pali to understand. Therefore, it is translated figuratively as "they (the deities) well-guard (that monk's) requisites."
2. Here too, the phrasing is slightly modified for easier understanding.
3. Translated by taking it as a causative attribute (hetumanta-visesana). Connect this causal term with "abandons."
4. If translated literally as "having developed spiritual urgency," it is not very clear or distinct. Therefore, the phrasing is changed to "developing spiritual urgency."

Because it is very beneficial and is desired in all matters (as a precursor) [Note 1], and because it is the cause for the essential practice of meditation, it is called sabbatthaka-kammaṭṭhāna [Note 2] (universally beneficial meditation subject).

Among the forty meditation subjects, the one that suits the practitioner's temperament is called pārihāriya-kammaṭṭhāna [Note 3] (meditation to be constantly maintained), because it must always be maintained by that practitioner and because it is the proximate cause for higher and higher stages of meditation. One who gives these two kinds of meditation subjects is called a "giver of meditation subjects" (kammaṭṭhāna-dāyaka).

A "good friend" (kalyāṇamitta) is described as:

"Endearing, respectful, and worthy of praise; a speaker and patient of speech; a speaker of deep discourse (such as the Truths and Dependent Origination); and one who does not urge one toward improper things."

Notes
1. "In all matters" means in all duties of a monk, or in all meditation practices.
2. Sabbatthaka (desired in all matters) + kamma (meditation practice) + ṭhāna (cause).
3. Pārihāriya (to be constantly maintained) + kamma (higher meditation practice) + ṭhāna (proximate cause).

A good friend is one endowed with such qualities, who truly seeks one's welfare and stands on the side of growth in virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and wisdom (paññā).

[95] Because of the teaching, "Ānanda, by relying on me as a good friend, beings subject to birth are freed from birth," etc., the Buddha alone is the good friend endowed with all attributes. Therefore, while the Buddha is alive, it is best [Note 1] to take a meditation subject in the presence of the Buddha. If the Buddha has entered Parinibbāna, one should take it in the presence of one of the eighty Great Disciples (Mahāsāvaka) who is still living. If such a Great Disciple is not available, one should take it in the presence of an Arahant who has reached the destruction of taints (āsavakkhaya) by developing insight (vipassanā) based on [Note 2] the fourth or fifth jhāna produced through the power of the desired meditation subject.

Notes
1. If it were said "the meditation subject taken is a well-taken meditation subject," it would be difficult for those unfamiliar with Pali to understand. Therefore, the phrasing is changed to "it is best to take a meditation subject."
2. If translated literally as "developing insight which has jhāna as its proximate cause," some might not understand. Therefore, it is modified as above.

Question: Does an Arahant reveal his own quality by saying, "I am an Arahant"? How could there be such a question? If he knows, "This is a practitioner of meditation," he may reveal it. Did not the Elder Assagutta, knowing a monk to be a practitioner of meditation, spread a piece of leather in the sky and, sitting cross-legged on that leather, preach the meditation subject? [Note 1] This is the answer.

Therefore, if one finds an Arahant (who can give meditation subjects), it is very good. If one does not find an Arahant, then among Non-returners (Anāgāmī), Once-returners (Sakadāgāmī), Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna), worldlings (puthujjana) who have attained jhāna, and worldlings who have mastered the three Pitakas, two Pitakas, or one Pitaka, the former...

Notes
1. In this context, when it is said that an Arahant shows his quality to a practitioner of meditation, it should be understood that he shows it only to a monk, not to laypeople or novices.
95:
For if one tells or shows their own state of a Noble One or Arahantship to a layperson or novice, it is a Pācittiya offense of bhūtārocana (telling the truth about superior human states). Moreover, no Noble One ever intentionally violates a Vinaya rule; that is why.

2. Up to this point, persons endowed with both types of knowledge—āgamasuta (learning) and adhigamasuta (realization)—are shown. Among them, those up to the stage of Stream-enterer (sotāpanna) are persons endowed with both mundane and supramundane adhigamasuta. A worldling (puthujjana) who has attained Jhana is a person endowed only with one type of adhigamasuta, namely, mundane Jhana. After that, worldlings who are bearers of the Three Pitakas (tipiṭakadhara), etc., are endowed only with learning (āgamasuta).

[One should take the meditation subject] from [such a person]. If even a bearer of one Pitaka is not available, one should take it from one who has thoroughly mastered at least one Nikaya along with its commentary and is a conscientious (lajjī) person. Such a teacher, who preserves the tradition (tanti) and protects the lineage (vaṃsa), maintaining the succession of teachers, presents only the view of his teachers (ācariyāmata) and not his own opinion. Therefore, the great elders of old said three times: "A conscientious person will protect [the Sasana]; a conscientious person will protect [the Sasana]."

Among these "good friends" (kalyāṇamitta) who are meditation teachers, those mentioned earlier, such as Arahants, teach only the path they themselves have attained. However, a learned (bahussuta) meditation teacher, having purified his learning through approaching various teachers and through study and inquiry, notes the Suttas and the reasons from various Nikayas.

Note:
These are persons endowed [with knowledge]. It means they are persons with mere theoretical knowledge of the scriptures. However, it is further shown that such noble persons are also worthy of respect.
1. "Ita cito ca"—"from here and there"—is a suitable Burmese translation. This Pali is a copy of the Sanskrit "itas tatas," so it should only be "ito tato." However, in modern texts, it always appears as "ita cito ca" with the word "ca." In the sub-commentary (ṭīkā), it is explained with a sense of selection (niddhāraṇa) from the five Nikayas, so it is translated here as "from various Nikayas," explicitly mentioning the selection.

[The learned teacher], well-noting the Sutta [appropriate to the meditation subject] and the logical reasoning [following that Sutta], and connecting what is suitable and unsuitable, will teach the meditation subject, showing the "Great Road" (the method of meditation) like a great elephant moving through a dense thicket. Therefore, one should approach such a "good friend" who can give a meditation subject, perform the duties (vatta) toward that teacher, and receive the meditation subject.

[96] If one finds this "good friend" meditation teacher in one's own monastery, that is excellent. If not [in one's own monastery], one should go to the monastery where that "good friend" meditation teacher resides.

Note:
1. Translated in accordance with the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) "suttānugataṃ yuttiñca." Here, "logical reasoning following the Sutta" should be understood as reasoning that enters and follows in accordance with the Sutta when the Sutta is taken.
2. By connecting what is suitable or unsuitable for the pupil who is receiving the meditation subject, through searching for the appropriate logic (yuttimaggatena), investigation, and reflection. Alternatively, by keeping well in mind what is suitable or unsuitable for the pupil (Sub-commentary). The translation above follows the first explanation of the sub-commentary. This means directing the pupil to resort to what is suitable and avoid what is unsuitable. According to the second explanation in the Pyay Mu Nissaya, it is "keeping it well in his own heart." In that sense, it refers to the teacher's mindfulness of suitability. It is also appropriate if taken as instilling it in the pupil's mind.

A monk who goes [to the teacher] should not go surrounded by disciples, having washed his feet and anointed them with oil, wearing sandals, carrying an umbrella, and having others carry oil-tubes, honey, molasses, and so on. Having fulfilled the duties of a traveler, he should carry his own bowl and robes himself. Along the way, he should perform the duties (the duty of an arriving guest, āgantukavatta, and the duty of a departing monk, gamikavatta) at every monastery he enters, and he should travel with light requisites and live a very frugal life.
96:
A monk who is about to enter the monastery of a meditation teacher (kammaṭṭhānācariya), who is a good friend, should have a tooth-stick made 'allowable' (kappiya) while on the way and bring it with him. He should not enter another compound with the intention, 'I will rest for a moment, wash and oil my feet, and then go to the teacher.' Why? Because if there are monks in that compound who are incompatible with the teacher, they might ask the reason for his arrival and speak ill of the teacher, saying, 'You are ruined if you have come to him,' thereby causing him dissatisfaction. Because of this, he might even turn back from that very compound. Therefore, he should ask for the teacher's residence and go directly to that monastery.

If the meditation teacher is junior (in seniority), the student should not allow him to take his bowl and robes. If the teacher is senior, the student should go, pay homage to the teacher, and remain standing. When told, 'Friend, set down your bowl and robes,' he should set them down. When told, 'Drink some water,' he should drink if he wishes. When told, 'Wash your feet,' he should not wash them immediately. For if the water was brought by the teacher, it would not be proper to wash. If the teacher says, 'Friend, wash; the water was not brought by me, but by others,' then he should sit and wash his feet in a secluded place where the teacher cannot see, or in an open space, or at one edge of the monastery.

If the teacher brings a tube of oil, the student should stand up and receive it respectfully with both hands. For if he does not accept it, the teacher might think, 'This monk is disrupting communion (sambhoga) from the very start,' and his mind might change. Having accepted it, he should not start by anointing his feet. For if that oil is for the teacher's body, it would not be proper. Therefore, he should apply it to his head [97] first, and then to his shoulders and so on. If the teacher gives permission, saying, 'Friend, this oil is for the whole body; apply it to your feet as well,' he should put a little on his head and then anoint his feet. Then he should ask, 'May I put this oil tube away, Bhante?' and if the teacher accepts, he should give it to him.

From the day of arrival, he should not yet request, 'Bhante, please teach me the meditation subject.' From the next day onwards, if there is a regular attendant of the teacher, he should ask permission from that attendant and perform the duties (vatta) for the teacher.
97:
Even if requested, if [the regular attendant] does not grant permission, one should perform [the duties to the teacher] only when an opportunity arises. A monk performing the teacher's duties should offer three types of tooth-sticks: small, medium, and large. He should prepare two kinds of water for washing the face and for bathing: cold and hot. From those two kinds of water—

Note 1: 'Oil for all purposes' (sabbapārihāriyatela) means oil that should be carried or applied for all parts of the body or for all monks. (Sub-commentary) In this context, if it were 'pariharitatela,' it could be translated as 'carried oil,' but because it contains the '-tabba' suffix, it should only be translated as 'oil that should be carried or applied.'
Note 2: Applying a little to the head is a sign of respect.
Note 3: Connect 'From the next day... perform the teacher's duties.'

One should consistently offer the same kind of water that the teacher has used for three days. For a teacher who uses any water without preference, one should offer whatever is available. There is no benefit in much elaboration. (Note 1: This means there is no need for further detail because the Buddha's words are clearly present in the Mahāvagga and Cullavagga Khandhakas.)

'Monks, a resident pupil (antevāsika) should conduct himself properly toward his teacher (ācariya). This is the proper conduct: [The pupil] should rise early, and having removed his sandals and arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, he should give the tooth-stick. He should give the water for washing the face. He should prepare the seat. If there is gruel, he should wash the bowl and offer the gruel.' All such duties to the teacher well-prescribed by the Blessed One in the Khandhaka must be performed.

While pleasing the teacher through the perfection of these duties as mentioned, [the monk seeking meditation instructions] should pay homage in the evening and depart only when dismissed by the teacher saying, 'Go.' (Note 2: Connect 'Having paid homage... depart only when dismissed.') When the teacher asks, 'Why have you come?' he should explain the reason for his arrival. If the teacher does not ask but accepts the service, after ten or fifteen days have passed (Note 3: In this regard, the instruction to wait for 10 or 15 days before asking for meditation instructions is worth considering. Has it not been shown in the [Visuddhimagga] that one should ignore illnesses that cannot be cured within a few days and quickly strive in the Dhamma? If one were to die during those waiting days, would it not be a great loss? Has the Blessed One not taught, 'Today the effort should be made, who knows if death will come tomorrow?' indicating that one should strive immediately without delay? When Bāhiya Dārucīriya met the Blessed One, did the Blessed One not teach him meditation instructions while standing even during the alms round? A meditation teacher who is a benevolent good friend (kalyāṇamitta) should not be reluctant to teach meditation to one who wishes to strive. Indeed, the teacher should even encourage and urge the student to practice quickly. Thus, there is no reason to be overly hesitant or shy toward the meditation teacher. If one cannot yet strive due to exhaustion from travel, one should wait only one day and ask for instructions the next day. If one is not exhausted and is able to strive, one should ask for instructions and begin practicing at a suitable time on the very day of arrival.), even if dismissed on a certain day, he should not go but should ask for an opportunity and state the reason for his arrival. Otherwise (or in another way, Note 1: This means if one wishes to explain in another way than previously shown), having gone at an unofficial time, if asked 'For what purpose have you come?' he should explain [the reason for his arrival]. If the teacher says, 'Come in the morning,' he should go in the morning.

However, if at that time the pupil's bile is bothering him and burning his stomach, or if his food is not digesting due to weak digestive fire, or if any other illness afflicts him, he should disclose the illness as it is, inform the teacher of a suitable time for himself, and approach at that time. The reason for changing the time is that if meditation instructions are given at an unsuitable time [due to illness], it is not possible to attend to them properly. This is the detailed explanation of 'approaching a good friend (a noble teacher) who gives meditation instructions'.

## Explanation of Temperaments

[98] 43. Now, regarding the phrase 'suitable to one's temperament,' [I shall explain] the detail of the word 'temperament' (carita).
98:
## Description of Temperaments (Cariyāvaṇṇanā)

Temperaments, which are the states of frequent occurrence, are six: the greed-temperament, the hatred-temperament, the delusion-temperament, the faith-temperament, the wisdom-temperament, and the speculative-thought-temperament. Some teachers, however, desire fourteen temperaments, including these eight: four others by way of the combination (saṃsagga) and conjunction (sannipāta) of greed, etc., and likewise four for faith, wisdom, and speculative thought. If such divisions are mentioned, there would be many temperaments when greed, etc., are combined with faith, etc.1 Therefore, temperaments should be understood as only six in brief. (Cariyā)—frequent occurrence, nature (pakati), and predominance (ussannatā) are identical in meaning. By way of these temperaments, there are six types of persons: the one of greed temperament, the one of hatred temperament, the one of delusion temperament, the one of faith temperament, the one of wisdom temperament, and the one of speculative-thought temperament.

Among these six persons, for the one of greed temperament, faith is strong when wholesome states arise. This is because faith is close in quality to greed. To clarify:

Note
1. The way many temperaments occur: (1) Greed temperament, (2) Hatred temperament, (3) Delusion temperament, (4) Greed-Hatred, (5) Greed-Delusion, (6) Hatred-Delusion, (7) Greed-Hatred-Delusion, totaling 7. (1) Faith temperament, (2) Wisdom temperament, (3) Speculative-thought temperament, (4) Faith-Wisdom, (5) Faith-Speculative-thought, (6) Wisdom-Speculative-thought, (7) Faith-Wisdom-Speculative-thought, totaling 7. Combined with the previous 7, it makes 14. Among those, if the first 7 are taken as a base and paired with the latter 7, 49 (7x7) are obtained. The pairing is: (1) Greed-Faith, (2) Greed-Wisdom, (3) Greed-Speculative-thought, (4) Greed-Faith-Wisdom, (5) Greed-Faith-Speculative-thought, (6) Greed-Wisdom-Speculative-thought, (7) Greed-Faith-Wisdom-Speculative-thought. Thus, 7 are obtained by pairing with Greed. Similarly, 7 each are obtained by pairing with Hatred, Delusion, Greed-Hatred, Greed-Delusion, Hatred-Delusion, and Greed-Hatred-Delusion. Therefore, there are 49. Combined with the initial 14, there are 63 temperaments. According to the view of "some" (keci), if one temperament of views (diṭṭhi) is added, there are 64. Referring to this occurrence, it is said, "many temperaments occur." This expansion of 63–64 temperaments is taken from Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī 256 and Abhidhammatthavikāsinī Vol. 2, 216.

On the unwholesome side, greed is smooth and not very coarse; so on the wholesome side is faith. Just as greed seeks out the objects of sensual desire (vatthukāma), so faith seeks out qualities such as virtue (sīla). Just as greed does not give up what is harmful, so faith does not give up what is beneficial. Therefore, the one of faith temperament is similar in nature to the one of greed temperament.

For the one of hatred temperament, wisdom is strong when wholesome states arise. This is because wisdom is close in quality to hatred. To clarify: just as on the unwholesome side, hatred is without affection and does not cling to the object, so on the wholesome side is wisdom. Just as hatred seeks out only faults, even if they are unreal, so wisdom seeks out only the faults (of formations) that are real. Just as hatred occurs in the manner of avoiding beings, so wisdom occurs in the manner of avoiding formations (saṅkhāra). Therefore, the one of wisdom temperament is similar in nature to the one of hatred temperament.

For the one of delusion temperament, when striving to give rise to wholesome states that have not yet arisen, there mostly arise wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) that cause obstacles. This is because speculative thought is close in characteristic to delusion. To clarify: just as delusion is unsteady because of its confused state, so speculative thought is unsteady because of its thinking in various ways. Just as delusion is wavering because of its inability to penetrate the object, so speculative thought is wavering because of its quickness in imagining. Therefore, the one of speculative-thought temperament is similar in nature to the one of delusion temperament.

Other teachers also speak of three other temperaments by way of craving (taṇhā), conceit (māna), and views (diṭṭhi). Among those three, craving is just greed, and conceit is associated with that craving.
99: Therefore, those two (craving and pride) do not occur beyond the greedy temperament. Because wrong view has delusion as its root, the speculative temperament follows, or enters into, the deluded temperament. 44. What is the cause of these temperaments? "This person is of a greedy temperament, this person is of a temperament of one of the others such as hate"—how is this to be known? What is suitable for a person of what temperament, such as a dwelling or a couch? This is the inquiry. In that inquiry, (the answer is): "The three temperaments of greed, hate, and delusion that occurred previously arise due to the cause of habituation in a past life. They arise due to the cause of the humors such as the elements beginning with earth, and wind and phlegm." Thus some teachers (such as Elder Upatissa) say (in the Vimuttimagga). According to those teachers: one who, in a past life, frequently performed pleasant gestures and beautiful deeds becomes one of a greedy temperament. One who has passed away from heaven and is reborn here is also (of a greedy temperament). One who, in a past life, frequently performed acts of cutting, killing, binding, and enmity becomes one of a hating temperament. One who has passed away from hell or the realm of nagas and is reborn here in this human world is also (of a hating temperament). One who, in a past life, drank much liquor and was deficient in hearing and inquiring becomes one of a deluded temperament. One who has passed away from the animal realm and is reborn here in this human world is also (of a deluded temperament). Thus they say (the three temperaments of greed, hate, and delusion) arise due to the cause of habituation in a past life. As for arising due to the elements and humors: a person becomes one of a deluded temperament due to the excess of the two elements, earth and water. Due to the excess of the other two (fire and air), one is of a hating temperament. If all four elements are equal, one is of a greedy temperament. Among the humors such as wind and phlegm, one with an excess of phlegm is of a greedy temperament. One with an excess of wind is of a deluded temperament. Alternatively, one with an excess of phlegm is of a deluded temperament, and one with an excess of wind is of a greedy temperament. Thus they say they arise due to the cause of elements beginning with earth and humors such as wind and phlegm. In that statement (of some teachers), (if examined): not all those who frequently performed pleasant gestures and beautiful deeds in a past life, nor all those who passed away from heaven and were reborn here in this human world, are only of a greedy temperament. Others are not only of a hating or deluded temperament. Likewise, there is no such fixed rule of excess of elements in the manner stated. In the fixed rule of humors, only the two, greed and delusion, are mentioned. Those two also contradict what precedes and follows.
