And among the temperaments of faith, etc., the cause of even one is not mentioned. Therefore, all this is an indefinite statement. This is the decision here according to the opinion of the teachers of the Commentaries; for this was said in the section called Ussada-kittana (Description of Predominance): "These beings, by the law of determination of past roots, are predominant in greed, predominant in hate, predominant in delusion, predominant in non-greed, predominant in non-hate, and predominant in non-delusion."
100: In the text of the Vimuttimagga seen by the teacher Buddhaghosa, the passage "one with an excess of bile humor is of a hating temperament" seems to be missing. The above statement also appears in a similar place in the introduction to this Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga. This also is merely contradictory. Among the temperaments of faith, etc., the cause of even one temperament is not mentioned at all. Therefore, all these statements of some teachers are not words spoken with discernment. In stating the cause of these temperaments, the following is the decision (presented) by following the opinion of the teachers of the Commentaries. Indeed, this following statement was made by the teachers in the section called Ussada-kittana (Description of Predominance): "These beings, by the law of determination of past roots, are predominant in greed, predominant in hate, predominant in delusion, predominant in non-greed, predominant in non-hate, and predominant in non-delusion." [100] "To explain in detail: for a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, greed is strong and non-greed is weak, while non-hate and non-delusion are strong and hate and delusion are weak; that person's weak non-greed is unable to overcome the (strong) greed. But non-hate and non-delusion, being strong, are able to overcome the (weak) hate and delusion. Therefore, when that person is born by way of the rebirth-linking given by that kamma, he is greedy. He is gentle in body, speech, and mind; he is not prone to anger; he is wise, possessing knowledge as sharp as a diamond point. (1) "But for a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, greed and hate are strong and non-greed and non-hate are weak, while non-delusion is strong and delusion is weak; that person, by the previous method (when born by the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is both greedy and hateful. However, he is wise, possessing knowledge as sharp as a diamond point, like the Elder Datta-Abhaya. (2) "For a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, greed, non-hate, and delusion are strong and non-greed, hate, and non-delusion are weak; that person, by the previous method (when born by the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is greedy and dull-witted. However, he is gentle in body, speech, and mind; he is not prone to anger, similar to the Elder Bākula. (3) "Furthermore, for a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, all three—greed, hate, and delusion—are strong and non-greed, non-hate, and non-delusion are weak; that person, by the previous method (when born by the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is both greedy and hateful, and is also deluded. (4) "For a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, non-greed, hate, and delusion are strong and greed, non-hate, and non-delusion are weak; that person, by the previous method (when born by the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is low in greed and low in defilements; even on seeing a divine object, he is unshaken. However, he is also hateful and dull-witted. (1) "For a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, non-greed, non-hate, and delusion are strong and greed, hate, and non-delusion are weak; that person, by the previous method (when born by the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is not greedy, not hateful, and is gentle in body, speech, and mind; however, he is dull-witted. (2) "Furthermore, for a person in whom, at the moment of the accumulation of kamma, non-greed, hate, and non-delusion are strong and greed, non-hate, and delusion are weak..."
101:
That person, by the previous method (through the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is not greedy but possesses great wisdom. However, they are prone to anger and are often irritable. (3)

[101] “For one in whom, at the moment of accumulating kamma, all three—non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are strong, while greed, hatred, and delusion are weak: that person, by the previous method (through the rebirth-linking given by that kamma), is not greedy or hateful but is wise. Such a person is like the Elder Mahāsaṅgharakkhita.” (4)

Note: This indicates that even when seeing such an object, there is no agitation; it goes without saying that there is no agitation upon seeing worldly objects. Therefore, the word 'pi' (even/also) is a contextual application (ṭhāna-payoga) placed where it is appropriate. However, in Burmese, it is smoother and clearer when applied as 'even when seeing a celestial object, there is no agitation,' even if it is not its literal place.

In the aforementioned explanation of the predominance of traits (ussada-kittana), the person called 'greedy' is one of lustful temperament (rāgacarita). Those who are very hateful or dull-witted are (respectively) of hateful temperament (dosacarita) and deluded temperament (mohacarita). The one with great wisdom is of intelligent temperament (buddhicarita). Those who are not greedy or hateful are of faithful temperament (saddhācarita) because of their naturally clear disposition. Alternatively, just as one born through kamma accompanied by non-delusion is of intelligent temperament, so one born through kamma accompanied by strong faith is of faithful temperament. One born through kamma accompanied by thoughts of sense-desire and so on is of speculative temperament (vitakkacarita). One born through kamma accompanied by a mixture of greed and so on is of mixed temperament (vomissacarita). (This concludes one section.) Thus, it should be understood that the kamma producing rebirth-linking, accompanied by one or another of these factors like greed, etc., is the root cause of the temperaments.

45. As for the question, “How is it to be known that this person is of lustful temperament?” and so forth, the following is the method of knowing:

One should explain the temperaments by way of posture, activity, food, seeing, and the occurrence of mental states (such as deceit and hypocrisy). This is the method of knowing.

Note: 1. The phrase in parentheses is the translation of the concluding word 'iti' in Pali; while it serves a purpose in Pali, it seems redundant in Burmese, so it is set apart with parentheses. The same applies hereafter.

Among these five, regarding 'by way of posture': (In detail) a person of lustful temperament, when walking in their natural way, walks gracefully. They set their foot down slowly, set it down evenly, and lift it up evenly. Their footprint is arched in the middle. A person of hateful temperament walks as if digging with their toes. They set their foot down hurriedly and lift it up hurriedly. Their footprint is dragged at the heel. A person of deluded temperament walks with a confused gait. They set their foot down as if trembling and lift it up as if trembling. Their footprint is that of one who has pressed down suddenly. It is also said in the account of the Māgaṇḍiya Sutta:

“The footprint of one affected by lust is arched in the middle;
The footprint of one affected by hate is dragged at the heel;
The footprint of one who is deluded is suddenly pressed down;
But such as this is the footprint of one who has drawn back the veil (the Buddha).”
102:
“A footprint of this nature (even and well-pressed) is the footprint of one who has opened the roof (of defilements).”

[102] The standing of a person of lustful temperament is graceful, refined, and pleasant in appearance. The standing of a person of hateful temperament is stiff in appearance. The standing of a person of deluded temperament is untidy and confused in appearance. The same applies to sitting. A person of lustful temperament, without hurrying, prepares their bed evenly, lies down slowly, keeps their limbs well-arranged, and sleeps in a graceful manner.

When woken up, they do not rise quickly but give a slow response as if hesitant or shy. A person of hateful temperament prepares their bed hurriedly and haphazardly, throws their body down, and sleeps with a frown. When woken up, they rise quickly and give a response as if angry. A person of deluded temperament prepares their bed poorly and untidily, throws their limbs about in a disorganized way, and mostly sleeps face down. When woken up, they rise heavily, making a grunting sound, and rise slowly. Those of faithful temperament, etc., because they are similar to those of lustful temperament, etc., have similar postures. (This concludes one section.) Thus, first, the temperaments should be explained by way of posture.

Regarding 'by way of activity': (In detail) in activities such as sweeping, a person of lustful temperament holds the broom well and sweeps cleanly and evenly without hurrying, not scattering the sand, as if spreading a carpet of Sinduvāra flowers. A person of hateful temperament holds the broom tightly and sweeps hurriedly, pushing the sand to both sides with a harsh sound, leaving it unclean and uneven. A person of deluded temperament holds the broom loosely and sweeps in a swirling, confused manner, leaving it unclean and uneven.

As with sweeping, so in all activities such as washing and dyeing robes, the person of lustful temperament acts skillfully, gently, evenly, and carefully. The person of hateful temperament acts tightly, stiffly, and unevenly. The person of deluded temperament acts unskillfully, confusedly, unevenly, and indecisively. Furthermore, the way a person of lustful temperament wears their robe is neither too tight nor too loose; it is graceful and well-rounded. For a person of hateful temperament, it is too tight and not well-rounded. For a person of deluded temperament, it is loose and messy. Those of faithful temperament, etc., should be known by following the behavior of those of lustful temperament, etc., because they share the same nature. (This concludes one section.) Thus, the temperaments should be explained by way of activity.

Regarding 'by way of food': A person of lustful temperament likes oily and sweet food. When eating, they make a well-rounded mouthful that is not too large, and they eat without hurrying, savoring the taste. When they get something delicious, they feel joy...
103:
By way of food: A person of lustful temperament likes soft and delicious food. When eating, he makes well-rounded mouthfuls of moderate size and eats slowly, savoring the taste. He is delighted when receiving something sweet. [103] A person of hateful temperament likes coarse and sour food. When eating, he makes mouthfuls that fill the mouth and eats hurriedly without savoring the taste. He becomes unhappy when receiving something that is not tasty. A person of deluded temperament has no fixed preference in food. When eating, he makes small, uneven mouthfuls, scattering grains of rice in the bowl and smearing his lips. With a distracted mind, he eats while thinking of various things. Those of faithful temperament and so on should be understood by following the manner of those of lustful temperament and so on, because of their similarity in nature. Thus, temperaments should be explained by way of food.

By way of seeing and so on: A person of lustful temperament, upon seeing even a slightly pleasing form, looks for a long time as if amazed. He becomes attached even to minor virtues and does not grasp actual faults. When departing, he leaves with longing, looking back as if unwilling to let go. A person of hateful temperament, upon seeing even a slightly unpleasing form, does not look for long, as if weary. He is irritated even by minor faults and does not grasp actual virtues. When departing, he leaves without longing, as if wanting to let go. A person of deluded temperament, upon seeing any form, relies on others; hearing others blame, he blames; hearing others praise, he praises; but he himself remains indifferent through the indifference of ignorance. This is the method for hearing sounds and so on as well. Those of faithful temperament and so on should be understood by following the manner of those of lustful temperament and so on, because of their similarity in nature. Thus, temperaments should be explained by way of seeing and so on.

By way of the occurrence of states (such as deceit and treachery): In a person of lustful temperament, states such as deceit (māyā), treachery (sāṭheyya), pride (māna), evil wishes (pāpicchatā), great greed (mahicchatā), discontent (asantuṭṭhitā), vanity (siṅga), and frivolity (cāpalya) frequently occur. In a person of hateful temperament, states such as anger (kodha), enmity (upanāha), disparaging (makkha), rivalry (paḷāsa), envy (issā), and avarice (macchariya) occur. In a person of deluded temperament, states such as sloth (thina), torpor (middha), restlessness (uddhacca), remorse (kukkucca), doubt (vicikicchā), tenacious grasping (ādhānaggāhitā), and difficulty in relinquishing (duppaṭinissaggitā) occur. In a person of faithful temperament, states such as generosity (muttacāgatā), desire to see the noble ones (ariyānaṃ dassanakāmatā), desire to hear the true Dhamma (saddhammaṃ sotukāmatā), abundance of joy (pāmojjabahulatā), honesty (asaṭhatā), lack of deceit (amāyāvitā), and confidence in inspiring things (pasādanīyesu ṭhānesu pasādo) occur. In a person of intellectual temperament, states such as obedience (sovacassatā), good friendship (kalyāṇamittatā), moderation in eating (bhojanemattaññutā), mindfulness and clear comprehension (satisampajañña), devotion to wakefulness (jāgariyānuyoga), a sense of urgency (saṃvega) in inspiring places, and wise effort (yoniso padhāna) for one who has a sense of urgency occur. In a person of speculative temperament, states such as talkativeness (bhassabahulatā), delight in groups (gaṇārāmatā), lack of delight in wholesome application (kusalānuyoge arati), unsteadiness in tasks (anavaṭṭhitakiccatā), at night...
104:
1. In the preceding paragraph, the phrase 'saddhācaritādayopi' appeared, and it was translated in a conjunctive sense (sampiṇḍana) as 'also those of faithful temperament, etc.' Here, however, because it is accompanied by 'pana', it is translated in an alternative sense (pakkhantara); both are appropriate.

Although it has been said that temperaments should be demonstrated through postures and so forth as described, this method of demonstrating temperaments does not appear at all in the Pāḷi [Canon], nor does it appear in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). It is stated merely by following the opinions of teachers, independent of the Pāḷi and Commentaries. Therefore, it should not be accepted as essential. The reason is: if those of hating temperament, etc., act with heedfulness and mindfulness, they are also capable of performing the postures, etc., said to belong to those of lustful temperament. Furthermore, in a single individual of mixed temperament (lust, hate, etc.), postures with such distinct characteristics should not occur. It is for these two reasons. However, only the method of demonstrating temperaments mentioned in the Commentaries should be accepted as essential. Indeed, it is said: 'A teacher who possesses the knowledge of penetrating others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa) will teach the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) after knowing the temperament; a teacher who does not possess it should question the pupil.' Therefore, one should know, either through the knowledge of penetrating others' minds or by questioning that person, 'This person is of lustful temperament; this person is of one of the temperaments such as hating, etc.'

46. Regarding the statement, 'What kind of dwelling, couch, and so forth is suitable for a person of what temperament?', first, the dwelling will be described. For a person of lustful temperament, a suitable dwelling is one of the following: a dwelling with a dirty terrace, a single-story ground-level dwelling, an unrenovated mountain cleft, a grass-roofed hut, or a leaf-thatched hut. Furthermore, such a dwelling is covered in dust, full of bats, and in a state of ruin. It may be too high or too low, situated on parched and rough ground, or be a place of dread (due to lions, tigers, etc.), with an unclean and uneven path. In that dwelling, there is a couch or stool that is full of bedbugs, ugly, and misshapen. To one who looks at such a dwelling, a feeling of loathing arises just by seeing it. Such a dwelling is suitable (for one of lustful temperament).

(As for robes:) A robe with tattered edges and tangled, dangling threads; a robe full of holes like a net cake; a robe rough to the touch like a plank studded with nails; a robe that is soiled and heavy; a robe that is burdensome to carry (due to its weight or the need for frequent repairs)—such inner and outer robes are suitable (for a person of lustful temperament). The alms-bowl, too, is suitable if it is a discolored clay bowl, or a heavy, misshapen iron bowl that is unsightly with plugs, repairs, and lumps, resembling a human skull and thus loathsome. The path for alms-round is suitable if it is unpleasant, far from the village, and uneven. The alms-resort village is suitable if it is a village where people go about as if they do not see (the alms-collecting monk); where, even if a monk leaves without receiving alms from a single house, and someone calls, 'Come, Bhante,' leads him into the refectory, gives him gruel or rice, and then they leave without even a sidelong glance, like cattle being driven into a pen—such a village is suitable. The attendants are suitable if they are unattractive, ill-favored, dressed in soiled clothes, foul-smelling, and loathsome, serving gruel and rice disrespectfully as if they were throwing it away.
105:
Rice gruel, alms-food, and snacks made of coarse grains such as millet, wild rice, and broken rice, as well as sour gruel, fermented water, and vegetable soup—whatever is just enough to fill the stomach—are suitable. For the person of lustful temperament, the suitable postures are standing and walking. As for the meditation object, any of the color kasinas like blue, etc., that is of an impure color is suitable. All these are suitable for the person of lustful temperament.

For the person of hateful temperament, a lodging that is neither too high nor too low, endowed with shade and water, with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and stairs, decorated with fine paintings and floral designs, with a smooth and soft floor, like a celestial mansion, adorned with flower garlands and colorful cloth canopies, with well-arranged clean and pleasant beds and chairs, and fragrant with the scent of flowers placed here and there—such a lodging that generates joy and delight just by seeing it—is suitable. The path to that lodging should be free from all dangers, clean, level, and well-decorated. To prevent pests like cockroaches, bugs, snakes, and mice, the requisites should not be too many; just one bed and one chair are suitable. The inner and outer robes should be made of fine materials such as Chinese silk, Somāra silk, silk, fine cotton, or fine linen—whatever is of high quality, light, well-dyed in a color suitable for a monk, and clean, whether single-layered or double-layered. The alms-bowl should be well-shaped like a water bubble, smooth like a gem, stainless, and of a color suitable for a monk; a very clean iron bowl is suitable. The alms-round path should be safe, level, pleasant, and neither too far from nor too close to the village. The alms-round village should be one where people, expecting the venerable one to arrive, prepare seats in swept and sprinkled areas, come out to meet him, take his bowl, invite him inside, seat him on the prepared seat, and serve him respectfully with their own hands. Such an alms-round village is suitable. The attendants should be handsome, pleasant, well-bathed, well-anointed, fragrant with incense and flowers, adorned with clean and attractive clothes of various colors, and respectful. The rice gruel, alms-food, and snacks should be endowed with color, scent, and taste, nutritious, delightful, excellent in every way, and available as much as desired. For the person of hateful temperament, the suitable postures are lying down and sitting. The meditation object should be any of the color kasinas like blue, etc., that is of a very pure color. All these are suitable for the person of hateful temperament.

For the person of deluded temperament, a lodging that faces an open space and is not cramped, where the horizons are clearly visible to one sitting there, is suitable.
106:
Among the postures, walking is suitable. For the person of deluded temperament, a small kasina disk the size of a small winnowing tray or a saucer lid is unsuitable. Because the mind becomes more confused in a cramped space, a large and wide kasina disk is suitable. The remaining details are the same as those described for the hateful temperament. All these are suitable for the person of deluded temperament.

For the person of faithful temperament, all the arrangements mentioned for the hateful temperament are suitable. Among meditation objects, the recollections (anussati) are also suitable.

For the person of intellectual temperament, there is nothing that can be called 'unsuitable' regarding lodging and so on.

For the person of speculative temperament, a lodging that is open and faces the horizons is unsuitable. In such a lodging, delightful parks, forests, ponds, villages, market towns, districts, and blue-colored mountains are visible to one sitting there; such a lodging is unsuitable because it serves as a condition for the mind to wander in thoughts. Therefore, one should dwell in a lodging such as a deep mountain cleft, a place hidden by forest, or a cave like the Mahinda Cave which is like the belly of an elephant. For the person of speculative temperament, a large kasina disk is unsuitable, as it causes the mind to wander through discursive thoughts. A small kasina disk, however, is suitable. The remaining details are the same as those described for the lustful temperament. All these are suitable for the person of speculative temperament.

This detailed explanation is an elaboration of the divisions, causes, signs, and suitability of the temperaments mentioned in the phrase 'suitable to one's own temperament.' However, the meditation subjects suitable to each temperament have not yet been fully revealed in all their aspects. They will become clear in the detailed explanation of the following headings (mātikā).

## Explanation of the Forty Meditation Subjects

47. Therefore, regarding the statement 'having taken one of the forty meditation subjects,' the determination of meditation subjects should be understood through these ten aspects: (1) Enumeration, (2) Inducing access and absorption, (3) Types of jhana, (4) Transcending, (5) Increasing and not increasing, (6) Object, (7) Plane, (8) Grasping, (9) Condition, and (10) Suitability to temperament.
108:
Among these two types, in the fourteen meditation subjects—namely the first three divine abodes (brahma-vihāra) which are the objects of three jhānas, and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) and the ten kasinas which are the objects of four jhānas—there is the 'overcoming of factors' (aṅgasamatikkama). This is because one attains the second jhāna and so on by overcoming the jhāna factors such as initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) while remaining on those same objects (of the divine abodes, mindfulness of breathing, and kasinas). The same applies to the fourth divine abode. For that fourth divine abode is also attained by overcoming joy (somanassa) while remaining on the objects of loving-kindness (mettā) and so on. In the four formless states (āruppa), there is the 'overcoming of objects' (ārammaṇasamatikkama). Indeed, one attains the base of infinite space by overcoming one of the nine preceding kasinas. And one attains the base of infinite consciousness and so on by overcoming the concept of space and so forth. In the remaining twenty-one meditation subjects, there is no overcoming of factors or objects. Thus, the decision should be understood by way of overcoming factors and objects.

(5) Regarding 'by way of distinguishing what should and should not be developed (expanded)': Among these forty meditation subjects, only the ten kasinas should be developed (expanded). The benefit is that within the extent to which the kasina is pervaded, one is able to hear sounds with the divine ear element (dibba-sota-dhātu), see forms with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), and know the minds of other beings with the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa). However, mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) and the foulness subjects (asubha) should not be developed. Why? Because they are delimited by their own location and because there is no benefit. Their delimitation by location will become clear in the method of meditation. If those are developed, only a heap of corpses increases, and there is no benefit whatsoever. This is also stated in the explanation of the questions of the novice Sopāka: 'Venerable Sir, the perception of form (kasina) is well-manifested (vibhūta), but the perception of bones is not well-manifested (avibhūta).' Here, 'the perception of form is well-manifested' is said in terms of the expansion of the sign (nimitta). 'The perception of bones is not well-manifested' is said in terms of non-expansion.

As for the statement, 'He pervaded this whole earth with the perception of bones,' this was said in terms of the mode of appearance to an Elder who had attained the perception of bones (and reached mastery). It is not said in terms of expanding the counterpart sign. For example, just as in the time of King Dhammāsoka, a Karavīka bird, seeing its own reflection in the mirror-walls all around, perceived Karavīka birds in all directions and uttered a sweet cry; so too, the Elder (Siṅgālapitu), because of his mastery of the perception of bones, seeing the sign appearing in all directions, thought, 'The whole earth is filled with bones.'

If so, does not the statement (in the Dhammasaṅgaṇī) that the jhānas of foulness have immeasurable objects (appamāṇārammaṇa) contradict this? It does not contradict. For one yogi takes the sign in a large bloated corpse or a large skeleton. Another takes it in a small one. By this reason, one yogi has a jhāna with a limited object (pariṭṭārammaṇa), while another has a jhāna with an immeasurable object (appamāṇārammaṇa). This is one answer to the objection. Alternatively, some yogi develops (expands) it because he does not see the disadvantage in expanding that foulness sign. With reference to such a person, it is said to have an 'immeasurable object.' However, because there is no benefit, they should not be developed. This is another answer.
109:
## [109]
Just as these foulness subjects and others should not be expanded, so too the remaining meditation objects such as mindfulness of breathing should not be expanded. Why? Because among those meditation subjects, if one expands the sign of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-nimitta), only the mass of air expands, and it is a meditation subject delimited by its location (such as the tip of the nose and the upper lip). Thus, because of this disadvantage (of only expanding the mass of air) and because it is a meditation subject delimited by its location, it should not be expanded.

The Divine Abidings (Brahmavihāras) have the concept of beings (satta-paññatti) as their object. If one expands the sign of those Divine Abidings, only the mass of beings would expand, and there is no benefit in the expansion of that mass of beings. Therefore, the objects of those Divine Abidings should also not be expanded. As for the statement beginning with "pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness," it is spoken only in terms of encompassing (pariggaha) [the object of meditation that has not yet been grasped]. (It is not spoken in terms of expanding the object that has already been grasped). Encompassing beings in one direction in sequence, such as those living in one house, two houses, etc., and developing [meditation] is called "pervading one direction." It does not mean expanding the sign. In this development of the Divine Abidings, there is no counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) at all that this yogi could expand¹. In this development of the Divine Abidings, having a limited (narrow) object or an immeasurable (great) object should be understood only in terms of encompassing (a few or many individuals)².

Note
1. Only the counterpart sign can be expanded; in Divine Abidings, even the counterpart sign does not appear, so the object should not be expanded—this is the meaning.
2. Jhana of loving-kindness etc. developed towards a few individuals like one or two is called parittārammaṇa—having a limited object; likewise, Jhana developed towards [many] individuals is called appamāṇārammaṇa—having an immeasurable object—this is the meaning.

Among the formless (āruppa) objects, the concept of space (ākāsa-paññatti) is the sign obtained by removing the kasina; therefore, that conceptual object [should not be expanded]¹. That concept of space should be attended to only in terms of the removal of the kasina. Even if one expands beyond that removal of the kasina, there is no benefit whatsoever. The object of the first formless consciousness² is a natural phenomenon (sabhāva-dhamma); therefore, that consciousness object [should not be expanded]. Indeed, it is not possible to expand a natural phenomenon. The object of the absence of the first formless consciousness (natthibhāva-paññatti) is merely the non-existence of that consciousness; therefore, that object [should not be expanded]. The object of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception should also not be expanded precisely because it is a natural phenomenon. The remaining meditation subjects (such as recollection of the Buddha) [should not be expanded] because they are not counterpart signs. Indeed, only that which is a counterpart sign can be said to be expandable. The objects of the recollection of the Buddha etc. do not become counterpart signs³. Therefore, the objects of those recollections [Buddha etc.] should not be expanded. Thus, [the decision] should be understood by way of defining what is to be expanded and what is not.

Note
1. Translated with slight additions and modifications for ease of understanding.
2. Refers to the Ākāsānañcāyatana consciousness which is the object of the Viññāṇañcāyatana Jhana.
3. It means they do not reach the state of a counterpart sign and are not called counterpart signs.

(6) Regarding "by way of defining the object": Among these forty meditation subjects, these twenty-two—the ten kasinas, the ten foulness subjects, mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness occupied with the body—have the counterpart sign as their object. The remaining eighteen meditation subjects do not have the counterpart sign as their object. Furthermore, among the ten recollections, excluding mindfulness of breathing and mindfulness occupied with the body, the remaining eight recollections, the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, the defining of the four elements, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these twelve meditation subjects have natural phenomena (sabhāva-dhamma) as their objects. The ten kasinas, the ten foulness subjects, mindfulness of breathing, and mindfulness occupied with the body—these twenty-two have the sign (nimitta) as their object. The remaining six—the four Divine Abidings, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of nothingness—have objects that are "not-to-be-called" (na-vattabba), meaning they are neither natural phenomena nor counterpart signs. Furthermore, the eight subjects—the livid (vipubbaka), the blood-stained (lohitaka), the worm-infested (puḷuvaka), mindfulness of breathing, the water kasina, the fire kasina, the air kasina, and the object of the circle of light from the sun etc. (entering through a lattice window etc.) in the light kasina—are "moving objects" (calitārammaṇa). Those eight meditation subjects are "moving" only in the preliminary stage (before the counterpart sign arises).
110:
The counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is indeed peaceful. The remaining thirty-eight meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) are unmoving objects. Thus, the decision should be understood by way of analyzing the object.

(7) "By way of plane (bhūmi)": In this regard, these twelve meditation subjects—the ten kinds of foulness (asubha), mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati), and the perception of repulsiveness in food (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā)—do not occur in the celestial planes of the sense sphere. These twelve and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), making thirteen, do not occur in the Brahma-world. In the formless (arūpa) plane, none occur except for the four formless states. In the human plane, all meditation subjects occur. Thus is the decision by way of plane.

(8) "By way of acquisition (gahana)": In this regard, the decision should be understood by way of acquisition through what is seen, what is touched, and what is heard among these forty meditation subjects. Among them, excluding the air kasiṇa (vāyokasiṇa), the remaining nine kasiṇas and the ten kinds of foulness—these nineteen—are to be acquired by sight. This means that in the preliminary stage, one should look with the eyes and grasp their sign (nimitta). In mindfulness occupied with the body, the skin-pentad (tacapañcaka) is to be acquired by sight, and the rest, such as the kidney-pentad (vakkapañcaka), by hearing (i.e., through description). Thus, the object of that mindfulness occupied with the body is to be acquired by sight and hearing. Mindfulness of breathing is to be acquired by touch. The air kasiṇa is to be acquired by sight and touch. The remaining eighteen meditation subjects are to be acquired by hearing. Among these forty meditation subjects, the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā-brahmavihāra) and the four formless states are not to be acquired by a beginner (at the start). The remaining thirty-five are to be acquired (by a beginner). Thus is the decision by way of acquisition.

(9) "By way of condition (paccaya)": In this regard, among these forty meditation subjects, excluding the space kasiṇa (ākāsakasiṇa), the remaining nine kasiṇas are conditions for the formless attainments. The ten kasiṇas are conditions for the direct knowledges (abhiññā). The first three divine abidings (brahmavihāra) are conditions for the fourth divine abiding. Each lower formless state is a condition for the one immediately above it. The base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). All meditation subjects are conditions for abiding in happiness in this very life, for insight (vipassanā), and for the excellence of future existence (bhavasampatti). Thus is the decision by way of condition.

(10) "By way of suitability to temperament (caritānukūla)": In this regard, the decision should be understood by way of suitability to temperaments among the forty meditation subjects. How is it suitable to temperaments? Among these forty meditation subjects, the eleven subjects consisting of the ten kinds of foulness and mindfulness occupied with the body are suitable for one of lustful temperament (rāgacarita). The eight subjects consisting of the four divine abidings and the four color kasiṇas (blue, yellow, red, and white) are suitable for one of hating temperament (dosacarita). Only the single meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing is suitable for one of deluded temperament (mohacarita) and for one of discursive temperament (vitakkacarita). The first six recollections (anussati) are suitable for one of faithful temperament (saddhācarita). The four subjects consisting of mindfulness of death (maraṇassati), the recollection of peace (upasamānussati), the definition of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna), and the perception of repulsiveness in food are suitable for one of intelligent temperament (buddhicarita). The remaining six kasiṇas and the four formless states are suitable for all temperaments. Furthermore, among the kasiṇas, any that is limited (small) is suitable for one of discursive temperament, and any that is measureless (large) is suitable for one of deluded temperament.
111:
Thus is the decision by way of suitability to temperament to be understood. This concludes one part.

Furthermore, all this (stated regarding suitability to temperament) is said by way of direct opposition and by way of extreme suitability. However, there is no wholesome development (kusalabhāvanā) that does not suppress lust and so on, or that does not benefit faith and so on. This was also said in the Meghiya Sutta:

“Four things should be further developed: Foulness (asubha) should be developed for the abandoning of lust (rāga). Loving-kindness (mettā) should be developed for the abandoning of ill-will (byāpāda). Mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati) should be developed for the cutting off of discursive thoughts (vitakka). The perception of impermanence (aniccasaññā) should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit 'I am' (asmimāna).”

This was taught (specifically for the Elder Meghiya).

In the Rāhula Sutta as well, seven meditation subjects were taught to the single person, the Venerable Rāhula, in the way beginning: “Rāhula, develop the meditation on loving-kindness.” Therefore, without being rigidly attached merely to the words, one should seek the intention in every instance. This is the decision in the discussion of meditation subjects under the phrase “having taken a meditation subject.”

48. The following is an explanation of the meaning of the word “having taken” (gahetvā). In the phrase “that meditator, having approached a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) who is a giver of a meditation subject,” one should approach a good friend of the kind already described (possessing qualities such as being lovable, venerable, etc.) and, having surrendered oneself to the Blessed Buddha or to the teacher, and being possessed of a fulfilled inclination and a fulfilled resolution, one should ask for a meditation subject.

In that regard, one should surrender oneself to the Blessed Buddha in this way: “Venerable Sir, I surrender this individuality (attabhāva) to you.” For if he does not surrender himself and lives in remote dwellings, he might be unable to stand firm when fearful objects come into focus; he might then return to the vicinity of a village, associate with laypeople, fall into wrong livelihood, and come to ruin. But for one who has surrendered his individuality, even when fearful objects come into focus, fear does not arise. Reflecting, “Wise man, did you not previously surrender yourself to the Buddha?”, joy alone arises in that meditator.
112:
For example, a person might possess a fine cloth made in the Kāsī country. If a rat or an insect were to bite that cloth, that person would become unhappy. However, if that person were to donate that cloth to a monk who has no robes, even if he sees that monk cutting the cloth into small pieces, only joy and gladness would arise in him. In the same way as this analogy, the meaning of the following should be understood.

A meditator who surrenders himself to the meditation teacher should also say, 'Venerable sir, I surrender this person (myself) to you.' The disadvantage of not surrendering in this way is that a meditator who has not surrendered himself to the teacher is someone the teacher has no right to rebuke. He becomes difficult to admonish, not following the teacher's advice. He goes wherever he pleases without asking the teacher, wandering as he likes. The teacher does not support such a meditator with material requisites or with the Dhamma (instruction), nor does he teach him the profound and difficult scriptures. Not receiving these two kinds of support, he finds no footing in the Sasana and soon falls into immorality or returns to the life of a layman. The benefit of surrendering is that a meditator who has surrendered himself to the teacher is someone the teacher has the right to rebuke. He does not go wherever he pleases without asking. Being easy to admonish, his livelihood and conduct remain dependent on the teacher. Receiving the two kinds of support from the teacher, he attains growth, increase, and prosperity in the Sasana, like the resident disciples of the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa.

It is said that three monks came to the presence of that Elder. Among them, one said, 'Venerable sir, if you were to say it is for your sake, I would dare to jump into a hundred-fathom deep abyss.' The second monk said, 'Venerable sir, if you were to say it is for your sake, I would dare to grind this body on a stone slab starting from the heels until nothing remains.' The third monk said, 'Venerable sir, if you were to say it is for your sake, I would dare to stop my inhalation and exhalation until I die.' The Elder, reflecting, 'These monks are indeed capable persons,' taught them a meditation subject. Those three monks, established in the advice of the Elder, all attained Arahantship. This is the benefit of surrendering oneself to the Buddha and the teacher. Therefore, I have said, 'Having surrendered oneself to the Blessed Buddha or to the teacher.'

49. Regarding the phrase 'being endowed with noble intentions and noble inclinations,' the meditator should be endowed with noble intentions through the six aspects such as non-greed. The benefit is that a person with such noble intentions attains one of the three types of Bodhi (Enlightenment: Sāvaka-bodhi, Pacceka-bodhi, or Sammā-sambodhi). As it is said:

'Six intentions of Bodhisattas lead to the ripening of their Bodhi. Bodhisattas with the intention of non-greed see the danger in greed.'
113:
'Bodhisattas with the intention of non-hatred see the danger in hatred. Bodhisattas with the intention of non-delusion see the danger in delusion. Bodhisattas with the intention of renunciation see the danger in household life. Bodhisattas with the intention of seclusion see the danger in society and defilements. Bodhisattas with the intention of escape see the danger in all realms of existence and destinies.'

The reason why one should be endowed with noble intentions in these six aspects is that all the Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, Arahants, Pacceka-buddhas, and Sammā-sambuddhas of the past, future, and present attained their respective distinctions only through these six aspects. Therefore, one should be endowed with noble intentions through these six aspects. Furthermore, one should be endowed with noble inclinations by leaning towards concentration and Nibbāna. This means being one who inclines towards concentration, values concentration, and leans towards concentration; and being one who inclines towards Nibbāna, values Nibbāna, and leans towards Nibbāna.

50. When a person endowed with such noble intentions and inclinations requests a meditation subject, a teacher who possesses the supernormal knowledge of encompassing the minds of others (cetopariya-ñāṇa) should know the student's temperament by observing the movements of his mind. A teacher who does not possess this knowledge should know the temperament by asking in ways such as: 'What is your temperament? What states occur frequently in you? Upon what state do you reflect with comfort? In which meditation subject does your mind take interest?' Having known this, he should teach a meditation subject suitable to the temperament.

When teaching the meditation subject, the teacher should teach in three ways: (1) For a meditator who has previously learned and reflected on it, he should have him recite it for one or two sessions in his presence and then give it. (2) For a meditator living nearby, he should teach it at every moment he comes. (3) For a meditator who wishes to go elsewhere after learning, he should teach it making it neither too brief nor too extensive.

Among those meditation subjects, when teaching the earth kasiṇa first, the teacher should explain nine aspects: the four faults of a kasiṇa, the making of the kasiṇa, the method of developing the completed kasiṇa, the two types of signs (nimitta), the two types of concentration (samādhi), the seven types of suitability and unsuitability, the ten skills in absorption (appanā-kosalla), the balancing of energy and concentration, and the procedure for absorption. In other meditation subjects as well, he should teach what is appropriate for each. All of this will be made clear in the section on the methods of development.
114: In this way, while the meditation subject is being taught, that yogi should listen by taking the sign (for the sake of remembering). In the phrase 'taking the sign,' it means: 'This is the preceding word, this is the following word, this is the [114] meaning of this word, this is the intended sense of this word, this is the simile'—thus binding and marking various aspects in the mind. Indeed, for a yogi who listens respectfully by taking the sign in this way, the meditation subject is well-grasped. When it is well-grasped, the attainment of special distinction is accomplished for that yogi by depending on that meditation subject; it is not so for another. This is the explanation of the meaning of the word 'taking.' By this sequence of words, the phrase 'having approached a good friend and having taken one of the forty meditation subjects suitable to one's own temperament' has been explained in detail in all its aspects. Here ends one part. This is the third chapter, called the Description of the Taking of the Meditation Subject, in the Section on the Development of Concentration in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the purpose of gladdening good people. ## The Description of the Taking of the Meditation Subject is finished.
115:
This is the third chapter, the "Description of Taking a Meditation Subject" (Kammaṭṭhānaggahana-niddesa), in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## The detailed description of taking a meditation subject is finished.

Note 1: This means the entire task of detailed exposition is complete.

## 4. Pathavīkasiṇa-niddesa
## Detailed Description of the Earth Kasiṇa

[115] 51. Now, regarding the statement: "Having left a dwelling unsuitable for the development of concentration and living in a suitable dwelling" (the following is the detailed explanation). A bhikkhu for whom it is comfortable and suitable to live in the same dwelling with his teacher should stay in that very dwelling where the teacher resides, while fully clearing up any difficulties in his meditation subject. If it is not comfortable or suitable there, and if there is another suitable dwelling at a distance of a gāvuta, half a yojana, or even a yojana, he should live there. The benefit of living thus is: if any doubt or forgetfulness arises regarding any part of the meditation subject, he can perform his duties at the monastery early in the morning, go for alms on the way, and only after finishing his meal, go to the teacher's residence. Having cleared up the meditation subject in the presence of the teacher for that whole day, he can pay respects to the teacher the next day, depart, go for alms on the way, and return to his own dwelling without fatigue. If he cannot find a comfortable and suitable place even within the distance of a yojana, that yogi should cut off all difficulties (knots) in the meditation subject, making it very pure and "connected to adverting" (so that it appears easily just by reflecting on it)¹, and then, even if he has to go far², he should leave the dwelling unsuitable for the development of concentration and live in a suitable dwelling.

## Unsuitable Dwelling

52. Between those two types—suitable and unsuitable dwellings—an unsuitable dwelling is one possessed of any one of the eighteen faults. These are the eighteen faults in that unsuitable dwelling:

(1) A large monastery³,
(2) A new monastery,
(3) A dilapidated monastery,

Note 1: "Connected to adverting" (āvajjanapaṭibaddhaṃ) means making it so that it appears easily and quickly just by reflecting or turning the mind to it. Therefore, it is translated as above.
Note 2: Connect "going... should live."
Note 3: Although "mahattaṃ" literally means "the state of being large," it is translated primarily as "a large monastery" because the literal translation might not be widely understood. In translating it as "a large monastery," the quality of "largeness" itself should be taken as a fault because it can be a disturbance to the yogi monk.

(4) A monastery near a main road¹,
(5) A monastery with a rock pool,
(6) A monastery with a vegetable garden,
(7) A monastery with flowering plants,
(8) A monastery with fruit trees,
(9) A monastery that is famous and sought after,
(10) A monastery near a city or village,
(11) A monastery with many trees and bamboos,
(12) A monastery connected to arable fields,
(13) A monastery where there are incompatible persons,
(14) A monastery near a port or landing place,
(15) A monastery in a remote border region,
(16) A monastery on the frontier of a kingdom,
116:
Note: In the case of a dilapidated monastery and so forth, it is the same; the specific attributes and characteristics of those monasteries, such as being new or being old and dilapidated, should be taken as faults.

1. *Panthanissita*—By the phrase 'depending on a road,' it means being near a main road; therefore, the meaning is translated accordingly. Later, the meanings of the terms *sannissita* and *sannissaya* are also translated according to their intended sense.

(17) An unsuitable monastery,
(18) A monastery without good friends—
Among these eighteen types of faults, a monastery endowed with any one of these faults is called an unsuitable monastery. One should not reside in such a monastery.

Why? (1) In a **large monastery** (*Mahāvihāra*), monks with various desires gather. Because they are in conflict with one another, they do not perform duties (such as at the *Bodhiyaṅgaṇa*); they do not sweep the Bodhi-tree platform and so forth, nor do they set out drinking water or water for use. In a monastery where these major and minor duties are not performed, when this yogi monk, [116] thinking 'I will go for alms in the village,' takes his bowl and robes and goes out, if he sees that the duties like sweeping the *Bodhiyaṅgaṇa* have not been done, or if he sees there is no water in the water pot, he must perform the duty; he must set out the water pot (by filling it). If he does not do so, he incurs an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkhaṭa*) due to the breach of duty. If he does perform them, time passes, and by the time he enters for alms late in the day, the alms-giving is finished and he receives nothing. If he returns to his place of seclusion, his mind becomes distracted by the loud voices of novices and young monks, and by the sounds of Sangha activities. However, if all duties are already performed and there are no other disturbances besides the duties, then one may reside in such a large monastery.

(2) In a **new monastery** (*Navavihāra*), there is much construction work (*navakamma*); they criticize a monk who does not participate. If the monks have said (given permission), 'Venerable sir, please strive in the recluse's Dhamma as you please; we will do the construction work,' then one may reside in such a new monastery.

(3) In an **old/dilapidated monastery** (*Jiṇṇavihāra*), there are many things to be cleaned and repaired; they criticize a monk who does not clean or repair at least his own sleeping place. For the monk who does the cleaning and repairing, his meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) declines.

(4) In a **monastery near a main road** (*Panthanissita*), visitors (*āgantuka*) gather day and night. One has to give one's own sleeping place to visitors who arrive at an improper time and (one must) live at the foot of a tree or on a stone slab. The next day is the same. Therefore, there is no opportunity to practice meditation. If there is no such crowding by visitors, then one may reside in such a monastery near a main road.

(5) In a **monastery with a rock pool** (*Soṇḍī*), many people gather to fetch water. The resident pupils of the King's teacher-elders who live in the city come for the purpose of dyeing work; to those monks who ask for dyeing pots, wood for boiling dye, and wooden dyeing troughs, etc., one must show them, saying 'in such and such a place.' Thus, at all times, one is constantly occupied.

Note: 1. Since the meaning of the term *soṇḍī* has been clearly translated as 'a monastery with a rock pool,' the explanation of that term is omitted here.

(6) In a **monastery with various vegetables**, even when that monk has taken his meditation subject and is sitting for the day-abiding, women gathering vegetables nearby sing songs while picking leaves, and by the impact of dissimilar sounds (*visabhāga-sadda*), they cause an obstacle to meditation.
117:
(7) In a **monastery where various flowering shrubs** are in full bloom, there is the same kind of danger that is encountered in the monastery with a vegetable patch.

[117] (8) In a **monastery with various fruits** such as mango, rose-apple, and jackfruit, those who want fruit come and beg; they get angry with a monk who does not give, or they take by force. In the evening, when a monk walking on the ambulatory in the middle of the monastery sees those picking fruit and says, 'Lay followers, why do you do this?', they insult him as they please. They also strive to make it impossible for that monk to stay (in that monastery).

(9) In a **monastery that is sought after** (by people) and designated as venerable, such as Dakkhiṇagiri, Hatthikucchi, Cetiyagiri, and Cittala-pabbata—

Note: 1. The reading *leṇasammate* in the new edition of the Visuddhimagga is not suitable; only the old reading *lokasammate* is suitable. It means a monastery designated as venerable by the public, such as a place where many Arahants have lived or a place where Arahants reside.

—people who wish to pay homage, praising the monk living there, saying 'This venerable one is an Arahant,' flock from all around. Therefore, it is not pleasant for that yogi. However, for a yogi for whom that monastery is suitable, he should go elsewhere during the day and stay there at night.

(10) In a **monastery near a city** (*Nagarasannissita*), incompatible objects (*visabhāgārammaṇa*) appear. Water-carrying slave girls also go about bumping into one another with their water pots; they do not step aside to give way. Powerful people also sit in the middle of the monastery after surrounding themselves with screens.

(11) In a **monastery near wood/timber** (*Dārusannissaya*), where there is firewood and trees suitable for making parts of buildings like houses, women gathering firewood cause unpleasantness (to the meditation) just like the women gathering vegetables mentioned before. Thinking 'We will cut the trees in the monastery and build houses,' people come and cut (those trees). If—

Note: 1. Here, *visabhāga*—incompatible object—since it is for a monk, seems to intend only the object of a woman which causes lust. However, in the Commentary (*Ṭīkā*), it is explained: 'Incompatible objects include both desirable objects (*iṭṭhārammaṇa*) and undesirable objects (*aniṭṭhārammaṇa*). Indeed, to show the appearance of undesirable objects, it says "bumping into one another with water pots" and so forth.'

—the yogi monk, while coming out of the meditation hall in the evening and walking on the ambulatory in the middle of the monastery, sees those people and says, 'Lay followers, why do you do this?', they insult him as they please. They also strive to make it impossible for that monk to stay.

(12) In a **monastery connected to fields** (*Khettasannissita*), being surrounded by fields on all sides, people make a threshing floor in the very middle of the monastery and thresh grain. They sleep in the porches. They also cause many other kinds of unpleasantness. Also, in a monastery where there is much Sangha property in the form of fields, the monastery attendants block the donors' cattle (to prevent them from eating the crops) and prohibit the donors' turn for irrigation water. People bring ears of paddy and show them to the Sangha, saying, 'Look at the actions of your monastery attendants.' For various such reasons, one has to go to the doors of the houses of kings and great ministers. Such a monastery is also included in the 'monastery connected to fields.'

(13) **Presence of incompatible persons**: where monks who are mutually incompatible enemies reside. Those who, when being restrained while quarreling, saying 'Venerable sirs, do not do this,' say, 'Since the time this rag-robe wearer (*pāṃsukūlika*) arrived, we have been ruined.'
118:
(13) Monasteries with incompatible people: These are monasteries where monks live as enemies due to mutual incompatibility. When [a yogi monk] tries to mediate during their quarrels, saying, "Venerable sirs, do not do this," they are likely to say, "We have been ruined ever since this rag-robe-wearing monk arrived."

Note 1: The literal meaning of 'parivārito' is 'surrounded.' However, to make it understandable for those not proficient in Pali, it has been slightly modified in the translation above.

(14) Monasteries near a water-port or a land-port: People constantly arriving by boat or cart cause discomfort by [frequently requesting], "Give us a place to stay, give us drinking water, give us salt."

(15) Monasteries in border regions: People do not have faith in the Triple Gem, such as the Buddha.

(16) Monasteries near national boundaries: There is danger from kings. A king might strike that region, thinking, "This place is not under my authority," and the other king does the same. This monk sometimes wanders in the territory of one king and sometimes in the other's. While so wandering, they might bring him to ruin, thinking, "This man is a spy (carapuriso)."

(17) Unsuitable monasteries: These are unsuitable due to the convergence of disagreeable objects like unsuitable sights (visabhāga-rūpa), or because they are possessed by non-human beings (amanussa). Here is a story regarding this unsuitability: An Elder lived in a forest monastery. A female yakkha (yakkhinī) stood at the door of his leaf-hut and sang. The Elder went out and stood at the door. She went and sang at the head of the walkway (caṅkamana). The Elder went to the head of the walkway. She stood at the edge of a cliff a hundred men deep (sataporisa) and sang. The Elder turned back. Then she came swiftly, grabbed the Elder [by the shoulder], and said, "Venerable sir, I have eaten not just one or two monks like you, but many."

(18) Monasteries where good friends are not obtained: This refers to a monastery where one cannot find a good friend (kalyāṇamitta) such as a teacher, one equal to a teacher, a preceptor (upajjhāya), or one equal to a preceptor. Not finding such good friends in that monastery is indeed a great fault [for meditation]. Thus, a monastery possessed of any one of these eighteen faults should be understood as "unsuitable." There are also these words [three verses] mentioned in the Commentaries:

"A large monastery, a new one, a dilapidated one, one near a road, one with a pond, one with leafy greens, one with flowers, one with fruits, one that is famous, one near a city, one with timber, one near a field, one with incompatible people, one near a water-port or land-port, one in a border region, one near a national boundary, one that is unsuitable, and one where a friend is not found—a wise man, knowing these eighteen places to be unsuitable for meditation, should avoid them from afar, just as one avoids a dangerous path."
119:
## Suitable Monastery

53. A monastery endowed with five factors, such as being neither too far from nor too near to an alms-resort village, is called a suitable monastery. Indeed, it was said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, how is a lodging endowed with five factors? Here, monks, (1) a lodging is neither too far nor too near, and is well-provided with a route for coming and going; (2) it is not crowded with people by day and is quiet by night, free from noise and tumult; (3) there is little contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, burning sun, and reptiles; (4) for a monk living in that lodging, the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal supports for the sick arise easily and without difficulty; (5) in that lodging, there dwell elder monks who are learned (bahussuta), masters of the scriptures (āgatāgama), experts in the Dhamma (dhammadhara), experts in the Vinaya (vinayadhara), and experts in the Summaries (mātikādhara), who are established in virtues such as firm morality. From time to time, he approaches them and asks: 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' He inquires about the Pali text and the meaning. Those venerable ones then reveal what was not revealed, clarify what was not clear, and dispel doubts regarding various doubtful points of the Dhamma. In this way, monks, a lodging is endowed with five factors." (Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.11).

This is the detailed explanation of the phrase: "Having abandoned a monastery unsuitable for the development of concentration and dwelling in a suitable monastery."

## Severing Minor Impediments

54. Regarding the phrase "having severed minor impediments": A monk dwelling in a suitable monastery as described should also sever whatever minor impediments (khuddaka-palibodha) he may have. What are these minor impediments? Long hair, nails, and beard should be cut. Patching or sewing should be done on worn-out robes. Dirty ones should be dyed. If there is a stain on the bowl, the bowl should be baked. Beds, chairs, and so on should be cleaned. These are the minor impediments. This is the detailed explanation of the phrase: "having severed minor impediments."

## Meditation Procedure

55. Now, regarding the phrase "one should develop [meditation] without neglecting any part of the meditation procedure": This is the detailed explanation according to all meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), beginning with the Earth Kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa).
120:
[120] As described, a yogi who has cut off minor impediments (palibodha), having returned from the alms-round after the meal and dispelled the drowsiness caused by the food, should sit comfortably in a secluded place and take the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) from either prepared earth or unprepared natural earth. Indeed, the following has been stated (in the ancient commentaries):

“A yogi who learns the earth kasiṇa takes the sign in a specific type of earth: whether it is prepared or unprepared; it must be limited, not unlimited; with boundaries, not without boundaries; circular, not non-circular; with a periphery, not without a periphery; the size of a small winnowing basket or the size of a large pot-lid. That monk takes that learning sign well (so that it appears clearly even when his eyes are closed), grasps it firmly so that it remains in his memory, and defines it by contemplating it repeatedly. Having taken that learning sign well, grasped it firmly, and defined it by contemplating it repeatedly, seeing the benefits and perceiving it as a treasure, he arouses a sense of respect, and being full of endearment, he binds his mind to that object of the learning sign, thinking: ‘Surely, by this practice, I shall be freed from aging and death.’ That yogi, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... enters and dwells in the first jhāna.”

In the above commentary passage (in detail), for a monk who, in a past life, either in the Dispensation (of a Buddha) or having gone forth as a hermit, has previously produced the fourfold or fivefold jhānas in the earth kasiṇa—for such a meritorious yogi endowed with strong supporting conditions—the learning sign arises even on unprepared ground, such as in a plowed area or on a threshing floor, as it did for the Elder Mallaka. It is said that while that venerable one was looking at a plowed area, the learning sign arose for him, having the same extent as that area. That Elder, having expanded that sign and produced the fivefold jhānas, and having established insight (vipassanā) with the jhāna as a basis, attained Arahantship.

However, a yogi who has not performed such previous practice should make a kasiṇa disk while avoiding the four defects of the kasiṇa, without deviating from the method of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) learned in the presence of a teacher. The defects of the earth kasiṇa are fourfold, due to the mixture of blue, yellow, red, and white colors. Therefore, without taking clay of colors such as blue, etc., one should make the kasiṇa disk with fine dawn-colored clay, similar to the clay found in the banks eroded by the current of the Ganges River. Furthermore, that kasiṇa disk should not be made in the middle of the monastery in a place where novices and others walk about. It should be made in a secluded place at the edge of the monastery, in a mountain cleft or in a leaf-hut, either as a portable kasiṇa or as a fixed one.
121:
Of these two types of kasina disks, the portable one should be made by tying a rag, leather, or a matting to four sticks. On that rag, etc., one should apply well-kneaded fine clay, from which grass, roots, pebbles, and potsherds have been removed, in a circle of the aforementioned size (a small winnowing basket or a large saucer lid). When first practicing, this portable kasina disk should be spread on the ground and looked at. As for the fixed kasina disk, it should be made by driving stakes into the ground in the shape of a lotus calyx and binding them with creepers.

If that dawn-colored clay is insufficient, other clay should be placed underneath, and on the upper part, a circle of well-purified dawn-colored clay, one span and four fingers in diameter, should be made. Referring to this very size, it was said: "the size of a small winnowing basket or the size of a large saucer lid." The words "limited, not unlimited," etc., were said for the purpose of defining the extent of that kasina disk.

56. Therefore, having defined the extent as mentioned, and because a wooden hand-tool (such as one made of sandalwood) produces a color dissimilar to the dawn-colored clay, one should not use it but instead rub it with a stone hand-tool to make it smooth like the surface of a drum. Having done so, one should sweep that place, bathe, return, and sit on a well-spread chair with legs a span and four fingers high, placed at a distance of two and a half cubits from the kasina disk. For the yogi sitting further than two and a half cubits, the kasina does not appear clearly. For one sitting closer than that, the defects of the kasina become apparent. If sitting on a chair that is higher than that, one has to look down by bending the neck. If sitting on a chair that is lower than that, the knees become painful. 

Therefore, having sat in the manner described, one should contemplate the danger in sense pleasures through the method beginning with "Sense pleasures provide little gratification." Then, having aroused a desire for renunciation (nekkhamma), which is the means of escape from sense pleasures and the way to transcend all suffering, and having generated joy and happiness by recollecting the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, one should arouse respect for the practice, thinking: "This is the path of renunciation practiced by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Noble Disciples." Then, having aroused effort, thinking: "I shall surely share the taste of the bliss of seclusion (viveka-sukha)," one should open the eyes in a moderate manner and develop the practice by taking the sign (nimitta).

For the yogi who opens the eyes too wide, the eyes become fatigued, and the disk becomes too distinct; thus, the sign does not arise for him. For one who opens the eyes too narrowly, the disk is not distinct, and the mind becomes sluggish; in this way, too, the sign does not arise. Therefore, like one looking at the reflection of his face on the surface of a mirror, one should open the eyes in a moderate manner, take the sign, and develop it. The color should not be contemplated, nor should the characteristic (of hardness) be given attention. Rather, [122] without letting go of the color, one should make it have the appearance of the supporting earth, and giving attention to the over-prominent quality (of the earth element), one should place the mind on the conceptual designation (paññatti) 'earth' (pathavī).
122:
Among the names for earth such as pathavī, mahī, medinī, bhūmi, vasudhā, and vasundharā, one should recite the name that one desires and that is suitable to one's [previous] perception. However, since the name 'pathavī' is the most well-known, one should develop it using this well-known name as "Pathavī, pathavī" (Earth, earth).

Note 1: This is an instruction to avoid mixing with color kasinas.
Note 2: This is an instruction to avoid mixing with the definition of elements (dhātu-vavatthāna).
Note 3: This is translated based on the Tika explanation found in the Pyay edition: "In the same manner as the support... it means one should attend to it as 'earth' together with the color, following the nature of that earth which the color depends on." It means one should contemplate it as 'earth' according to the shape of the earth-kasina disk.

One should contemplate it, opening the eyes at one time and closing them at another. As long as the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) does not arise, one should continue to develop it in this manner for a hundred times, a thousand times, or even more.

57. For the monk developing it in this way, when the sign appears to him while his eyes are closed just as it did when they were open, then the learning sign is said to have arisen. From the time that learning sign has arisen, he should no longer sit in that place. He should enter his own dwelling and develop it while sitting there. To avoid the delay of washing his feet, he should have single-soled sandals and a walking stick (to protect against dangers). If his tender concentration is lost due to some unsuitable cause, he should put on his sandals, take his walking stick, go to that place, grasp the sign, return, and sitting comfortably, develop it. He should apply his mind to it again and again; he should strike it with thought (takkāhata) and strike it with applied thought (vitakkāhata). 

Note 1: Takkāhata - struck by thought + āhata - struck/hit. Striking with thought means attending to and thinking about the object effectively, just as one strikes or hits with a stick. Therefore, the Tika says: "Takkāhata vitakkāhata means... one should repeatedly perform the act of striking the meditation object with right thought (sammā-saṅkappa)... one should many times arouse the attention which is powerful thought."

As he does so, by the sequence of development, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are suppressed, the defilements (kilesa) subside, the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) arises.

Note 1: In this context, there is no other sequence of development besides preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā) and access development (upacāra-bhāvanā). Therefore, it means that as the development becomes stronger, the hindrances such as sensual desire become fewer and more sparse until they are removed. Thus, the Tika says: "Anukkamena - gradually - means by the sequence of development... when the faculties such as faith become very pure and sharp... the factors of jhāna which are only of the sense sphere, such as applied thought, appear many times."

Between the learning sign and the counterpart sign, this is the difference: in the learning sign, the defects of the kasina (such as finger marks or the edge of the disk) are apparent. But the counterpart sign appears like a mirror-disk taken out of a bag, like a well-washed conch-shell, like the moon's disk coming out from behind a cloud, or like cranes against a rain cloud. It appears as if it has broken through the learning sign and come out, being a hundred times, a thousand times more purified. Furthermore, it has neither color nor shape. If it were such, it would be cognizable by eye-consciousness, gross, subject to comprehension [by the three marks], and struck by the three marks. But it is not like that. It is merely a mode of appearance for one who has attained concentration, born of perception. This is the difference between the counterpart sign and the learning sign.

Note: Seven powers (bala) support it, and the jhāna factors such as applied thought (vitakka), which are only of the sense sphere, appear many times.

58. From the time it arises, the hindrances are indeed suppressed, the defilements have subsided, and the mind is concentrated with access concentration.
123:
Therefore, the hindrances such as sensual desire, which are the direct opposites of those jhāna factors, along with the unwholesome states that share the same basis, become remote. Simultaneously with the arising and appearance of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta), access concentration (upacāra-jhāna) arises, taking that counterpart sign as its object. Thus, it is explained: "the hindrances are abandoned," and so forth.

The benefit is that from the time the counterpart sign appears, the hindrances are already abandoned, and the defilements that share the same basis are also suppressed. The mind is well-established by access concentration. This concludes one section.

[123] Indeed, concentration is of two kinds: access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and attainment concentration (appanā-samādhi). The mind is unified and well-established in two ways: at the stage of access and at the stage of attainment (due to remoteness from the opposites of jhāna and reaching firmness). In these two stages, at the stage of access, the mind is well-established through the abandoning of the hindrances. At the stage of attainment, it is well-established through the manifestation of the jhāna factors.

Note:
1. This is the meaning of "pana" as stated in the Pyay edition. In connection with the preceding statement "the counterpart sign arises," which shows the initial arising of the counterpart sign, it should also be a statement that shows the specific details after the counterpart sign has arisen.
2. It means the hindrances have already been abandoned, the task of abandoning is finished, and there is no longer a need to strive to abandon them.
3. "Tadekaṭṭha"—defilements that share the same basis with those hindrances—are of two kinds: "sahajātakaṭṭha," defilements associated within a single consciousness-arising, and "pahānekaṭṭha," similar defilements occurring within the same continuity.

The following explains the distinction and the ability to differentiate between access concentration and attainment concentration. In access concentration, the jhāna factors are not yet strong. Because the jhāna factors are not yet strong, just as a young child, though lifted and set on his feet, falls to the ground again and again, so too, when access concentration arises, the mind sometimes takes the counterpart sign as its object and sometimes sinks into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). In attainment concentration, however, the factors are strong. Because the factors are strong, just as a strong man might rise from his seat and stand all day, so too, when attainment concentration arises, the mind, having once cut off the flow of the life-continuum, remains for the whole night or the whole day, proceeding only by way of the sequence of wholesome impulsion (kusala-javana). This is the reason for their distinction.

Between the two, the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta), the arising of the counterpart sign together with access concentration is extremely difficult. Therefore, if one can develop that sign and reach attainment in that very sitting, it is well. If not, the monk must guard that sign with diligence, like the embryo of a universal monarch. For it is said:

Note:
1. "Bhavaṅgavāra"—the turn of the life-continuum—refers here to the flow of the life-continuum that occurs continuously in its turn. Therefore, it is translated as above.

For the yogi who guards the counterpart sign, there is no loss of the counterpart sign already gained. In the absence of such guarding, what is gained is repeatedly lost.

## Explanation of the Seven Suitable Things

59. In this context, the following is the method of guarding:

Dwelling, resort, speech, person, food, climate, and posture—these seven unsuitable things (asappāya) should be avoided.

One should cultivate the seven suitable things (sappāya). For one practicing thus, attainment (appanā-jhāna) arises before long for some yogis.

Among these (seven things such as dwelling, etc.), a dwelling where the sign has not arisen does not arise, or where the arisen sign perishes, where unestablished mindfulness does not become established, and the unconcentrated mind does not become concentrated—this is an unsuitable dwelling. A dwelling where the sign arises and becomes firm, [124] where mindfulness is established and the mind becomes concentrated—as happened to the Elder Padhāniya-Tissa residing at Nāgapabbata monastery—this is a suitable dwelling. Therefore, in a monastery with many dwellings, one should try living in each for three days, and stay in the one where the yogi attains concentration.
124:
To demonstrate the benefit of such living, five hundred monks residing in the Cūḷanāga Cave on the island of Tambapaṇṇi attained Arahantship right there in that Cūḷanāga Cave, having taken up their meditation subject due to the suitability of the dwelling. Furthermore, the number of those such as Stream-enterers and so forth [Note 1], as well as those who, having reached the stage of Noble Ones elsewhere, attained Arahantship in that Cūḷanāga Cave, is beyond count—it is very many. The same applies to other places like the Cittalapabbata Monastery and so forth.

Note 1: This is the meaning of the term 'Sotāpannādīnaṃ' according to the Nissaya of the Pyay version. According to this meaning, it should be understood that the number of individuals who became Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners in that cave is also very many. However, since it does not say 'Sotāpattiphalādippattānaṃ' (those who reached the fruit of stream-entry, etc.) in the same way as 'Arahattappattānaṃ' (those who reached Arahantship), whether this meaning accords with the intention of the Commentator should still be considered. It could also be a statement showing only that the number of individuals such as Stream-enterers, etc., who had already attained those stages in other places and then reached Arahantship in this cave, is many.
