According to that intention, this sentence should be translated as: 'Furthermore, the number of Stream-enterers and so forth who, having already reached the stage of Noble Ones (such as the fruit of stream-entry) in other monasteries and places, then reached Arahantship in that Cūḷanāga Cave, is beyond count—it is very many.'

Furthermore, an alms-resort village that is located either to the north or to the south [Note 1] of the monastery, not too far away—within a distance of one and a half kosas [Note 2]—and where suitable alms-food is easily obtainable [Note 3], is suitable. The opposite is unsuitable.

Note 1: Indicating that the monastery and the alms-resort village should be situated to the north and south is to prevent facing the sun directly while going to and returning from alms-round.
Note 2: One and a half kosas is 600 rods (tā) by the 7-cubit measure; it is 1050 rods by the 4-cubit dhanu-tā measure. In the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā), it is stated as a distance of 1000 dhanu-tā. This statement likely follows the paribhāṣā rule that 'a slight deficiency or excess is not counted,' thus not counting the extra 50 rods.
Note 3: 'Sulabhasampannabhikkho'—literally 'there is easily obtainable and complete alms-food'—is translated as above to make it easier to understand.

Regarding speech, talk that is included within the thirty-two types of 'animal talk' [Note 4] (which are contrary to heaven and the path to liberation) is unsuitable. The fault is that such unsuitable talk leads to the disappearance of the yogi's acquired sign (nimitta) [Note 1]. Talk based on the ten subjects of talk (kathāvatthu) [Note 2] (such as fewness of wishes, etc.) is suitable, but even such suitable talk should be spoken in moderation.

Note 4: Here, the thirty-two types of contrary talk are: talk about kings, thieves, ministers/officials, armies, dangers, battles, food, drink, clothing, beds, garlands, perfumes, relatives, vehicles, villages, market towns, cities, districts, women, (men), heroes, streets, watering places, the dead, miscellaneous talk, the world, the ocean, and talk about becoming and non-becoming (prosperity and decline). These contrary talks can be seen in the Burmese translation of the Sīlakkhandhavagga Pāḷi, page 7, etc. To complete the thirty-two types, the Sub-commentary indicates adding talk about forests, mountains, rivers, and islands.
Note 1: The literal translation 'leads to the disappearance of the acquired sign' is replaced as above to make it clearer for some readers.
Note 2: The ten subjects of talk are: (1) Appicchatā—fewness of wishes, (2) Santuṭṭhi—contentment, (3) Paviveka—seclusion, (4) Asaṃsagga—non-association, (5) Vīriyārambha—arousing energy, (6-10) Sīla (virtue), Samādhi (concentration), Paññā (wisdom), Vimutti (liberation), and Vimuttiñāṇadassana (knowledge and vision of liberation). Talk related to fewness of wishes, etc., is also called 'kathāvatthu'; see footnote (1) on page 292 regarding the showing of 'attachment to families' (kulapalibodha).

A suitable person is one who does not speak contrary talk (to heaven and liberation) and is endowed with virtues such as morality (sīla). Depending on such a person, the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated, and the concentrated mind becomes firmer. Such a person is suitable. However, a person who is frequently occupied with physical fitness and who speaks contrary talk is unsuitable. The fault is that just as muddy water makes clear water turbid, such a person (makes the yogi defiled); depending on such a person, even the attainment (samāpatti) of the young monk residing at Koṭapabbata Monastery was lost—what then need be said of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta)?

Regarding food, for some yogis, sweet food is suitable; for others, sour food is suitable. Regarding climate, for some yogis, a cold climate is suitable; for others, a hot climate is suitable. Therefore, whatever food or climate one uses that results in comfort, where the unconcentrated mind becomes concentrated and the concentrated mind becomes firmer, that food and that climate are suitable. Food and climate other than these are unsuitable.

Among the postures, for some yogis, walking is suitable; for others, one of the postures of lying, standing, or sitting is suitable.
125:
Therefore, just as (investigating) the monastery, one should investigate that posture (among the various postures) for three days each (by practicing) and know: "The posture that makes the unconcentrated mind concentrated and makes the already concentrated mind firmer is suitable (for the yogi). Postures other than this are unsuitable."

In this way, having avoided the seven kinds of unsuitable things (asappāya) and having cultivated the seven kinds of suitable things (sappāya), for some yogis who practice thus and frequently cultivate the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta), absorption (appanā) arises before long.

## Ten Skills for Absorption

60. For the yogi who, despite practicing in this way, does not achieve absorption, he should fulfill the ten kinds of skill in absorption called appanā-kosalla. In fulfilling them, this is the method of knowing; skill in absorption should be desired through ten ways:
(1) Cleansing the physical basis,
(2) Balancing the faculties,
(3) Skill in the sign,
(4) Exerting the mind when it should be exerted,
(5) Restraining the mind when it should be restrained,

## (1) Cleansing the Physical Basis

61. Therein, "cleansing the physical basis" means making the internal and external physical bases clean. To elaborate:
When the hair, fingernails, toenails, and beard are long, or when the body is smeared with sweat and dirt, the internal physical basis is unclean and impure. When that yogi's robes are worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling, or when the monastery is cluttered with rubbish, the external physical basis is unclean and impure. When the internal and external physical bases are unclean, the wisdom (associated with) the consciousness and mental factors that arise is also unclean and impure. (To give an example) It is like the light of a lamp flame produced depending on an impure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. For the yogi who contemplates formations with impure wisdom, the formations also do not appear clearly. For the yogi who is devoted to the meditation subject, the meditation subject also does not reach growth (by the clear appearance of its factors), development (by mastery), or abundance (by reaching complete proficiency in every way). 

However, when these internal and external physical bases are clean, the wisdom (associated with) the consciousness and mental factors that arise is also clean and pure. (To give an example) It is like the light of a lamp flame produced depending on a pure lamp-bowl, wick, and oil. For the yogi who contemplates formations with pure wisdom, the formations also appear clearly. For the yogi who is devoted to the meditation subject, the meditation subject reaches growth, development, and abundance.

## (2) Balancing the Faculties

62. "Balancing the faculties" means making the faculties such as faith and so on equal (in their functions), neither deficient nor excessive.
If, for that yogi, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is strong and the other faculties are weak, then because of that (strength of faith and weakness of others), the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) cannot perform the function of exerting, the faculty of mindfulness (satindriya) cannot perform the function of establishing (on the object), the faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) cannot perform the function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) cannot perform the function of seeing and knowing. Therefore, the faculty of faith should be diminished by investigating the nature of things (such as cause and effect) and by not attending to the meditation subject in a way that increases the faculty of faith.
126:
In the case of excessive faith, the story of the Elder Vakkali is an example. If—

Note 1: By contemplating the nature of the Dhamma—this means that when one focuses on the noble qualities of a person who is an object of faith and devotion, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) becomes powerful due to the intensity of that conviction. It means investigating and contemplating the cause and effect of that object of devotion according to reality (as it is). (Sub-commentary). In this sub-commentary, "cause and effect, etc." includes the analysis of hair, body hair, etc., or the five aggregates as mere mind and matter, or as mere impermanence, suffering, and non-self. If one contemplates by such analysis, the person and qualities to be devoted to disappear, and thus excessive devotion can be reduced.

Note 2: By not attending in that manner—this means that if the faculty of faith is strong for a yogi who practices meditation in a certain way, it should be reduced by not practicing meditation in that same way. (Sub-commentary).

Note 3: The Elder Vakkali, having made a resolution for the position of one foremost in faith (saddhādhimutta) and performed special meritorious deeds, was extremely devoted to the Blessed One. Therefore, he spent his time only striving to behold the physical body (rūpakāya) of the Buddha. He did not strive in the practice of meditation. Thus, at a suitable time, the Blessed One gave him an exhortation, saying, "Vakkali, what is the use of you looking at this foul body of mine? He who sees the Dhamma sees me, Vakkali," and so on, and urged him to practice meditation. However, because he did not practice and remained only near the Buddha, the Buddha dismissed him to go elsewhere. At that time, the Elder Vakkali became very distressed and climbed a cliff on Mount Gijjhakūṭa to commit suicide by jumping off. Then the Blessed One, while staying at the Veḷuvana monastery, emitted a radiance to let Vakkali see him and—

Spoke this verse: "The monk who is full of joy and has faith in the Buddha's Dispensation can reach the state of peace (Santa-pada), which is the cessation of formations, the bliss of Nibbāna."

And said, "Vakkali, come!" Then the Elder Vakkali, feeling as if he were sprinkled with the nectar of immortality, became joyful and developed insight (vipassanā). However, because his faith was too strong, he was unable to enter the correct path of insight. Then the Blessed One, bringing about the balance of the faculties, purified the meditation subject for him. The Elder Vakkali, practicing insight by the method given by the Blessed One, attained the fruit of Arahantship through the sequence of the paths. (Sub-commentary). This story can also be seen in the Dhammapada Commentary (Vol. 2, p. 380), though it differs slightly. In the Vakkali Sutta of the Khandhavagga Saṃyutta (p. 97), it is stated that the Elder Vakkali was seriously ill in a potter's house, that the Blessed One visited and gave him exhortation, and that he then moved to the Isigili slope. There, the Elder Vakkali took his own life with a razor, but while doing so, he practiced insight and became an Arahant before passing away (parinibbāna).

—if the faculty of energy (vīriyindriya) is too strong, the faculty of faith cannot perform its function of conviction, nor can the faculty of mindfulness, etc., perform their specific functions such as establishing themselves on the object. Therefore, that faculty of energy should be reduced by developing the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga), etc. In the case of excessive energy, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be shown as an example.

Note 1: The Venerable Elder Soṇa, who had ordained from the life of a wealthy man's son and was so delicate that hair grew on the soles of his feet, took a meditation subject from the Blessed One. While staying in the Sitavana cemetery near Rājagaha, he thought, "My body is delicate; it is not possible to attain the bliss of Nibbāna by living comfortably and easily. I should practice the monk's Dhamma even by exhausting my body." He then undertook only standing and walking meditation. Although blisters developed on the soles of his feet, he ignored the painful feelings and made firm effort. Because his energy was excessive, he was unable to attain the higher Dhamma. Then the Blessed One went to that Sitavana cemetery and admonished him with the simile of the lute, showing him the method of balancing energy and purifying his meditation subject. The Blessed One then returned to Mount Gijjhakūṭa. The Venerable Elder Soṇa, applying the balance of energy according to the method given by the Blessed One, practiced insight and was established in the fruit of Arahantship. (Sub-commentary). Details are in the Cammakkhandhaka of the Mahāvagga Pāḷi, Vinaya Piṭaka.

Similarly, among the remaining faculties, it should be understood that if one faculty is too strong, the others are unable to perform their own functions. In particular, among these five faculties, the equality of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is praised (by the teachers). For one with strong faith but weak wisdom is blindly devoted; he is devoted to a person without merit. Or, he is foolishly devoted without investigation. He is devoted to an object that is not worthy of devotion. One with strong wisdom but weak faith tends towards the side of craftiness; like a disease caused by medicine, he is difficult to cure. When both faith and wisdom are balanced, one is devoted only to an object worthy of devotion.

Note 1: Here, the first meaning corresponds to the reading 'mudhappasanno' (devoted to the useless). The second meaning corresponds to the reading 'muddhappasanno' (foolishly devoted). 'Mudha' means uselessly, or towards a useless person + 'pasanno' means devoted. Here, the meaning of being devoted to a useless person—one not worthy of devotion—agrees with the subsequent words 'avatthusmiṃ pasīdati' (he is devoted to an object not worthy of devotion). However, in the words 'Supabbā nāma upāsikā mudhappasannā' (the laywoman named Supabbā is uselessly devoted) found in the Vinīta-vatthu of the first Pārājika in the Vinaya Pāḷi, only the meaning of being devoted uselessly or without benefit seems appropriate. The second meaning, 'foolishly devoted without investigation,' agrees with the sub-commentary's explanation 'na aveccappasanno' (not devoted through penetrating with wisdom and investigation).

Note 2: 'Kerāṭika-pakkhaṃ' means he approaches the side of craftiness. With weak faith and through speculative reasoning, he thinks, "Even without giving a gift, just by thinking about it, the merit of dāna occurs," and so on. He is deceived by false reasons. Because such a person's speculative thinking has robbed and destroyed his good intentions, he does not listen to the words of the wise. Even when explained with logical reasons, he no longer reaches a state of understanding. Therefore, it is said, "Like a disease caused by medicine, he is difficult to cure." (Sub-commentary).

Since concentration has the nature of laziness, one with strong concentration but weak energy is overcome by laziness. Since energy has the nature of restlessness, one with strong energy but weak concentration is overcome by restlessness (uddhacca). If concentration is balanced with energy, it cannot fall into the side of laziness. If energy is balanced with concentration, it cannot fall into the side of restlessness. Therefore, both faith and wisdom, and concentration and energy, should be made equal in their functions. The benefit is that when these two pairs are balanced, absorption (appanā) occurs.

Alternatively, for one who practices serenity (samatha), even strong faith is suitable. Believing that "the method taught by the Blessed One will surely be fulfilled," and being fully convinced (sinking into the object), the yogi practicing serenity will reach absorption. Between concentration and wisdom, for a yogi practicing serenity, strong concentration is suitable. In this way, with strong concentration, that yogi reaches absorption. For a yogi practicing insight (vipassanā), strong wisdom is suitable. In this way, with strong wisdom, that yogi reaches the penetration of the characteristics (such as impermanence). However, by the equality of both concentration and wisdom, absorption also certainly occurs.

Mindfulness (sati), however, is suitable when it is strong in all instances. For strong mindfulness protects the mind from falling into restlessness through the power of faith, energy, and wisdom, which belong to the side of restlessness. It protects the mind from falling into laziness due to concentration, which belongs to the side of laziness. Therefore, that mindfulness is desired in all meditation subjects, just as salt is desired in all dishes, or as a chief minister who understands all affairs is desired in all royal duties. Or rather, it is desired in all states of shrinking or scattering. Therefore (in the Commentary) it is said:

"But mindfulness has been said by the Blessed One to be required everywhere. For what reason? Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; without mindfulness, there is no exerting or restraining of the mind."

## 4. Exerting the Mind

[127] 64. How is the mind exerted at the time it should be exerted? When the mind is sluggish due to excessively lax energy and so forth, one exerts it by not developing the three factors such as the enlightenment factor of tranquility, but by developing the three enlightenment factors such as investigation of states. Indeed, the Blessed One has spoken these words:

“Monks, suppose a man wants to make a small fire blaze up. He throws wet grass, wet cow-dung, and wet wood into it; he blows on it with water-laden wind and sprinkles it with dust. Monks, would that man be able to make that small fire blaze up?” “No, venerable sir.” “In the same way, monks, when the mind is sluggish, it is the wrong time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility; it is the wrong time to develop the enlightenment factor of concentration... it is the wrong time to develop the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Why is that? Because, monks, the mind is sluggish, and it is difficult to arouse it with these states. But, monks, when the mind is sluggish, it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of investigation of states; it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of energy; it is the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of joy. Why is that? Because, monks, the mind is sluggish, and it is easy to arouse it with these states. Monks, suppose a man wants to make a small fire blaze up. He throws dry grass, dry cow-dung, and dry wood into it; he blows on it with his mouth and does not sprinkle it with dust. Monks, would that man be able to make that small fire blaze up?” “Yes, venerable sir.” (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.234).

By producing these states in these ways as mentioned, one is said to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga), etc. Restraining the mind when it should be restrained is also done in this manner.

## (6) Gladdening the Mind

66. How is the mind gladdened when it should be gladdened? When the practitioner's meditation mind is devoid of joy due to weak application of wisdom or failure to attain the bliss of peace, then one should gladden and strengthen that mind by reflecting on the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (saṃvega-vatthu). The eight grounds for spiritual urgency are: (1-4) birth, aging, sickness, and death; (5) the suffering of the woeful planes; (6) the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the past; (7) the suffering rooted in the round of rebirths in the future; and (8) the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present life. Furthermore,

Notes:
1. Birth, aging, sickness, and death occur appropriately in both the happy and unhappy realms. Therefore, apart from these four, the suffering caused by being bound with fivefold bonds (in hell), the suffering of hunger and thirst (in the realm of hungry ghosts and asuras), and the suffering of mutual oppression (in the animal realm) are specifically noted as the suffering of the woeful planes. All these (birth, aging, sickness, death, and the suffering of the woeful planes) are taken as pertaining to the present life of those beings. Therefore, the sufferings rooted in the round of rebirths in the past and future are taken separately. Furthermore, among beings who live depending on food, the suffering caused by the search for food for those who live by effort does not apply to those who do not have to search for food. The suffering caused by that livelihood of searching for food is stated as the eighth ground for spiritual urgency. (Ṭīkā)

One should also cause clarity of the mind by repeatedly recollecting the qualities of the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. Gladdening the mind when it should be gladdened is done in this manner.

## (7) Equanimity towards the Mind

How is the mind treated with equanimity when it should be treated with equanimity? When the meditation mind of the practitioner who practices in this way is neither shrinking nor distracted, not devoid of joy, and proceeds evenly on the object, following the right path of tranquility (samatha), then the practitioner need not concern himself with uplifting, restraining, or gladdening the mind. It is like a charioteer with horses that are running evenly. Treating the mind with equanimity when it should be treated with equanimity is done in this manner.

## (8) Avoiding the Unconcentrated

Avoiding the unconcentrated person means keeping far away and departing from those who have never entered or traveled the path of practice for attaining jhāna, who are busy with many affairs, and whose hearts are distracted.

## (9) Associating with the Concentrated

Associating with the concentrated person means approaching from time to time those who have traveled and practiced the path for attaining jhāna and who have attained access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi).

## (10) Inclining the Mind towards Absorption Concentration

[132] Inclining the mind towards absorption concentration means the application of mind and constant effort in producing (or for the sake of producing) absorption concentration. It means honoring concentration, leaning towards concentration, inclining towards concentration, and being prone to concentration. (10)

In this way, the ten kinds of skillfulness in absorption (appanā-kosalla) should be perfected.

67. The benefit is: For the practitioner who thus perfects the skillfulness in absorption when the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) has been obtained, absorption arises.

If that absorption does not arise for the practitioner who practices in this way, even so, the wise practitioner should not give up the effort but should continue to strive.

There is no possibility that a person can attain even a slight distinction in the Dhamma by abandoning or slackening right effort (sammā-vāyāma).

Therefore, the wise one, carefully noting the manner in which the mind occurs, should repeatedly apply effort so that it is balanced (with concentration).

If the mind shrinks even slightly, one should certainly uplift it. Restraining the effort that is too strenuous, one should make it proceed evenly.

Just as the behavior of bees and others regarding pollen, lotus leaves, spider webs, boats, and oil tubes is well explained (in the Commentary as examples).

Likewise, having freed the mind entirely from sluggishness and distraction, one should direct the meditation mind towards the counterpart sign.

## Directing towards the Sign

68. The following is the explanation of the meaning of the two verses regarding pollen, etc.—Just as an unskillful bee, knowing that a flower has bloomed on a certain tree, rushes with great speed, overshoots the tree, and having to turn back, arrives only when the pollen is exhausted. Another unskillful bee, rushing with slow speed, arrives only after the pollen is already gone. But a skillful bee, rushing with even speed, reaches the cluster of flowers easily, takes as much pollen as desired, produces honey, and enjoys the sweet taste.
133:
[133] Furthermore, when the pupils of a surgeon are learning the art of making incisions and such on a lotus leaf placed in a bowl of water, one unskilled pupil strikes with the knife with such force that he either cuts the lotus leaf in two or sinks it into the water. Another unskilled pupil, fearing he might cut it or sink it, does not even dare to touch it with the knife. But a skilled pupil, through balanced effort—neither too fast nor too slow—demonstrates the incision on the lotus leaf, and having mastered the craft, performs such operations as bloodletting in appropriate cases and earns his fee.

Note 1: Here, according to the Sinhalese variant 'aticcheko', the meaning 'an excessively clever bee' is also appropriate.

Furthermore, when a king announces, "Whoever brings a spider's thread four fathoms (sixteen cubits) long shall receive four thousand pieces of money," one unskilled man, pulling the spider's thread with haste, only breaks it here and there. Another unskilled man, fearing the thread might break, does not even dare to touch it with his hand. But a skilled man, starting from the end, winds it onto a small stick with balanced effort and, by bringing it, receives the reward.

Furthermore, an unskilled skipper, by filling the sails in a strong wind, causes the ship to drift away from its destination. Another unskilled skipper, by lowering the sails in a weak wind, causes the ship to remain stationary. But a skilled skipper fills the sails completely in a weak wind and uses half-sails in a strong wind, reaching the desired destination safely.

Furthermore, when a teacher tells his pupils, "Whoever fills an oil tube without spilling any oil shall receive a reward," one unskilled pupil, out of greed for the reward, pours too quickly and spills the oil. Another unskilled pupil, fearing the oil might spill, does not even dare to pour it. But a skilled pupil fills it with balanced effort and receives the reward.

In the same way, when the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) has arisen, one monk exerts strenuous energy, thinking, "I shall reach absorption (appanā) very quickly." His mind, due to over-exerted energy, falls into restlessness (uddhacca), and he is unable to reach absorption. Another monk, seeing the fault in over-exerting energy, slackens his effort, thinking, "What is the use of striving for absorption now?" His mind, due to excessively slackened energy, falls into sloth (kosajja), and he too is unable to reach absorption. But the monk who frees the meditative mind from slackness whenever it is slightly slack, and from restlessness whenever it is slightly restless, directs the mind towards the sign with balanced [134] energy...

That monk reaches absorption (appanā); he should be like one who has reached absorption. With reference to this meaning, I have said:

“Just as the movement of bees and others on pollen, lotus petals, spider threads, boats, and oil tubes is well-described [in the Commentaries], so too, having completely freed the mind from sluggishness and agitation, one should direct the meditation-mind towards the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) at all times.”

## Explanation of the First Jhāna

69. In this way, as described, for the yogi who directs the meditation-mind towards the sign, [at the moment when it should be said] “Now absorption will be accomplished,” the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is interrupted [1], and taking that very earth-kasina counterpart sign as the object, which has appeared through the practice of contemplating “earth, earth” [1], the mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana) arises [2]. Following that mind-door adverting, four or five impulsions (javanas) occur on that same earth-kasina counterpart sign object [3]. Among those four or five impulsions, the last single impulsion is a fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara) impulsion; the remaining impulsions are sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) impulsions [4]. These three or four sense-sphere impulsions, which possess initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), zest (pīti), happiness (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittēkaggatā) that are stronger than those in ordinary minds, are called “preparatory” (parikamma) because they prepare in advance for absorption [1]. Just as the vicinity of a village or a city is called the “access” (upacāra) of the village or city, so too, they are called “access” (upacāra) because they are close to absorption or because they occur in the [not too distant] proximity of absorption [2, 3]. From this single-adverting process (ekāvajjana-vīthi) [4],

1. Connect “interrupted,” “taking as object,” and “arises.”
2. This shows the arising of the adverting mind which has the same process (vīthi) as the absorption jhāna mind.
3. For an individual with quick realization (khippābhiññā), the impulsions occur four times. For an individual with slow realization (dandhābiññā), the impulsions occur five times. This rapid occurrence of impulsion-minds is what is meant by “javana.”
4. If four impulsions occur, the fourth and last is the fine-material sphere absorption jhāna impulsion, and the preceding three are sense-sphere impulsions. 2. If the name “upacāra” is given because of closeness to absorption, it might be argued that the name “upacāra” should only belong to “gotrabhū” which is even closer to absorption. Therefore, the commentator says “because they occur in the proximity.” Indeed, even if not extremely close, if it occurs in a place that is not too far, it is called “samīpacārī” (occurring in the proximity). The adverting of the sense-sphere impulsions called parikamma, upacāra, anuloma, and gotrabhū is this very adverting; the adverting of the absorption jhāna impulsion is also this very adverting. Thus it is said to have a single or same adverting.

they are called “conformity” (anuloma) because they conform to the preparatory acts in the previously occurring multiple-adverting processes (nānāvajjana-vīthi) [1] and to the absorption above [2]. Among these three or four impulsion-minds—parikamma, upacāra, and anuloma—the third or fourth mind, which is the last of all [3], is also called “change-of-lineage” (gotrabhū) because it overcomes and transcends the sense-sphere lineage and because it evolves the sublime (mahaggata) lineage. Among these three or four minds, if counted without repeating what has already been taken, the first mind is called parikamma, the second is upacāra, the third is anuloma, and the fourth is gotrabhū. In another way of counting [1], the first mind is called upacāra, the second is anuloma, the third is gotrabhū, and the fourth or fifth mind [2] is called the absorption (jhāna) mind. Indeed, only the fourth mind or only the fifth mind becomes absorption (i.e., enters into the object). That occurrence of absorption [not being fixed as the fourth or fifth] is according to the capacity of the individual with quick realization or the individual with slow realization [3]. After that fourth or fifth impulsion-mind, the [sixth or seventh] impulsion, having exhausted its momentum, is as if it falls, and it is then the turn of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) mind.

In the meditation processes practiced before the occurrence of absorption jhāna, there were as many advertings as there were process cycles. Those advertings are also different from the adverting of the absorption jhāna included in the final absorption process. Therefore, those earlier meditation processes are called nānāvajjana—processes with many or different advertings.
2. The sense-sphere meditation impulsions included in the absorption jhāna process conform to the preparatory meditation impulsions included in the earlier multiple-adverting processes, and they also conform to the absorption impulsion that is about to occur. 3. If three sense-sphere impulsions occur, it means the third mind; if four occur, it means the fourth mind.

Because it occurs appropriately in that manner, it is not stated as a fixed, absolute rule, but rather as these two alternatives.

In the sense-sphere impulsion process (kāma-javana-vīthi), where seven impulsions occur, the second impulsion is stronger than the first, the third is stronger than the second, and the fourth is stronger than the third. The fifth impulsion begins to weaken; below that—

However, the Elder Godatta, a master of the Abhidhamma, recited the Paṭṭhāna passage: "Preceding wholesome states are a condition for succeeding wholesome states by way of repetition (āsevana-paccaya)," and argued that because succeeding states are stronger due to the repetition condition, absorption (appanā) can also occur at the stage of the sixth and seventh impulsions. That statement was rejected in the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), saying, "This is merely the personal opinion of the Elder (the Abhidhammika Godatta)." In reality, absorption occurs only at the fourth and fifth impulsions. After those impulsions, the sixth or seventh is said to fall away. [135] (The Commentaries state) this is because they are too close to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Since this statement (in the Commentaries) is made after careful investigation, it is impossible to reject it. Just as a man running towards a precipice, even if he wishes to stop, is unable to stand still by placing his foot at the very edge and falls into the abyss, so too, one is unable to attain absorption at the sixth or seventh moment because of the proximity to the life-continuum.

Note: The sixth impulsion weakens, and the seventh impulsion below it weakens further until its momentum is exhausted; therefore, only the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs after that seventh impulsion. Similarly, in this absorption-jhāna process, the momentum increases sequentially up to the fourth sense-sphere impulsion. Although the fifth moment is usually where strength begins to decline, because it is an absorption-jhāna impulsion which is more powerful than a sense-sphere impulsion, it does not weaken but is at its strongest. If absorption does not occur at the fifth moment and only a sense-sphere impulsion occurs, then from that fifth moment onwards, the momentum of the impulsions would have already begun to decline and drop; thus, an absorption impulsion cannot occur, and it is the turn for the life-continuum to arise.

Therefore, it should be understood that absorption occurs only at the fourth and fifth impulsion stages.

Furthermore, that absorption-jhāna impulsion lasts for only a single mind-moment. Indeed, in seven instances, there is no fixed duration: in the first absorption, in the mundane direct knowledges (lokiya-abhiññā), in the four paths (magga), in the fruition (phala) impulsions immediately following the path, in the jhāna-mind which is the life-continuum in the fine-material and immaterial realms, in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana) which serves as a condition for cessation (nirodha), and in the fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti) of a non-returner or an arahant emerging from cessation. Among these seven instances, the fruition mind following immediately after the path does not occur more than three times. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception jhāna serving as a condition for cessation does not occur more than twice. There is no fixed limit to the (number of) life-continuum minds in the fine-material and immaterial realms. In the remaining instances (the first absorption, mundane direct knowledge, the path-moment, and the fruition-moment of a non-returner or arahant emerging from cessation), the mind occurs only once.

Note: 1. As shown in Note 4 on page 425, if absorption does not occur at the fifth moment, the momentum will decrease and drop starting from that fifth moment. Since the sixth and seventh moments are the turn for the life-continuum to arise, they are said to be "close to the life-continuum," meaning the mental momentum is weak and near to becoming the life-continuum.

Thus, the first absorption lasts for only a single mind-moment. After that single absorption-jhāna mind, the life-continuum occurs. Then, having interrupted the life-continuum, an adverting mind (āvajjana) arises for the purpose of reviewing the jhāna; thereafter, reviewing impulsions (paccavekkhaṇā-javana) that review the jhāna occur. This is the sequence of attaining the first jhāna.

To continue: through this much of the meditative development, this meditator, "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), with rapture (pīti) and happiness (sukha) born of seclusion." A meditator dwelling thus has attained the first jhāna which takes the earth-kasiṇa as its object, having abandoned five factors, being possessed of five factors, having three types of excellence, and being endowed with ten characteristics.

## Commentary on the Discourse on Jhāna

70. In the passage describing the first jhāna, "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures" means being secluded from, being without, having departed from, or having moved away by way of abandonment from sensual pleasures (both objective sensual pleasures, vatthu-kāma, and defilement-based sensual pleasures, kilesa-kāma). Furthermore, in the phrase "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," the word "quite" (eva) should be understood as having the sense of restriction (niyama). Because it has the sense of restriction, it shows that although sensual pleasures are not manifest at the time of entering and dwelling in the first jhāna, they are the opposites of that first jhāna, and that the first jhāna is attained only by the abandonment of sensual pleasures.

How does it show this? When this restriction is made as "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures," the following benefit becomes clear: "Sensual pleasures are indeed the opposites of jhāna; when those sensual pleasures are present, this jhāna does not occur, just as there is no light from a lamp when there is darkness. Only by abandoning (secluding oneself from) those sensual pleasures [136] is that jhāna attained, just as reaching the further shore is achieved only by leaving this shore." Because this is clear, the restriction is made. Here ends one part of the commentary.

Note: 1. This phrase explains the term "from sensual pleasures."

Therefore, in the Burmese translation of this term, it is supplemented as "from (objective and subjective) sensualities."

2. With these three words starting from "quite secluded," the term "quite secluded" is explained step by step.

In this context [Note 1], one might ask: "Why is this restrictive word 'only' (eva) spoken only in the preceding phrase and not in the subsequent phrase? Could one enter and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from unwholesome states such as the hindrances?" [Answer:] The statement of the restrictive word "only" in the preceding phrase should not be understood as the questioner suggests. To explain further, because [this jhāna] is the escape from, the departure from, and the cause for departing from those sensualities [Note 2], the restrictive word "only" is spoken in the preceding phrase. Even though it is spoken only in the preceding phrase, it should be brought forward and applied to the subsequent phrase as well [Note 1], just as in the statement: "Monks, only here is there a recluse; here [only] [Note 2] is there a second recluse" (MN 1.139). In this statement, the restrictive word "only" should be brought forward and spoken [in the second part]. Indeed, it is impossible to enter and dwell in jhāna without being secluded from other unwholesome states known as the hindrances. Therefore, the word [only] should be understood as connected to both phrases: "quite secluded from objective and subjective sensualities, quite secluded from unwholesome states."

Note 1: Connect with: "In the subsequent phrase as well... it should be brought forward and spoken."

Furthermore, in both phrases, by this word "secluded" [Note 1], all types of seclusion—such as tadaṅga-viveka, vikkkhambhana-viveka, samuccheda-viveka, paṭipassaddhi-viveka, and nissaraṇa-viveka, as well as kāya-viveka, citta-viveka, and upadhi-viveka—are included. Although all these seclusions are included, only the three seclusions—physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion by suppression (vikkkhambhana-viveka)—should be understood in this description of jhāna.

By the term "from sensualities" [Note 2], one should understand that it encompasses both objective sensuality (vatthu-kāma)—as taught in the Mahāniddesa: "What are objective sensualities? Pleasing forms," etc.—and subjective sensuality (kilesa-kāma), as taught in the Mahāniddesa and Vibhaṅga: "Desire is sensuality, lust is sensuality, desire and lust are sensuality, intention is sensuality, lust is sensuality, intentional lust is sensuality; these are called sensualities." All of these should be understood as being included.

Note 1: Connect with: "By the word... they are included." Note 2: Connect with: "By this term... both objective and subjective sensualities are included."

The benefit of this inclusion is that in the phrase "quite secluded from sensualities," the meaning "quite secluded from objective sensualities" becomes appropriate; by seclusion from objective sensualities, physical seclusion (kāya-viveka) is expressed. In the phrase "quite secluded from unwholesome states," the meaning "quite secluded from subjective sensualities and all unwholesome states" becomes appropriate; by seclusion from subjective sensualities and all unwholesome states, mental seclusion (citta-viveka) is expressed. Furthermore, in these two phrases, because the first phrase [Note 1] teaches seclusion from objective sensualities, it clarifies the abandoning of the pleasure of enjoying objective sensualities. Because the second phrase [Note 2] teaches seclusion from defilements, it clarifies the attainment (acceptance) of the pleasure of renunciation (nekkhamma-sukha).

Note 1: The translation "by the first phrase" is to be consistent with similar terms to follow. According to the Ṭīkā, which explains 'purimena' as 'by the physical seclusion,' it could be translated as 'by the preceding physical seclusion.'
Note 2: Here too, according to the Ṭīkā, it should be translated as 'by the second mental seclusion.'

Thus, by teaching seclusion from objective and subjective sensualities, in these two phrases, the first phrase [Note 1] clarifies the abandoning of the objects that cause defilements like craving, while the second phrase clarifies the abandoning of the defilements themselves. Furthermore, by the first phrase, the relinquishing of the cause of instability (objective sensuality) is shown; by the second, the abandoning of the cause of foolishness and ignorance. Furthermore, by the first phrase, the purity of the conduct of body and speech is shown; by the second, the cultivation and purification of the mental disposition (ajjhāsaya).

Regarding the aspect of defilement sensuality (kilesakāma), "sensuality" (kāma) is intended only as sensual desire (kāmacchanda), which has many varieties such as longing, attachment, and so forth. Although this sensual desire is included among unwholesome states, it is taught separately in the Vibhaṅga as the opponent of jhāna, in such ways as: "Therein, what is sensuality? However, to distinguish them in the compound 'paccanīkapaṭipakkhabhāvadassanato', 'paccanīka' is translated as 'adversary' and 'paṭipakkha' as 'opponent'. The hindrances are the adversaries of the jhāna factors, and the jhāna factors are the opponents of those hindrances. Therefore, connect the term "of the jhāna factors" with the part of the phrase "being the opponent."

This means that the hindrances are the adversaries of the jhāna factors, and the jhāna factors themselves are the opponents of those hindrances, being the states that destroy and strike them down. For it is said in the book called Peṭaka:

"Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire; rapture is the opponent of ill will; initial application is the opponent of sloth and torpor; happiness is the opponent of restlessness and remorse; and sustained application is the opponent of doubt."

Note 1: "By showing" means "teaching while showing."
Note 2: The Peṭaka is a commentary on the Tipiṭaka taught by the Venerable Mahākaccāyana. According to the Ṭīkā, it refers to either the Netti or the Peṭakopadesa. However, the Vimativinodanī (Vol. 1, p. 72) states that the Peṭaka is a work following the method of the Netti composed by Mahākaccāyana, called Peṭaka because it opens up the Tipiṭaka. Thus, it should be understood as the Peṭakopadesa. However, the specific citation "Concentration is the opponent of sensual desire..." is not found in the current versions of the Netti or Peṭakopadesa.

In this way, by the phrase "quite secluded from sensualities," seclusion by suppression (vikkhambhana-viveka) of sensual desire is taught. By the phrase "secluded from unwholesome states," seclusion by suppression of all five hindrances is taught. If counted by the method of including what has not yet been included: by the first phrase, the seclusion of sensual desire is taught; by the second, the seclusion of the remaining hindrances.

Likewise, by the first phrase, the seclusion of greed (lobha) directed towards the five varieties of sensual cords is taught; by the second, the seclusion of hatred (dosa) and delusion (moha) directed towards the nine varieties of the objects of resentment (āghātavatthu), and so on. Alternatively, among unwholesome states such as the floods (ogha), by the first phrase, the seclusion of the flood of sensuality (kāmogha), the bond of sensuality (kāmayoga), the taint of sensuality (kāmāsava), the clinging to sensuality (kāmupādāna), the bodily tie of covetousness (abhijjhākāyagantha), and the fetter of sensual lust (kāmarāgasaṃyojana) is taught; by the second phrase, the seclusion of the remaining floods, bonds, taints, clingings, ties, and fetters.

By the first phrase, the seclusion of craving (taṇhā) and its associated states is taught; by the second, the seclusion of ignorance (avijjā) and its associated states.

Note 1: Connect this with the phrase "seclusion by suppression is taught."
Note 2: "Five varieties of sensual cords" refers to the five types of pleasant objects associated with different domains.

To show another way: by the first phrase, the seclusion by suppression of the eight types of consciousness associated with greed is taught; by the second, the seclusion of the remaining four types of unwholesome consciousness. This is the explanation of the meaning of the phrase "quite secluded from sensualities, secluded from unwholesome states."

[138] 71. Having thus shown the factors to be abandoned in the first jhāna through this much explanation, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with "accompanied by initial application and sustained application" in order to show the associated factors. In that phrase, "thinking" is called initial application (vitakka); it means the act of thinking. This initial application has the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object.

Note 1: Connect as: "Having shown... through this much explanation."
Note 2: The mind seems to ascend to the object by the power of thinking.
138:
Therefore, this *vitakka* (initial application) is said to have the characteristic of directing the mind onto the object. For example, just as a person might enter the king's palace by relying on a relative or a friend who is an acquaintance of the king, and follow them inside, in the same way, the mind reaches the object by relying on *vitakka*. If this is so, how does a mind without *vitakka* (such as the second *jhāna* and so forth) reach the object? It reaches it only through the power of *vitakka*. To explain further: just as the aforementioned man, having gained familiarity (through frequent visits), can enter the king's palace without hesitation even without that guiding relative or friend, in the same way, the mind, having gained familiarity (through frequent reaching of the object), [can reach the object even without *vitakka*].

It has the function (rasa) of striking at the beginning and striking all around (threshing) [the object].1 Therefore, it is said that by means of that *vitakka*,2 the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) performs the initial striking of the object and the striking all around the object with *vitakka*.

Note:
Even without *vitakka*, the mind devoid of *vitakka* (such as the second *jhāna* and so forth) reaches the object. 'Gaining familiarity' means having acquired the habit called *vitakka-bhāvanā* (the development of initial application) within the mental continuity. Indeed, through the power of *vitakka* occurring repeatedly in the mental continuity, the mind's reaching of the object has been practiced for a long time; therefore, even when that mind is occasionally devoid of *vitakka*, it still occurs within that familiar object. For example, just as a mind that has been practiced for a long time through the power of investigating with wisdom may occasionally occur through the power of investigation even when not associated with wisdom; or, for another example, just as a mind that has occurred in association with defilements may still occur through the power of the habit (*vāsanā*) of defilements even when it is free from defilements (as in the case of an Arahant); in this same way, the manner in which the mind reaches the object while devoid of *vitakka* should be understood. (Ṭīkā)

1. Striking at the beginning (or first) is called *āhanana*. Striking from all sides, or striking repeatedly, is called *pariyāhanana*. The occurrence [of mindfulness/attention] such as "matter, matter" or "earth, earth" should be understood as "striking at the beginning, striking directly, striking all around, and striking repeatedly." (Ṭīkā)
2. Connect with: "...is said to perform [this] by means of that *vitakka*."

It is manifested to the [meditator's] knowledge as the state that brings the mind to the object or draws it in.1

*Vicāra* (sustained application) means roaming around the object, or, examining and threshing it; it means the repeated wandering to and fro upon the object, or, the repeated engagement with the object. That *vicāra* has the characteristic of repeatedly threshing (examining) the object. It has the function of yoking conascent states to that object. It is manifested to the [meditator's] knowledge as the state that continuously binds the mind to the object.

Although *vitakka* and *vicāra* are inseparable in certain types of consciousness (such as the first *jhāna* and sense-sphere consciousness), *vitakka* is the first impact of the mind on the object, like the initial strike of a bell, because of its grossness and its state as the precursor (to *vicāra*).2

Note:
1. Bringing the mind to the object—delivering it—is called *ānayana*. Alternatively, drawing it (to the object) is called *ānayana*. (Ṭīkā)
2. Because it is grosser than *vicāra*, and because it is the precursor to *vicāra* itself, *vitakka* is like the sound of striking a bell, which is grosser than and the precursor to the subsequent ringing/reverberation. The similarity lies in the fact that the sound of striking the bell is the first to occur; in the same way, *vitakka* is the first impact of the mind on the object because of its nature of directing the mind to the object first. (Ṭīkā)

Because of its nature as the first impact of the mind on the object, like the initial sound of a bell, it is called *vitakka*. Because of its subtle nature (compared to *vitakka*) and its nature of repeatedly threshing the object, like the continuous reverberation of a bell, the state that continuously binds [the mind to the object] is called *vicāra*. Furthermore, between these two, *vitakka* is vibratory; it is the state of the mind's vibration at the moment of initial occurrence.1 It is like the flapping of the wings of a large bird wishing to fly up into the sky. It is also like the bee's diving towards a lotus with its mind following the scent. *Vicāra* has a peaceful occurrence; it is the state of the mind not vibrating excessively. It is like the spreading of the wings of a large bird that has already flown up into the sky. It is also like the bee hovering over the lotus after having dived towards it. However, in the Commentary on the Duka-nipāta, it is stated:

Note:
1. Here, 'vibration' does not mean distraction or instability; it only means being active and energetic as the opposite of sloth and torpor. Therefore, in the Sāratthadīpanī-ṭīkā (Vol. 1, p. 360), it is stated: "In this context, the vibration (*vipphāra*) of *vitakka* is the opposite of sloth (*thīna-middha*), being the non-shrinking and non-contraction towards the object. However, this non-shrinking and non-contraction is similar to vibration in its nature of directing [the mind] onto the object. Therefore, it is intentionally called 'the vibratory nature of the mind.'"

"*Vitakka* is the state that occurs by way of directing the mind towards the object, like the movement of a large bird flying in the sky, catching the wind with both wings and then steadying the wings. *Vicāra* is the state that occurs by way of repeatedly threshing the object, like the movement of a bird flapping its wings to catch the wind."

This statement is appropriate regarding the continuous occurrence (in either access or absorption concentration). This distinction between *vitakka* and *vicāra* becomes clear in the first and second *jhānas*.

To give another illustration: *vitakka* is like the hand that firmly holds a tarnished bronze bowl, while *vicāra* is like the other hand that rubs and polishes it with a woolen pad smeared with soap powder and oil. Similarly, it is like the hand of a potter that presses down while turning the wheel with a stick to make a vessel, whereas *vicāra* is like the hand that moves to and fro [shaping it].
139:
Vicāra (sustained thought) is like a hand that circles and rubs. Vitakka (applied thought) is like the hand of a potter who, while spinning the wheel with a stick to make pots, presses down on the clay; vicāra is like the hand that moves around and examines here and there. Furthermore, vitakka, which directs the mind towards the object, is like the central point of a compass [139] that remains pressed down in the middle while drawing a circle (on a copper plate, etc.). Vicāra, which repeatedly examines the object, is like the outer point of the compass that circles around. Just as a tree exists together with its flowers and fruits, this jhāna is called "with applied thought and sustained thought" (savitakka savicāra) because it occurs together with this vitakka and this vicāra. In the Vibhaṅga, however, the teaching is presented in terms of a person (puggala-adhiṭṭhāna), such as "He is endowed with, fully endowed with, this vitakka and this vicāra." The meaning there should also be understood in the same way as it is explained here in this Visuddhimagga.

In the phrase "born of seclusion" (vivekaja), seclusion (viveka) means being solitary; it means the removal of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa). Or, it is called viveka because it is secluded or it causes seclusion; it refers to the group of states associated with jhāna that are secluded from the hindrances. Therefore, it is "born of seclusion" because it is born from that seclusion, or it is born in that seclusion. Thus, due to these two reasons—being born from seclusion or being born in seclusion—it is called "born of seclusion."

Notes:
1. This is the meaning of the term nīvaraṇavigamo. While "the seclusion of the hindrances" might seem more appropriate, it is translated according to the common convention to be consistent with the two subsequent explanations.
2. In the Pali, the word vivekajaṃ is explained in two ways according to the grammatical cases: "born from seclusion" and "born in seclusion" (the group of states that are secluded). Here, only the first method, "born from seclusion," was translated previously.

72. In the phrase "having rapture and happiness" (pītisukha), it is called rapture (pīti) because it refreshes. That rapture has the characteristic of endearing. Its function is to refresh the body and mind, or its function is to pervade the body with excellent mind-produced matter (cittaja-rūpa). It is manifested as elation. That rapture is of five kinds: (1) minor rapture (khuddikā pīti), (2) momentary rapture (khaṇikā pīti), (3) showering rapture (okkantikā pīti), (4) uplifting rapture (ubbegā pīti), and (5) pervading rapture (pharaṇā pīti). Among these five kinds of rapture: (1) Minor rapture is only able to make the hair on the body stand on end. (2) Momentary rapture arises repeatedly like flashes of lightning. (3) Showering rapture breaks over the body again and again like waves breaking on the seashore. (4) Uplifting rapture is powerful; it reaches the extent of lifting the body up and making it leap into the air. To provide an example of this: The Elder Mahā Tissa, who resided at Puṇṇavallika Monastery, went to the courtyard of the shrine on a full moon evening. Looking at the moonlight and facing the Mahācetiya, he thought, "At this time, the four assemblies will be worshipping the Mahācetiya." Through the power of the object of the shrine seen previously, he aroused uplifting rapture with the Buddha as the object. Like a colorful ball thrown onto a plastered floor, he sprang into the air and landed right in the courtyard of the Mahācetiya. Similarly, a certain daughter of a noble family in Vattakālaka village near Girikaṇḍaka Monastery also flew into the air through powerful uplifting rapture with the Buddha as the object.

When her parents were going to the monastery to hear the Dhamma in the evening, they said, "Dear daughter, you are heavy with child and cannot travel at an improper time. We will listen to the Dhamma and share the merit with you."
140:
"We will listen to the Dhamma and share the merit with you," they said and left. Although she wanted to go, she was unable to refuse her parents' words [140] and stayed behind at home. Standing on the floor in front of the house, looking at the pagoda situated on the mountain peak at Girikaṇḍaka Monastery by moonlight, she saw the lamp offering made to the pagoda. She saw the fourfold assembly circumambulating the pagoda clockwise after making offerings of flowers, scents, and so forth, and she heard the sound of the group chanting by the Saṅgha of monks. Then, reflecting, "How fortunate are these people who have the opportunity to go to the monastery, walk on such a pagoda courtyard, and listen to such sweet Dhamma talks," she experienced uplifting joy (ubbegā-pīti) while gazing at the pagoda, which resembled a heap of pearls. By the power of that uplifting joy, she flew into the sky and descended onto the pagoda courtyard even before her parents. She paid homage to the pagoda and stood listening to the Dhamma. Then her parents arrived and asked her, "Dear daughter, by which path did you come?"

She replied, "I came through the sky, not by the ground path." They said, "Dear daughter, only Arahants travel through the sky.1 How could you come that way?" Then she said, "While I was standing looking at the pagoda by moonlight, powerful joy (pīti) arose with the Buddha's qualities as the object. At that time, I did not know whether I was standing or sitting; only because of the acquired sign (nimitta) of merit did I fly into the sky and find myself standing on the pagoda courtyard."

Thus, uplifting joy (ubbegā-pīti) has the extent of leaping and flying upwards. When pervading joy (pharaṇā-pīti) arises, the entire body is continuously touched and pervaded, like a bladder filled with blown air or like a mountain cavern into which a great flood of water has rushed.

Furthermore, when these five types of joy reach maturity (literally, 'conceiving'), they fulfill the two kinds of tranquility (passaddhi): bodily tranquility (kāya-passaddhi) and mental tranquility (citta-passaddhi). When tranquility reaches maturity, it fulfills the two kinds of happiness (sukha): bodily and mental. When happiness reaches maturity, it fulfills the three kinds of concentration (samādhi): momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Among these five types of joy,1 the pervading joy (pharaṇā-pīti) which, being the root of absorption concentration, grows and reaches association with absorption concentration, is what is intended here by the term "joy" (pīti).

Note
1- Non-returners, Once-returners, Stream-enterers, and worldlings who have attained psychic powers (abhiññā) can also travel through the sky. Therefore, saying "only those with psychic powers can travel" would be more comprehensive. However, the woman's parents might have said this due to lack of knowledge, or they might have mentioned the highest person (Arahant) to represent the best.

73. As for the meaning of the term happiness (sukha) other than joy: happiness is that which is pleasant. Alternatively, it is called sukha because it thoroughly "eats" (khādati) or "digs up" (khanati) the afflictions of body and mind.2 This happiness has the characteristic of being pleasant, the function (rasa) of strengthening associated states, and manifests as assistance.

Note
1- Connect this with: "Among these five types of joy... the joy that reaches association... is what is intended."
2- In this alternative explanation, the etymology of the word 'sukha' is explained as 'su' (well) + 'khā' (to eat) or 'su' + 'khana' (to dig). While this is significant in Pali, it is not very beneficial in Burmese translation. However, it is translated in full for those who wish to know.

To explain further, although joy and happiness are inseparable in certain states of mind such as the first jhāna, joy (pīti) is the delight in obtaining a desired object,1 while happiness (sukha) is the experiencing of the taste of the object already obtained.2 Where there is joy, there is happiness; but where there is happiness, there is not necessarily joy. Joy is included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), while happiness is included in the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha).
141:
[141] Rapture (pīti) [which occurs when obtaining a desired object] should be understood as being like the rapture of a man exhausted by traveling through a waterless desert upon seeing or hearing of a forest and water. Happiness (sukha) [which occurs when experiencing the taste of an object already obtained] should be understood as being like the happiness of that man upon entering the forest shade and using the water. This statement should be understood as being said because of the manifestation of rapture and happiness at those respective times of seeing, hearing, using, obtaining, and experiencing. As stated, this rapture and this happiness belong to this jhāna, or exist in this jhāna; therefore, this jhāna is said to have 'rapture and happiness' (pītisukhaṃ).

Note:
1. At the moment of first obtaining a desired object, the sense of refreshment and joy is more prominent; at that moment, happiness also exists, but because it has not yet been used or experienced, that happiness is not yet very prominent.
2. When using and experiencing an object already obtained, the happiness and joy of body and mind are more prominent; at that moment, although rapture exists, that rapture is not very prominent.

Alternatively, rapture and happiness together are 'rapture-happiness' (pītisukhaṃ), to be understood like the terms 'Dhamma-Vinaya' etc. Rapture and happiness born of seclusion (viveka) belong to this jhāna, or exist in this jhāna; therefore, it is also a jhāna that has 'rapture and happiness born of seclusion.' Indeed, just as the jhāna is born of seclusion, so too the rapture and happiness in this jhāna are born only of seclusion. Since this rapture and happiness born of seclusion exist in that jhāna, it is appropriate to say 'jhāna having rapture and happiness born of seclusion' in a single phrase. In the Vibhaṅga, however, it is stated in this manner: 'This happiness is associated with this rapture,' etc. The meaning there should also be understood in the same way as this commentary's explanation.

Note:
1. These last two sentences show that in the term 'pītisukhaṃ' (having rapture and happiness), it is formed by combining a Dvandva compound with an Assatthi-taddhita suffix. Although this explanation is very beneficial in Pali, it is not as beneficial in the Burmese translation. This note is provided so that those who do not know Pali may realize it is not their field, and having realized this, they should not be discouraged or complain even if they do not understand these explanations.
2. This shows how the words 'pīti' and 'sukha' are combined as a Dvandva compound; it is only for those who know Pali.
3. This shows how the term 'vivekajaṃ' (born of seclusion) and 'pītisukhaṃ' (rapture-happiness) are combined as a Bahubbīhi compound into a single term. According to this explanation, the attribute 'born of seclusion' should be connected with 'rapture-happiness.' According to the previous explanation where 'vivekajaṃ' and 'pītisukhaṃ' were explained separately, the attribute 'born of seclusion' should be connected with the word 'paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ' (first jhāna).

The term 'first jhāna' (paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ) will be clarified later. 'Having attained' (upasampajja) means having approached or reached. Alternatively, it means having fulfilled or produced. In the Vibhaṅga, it is stated: 'Having attained (upasampajja) means the gain, the regaining, the reaching, the arrival, the touching, the realization, the attainment of the first jhāna.' The meaning of that statement in the Vibhaṅga should also be understood in the same way as this commentary's explanation.

'Abides' (viharati) means that, being endowed with the jhāna of the aforementioned nature through a posture suitable for that first jhāna, one brings about the dwelling—which consists of the movement, occurrence, protection, maintenance, sustenance, and conduct of the individual existence (attabhāva). Indeed, it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: 'Abides (viharati) means one moves, occurs, protects, maintains, sustains, conducts, and dwells; therefore, it is said "abides".'

Note:
1. Connect as: 'brings about the movement of the individual existence,' 'brings about the occurrence of the individual existence,' 'brings about the maintenance of the individual existence,' etc.
2. It means 'brings about the protection of the individual existence.'
3. In the root word 'viharati' (abides), it is explained as 'vi' (cutting off) + 'harati' (carries) = 'viharati'. It means carrying on by changing through other postures, thereby cutting off the weariness and pain occurring in a single posture.

## Abandoning Five Factors etc.
74. Regarding the statement 'abandoning five factors and possessing five factors,' the state of having abandoned five factors should be understood through the abandonment of these five hindrances (nīvaraṇa): sensual desire (kāmacchanda), ill-will (byāpāda), sloth and torpor (thina-middha), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca), and doubt (vicikicchā). Indeed, jhāna does not arise when these are not abandoned. Therefore, these are called the 'factors of abandonment' of that jhāna. To clarify further, although other unwholesome states are also abandoned (by way of suppression) at the moment of jhāna, these hindrances specifically act as obstacles to jhāna. To elaborate, a mind lured by various objects through sensual desire does not become well-concentrated on a single object. Alternatively, a mind overcome by sensual desire does not practice the path which is the practice for abandoning the sensual realm (kāmadhātu). A mind struck by ill-will towards an object does not [occur] continuously [142] (due to distraction). A mind overcome and struck by sloth and torpor is not fit for the work of meditation, or is unsuitable for the work of meditation. A mind struck by restlessness and remorse is only unpeaceful and wanders about.
142:
The mind oppressed by doubt (vicikicchā) does not ascend to the path of practice that leads to the attainment of jhana. Because they specifically obstruct jhana, only these five hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are called the 'factors to be abandoned' (pahānaṅga). This concludes one section.

To further explain the possession of factors in detail: Vitakka (initial application) directs the mind onto the object; Vicāra (sustained application) binds the mind to the object continuously. For the mind whose practice has been accomplished for the sake of non-distraction through these two, rapture (pīti) produces refreshment and happiness (sukha) produces intensification. When this occurs, one-pointedness (ekaggatā)—supported by that directing, binding, refreshing, and intensifying of the mind along with its associated states—is placed evenly and rightly on a single object (due to the equilibrium of the five faculties, and by way of being far from opposites, free from shrinking, and free from distraction). Therefore, it should be understood that the first jhana is possessed of five factors through the arising of these five: vitakka, vicāra, pīti, sukha, and ekaggatā. Indeed, when these five arise, it is called the arising of jhana. Thus, these five are called its constituent factors. One should not assume there is a jhana separate from these five factors. To illustrate with an analogy: just as an army is called 'four-fold' or music 'five-fold' or the path 'eight-fold' based on its constituents alone, so too this jhana is called 'five-fold' or 'possessed of five factors' based on its constituents alone.

Furthermore, although these five factors exist even at the moment of access (upacāra) [and in the moment of the ordinary sense-sphere mind], they are stronger in access than in the ordinary mind. However, here (in jhana), they are even stronger than in access, having reached the characteristic of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). To elaborate: among these five jhana factors, vitakka arises directing the mind onto the object in a very clear manner. Vicāra arises intensely contemplating the object. Rapture and happiness pervade the entire body. Hence it is said: 'There is no part of his whole body untouched by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion' (D. i. 228). One-pointedness also arises touching the object, like an upper lid fitting onto a lower casket; this is their distinction from the others (in access). Although one-pointedness is not explicitly mentioned in the passage 'with vitakka and vicāra,' it is nonetheless a factor because the Vibhaṅga states: 'Jhana is vitakka, vicāra, pīti, sukha, and one-pointedness of mind.' The intention with which the Blessed One made the brief exposition (uddesa) is the same intention he revealed in the Vibhaṅga. This concludes one section.

## The Three Goodnesses

[143] 75. In the phrase 'possessed of ten characteristics with three goodnesses,' it should be understood that there are three goodnesses by way of the beginning, middle, and end (of the jhana). It should also be understood that it is possessed of ten characteristics by way of the signs to be noted—or the signifying characteristics—of that jhana's beginning, middle, and end. In explaining these goodnesses and characteristics, the following is the canonical Pali text:
143:
“The purity of the path to attaining jhāna is the beginning of the first jhāna; the development of equanimity is the middle; exultation is the end. The purity of the path to attaining jhāna is the beginning of the first jhāna. How many are the characteristics of the beginning? There are three characteristics of the beginning: (1) the mind is purified from the obstacles (hindrances) of that first jhāna; (2) because it is purified, the mind practices the intermediate sign of serenity (samatha-nimitta)¹; (3) because it practices, the mind enters into that sign of serenity. These three—(1) the mind being purified from obstacles, (2) the mind practicing the intermediate sign of serenity because it is purified, and (3) the mind entering into that sign of serenity because it practices—are the characteristics of the beginning, which is the purity of the path of the first jhāna. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is accomplished with the beauty of the beginning and with the three characteristics.”

“The development of equanimity is the middle of the first jhāna. How many are the characteristics of the middle? There are three characteristics of the middle: (1) it looks on with equanimity at the purified mind; (2) it looks on with equanimity at the mind that has entered the path of serenity; (3) it looks on with equanimity at the absorption mind (appanā) established in singleness (without the company of defilements). These three—(1) looking on with equanimity at the purified mind, (2) looking on with equanimity at the mind that has entered the path of serenity, and (3) looking on with equanimity at the absorption mind established in singleness—are the characteristics of the middle, which is the development of equanimity of the first jhāna. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna is accomplished with the beauty of the middle and with the three characteristics.”

“The exultation of the first jhāna is the end. How many are the characteristics of the end? There are four characteristics of the end: (1) exultation in the sense of non-transgression among the states arisen in that first jhāna; (2) exultation in the sense of the faculties having a single function; (3) exultation in the sense of conveying energy appropriate to those faculties; (4) exultation in the sense of repetition (cultivation). These four are the characteristics of the end, which is the exultation of the first jhāna. Therefore, it is said that the first jhāna has the beauty of the end and is accomplished with the four characteristics.”

[144] In that scriptural passage, some teachers (of the Abhayagiri tradition) say: “The purity of the path to jhāna refers to access concentration (upacāra)³ along with its preliminary preparations (parikamma)¹—the equipment². The development of equanimity refers to absorption (appanā). Exultation refers to the reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā) of the jhāna.” However, because it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali that “the absorption mind, having reached the state of having a single function, also attains the purity of the path to jhāna, develops equanimity⁴, and is gladdened by knowledge,” the purity of the path to jhāna should be understood only within the absorption (the moment of jhāna) by virtue of the preceding cause (the preliminary stage)¹.

Notes:
1. 'Practices the sign of serenity'—this translation follows the standard rendering of the text 'samathanimittaṃ paṭipajjati'; it means 'reaches the sign of serenity.' Such reaching, according to the method of singleness, is merely being connected with that sign of serenity. This will be explained in detail later.
1. 'Preliminary preparations' (parikamma) refers to the meditative processes that occurred prior to the jhāna process. By saying 'along with those equipments,' it means those preliminary meditations are also included in the purity of the path to jhāna.
2. This is the meaning of the word 'sambhāra'; it refers to the fundamental causes that nurture or produce the jhāna. Just as wood and bamboo, which are parts of a house, are called the 'sambhāra' or materials of the house.
3. 'Access concentration' (upacāra) refers to the sense-sphere impulsions (kāmāvacara javana) included within the jhāna process.
4. 'Also develops equanimity'—this meaning is a concise translation based on the Pyay version of the Nissaya. However, because it is the meaning of the term 'upekkhānubrūhitañca' and shares the same referent as the word 'cittaṃ' (mind), the meaning 'that mind is developed by equanimity' is also appropriate.
144:
The intensification of equanimity (*upekkhānubrūhanā*) should be understood through the function of specific-neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā-upekkhā*). Gladdening (*sampahaṃsanā*) should also be understood through the accomplishment of the function of knowledge that purifies by achieving the state of non-overrunning of the states of concentration and wisdom, and so on.

How is it to be understood? In the process of absorption (*appanā*), the group of defilements known as hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) is the danger to that jhāna; the mind is purified from those hindrances which are the dangers to jhāna. Because it is purified and free from the obstructing hindrances, it practices the middle sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*). (Note: Here, 'practices the sign of serenity' means it reaches the sign of serenity.) Absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) which occurs evenly is indeed called the middle sign of serenity. Immediately following that—or rather, the preceding change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhū-citta*) which is beneficial to that absorption concentration—by the method of unity (*ekatta-naya*), inclining towards a single continuum, is said to practice the middle sign of serenity. (Note: The 'method of unity' refers to the way it is understood to have reached stability by changing or inclining within a single mental continuum, just as milk becomes curds or sour milk; even though there is a distinction between sense-sphere consciousness and sublime consciousness, or between cause and effect, it is understood as a single mental process. - Sub-commentary). By such practicing, as it reaches stability through the power of absorption concentration, it is said to 'enter into' that sign of serenity. Thus, the purification of the way (*paṭipadā-visuddhi*) should be understood by way of its arrival (preliminary work) only at the moment of arising (*uppāda-khaṇa*) of the first jhāna, which accomplishes the characteristics present in the preceding change-of-lineage consciousness. (Note: 'Accomplishing... purification' means accomplishing the characteristics of purification from the danger of hindrances, reaching the middle sign of serenity, and entering into it, which are present in that change-of-lineage consciousness. This is the intended meaning. Indeed, those characteristics called 'purification of the way' which are included in the moment of jhāna due to special causes are preached as if they accomplish that specific purification of the way of jhāna. - Sub-commentary).

Since there is no further need to cleanse that mind which has been thus purified, the yogi who does not concern himself with cleansing—or rather, the lack of concern—is said to look on with equanimity at the purified mind. Having reached the state of serenity, the yogi who does not concern himself with the further steadying of the mind that is practicing the path of serenity—or rather, the lack of concern—is said to look on with equanimity at the path of serenity. Because it is practicing the path of serenity, having abandoned the company of defilements and being established in unity, the yogi who does not concern himself with the further establishment in unity—or rather, the lack of concern—is said to look on with equanimity at the mind established in unity. Thus, the intensification of equanimity should be understood through the function of specific-neutrality.
