2. The text in parentheses is added to bridge the preceding and following sentences.
3. "Becomes familiar" means reaching a state where the corpse is no longer perceived as repulsive, similar to a cemetery keeper who cremations corpses (Sub-commentary).

In the meditation on the gnawed (vikkhāyitaka), one should develop the mental attention: "Repulsive gnawed corpse, repulsive gnawed corpse," referring to a corpse gnawed in various ways by dogs, jackals, etc. Furthermore, in this meditation on the gnawed, the learning sign appears just as it is, gnawed in various places. The counterpart sign appears as a complete whole without any gnawed marks.

For a corpse that has been scattered in various places (vikkhittaka), one should also follow the method mentioned for the cut-in-half, having the parts placed a finger's breadth apart or doing it oneself, and develop the mental attention: "Repulsive scattered corpse, repulsive scattered corpse," referring to parts gnawed and scattered here and there by dogs, jackals, etc. In this meditation on the scattered, the learning sign appears with distinct gaps between the parts. The counterpart sign, however, appears as a complete whole.

A hacked and scattered corpse (hatavikkhittaka) can also be found in the same types of places mentioned for the cut-in-half. Therefore, having gone to such a place, one should follow the same method, having the parts placed a finger's breadth apart or doing it oneself, and develop the mental attention: "Repulsive hacked and scattered corpse, repulsive hacked and scattered corpse." Furthermore, in this meditation on the hacked and scattered, the learning sign appears like the visible marks of sword cuts. The counterpart sign appears as a complete whole.

A bloody corpse (lohitaka) can be found on battlefields and such, on the severed hands and feet of those who have received weapon wounds, or when blood is oozing from the openings of burst boils, carbuncles, and the like. Therefore, seeing such a corpse, one should develop the mental attention: "Repulsive bloody corpse, repulsive bloody corpse." In this meditation on the bloody, the learning sign appears with a moving quality, like a red banner fluttering in the wind. The counterpart sign, however, appears still and quiescent.

The worm-infested corpse (puḷavaka) occurs two or three days after death, at the time when a mass of worms oozes from the nine openings of the carcass.
186:
Alternatively, that worm-infested foulness (puḷavaka-asubha) has the body size of a dog, a jackal, a human, an ox, a buffalo, an elephant, a horse, a python, and so on, and it remains like a heap of sali rice. [186] Among those (carcasses of dogs, etc.), in any one of the rotting carcasses, one should bring to mind: "A foul corpse full of worms, a foul corpse full of worms." Indeed, it is appropriate to contemplate any such corpse. To the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissa, the sign appeared in the carcass of an elephant within the Kāḷadီghavāpi reservoir. In this meditation on the worm-infested (puḷavaka-kammaṭṭhāna), the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) appears as if it were moving. The counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) appears motionless and still, like a heap of sali rice.

The foulness of the skeleton (aṭṭhika-asubha) has been taught in various ways, such as: "As if one were to see a body cast away in a charnel ground, a skeleton with flesh and blood, held together by sinews," and so forth. In that meditation on the skeleton, one should go to the place where the skeleton is cast away in the manner previously described. Having established the sign and the object by means of surrounding stones and so on, and having characterized it according to its own nature as "This is a skeleton," the sign should be grasped in eleven ways by means of color and so forth.

119. To further explain the distinction: for one who looks at that skeleton as "white" by way of color, it does not appear (as foulness); it becomes mixed with the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa). Therefore, it should be viewed only by way of its foulness as "a foul skeleton." Here, "mark" (liṅga) is the name for the hands and so forth. Therefore, it should be defined by way of its marks as hands, feet, head, chest, arms, hips, thighs, and calves. Furthermore, it should be defined by way of its shape as long, short, round, square, small, or large. Direction (disā) and location (okāsa) are as previously described. Having defined it by way of the boundaries of each bone, one should take whichever bone appears clearly and reach absorption (appanā). Furthermore, it should be defined by way of the low and high places of each bone, as concave and convex. It should also be defined by way of its position: "I am standing in a low place, the bone is in a high place; I am standing in a high place, the bone is in a low place." Moreover, it should be defined by way of the joints where two bones meet. It should be defined by way of the gaps between the bones themselves. Moreover, one should let knowledge range over all the bones and define them all around as "This bone is in this place." If the sign still does not appear even when defined in this way, the mind should be well-fixed on the forehead bone.

120. Just as in this foulness of the skeleton, the way of grasping the sign in these eleven ways should also be noted in the previously mentioned foulness of the worm-infested and so forth, as applicable. To continue, this meditation on the skeleton can be accomplished with a whole skeleton or even with a single bone. Therefore, having grasped the sign in eleven ways in either the whole skeleton or a single bone, one should bring to mind: "Foul skeleton (foul bone), [187] foul skeleton (foul bone)." In this meditation on the skeleton, it is said (in the ancient Commentaries) that the learning sign and the counterpart sign are exactly the same. That statement is appropriate for a single bone. However, for a skeleton, it is appropriate that there are visible gaps in the learning sign, while in the counterpart sign, it appears completely filled. Furthermore, even with a single bone, the learning sign might be ugly and frightening, whereas the counterpart sign, because it brings about access concentration (upacāra-samādhi), might produce rapture and joy (pīti-somanassa).
187:
Indeed, in this matter, the statement made in the Commentaries is made by leaving the door open. The manner of leaving the door open is as follows: "In the four divine abidings (brahmavihāras) and the ten foulness meditations (asubhas), there is no counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). Truly, in the divine abidings, the breaking down of boundaries (sīmāsambheda) is itself the sign. In the ten foulness meditations, if one makes it free from conceptualization and sees only the state of repulsiveness, that is called the sign." Having said this, [the Commentary] does not stop there, but immediately adds: "In this foulness meditation, the sign is of two kinds: the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). The learning sign appears as distorted, ugly, and frightening." Such statements are again mentioned in those Commentaries. Therefore, only the statement we have made after careful investigation (that the sign is suitable in a single bone, but in a skeleton, the learning sign appears with gaps, etc.) is appropriate in this context of the sign of the bone meditation.

Alternatively, as an illustration, for the Elder Mahā Tissa (who was traveling from Cetiya Mountain to Anurādhapura for alms), the perception of the entire body of a woman as a skeleton, triggered by merely seeing her teeth-bones when she laughed, serves as a clear example in this bone meditation (showing the distinction between the learning sign and the counterpart sign).

The Buddha, whose fame is praised by the Thousand-Eyed One (Sakka) who possesses ten times a hundred eyes, who is endowed with the Ten Powers and the quality of pure beauty (being pure and free from the stains of defilements along with their latent tendencies), taught these ten kinds of foulness, each being a cause for the first jhāna, as described. Having understood these and the method of their development as explained, one should further understand this miscellaneous discussion regarding them.

## Miscellaneous Discussion

121. Among these, a person who has attained jhāna in any one of the foulness meditations, because lust is well-suppressed, becomes like one free from lust, devoid of flighty or greedy behavior. Even so, the reason these different types of foulness are taught is according to the natural state of the body and the different temperaments of those prone to lust. To explain: when a corpse reaches a state of repulsiveness, it might reach the state of being bloated (uddhumātaka), or it might reach one of the states such as being livid (vinīlaka). In this way, whatever state is possible to obtain in a corpse, the sign should be grasped as "the bloated repulsive corpse" or "the livid repulsive corpse." Therefore, it should be understood that the ten types of foulness are taught according to the natural state of the body (such as bloating, etc.).
188: Furthermore, among these ten kinds of foulness, the bloated corpse (uddhumātaka) is particularly suitable for one whose lust is strong regarding the shape of the body, as it shows the distortion and destruction of the body's form.
189: [189] The sign of foulness (asubha-nimitta) also appears in the body of a living person. Indeed, just like a dead body, the living body is also foul, loathsome, and unattractive. However, in this living body, because it is concealed by adventitious adornments (such as bathing, cleaning, and applying perfumes), the characteristic of foulness, which is the mark of its unattractiveness, does not appear to most people. By its very nature, this body is a heap of over three hundred bones, joined by one hundred and eighty joints, bound by nine hundred tendons, plastered with nine hundred pieces of flesh, enveloped in moist skin, and covered by the epidermis. It is full of many small openings (such as pores for hair and sweat), and like a pot of fat, it is constantly oozing and trickling from above and below. It is inhabited by a multitude of worms, the abode of diseases, and the basis for painful states. Like an old, burst boil, it constantly discharges from nine wound-like openings. From its two eyes, eye-filth trickles; from the ear-holes, ear-filth; from the nostrils, snot; from the mouth, food, bile, phlegm, and blood are vomited; from the lower orifices, excrement and urine are discharged; and from the ninety-nine thousand pores, loathsome sweat trickles. Bluebottles and other flies surround and settle upon it. If one does not tend to this body by brushing the teeth, washing the face, oiling the head, bathing, and wearing clothes, but wanders from village to village in its natural state with coarse, disheveled hair, then even a king would be no different from a flower-scavenger or an outcaste (caṇḍāla), as their bodies would be equally loathsome. Thus, in terms of being impure, foul-smelling, and disgusting, there is no difference between the body of a king and that of an outcaste. Although there is no such difference, people clean the teeth-filth and so on by brushing and washing, conceal the private parts that should be hidden with various garments, smear the body with fragrant perfumes of various colors, and adorn it with flowers and ornaments, thereby bringing it to a state where it can be grasped as 'I' and 'mine.' Because it is thus concealed by these adventitious adornments, men feel delight in women and women in men, failing to recognize the characteristic of foulness, which is the body's true and inherent nature. In the ultimate sense (paramattha), however, there is not even an atom's worth of anything in this body that is fit to be delighted in. Because this is so, if even a single part such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, saliva, snot, excrement, or urine falls outside the body, people do not even wish to touch it with their hands; they are repelled by it, ashamed of it, and loathe it. Yet, as for the parts remaining inside this body, although they are just as loathsome as those that have fallen out, people—being enveloped in the darkness of ignorance (avijjā) and stained by the lust (rāga) of self-love—grasp them as 'desirable, lovely, permanent, pleasant, and self (attā).' Grasping them in this way, they become like an old jackal in the forest who, seeing a kiṃsuka tree in bloom, is distressed by mistaking the flowers that have not yet fallen from the tree for pieces of meat. Therefore—
190:
The following three verses were spoken (by the ancient teachers):

“This body (which is a collection of thirty-two parts) has a foul, rank, and evil smell. Though repeatedly washed and cleaned, it is impure. It is like the rotting carcass of a dog or a snake, and like a cesspit. It is censured by those who possess the eye of wisdom. But fools, who lack the eye of wisdom, delight in and cherish this body (perceiving it as fragrant and so forth).

Indeed, the loathsome nature of the living body should also be contemplated. The following three verses were spoken (by the ancient teachers):

*Dugghandho asuci kāyo, kuṇapo ukkarūpamo.*
*Nindito cakkhubhūtehi, kāyo bālābhinandito.*

This body (the collection of thirty-two parts) has a foul, rank, and evil smell.

Note: Because it is not difficult to understand, and for the benefit of those who wish to memorize and contemplate it, the Pali of these three verses is presented and translated using the Nissaya method.

It is impure (even though it is repeatedly washed and groomed). It is like the rotting carcass of a dog or a snake. It is like a cesspit. This body is censured by those who possess the eye of wisdom. But fools, who lack the eye of wisdom, delight in and cherish it (perceiving it as fragrant and so forth).

*Allacamma-paṭicchanno, navadvāro mahāvaṇo.*
*Samantato paggharati, asuci pūtigandhiyo.*

(This body, which is so cherished by the ignorant,) is covered with moist skin. It has nine prominent openings. It is like a great wound with many orifices. From all around, it constantly trickles and oozes impure, loathsome, and foul-smelling substances such as excrement and urine.

*Sace imassa kāyassa, anto bāhirako siyā.*
*Daṇḍaṃ nūna gahetvāna, kāke soṇe nivāraye.*

If the inside of this body were to be turned outside, one would surely have to take a stick to drive away the crows and dogs.

Therefore, a monk of a wise nature (one who is capable of attaining the special states of jhāna, path, and fruit) should take the sign of foulness (asubha-nimitta) wherever the aspect of foulness appears, whether in a living body or a dead body. Having produced the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) and established himself in access concentration (upacāra-jhāna), he should develop that meditation and bring the foulness meditation to absorption concentration (appanā-jhāna). Here ends one part.

This is the Sixth Chapter, titled 'Description of Foulness as a Meditation Subject' (Asubhakammaṭṭhāna-niddesa), in the section on the Development of Concentration in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## The Detailed Explanation of Foulness as a Meditation Subject Ends.

## 7. Cha-anussati-niddesa: Detailed Explanation of the Six Recollections

## Explanation of the Meaning of the Ten Recollections

[191] 123. Immediately after the foulness meditation, among the ten recollections previously mentioned in brief: Mindfulness (sati) itself is called 'recollection' (anussati) because it occurs repeatedly. Alternatively, it is called 'recollection' because it is mindfulness appropriate for a son of good family who has gone forth out of faith (saddhā-pabbajita), occurring only in the proper place where it should occur.
191:
(1) The recollection (anussati) that arises by taking the Buddha as the object is called Buddhānussati (Recollection of the Buddha).

Notes:
1. Among the ten, connect with "is called Buddhānussati," etc.
2. In the term 'anussati', the meaning of the prefix 'anu' is shown; it should be translated as 'repeatedly'.
3. Anu (repeatedly) + sati (recollection) = anussati (repeated recollection).
4. Another meaning of 'anu' is shown; it should be translated as 'accordingly' or 'suitable'.
5. Anu (accordingly/suitable) + sati (recollection) = anussati (suitable recollection). Here, 'suitable' refers both to the object worthy of recollection and to the noble disciple who has gone forth out of faith; both meanings should be taken.
6. The name 'Buddha' is designated to the Blessed One based on certain qualities. Taking those qualities of the Buddha together, this name (Buddhānussati) is a designation for the mindfulness (sati) that takes the qualities of the Buddha as its object.

(2) The recollection that arises by taking the Dhamma as the object is called Dhammānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-proclaimed (svākkhātata), as its object.

(3) The recollection that arises by taking the Saṅgha as the object is called Saṅghānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its good conduct (suppaṭipannatā), as its object.

(4) The recollection that arises by taking one's own virtue (sīla) as the object is called Sīlānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the qualities of virtue, such as its being untorn (akhaṇḍatā), as its object.

(5) The recollection that arises by taking one's own generosity (cāga) as the object is called Cāgānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the qualities of generosity, such as being liberal in giving (muttacāgatā), as its object.

Note:
It says "taking the Buddha as the object." Therefore, it is stated: "This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the qualities of the Buddha as its object" (Commentary). Because it is shown thus in the Commentary, although it says "taking the Buddha as the object," one should take the meaning as "taking the qualities of the Buddha as the object." The same applies to "taking the Dhamma as the object," etc.

(6) The recollection that arises by taking deities (devatā) as witnesses is called Devatānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes one's own qualities, such as faith (saddhā), as the object, while placing the deities in the position of witnesses.

(7) The recollection that arises by taking one's own death (maraṇa) as the object is called Maraṇānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the interruption of the life faculty (jīvitindriya) as its object.

(8) Mindfulness that goes to the physical body consisting of thirty-two parts such as hair, etc., or mindfulness that occurs in the body, is called Kāyagatāsati. According to grammatical rules, it should be called 'Kāyagatasati', but it is taught as 'Kāyagatāsati' without shortening the 'ā' in 'gatā'.

Notes:
1. In the Sinhalese version, the term 'anu' is omitted here, and it appears as "the mindfulness that arises is called Maraṇassati," which agrees with the Aṅguttara Nikāya (II, 268).
2. The translation has been slightly modified from the literal Pali to make it easier for those not proficient in Pali to understand.
3. When the terms 'kāyagatā' and 'sati' are joined in a kammadhāraya compound, the 'ā' in 'gatā' should be shortened; however, it should be known that it is taught as 'Kāyagatāsati' without such shortening.

This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the sign (nimitta) of the body parts (koṭṭhāsa), such as hair, as its object.

(9) Mindfulness that arises by taking the in-breaths and out-breaths as the object is called Ānāpānassati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes the sign of the in-breaths and out-breaths as its object.

(10) The recollection that arises by taking peace (upasama)—that is, Nibbāna, the stilling of all formations—as the object is called Upasamānussati. This name is a designation for the mindfulness that takes Nibbāna, the stilling of all suffering, as its object.

Notes:
1. "Taking the sign of the body parts" means taking the sign of foulness in parts like hair. In the seven recollections prior to this, there is no occurrence of a 'sign'; it is mentioned here to show that a sign exists in this mindfulness occupied with the body (Commentary).
2. Āna (in-breath) + apāna (out-breath) + sati (recollection) = Ānāpānassati (mindfulness of in-breathing and out-breathing).
3. 'Upasama' refers to the stilling of all formations, meaning Nibbāna (Commentary). Upasama (Nibbāna, the stilling of all formations) + anussati (repeated recollection) = Upasamānussati (repeated recollection of Nibbāna, or repeated recollection of the quality of Nibbāna as the stilling of the suffering of formations).

## 1. Explanation of the Development of Buddhānussati

124. Among these ten recollections, a meditator who wishes to develop the first, Buddhānussati, and who is possessed of unwavering confidence (aveccappasāda) gained through understanding, should go to a suitable dwelling (possessing the five factors) and stay in seclusion. Withdrawing from external objects and being well-concentrated on the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), he should repeatedly recollect the qualities of the Blessed Buddha in this way:

"Iti pi so bhagavā arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno sugato lokavidū anuttaro [192] purisadammasārathi satthā devamanussānaṃ buddho bhagavā."

In the manner provided by this Pali text, the qualities of the Blessed Buddha should be repeatedly recollected.

Notes:
1. The clarity and confidence that arise after knowing the qualities of the Buddha truly through understanding is called 'aveccappasāda'; it is the faith associated with the Noble Path. Alternatively, faith similar to that of the Noble Path is also called 'aveccappasāda'; such faith is not shaken by the winds of wrong view, nor can those winds move it. It refers to one possessed of such unwavering confidence. For such a person, the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha will reach completion and perfection. For others, it may not reach completion or perfection (Commentary).
2. By the phrase "stay in seclusion," physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), which is the absence of company, is shown.
192:
(Ṭīkā)
In this context (regarding the phrase "should be recollected repeatedly"), the following is the method of repeated recollection:
"For this reason, the Blessed One is Arahaṃ; for this reason, he is Sammāsambuddho... [etc.]... for this reason, he is Bhagavā." Thus, the yogi recollects repeatedly (or, it should be recollected repeatedly).¹

Note:
1. Here, the first meaning is the literal translation of the existing word *anussarati*. The second meaning in parentheses is consistent with the word *anussaritabbā* (should be recollected) at the end of the previous paragraph. Following this, there is an explanation of the word *itipi*: "*Itipi* means 'for this reason and for that reason'." Since that meaning has already been translated as "For this reason, he is Arahaṃ," etc., and because showing that explanation in the Burmese translation does not provide much benefit, that specific explanation is omitted.

## Explanation of the Quality of Arahaṃ
125. Regarding those qualities, the meaning is: The Blessed One is called Arahaṃ for these reasons: because of being remote (from defilements), because of having killed the enemies, because of having destroyed the spokes (of the wheel of Saṃsāra), because of being worthy of requisites and so on, and because of the absence of secrecy in doing evil. To explain further:
Because the Blessed One has destroyed the defilements along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) by means of the (Noble) Path, he is remote (*ārakā*) from all defilements; he stands at an extreme distance from defilements. Because of being thus remote, he is called Arahaṃ.¹

Note:
1. This means the word *Arahaṃ* is derived from *ārakā* (remote). Therefore, according to this explanation, one should repeatedly recollect: "The Blessed One is Arahaṃ, being remote and pure from the 1,500 defilements along with their habitual tendencies." (For the calculation of the 1,500 defilements, see Dependent Origination, Vol. 2, p. 348). Noble Arahant disciples are also free from all defilements; however, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from when they had defilements may still remain. For instance, the Venerable Pilindavaccha, due to his past habits as a Brahmin, had the habit of addressing others rudely as "outcaste" (*vasala*). The Blessed One, however, is free even from such habitual tendencies. In this regard, one can also recollect specifically, such as "The Blessed One is free from greed," "The Blessed One is free from hatred," etc., rather than just collectively.

"The Noble One in whom those defilements do not arise¹ (or, do not cling or adhere), that Noble One is said to be remote from those defilements. Our refuge, the Blessed One, is also remote, as defilements and faults do not arise in him; therefore, he should be known as Arahaṃ." (1)

126. Furthermore, the Blessed One has killed those enemies known as defilements with the weapon of the Noble Path. Because he has killed the enemies of defilements, he is also called Arahaṃ.²

Note:
In this context, one can also recollect: "The Blessed One who has abandoned greed," "The Blessed One who has abandoned hatred," etc.
1. In this sentence, a literal translation would be "the non-arising of those defilements of that Noble One occurs." Such a translation is not smooth in Burmese, so it has been slightly modified as above.
2. From *ari* (enemies) + *hata* (killed) = *Arahaṃ*: The Blessed One who has abandoned and killed the enemies of defilements.

"Our refuge, the Blessed One, has killed all enemies known as greed and so on¹ with the sword-weapon of the wisdom of the Noble Path. Because he has thus killed the enemies of defilements, he should be known as Arahaṃ." (2)

127. Furthermore, the wheel of Saṃsāra² has a hub made of ignorance and craving, spokes consisting of meritorious formations, demeritorious formations, and imperturbable formations, and a rim of aging and death. It is pierced by an axle made of the origin of taints and is well-fitted to the chariot of the three realms (sensual, fine-material, and immaterial).¹ It has been revolving for a time without beginning. The Blessed One, standing on the ground of virtue (*sīla*) at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhi-maṇḍa*) with the feet of energy (*vīriya*), took the axe of knowledge (*ñāṇa*) which brings an end to kamma with the hand of faith (*saddhā*) and destroyed all the spokes.² Because he has thus destroyed the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra, he is also called Arahaṃ.³

Note:
In this context, one can also recollect: "The Blessed One who has killed greed," "The Blessed One who has killed hatred," etc.
1. In the phrase *sabbepi* (all also), the word "also" (*pi*) indicates that he has killed not only the collective group of all defilement-enemies but also each individual defilement-enemy. However, in Burmese usage, it is not common to speak that way, so the meaning of the word *pi* (also) is shown in parentheses.
2. Connect as: "That wheel of Saṃsāra... having a hub... being well-fitted... revolves continuously." This means the wheel of Saṃsāra revolves continuously because it has such a hub, spokes, and rim, and is fitted with such an axle.
1. (Repeated note in source).
2. Connect as: "Destroyed all the spokes."
3. *Ara* (spokes) + *hata* (destroyed) = *Arahaṃ*: The Blessed One who has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra, which are the three types of formations (*saṅkhāra*).

128. Alternatively, regarding the destruction of spokes: The cycle of Saṃsāra is called the wheel of Saṃsāra because its beginning cannot be known when one reflects back step by step (i.e., it is *Anamatagga*).¹

Note:
This means that by destroying the spokes of formations—meritorious and demeritorious kamma—new existence of mind and matter (*nāma-rūpa*) does not arise at all and ceases. Therefore, the great wheel of Saṃsāra, which is the process of mind and matter, can no longer revolve. It means the Blessed One has destroyed the spokes so that it cannot revolve.
1. *Anu* (following step by step) + *amatagga* (beginning not known) = *Anamatagga*: Saṃsāra whose beginning cannot be known when reflecting back step by step. This means that because there are effects like consciousness and mind-matter in the present life, it is known that the causes of those effects, such as ignorance and craving, existed in the past life. In that past life too, causes like ignorance and craving arose depending on effects like consciousness.
193:
Since the effects that depend on those causes also existed in that life, the causes of those effects also existed in a previous life. Thus, by tracing back step by step, the beginning of Saṃsāra cannot be found or known. Therefore, the process of the aggregates of mind and matter, known as Saṃsāra, is said to have an unknowable beginning—or rather, no beginning at all.

Because ignorance (avijjā) is the root cause, it is called the hub of this wheel of Saṃsāra. Because aging and death (jarāmaraṇa) are the end, they are called the rim. The remaining ten factors (from volitional formations to birth) are called the spokes, because they have ignorance as their root and aging and death as their end. In that statement (to elaborate), not knowing the truths of suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path (or delusion that knows wrongly) is ignorance (avijjā).

(To further show how it is the root cause:) In the sense realm (kāmabhava), ignorance (avijjā) assists volitional formations (saṅkhāra).1 In the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), ignorance assists volitional formations. In the immaterial realm (arūpabhava), ignorance assists volitional formations. In the sense realm, volitional formations assist rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhivinnāṇa); the same applies to the other two, the fine-material and immaterial realms. In the sense realm, rebirth-consciousness assists name-and-form (nāmarūpa). The same applies to the fine-material realm. In the immaterial realm, it assists name (nāma) only. In the sense realm, name-and-form assists the six sense bases (saḷāyatana). 

Note: 
1. Here, 'assists' (paccaya) means to be a support in some way for the arising of the respective effect. There are 24 such modes of support, such as root-condition (hetu-paccaya), object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya), etc. For details, see the Burmese translation, Vol. 4, pp. 54, 88, etc.

In the fine-material realm, name-and-form assists three sense bases.1 In the immaterial realm, name assists one sense base, the mind base (manāyatana). In the sense realm, the six sense bases assist the sixfold contact (phassa). In the fine-material realm, the three sense bases assist the three types of contact.2 In the immaterial realm, the one sense base assists the one type of mind-contact (manosamphassa). In the sense realm, the six types of contact assist the six types of feeling (vedanā). In the fine-material realm, the three types of contact assist the three types of feeling in that very realm. In the immaterial realm, the one type of mind-contact assists the one type of feeling in that very realm. In the sense realm, the six types of feeling assist the six groups of craving (taṇhā-kāya).3 In the fine-material realm, the three types of feeling assist the three groups of craving in that very realm.

Note: 
1. The three sense bases are the eye, ear, and mind bases.
2. The three types of contact are eye-contact, ear-contact, and mind-contact.
3. The term 'taṇhā-kāya' is translated as 'groups of craving.' The collection of cravings for various forms is called 'rūpa-taṇhā-kāya' (group of craving for forms). The same applies to craving for sounds, etc.
194:
Volitional formations are effects produced by causes. The wisdom in discerning the causes, such as "Both of these (ignorance and volitional formations) are also effects produced by causes," is called the Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena (Dhammaṭṭhiti-ñāṇa). In the past duration known as the previous life, and in the future duration known as the next life, "Ignorance is the cause, volitional formations are the effects produced by the cause, and both of these are effects produced by the cause"—the wisdom in thus discerning the causes is called the Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena. In this same manner, all terms (such as volitional formations as cause and consciousness as effect, etc.) should be expanded and understood.

In that Wheel of Saṃsāra, ignorance and volitional formations constitute one section; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling constitute one section; craving, clinging, and existence constitute one section; and birth, aging, and death constitute one section. Furthermore, among these four sections, the first section is the past duration. The middle two sections are the present duration. Birth, aging, and death (the final section) are the future duration.

Note: 1. Since ignorance also arises due to the arising of taints (āsava-samudaya), both are referred to as effects produced by causes.

To explain further, in these four sections, by taking ignorance and volitional formations (in the section of past causes), craving, clinging, and existence (which are inseparable associates) are also taken. Therefore, these five factors are called the round of kamma (kamma-vaṭṭa) in the past duration or past life. The five factors starting with consciousness are called the round of resultants (vipāka-vaṭṭa) in the present duration of this life. By taking craving, clinging, and existence (in the section of present causes), ignorance and volitional formations (which are inseparable associates) are also taken. Therefore, these five factors are called the round of kamma in the present duration of this life. By indicating birth, aging, and death, the task of describing consciousness and so on (which are the bases of birth, aging, and death) is accomplished; therefore, these five factors (consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling) are called the round of resultants in the future duration or future life. Thus, these four sections consist of twenty modes.

Note: 1. If the term 'niddiṭṭhattā' were translated literally as 'because of being pointed out,' those with little scriptural knowledge might not understand. Therefore, it is translated using an easier synonymous method as above. 2. Following the traditional translation, 'ākāra' is translated as 'modes' (literally 'aspects'). According to the sub-commentary's definition 'ākīriyanti pakāsīyanti,' it should be understood as 'factors that are further explained.'

Furthermore, in this Wheel of Saṃsāra, there is one connection between volitional formations and consciousness, one connection between feeling and craving, and one connection between existence and birth.

As stated, the Blessed One knows, sees, realizes, and penetrates in every way this Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), called the Wheel of Saṃsāra, which has four sections, three durations, twenty modes, and three connections. That knowing is called 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing, and 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of knowing specifically. Therefore, it is said: "Wisdom in discerning causes is the Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena."

Note: 1. Although there are four adjectives ending in 'having,' they are combined into pairs to maintain the flow of the sentence. 2. This is the translation of the term 'pajānanaṭṭhena.' Although it does not explicitly say 'knowing specifically' with the prefix 'pa-', it refers to the same knowing of wisdom (ñāṇa) that is equivalent to 'paññā.' Therefore, one should not conclude that 'jānāti' (knows) or 'janana' (knowing) without the 'pa-' prefix does not refer to the knowledge of wisdom. In this regard, one should also note the meanings of terms like 'Sabbaññū' (The Omniscient One) because He knows all (sabbaṃ jānāti), and 'Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa' (Omniscient Knowledge).

With this Knowledge of the Stability of Phenomena, the Blessed One, having known those factors such as ignorance as they truly are, became weary of them, became dispassionate, and was liberated; He struck, destroyed, and demolished the spokes (ara) of this Wheel of Saṃsāra with its various modes as described. Because He has thus destroyed the spokes, He is called 'Arahaṃ.'

Since the spokes of the Wheel of Saṃsāra were destroyed with the sword of knowledge by the Protector of the World, He is therefore called 'Arahaṃ.' (3)

Note: 1. Ara (spokes) + hata (destroyed) = Arahaṃ; the Blessed One who has struck and destroyed the spokes of the Wheel of Saṃsāra with the sword of the Path of Arahantship.

## Diagram (1) of the Wheel of Dependent Origination
This first diagram is drawn in accordance with paragraph 128 of the Visuddhimagga mentioned above. In that circle, merit-producing volitional formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) caused by ignorance are divided into two types: sense-sphere and fine-material sphere. Among them, sense-sphere merit-producing formations can lead to four rims: (1) aging and death in the woeful states, (2) aging and death in the human and celestial realms, (3) aging and death in the fine-material realm, and (4) aging and death in the immaterial realm; thus it is shown in four sections. In the same way, fine-material merit-producing formations are divided into 3 sections, demerit-producing formations into 2 sections, and imperturbable formations into 2 sections.

In accordance with the sub-commentary's explanation of 'Anamatagga' (without discoverable beginning):
(1) If a plant is found, its seed can be known and inferred.
(2) If there is a seed, its plant must have existed before.
(3) By searching in this way, the beginning is not found.
(4) Searching similarly, the beginning of Saṃsāra is not found.
(5) Since there is an effect in the present life, there was a cause in the past.
(6) Depending on that cause, the five effects existed at that time.
(7) To produce those effects, five causes existed in the past.
(8) By searching in this way, the beginning is not found.

## Diagram (2) of the Wheel of Dependent Origination
This second diagram is to be compared with the Burmese translation of the Visuddhimagga, Volume 4, page 191, paragraph 652, etc. To understand the details:
Two roots, two truths, four layers, three rounds, three connections, twelve factors, three durations, and twenty modes—among these eight categories, for one who clearly sees and knows the five present effects, the round of craving does not arise from feeling, the cycle is severed, and suffering ceases.
195:
In the aforementioned summary verse, 'one who clearly and personally perceives the fivefold present results' means: one who, at every moment of occurrence—whether seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, or cognizing—clearly and thoroughly perceives the five present results, namely consciousness (viññāṇa) along with mind-and-matter (nāma-rūpa), the sense bases (āyatana), contact (phassa), and feeling (vedanā), through their natural characteristics, their arising and passing away, and the characteristics of impermanence (anicca), suffering (dukkha), and non-self (anattā).

Regarding 'the root of the round of craving does not arise due to feeling,' it means: for one who perceives thus thoroughly, at every moment of insight, the craving that could arise—known as the latent tendency for craving towards an object (ārammaṇānusaya)—ceases momentarily (tadaṅga-nirodha) regarding the mind-and-matter objects rightly known through their aspect of impermanence, etc. Consequently, clinging (upādāna), becoming (bhava), birth (jāti), and aging-and-death (jarā-maraṇa), which would have followed from that craving, also cease. After such cessation through insight, at the moment of the Noble Path (ariya-magga), the latent tendency of craving within the continuity (santānānusaya) is eradicated (samuccheda-nirodha), and clinging, etc., cease once and for all. Referring to this mode of cessation, it is stated in the Sammāsa Sutta of the Nidānavagga Saṃyutta (p. 333):

'Whatever in the world is of a lovely and pleasant nature, they see it as impermanent, they see it as suffering, they see it as non-self. They abandon craving. They abandon the acquisitions (upadhi), they abandon suffering.' This means those who perceive seeing, hearing, etc., which are called lovely and pleasant things, as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, abandon craving, abandon the aggregates called acquisitions, and abandon suffering.

In the Dukkha Sutta and others of that same Nidānavagga Saṃyutta (p. 300), it is also taught: 'With the remainderless fading away and cessation of that very craving (which would arise due to feeling), there is the cessation of clinging,' and so forth.

129. Furthermore, because he is the most supreme recipient of offerings, the Blessed One is worthy of requisites such as robes and special veneration. Because he is so worthy, when the Tathāgata appeared, all the powerful deities and humans with great retinues did not offer veneration to any other place or person. To demonstrate the truth of this: the Great Brahmā Sahampati venerated the Tathāgata with a jeweled garland the size of Mount Sineru. Other deities such as Sakka, and humans such as King Bimbisāra and King Kosala, venerated him to the best of their ability. Moreover, dedicated to the Blessed One even after his Parinibbāna, the Great King Asoka spent ninety-six crores of wealth and established eighty-four thousand monasteries throughout the whole of Jambudīpa. What need is there to mention other special forms of veneration (by ordinary deities and humans)? Because he is worthy of requisites and so forth in this manner, he is called 'Arahaṃ'.

Since this Lord of the World is worthy of special veneration along with the four requisites, the Victor (Jina) is worthy of this name 'Arahaṃ,' which accords with its meaning in the world.

Note 1: Formed from the root 'arah' + the suffix 'anta', it becomes 'arahanta' or 'arahaṃ'. It grammatically means 'one who is worthy'. Therefore, one should repeatedly reflect: 'The Blessed One is the Arahaṃ, who is worthy of receiving the special veneration of all beings, including humans, deities, and Brahmas.'

131. Furthermore, just as in the world some fools who imagine themselves to be wise commit evil in secret for fear of ill-repute (thinking others might see or hear), this Blessed One never does so (because the defilements that cause evil were well-abandoned at the seat of enlightenment). Because of the absence of secrecy in committing evil, he is called 'Arahaṃ'.

Note 2: The word 'fools' alone implies all fools without distinction; therefore, to avoid verbosity and for ease of understanding, the translation of the word 'yekeci' (whosoever) is omitted.

Since there is no such thing as secrecy in the evil deeds of such a one (the Buddha), who is endowed with the quality of 'tādi' (equanimity/steadfastness), he is renowned as 'Arahaṃ' due to that absence of secrecy.

Note 1: 'A' (none) + 'raha' (secrecy) = 'Arahaṃ', the Blessed One who has no secrecy. It means the Blessed One who does not commit evil in secret because he is pure in all ways, both in public and in private.

Thus, in every way:
(1) Because of being remote from defilements,
(2) because of having killed the enemies which are the defilements,
(3) because the spokes of the wheel of Saṃsāra have been destroyed,
(4) because of being worthy of requisites and so forth,
(5) because he does not commit evil in secret and there is no secrecy for him to commit evil,
that Blessed One (who is the true refuge of the whole world) is called 'Arahaṃ'.

Note 1, 2, 3: In the Pali text regarding these three reasons, they are presented appropriately according to the poetic meter as it is a verse.

## (The Explanation of the Quality of Arahaṃ Ends.)

## (2) The Explanation of the Quality of Sammāsambuddha

131. Furthermore, because he has known all things rightly (sammā) and by himself (sāmaṃ), he is the 'Sammāsambuddha' (Perfectly Enlightened One). Indeed, he has known all things rightly and by himself: he has known things that should be known through higher knowledge (abhiññeyya) as such; things that should be fully understood (pariññeyya) as such; things that should be abandoned (pahātabba) as such; things that should be realized (sacchikātabba) as such; and things that should be developed (bhāvetabba) as such. Therefore, he said:

'What should be known through higher knowledge has been known by me; what should be developed has been developed; what should be abandoned has been abandoned by me; therefore, O Brahmin, I am the Buddha.' (M. Ni. 2.399; Su. Ni. 563)
196:
If translated strictly according to the Pali, it would differ from the previous two points and become inconsistent; therefore, in this Myanmar translation, priority is given to the smoothness of the Myanmar language, capturing only the essential meaning to ensure clarity.

4. Regarding 'Sāmañca' (and by himself), the word 'ca' has the sense of conjunction with 'Sammā' (rightly known). Thus, it is translated as above. In the Commentary (Ṭīkā), 'Sāman' is explained as 'Sayam-eva' (by oneself). This is because the term 'Sāman' alone can imply the restrictive sense of 'by oneself without receiving guidance from others,' and it is used to show that he did not receive instructions from anyone else.

To elaborate: This Blessed One knows all things rightly and knows them by himself. He has known the four truths that should be known by higher knowledge (abhiññeyya) as abhiññeyya; he has known the truth of suffering that should be fully understood (pariññeyya) as pariññeyya; he has known the truth of origin that should be abandoned (pahātabba) as pahātabba; he has known the truth of cessation that should be realized (sacchikātabba) as sacchikātabba; and he has known the truth of the path that should be developed (bhāvetabba) as bhāvetabba. Therefore, the Blessed One uttered the following verse:

'O Sela, what should be known by higher knowledge, I have known; what should be developed, I have developed; what should be abandoned, I have abandoned; therefore, O Brahmin, I am a Buddha.'

Note: Regarding the realization of Nibbāna, it is said 'the truths that should be realized (sacchikātabba).' The use of the plural is to include the different aspects such as Nibbāna with elements of clinging remaining (sa-upādisesa-nibbāna), etc. Alternatively, this is a concise teaching of the Four Noble Truths, showing the existence of the phenomena without defining their specific limits, similar to the Abhidhamma Mātikā.

132. Alternatively: The eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda) is the Truth of Suffering. The craving (taṇhā) from the past life, which is the root cause for the arising of that eye, is the Truth of the Origin. The non-arising of both these truths is the Truth of Cessation. The practice (the Eightfold Path) that knows cessation distinctly is the Truth of the Path. In this way, by taking each item such as the eye, he knows all things rightly and by himself. The same method applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

By this same method, one should apply: the six bases such as the visible form base; the six groups of consciousness such as eye-consciousness; the six contacts such as eye-contact; the six feelings born of eye-contact; the six perceptions such as perception of forms; the six volitions such as volition regarding forms; the six cravings such as craving for forms; the six thoughts (vitakka) such as thought regarding forms; the six sustained thoughts (vicāra) such as sustained thought regarding forms; the five aggregates such as the aggregate of form; the ten kasinas; the ten recollections; the ten perceptions such as the perception of a bloated corpse (asubha); the thirty-two parts of the body such as hair; the twelve bases; the eighteen elements; the nine existences (bhava) such as the sensual existence; the four jhānas such as the first jhāna; the four immeasurables such as the meditation on loving-kindness; the four formless attainments; the factors of Dependent Origination in reverse order starting from aging and death; and the factors of Dependent Origination in forward order starting from ignorance.

In that context, the following is the application for the last item: Aging and death are the Truth of Suffering. Birth is the Truth of the Origin. The escape from and the end of both is the Truth of Cessation. The practice that knows cessation distinctly is the Truth of the Path. Thus, by taking each item, he knows all things rightly and by himself; he has understood them accordingly and penetrated them. Therefore, I have said: 'Because he knows all things rightly and by himself, he is called Sammāsambuddha.'

## (End of the explanation of the quality of Sammāsambuddha.)

## (3) Explanation of the quality of Vijjācaraṇasampanna

133. Furthermore, because he is endowed with the special knowledges called 'vijjā' and the foundational conduct called 'caraṇa', he is called Vijjācaraṇasampanna. Among 'vijjā' and 'caraṇa', 'vijjā' refers to the three special knowledges or the eight special knowledges. The three special knowledges should be understood as taught in the Bhayabherava Sutta. The eight special knowledges should be understood as taught in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta. In the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, the eight special knowledges are taught by including insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and the mind-made power (manomayiddhi) along with the six higher powers (abhiññā).

'Caraṇa' (Conduct) consists of fifteen things: (1) restraint by the Pātimokkha virtue, (2) guarding the doors of the sense faculties, (3) moderation in eating, (4) devotion to wakefulness, (5-11) the seven good qualities (saddhamma) [faith, shame, fear of wrongdoing, great learning, energy, mindfulness, wisdom], and (12-15) the four fine-material sphere jhānas. These fifteen things should be known as 'caraṇa'. Indeed, the noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) travels to the deathless region of Nibbāna by means of these fifteen good qualities; because they are the means of going to Nibbāna, these fifteen qualities are called 'caraṇa'. As it is said in the discourse:

'Mahānāma, here, a noble disciple is virtuous...' All this should be understood as taught in the Sekha Sutta of the Majjhima Paṇṇāsa. The Blessed One is endowed with these three or eight special knowledges and these fifteen foundational conducts. Therefore, he is called Vijjācaraṇasampanna.
197:
[197] In this quality of 'Vijjācaraṇasampanna' (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct), the fulfillment of the special knowledges (vijjā) stands as the fulfillment of the Blessed One's omniscience (sabbaññuta). The fulfillment of the basic conduct (caraṇa) stands as the fulfillment of His Great Compassion (mahākāruṇikatā). Because He knows the benefit and harm of all beings through His omniscience, and because He is the Great Compassionate One, He leads them to avoid harm and engages them in what is beneficial. Such engagement is the natural practice of one endowed with knowledge and conduct. Because He engages them in benefit in this way, the disciples (sāvakas) of this Blessed One are well-practiced (suppaṭipanna); they are not ill-practiced like the disciples of sectarian teachers who lack knowledge and conduct, such as those who are self-tormentors (attantapa).

## (The explanation of the quality of Vijjācaraṇasampanna ends.)

## (4) Explanation of the quality of Sugata

134. He is called 'Sugata' because He has a beautiful going, because He has gone to a beautiful place, because He has gone rightly, and because He speaks rightly.

To explain further: 'Going' is also called 'gata'. That going of the Blessed One is beautiful, pure, stainless, and faultless. What is that going? It is the Noble Path (ariya-magga). Indeed, by that beautiful going of the Noble Path, He has gone to the region of safety (Nibbāna) without clinging. Because He has such a beautiful going, He is called Sugata. (1)

Furthermore, He has gone to a beautiful place, which is the Deathless Nibbāna. Because He has gone to such a beautiful place, He is called Sugata. (2)

Furthermore, He has gone rightly, meaning He does not return to the defilements already abandoned by each respective path. For it is said (in the Mahāniddesa): "The defilements abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) do not return, do not come back, do not recur; therefore He is Sugata... [as with the other paths] ... the defilements abandoned by the path of arahantship (arahatta-magga) do not return, do not come back, do not recur; therefore He is Sugata." Alternatively, He has gone rightly because, from the time at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Seat of Enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), He practiced the right conduct of fulfilling the thirty perfections (pāramīs) solely for the welfare and happiness of the entire world, and He has gone without falling into the extremes of eternalism (sassata), annihilationism (uccheda), sensual indulgence (kāmasukha), and self-mortification (attakilamatha). Because He has gone rightly in this way (through the Noble Path and the prior right practice), He is called Sugata. (3)

Furthermore, He speaks rightly; He speaks only appropriate words in appropriate situations. Because He speaks such good and appropriate words rightly, He is called Sugata. The following discourse is the evidence for this:

"The Tathāgata knows a word to be false, incorrect, and unbeneficial, and that word is also unpleasant and disagreeable to others; such a word the Tathāgata does not speak. (1)

The Tathāgata knows a word to be true and correct but unbeneficial, and that word is also unpleasant and disagreeable to others; such a word the Tathāgata does not speak. (2)

The Tathāgata knows a word to be true, correct, and beneficial, but that word is unpleasant and disagreeable to others; in such a case, the Tathāgata knows the right time to speak that word. (3)

The Tathāgata knows a word to be false, incorrect, and unbeneficial, but that word is pleasant and agreeable to others; such a word the Tathāgata does not speak. (4)"
198:
The Blessed One knows: 'This is true, this is factual, but it is not beneficial.' Others may like and appreciate such words, but the Blessed One does not speak them (5)¹. The Blessed One knows: 'This is true, this is factual, and it is beneficial.' [198] Others may like and appreciate such words, and in that case, the Blessed One knows the proper time to speak those words (6)². (This is from the Sādhaka Sutta). Because he speaks in such a good manner as described, he should be known as 'Sugato' (The Well-Gone).

## (The explanation of the attribute 'Sugato' ends.)

## (5) Explanation of the attribute 'Lokavidū'

135. Furthermore, he is called 'Lokavidū'³ because he has known the world in all its aspects. To explain further: That Blessed One, called Lokavidū, has known, understood, and penetrated the world in all its aspects—by its nature, by its origin (samudaya), by its cessation (nirodha), and by the means to its cessation.

Notes:
1. These words in (5) refer to slanderous speech, factual but useless talk (tiracchānakathā), or flattering speech directed at lay devotees for the sake of gain.
2. These words in (6) refer to talk on giving (dāna), virtue (sīla), and other topics related to worldly welfare, spoken at the appropriate time and place.
3. Loka (world) + Vidū (knower) = Lokavidū (The Knower of the Worlds).

This is in accordance with the following words spoken by the Blessed One:

'Friend Rohitassa, where one is not born, does not age, does not die, does not pass away, and is not reborn¹, that end of the world, I say, cannot be known, seen, or reached by traveling. Yet, friend Rohitassa, I also say that without reaching the end of the world, there is no making an end to suffering. Rather, friend Rohitassa, it is in this very fathom-long body, endowed with perception and mind, that I declare the world², the origin of the world, the cessation of the world³, and the way leading to the cessation of the world.'

Notes:
1. The commentaries and sub-commentaries state that these two terms show the continuity of not dying and not being born. Some teachers say they refer to spontaneous rebirth (upapāta); the sub-commentary notes this view as plausible.
2. 'The world' refers to the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca); 'the way' refers to the Truth of the Path (magga-sacca). By this, the Buddha shows: 'Friend Rohitassa, I do not declare these Four Noble Truths in grass or wood, but within this very body of a being dependent on the four great elements.'
3. 'Cessation of the world' refers to the cessation of the world of formations, or specifically, Nibbāna.

'The end of the world can never be reached by walking,
Yet without reaching the end of the world, there is no release from suffering.
Therefore, truly, the wise one, the Knower of the Worlds,
The reacher of the world's end, who has lived the holy life,
Having known the end of the world, being at peace,
Does not long for this world or the next.' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.107, Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.45).

136. Moreover, there are three kinds of worlds: the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of space (okāsaloka). Among these:

In the passage, 'One world: all beings¹ subsist on nutriment,' the world of formations² should be understood. In the passage, 'The world is eternal' or 'The world is not eternal,' the world of beings is meant³.

'As far as the sun and moon revolve, shining and illuminating the quarters,
So far the thousandfold world extends; there your power holds sway.'⁴

Notes:
1. 'Beings' refers to the formations of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa-saṅkhāra) which are called 'beings' based on the individual.
2. Both animate formations (with faculties) and inanimate formations (without faculties) are called the world of formations.
3. The conceptualization of 'self' or 'world' by those with wrong views as eternal, etc., is based on the concept of a being, not on mere formations. Thus it is called the world of beings.
4. The area illuminated by the sun and moon is one universe (cakkavāḷa); a thousand such universes constitute a thousandfold world system (the domain of a Brahmā). Here, the light of the sun is the primary focus; the moon is mentioned according to common usage.

In this passage, the world of space is meant. The Blessed One knew these three worlds in every way.

To explain further: 'One world: all beings subsist on nutriment. Two worlds: name and form. Three worlds: three kinds of feeling. Four worlds: [199] four kinds of nutriment. Five worlds: five aggregates of clinging.'
199: The six internal bases are the six worlds. The seven stations of consciousness [1] are the seven worlds. [Footnote 1: (1) Different bodies and different perceptions, (2) different bodies and uniform perceptions, (3) uniform bodies and different perceptions, (4) uniform bodies and uniform perceptions, (5) perception of the base of infinite space, (6) perception of the base of infinite consciousness, (7) perception of the base of nothingness. These 7 are called the seven stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhiti). For their meanings, see the footnotes on pages 145-6 of the fourth volume of the Burmese translation of Visuddhimagga, first edition. This relates to paragraph 637.] The eight worldly conditions are the eight worlds. The nine abodes of beings [1] are the nine worlds. [Footnote 1: If the abode of unconscious beings and the abode of beings with neither-perception-nor-non-perception are added to the seven stations of consciousness, they become the nine abodes of beings (sattāvāsa).] The ten material bases are the ten worlds. The twelve bases are the twelve worlds. The eighteen elements are the eighteen worlds. (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.112). This world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) has also been known by the Blessed One in every way. Furthermore, the Blessed One knows the inclinations (āsaya) [2] of all beings, knows their underlying tendencies (anusaya) [3]. [Footnote 2: The dwelling place of the mind is called inclination (āsaya). One who is habituated to the view of eternalism, even if they occasionally accept the view of annihilationism or right view, tends to return to their eternalist view. Similarly for annihilationism. Therefore, eternalism and annihilationism are the inclinations where the minds of worldlings dwelling in the round of rebirth reside. Insight knowledge and path knowledge are the inclinations where the minds of noble ones dwelling beyond the round of rebirth reside. These four are called inclinations. Footnote 3: The seven defilements that can arise when conditions are met—sensual lust, aversion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, lust for existence, and ignorance—are called underlying tendencies (anusaya).] He knows their temperaments (carita) [1], knows their dispositions (adhimutti) [2]. [Footnote 1: Temperament refers to good conduct and bad conduct. Alternatively, the six temperaments: lustful, hateful, deluded, faithful, intellectual, and speculative. (Ṭīkā). Footnote 2: Disposition refers to the mental attitude or inclination. Some have low dispositions (hīnādhimutti), while others have noble dispositions (paṇītādhimutti).] He knows beings with little dust in their eyes and those with much dust in their eyes, those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good qualities and those with bad qualities, those easy to teach and those hard to teach, and those who are capable and those who are incapable of realizing the Dhamma. Because he knows thus, the Blessed One has known the world of beings (sattaloka) in every way. 137. Just as he knows the world of beings, so too he knows the world of locations (okāsaloka). To explain: a single world-system (cakkavāḷa) is 1,203,450 yojanas in length and breadth. As for its circumference: The entire circumference of a world-system is 3,610,350 yojanas [1]. [Footnote 1: Modern science mentions Pluto... for comparison.] In that world-system: This great earth (vasundharā) is said to be 240,000 yojanas in thickness [2]. [Footnote 2: Modern science says the earth is a sphere... difficult to deny.] The water that supports this very earth is 480,000 yojanas in thickness and rests on air. The air that supports that water extends 960,000 yojanas into the sky. This is the constitution of the world of locations. To continue: in this world-surface thus well-constituted— [200] The noble Mount Sineru is submerged 84,000 yojanas in the great ocean [1] and rises 84,000 yojanas into the sky. [Footnote 1: This means Mount Sineru is 84,000 yojanas below and 84,000 yojanas above.]
200:
Below the dimensions of Mount Sineru, in descending order by half the measure of each preceding one, submerged below and rising above,¹ are the divine mountains adorned with various jewels,² which are the dwellings of the gods:

The great Yugandhara mountain, Īsadhara mountain, Karavīka mountain, Sudassana mountain, Nemindhara mountain, Vinataka mountain, and Assakaṇṇa mountain—

These seven great mountains stand around Mount Sineru; they are the abodes of the Great Kings and are inhabited by devas and yakkhas.

Mount Himavā is five hundred yojanas high,² and three thousand yojanas in length and breadth. It is as if adorned with eighty-four thousand peaks. 

The Jambu (rose-apple) tree, named 'Naga' (immobile),³ has a trunk circumference of fifteen yojanas. The length of its trunk and branches is fifty yojanas each, and it spreads out to a width of one hundred yojanas. It rises to that same height (one hundred yojanas).¹ By the power of this Jambu tree, the continent is known as Jambudīpa.

Furthermore, the dimensions of this Jambu tree are the same as the Citrapāṭali (Trumpet flower) tree of the Asuras, the Simbali (Silk-cotton) tree of the Garuḍas, the Kadamba tree in the western continent of Aparagoyāna,² the Kapparukkha (Wishing tree) in the northern continent of Uttarakuru,² the Sirīsa (Acacia) tree in the eastern continent of Pubbavideha,² and the Pāricchattaka (Coral tree) in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

“The Pāṭali, the Simbali, the Jambu, the Pāricchattaka of the gods, the Kadamba, the Kapparukkha, and the Sirīsa is the seventh.”

The Cakkavāḷa mountain is submerged eighty-two thousand yojanas in the great ocean, and rises just as much (eighty-two thousand) above the water's surface. This Cakkavāḷa mountain stands encircling the entire world-system (loka-dhātu).¹

In that world-system, the moon's disk is forty-nine yojanas.² The sun's disk is fifty yojanas.³ The realm of Tāvatiṃsa is ten thousand yojanas. Likewise, the Asura realm, the Avīci great hell, and Jambudīpa (India)¹ are each ten thousand yojanas. The continent of Aparagoyāna is seven thousand yojanas. The continent of Pubbavideha is likewise seven thousand yojanas. The continent of Uttarakuru is eight thousand yojanas. Each of these four great continents is surrounded by five hundred small islands.² All these together are called one Cakkavāḷa or one world-system. Between three such world-systems lie the Lokantarika hells.³

Notes
1. Modern oceanographers state that the deepest part of the ocean is only over 5 miles. Therefore, one should consider what kind of yojana is referred to here.
1. Connect these adjectives (rising, divine, adorned with jewels) to the 'great mountains'.
2. Modern measurements of Mount Himavā (Himalayas) by those who have reached the summit state it is only over 5 miles high. Therefore, the yojana and ancient measurement methods shown here are points for consideration.
3. This is the meaning of the word 'Nagavhaya'. 'Naga' means a tree that does not move; it is synonymous with 'rukkha' (tree). 'Avhaya' means name or title; it is used here merely to complete the eight syllables of the Pali verse and has no special additional meaning.
1. Where is this great Jambu tree located? According to the Aṅguttara Commentary (Vol. 1, p. 377), it grows on Mount Himavā and lasts for the duration of the aeon. Furthermore, the Sāratthadīpanī Ṭīkā (Vol. 1, p. 259) states that each of its side branches is fifty yojanas long, and great rivers flow from these large branches.
2. The specific locations of these Kadamba, Kapparukkha, and Sirīsa trees are not clearly mentioned in the scriptures.
1. According to scientists, the Earth is a sphere and such a Cakkavāḷa mountain does not exist, nor would it be necessary.
2. Scientists state that the moon's diameter is about 2,000 miles, its circumference is about 6,000 miles, and it orbits the Earth at a distance of about 240,000 miles.
3. Scientists state that the sun's diameter is about 864,393 miles, its mass is equivalent to 329,000 Earths, and it is about 92,897,000 miles away from the Earth.
1. Jambudīpa is understood to be India because Ashokan inscriptions mention neighboring countries, commentaries state King Siridhamma-asoka ruled the entire island of Jambudīpa, and the Mahāgovinda Sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya describes the map of Jambudīpa as wide in the north and shaped like the front of a cart in the south.
2. Nowadays, it is said that there are far more than five hundred small islands; Indonesia alone has over three thousand islands. Therefore, the 'five hundred small islands' mentioned here should be understood as referring only to inhabited islands like Sri Lanka, or as the state of the world at its beginning.
3. Just as when three large plates are placed together, the Lokantarika hells exist in the space where three world-systems meet.
201:
In the manner described, the Blessed One, with his infinite Buddha-knowledge, has known and penetrated the infinite world-elements known as the infinite universes. In this way, the world of space (Okāsaloka) was also fully known by him.

Note:
There exist hells (in the intervals between world systems). In those hells, there is no light from the moon or sun; it is absolute darkness. The beings fallen into those hells crawl like bats on the cliffs at the edge of the universe. When they touch and encounter one another, they perceive each other as food and try to seize and kill one another. In doing so, they fall from the cliffs they were clinging to and drop into the water supporting the world. Upon falling, they dissolve like flour in the extremely caustic water. If their karma is not yet exhausted, they reappear on the cliffs. For what karma are they born in that hell? It is said they are born there due to unwholesome kamma such as cruel offenses, daily acts of violence, and persecution against parents and virtuous monks who observe the Dhamma. (Dīgha Nikāya Mahāvagga Aṭṭhakathā, p. 26). The space between three or four solar systems can also be called Lokantarika.

A point to be specially noted here: Detailed descriptions of the earth and the structure of the universe are not found in the Pali scriptures. Even in the Vimuttimagga, believed to have been composed in India, such descriptions are not present in the explanation of the attribute Lokavidū.

This Blessed One has known [the world] in every respect.1 Because he has thus known the world in every respect according to the way he knows the three worlds, he is called 'Lokavidū'.

## (End of the explanation of the attribute Lokavidū.)

## (6-a) Explanation of the attribute Anuttaro

138. Furthermore, because there is no one superior or more excellent than him in qualities,2 there is no one higher than this Blessed One; therefore, he is called 'Anuttaro'.3 This is indeed true—this Blessed One surpasses the entire world (of all beings) by his quality of virtue (sīla); he also surpasses it by his qualities of concentration (samādhi), wisdom (paññā), liberation (vimutti), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimutti-ñāṇadassana).

Note:
1. This sentence is a concluding statement. Therefore, it should not be thought of as identical to the previous sentence.
2. In the phrase "no one superior or more excellent," the word "superior" is used as an explanation of the term 'Anuttaro' (none higher or more excellent). It is not said because there are others who are merely excellent; for indeed, in the world with its devas, there is no one even nearly equal (sadisappa) to the Blessed One. Where could there be an equal? It goes without saying that there is no one superior. (Ṭīkā)
3. Ana (none) + Uttara (higher/more excellent) = Anuttaro: The Blessed One who has no one higher or more excellent, being the Most Excellent.

He surpasses [the world] by the quality of virtue; he is also peerless (in the same era). He is equal only to the Buddhas of the past and future, who are also peerless. He is without a likeness, without a counterpart, without a rival... etc... He is also peerless and without a rival in the quality of the knowledge and vision of liberation. This statement is in accordance with the following words spoken by the Blessed One:

"Monks, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its devas and humans, I do not see any other recluse or brahmin who is more accomplished in virtue than myself." This and other such passages should be understood in detail. Likewise, the Aggappasāda Sutta and others should also be understood.1 Verses beginning with "No teacher have I" should also be expanded upon.

## (End of the explanation of the attribute Anuttaro.)

Note:
1. "Monks, as far as there are beings—whether without feet, with two feet, with four feet, or with many feet; whether with form or without form; whether percipient, non-percipient, or neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient—of all these beings, the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One, is called the foremost. Monks, those who have faith in the Buddha have faith in the foremost..." (Aggappasāda Sutta).

## (6-b) Explanation of the attribute Purisadammasārathi

139. He is called 'Purisadammasārathi'1 because he drives or guides men (beings) who are fit to be tamed. (By the word "drives," it is meant that) he tames or disciplines them. In that phrase, "men to be tamed" (purisadamma) refers to animal-men, human-men, and non-human-men who are untamed but fit to be tamed. This is indeed true—the Blessed One tamed animal-men such as the Nāga king Apalāla, Cūḷodara, Mahodara, Aggisikha, Dhūmasikha, the Nāga king Aravāḷa,2 the elephant named Dhanapālaka (also known as Nāḷāgiri), and so on; he made them harmless and established them in the refuges and the precepts. He also tamed human-men such as Saccaka the son of a Nigaṇṭha, the young man Ambaṭṭha, the brahmins Pokkharasāti, Soṇadaṇḍa, Kūṭadanta, and others. He also disciplined non-human-men such as the yakkhas Āḷavaka, Sūciloma, and Kharaloma, and Sakka the king of devas, and so on, taming them through various diverse methods of discipline. Indeed, in this context, the sutta beginning with "Kesi, I train a man to be tamed sometimes with gentleness, sometimes with harshness, and sometimes with both gentleness and harshness" should be understood in detail.1

Furthermore, the Blessed One, while teaching the first jhāna and so on to those of pure virtue, and teaching the practice of the higher paths to Stream-enterers (Sotāpanna) and others, also tames those who are already (partially) tamed (to make them fully tamed).

## (End of the explanation of the attribute Purisadammasārathi.)

Note:
1. Purisa (man/being) + Damma (to be tamed) + Sārathi (driver/guide/tamer) = Purisadammasārathi: The Blessed One who drives or tames men fit to be tamed.
2. Apalāla is a Nāga king living in the Himālaya. Cūḷodara and Mahodara are Nāga kings living on the island of Nāgadīpa. Aggisikha and Dhūmasikha are Nāgas living on the island of Sīhaḷa (Sri Lanka). (Ṭīkā). The Nāga king Aravāḷa is mentioned in the Vinaya Aṭṭhakathā (p. 48) as living in Kasmīra-Gandhāra.
1. In that sutta, it is taught that taming by showing the benefits of good conduct is "gentle," and taming by showing the faults of misconduct is "harsh," etc.

## (6-g) Explanation of the attribute Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi

[202] Alternatively, this term 'Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi' is a single attribute expressing one meaning. Indeed,
202:
The Blessed One makes men who are to be tamed go—while sitting in a single cross-legged posture—to the eight directions (of the attainments) without any hindrance or delay. Therefore, he is called *Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi* (Incomparable Charioteer of Men to be Tamed). Indeed, in this context, the discourse beginning with "Monks, when an elephant-tamer makes an elephant to be tamed go—when he drives it—it runs in only one direction" should be understood in detail.

## (The explanation of the quality of Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi ends.)

Notes
1. It means the Blessed One is the most excellent and best among those who instruct, teach, guide, and discipline individuals who are to be tamed.
2. After showing that a horse trained by a horse-trainer also runs in only one direction when driven, the discourse explains that the Blessed One is called *Anuttaro Purisadammasārathi* because he can instruct and guide one to reach the eight directions in a single sitting: (1) Kasina of color in internal form, (2) Kasina of color in external form, (3) *Subha-jhāna*, (4-7) the four *Arūpa-jhānas*, and (8) *Nirodha-samāpatti*.

## (7) The explanation of the quality of Satthādevamanussānaṃ

140. He is called *Satthā* (Teacher) because he instructs and teaches according to what is appropriate regarding the welfare of the present life, the welfare of future lives, and the supreme welfare (Nibbāna). Alternatively, he is called *Satthā* because he is like a caravan leader, the head and leader of a group of merchants. This refers to the Blessed One as the caravan leader. For example, a caravan leader helps merchants cross through difficult terrains: a wilderness of robbers, a wilderness of wild beasts, a wilderness of famine, a wilderness of waterlessness...

Notes
1. Since the verb *anussāsati* (instructs) should have two objects, the welfare being taught should also be an object. However, because it is stated as *paramatthehi* in the instrumental case, and the sub-commentary also explains the meaning using the instrumental case *tehi*, and because language can follow the speaker's intention, it is translated here in the instrumental sense as it appears in the Pali.
2. In this sense, the meaning of *Satthā devamanussānaṃ* as "the Blessed One who is the teacher of gods and humans" should be understood.
3. In this sense, the meaning of *Satthā devamanussānaṃ* as "the Blessed One who is the great leader and guide, like a caravan leader for gods and humans" should be understood.

...he makes them cross over, pass through, and escape, bringing them to a land of safety. Similarly, the Blessed One, as the caravan leader, makes beings cross the wilderness; he makes them cross the wilderness of birth (*jāti*), (the wilderness of aging (*jarā*), the wilderness of sickness (*byādhi*), and the wilderness of death (*maraṇa*); he makes them pass through). In this way, the meaning of the word *Satthā* should be understood according to the method of the *Niddesa*. *Devamanussānaṃ*—of gods and humans—means he is the teacher of both gods and humans. This statement "Teacher of gods and humans" is made by way of defining the most noble beings and by way of defining those capable of liberation (*bhabba-puggala*). In reality, however, the Blessed One is also a teacher of animals by way of giving instruction. Indeed, those animals also, by listening to the Dhamma of the Blessed One, attain the fulfillment of supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), and through that very fulfillment of supporting conditions, they become partakers of the Path and Fruit in their second or third existence. In this matter, the frog-deity (*Maṇḍūka-devaputta*) and others are examples.

To elaborate: While the Blessed One was preaching the Dhamma to the residents of Campā on the bank of Lake Gaggarā, a frog took the sound of the Blessed One's voice as a sign (of the Dhamma) and was listening. A cowherd, standing there leaning on his staff while absentmindedly listening, pressed his staff down on the frog's head. That frog died at that very moment and was reborn in a golden mansion twelve leagues in size in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Like one waking from sleep, seeing himself surrounded by a host of celestial nymphs in that mansion, he reflected: "Oh, even a frog like me has been reborn in this golden celestial mansion! What kind of deed did I perform?" He saw no other merit than having taken the sound of the Blessed One's voice as a sign. (Therefore,) that frog-deity immediately came with his golden mansion and paid homage at the Blessed One's feet with his head. The Blessed One, though knowing, asked:

"Who is it that pays homage at my feet, shining with psychic power and glory, illuminating all directions with such magnificent beauty?"
203:
"Who is this, shining with divine power and retinue, illuminating all directions with such an exceedingly pleasing appearance, bowing at my feet?"

[203] "In my previous life, I was a frog dwelling in the water. While I was listening to your Dhamma, a cowherd killed me (by pressing down with a bamboo staff)," he replied.
