(Sub-commentary) According to this second explanation of the Sub-commentary, in the phrase "manasā sajjhāyo" (mental recitation), the word "sajjhāya" is not derived from "saṃ + ajjhāya" but from "saṃ + jhāy." Therefore, that word "sajjhāyo" should be translated as "contemplating or thinking."

Mental contemplation-recitation supports the penetration and understanding of the characteristics of foulness (asubha-lakkhaṇa) (or the ability to remember the nature of loathsomeness). (2)

## Defining by Color and So Forth
By way of color: the color of head-hairs and so forth should be defined and noted. (3)

By way of shape: the shape of those same head-hairs and so forth should be defined and noted. (4)

By way of direction: in this body, the part above the navel is the upper direction, and below is the lower direction. Therefore, the direction should be defined as, "This part is in such and such a direction." (5)

By way of location: the location of each part should be defined as, "This part is situated in such and such a location." (6)

By way of delimitation: there are two kinds of delimitation—similar delimitation (sabhāga-pariccheda) and dissimilar delimitation (visabhāga-pariccheda). Therein, similar delimitation should be known as, "This part is delimited below, above, and across by such and such." Dissimilar delimitation should be known by way of non-mixture, such as, "Head-hairs are not body-hairs, and body-hairs are not head-hairs." (7)

When explaining the skill in the sevenfold learning in this way, one should explain after knowing that this meditation subject is taught by way of loathsomeness in such and such a Sutta, and by way of elements in such and such a Sutta. For this is taught by way of loathsomeness only in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. It is taught by way of elements in the Mahāhatthipadopama, Mahārāhulovāda, and Dhātuvibhaṅga Suttas. In the Kāyagatāsati Sutta, however, the four jhānas are analyzed with reference to the one to whom it appears by way of color. Therein, what is taught by way of elements is the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā). What is taught by way of loathsomeness is the meditation subject of tranquility (samatha). And that is what is meant here as the tranquility meditation subject.
236:
The lower part is called the downward direction; therefore, one should define the direction as "this part is in this direction." (5)

By location: This means one should define the location of each part as "this part is located in this place." (6)

By delimitation: There are two kinds of delimitation: delimitation by its own kind (sabhāga-pariccheda) and delimitation by a different kind (visabhāga-pariccheda). Among these, "this part is bounded below, above, and around by such and such" is how one understands delimitation by its own kind. "Hairs are not body hairs, and body hairs are not hairs"—in this way, one understands delimitation by a different kind through the power of non-mixture. (7)

Furthermore, a teacher who explains the skill in learning (uggahakosalla) in these seven ways as just described should understand and explain that this meditation on mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) is taught in such and such a sutta by way of the perception of repulsiveness (paṭikkūla), and in such and such a sutta by way of elements (dhātu). To elaborate: this meditation on mindfulness of the body is taught only by way of repulsiveness in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. In the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa, it is taught by way of elements. However, in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta of the Uparipaṇṇāsa, it is taught by classifying the four jhānas for the sake of a person to whom it appears by way of color (vaṇṇa). Among these, the meditation taught by way of elements is insight meditation (vipassanā), while the meditation taught by way of repulsiveness is serenity meditation (samatha).

Note
1. When searching for hair, etc., if a dark color appears, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) of the blue kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa) appears, and one attains the four fine-material jhānas. When contemplating bones, if a white color appears, the counterpart sign of the white kasiṇa (odāta-kasiṇa) appears, and one attains the four fine-material jhānas. This sutta shows the attainment of the four jhānas for such a person.

This meditation on the thirty-two parts (dvattiṃsākāra) found in the Kāyagatāsati Sutta is only serenity meditation in the context of this mindfulness of the body. Here ends the explanation of skill in learning.

## Explanation of Skill in Attention (Manasikārakosalla)

[236] 181. Having explained the skill in learning in the seven ways as mentioned, one should explain the skill in attention in these ten ways: (a) in order (anupubbato), starting from hair, body hair, etc.; (b) not too fast (nātisīghato); (c) not too slow (nātisaṇikato); (d) warding off distraction (vikkhepapaṭibāhanato); (e) transcending the concept (paṇṇattisamati-kkamanato) of hair, etc.; (f) dropping the indistinct (anupubbamuñcanato); (g) by way of absorption (appanāto); and (h, i, j) the three Suttas. Among these:

(a) In order: This means that a yogi practicing this mindfulness of the body should attend to it in the order of hair, body hair, etc., starting from the recitation; one should not attend to it by skipping every other part.

Note
1. In the context of mindfulness of the body as shown in the Visuddhimagga. The Commentary (Ṭīkā) explains it as "in this section on the attention to repulsiveness."
2. One should not attend by skipping one part, let alone skipping two or more. (Ṭīkā)

The fault is: if one attends by skipping parts, just as an unskilled man climbing a thirty-two-step ladder by skipping steps might fall due to physical exhaustion and fail to complete the climb, so too, because of not attaining the satisfaction (assāda) that should be reached through the perfection of development (bhāvanā), one falls due to mental exhaustion and fails to complete the development.

(b) A yogi attending in order should also not attend too fast.
237:
The fault is: for a yogi who attends too fast, just as a man traveling a three-league journey who does not notice the places he should or should not go, even if he runs back and forth a hundred times with great speed, the journey is indeed finished, but he must still ask his way as he goes. Similarly, the meditation merely reaches the end, but it does not become clear and does not bring about distinction. Therefore, one should not attend too fast.

(c) Just as one should not attend too fast, so too one should not attend too slow. The fault is:

Note
1. Connect as: "If one attends by skipping parts... similarly... one falls due to mental exhaustion because of not attaining satisfaction."
2. Connect as: "For the yogi... similarly, the meditation merely reaches the end..."

For a yogi who attends too slow, just as a man who wants to travel a three-league journey in a single day but lingers at trees, mountains, or lakes along the way, the journey does not reach its end and must be finished in two or three days. Similarly, the meditation does not reach its conclusion and does not become a condition for attaining distinction.

(d) Warding off distraction: This means that one should ward off the distraction of the mind toward various external objects after letting go of the meditation subject. The fault is: for one who does not ward it off, just as a man traveling a narrow cliff-path only a foot wide who does not carefully notice where he steps but looks here and there, his footing will fail and he will fall into a hundred-fathom-deep abyss. Similarly, when there is distraction toward external objects, the meditation subject declines and perishes. Therefore, one should attend by warding off distraction.

[237] (e) Transcending concepts: This means one should transcend the names and concepts such as "hair," "body hair," etc., and fix the mind on the repulsiveness. To give an analogy: in a time when water is scarce, people find a well in the forest and tie some sign like a palm leaf there. They come by that sign to bathe and drink. But when the path of their coming and going becomes clear through frequent travel, they no longer have any need for the sign; they go whenever they wish to bathe and drink. Similarly, for a yogi who attends by way of the concepts "hair," "body hair," etc., in the preliminary stage, the state of repulsiveness becomes clear. At that time, the yogi should transcend the concepts "hair," "body hair," etc., and fix the mind only on the state of repulsiveness.

(f) Dropping the indistinct: This means that whichever part does not appear clearly, one should drop that part and attend by dropping the indistinct in order. To elaborate: for a beginner, when attending to "hair," the attention goes and stops only at "urine," the final part. And when attending to "urine," the attention goes in reverse and stops only at "hair," the first part. Then, as he attends repeatedly, some parts appear to him and some do not. He should perform the work of attention only on those parts that appear.

Here is an analogy: just as a hunter who wants to catch a monkey living in a grove of thirty-two palm trees might shoot an arrow at a leaf of the first palm tree and shout. Then that monkey, jumping from tree to tree in order, would go to the very last palm tree. When the hunter does the same there, the monkey would return to the first tree in the same manner. Being repeatedly chased like this, the monkey would jump from the places where the shouts were made and eventually land on a single tree. Grabbing firmly onto the spike of a young palm leaf in the middle of that tree, it would not jump even if shot at. This should be understood in the same way.

Here is the application of the analogy: the thirty-two palm trees in the grove are like the thirty-two parts in this body. The monkey is like the mind. The hunter is like the yogi. The monkey's dwelling in the thirty-two-palm-tree grove is like...
238:
(To what extent?) One should practice attention until only two parts (koṭṭhāsa) appear, and among those two, until one appears more clearly. By repeatedly attending to that one part which appears more clearly, one should bring about absorption (appanā-jhāna).

In this regard, there is this simile: A hunter wishing to catch a monkey living in a grove of thirty-two palm trees would shoot an arrow at the leaf of the first palm tree and make a loud shout to frighten it. Then, that monkey would jump from tree to tree in succession and reach the last palm tree. If the hunter goes to that tree and likewise shoots an arrow and shouts to frighten it, the monkey would return to the first tree in the same manner. When the monkey is made to jump repeatedly to its full capacity, it would rise only at the places where the shouts occur and jump to a certain tree in succession. 

(Note: 'pari-pāṭiyamāna' means being made to jump all around, which refers to making it jump to its full capacity.)

In the middle of that tree, holding firmly to the spike of the young palm leaf and not rising even when shot at with an arrow, it would remain still. This method of attention should be understood as being similar to this simile.

In that simile, the following is the correlation between the simile and the thing illustrated: The thirty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) in this body should be understood as the thirty-two palm trees in the grove. The mind should be understood as the monkey. The yogi should be understood as the hunter. The repeated occurrence and wandering of the yogi's mind by way of the object in the body of thirty-two parts should be understood as the monkey's living in the grove of thirty-two palm trees. Just as when the hunter shoots an arrow at the leaf of the first tree and shouts, the monkey jumps to various trees and reaches the last tree; so too, when the yogi begins to attend to 'hairs of the head,' the mind proceeds in succession and comes to rest only at the final part. The same applies to the return journey. Just as the monkey rises only at the places of shouting when made to jump repeatedly to its full capacity; so too, for the yogi who attends repeatedly, when only certain parts appear, he should abandon those that do not appear and perform the preliminary work (parikamma) only on those that do appear. 

(Note: 'holding firmly... it would remain without rising' and 'this method of attention... should be understood' are connected.)

Just as, in the end, having jumped to a single tree and holding firmly to the spike of the young palm leaf in the middle of that tree, the monkey does not rise even when shot at with an arrow; so too, in the end, when two parts appear, one should repeatedly attend only to the part that appears more clearly and bring about absorption (appanā-jhāna).

Another simile is this: An alms-collecting monk living in dependence on a village of thirty-two houses, if he receives alms for two houses at the very first house, he would let go of the alms from one house further on. Again, on the next day, if he receives alms for three houses at one house, he would let go of the alms from two houses further on. On the third day, if he receives a full bowl at the very first house, he would go to the sitting hall and consume it (without going to other houses). This method of attention should be understood as being similar to this simile.

The correlation between the simile and the thing illustrated is as follows: The thirty-two parts should be understood as the village of thirty-two houses. The yogi should be understood as the alms-collecting monk. The yogi's performing of the preliminary work on the thirty-two parts should be understood as the monk's living in dependence on that village. Just as receiving alms for two houses at the first house and letting go of the alms from one house further on, and just as receiving alms for three houses on the second day and letting go of the alms from two houses further on; so too, while attending, one should abandon those that do not appear and perform the preliminary work on those that appear, down to two parts.
239:
Just as on the third day, receiving a full bowl at the very first house (without going to other houses), going to the refectory, sitting down, and consuming the food; so too, one should understand the arising of absorption (appanā jhāna) by repeatedly reflecting only on the most prominent part among the two parts.

(g) Regarding 'by way of absorption' (appanā)—it should be understood that absorption occurs in one of the parts, such as the hair, etc., within the part where absorption arises. This is the intended meaning here.

(h, i, j) Regarding 'the three suttas'—these three suttas, namely the Adhicitta Sutta, the Sītibhāva Sutta, and the Bojjhaṅgakosalla Sutta, should be known for the purpose of balancing effort (vīriya) and concentration (samādhi). This is the intended meaning here. Among those—

[239] "Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind (adhicitta)—the mind of extraordinary samatha and vipassanā—should from time to time attend to three signs (nimitta). From time to time, he should attend to the sign of concentration (samādhi-nimitta); from time to time, he should attend to the sign of exertion (paggaha-nimitta); from time to time, he should attend to the sign of equanimity (upekkhā-nimitta).

Notes:
1. Connect 'Among those...' with 'should be known as the Adhicitta Sutta,' etc.
2. Adhi- (extraordinary/superior) + citta (mind of samatha and vipassanā).
3. The sign of concentration is the very state of stability that is to be noted. 'Should attend to' means it should be made in the mind, 'should be brought into being'—this is the meaning of 'should be made.' Alternatively, the object which is the cause of concentration is called the sign of concentration; it means that should be reflected upon. The same method applies to the sign of exertion and the sign of equanimity (meaning, take two meanings for each). (Ṭīkā)

Bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind should attend only to the sign of concentration exclusively, it is possible that his mind may lead to laziness (kosajja). If he should attend only to the sign of exertion exclusively, it is possible that his mind may lead to restlessness (uddhacca). If he should attend only to the sign of equanimity exclusively, it is possible that his mind may not be properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints (āsava).

But, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind from time to time attends to the sign of concentration, from time to time attends to the sign of exertion, and from time to time attends to the sign of equanimity, then that mind becomes malleable (mudu), wieldy (kammañña), and radiant (pabhassara); it is not brittle (na ca pabhaṅgu) and is properly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.

Bhikkhus, suppose a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice prepares a crucible. Having prepared the crucible, he heats the mouth of the crucible. Having heated the mouth of the crucible, he takes the gold with tongs, puts it into the mouth of the crucible, and from time to time blows on it, from time to time sprinkles it with water, and from time to time looks on at it. Bhikkhus, if the goldsmith or his apprentice were to blow on that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would burn. If he were to sprinkle it with water exclusively, it is possible that the gold would cool down. If he were to look on at it exclusively, it is possible that the gold...

Notes:
1. This is the meaning of the word 'ekantaṃ'; it means if one observes only one type exclusively.
1. 'Pabhassaraṃ' means it is completely pure and bright because it is free from the defilements (upakkilesa) that cause tarnish. (Ṭīkā) In accordance with this explanation, 'radiant' should be understood as being clean and pure.
2. 'Na ca pabhaṅgu' means it does not fail or break because it has reached a state of strength and capability in the work of meditation, just as pure gold that has been well-refined is capable of being made into desired ornaments. (Ṭīkā)
240:
...would not reach proper maturity. But, bhikkhus, when the goldsmith or his apprentice from time to time blows on that gold, from time to time sprinkles it with water, and from time to time looks on at it, then that gold becomes malleable, wieldy, and radiant; it is not brittle and is well-suited for work. Whatever kind of ornament he wishes for—whether a tiara (paṭika), earrings (kuṇḍala), [240] a necklace (gīveyya), or a golden wreath (suvaṇṇamālā)—he can achieve the purpose of whatever ornament he desires.

In the same way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu devoted to the higher mind attends to the three signs... (as before) ...and is well-concentrated for the destruction of the taints. To whatever state realizable by direct knowledge (abhiññā) he inclines his mind for realization by direct knowledge, he attains the ability to be a witness (or attains the realization) in that very state, whenever the conditions (such as previous causes) are present."

Notes:
1. This is the meaning of 'yadi gīveyyāya'. Since the word 'gīveyya' is neuter, it is clear that 'gīveyyāya' is formed with the fourth case (dative) in the sense of 'for that purpose'. Therefore, similar words like 'yadi paṭikāya' are also translated in the dative sense as 'whether for a tiara', etc.
1. This is the meaning of the phrase 'sati sati āyatane'. The Ṭīkā explains 'tasmiṃ tasmiṃ pubbhetu-ādike kāraṇe sati' (when those various causes such as previous merit exist), using the distributive (vicchā) sense to show that the two words 'sati sati' are distributive. For a detailed decision, see Mahāṭīkā Nissaya, Vol. 2, p. 195.

This sutta should be known as the Adhicitta Sutta.

"Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness (nibbāna). What are the six? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu restrains the mind on the occasion when it should be restrained. He exerts the mind on the occasion when it should be exerted. He gladdens the mind on the occasion when it should be gladdened. He looks on at the mind with equanimity on the occasion when it should be looked on with equanimity. He is intent on the sublime (magga-phala) and delights in Nibbāna. Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu possessed of these six qualities is capable of realizing the unsurpassed state of coolness."

This sutta should be known as the Anuttara Sītibhāva Sutta.

As for the Bojjhaṅgakosalla Sutta, it has already been shown in the discussion on skill in absorption (Appanākosalla-kathā, Vol. 1, p. 400) as: "Bhikkhus, in the same way, when the mind is sluggish, it is not the right time to develop the enlightenment factor of tranquility (passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga)," and so forth.

Thus, having well-grasped this sevenfold skill in learning (uggahakosalla) and having thoroughly defined this tenfold skill in attention (manasikārakosalla), the yogi should properly learn the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) by way of both skills. To say further: if it is convenient for that yogi to stay in the same monastery as the meditation teacher, he should not have the meditation subject taught in full detail at once, but should define it well and, while practicing, after attaining distinction in meditation, have it taught further and further (progressively).

If he wishes to live elsewhere, he should have it taught in detail according to the stated method, review it repeatedly to cut off all knots of doubt, and then, leaving aside unsuitable lodgings as mentioned in the description of the earth kasiṇa...
241:
A practitioner who wishes to reside in another place or another monastery should have the instructions explained in detail as previously described, resolve all knots and difficult points, and then, following the method mentioned in the description of the earth kasiṇa (pathavī-kasiṇa-niddesa), reject an unsuitable monastery and [241] reside in a suitable monastery. Having cut off minor impediments, he should perform the preliminary work (parikamma) for the meditation on mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati), which involves contemplating repulsiveness.

## Performing the Preliminary Work
The practitioner performing this preliminary work should first take the sign (nimitta) of the hair of the head (kesā) as being foul (asubha). How? Having plucked one or two hairs and placed them on the palm of the hand, he should first determine their color. It is also appropriate to look at the hair in the place where it has been shaved. It is also appropriate to look at the reflection in a bowl of water or a bowl of gruel. When they are black, he should attend to them as 'black.' When they are white, he should attend to them as 'white.' When they are mixed, he should attend to them according to the predominant color. Just as with the hair of the head, so too with the entire skin-pentad (taca-pañcaka), he should take the sign only after seeing them.

## Explanation of Defining the Parts (Koṭṭhāsa)
182. Having taken the sign in this way, and having defined all the parts (koṭṭhāsa) by way of color, shape, direction, location, and limit, he should then define their repulsiveness in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, habitat, and location.

In this regard, the following is the progressive explanation for all the parts.

## (1) Hair of the Head (Kesā)
Regarding the hair of the head (kesā), by their natural color, they are black, the color of a wet soap-nut (ariṭṭhaka). By shape, they are long and round, the shape of a balance-rod. By direction, they grow in the upper direction. By location, they are bounded on both sides by the ear-tips, in front by the edge of the forehead, and behind by the nape of the neck. The moist skin covering the skull is the location of the hair. By limit, each hair is fixed by entering the skin covering the head to the depth of the tip of a grain of rice. It is limited below by the surface of its own root, above by space, and around by other hairs. No two hairs grow together in one place; this is the 'limit as to its own kind' (sabhāga-pariccheda). Hair of the head is not hair of the body (lomā), and hair of the body is not hair of the head; in this way, being unmixed with the remaining thirty-one parts, the hair of the head is a separate part; this is the 'limit as to what is different' (visabhāga-pariccheda). This is the definition of the hair of the head by way of color and so on.

Note:
1. Hair is visible to everyone; it is black in youth, reddish in some races, and turns white in old age. This is easily known, so a metaphor is not strictly necessary, but metaphors are provided here as they will be used for later parts that are harder to perceive. Thus, one need not overthink the 'soap-nut' metaphor; one should simply note the color of hair as seen.
2. The metaphor of the balance-rod is used to indicate the roundness; since it is visible, the metaphor is not critical. The 'Kāyānupassanā' by the Minister of Yaw states it is 'like a black silk thread.'
3. Although the Pali term 'disā' should be translated as 'direction,' from this point onward, it will be translated simply as 'region' or 'direction.'

Regarding the location, the hair is bounded by the ear-tips and other landmarks. The term 'paricchinna' (bounded/limited) is used here to mean that the area where hair grows is delimited by these signs. Regarding the limit, each hair enters the skin to the depth of the tip of a grain of rice; it is bounded below by its root, above by space, and laterally by other hairs. No two hairs grow in the same spot—this is the 'delimitation of the similar' (sabhāga-pariccheda).

183. The following is the definition of their repulsiveness in five ways by way of color and so on. These hairs are repulsive by way of color, repulsive by way of shape, repulsive by way of smell, repulsive by way of habitat, and repulsive by way of location.
242:
By way of location, they are also repulsive.

[242] To explain in detail—even if food is pleasant, if one sees something with the color of hair in a bowl of gruel or rice, one feels disgusted, saying, 'This food is mixed with hair. Take it away.' Thus, hair is repulsive by way of color.

Those eating at night, even if they just touch a fiber of akkayāka or makaci that has the shape of hair, they feel disgusted in the same way. Thus, hair is repulsive by way of shape.

The smell of hair that is devoid of preparation such as oiling, flowers, and incense is extremely disgusting. The smell of hair thrown into fire is even more disgusting. Indeed, hair might not be repulsive by way of color and shape, but it is certainly repulsive by way of smell. For example, the stool of a suckling infant is turmeric-colored by way of color and like a lump of turmeric by way of shape.

Furthermore, the bloated carcass of a black dog discarded in a rubbish heap is the color of a ripe palmyra fruit by way of color; by way of shape, it is like a smooth, rounded mudiṅga drum (Note 1). Even its fangs are like jasmine buds. Thus, both the infant's stool and the rotting dog carcass might not be repulsive by way of color and shape, but they are certainly repulsive by way of smell. Similarly, hair might not be repulsive by way of color and shape, but it is certainly repulsive by way of smell (Note 2).

Furthermore, just as vegetables grown in an impure place (near a village) by the drainage of the village are disgusting to city-dwellers and unfit for consumption, so too hair is disgusting because it grows from the drainage of pus, blood, urine, feces, bile, phlegm, and so on. This is their repulsiveness by way of origin (āsaya) (Note 3).

And these hairs grow in the mass of the thirty-one parts like a fungus on a heap of dung. Because they grow in an impure place, like vegetables growing in a cemetery or rubbish heap, or like lotuses and lilies growing in a moat, they are extremely disgusting. This is their repulsiveness by way of location (okāsa).

As with hair, so too for all the other parts (Note 4), repulsiveness should be understood in five ways: by way of color, shape, smell, origin, and location. Furthermore, all parts should be defined separately by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation.

Note 1: Regarding the phrase 'vissaṭṭha-mudiṅga-saṇṭhānaṃ'—the Nissaya translates it as 'shaped like a prepared drum.' However, 'prepared' does not add much meaning. Assuming 'vissaṭṭha' should be 'vimaṭṭha,' it is translated here as 'smooth.' The point is the similarity between the rotting dog and the drum.
Note 2: The term 'paṭikkūla' is translated here as 'repulsive,' 'having repulsiveness,' or 'disgusting' as fits the flow of the language.
Note 3: 'Paṭikkūlyaṃ'—the state of being repulsive, the fact of having repulsiveness, or the quality of being disgusting; these four meanings are essentially the same.
Note 4: Connect this with: 'the repulsiveness of all the remaining parts should be understood.'

## (2) Body Hairs

184. Therein, first, body hairs (lomā) in their natural color are not pure black like head hair, but are blackish-brown. By way of shape, they have downward-curving tips and are shaped like the root of a palmyra tree. By way of direction, they grow in two directions. By way of location, except for the location where head hair is established and the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, they mostly grow on the skin that envelops the rest of the body. By way of delimitation, they are fixed in the skin that envelops the body to the depth of a likkhā (Note 5) [243] below by their own roots...

Note 5: A particle too small to be seen by the naked eye is called a paramāṇu. A cluster of 36 paramāṇu is an aṇu. This aṇu can be seen in sunbeams passing through small holes in a wall. A cluster of 36 aṇu is a tajjārī, which is the dust seen rising into the air on cart tracks. A cluster of 36 tajjārī is a rathareṇu.
243:
This is the dust that exists on the ground in cart tracks, chariot paths, and so on. A mass of thirty-six such chariot-dust particles (rathareṇu) is called a louse-egg particle (likkhā). It is also called stylus-filings or stylus-residue dust. It means that [the hair] remains embedded in the skin to the extent of such a likkhā particle.

2. Connect with "by the root... which remains embedded."

Above, it is bounded by space; transversely, it is bounded by each other. No two body hairs are together. This is their delimitation by similar parts (sabhāgapariccheda). As for their delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāgapariccheda), it is just the same as for the head hairs.

## (3) Nails

185. Nakhā (Nails) is the name for the twenty nail-plates. In color, they are all white. In shape, they are like fish scales. In direction, the toenails are in the lower direction, and the fingernails are in the upper direction; thus they are produced in two directions. In location, they are fixed on the tips of the backs of the fingers and toes. In delimitation, they are bounded in two directions by the flesh of the tips of the fingers and toes, internally by the flesh of the backs of the fingers and toes, externally and at the tips by space, and transversely by each other. No two nails are together. This is their sabhāgapariccheda.

Note
1. These names, sabhāgapariccheda and visabhāgapariccheda, will be referred to hereafter using only their Pali terms.

Their visabhāgapariccheda is just the same as for the head hairs.

## (4) Teeth

186. Dantā (Teeth) refers to the thirty-two teeth-bones of one who has a full set of teeth. They are also white in color. In shape, they have various shapes. To explain in detail: among them, in the middle of the lower row of teeth, four teeth are shaped like gourd seeds set in a row in a lump of clay. On each of their two sides, there is one tooth with a single root and a single point, shaped like a jasmine bud. Next to each of those is one with two roots and two points, shaped like a cart-prop. Next to those, on each side, are two with three roots and three points. Next to those, on each side, are two with four roots and four points. The same applies to the upper row of teeth. In direction, they are produced in the upper direction. In location, they are fixed in the two jawbones. In delimitation, they are bounded below by their own root-surfaces fixed in the jawbone, above by space, and transversely by each other. No two teeth are together. This is their sabhāgapariccheda. Their visabhāgapariccheda is just the same as for the head hairs.

## (5) Skin

187. Taco (Skin) refers to the thick skin that stands wrapping around the whole body. Above that thick skin is what is called the thin skin (chavi), which has colors such as black, dark brown, or yellow. If this thin skin is stripped from the whole body and rolled up, it is only the size of a jujube seed. The thick skin itself is white in color. The whiteness of this thick skin becomes apparent when the thin skin is scorched by the heat of a flame or damaged by a blow from a weapon, etc. In shape, it is simply the shape of the body. This is the summary here.

[244] In detail, however, the skin of the toes is like the shape of a silkworm's cocoon. The skin of the back of the foot is like the shape of a covered shoe.
244:
The skin of the calves is like a palm-leaf rice packet; the skin of the thighs is like a long bag filled with rice. The skin of the buttocks is like a cloth water filter filled with water; the skin of the back is like leather stretched over a wooden board; the skin of the abdomen is like leather stretched over the body of a lute.

Note:
1. The above simile is rarely seen nowadays. It can be seen if one visits a silk-rearing station. Since it can be known by looking at the toes, this simile is not of great benefit.

The skin of the chest is mostly square; the skin of both arms is like leather stretched over a quiver; the skin of the back of the hand is like a razor case [1], or otherwise, like a comb bag [2]; the skin of the fingers is like a key case; the skin of the neck is like a neck-wrap [3]; the skin of the face is full of holes (due to the mouth, nose, and eye sockets) and is like an insect's nest (or a bird's nest); the skin of the head is like an alms-bowl bag.

Note:
1. This refers to the case of a razor used in ancient times. In the Kāyānupassanā text, it is said to be like a Chinese tinderbox bag. That tinderbox bag is also difficult to know nowadays. Since the back of the hand can be known simply by looking at it, it is not important to know the simile here.
2. Phanakatthavika—the meaning 'comb bag' (or brush bag) is the interpretation from the Pyay version of the Nissaya. The Pyay Nissaya also mentions that in ancient Nissayas, it was translated as a 'Phanaik' dagger sheath. Since comb bags and Phanaik dagger sheaths do not exist in the present time, these similes are also not of much benefit.
3. The word Kañcuka refers to a garment called 'Thin-daing' in ancient times; therefore, in the Nissaya, Galakañcuka is translated as a neck-wrap garment. In the Ṭīkā, it is called Kaṇṭhatthāṇakaṃ—a garment that protects the neck; thus, the Pyay Nissaya states that it refers to a protective garment worn around the neck to guard against weapons, etc. In any case, the meaning 'neck-wrap' is appropriate and well-known.

To continue with the method of defining and noting: A meditator (yogī) who grasps the skin should send their knowledge (insight) from the upper lip towards the upper face, first defining the skin that stays enveloping the face [1]. Then the skin of the forehead. Then, just as one might pass a hand between an alms-bowl and its bag, one should send knowledge between the skull and the scalp, separating the skin's connection with the bone and defining the scalp. Then the skin of the shoulders. Then, in forward and reverse order, the skin of the right arm. Then, in the same manner, the skin of the left arm. Then the skin of the back. Having defined that, in forward and reverse order, the skin of the right leg. Then, in the same manner, the skin of the left leg. Then, in due order, the skin of the bladder, abdomen, chest, and neck. Then, immediately after the neck skin, one should define the skin of the lower jaw and conclude by reaching the end of the lower lip. For the meditator who grasps the coarse skin in this manner,

Note:
1. This is the meaning of the word Vavatthapetabbaṃ; therefore, the meaning 'should be noted' or 'should be determined' should be taken. It is the same in subsequent instances.

the subtle skin also becomes clear [1]. In terms of direction, it arises in two directions: upper and lower. In terms of location, it stays enveloping and wrapping the entire body. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited below (internally) by the surface it rests on, and above (externally) by space [2]. This is its delimitation by similar parts (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

## (6) Flesh
188. 'Flesh' (Maṃsa) refers to the nine hundred pieces of flesh. All of it is red in color, like the Kimsuka flower. In terms of shape, the calf muscle is like a palm-leaf rice packet; the thigh muscle is like a grinding stone (a small stone pestle) [3]; the buttock muscle is like

Note:
1. 'The subtle skin also' refers to the skin inside the mouth, etc., which is subtler than the coarse skin mentioned.
2. This is the meaning of the word Paricchinno. If translated precisely as 'is delimited,' it might be confused with the meaning of Vavatthapetabbaṃ (should be defined); therefore, the phrasing has been varied. It is the same in similar cases hereafter.
3. The small stone refers to Silāputtako—a stone pestle (Ṭīkā).

the corner of an oven; the back muscle is like a slab of palm sugar [1]; the flesh of the two sides (ribs) is like a thin layer of clay plastered on the wall of a granary; the breast muscle is like a ball of clay that has been rolled and dropped.
245:
[245] The flesh of the two upper arms is like the shape of a large skinless rat placed one on top of the other. To the yogi who thus grasps the gross flesh, the subtle flesh also becomes clear. In terms of direction, it occurs in both directions (upper and lower). In terms of location, it stands smeared and attached to the three hundred and twenty (320) bones. In terms of delimitation, it is bounded below by the surface of the bone-assembly, above by the skin, and transversely by one another. This is its delimitation of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Its delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair of the head.

Note
1. Tālaguḷapaṭala—a palm sugar sheet refers to a sheet obtained by smearing cooked palm juice on a palm-leaf mat or similar, drying it, and then peeling it off. (Sub-commentary) In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, it is said that the flesh on both sides of the back is shaped like an unopened palm-spadix or an unopened betel-nut bud.

## (7) Sinews

189. Sinews (nhārū) refers to the nine hundred (900) sinews. All these sinews are white in color. In shape, they have various shapes. To elaborate: among these nine hundred sinews, sixty major sinews called 'body-supporters' (sarīradhāraka) descend, binding the body together, starting from the upper part of the neck. Five descend by the front side, five by the back side, five by the right side, and five by the left side. Also, binding the right arm, five are in the front of the arm and five in the back. Likewise, binding the left arm (five in front and five in back). Binding the right leg, five are in the front of the leg and five in the back. Likewise, binding the left leg (five in front and five in back). In this way, the sixty major sinews known as 'body-supporters' descend, binding the body together. These major sinews are also called kaṇḍarā. All of them are shaped like a kandala bud. Other sinews remain covering and spreading over various parts of the body. Those more subtle than them are shaped like strings.

Note
1. In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, it is said they are shaped like a cotton bud, and it is also stated that the translation of kaṇḍala as 'byu-daing khat-tar' (crinum lily) is due to a lack of better terminology.

Those more subtle than them are shaped like strings (suttarajjuka). Those even more subtle are shaped like the pūtilatā creeper. Those even more subtle are shaped like the strings of a large lute (vīṇā). Others are shaped like coarse thread. The sinews on the backs of the hands and feet are shaped like a bird's foot. The sinews on the head are shaped like a net-cap for children. The sinews on the back are shaped like a wet net spread out in the sun. The remaining sinews following the various large and small limbs are shaped like a net-jacket worn on the body. In terms of direction, they occur in both directions (upper and lower). In terms of location, they stand binding the bones throughout the whole body. In terms of delimitation, they are bounded below by the surfaces resting on the three hundred bones, above by the areas touching the flesh and skin, and transversely by one another. This is their delimitation of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Their delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair of the head.

Note
1. The meaning 'shaped like a string' is the translation for the text 'suttarajjuka-saṇṭhānā'. The meaning is not clear. In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, based on the text 'sūkaravāgurārajju-saṇṭhānā' from the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, it is said they are shaped like the rope of a pig-trap, and the text in the Visuddhimagga is suggested to be a corruption.
2. In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, the word 'pūtilatā' is translated as 'ka-leim-phyu' vine, and it is said they are shaped like the ka-leim-phyu vine.
3. In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, the word 'vīṇā' is translated as 'violin', and it is said they are shaped like large violin strings.

## (8) Bones

190. Bones (atthi) refers to the bones which, excluding the thirty-two teeth, [the rest] consist of sixty-four hand bones, sixty-four foot bones, sixty-four soft bones dependent on flesh, two heel bones (paṇhika), two ankle bones (gopphaka) in each foot (totaling four), and two shin bones (jaṅgha) in each leg.

Note
1. Connect this with: 'the remaining bones are about three hundred'.
2. The counting of foot bones is shown in the Kāyānupassanā treatise as follows: (In anatomy texts, there are 5 distal phalanges, 4 middle phalanges—the big toe has no middle phalanx—5 proximal phalanges, 5 metatarsals, 1 calcaneus, and 6 tarsal bones between the tibia/fibula and the metatarsals/calcaneus, plus 5 sesamoid bones, totaling 31 in one foot and 62 in both feet. This is 2 less than the Commentary's count).
3. In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, it is said that since the ankle bones are merely the two bony protrusions at the ends of the two leg bones (tibia and fibula), they should not be counted separately. If they are counted separately, the wrist bones would also have to be counted separately.
246:
Therefore, it is not found in the ancient commentaries. The evidence is in the passage "Thus, about three hundred":

1 knee bone each, 1 thigh bone each, 2 hip bones, 18 backbone segments (vertebrae)¹, 24 ribs, 14 chest bones, 1 breastbone (sternum), 2 collarbones (clavicles), 2 shoulder blades (scapulae), 2 upper arm bones (humeri), 2 forearm bones each (4 total), 7 neck bones, 2 jawbones, 1 nose bone, 2 eye socket bones, 2 ear bones, 1 forehead bone, 1 crown bone, and 9 skull bones—thus, the bones are about three hundred in number. All of these are white in color and possess various shapes.

To elaborate: Among them, the bones of the tips of the toes are like clearing-nut seeds (*kataka-bīja*). The middle joints next to them are like jackfruit seeds (*panasa-bīja*). The base joints are like small drums (*paṇava*). The bones of the back of the foot (metatarsals) are like a cluster of crushed roots of the *khandala* plant². The heel bone is like the seed of a single-seeded palmyra fruit. The ankle bones are like toy marbles tied together with string. The place where the leg bones rest on the ankle bones is like a peeled date-palm shoot (*sindī-kaḷīra*)³.

Note:
It should be understood that the Vibhaṅga Mūla-Ṭīkā states that the ankle bones are not explicitly mentioned due to the words "Thus" and "about."
1. The 18 backbone segments include the lumbar (waist) vertebrae.
2. The Kāyānupassanā text says they are like the shape of crushed bamboo roots.
3. The Nissaya translates this as the shoot of a *thin-baung* plant; however, the New Abhidhāna Nissaya and the Kāyānupassanā translate *sindī* as date palm.

The smaller leg bone (fibula) is like the frame of a small toy bow. The larger leg bone (tibia) is like the back of a withered snake. The knee bone (patella) is like a piece of foam broken on one side. The place where the leg bone rests on that knee bone is like a cow's horn with a blunt tip. The thigh bone (femur) is like the handle of a poorly planed adze or axe. The place where the thigh bone rests in the hip bone is like a toy marble. The place where the hip bone meets that thigh bone is like a large *punnāga* fruit with the tip cut off.

If the two hip bones are joined together, they are like a potter's kiln. If they are separate, they are like a blacksmith's pincers¹. The hip bone at the end (sacrum/coccyx) is like the hood of a hanging snake, with holes in seven or eight places. From the inside, the backbone segments (vertebrae) are like lead sheets stacked one upon another. From the outside, they are like a row of rings (or a series of circles)¹.

Note:
1. The Nissaya translates this as the handle of a blacksmith's hammer or the rope tied to the handle. However, because a similar term *ayokūṭa-yottaka* is later translated as "pincers" for the lower jaw, and the Kāyānupassanā translates both terms as "pincers," and because scientific diagrams of the hip bone resemble pincers like the jawbone, it is translated here as "pincers."

Between those backbone segments, there are two or three thorn-like projections like saw teeth. Among the twenty-four ribs, the incomplete ones are like incomplete scimitars (curved swords)², and the complete ones are like complete scimitars. All the ribs together are like the spread wings of a white cock. The fourteen chest bones are like the frame of an old palanquin¹. The breastbone is like the blade of a wooden ladle.

Note:
1. The Nissaya translates *vaṭṭanāvaḷi* as "the sequence of threads wound around a spindle." The Kāyānupassanā translates it as "a series of threadless bobbins" and criticizes the Nissaya's translation as inconsistent with the sub-commentary and anatomical shapes. It could also be described as a stack of threadless spools.
2. The Nissaya translates *aparipuṇṇa-asi* as a scimitar with an incomplete hilt or blade. The Kāyānupassanā translates it as: "short ribs are like unfinished curved knives, and long ribs are like finished curved knives." The Khuddakapāṭha Commentary says they are like incomplete and complete Sinhalese sickles. Since sickles are long and curved, the Kāyānupassanā concludes that the "scimitar" mentioned should be understood as a curved knife.

The two collarbones are like the handles of small iron adzes. The two shoulder blades are like a Sinhalese hoe worn down on one side². The two upper arm bones are like the handles of mirrors. The forearm bones are like twin palmyra trunks. The wrist bones are like lead sheets joined together. The bones of the back of the hand are like crushed *khandala*...

Note:
1. The meaning "palanquin" comes from the reading *sandamānika*. The Kāyānupassanā uses the reading *sandana* and translates it as the frame of a broken chariot. Current editions use *sandamānika*.
2. Since this commentary was written by Sinhalese teachers, they used the well-known Sinhalese hoe as a metaphor. For Burmese people, the shape of a Sinhalese hoe is difficult to know, so this metaphor is not very helpful. However, there is no need for discouragement; one can understand the shape by examining the shoulder blade, studying skeletons, or looking at scientific anatomical diagrams.
247:
Therefore, if there are any parts among the thirty-two parts of the body that are not understood according to this Burmese translation, please look at the diagrams of the body parts provided by scientists. The teachers of the Sinhalese Commentaries also took and described these from the famous Indian medical treatises of that ancient time. In the Buddha's teaching, there are only brief headings. Detailed analysis:

...the two forearm bones are like a pair of palm-shoots, palm-sprouts, or palm-roots joined together. The wrist bones are like lead sheets rolled and joined together. The bones of the back of the hand are like a bundle of fibers of a flattened bryophyllum plant. Among the finger bones, the base joints are like the shape of a paṇava drum; the middle joints are like the shape of unripe jackfruit seeds; the tip joints are like the shape of kataka seeds.

The seven neck bones are like bamboo shoot rings threaded and arranged in order on a stick. The lower jaw bone is like a blacksmith's iron hammer. The upper jaw bone is like a knife for scraping sugarcane. The eye-socket and nose-socket bones are like young palm seeds with the kernels removed. The forehead bone is like a broken conch-shell bowl placed face down. The temple bones are like a barber's razor case. Above the forehead and temple bones, in the place where the headband is tied, the bone is wrinkled and like a piece of cloth filled with ghee.

Note: This mirror handle is also a mirror handle used in ancient Sri Lanka.

The bone at the top of the head is like a curved coconut shell with the opening cut off. The (back) skull bones are like a cracked gourd shell that has been sewn together.

By direction, they occur in two directions: upper and lower. By location, generally speaking, they are situated throughout the whole body. Specifically, among those bones, the head bones rest on the neck bones. The neck bones rest on the spinal bones. The spinal bones rest on the hip bones. The hip bones rest on the thigh bones. The thigh bones rest on the knee bones. The knee bones rest on the shin bones. The shin bones rest on the ankle bones. The ankle bones rest on the foot bones.

By delimitation, they are bounded internally by the bone marrow, above and externally by the flesh, and at the ends and bases by each other. This is their delimitation of the similar (sabhāga-pariccheda). The delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

Note: 1. This is the meaning of the term 'saṅkuṭita-ghata-puṇṇa-paṭala-khaṇḍa-saṇṭhānaṃ'. Here, the word 'saṅkuṭita' is translated as 'wrinkled' as it appears in the Nissaya. However, in the Kāyānupassanā treatise, it says: 'Above the two temple bones on the left and right, the two frontal bones are curved at the edges and are like a piece of cloth filled with ghee.' In bone diagrams, these bones are indeed seen to be curved. Therefore, saying 'curved' for 'saṅkuṭita' seems more appropriate. In the Khuddakapāṭha Commentary, this word 'saṅkuṭita' is not included, and the text reads 'bahala-ghata-puṇṇa-paṭa-piloṭika-saṇṭhānaṃ', which would be translated as 'like a piece of coarse cloth filled with thick ghee.' However, the shape is not clear.
2. In the Kāyānupassanā treatise, it says: 'The five bones at the back of the head are like five pieces of an old cracked gourd shell sewn together.'

## (9) Bone Marrow

191. Bone marrow (aṭṭhimiñja) is the marrow found inside various bones. In color, it is white. In shape, the marrow inside large bones is like a large rattan shoot steamed in a bamboo tube. The marrow inside small and very small bones is like a thin rattan shoot steamed in small bamboo joints. By direction, it occurs in two directions: upper and lower. By location, it is situated inside the bones. By delimitation, it is bounded by the inner surfaces of the bones. This is its delimitation of the similar. The delimitation of the dissimilar is just like that of the hair.

## (10) Kidneys

192. Kidneys (vakka) are two lumps of flesh attached to a single stalk. In color, it is slightly red, the color of pālibhaddaka seeds. In shape, it is like a pair of playing marbles for children; or it is like a pair of mangoes attached to a single stalk. By direction, it occurs in the upper direction. By location, starting from the throat with a single base stalk, going down a little and attached by a large vein that splits into two, it stands surrounding the heart.

Note: 1. These 'vakka' are commonly called kidneys. However, in the Kāyānupassanā treatise, it points out faults such as the kidneys being located too low, rejects that view, and suggests it should be an organ that takes in food, stating as follows:
'In anatomy books, behind the uvula, the opening where water and food enter is at the back, and the opening where air is breathed in is at the front, thus there are two openings.'
248:
Between those two, the opening towards the chest where the breath enters has two levels like a funnel. Among these two levels, the outer funnel, when felt with the hand, consists of the hard cartilaginous nodules found in the throat. This outer funnel rises and closes when swallowing water or food to prevent them from entering the windpipe towards the chest. Below this outer funnel, on the left and right of the windpipe opening, this sinew (connective tissue) remains attached. It is said that people living in areas where they drink hard water containing much lime or salt, or water with a white appearance, are prone to developing goiter.

In terms of delimitation, the sinew is delimited by its own part. This is its delimitation by similar parts (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāga-pariccheda) is the same as that of the hair.

## (11) Heart

193. Hadaya (Heart) refers to the heart-flesh. In color, it is red, having the color of the back of a red lotus petal. In shape, it has the shape of a red lotus bud positioned upside down with the outer petals removed; it is smooth on the outside, and the inside is like the interior of a sponge gourd (luffa). For those with wisdom, it is slightly open; for those of dull wisdom, it remains a bud. Inside that heart, there is a small cavity about the size of a Punnāga seed's place, where about half a handful of blood remains. Depending on this blood (or rather, depending on the heart-base matter [hadaya-vatthu] located in this blood), the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu) arise. Furthermore, this heart-blood—

Note: This statement in the anatomy text agrees with the current understanding of the position of the sinew (connective tissue).
1. When two hands are joined to receive something, it is called a 'handful' (lakkhope); when one hand is used, it is called a 'scoop' (lak-sun). Half of that scoop is called 'half a scoop' (pasata).
2. The 1 five-door adverting consciousness and 2 receiving consciousnesses—these 3 types of consciousness are called the mind-element (manodhātu). The 10 types of fivefold sensory consciousness (eye-consciousness, etc.) and the 76 types of consciousness remaining after excluding these 3 mind-elements are called the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu).

For one of lustful temperament, it is red; for one of hateful temperament, it is black; for one of deluded temperament, it is like the color of meat-wash water; for one of discursive temperament, it is the color of bean soup (Kulattha broth). For one of faithful temperament, it is the color of a Kanikāra flower; for one of wise temperament, it is clear, exceptionally translucent, undisturbed, pure, clean, and appears radiant like a well-polished genuine ruby.

Note: It is meant that these 76 types of consciousness and the 3 mind-elements arise depending on the matter called the heart-base (hadaya-vatthu) which is constantly arising in the heart-blood. Regarding this statement, a question may arise: In modern times, when a heart is being treated by removing the old heart and replacing it with a new one, upon what do those consciousnesses depend to arise? If one wishes to take the commentary's statement strictly, one should hold that 'during the time the new heart and the body's blood have not yet connected, they arise depending on the heart-base matter in the old heart; from the time they connect, the heart-base matter arises in the new heart and they arise depending on that heart-base matter.' If one does not take it so strictly and holds that 'the heart-base matter arises in the blood within the heart and in the blood pumped out from the heart, and they arise depending on that heart-base matter,' then such a question would not even arise.
1. 'One of lustful temperament' means one in whom lust frequently occurs. Therefore, instead of saying 'one of lustful temperament,' it is stated here as 'one in whom lust is powerful.' The same applies to 'one in whom hate is powerful,' etc.

In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated inside the body in the middle between the two breasts. In terms of delimitation, the heart is delimited by its own part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. Its delimitation by dissimilar parts is the same as that of the hair.

Note: Here, I shall summarize the statements of modern Western doctors. The heart is situated between the two lungs inside the thoracic cavity of the body; in size, it is about the size of a clenched fist. It is shaped like a pear. The lower left tip appears pointed. It is the organ that sends blood to the entire body. In that heart, there are two chambers, left and right. In the left chamber, there are two rooms, upper and lower; similarly, in the right chamber, there are also two rooms, upper and lower. Blood returning from the entire body through the veins enters the upper right room of the heart through the main vein, and from the upper room, it enters the lower room. When that room is full, the heart squeezes that blood out. That blood exits through the main artery and enters the two lungs, right and left, through large vessels that branch off to the right lung and the left lung. Inside those lungs, the blood spreads through very small, minute blood vessels. The inhaled breath provides the necessary gas called oxygen into that blood. The exhaled air carries away the unnecessary gas called carbon dioxide—

## (12) Liver

194. Yakana (Liver) refers to the twin-lobed slab of flesh. In color, it is red, having a pale quality, not excessively red, the color of the back of a white water lily petal. In shape, it is single at the base and twin-lobed at the tip, having the shape of a Kovilāra (Bauhinia) leaf. That liver is single and large for those of dull wisdom, but for those with wisdom, there are two or three small ones. In terms of direction, it is in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated inside between the two breasts, depending on the right side.

## Note

—by carrying away the gases, it purifies the blood. That purified blood exits the lungs through the main veins and enters the upper left room of the heart. From the upper room, it enters the lower room. When that room is full, the heart squeezes out that pure blood. That pure blood spreads through the main artery to the upper and lower parts of the entire body. Within about one minute, that blood returns through the veins and reaches the heart again. It is said that the heart squeezes out blood about seventy times per minute. If you wish to know more extensively, please look at books and documents that describe the parts of the body.
1. The position of this liver will also be more clearly understood if viewed in those books and documents showing the parts of the body.

In terms of delimitation, the liver is delimited by its own part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. Its delimitation by dissimilar parts is the same as that of the hair.

## (13) Membrane

195. Kilomaka (Membrane) refers to the two types of flesh-covering membranes, categorized as the concealed and the unconcealed. Both types are white in color, having the color of a coarse white cloth. In shape, it has the shape of its own location. In terms of direction, the concealed membrane is in the upper direction; the other membrane is in both directions. In terms of location, [249] the concealed membrane stands covering the heart and the sinew (connective tissue); the unconcealed membrane stands covering the flesh beneath the skin throughout the entire body.
249:
In terms of delimitation, it is bounded below by the flesh, above by the skin, and transversely by the part of the membrane itself. This is its delimitation of the similar (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

Note: 1. In the Kāyānupassanā text, the coarse white cloth (dukũla-pilotika) is described as follows: "Dukũla is a cloth woven from the fiber of the linseed plant which produces seeds like the weight of a diamond rati. The word pilotika also refers to a coarse cloth. Therefore, in the Suvaᅇᅇasāma Jātaka, it is said to be called dukũla because it was received with a coarse cloth woven from dukũla fiber when the fisherman's son was born."

## (14) Spleen

196. Pihaka (Spleen) is a piece of flesh called the "stomach-flap" (waist-layer) located on the upper side of the stomach. In color, it is blue, like the color of the nigguᅇᅇĩ flower. In shape, it is seven finger-breadths in size, without attachment, and shaped like the tongue of a black calf. In direction, it is in the upper direction. In location, it is situated on the left side of the heart, relying on the upper side of the stomach-membrane. When this spleen comes out due to a blow or strike from a weapon, the life of beings comes to an end. In terms of delimitation, it is bounded by the part of the membrane itself. This is its delimitation of the similar.

Note: 1. In the Kāyānupassanā text, it says: "It is a piece of flesh that hangs down and was called pihaka in ancient times; later it was called thayet-ywet (mango leaf) because it resembles a mango leaf." Furthermore, it also shows the statement from the Anatomy text: "The spleen, counting from the 6th rib from the top, extends downwards for one span, pressing against the upper left part of the stomach inside the left side, and is situated along the length of the human body."

This is its delimitation of the similar (sabhāga-pariccheda). Its delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāga-pariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

## (15) Lungs

197. Papphāsa (Lungs) is the flesh divided into two or three parts. In color, they are red, like the color of not-too-ripe cluster figs (udumbara). In shape, they are like a thick piece of cake cut unevenly. Because they are scorched and oppressed by the heat of the karma-born fire element (kammaja-tejo) that rises when there is no food inside, they are without essence or juice, like a wad of chewed straw. In direction, they are in the upper direction. In location, they are inside the body between the two breasts, hanging over and covering the heart and liver. In terms of delimitation, they are bounded by the part of the lungs themselves. This is its delimitation of the similar. Its delimitation of the dissimilar is just like that of the hair.

Note: 1. Here, the meaning "divided into two or three parts" is translated according to the Sinhalese reading "dvatti-maᅃsakhaᅇᅇappabhedaᅃ". Since the left lung has 2 parts and the right lung has 3 parts, it is stated as "dvatti" (two or three). If one looks at the anatomical diagrams of the body parts, the form of the lungs is seen exactly like this. In Burmese texts, however, the reading is corrupted as "dvattiᅃsa" (thirty-two) in place of "dvatti".

## (16) Large Intestine

198. Anta (Large Intestine) is the coil of bowel, thirty-two cubits long in a man and twenty-eight cubits in a woman, folded and coiled in twenty-one places. In color, it is white, like the color of lime powder or plaster. In shape, it is like a decapitated snake coiled and placed in a red trough. In direction, it is in both directions. In location, it is situated inside the body, bound at the top to the gullet and at the bottom to the rectum (vacca-magga), thus extending from the beginning of the gullet to the end of the rectum. In terms of delimitation, it is bounded by the part of the large intestine itself. This is its delimitation of the similar. Its delimitation of the dissimilar is just like that of the hair.

## (17) Small Intestine

199. Antaguᅇa (Small Intestine) is that which is bound in the places of the coils of the large intestine.
250:
That small intestine is white in color, like the color of the root of the dakasĩtali (water-lily or moss). In shape, it is like the root of the dakasĩtali itself. In direction, it is in both directions. In location, it is situated between the twenty-one coils of the large intestine, binding them together so they do not slip, like the cord of a machine that binds the machine-plates together when the machine is pulled by those doing work with hoes or axes, or like the small cords situated as if sewn between the rings of a foot-wiping rope-mat.

Note: 1. Connect as: "...so that they do not slip... bound together... situated as if sewn..."

In terms of delimitation, it is bounded by the part of the small intestine itself. This is its delimitation of the similar. Its delimitation of the dissimilar is just like that of the hair.

## (18) Gorged Food

200. Udariya (Gorged Food) is the food that has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, which is in the stomach (udara). In color, it is the color of the swallowed food. In shape, it is like rice loosely tied in a water-strainer. In direction, it is in the upper direction. In location, it is in the stomach.

The stomach (udara) is the intestinal membrane like a bubble of air formed in the middle of a wet cloth being wrung from both ends. Outside it is smooth; inside it is like the fringe of a dirty cloth wrapping up meat-scraps and rotten meat. It can also be said to be like the inside of a rotten jackfruit skin. In this stomach,

Note: 1. Connect as: "...bound together... situated as if sewn..."

worms of thirty-two different families, such as takkoᅁaka, gaᅇᅇuppādaka, tālahĩraka, sũcimukhaka, and paᅁatantasuttaka, live in confusion, moving about in swarms. When there is no drink or food (in the stomach), they cry out and leap up, striking the heart-flesh. When drink and food are swallowed, they turn their mouths upwards and quickly snatch and eat the first two or three mouthfuls. This stomach is their maternity ward, their latrine, their hospital, and their cemetery. To give a simile: just as at the gate of an outcaste village, in a cesspool during the hot season when heavy rain falls, various kinds of corpses such as urine, excrement, pieces of skin, bone, and sinew, spit, snot, and blood, washed away by the rain, fall in and are mixed with mud and water; after two or three days, it is filled with families of worms, boiling with the heat of the sun, emitting bubbles of foam on top, dark blue in color, extremely foul-smelling and loathsome, such that it is not fit to be approached or looked at.

Note: 1. The thirty-two types of worms and eighty types of worms are shown in the Kāyānupassanā text, pages 180-182. However, here it is only essential to know that there are many types of worms in the stomach.
2. Connect as: "...having mouths... they snatch and eat."
3. Connect as: "In this stomach... in the same way, various kinds of food and drink... having fallen like dog's vomit... stay in a state that is quite loathsome."

It goes without saying that it is not fit to be smelled or consumed. In the same way, various kinds of food and drink, pounded and ground by the pestle of the teeth, turned and stirred by the hand of the tongue, smeared and wrapped with saliva and spit, at that very moment lose their good color, smell, and taste, and become like weaver's paste or dog's vomit...
251:
Note
1. The mass of foul, putrid, and slimy matter, having fallen... is disturbed... and mixed; seething—and so on, and finally, it should be connected as: "It remains in a state unfit even to approach or look at, let alone to smell or consume."
2. The food, drink, etc... being crushed... stirred... and smeared... being devoid of [its original state]... having fallen... and being enveloped... seething... swarming... and causing [bubbles] to rise... it remains in that state—this is how it should be connected.

Having fallen [into the stomach], it is covered and enveloped by bile, phlegm, and wind; it seethes with the heat of the stomach-fire and is swarming with thirty-two families of worms; later (or as time passes), it causes foam, clusters of bubbles, and froth to rise, and it remains in a state that is extremely putrid, foul-smelling, and loathsome. Even by merely hearing about this receptacle for undigested food (āmāsaya), a sense of dissatisfaction and lack of relish for food, drink, etc., is well-established; how much more so if one were to see it with the eye of wisdom. Furthermore, the drinks, food, etc., that fall into this receptacle for undigested food are divided into five parts: one part is eaten by worms, one part is burned by the stomach-fire, one part becomes urine, one part becomes feces, and one part turns into nutritive essence (rasa) to sustain the blood, flesh, and so on.

In terms of limit, it is bounded by the membrane of the stomach and by the portion of undigested food itself; this is its internal limit (sabhāgapariccheda). Its external limit (visabhāgapariccheda) is the same as that of the hair.

Note
1. Food, drink, etc... being crushed... stirred... and smeared... being devoid of [its original state]... having been digested... and being enveloped... seething... swarming... and causing [bubbles] to rise... it remains in that state—this is how it should be connected.

## (19) Feces (Karīsaṃ)

201. Karīsaṃ (feces) refers to excrement. In terms of color, it generally has the color of the food that was swallowed. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is produced in the lower direction. In terms of location, it stays in the receptacle for digested food (pakkāsaya). The receptacle for digested food is the place at the end of the intestines, between the navel above and the root of the spine below, measuring about eight finger-breadths in height, resembling a bamboo tube.

Note
1. The description of the large intestine (rectum) given by modern Western doctors starts from the upper part of the right pelvic cavity, goes up to the lower part of the liver on the right side, then crosses to the left under the stomach, and when it reaches below the spleen, it goes down again. Upon reaching the entrance of the left pelvic cavity, it becomes the sigmoid colon and then descends towards the anus. The section about 6 inches below the sigmoid colon is called the rectum. When this rectum is filled with feces, the urge to defecate arises. In the Visuddhimagga above, only this final, primary section is shown as the receptacle for digested food.

To illustrate this receptacle for digested food with a simile: just as rainwater falling on a high piece of ground flows down and stays filling a low piece of ground, even so, whatever drinks, food, etc., fall into the receptacle for undigested food, being made to foam by the stomach-fire, as each portion is digested, it becomes fine and smooth like something crushed on a grindstone; it then slides down through the intestinal cavity and remains accumulated like pale-colored clay packed into a bamboo tube. In terms of limit, it is bounded by the membrane of the receptacle for digested food and by the portion of feces itself; this is its internal limit (sabhāgapariccheda). Its external limit (visabhāgapariccheda) is the same as that of the hair.

## (20) Brain (Matthaluṅgaṃ)

202. Matthaluṅgaṃ (brain) is the mass of marrow situated inside the skull. In terms of color, it is white, having the color of a cluster of mushrooms; it may also be said to have the color of milk that has begun to curdle but has not yet become curd. In terms of shape, it has the shape of its location.

Note
1. In that receptacle for digested food... even so... it remains accumulated—this is how it should be connected.
2. Food, etc... as each portion is digested... having reached... sliding down... it remains accumulated—this is how it should be connected.

In terms of direction, it is produced in the upper direction. In terms of location, it stays inside the skull, joined together like four lumps of dough placed together, following the four sutures. In terms of limit, it is bounded by the inner surfaces of the skull and by the portion of the brain itself.
252:
It is delimited by the brain-part itself. This is its delimitation by similar parts (sabhāgapariccheda). Its delimitation by dissimilar parts (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hair.

## (21) Bile
203. Bile (Pitta) consists of two kinds: bound bile (baddha-pitta) and unbound bile (abaddha-pitta). Among them, bound bile is the color of thick madhuka oil. Unbound bile is the color of a withered kānchanāra flower. In shape, both have the shape of their location. In terms of direction, bound bile is produced in the upper direction; the other is produced in both directions. In terms of location, unbound bile—excluding the parts of the hair, body hair, teeth, and nails that are free from flesh and the hard dry skin—remains pervading the rest of the whole body like a drop of oil on water. When this unbound bile is disturbed, the eyes become yellow, they whirl, the body trembles, and it itches. Bound bile is situated in the bile-bladder, which is like the sheath of a large sponge-gourd (mahākosātakī) and is located near the liver-flesh between the heart and the lungs. When this bound bile is disturbed, beings become mad; with perverted minds, they cast off shame and fear of wrongdoing, doing what should not be done, saying what should not be said, and thinking what should not be thought. By delimitation, it is delimited by the bile-part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. Its delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

## (22) Phlegm
204. Phlegm (Semha) is the phlegm inside the body, measuring about one pattha. In color, it is white, the color of the juice of nāgabala leaves. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is produced in the upper direction. In terms of location, it is situated on the stomach lining. When swallowing food and drink, etc., to give an analogy: just as when moss or water-weeds on water are struck by a stick or a shard, they part in two and then cover the water again, so too, when food and drink fall, it parts in two and then covers the new food again. When this phlegm is deficient, the stomach becomes extremely loathsome with a smell of a corpse, like a ripe abscess or a rotten hen's egg. And from the smell rising from the stomach, the upward breath and the mouth become foul-smelling like a rotten corpse. Such a person deserves to be told, 'Go away, you smell foul.' And when it increases and becomes thick, it remains blocking the foul smell inside the stomach lining like a lid over a cesspit. By delimitation, it is delimited by the phlegm-part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. Its delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

## (23) Pus
253:
205. Pus (Pubba) is pus produced by the state of rotten blood. In color, it is the color of a pale, withered leaf. In a dead body, however, it is the color of thick, rotten rice-scum. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it occurs in both directions. In terms of location, there is no fixed location for pus where it remains collected. Wherever blood stagnates and matures in a part of the body struck by a stump, a thorn, a weapon, or a flame, or where boils and pimples arise, there it remains. By delimitation, it is delimited by the pus-part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. Its delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

## (24) Blood
206. Blood (Lohita) consists of two kinds: stored blood (sannicita-lohita) and circulating blood (saṃsaraṇa-lohita). Among them, stored blood is the color of thick, cooked lac-resin. Circulating blood is the color of clear lac-resin. In shape, both have the shape of their location. In terms of direction, stored blood is produced in the upper direction. The other is produced in both directions. In terms of location, circulating blood—excluding the parts of the hair, body hair, teeth, and nails that are free from flesh and the hard dry skin—remains pervading the entire clung-to body (upādinna-sarīra) following the network of veins. Stored blood fills the lower part of the liver's location, measuring about one pattha, and remains moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs by trickling slightly over the heart, kidneys, and lungs. Indeed, if that stored blood does not moisten the kidneys, heart, etc., beings become thirsty. By delimitation, it is delimited by the blood-part. This is its delimitation by similar parts. Its delimitation by dissimilar parts is just like that of the hair.

## (25) Sweat
207. Sweat (Seda) is the liquid element (āpo-dhātu) oozing from the pores of the body hair, etc. In color, it is the color of clear sesame oil. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In terms of direction, it is produced in both directions. In terms of location, there is no fixed location for sweat where it remains always like blood. But when the body is heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, or climatic changes, etc., it oozes from all the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair, like a bundle of lotus stalks, lotus roots, and white lily stems cut unevenly and just pulled out of the water. Therefore, its shape should be understood according to the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair. Furthermore, the meditator who grasps the sweat should mindfully consider it as situated filling the openings of the pores of the hair and body hair.
254:
[254] In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of sweat. This is its delimitation of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). As for the delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda), it is just like that of the hair of the head.

## (26) Fat (Medo)
(208). Fat (medo) is solid fat. In color, it is the color of sliced turmeric. In shape, in a stout person, it has the shape of a piece of turmeric-colored coarse cloth placed between the skin and the flesh. In a lean person, it has the shape of a piece of turmeric-colored coarse cloth placed in two or three layers, depending on the flesh of the calves, the flesh of the thighs, the flesh of the back near the spine, and the flesh of the belly. In direction, it is found in both directions (upper and lower). In location, in a stout person, it is spread over the whole body; in a lean person, it is located depending on the flesh of the calves and so on. Although it is called grease or oil, because of its extreme loathsomeness, it is not taken for the purpose of head oil, nor for the purpose of nasal oil and so on. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited below by the flesh, above by the skin, and all around by its own portion of fat. This is its delimitation of the similar. As for the delimitation of the dissimilar, it is just like that of the hair of the head.
