## (27) Tears (Assu)
208. Tears (assu) are the water element (āpodhātu) that trickles from the eyes. In color, they are the color of clear sesame oil. In shape, they have the shape of their location. In direction, they belong to the upper direction. In location, they are situated in the eye sockets. However, these tears do not always remain collected in the eye sockets like bile in the gall-bladder. Rather, they are produced when beings are joyful and laugh loudly, or when they are sorrowful and weep or lament, or when they eat unsuitable food of such a nature (that causes tears), or when their eyes are affected by smoke, dust, grit, and so on. At such times, being originated by joy, sorrow, unsuitable food, or temperature (utu), they fill the eye sockets and either stay there or trickle out. A meditator who grasps tears should grasp them as they stay filling the eye sockets. In terms of delimitation, they are delimited by their own portion of tears. This is their delimitation of the similar. As for the delimitation of the dissimilar, it is just like that of the hair of the head.

## (28) Grease (Vasā)
209. Grease (vasā) is melted fat. In color, it is the color of coconut oil. It may also be said to be the color of oil poured on the scum of rice water. In shape, it has the shape of a drop of oil spreading over the surface of clear water at the time of bathing. In direction, it is found in both directions. In location, it is mostly situated on the palms of the hands, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the tip of the nose, the forehead, and the points of the shoulders. Furthermore, this grease does not always remain in a melted state in these locations. Rather, when those parts are [255] heated by the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, or by an imbalance of the temperature or the elements (dhātu) such as blood and wind,
255:
at that time, it moves here and there in those places like a drop of oil spreading on clear water during a bath. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of grease. This is its delimitation of the similar. As for the delimitation of the dissimilar, it is just like that of the hair of the head.

## (29) Spittle (Kheḷo)
210. Spittle (kheḷo) is the water element mixed with froth inside the mouth. In color, it is white, the color of froth. In shape, it has the shape of its location. It may also be said to have the shape of froth. In direction, it belongs to the upper direction. In location, it descends from both sides of the cheeks and stays on the tongue. Furthermore, this spittle does not always remain collected there. Rather, when beings see or remember food of such a nature that causes spittle, or when they put something hot, bitter, pungent, salty, or sour into their mouths, or when their heart is distressed (or disturbed), or when disgust arises for something, then the spittle is produced and, descending from both sides of the cheeks, stays on the tongue. It should be noted that this spittle is thin at the tip of the tongue and thick at the root of the tongue. Moreover, it is able to moisten flattened rice, raw rice, or any other edible put into the mouth without being exhausted, like the water in a small well dug in a sandbank in a river. In terms of delimitation, it is delimited by its own portion of spittle. This is its delimitation of the similar. As for the delimitation of the dissimilar, it is just like that of the hair of the head.

## (30) Snot (Siṅghāṇikā)
211. Snot (siṅghāṇikā) is the impurity that trickles down from the brain (matthaluṅga). In color, it is the color of the kernel of a young palmyra nut. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In direction, it belongs to the upper direction. In location, it stays filling the nostrils. Furthermore, this snot does not always remain collected in the nostrils. Rather, to give an illustration, just as if a man were to wrap curd in a lotus leaf and prick it underneath with a thorn, then the clear whey would leak through the hole and fall outside and downwards; even so, when beings weep, or when there is a disturbance of the elements caused by unsuitable food or temperature, then the brain inside the head, having turned into putrid phlegm, leaks out and, descending through the opening in the roof of the palate, stays filling the nostrils or trickles out.

Note: In modern medical and scientific texts, it is explained that nasal fluid comes from the nasal sinuses; there is no mention of the brain decaying to become nasal fluid. Therefore, the above statement may have been taken from a prominent text of that ancient era.
256:
To continue—the meditator who grasps snot should grasp it only by way of its being established filling the nostrils; by delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of snot. This is its delimitation of the similar (sabhāgapariccheda). Its delimitation of the dissimilar (visabhāgapariccheda) is just like that of the hairs.

## (31) Synovial Fluid

212. Lasikā (synovial fluid) is the slippery putrid grease inside the joints of the body. In color, it is like the color of the resin of the kaṇikāra tree. In shape, it has the shape of its location. In direction, it occurs in two directions. In location, it stays within the one hundred and eighty joints, performing the function of lubricating the bone joints. Specifically, in one who has little of this synovial fluid, when getting up, sitting down, moving forward, retreating, bending, or stretching, the bones creak (making a 'kat-kat gut-gut' sound), moving as if making a finger-snapping sound. If such a person travels a distance of about one or two leagues (yojana), the air element (vāyodhātu) becomes disturbed, and the limbs ache. In one who has much of it, the bones do not creak when getting up, sitting down, etc.; even after traveling a long distance, the air element is not disturbed, and the limbs do not ache. By delimitation, it is delimited by the portion of synovial fluid. This is its delimitation of the similar. Its delimitation of the dissimilar is just like that of the hairs.

## (32) Urine

213. Mutta (urine) is the liquid of urine. In color, it is like the color of bean-alkali water (māsakhārodaka). In shape, it has the shape of water inside a water pot placed upside down. In direction, it occurs in the lower direction. In location, it stays inside the bladder (vatthi). The bladder is called the bladder-sac (vatthipuṭa). To give an analogy, just as cesspool-water enters a filter-pot (yavanaghaṭa) that has no [obvious] opening when placed in a cesspool, and its path of entry is not apparent, so too urine enters [the bladder] from the body, and its path of entry is not apparent, but its path of exit is clear. When the bladder is full of urine, the urge of beings to urinate occurs. By delimitation, it is delimited by the interior of the bladder and by the portion of urine. This is its delimitation of the similar. Its delimitation of the dissimilar is just like that of the hairs.

## (Here ends the definition of the parts).

Note:
1. The meaning of 'bean-alkali water' is the meaning of the term māsakhāra. The Ṭīkā states: 'The liquid obtained by burning the whole bean plant including the roots and filtering the ash is called māsakhāra.' The Kāyānupassanā treatise, however, states: 'It is the clear liquid obtained by roasting mās beans, mixing the ash with water, and filtering it,' and rejects the interpretation of using the ash of the whole plant.
2. A cesspool (candanikā) is a place for discarding dishwater, waste from pregnancy, etc. (Ṭīkā). According to this Ṭīkā, a pit or hollow where foul and stagnant water stays is called a cesspool.
3. A filter-pot called a yavanaghaṭa naturally has no [obvious] entry hole. The reason for the qualifier 'without an opening' (amukhe) is to show that even if the filter-pot has no crack or hole as small as a needle-point for water to enter, its path of entry is not apparent. Similarly, urine enters from the body, but its path of entry is not apparent; the path of exit, however, is clear. To show such a good filter-pot, it is said: 'amukhe yavanaghaṭe—in a Yavana filter-pot without an opening.' (Ṭīkā). This filter-pot is a type made of fine clay and baked, with a large body like a squat bottle. It is placed inside a drinking-water pot. The water that seeps into this filter-pot is poured out and drunk. Since it was used by the Yavana (Greek, Persian, or Muslim) people in ancient times, it was called a yavanaghaṭa. Although it has a mouth-opening like a bottle for pouring water out, it has no apparent opening for water to enter; it can only enter by seeping. Therefore, it is said to have 'no entry opening' (amukhe).

Note:
The statement that there is no path for urine to enter the bladder is intended by the Commentators to mean that it is not clearly visible to ordinary people. Modern Western doctors explain the formation of urine as follows: food that is somewhat digested in the stomach reaches the small intestine, where it is further digested. Within the small intestine, tiny fleshy fibers called villi absorb the nutrient essence (rasadhātu) that can become blood, etc., and send it through small vessels to the main blood vessels. From these main vessels, two large arteries send blood to the two kidneys. Inside each kidney, there are over a million mechanisms for filtering waste, which filter out waste water from the blood and send it to the bladder through two ureters. From the bladder, it exits through the urethra.

## Method of Contemplation and Progress

214. Having thus defined the thirty-two parts such as the hairs by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, and then attending to them as 'repulsive, repulsive' in five ways by way of color, shape, smell, origin, and location, using the methods of 'in order', 'not too fast', etc.—at the end of transcending the concept (paṇṇatti), just as a man with good eyesight looking at a garland of thirty-two kinds of flowers strung on a single thread sees all the flowers clearly without confusion of order, so too, for one looking at this body, 'there are in this body hairs...', all these parts become clear.
257:
In this sense, it should be said that the bladder has two inlets and one outlet.

1. It means 'by way of the fivefold classification such as color, shape, etc.'

For a meditator who contemplates 'repulsive,' at the end of transcending the conceptual name, to give a simile: just as when a man with good eyesight looks at a garland of flowers of thirty-two colors strung on a single thread, all the flowers appear clearly and simultaneously, as if without before or after; even so, while looking at this body [with wisdom] as 'there are hairs in this body,' and so on, all those parts (koṭṭhāsa) appear clearly and simultaneously, as if without before or after. Therefore, in the explanation of skill in attention (manasikāra-kosalla) (page 288), I have said: 'To explain further—for a beginner contemplating "hair," the attention goes [according to the rote learning] and reaches and stays only at the final part, which is "urine."' 

Note:
1. This statement shows the method of contemplation. A person who wishes to practice this meditation of mindfulness occupied with the body (kāyagatāsati) must first define and understand the hairs, etc., by way of the five aspects: color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation. Then, when contemplating, one should attend to and contemplate the repulsiveness by way of color, etc. This refers to the meditator who is thus attending and contemplating.
2. 'Reaches and stays only at the final part'—this statement is made by taking it as 'the attention to the meditation subject occurs at the beginning by following the sequence of the meditation text (which is learned by heart).' (Sub-commentary). In accordance with this sub-commentary:

Furthermore, if one applies the attention to the external [bodies of others] as well (as being purely repulsive, just as in one's own continuity), then when all the parts become clear to that meditator as described, beings such as humans and animals who are wandering about lose the appearance of a 'being' (or, are devoid of the appearance of a 'being') and appear only as a heap of repulsive parts. Even the food and drink consumed by those humans and animals appears as if it were being thrown into a heap of repulsive parts.

Then, by way of abandoning the sequence and so on, for that meditator who contemplates 'repulsive, repulsive' repeatedly, absorption (appanā) arises in due course. In that process, the appearance of hair and so on by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation is the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta). The appearance by way of repulsiveness in every aspect is the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta).

Note:
The statement from the sub-commentary (kammaṭṭhāna-tanti-anusārena) on page 288 was also shown in parentheses. As shown in that explanation, it is also presented here. However, in this context, whether the statement of the Commentary refers to following the sequence of the text learned by heart is still to be considered.
1. Connect 'when they appear...' with '...they appear' and '...it appears.'

For the meditator who repeatedly associates with and develops that counterpart sign (or, the attention having that counterpart sign as its object), absorption arises only by way of the first jhāna, just as in the foulness meditations (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) mentioned previously.

That absorption arises as only one for a person to whom only one part is clear, or for one who, having reached absorption in one part, does not make further effort in another part. For these two types of persons, only one absorption arises. However, for a person to whom many parts are clear, or for one who, having reached jhāna in one part, makes further effort in another part as well, the first jhānas arise according to the number of parts (perceived or attended to), just as they did for the Elder Mallaka (Mallaka Thera).

It is heard that the Venerable Mallaka Thera, taking the hand of the Elder Abhaya, the Dīgha-reciter (Dīgha-bhāṇaka), said: 'Friend Abhaya, please learn this problem first,' and then said: 'The Elder Mallaka obtained thirty-two first jhānas in the thirty-two parts. If he enters one jhāna at night and one during the day, he enters them all again in just over half a month (i.e., 17 days). If he enters only one jhāna daily, he enters them all again in just over a month.'

To continue—although this meditation is accomplished by way of the first jhāna as described, it is called 'mindfulness occupied with the body' (kāyagatāsati) because it is accomplished through the power of mindfulness regarding color, shape, and so on.

The benefit is: a monk devoted to this meditation of mindfulness occupied with the body becomes a conqueror of boredom and delight (arati-rati-saho); boredom does not conquer him; he dwells having repeatedly overcome boredom and delight that have arisen. He becomes a conqueror of fear and dread; fear and dread do not conquer him; he dwells having repeatedly overcome fear and dread that have arisen. He is one who endures cold, [Page 258] heat, hunger, thirst, and the touch of gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and the bite and contact of snakes and scorpions.
258:
He endures harsh words that are spoken badly and that come badly. He is of a nature to endure painful, racking, sharp, piercing, disagreeable, unpleasant, and life-threatening bodily feelings that have arisen within. Based on the distinction of colors such as hair and so forth—blue, yellow, red, and white—he becomes an attainer of the four jhānas. He penetrates and attains the six supernormal knowledges (abhiññā).

Therefore, indeed, the wise person, being vigilant, should apply himself to this mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati), which is thus endowed with many benefits. This is the introduction to the detailed explanation of mindfulness of the body.

## (Mindfulness of the Body is finished).

## 9. Explanation of the Development of Mindfulness of Breathing (Ānāpānassati)

215. Now, the Blessed One, having praised it thus: "Bhikkhus, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-samādhi), when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated and happy dwelling, and it causes evil unwholesome states to disappear and settle at once whenever they arise"—

[Note: The time has now come to explain the method of development. The Blessed One, having praised it, taught and pointed it out.]

"Bhikkhus, how is concentration through mindfulness of breathing developed, and how is it cultivated so that it is peaceful and sublime, an unadulterated and happy dwelling, and causes evil unwholesome states to disappear and settle at once whenever they arise? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, having gone to the forest, or to the root of a tree, or to an empty hut, sits down, having folded his legs crosswise, set his body erect, and established mindfulness in front of him. Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out."

[Note: According to the Vinaya Commentary and secular texts, assāsa is out-breath and passāsa is in-breath. However, to be consistent with the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali to be shown later, and because one usually begins with the in-breath at the start of practice, here assasati is translated as 'breathes in' and passasati as 'breathes out.' This translation also accords with the meaning of the word ānāpāna.]

"Breathing in long, he understands it clearly: 'I breathe in long.' Breathing out long, he understands it clearly: 'I breathe out long.' Breathing in short, he understands: 'I breathe in short.' Breathing out short, he understands: 'I breathe out short.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the whole body.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in calming the bodily formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing rapture.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing rapture.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing pleasure.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing pleasure.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in calming the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out calming the mental formation.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in experiencing the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out experiencing the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in gladdening the mind.' He trains thus: 'I shall breathe out gladdening the mind.'"

[Note: In the word pajānāti, the meaning of the prefix pa- is expressed as 'clearly.' However, in Burmese usage, simply saying 'knows' can convey the meaning of knowing distinctly or knowing with wisdom.]
259:
Because of the sense of knowing (ñātaṭṭhena), it is called knowledge (ñāṇa). In the context of the Pali language, such as in 'the Omniscient One' (Sabbaññū) and so on, even without the prefix 'pa-', the word 'knows' alone is sufficient to convey the meaning of knowledge and wisdom. Therefore, hereafter, the word 'pajānāti' will be translated simply as 'he knows'.

'He trains himself, "I will breathe out." He trains himself, "I will breathe in, setting the mind well." He trains himself, "I will breathe out, setting the mind well." He trains himself, "I will breathe in, liberating the mind." [259] He trains himself, "I will breathe out, liberating the mind." He trains himself, "I will breathe in, contemplating impermanence." He trains himself, "I will breathe out, contemplating impermanence." He trains himself, "I will breathe in, contemplating fading away (virāga)." He trains himself, "I will breathe out, contemplating fading away." He trains himself, "I will breathe in, contemplating cessation (nirodha)." He trains himself, "I will breathe out, contemplating cessation." He trains himself, "I will breathe in, contemplating relinquishment (paṭinissagga) (or: contemplating by way of letting go; or: contemplating so as to be able to let go)." He trains himself, "I will breathe out, contemplating relinquishment."'—

Thus, the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati-kammaṭṭhāna) with sixteen bases has been taught and pointed out. The method of developing that mindfulness of breathing has now come in sequence (to be explained). However, that method of development is complete in all aspects only if it is explained following the Pali commentary. Therefore, the following exposition is an extensive explanation preceded by the commentary on the Pali regarding this mindfulness of breathing meditation subject.

216. In the passage 'How, bhikkhus, is mindfulness of breathing concentration developed?' (Kathaṃ bhāvito ca, bhikkhave, ānāpānassati samādhi), the word 'How' (kathaṃ) is a question asked with the desire to explain the development of mindfulness of breathing in various ways. The phrase 'mindfulness of breathing concentration, when developed' is the indication of the Dhamma asked about with the desire to explain it in detail. In the passage 'How, when practiced frequently... [pe] ...can it bring to stillness?', the same method applies. Therein, 'developed' (bhāvito) means produced or increased. 'Mindfulness of breathing concentration' (ānāpānassati-samādhi) is concentration associated with mindfulness that grasps the in-breaths and out-breaths. Alternatively, concentration (arising) because of mindfulness of in-breaths and out-breaths is called mindfulness of breathing concentration (Note 1). 'Practiced frequently' (bahulīkato) means done again and again. 'Peaceful and sublime' (santo ceva paṇīto ca) means it is both peaceful and sublime (Note 2). In both terms, the emphasis (certainty) should be understood by the word 'only' (eva). What is meant? For instance, the meditation on foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna) is peaceful and sublime only by virtue of penetration (paṭivedha) (Note 1); however, by virtue of the object (ārammaṇa), it is neither peaceful nor sublime because it has a gross object and a repulsive object. Mindfulness of breathing is not like that—it is not unpeaceful or non-sublime for any reason. Rather, it is peaceful, specially stilled, and cooled even by the peacefulness of the object, and also by the peacefulness of the jhana factors known as penetration. It is sublime and unsatisfyingly good [meaning one never tires of its goodness] by the sublimity of the object, and also by the sublimity of the jhana factors. Therefore, it is said, 'It is peaceful and sublime.'

Note:
1— Of the two methods here, according to the first: Ānāpāna (in-breath and out-breath) + Sati (mindfulness) associated with + Samādhi (concentration) = Ānāpānassati-samādhi (concentration associated with mindfulness of in-breaths and out-breaths). According to the second: Ānāpānassati (mindfulness of in-breaths and out-breaths) because of which there is + Samādhi (concentration) = Ānāpānassati-samādhi (concentration arising because of mindfulness of in-breaths and out-breaths). This second method also shows that it arises because of the mindfulness that occurred at the moment of access (upacāra). This is explained based on the Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā).
2— In 'paṇīto ca', although 'eva' is not present, it is explained as being taken from 'santo ceva'. Therefore, based on this commentary, in the Burmese translation of the root sutta, 'paṇီတော စ' was translated as 'is also certainly sublime', adding the meaning of 'eva'.
1— It means it is peaceful and sublime only according to the jhana factors called penetration; according to the object, there is no peacefulness or sublimity.

In the phrase 'an unadulterated and pleasant dwelling' (asecanako ca sukho ca vihāro), (the meaning is) that concentration which has no 'sprinkling' cause (any cause that produces peacefulness and sublimity) is called 'asecanaka' (Note 1). It means a concentration with no sprinkling cause, unmixed with other assistance, separate, and unique. In this mindfulness of breathing concentration, there is no prior preparation of the object to be viewed (as in kasina jhana, etc.) (Note 2), nor is there peacefulness (only) by way of access (upacāra) (Note 3). (Rather,)

Note:
1— Although 'assa' is in the Pali, it is translated indefinitely so that even those with little learning can understand easily.
2— Preliminary work (parikamma), which is the cause of peacefulness, is also absent. Preliminary work refers to the prior actions starting from creating a kasina image up to the arising of the sign (nimitta). It is meant that such preliminary work is not present in this mindfulness of breathing concentration. Indeed, if there were preliminary work, the meditation subject would not be peaceful or sublime during that time because it would not be pleasant. (Ṭīkā) This is translated in accordance with the Sub-commentary. In the current Visuddhimagga book, the reading is 'parikammena vā'. According to that reading, it should be translated as 'there is no peacefulness by preliminary work or by access'.
3— The peacefulness of other concentrations arises due to the absence of hindrances and the manifestation of factors at the moment of access (upacāra); the peacefulness of this mindfulness of breathing concentration is not like that.
260:
This concentration is peaceful and sublime from the very first moment of attention; this is the meaning of the word 'asecanako'. Other teachers explain 'asecanako' as a concentration that is naturally sweet and delicious without any additives or infusions. Thus, this mindfulness of breathing concentration has nothing poured into it or added to it. It should be understood as a 'pleasant dwelling' (sukho vihāro) because it leads to the attainment of bodily and mental happiness at every moment of its attainment. 'Arisen and arisen' (uppannuppanne) refers to those [unwholesome states] that have not yet been suppressed. 'Evil' (pāpake) means lowly. 'Unwholesome states' (akusale dhamme) refers to states born of ignorance (avijjā), which is the cause of lack of skill and foolishness.

Note: It should be connected as: 'It is peaceful and sublime by its very nature.' (Ṭīkā)
1. In this context, 'arisen and arisen' (uppannuppanne) does not mean arising by way of production (uppāda), but refers to unwholesome states that are capable of arising because they have not yet been abandoned through suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna).
2. Ignorance (avijjā) is called 'lack of skill' (akosalla) because it is the cause of being unskillful and foolish; [it refers to] states born of that ignorance. Indeed, all unwholesome states are preceded by ignorance. (Ṭīkā)

'Instantly causes to disappear' (ṭhānaso antaradhāpeti) means it causes them to vanish or be removed in a single moment. 'Calms' (vūpasameti) means it stills them thoroughly. Alternatively, because it leads to penetration (nibbedhabhāgiya), when one reaches the growth of the Noble Path (ariya-magga) in due course, it cuts them off without remainder and stills them [through the Noble Fruit].

This is the summary of the meaning here: Monks, in what manner, in what way, and by what method is mindfulness of breathing concentration developed, and in what manner is it cultivated so that it is peaceful... and calms [unwholesome states]? This is the summary.

217. Now, wishing to explain that meaning in detail, the Blessed One said: 'Here, monks...' and so on. Therein, 'Here, monks, a monk' (idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu) means: Monks, in this Dispensation (Sāsana), a monk. For here, the word 'here' (idha) indicates the Dispensation which is the support for the person who produces mindfulness of breathing concentration in every way, and it excludes other dispensations from being such a support.

Note: 1. According to this second explanation, it means calming by leading to the Noble Path and Fruit.

For it is said: 'Only here, monks, is there a recluse (samaṇa)... other doctrines are void of recluses.' (M. Ni. 1.139). Therefore, I have explained it as 'a monk in this Dispensation'.

'Gone to the forest... or to an empty hut' (araññagato vā... suññāgāragato vā) indicates the selection of a dwelling suitable for the development of mindfulness of breathing concentration. For this monk's mind, which has for a long time wandered among sense objects such as visible forms, does not wish to mount the object of mindfulness of breathing concentration; it runs off the track like a carriage harnessed to a wild ox. Therefore, just as a cowherd, wishing to tame a wild calf that has grown up drinking all the milk of a wild cow, would take it away from the cow and tie it with a rope to a large post planted in a certain place—then that calf of his, struggling this way and that, unable to escape, would eventually sit down or lie down by that very post—in the same way, this monk, wishing to tame his corrupt mind which has grown up drinking the 'taste' [of pleasure] from sense objects like visible forms for a long time, should take it away from sense objects, enter a forest, the root of a tree, or an empty hut, and tie it to the post of in-breaths and out-breaths with the rope of mindfulness.
261:
When tied in this way, even though that monk's mind struggles here and there, since it does not find its previously accustomed objects, it is unable to break the rope of mindfulness and flee. Therefore, it stays and rests upon that very object of the in-breath and out-breath by the power of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). Therefore, the ancient teachers said:

“Just as a man who wishes to tame a young calf would tie it to a post,
So too, here in this Dispensation, a monk who wishes to tame his own mind
Should tie it firmly with mindfulness to the object of meditation.”

As just explained, this dwelling (such as the forest) of that yogi monk is suitable for meditation. Therefore, I have said: “This statement illustrates the monk's acquisition of a dwelling and bedding suitable for the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing.”

Alternatively, this Ānāpāna meditation is like the crown among the various meditation subjects. It is the proximate cause for the attainment of the special qualities of the Path and Fruition for all Buddhas, some Paccekabuddhas, and some disciples. It is also the proximate cause for dwelling happily in the present life. It is not easy to develop this mindfulness of breathing without leaving a village-outskirt dwelling crowded with the sounds of women, men, elephants, horses, and so on. This is because sound is a thorn to jhāna. Indeed, it is easy for this yogi monk, while dwelling in a forest far from a village and grasping this mindfulness of breathing, to produce the fourth jhāna (or the group of four jhānas) having the breath as its object, and then, using that very jhāna as a basis, to contemplate formations (saṅkhāras) and reach the highest fruit, Arahantship. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the dwelling suitable for that monk, spoke the words beginning with “gone to the forest.”

Truly, the Blessed One is like a master of site-selection (vatthuvijjā-ācariya). Just as a master of site-selection, after looking at and carefully examining a site for a city, points out, “Build the city here,” and when the city is successfully completed, he receives great honor from the royal family; even so, the Blessed One, like a master of site-selection, examines the dwelling suitable for the yogi monk and points out, “Meditation should be practiced in this place, such as the forest.” Then, when the yogi practicing meditation in that place reaches Arahantship through the sequence of concentration, insight, and the Noble Path, the Blessed One receives great honor (such as praise and devotion) in the form of the realization: “The Blessed One, our teacher, is indeed a truly Enlightened One who has known the truth correctly through his own higher knowledge.”

Furthermore, this yogi monk (practicing in the forest, etc.) is said to be like a leopard. To explain: Just as a great leopard, the king of the forest, relying on and hiding in a thicket of grass, a thicket of trees, or a thicket in the mountains, catches wild buffaloes, elks, pigs, and other prey; even so, this monk practicing meditation in places such as the forest [attains] in due order the Path of Stream-entry, the Path of Once-returning, the Path of Non-returning, and the Path of Arahantship...
262:
It should be understood that he also takes the four Noble Fruits. Therefore, the former teachers said:

[262] “Just as a leopard, having hidden, catches its prey, even so this son of the Buddha, a practitioner of insight (vipassanā) endowed with effort, having entered the forest, seizes the supreme Noble Fruit.”

Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to show the forest dwelling as a suitable ground for the momentum of that monk's effort in meditation, said: “Gone to the forest,” and so on.

218. In that passage, regarding “gone to the forest” (araññagato): “Forest (arañña) means everything outside the threshold (indakhīla) after exiting,” and “A forest dwelling (āraññakaṃ seနာsanaṃ) is at least five hundred bow-lengths away.” Having entered any such forest characterized by the bliss of seclusion. “Gone to the root of a tree” (rukkhamūlagato) means gone near a tree (under a tree). “Gone to an empty place” (suññāgāragato) means gone to a secluded, empty space. Furthermore, in this context, excluding the forest and the root of a tree, reaching any of the remaining seven types of dwellings¹ can also be called “gone to an empty place.”

Thus, having pointed out a dwelling (such as the forest) that is suitable for the three seasons, the three humors (phlegm, etc.), and the three temperaments (delusion, etc.)², and is appropriate for the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati), He said “sits” (nisīdati) to point out a calm posture that is on the side of non-sloth and non-restlessness. Then, wishing to show the stability of the sitting posture, the ease of maintaining the in-breaths and out-breaths, and the method of grasping the object for that yogi, He said “having folded his legs crosswise” (pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā), and so on. In that passage, “crosswise” (pallaṅkaṃ) means a sitting posture with the thighs locked all around. “Having folded” (ābhujitvā) means having bound¹. “Keeping the body erect” (ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya) means placing the upper body straight, aligning the eighteen vertebrae of the spine end to end. For when one sits in this way, the skin, flesh, and sinews do not bend. Consequently, the painful feelings that might arise moment by moment due to their bending do not arise. When those painful feelings do not arise, the mind becomes one-pointed and concentrated. The meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) does not fall away; it reaches growth and increase. “Setting up mindfulness in front” (parimukhaṃ satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā) means having established mindfulness directed towards the meditation object.

Note:
1. The remaining seven dwellings are: (1) a mountain, (2) a glen, (3) a mountain cave, (4) a cemetery, (5) a woodland, (6) the open air, (7) a heap of straw.
2. In the summer, the forest is suitable; in the winter, the root of a tree is suitable; in the rainy season, an empty place is suitable. For one with a phlegmatic humor, the forest is suitable; for one with a bilious humor, the root of a tree is suitable; for one with a windy humor, an empty place is suitable. For one of a deluded temperament, the forest is suitable; for one of a hateful temperament, the root of a tree is suitable; for one of a lustful temperament, an empty place is suitable. (Ṭīkā)

Note:
1. Such grammatical explanations are mostly beneficial in the Pali texts and less so in the Burmese translation; however, they are included here for completeness.

Alternatively, “pari” has the sense of grasping (pariggaha), “mukha” has the sense of leading out (niyyāna), and “sati” has the sense of establishment (upaṭṭhāna). Therefore, it is called “parimukhaṃ satiṃ.” The meaning should be understood here according to the method stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. This is the summary of the meaning in that commentary: having established mindfulness that is grasped and leads out (from the opposite state).

[263] 219. “Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out” (so satova assasati satova passasati) means that the monk, having sat as described and having established mindfulness as described, without abandoning that mindfulness, mindfully breathes in and mindfully breathes out; it means he is one who acts mindfully. Now, to show the ways in which he acts mindfully, He said “breathing in long” (dīghaṃ vā assasanto), and so on. Therefore, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, regarding this summary statement “so satova assasati satova passasati”...
263:
Note
1. In this entire section, all grammatical explanations are of little benefit in the Burmese translation; however, they are provided for completeness. Therefore, those who do not know Pali should not spend time pondering these explanations.

In the detailed analysis, the following words were spoken:

"He acts mindfully in thirty-two ways: through the power of the in-breath (preached as) long, for one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind, mindfulness is established; with that mindfulness and with that knowledge, he acts mindfully (1). Through the power of the out-breath (preached as) long... (2). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) short... (3). Through the power of the out-breath (preached as) short... (4). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) experiencing the whole body... (5). Through the power of the out-breath (preached as) experiencing the whole body... (6). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) calming the bodily formation... (7). Through the power of the out-breath (preached as) calming the bodily formation... (8). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) experiencing rapture... (9). Out-breath... (10). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) experiencing bliss... (11). ...Out-breath... (12). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) experiencing mental formation...

Note
1. 'Dīghaṃ assāsavasena' means by way of the in-breath which is preached as 'long'. The same applies to the remaining terms. This is translated in accordance with Paṭisambhidāmagga-aṭṭhakathā, Vol. 2, p. 281.

(13). ...Out-breath... (14). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) calming mental formation... (15). ...Out-breath... (16). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) experiencing the mind... (17). ...Out-breath... (18). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) gladdening the mind... (19). Out-breath... (20). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) concentrating the mind... (21). ...Out-breath... (22). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) liberating the mind... (23). ...Out-breath... (24). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) contemplating impermanence... (25). ...Out-breath... (26). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) contemplating fading away... (27). ...Out-breath... (28). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) contemplating cessation... (29). ...Out-breath... (30). Through the power of the in-breath (preached as) contemplating relinquishment... (31). Through the power of the out-breath (preached as) contemplating relinquishment, for one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind, mindfulness is established; with that mindfulness and with that knowledge, he acts mindfully (32)." (Burmese translation of the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali)

In that passage (beginning with 'breathing in long'), 'breathing in long' means 'producing a long in-breath.' It is stated in the Vinaya Commentary that 'assāsa is the wind going out, and passāsa is the wind coming in.' However, in the Suttanta Commentaries, it is explained in the reverse order (assāsa is the in-breath, passāsa is the out-breath). In this regard, for all beings born from a womb (gabbhaseyyaka), at the time of exiting the mother's womb, first the internal wind goes out. Later, the external wind, carrying subtle dust, enters inside and, striking the palate, is extinguished. Thus, in-breaths and out-breaths should be understood by their initial occurrence.

Furthermore, the length or shortness of those in-breaths and out-breaths should be understood by way of duration. To illustrate with an analogy: just as water or sand that stays spread over a long or short space is called 'long water, long sand' or 'short water, short sand,' so too, although the in-breaths and out-breaths are extremely subtle, in the bodies of elephants and snakes, they slowly fill the long extent of their physical forms and slowly exit. Therefore, they are called 'long.' In the case of dogs, rabbits, etc., they quickly fill the short extent of their physical forms and quickly exit. Therefore, they are called 'short.' Among humans, some breathe in and out long by way of a long duration, like elephants and snakes. Some breathe in and out short by way of a short duration, like dogs and rabbits. Therefore, for those humans, the breaths that go out and come in for a long duration [264] should be known as 'long,' and the breaths that go out and come in for a short duration should be known as 'short.'

In that passage (he knows he breathes in long, breathes out long), this yogi monk, through nine ways...

## Note
1. Translated by substituting with another method for easier understanding.
1. Although stated in the plural in Pali, it is translated without the plural suffix to make the Burmese phrasing smoother. Note similar terms hereafter in the same way.
2. Since the breaths of animals like elephants, snakes, dogs, and rabbits have already been fully shown in the preceding sentences, it is only necessary to show the breaths of humans in this context.
264:
Therefore, the word *nesaṃ* is translated as "of those people"; connect it as "of those people... those breaths." In the Ṭīkā, it is interpreted as "of those beings."

3. In the sense of "for a long duration" by way of time—in smooth Burmese, it means "for a long time" or "at a long time."

4. Connect it as "those breaths... should be known."

Breathing in long and breathing out long, one knows, "I breathe in long, I breathe out long." When one knows thus, it should be understood that the development of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā satipaṭṭhāna*) is fulfilled for that yogi (by one of the nine ways). In accordance with this, it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali:

“How, breathing in long, does one know 'I breathe in long'? Breathing out long, does one know 'I breathe out long'? One breathes in a long in-breath in a duration called long. One breathes out a long out-breath in a duration called long. One breathes in and breathes out a long in-breath and out-breath in a duration called long. While breathing in and breathing out a long in-breath and out-breath in a duration called long, desire (to strive further) arises [Note 1]. By the power of desire, one breathes in a long in-breath that is subtler than that. . . p . . . a long out-breath. . . p . . . one breathes in and breathes out a long in-breath and out-breath in a duration called long.

Note
1. Desire arises—this means when the meditation brings about a distinction from the previous state to the later state (i.e., when it becomes extraordinary), because of obtaining delight, wholesome desire characterized by the wish to act in that meditation work arises intensely. (Ṭīkā) Such desire is meant to arise during both inhalation and exhalation.

By the power of desire, while breathing in and breathing out a long in-breath and out-breath that is subtler than that in a duration called long, joy (*pāmojja*, i.e., tender rapture) arises. By the power of joy, one breathes in a long in-breath that is subtler than that. . . p . . . a long out-breath. . . p . . . one breathes in and breathes out a long in-breath and out-breath in a duration called long. By the power of joy, while breathing in and breathing out a long in-breath and out-breath that is subtler than that in a duration called long, the (meditative) mind turns away [Note 1] from the natural in-breath and out-breath (taught as long), and equanimity (*upekkhā*) is well-established [Note 1].

Note
1. Subtler than that—means because of the arising of desire as mentioned, (the breath) is subtler than the previous in-breath and out-breath. Indeed, when the heat and burning in the body are calmed by the power of meditation, the in-breaths and out-breaths become subtler. Joy arises—means because of the subtleness of the breaths and the greater tranquility of the object, and because the meditation of attention is on the right path, tender rapture such as minor rapture (*khuddikā pīti*) which arises with the meditative mind, occurs. The mind turns away—means when the in-breaths and out-breaths reach extreme subtleness in sequence,

By these nine ways, the long in-breaths and out-breaths are the body (*kāya*). The appearance or remembering is mindfulness (*sati*). The contemplation is knowledge (*ñāṇa*). The body is called only the foundation (*upaṭṭhāna*) because it is the object of mindfulness; it is not called mindfulness (as it is not the act of remembering). Mindfulness is called both foundation and mindfulness because it can appear and remember. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, one repeatedly contemplates that body, which is the collection of in-breaths and out-breaths. Therefore, it is called the development of mindfulness of the body as body (or contemplating the body in the body).” (This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga.)

Note
Because of not being apparent, some explain that the mind turns away from the in-breaths and out-breaths which have reached a state where they must be investigated whether they exist or not. In truth, when the breaths reach greater subtleness by the power of meditation, the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) arises in those breaths; at that time, the (meditative) mind turns away from the natural in-breath and out-breath. (Ṭīkā)
265:
1. Equanimity is well-established—means when concentration such as access (*upacāra*) or absorption (*appanā*) has arisen in that counterpart sign, equanimity occurs because there is no further need for concern to produce jhāna; this equanimity should be known as *tatramajjhattatā-upekkhā*. (Ṭīkā)

[265] The same method applies to the word "short" (*rassa*). This is the distinction: just as in the section just shown it was said "a long in-breath in a duration called long," so here in the short section it comes as "one breathes in a short in-breath in a duration called short" [Note 1]. Therefore, up to the concluding words "it is called the development of mindfulness of the body as body," it should be applied (by substituting) with the word "short."

As just explained, by way of long duration [Note 2] and by way of short time, this yogi who knows the in-breaths and out-breaths through these nine ways should be understood [Note 3] as "knowing when breathing in long, I breathe in long; when breathing out long. . . p . . . when breathing in short. . . p . . . when breathing out short, I breathe out short."

Of that monk who knows as stated:

Long and short in-breaths,
And out-breaths likewise,
These four types occur,
At the tip of the monk's nose [Note 1].

Note
1. It simply means it is stated so.
2. The word *addhāna* is translated as long duration; it simply means a long time.
3. *Veditabbo*—though it should be translated as "should be known," it is translated as "should be understood" to avoid confusion with the preceding and following words for "knows."

Note
1. In the verse, *vā* is shortened to *va* for meter. In *nāsikagge va*, the word *vā* has an indefinite sense; by that *vā*, the upper lip is included. (Ṭīkā) The indication to observe only at the tip of the nose or upper lip in these Pali, Commentaries, and Sub-commentaries is only for *samatha* concentration. Indeed, *samatha* concentration can only arise by focusing on a single spot. In the case of *vipassanā*, however, just as other winds like upward-going winds can be observed anywhere, it should be specially noted that these in-breaths and out-breaths can also be observed anywhere.

220. In "Training, I shall breathe in. . . p . . . experiencing the whole body (*sabbakāyapaṭisaṃvedī*)," the meaning is: training to breathe in while making known and clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire mass of in-breaths. Training to breathe out while making known and clear the beginning, middle, and end of the entire mass of out-breaths. Thus making them known and clear, one breathes in and out with a mind associated with knowledge. Therefore, it is said "one trains to breathe in and breathe out." Indeed, for one monk, in the mass of in-breaths or out-breaths spread as minute particles, only the beginning is clear, but not the middle and end. He is able to grasp only the beginning and becomes exhausted at the middle and end. For another, only the middle is clear, but not the beginning and end. For another, only the end is clear, but not the beginning and middle. He is able to grasp only the end and becomes exhausted at the beginning and middle. For another, everything is clear. He is able to grasp everything and does not become exhausted anywhere. To show that one should be such a person, it was taught: "Training, I shall breathe in while knowing the whole mass of in-breaths. . . p . . . breathe out."

[266] In that statement, "trains" (*sikkhati*) means: one exerts and makes effort in this manner. Alternatively, whatever restraint of mindfulness (*sati-saṃvara*) and restraint of energy (*vīriya-saṃvara*) such a monk has, this restraint is "training in higher virtue" (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) among the three trainings. Whatever concentration—the well-placing of the mind—such a monk has,
266:
This concentration is the training in higher mind (adhicitta-sikkhā). The wisdom of such a monk is the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññā-sikkhā). Thus, one trains in, frequents, develops, and cultivates these three trainings regarding that object [of the breath] with that mindfulness and that attention—this is the meaning to be understood in the word "sikkhati—he trains."

Among those [sixteen] bases of meditation, in the first two methods (where it is taught: "he knows he breathes in, he knows he breathes out" in connection with long and short breaths), there is only the act of breathing in and breathing out. There is no other task to be performed [Note 1]. However, from this third method onwards, effort must be made in the production of knowledge and so forth. Therefore, in those first two methods taught in connection with long and short breaths, the teaching is set forth only in the present tense as "he knows he breathes in, he knows he breathes out." But from this third method onwards, to show the manner of producing knowledge and so forth which ought to be done, the teaching is established by way of the future tense: "I shall breathe in experiencing the whole body," and so forth.

Note 1: Because of the presence of knowing the long and short breaths as they really are, the production of knowledge is indeed attained in those first two methods as well. However, because that production of knowledge is merely the grasping of those breaths as they occur, it is not very difficult to perform. Therefore, in those two methods, the connection with the present tense is made. In this third method and others, knowing is difficult; it is like a man walking on a path of razor blades. (Sub-commentary)

"Training thus: 'I shall breathe in... [etc.] ...I shall breathe out calming the bodily formation (kāyasaṅkhāra),'" the meaning is: he trains, thinking "I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out," while calming, further calming, ceasing, and specifically tranquilizing the coarse bodily formation (the in-breath and out-breath). In this regard, coarseness, subtlety, and calming should be understood as follows: In this meditating monk, before the time of grasping [the breath], the body and mind are distressed and coarse. When the coarseness of body and mind is not tranquilized, the in-breaths and out-breaths are also coarse; they proceed with great strength [Note 1], the nostrils are insufficient, and he may even stand breathing in and out through the mouth [Note 2]. But when his body and mind have been grasped [Note 3], then they become quiet and tranquil.

Note 1: This is an easy-to-understand Burmese translation of the Pali "balavatarā hutvā pavattanti." A literal translation would be: "they occur continuously, becoming particularly powerful."
Note 2: This passage up to here shows the coarseness of the breaths before meditating on ānāpāna.
Note 3: "Grasping the body and mind" means meditating on them.

They become specifically tranquil. When the body and mind are tranquil, the in-breaths and out-breaths proceed subtly, reaching a state where they must be investigated: "Do they exist or not?" [Note 1].

To give a simile: just as for a man who has stood still after running, or after descending from a mountain, or after removing a heavy burden from his head, his in-breaths and out-breaths are coarse, the nostrils are insufficient, and he stands breathing in and out through the mouth. But when he has dispelled that fatigue, bathed and drunk water, and lies down in the cool shade with a wet cloth on his chest, then his [267] in-breaths and out-breaths become subtle, reaching a state where they must be investigated: "Do they exist or not?" In the same way, in this meditating monk, before the time of grasping the in-breaths and out-breaths, the body and mind are distressed and coarse...

Note 1: From the time of meditating on ānāpāna, the breath gradually becomes subtle until it is so subtle that it is as if one is not breathing at any more.
267:
At that time, one might investigate and reflect, "Does the breath exist or not?" This shows the manner of occurrence. One should consider whether the practice of breathing in and out heavily is consistent with this statement.

When coarseness is not calmed, the in-breaths and out-breaths are also coarse; they occur with great force as they enter and exit, and the nostrils may be insufficient, such that one remains breathing in and out through the mouth. However, when the body and mind of that monk have been grasped (pariggahita), they become tranquil, especially tranquil. When the body and mind are tranquil, the in-breaths and out-breaths occur subtly as they enter and exit, reaching a state where one must investigate, "Do they exist or not?"

Why is this so? Because previously, before the time of grasping the in-breaths and out-breaths, this yogi monk did not have the intention, application, attention, and reflection to "calm the coarse bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra)"; but at the time of grasping, he does. Therefore, the bodily formations are subtler at the time of grasping than they were before grasping. Thus, the ancient teachers said:

"When the body and the mind are agitated, the breath proceeds excessively;
When the body is not agitated, it proceeds subtly."

221. Even during the time of grasping, it is still coarse; it is subtle in the access (upacāra) to the first jhāna. Even in that access to the first jhāna, it is still coarse; it is subtle in the first jhāna. It is coarse in the first jhāna and in the access to the second jhāna; it is subtle in the second jhāna.

It is coarse in the second jhāna and in the access to the third jhāna; it is subtle in the third jhāna. It is coarse in the third jhāna and in the access to the fourth jhāna; it is extremely subtle in the fourth jhāna, reaching a state of non-occurrence. This is the view of the reciters (bhāṇaka) of the Dīgha Nikāya and Saṃyutta Nikāya.

The reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya, however, hold that it is coarse in the first jhāna and subtle in the access to the second jhāna—thus desiring it to be subtler in the access to each higher jhāna than in the preceding lower jhāna. In brief, according to the view of all reciters, the bodily formation occurring before the time of grasping is calmed at the time of grasping; the bodily formation occurring at the (early) time of grasping is calmed in the access to the first jhāna; the bodily formation occurring in the access to the first jhāna is calmed in the first jhāna... and so on... the bodily formation occurring in the access to the fourth jhāna is calmed in the fourth jhāna. This is the method of knowing the calming in the context of tranquility (samatha).

In the context of insight (vipassanā), the bodily formation occurring before grasping is coarse; it is subtle when grasping the great elements (mahābhūta). That too is still coarse; it is subtle when grasping derived matter (upādārūpa). That too is still coarse; it is subtle when grasping all matter. That too is still coarse; it is subtle when grasping mentality (arūpa). That too is still coarse; it is subtle when grasping both mentality and materiality.

It is subtle when grasping the causes (paccaya). That too is still coarse; it is subtle when grasping mentality and materiality along with their causes. That too is still coarse; it is subtle in insight that perceives the characteristics (lakkhaṇa) of impermanence, suffering, and non-self. That too is still coarse in weak insight; it is subtle in strong (balava) insight. In such successive stages of subtlety, by the same method mentioned previously in the context of tranquility, [268] the calming of the preceding coarse bodily formation should be understood through the succeeding subtle bodily formation. In this phrase (calming the coarse bodily formation), coarseness, subtlety, and calming should be understood exactly as just described.

In the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, the meaning of this term¹ is stated along with the objection (codanā) and clarification (sodhana) as follows:

"How does one train, thinking, 'I shall breathe in... and so on... breathe out calming the bodily formation'? What are the bodily formations? Long in-breaths and out-breaths² occur in the body; these things
268:
Notes:
1. Connect with: "the meaning of this term... is stated."
2. In the Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali text, "long in-breaths" etc. is taught as one section, and "long out-breaths" etc. as another section separately; here, they are shown together in a summarized manner. The same applies hereafter.

...are bound up with the body and are called bodily formations. One trains calming, ceasing, and especially tranquilizing those bodily formations. [Short in-breaths and out-breaths... and so on... in-breaths and out-breaths (taught as) knowing the whole body of breath occur in the body; these things are bound up with the body and are called bodily formations. One trains calming, ceasing, and especially tranquilizing those bodily formations.¹] By whichever bodily formations of in-breath and out-breath there occurs the body's bending forward (ānamanā), bending sideways (vinamanā), bending all around (sannamanā), bending backward (paṇamanā), trembling (iñjanā), throbbing (phandanā), moving (calanā), or shaking (kampanā)², one trains, thinking, 'I shall breathe in calming such bodily formations'; one trains, thinking, 'I shall breathe out calming such bodily formations.' By whichever bodily formations there occurs no bending forward, no bending sideways, no bending all around, no bending backward, no trembling, no throbbing, no moving, and no shaking of the body, one trains, thinking, 'I shall breathe in calming such tranquil and subtle bodily formations'... and so on... 'I shall breathe out.'

If one were to train, thinking, 'I shall breathe in... breathe out calming the extremely subtle bodily formation' as just described, then there would be no development of the mind that gains the breath, no development of the in-breaths and out-breaths, no development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), and no development of concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing; nor would the wise enter into or emerge from that attainment (samāpatti). (This is the objection).

Notes:
1. The words within these brackets are taken from the Paṭisambhidāmagga to expand the ellipsis (peyyāla).
2. The Commentary (Ṭīkā) explains that the four terms starting with 'iñjanā' have the same meaning as the four terms starting with 'ānamanā', or that they denote slight trembling, etc. Among them, because the Pali term 'calanā' also denotes displacement, it is translated as 'moving' to avoid redundancy with other terms. Furthermore, in the original Paṭisambhidāmagga Pali, 'pakampanā' is found in place of 'kampanā'; its commentary explains it as 'bhusā kampanā'—violent shaking. Therefore, that term is translated as 'shaking'.

If one were to train, thinking, 'I shall breathe in... breathe out calming the extremely subtle bodily formation' as just described, then there indeed occurs the development of the mind that gains the breath. There occurs the development of the in-breaths and out-breaths. There occurs the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), and there occurs the development of concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing; and the wise can indeed enter into and emerge from that aforementioned attainment of ānāpāna. How is this so?

Just as when a bronze gong (kaṃsa) is struck, at first coarse sounds proceed. Because the sign (nimitta) of the coarse sounds is well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-considered, even when the coarse sounds have ceased, thereafter...
269:
They also emerge from that attainment. How?

Just as when a bronze dish is struck, gross sounds occur; because the sign of the gross sounds has been well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-sustained, even when the gross sounds have ceased, the subtle sounds subsequently continue to occur (perceived by the ear). Because the sign of the subtle sounds has been well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-sustained, even when the subtle sounds have ceased, the mind having the sign of the even more subtle sounds as its object continues to occur. In the same way, at first, gross in-breaths and out-breaths occur. Because the sign of the gross in-breaths and out-breaths has been well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-sustained, even when the gross in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths subsequently continue to occur (becoming clear to the meditating mind). Because the sign of the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths has been well-grasped, well-attended to, and well-sustained, even when the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased, the mind having the sign of the even more subtle in-breaths and out-breaths as its object does not go to distraction.

In that case (or: because of that), there is the development of the mind that has gained the in-breaths and out-breaths. There is the development of the in-breaths and out-breaths themselves. There is the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati). There is the development of concentration associated with mindfulness of breathing. Wise ones both enter into and emerge from such an attainment of mindfulness of breathing. 'Calming the bodily formation'—the in-breaths and out-breaths are the 'body' (kāya); the establishment is 'mindfulness' (sati); the contemplation is 'knowledge' (ñāṇa). The body is called 'establishment' (upaṭṭhāna) because it is what appears, but it is not called 'mindfulness'. Mindfulness is called both 'establishment' and 'mindfulness' because it is what establishes and remembers. With that mindfulness and that knowledge, one repeatedly contemplates that body (the collection of breaths). Therefore, it is called 'the development of the foundation of mindfulness of contemplating the body in the body'."

(This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga)

This is the sequential word-by-word commentary on the first tetrad, which was spoken in terms of the contemplation of the body in this meditation on mindfulness of breathing.

## Method of Practicing Ānāpānassati Meditation

222. Apart from the word-by-word commentary, the method of practice will now be shown: In that teaching (consisting of the sixteen bases mentioned), only this first tetrad is spoken of as the meditation subject for a beginner. The other three tetrads are spoken of in terms of the contemplation of feelings, the mind, and mental objects for one who has already attained jhāna in this first tetrad. Therefore, a clansman who is a beginner, wishing to reach Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges by developing this meditation subject and practicing insight based on the fourth ānāpāna jhāna,¹ should first perform all the preliminary duties such as the purification of virtue as previously mentioned, and then learn the fivefold meditation subject from a teacher of the kind described.

Note:
1. If translated strictly according to the Pali, it would be "by insight which has the fourth ānāpāna jhāna as its proximate cause." This is difficult for those with little scriptural knowledge to understand. Therefore, it is translated using the above phrasing.
270:
A clansman of good birth who, desiring to attain the fruit of Arahantship, has purified his virtue and performed all preliminary duties in the manner previously described, should learn the meditation subject in five parts from a teacher endowed with the aforementioned qualities.

[270] In this context, the five parts are: (1) learning (uggaha), (2) inquiry (paripucchā), (3) appearance (upaṭṭhāna), (4) absorption (appanā), and (5) noting (lakkhaṇa). Herein, 'learning' means learning the method of practicing the meditation subject by heart. 'Inquiry' means inquiring about the meaning of the meditation subject. 'Appearance' means the appearance of the meditation object's sign. 'Absorption' means reaching the end of the meditation development—the attainment of jhāna. 'Noting' means noting the meditation subject, which means observing the nature of the meditation subject as 'This meditation subject has such a characteristic nature.'

By learning the meditation subject in these five parts, one does not fatigue oneself, nor does one trouble the teacher. Therefore, after having the teacher recite a little and then reciting it back for a long time, and thus learning the meditation subject in five parts by heart, one should reside in a dwelling with the previously described features, whether in the presence of the teacher or elsewhere. Having cut off minor impediments and finished the meal, one should dispel the drowsiness following the meal. Sitting comfortably, one should gladden the mind by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem. Then, without confusing even a single word of the meditation procedure learned from the teacher, one should apply the mind to this mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati).

223. In such application of the mind, the following is the method of practice:
Counting (gaṇanā), following (anubandhanā), touching (phusanā), fixing (ṭhapanā), observing (sallakkhaṇā), turning away (vivaṭṭanā), purification (pārisuddhi), and reviewing them (paṭipassanā). This is the summary verse.

In this verse, 'counting' is just counting. 'Following' (anubandhanā) is the act of following and maintaining mindfulness. 'Touching' (phusanā) is the place of contact. 'Fixing' (ṭhapanā) is absorption (appanā), which is the fixing of the mind in jhāna. 'Observing' (sallakkhaṇā) is insight (vipassanā). 'Turning away' (vivaṭṭanā) is the Path (magga) (which turns away from the object of formations). 'Purification' (pārisuddhi) is the Fruit (phala). 'Reviewing them' (paṭipassanā) is the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇā) of the Path and Fruit.

Among these, the beginner clansman should first apply the mind to this meditation subject by way of counting. When counting, one should not stop below five, nor go beyond ten, nor show a gap in between. The fault is that if one stops below five, the arising of the mind fluctuates in a narrow range, like a herd of cattle shut in a narrow pen. If one goes beyond ten, the arising of the mind relies only on the counting. If one shows a gap in between, the mind wavers, thinking, 'Has my meditation reached the peak or not?' Therefore, one should count while avoiding these faults.

When counting, one should first count slowly, in the manner of a grain measurer. A grain measurer fills the measure, says 'one,' and pours it out. While filling it again, if he sees some rubbish and removes it, he continues to say 'one, one.' The same applies to 'two, two,' and so on. Similarly, this yogī, among the in-breaths and out-breaths, whichever breath is prominent, [271] that breath...

Notes:
1. This refers to the one who counts. The translation is adjusted for better flow in the target language.
2. 'Gap' (khaṇḍa) refers to a break in counting, such as counting 'one, three, five.' (Commentary)
3. It relies only on the counting, not on the meditation object. (Commentary)
4. The phrase 'reached the peak' is said in reference to one who has been applying the mind through counting for a very long time. (Commentary)
5. Based on the concentration gained from long-term counting, one should recollect and perceive as described. The Visuddhimagga states that gaps in counting cause the mind to waver; the commentary explains this as skipping numbers (e.g., 1, 3, 5). It is noted that it is difficult to understand how such skipping leads to doubt about reaching the end.
271:
In this regard, it is stated in the Pyay recension: if one stops for a short duration without counting in between, it is considered a break in the sequence. For such a yogi, it is said that by investigating whether the mind is inclined toward the meditation subject or not, it is even directed towards whether it has reached the peak, and so forth. In this sense, 'reaching the peak' (sikhāpatta) should be understood as the mind being intensely inclined toward the meditation object.

1. Before the second basket is poured, one simply says 'one basket, one basket.' After pouring the second basket, taking the third basket, one should count the incoming and outgoing breaths as they occur, starting from 'one, one' up to 'ten, ten.' While counting in this way, the incoming and outgoing breaths become clear to the yogi.

Then, discarding that slow counting, like that of a grain measurer, one should count with the fast counting, like that of a cowherd. To explain: A skilled cowherd, having taken pebbles in his pocket and holding a rope and a bamboo staff in his hand, goes to the pen early in the morning. Striking the cows on their backs and sitting on the top of the gatepost, he counts each cow as it reaches the gate by throwing a pebble, saying 'one, two,' and so on. The herd of cows, having stayed uncomfortably in a cramped space all night, comes out rapidly, huddling and rubbing against each other as they exit. That cowherd counts very quickly, 'three, four, five, ten,' and so on. Similarly, for this yogi, while counting by the previously mentioned slow method, the incoming and outgoing breaths become clear and move in and out rapidly and repeatedly. 

Then, knowing 'they move in and out repeatedly,' without taking them inside or outside, one should take only the incoming and outgoing breaths as they reach the nostrils and count quickly: 'one, two, three, four, five; one, two, three, four, five, six; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine; one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.' Indeed, in the meditation subject connected with counting, the mind becomes one-pointed and steady through the power of counting itself, just as a boat is held steady in a swift current by the power of a propping pole.

To the yogi counting quickly in this way, the meditation object appears as if it were occurring continuously without interruption. Then, knowing 'it is occurring continuously,' without attending to or grasping the air inside or outside, one should count quickly as before. Indeed, if one sends the mind inside along with the incoming air, the internal part of the body feels as if it were struck by wind or filled with fat. If one sends the mind outside along with the outgoing air, the mind becomes distracted by various external objects. However, for one who develops mindfulness by placing it only at the point of contact, the meditation reaches fulfillment. Therefore, I said: 'Without attending to or grasping the air inside or outside, one should count quickly as before.'

How long should this be counted? Until mindfulness stands firm on the object of the incoming and outgoing breaths without the need for counting. For counting is intended only for the purpose of cutting off external wandering thoughts and establishing mindfulness on the object of the incoming and outgoing breaths.
272:
In this way, it should be understood that one can count as desired within the rounds of five to ten. However, since the attainment of concentration is the essential goal, one should adopt the best method when personally practicing. In the Pali of the Buddha's words, counting is not shown; it only states: 'Mindfully he breathes in, mindfully he breathes out' (*sato va assasati sato passasati*)—showing that one should be mindful with every inhalation and exhalation. Therefore, it is also appropriate to meditate by fixing mindfulness at the point of contact of the incoming and outgoing air, noting it as 'breathing in, breathing out' or 'entering, exiting,' and so forth.

How long should one count these in-breaths and out-breaths? (One should count) until mindfulness is well-established on the object of the in-breath and out-breath without the need for counting. Indeed, counting serves only the purpose of cutting off distracted thoughts that wander externally and firmly establishing mindfulness on the object of the in-breath and out-breath.

## 224. After attending by way of counting (*gaṇanā*) as described, one should then attend by way of following (*anubandhanā*). 'Following' means giving up counting and following the in-breaths and out-breaths continuously without interruption by means of mindfulness. This, however, is not by way of following the beginning, middle, and end. To explain: for the air going out, the beginning is the navel, the middle is the heart, and the end is the nose-tip. For the air coming in, the beginning is the nose-tip, the middle is the heart, and the end is the navel. If a meditator follows that beginning, middle, and end, their mind becomes distracted, leading to distress and exhaustion, and the meditation subject becomes agitated. As it is said in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*:

'For one following with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breath (*assāsa*), the body and mind are distressed, trembling, and agitated due to the mind being distracted internally. For one following with mindfulness the beginning, middle, and end of the out-breath (*passāsa*), the body and mind are distressed, trembling, and agitated due to the mind being distracted externally.' (Ps. I, 157) [Note 1]

Therefore, a meditator attending by way of following should not do so by way of the beginning, middle, and end. Rather, one should attend by way of contact (*phusanā*) and by way of fixing (*ṭhapanā*). Indeed, there is no separate attendance by way of contact and fixing as there is with counting and following. However, by counting only at the point of contact, one is said to be attending by way of both counting and contact. Having given up counting at that same point, if one follows those breaths with mindfulness and fixes the mind by way of absorption (*appanā*), [Note 2] one is said to be attending by way of following, contact, and fixing. [Note 3] This meaning should be understood through the similes of the lame man and the gatekeeper mentioned in the Commentaries, and the simile of the saw mentioned in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*.

Note 1: In this *Paṭisambhidāmagga* Pali, it is stated that following the beginning, middle, and end of *assāsa* leads to internal distraction, and following the beginning, middle, and end of *passāsa* leads to external distraction. Thus, it is clear that *assāsa* refers to the in-breath and *passāsa* to the out-breath. Therefore, to be consistent with this Pali throughout, *assāsa* has been translated as 'in-breath' and *passāsa* as 'out-breath' from the beginning.

Note 2: 'Fixing the mind by way of absorption (*appanā*)' means: in whatever way absorption occurs. It means well-fixing the mind on the established sign (*nimitta*) in a manner that can produce absorption. (Ṭīkā)

Note 3: It is said that one attends by way of following and contact, or by way of following and fixing; these are two pairs. (Ṭīkā) If one follows by applying mindfulness at the point of contact, it is called attending by following and contact. If one follows by fixing the mind on the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*), it is called attending by following and fixing.

## 225. Herein, this is the simile of the lame man: Just as a lame man, swinging a swing for a mother and child playing on it, sits right there at the foot of the swing-post and sees both ends and the middle of the swing-plank as it comes and goes in succession, yet he is not preoccupied with the task of seeing the two ends and the middle; even so, this monk meditator, standing by the power of mindfulness at the foot of the post of binding (i.e., at the nose-tip or upper lip where the breath touches) [Note 4], swinging the swing of in-breaths and out-breaths, and sitting with mindfulness right there at the sign (*nimitta*) of the nose-tip and upper lip, sees the beginning, middle, and end of the in-breaths and out-breaths at the point of contact as they come and go in succession, following them with mindfulness and fixing the mind there, yet he is not preoccupied with the task of seeing them. This is the simile of the lame man.

Note 4: 'Standing at the foot of the post of binding' means standing at the nose-tip or upper lip where the in-breath and out-breath touch.
273: ## 226. Now, this is the simile of the gatekeeper: A gatekeeper does not examine people inside or outside the city, asking 'Who are you? Where do you come from? Where are you going? What is that in your hand?' and so forth.
274:
The exertion of effort is also manifested. The task of application is accomplished. The distinction is also attained.

What is the exertion of effort (padhāna)? The body and mind of the yogi who has aroused effort become wieldy and fit for developing meditation; this effort, which is the cause of this wieldiness, is 'exertion'.

What is the task of application (payoga)? In the continuity of the yogi who has aroused effort, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which defile the mind are abandoned (or, the hindrances depart), and wrong thoughts (micchā-vitakka) are stilled. This practice of noting and exerting, which is the cause for the cessation of these hindrances and wrong thoughts, is 'application'.

What is the distinction (visesa)? In the continuity of the yogi who has aroused effort, the fetters (saṃyojana) are abandoned (or, the fetters are exhausted), and the underlying tendencies (anusaya) that have the potential to arise are eradicated without a trace (reaching a state where they cannot arise through the Noble Path). This absence of fetters and defilements is the 'distinction'.
