As stated, although these three things are not the object of a single consciousness, they are not unknown but known. The mind does not fall into distraction. The exertion of effort is manifested. The task of application can be accomplished, and the distinction is attained.

"Whose mindfulness of breathing is full and well-developed in all aspects, practiced in due order as taught by the Buddha, that monk illuminates this world (such as his own body) like the moon freed from a cloud." This is from the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

This is the simile of the saw. In this simile, it should be understood that the mere non-attention to the coming and going of the breaths (paying attention only to the point of contact) is the purpose for that yogi monk.

228. For some individuals who pay attention to this mindfulness of breathing meditation subject, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) arises before long. The concentration called absorption (appanā), which is the placing of the mind adorned with the remaining jhāna factors, is also accomplished and fulfilled. For other individuals, however, from the time of paying attention by way of counting, as the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths gradually cease, the distress and fatigue of the body are stilled, and both body and mind become light. The body feels as if it has reached a state of leaping into the sky.

To give an illustration: when a person who has distress and fatigue of the body sits on a couch or a chair, the couch or chair sags, it makes a creaking sound, and the bedspread becomes wrinkled. But when a person who is free from distress and fatigue of the body sits, the couch or chair does not sag, it does not creak, and the bedspread does not wrinkle. The couch or chair feels as if it were filled with cotton. Why? Because a body without distress is light. Similarly, from the time of paying attention by way of counting, as the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths gradually cease, the distress and fatigue of the body are stilled, and both body and mind become light. The body feels as if it has reached a state of leaping into the sky.

[275] When the coarse in-breaths and out-breaths have ceased for that yogi, the consciousness arises having the sign of the subtle in-breaths and out-breaths as its object.
275:
When that subtle in-breath and out-breath also ceases, the mind continues to occur with the sign of the in-breath and out-breath as its object, which is progressively subtler and subtler. How is this? Just as a man might strike a bronze bowl or a bronze gong with a large iron rod; at the moment of striking, a loud sound arises.

Note 1: This means the mind occurs by taking the subtle sign of the in-breath and out-breath as its object.

For that man, the mind occurs with the coarse sound as its object. When the coarse sound ceases, then the mind occurs with the subtle sound-sign as its object. When that subtle sound ceases, the mind continues to occur with the sound-sign that is progressively subtler and subtler. It should be understood that it is just the same in this case. Indeed, there is this statement: "Just as when a bronze bowl is struck..." This should be understood in detail as shown on page 391.

229. Unlike other meditation subjects which become clearer and clearer in later stages, this meditation subject is not like that. Rather, as one develops it, it becomes subtler and may even not appear to be manifest. When it does not appear in this way, the meditating bhikkhu should not rise from his seat, shake out his leather mat, and leave. What should be done? He should not rise thinking, "I will ask the teacher," or "Now my meditation subject is lost." For to one who goes away after disturbing his posture, the meditation subject becomes entirely new again. Therefore, he should bring it back from the place where it was normally touching, while remaining seated as he was.

This is the method for bringing it back: After realizing the non-appearance of the meditation subject, that bhikkhu should reflect thus: "Where do these in-breaths and out-breaths exist? Where do they not exist? In whom do they exist? In whom do they not exist?" Then, upon reflecting thus, he knows: "These breaths do not exist in one inside the mother's womb, nor in those submerged in water, nor in those who are unconscious, nor in the dead, nor in those attained to the fourth jhāna, nor in those who have reached the fine-material or immaterial planes of existence, nor in those attained to the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti)."

Having known this, he should admonish himself: "O wise one, are you not one who is in the mother's womb? Are you not submerged in water, not unconscious, not dead, not attained to the fourth jhāna, not in the fine-material or immaterial planes, and not attained to the attainment of cessation? Indeed, the breaths exist in you, but because of your dull wisdom, you are unable to grasp and observe them." Then, he should direct his attention by placing his mind on the place where the breath normally touches. For those with a long nose, these breaths occur striking the nostril. For those with a short nose, they strike the upper lip. Therefore, this bhikkhu should fix the sign (nimitta) by noting, "They strike this particular place."

Note 1: To clarify the word 'ñatvā' (having known), it is translated as 'He knows; having known thus,' splitting the sentence.

He should fix the sign (nimitta) [Note 1] (or: he should place his mind on the sign of the 'post' which is the tip of the nose or the upper lip) [Note 2]. Indeed, it is because of this specific reason that the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, I do not say that the development of mindfulness of breathing is for one who is forgetful and lacks clear comprehension."

[276] 230. To explain further: Any meditation subject whatsoever is perfected only for one who is mindful and possesses clear comprehension. However—

Note 1: 'Fixing the sign' means establishing a firmer perception so that mindfulness may arise easily there. Indeed, mindfulness has firm perception as its proximate cause (Ṭīkā). It is difficult to reconcile the commentary with the sub-commentary. In the Pyay version of the Nissaya, 'nimitta' refers to the firmer perception that takes and notes the sign of the appearance previously grasped.
276:
‘Thapetabbaṃ’—should be placed, or should be established—is how it is translated. It is difficult to take the word ‘nimitta’ as meaning a firmer perception.

2. Here, an alternative interpretation is that in the context of ‘nimittaṃ thapetabbaṃ,’ it refers to ‘nimitte thapetabbaṃ’ or ‘cittaṃ thapetabbaṃ,’ and the translation follows that reading. In the Ṭīkā mentioned in Note 1, the word ‘tattha’ (therein) should be understood as explaining the word ‘nimitte.’ The explanation ‘thiratara-sañjānanaṃ’ (a firmer marking/perception) should be seen as an explanation added as a supplementary reading.

Other meditation subjects are clear to those who attend to them. But this Ānāpānassati meditation subject is profound (heavy) and a profound development (difficult to develop). It is the domain of attention only for Great Men—Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the Buddhas' sons (disciples). It is not trivial, nor is it practiced by trivial beings. The more it is attended to, the more peaceful and subtle it becomes. Therefore, strong mindfulness and wisdom are required in this Ānāpānassati meditation.

To give an analogy: when sewing a fine, smooth cloth, a fine needle is required. The tool for piercing the eye of the needle is required to be even finer than the needle itself. Similarly, when developing this meditation subject which is like a fine, smooth cloth, mindfulness, which is like the needle, is required to be strong. Wisdom associated with that mindfulness, which is like the tool for piercing the eye of the needle, is also required to be strong.

Furthermore, a monk endowed with such mindfulness and wisdom should not seek those breaths anywhere other than the place they normally touch (i.e., the tip of the nose and the upper lip). To give an analogy: a farmer, after plowing, releases his oxen, drives them toward the pasture, and rests in the shade. While he is resting, those oxen quickly enter the forest. If he is a skilled farmer, when he wishes to catch them and yoke them again, he does not wander through the forest following the tracks of those oxen. Instead, taking a rope and a goad, he goes straight to the watering hole where those oxen usually descend and either sits or lies down. While he is there, those oxen, having grazed for the day, descend to the watering hole, bathe, drink, and upon coming back up, he sees them, binds them with the rope, prods them with the goad, brings them back, yokes them, and performs his plowing again.

In the same way, that yogi monk should not seek those breaths anywhere other than the place they normally touch. Instead, taking the rope of mindfulness and the goad of wisdom, and placing the mind at the tip of the nose or the lip where the breath normally touches, he should carry out the attention. For one who attends in this way, before long, those breaths appear to him like the oxen at the watering hole. Then, binding them with the rope of mindfulness, yoking them at that very spot, and prodding with the goad of wisdom, he should repeatedly apply himself to the meditation subject.

231. For that yogi practicing in this way, before long, the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) appear. This appearing sign is not identical for everyone. Indeed, some teachers say that for some, it appears producing a pleasant touch like cotton, like silk-cotton, or like a draft of air.
277:
This ānāpāna-nimitta appears to some as like the light of a star, or like a ruby bead, or like a pearl bead. To some, it appears with a rough touch like a cotton stalk or a wooden needle. To some, it appears like a long sash-string, a flower garland, or a wisp of smoke. To some, it appears like a wide spider's web, a film of cloud, a lotus flower, a chariot wheel, the moon's disk, or the sun's disk.

Note 1: The sign (nimitta) here refers to the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) or the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta). Both signs are mentioned together in this context. The group of three similes starting with cotton is suitable for the uggaha-nimitta; the rest are suitable for both signs (according to the Ṭīkā). However, looking at the preceding and following context, it seems that only the paṭibhāga-nimitta is appropriate.

It appears in diverse ways because of the diversity of perception (saññā). To give an analogy: among many monks sitting and reciting a sutta, when one monk asks, "How does this sutta appear to you?", one says, "To me, it appears like a great mountain river." Another says, "To me, it appears like a forest." Another says, "To me, it appears like a shady tree, full of branches and laden with fruit." Just as that single sutta appears differently to those monks due to the diversity of their perception, so too this single meditation subject appears differently due to the diversity of perception. Indeed, this meditation sign is born of perception, has perception as its cause, and perception as its origin. Therefore, it should be understood that it appears differently due to the diversity of perception.

Among these three (the in-breath, out-breath, and the sign), the mind that has the in-breath as its object is one, the mind that has the out-breath as its object is another, and the mind that has the sign as its object is yet another. For someone in whom these three things do not exist (as meditation objects), their meditation can reach neither absorption (appanā) nor access (upacāra). But for someone in whom these three things exist, their meditation can reach both access and absorption. For it has been said:

"The sign, the in-breath, and the out-breath
Are not the object of a single mind.
For one who does not know these three things,
Development is not found.

The sign, the in-breath, and the out-breath
Are not the object of a single mind.
Only for one who knows these three things,
Is development found."

232. To continue: when the sign has appeared in this way, that monk should go to his teacher and report, "Venerable sir, an object of such a nature has appeared to me."

Note 1: This verse was also shown in paragraph 227. In that context, the sign was explained in the Ṭīkā as the 'binding sign' (upanibandhana-nimitta); because it binds the mind to the object, mindfulness is called upanibandhana; and because it is the place for noting the in-breaths and out-breaths, the tip of the nose and the upper lip are called the upanibandhana-nimitta. To make it easy to remember, we translated it as 'the place where the mind is bound by mindfulness.' However, in this context, since the preceding and following paragraphs describe the appearance of the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta), it seems to refer to that paṭibhāga-nimitta.

The teacher should not say, "That object is the sign," or "It is not the sign." He should say, "It happens like this, friend," and then tell him, "Pay attention to it again and again." The fault is this: if he says, "It is the sign," the monk might reach a state of complacency and stop his effort. If he says, "It is not the sign," the monk might lose hope and fall into weariness and regression. Therefore, without saying either, he should simply be urged to pay attention. This is the view of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas (Reciters of the Long Discourses).

The Majjhima-bhāṇakas (Reciters of the Middle Discourses), however, say: "Friend, this object is indeed the sign. Good man, pay attention to the meditation subject again and again." Then, his mind [should be fixed] on the sign itself...
278:
At that time, this yogi monk should place the mind only on the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta). From the appearance of this sign onwards, this meditation of the monk occurs by way of fixing (ṭhapanā). Indeed, the ancient teachers said:

“The wise yogi, making the various aspects (long and short) of the in-breath and out-breath clear in the beginning (or making them disappear in the end), binds his own mind, fixing it on the sign.”

Note: The second meaning is the primary interpretation of the sub-commentator. From the appearance of the counterpart sign, because one attends only to that sign, the aspects of long and short breaths disappear. This disappearance is explained as 'vibhāvento' or 'antaradhāpento'. The first meaning is according to other teachers mentioned in the sub-commentary.

For that yogi, from the appearance of the counterpart sign, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are suppressed, defilements are subsided, mindfulness is established, and the mind is well-concentrated with access concentration (upacāra-samādhi). Then, this yogi should not attend to the counterpart sign by way of color, nor contemplate it by way of natural characteristics like hardness or motion, or general characteristics like impermanence. Rather, it should be carefully guarded like a queen guarding the embryo of a Wheel-turning Monarch, or a farmer guarding the grain of rice, avoiding the seven unsuitable things (lodging, etc.) and cultivating the seven suitable things. Guarding it thus, making it grow and flourish through repeated attention, he should fulfill the ten kinds of skill in absorption (appanā-kosalla) and balance energy (vīriya) with concentration. For the yogi striving thus, the four or five jhānas arise in that counterpart sign, following the sequence mentioned in the earth kasiṇa.

## How to Practice Vipassanā

233. To show the way to practice Vipassanā: Having attained the four or five jhānas in this mindfulness of breathing (Note: This is the meaning of 'ettha'. The sub-commentary explains it as 'in this mindfulness of the body'. Since the word 'mindfulness of the body' does not appear immediately before, it should be considered.), if the monk wishes to reach the fruit called purification (pārisuddhi) by developing the meditation through defining (sallakkhaṇā) and turning away (vivaṭṭanā), he should master that same jhāna in five ways, then define mind and matter (nāmarūpa) and initiate Vipassanā. How? Emerging from the attainment (samāpatti), he sees that the physical body and the mind are the causes of the in-breaths and out-breaths. Just as when a blacksmith's bellows are blown, the air moves depending on the bellows and the man's appropriate effort, so too, depending on the body and the mind, the in-breaths and out-breaths move. Then he defines the in-breaths and out-breaths and the body as 'matter' (rūpa), and the mind and its associated mental factors as 'mind' (nāma). This is the summary here. The detailed definition of mind and matter will be clear later in the Diṭṭhivisuddhi-niddesa. Having defined mind and matter, he searches for their causes. Seeing the causes, he transcends doubt regarding the occurrence of mind and matter in the three periods of time.
279:
Having transcended doubt, he applies the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa) by way of group-contemplation (kalāpa-sammasana). He abandons the ten imperfections of insight (vipassanupakkilesa) like light, etc., which arise in the early stage of the knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Defining the path-knowledge (paṭipadā-ñāṇa) free from imperfections as the 'path' (magga), he abandons 'arising' and reaches the knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga-ñāṇa). Through continuous contemplation of dissolution, becoming disenchanted, dispassionate, and liberated from all formations (saṅkhāra) appearing as passing away, he reaches the four noble paths (ariya-magga) in sequence. Established in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala), reaching the end of the nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa), he becomes the supreme recipient of offerings (aggadakkhiṇeyya) for the world including the devas.

With this sequence of words, the development of mindfulness of breathing concentration (ānāpānassati-samādhi-bhāvanā), starting from counting (gaṇanā) and ending in insight (vipassanā), is complete. This is the explanation of the first tetrad in all its aspects.

## Explanation of the Second Tetrad, etc.

234. In the other three tetrads, there is no separate method for developing the meditation. Therefore, their meaning should be understood according to the word-by-word explanation as follows.

'Experiencing rapture' (pītipaṭisaṃvedī): He trains, thinking 'I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out,' making rapture known and clear. In this phrase, rapture is experienced in two ways: by way of object (ārammaṇa) and by way of non-delusion (asammoha).

How is rapture experienced by way of object? He attains the two jhānas (first and second) that possess rapture. At the moment of attainment, because of the attainment of jhāna, he experiences rapture by way of the object (the counterpart sign). Why? Because the object is experienced (with the jhāna that has rapture). (Note: Just as when one joyfully perceives an object, that joy is also clearly known.) How by way of non-delusion? Having attained the two jhānas with rapture and emerged, he contemplates the rapture associated with the jhāna as 'exhausting' and 'perishing'. At the moment of insight, he experiences rapture by way of non-delusion through the penetration of characteristics. Indeed, it is said:

“For one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind by way of the long in-breath, mindfulness is established. Through that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced. ... (repeats for short breath, whole body, calming bodily formation) ... for one who knows the one-pointedness and non-distraction of the mind, mindfulness is established. Through that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is experienced. For one who attends, that rapture is experienced; for one who knows, sees, reviews, concentrates the mind, resolves with faith, exerts energy, establishes mindfulness, composes the mind, knows with wisdom, knows the things to be known with direct knowledge (abhiññeyya), knows the things to be fully understood with full understanding (pariññeyya), abandons the things to be abandoned (pahātabba), develops the things to be developed (bhāvetabba), and realizes the things to be realized (sacchikātabba), that rapture is experienced.”
280:
"Thus, one experiences that rapture."

In this same manner, the meaning of the remaining terms [such as sukha-paṭisaṃvedī and cittasaṅkhāra-paṭisaṃvedī] should also be understood. This is the distinction here: experiencing bliss (sukha) should be understood by way of the first, second, and third jhānas, and experiencing the mental formation (cittasaṅkhāra) by way of all four jhānas. "Mental formation" refers to the two aggregates: feeling (vedanā) and perception (saññā). Regarding the term sukha-paṭisaṃvedī (experiencing bliss), it is stated in the Paṭisambhidāmagga: "Bliss is twofold: bodily bliss and mental bliss," in order to show the plane of insight (vipassanā-bhūmi).

Note 1: "To show the plane of insight" means to show the plane of insight by way of reviewing miscellaneous formations (pakiṇṇaka-saṅkhāra). (This is because there is no bodily bliss (kāyika-sukha) within the serenity of jhāna (samatha-jhāna). (Sub-commentary) There are two ways of practicing insight: one is emerging from jhāna and reviewing the jhāna factors, and the other is emerging from jhāna and reviewing whatever objects arise, such as seeing, hearing, etc. Among these, reviewing whatever arises, such as seeing and hearing, is called "reviewing miscellaneous formations." Reviewing bodily bliss, which arises due to a very distinct bodily contact after emerging from jhāna, is included within the review of miscellaneous formations. Therefore, in the Paṭisambhidāmagga, bodily bliss—which should and can be reviewed after emerging from ānāpāna-jhāna—is analyzed and taught as an object that is the plane of insight. If only pure serenity (samatha) were intended, there would be no reason to include bodily bliss, as it does not exist within the jhāna itself. In this sub-commentary statement, the method of reviewing miscellaneous formations should be particularly noted. For those who follow the vehicle of pure insight (suddha-vipassanā-yānika), since they do not possess jhāna, they must review whatever arises, such as seeing and hearing, which are called miscellaneous formations. This point should also be particularly noted.)

Passambhayaṃ cittasaṅkhāraṃ (tranquillizing the mental formation) means tranquillizing, or "ceasing," the grosser and grosser mental formations. The detailed explanation of this tranquillizing should be understood in the same way as described under the section on bodily formations (kāyasaṅkhāra).

Alternatively, among these four terms, in the phrase "experiencing rapture," feeling (vedanā) is taught with rapture (pīti) as the heading. In the phrase "experiencing bliss," feeling is taught in its own form. In the two phrases "experiencing the mental formation" and "tranquillizing the mental formation," feeling associated with perception is taught, because it is said: "Perception and feeling—these states are mental, bound to the mind; they are mental formations." Thus, it should be understood that this second tetrad is spoken by way of the contemplation of feeling (vedanānupassanā).

235. In the third tetrad also, experiencing the mind (cittapaṭisaṃvedī) should be understood by way of the four jhānas. Abhippamodayaṃ cittaṃ (gladdening the mind) means: gladdening the mind, greatly gladdening it, cheering it, greatly cheering it, he trains thus: "I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out." In that context, gladdening occurs in two ways: by way of concentration (samādhi) and by way of insight (vipassanā).

How is it by way of concentration? One enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture. At the moment of attainment, he gladdens and greatly gladdens the mind with the associated rapture. How is it by way of insight? Having entered the two jhānas accompanied by rapture and emerged from them, he reviews the rapture associated with the jhāna as being subject to exhaustion and vanishing. Thus, at the moment of insight, taking the rapture associated with the jhāna as the object, he gladdens and greatly gladdens the mind. [281] A person who practices in this way is said to "train thus: 'Gladdening the mind, I shall breathe in, I shall breathe out.'"
281:
Concentrating the mind (samādahaṃ cittaṃ) means placing the mind evenly and well on the object by means of the first jhana and so on. Alternatively, for one who, after emerging from those jhanas, contemplates the mind associated with the jhana as passing away and vanishing, momentary concentration (khanika-samādhi) called momentary one-pointedness of mind (khanika-cittekaggatā) arises through the penetration of characteristics [such as impermanence] during the moment of insight. One who places the mind evenly on the object by means of such momentary concentration is also said to "train thus: 'I shall breathe in... breathe out concentrating the mind.'"

Liberating the mind (vimocayaṃ cittaṃ) means liberating the mind, or making it especially free, from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) by the first jhana; from initial and sustained thought (vitakka-vicāra) by the second; from rapture (pīti) by the third; and from pleasure and pain (sukha-dukkha) by the fourth. Alternatively, after emerging from those jhanas,

Note: Momentary one-pointedness of mind (khanika-cittekaggatā) is concentration that lasts only for the moment of insight. It is appropriate to mention this concentration because when this momentary concentration occurs continuously without interruption in a uniform mode of steadiness, and is not overwhelmed by opposing states, it can keep the mind from wavering just like attainment concentration (appanā-jhāna). Therefore, the Visuddhimagga states: "One who places the mind evenly on the object by means of such momentary concentration... [and so on] ... is said to train thus." (Sub-commentary). Anyone who has fully practiced and personally experienced this momentary concentration can well understand how the mind can be well-concentrated through it, in accordance with these Commentaries and Sub-commentaries.

one contemplates the mind associated with the jhana as passing away and vanishing. At the moment of insight, such a person breathes in and breathes out while liberating the mind from the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā); from the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā); from the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self (anattānupassanā); from delight through the contemplation of disenchantment (nibbidānupassanā); from lust through the contemplation of fading away (virāgānupassanā); from origination through the contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā); and from grasping through the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā). Therefore, it is said: "He trains thus: 'I shall breathe in... breathe out liberating the mind.'" It should be understood that this third tetrad is taught by way of the contemplation of the mind (cittānupassanā) as described.

236. In the fourth tetrad, regarding the term "contemplating impermanence" (aniccānupassī), first, "impermanence" (anicca) should be understood; "impermanency" (aniccatā), which is the characteristic of impermanence, should be understood; "contemplation of impermanence" (aniccānupassanā) should be understood; and "one who contemplates impermanence" (aniccānupassī) should be understood.

Therein, "impermanence" (anicca) refers to the five aggregates. Why? Because they have the nature of arising, vanishing, and changing.

Note: Having the nature of arising (uppāda), having the nature of vanishing (bhaṅga), and having the nature of being otherwise (ṭhiti) apart from arising and vanishing. Therein, "being otherwise" means the state of maturing while remaining for a brief moment, distinct from arising and vanishing. It is called ṭhiti. Therefore, to translate briefly and clearly:

"Impermanency" (aniccatā)—the state of being impermanent (or the characteristic of impermanence to be noted as impermanent)—refers to the very arising, vanishing, and changing (i.e., maturing) of those aggregates. Or, it is arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga). Alternatively, it is the non-existence after having come into being—the disappearance. It means the breaking up through momentary dissolution of things that have arisen, not remaining in that same state. "Contemplation of impermanence" (aniccānupassanā) is the contemplation of materiality and so on as impermanent by way of that impermanency, which is the characteristic of impermanence consisting of arising-presence-dissolution, or the characteristic of impermanence consisting of vanishing after having arisen.

Note: It can also be translated as "because of having arising, presence, and dissolution." Therefore, the Sub-commentary explains as follows: In the phrase "uppādavayaññathattabhāva," arising (uppāda) is the coming into being, the manifestation of its own nature, of conditioned things (saṅkhāra) due to their primary and supporting causes. Vanishing (vaya) is the cessation, destruction, or disappearance of those conditioned things that have arisen. Changing (aññathatta) is the occurrence in another way through maturing or aging (jarā). (Sub-commentary).
282:
If a certain phenomenon arises, matures, and then perishes, that phenomenon should be known as anicca (impermanent). In such recognition, the characteristic marks for identifying impermanence are indeed arising (uppāda), presence (ṭhiti), and dissolution (bhaṅga). Therefore, these three—arising, presence, and dissolution—are called the characteristic of impermanence (anicca-lakkhaṇa). Alternatively, it is the contemplation of impermanence in the five aggregates: materiality, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. One who contemplates impermanence (aniccānupassī) is one endowed with that insight and vision of impermanence. Thus, one who breathes in and breathes out while contemplating impermanence in this way should be understood as: 'He trains himself, thinking: "I shall breathe in... I shall breathe out contemplating impermanence."' 

Note: If a phenomenon disappears after arising, it should be known as anicca (impermanent), just as one recognizes a flash of lightning that appears and then vanishes. In such recognition, the characteristic mark of impermanence is the very disappearance after having appeared. Therefore, 'non-existence after having been' (hutvā abhāvo) is another way the characteristic of impermanence is described. 

1. While observing the arising of materiality and mentality (rūpa-nāma), if one sees them perish and disappear after staying for a brief moment, and thus understands and accepts them as impermanent, this is called contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) through the characteristic of arising, presence, and dissolution. This contemplation typically occurs at the stages of knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa) and tender knowledge of arising and passing away (taruṇa-udayabbaya-ñāṇa). Furthermore, understanding and accepting impermanence by seeing the disappearance of the observed materiality and mentality after they appear is also called contemplation of impermanence. This typically occurs at the stages of mature knowledge of arising and passing away (balava-udayabbaya-ñāṇa), knowledge of dissolution (bhaṅga-ñāṇa), and so on. 

Regarding the term virāgānupassī (contemplating fading away), there are two kinds of fading away (virāga): fading away as destruction (khaya-virāga) and absolute fading away (accanta-virāga). Among these, the momentary dissolution of formations (saṅkhāra) is called fading away as destruction. Nibbāna is called absolute fading away. Insight (vipassanā) and the noble path (ariya-magga), which proceed by way of seeing these two kinds of fading away, are called contemplation of fading away (virāgānupassanā). One who breathes in and breathes out while endowed with these two kinds of contemplation should be understood as: 'He trains himself, thinking: "I shall breathe in... I shall breathe out contemplating fading away."' The same method applies to the term nirodhānupassī (contemplating cessation). 

Regarding the term paṭinissaggānupassī (contemplating relinquishment), there are also two kinds of relinquishment (paṭinissagga): relinquishment as giving up (pariccāga-paṭinissagga) and relinquishment as entering into (pakkhandana-paṭinissagga). Relinquishment itself is the contemplation; hence it is called contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā). This is a designation for both insight and the noble path. 

## Note 

1. It should be understood distinctly: Insight sees fading away as destruction (khaya-virāga); the noble path sees absolute fading away (accanta-virāga). 

2. The similar method for cessation (nirodha): There are two kinds of cessation—cessation as destruction (khaya-nirodha) and absolute cessation (accanta-nirodha). The momentary dissolution of formations is called cessation as destruction. Nibbāna is called absolute cessation. Insight and the noble path that see these two kinds of cessation are called contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā). One who breathes in and breathes out while endowed with these two kinds of contemplation should be understood as: 'He trains himself, thinking: "I shall breathe in... I shall breathe out contemplating cessation."' This is the similar method. 

Relinquishment as giving up and relinquishment as entering into: To elaborate—Insight gives up defilements (kilesa) along with the resultant aggregates and the volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra)—both wholesome and unwholesome—by way of substitution of opposites (tadaṅga). Therefore, it is called relinquishment as giving up. Furthermore, because it sees the faults of conditioned things (saṅkhata), it enters into Nibbāna, which is the opposite (the state free from conditioned things), by way of inclination towards it. Therefore, it is also called relinquishment as entering into. 

Note: 

1. Regarding the phrase 'by way of substitution of opposites' (tadaṅga): Contemplation of impermanence gives up the perception of permanence (nicca-saññā) by way of abandonment by substitution of opposites. In giving up, if the contemplation of impermanence did not occur, certain defilements would arise through the grasp of permanence, as would volitional formations (wholesome and unwholesome) rooted in those defilements, and resultant aggregates (vipāka-kkhandha) rooted in those defilements and volitional formations in the future. It gives them up by preventing these defilements, kamma, and aggregates from arising. Contemplation of suffering (dukkhānupassanā), etc., give up in the same way. (Ṭīkā) 

2. 'Entering into' means the mind's inclination towards Nibbāna. 

It is called relinquishment as entering into. The noble path gives up defilements along with the resultant aggregates and volitional formations by way of eradication (samuccheda). Therefore, it is called relinquishment as giving up. Furthermore, it enters into Nibbāna by making it the object. Therefore, it is also called relinquishment as entering into. Both insight and the path are called contemplation (anupassanā) because they contemplate repeatedly following preceding knowledges. One who breathes in and breathes out while endowed with these two kinds of contemplation of relinquishment should be understood as: 'He trains himself, thinking: "I shall breathe in... I shall breathe out contemplating relinquishment."' 

Note: 

1. In the Visuddhimagga, the two kinds of relinquishment are combined in a single sentence. Here, they are shown separately for the ease of those with less scriptural knowledge. 

2. In the continuity of one for whom the noble path has arisen, various defilements such as wrong view (diṭṭhi) and doubt (vicikicchā), various volitional formations such as kamma that leads to states of deprivation, and resultant aggregates such as aggregates in states of deprivation or aggregates beyond seven births, can no longer arise. This means the four noble paths give up these defilements, volitional formations, and resultant aggregates by eradicating them so they cannot arise. 

3. The path knowledge is also called contemplation (anupassanā) because it sees Nibbāna immediately after the change-of-lineage knowledge (gotrabhū-ñāṇa). This translation follows the meaning of the phrase 'contemplating repeatedly following preceding knowledges' (purimapurimañāṇānaṃ anu anu passanato) in accordance with the Mūla-ṭīkā. 

This fourth tetrad is taught solely by way of pure insight (suddha-vipassanā). The previous three tetrads, however, are taught by way of both calm (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). In this way, the development of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati) with its sixteen bases should be understood by way of the four tetrads. 

237. To further show the benefits: This mindfulness of breathing, (developed) by way of the sixteen bases as described, is of great fruit and great benefit. Regarding the phrase 'of great benefit,' its great benefit should be understood by way of its being peaceful, etc., as the Buddha taught: 'Bhikkhus, this concentration through mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, is peaceful and sublime...' 

Note: 

1. This is the meaning of the particles 'ca pana'. 

2. In the phrase 'by way of the sixteen bases' (soḷasavatthuvaseana ca), the word 'ca' has the sense of connecting 'by way of the sixteen bases' and 'by way of being peaceful, etc.,' which will be mentioned. (Ṭīkā) Although the sub-commentator says this, since 'being peaceful, etc.' is not the mode of development, it does not seem appropriate. Therefore, the word 'ca' is translated only as a sentence-linker (vākya-jotaka). 

3. Connect with: 'The fact that this mindfulness of breathing has great benefit should be known.' The meaning 'of that mindfulness of breathing' is...
283:
It should be understood that mindfulness of breathing has great benefits by virtue of its ability to cut off unwholesome thoughts (micchāvitakka). Indeed, because this mindfulness of breathing is peaceful, sublime, unadulterated, and a happy dwelling, it cuts off the mind's wandering to various objects through the power of unwholesome thoughts that obstruct concentration, and it makes the mind directed solely toward the object of the in-breath and out-breath. Therefore, it was said: “Mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of unwholesome thoughts” (A. Ni. 9.1).

Furthermore, its great benefit should be understood as the root cause for the fulfillment of knowledge and liberation (vijjā-vimutti). Indeed, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, mindfulness of breathing, when developed and cultivated, fulfills the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna); the four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga); the seven factors of enlightenment, when developed and cultivated, fulfill knowledge and liberation” (M. Ni. 3.147).

[Note: Regarding the term 'assā' (of her/it), it refers back to 'ānāpānassatiyā' mentioned in the previous sentence. However, in the Ṭīkā (sub-commentary), in view of the supporting sutta to be cited, it is explained as 'assa' meaning 'of mindfulness of breathing concentration' (ānāpānassatīsamādhissa). The Pyay-mu Nissaya observes that while the Ṭīkā's interpretation fits the supporting Pali text, it deviates from the flow of the preceding sentence.]

Moreover, its great benefit should be understood by making known the final in-breaths and out-breaths. Indeed, the Blessed One said: “Rāhula, when mindfulness of breathing is thus developed and cultivated, even those final in-breaths and out-breaths are known as they cease, not unknown” (M. Ni. 2.121).

238. In that context, by way of cessation, there are three kinds of final breaths: final in terms of existence (bhava-carimaka), final in terms of jhāna (jhāna-carimaka), and final in terms of death (cuti-carimaka). To elaborate: among the three spheres of existence, in-breaths and out-breaths occur in the sense-sphere existence (kāma-bhava), but they do not occur in the fine-material (rūpa) and immaterial (arūpa) existences; therefore, those breaths (occurring in the final sense-sphere existence) are called final in terms of existence.

[Note: This means that for Anāgāmins who pass away from the sense-sphere and are reborn in the fine-material or immaterial spheres, the breaths in their final sense-sphere existence are 'final' in terms of existence. The same applies to Sotāpannas and Sakadāgāmins. For Arahants attaining Parinibbāna in the sense-sphere, their breaths should also be called 'final' in terms of existence. If taken this way, the distinction of 'final' (carimaka) is meaningful. The Ṭīkā, however, explains 'bhava-carimaka' as being final in terms of the inferior (nihīna) sense-sphere existence. By that logic, all breaths would be 'final' since they only occur in the sense-sphere. If so, the qualifier 'final' would be redundant. The wise should consider this carefully.]

Among the jhānas, breaths occur in the lower three jhānas but not in the fourth jhāna; therefore, those breaths (occurring in the lower jhāna immediately preceding the fourth) are called final in terms of jhāna. Furthermore, those breaths which arise together with the sixteenth mind-moment before the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) and cease together with the death-consciousness are called final in terms of death. These are what are intended here as “final.”

[Note: This means when one enters the fourth jhāna after the lower three, the breaths occurring in the lower jhāna immediately preceding the fourth are 'final' in terms of jhāna, as they cease in the fourth jhāna. This aligns with the Pali texts describing the cessation of bodily formations (kāya-saṅkhāra) upon entering the fourth jhāna.]

For a bhikkhu devoted to this meditation subject, because the object of mindfulness of breathing is well-grasped, when he adverts to the arising at the moment of the arising of the sixteenth mind-moment before the death-consciousness, their arising becomes clear to him. When he adverts to the presence, their presence becomes clear. When he adverts to the dissolution, their dissolution becomes clear.

For a bhikkhu who has attained Arahantship after developing another meditation subject, the limit of his life-span is either delimited or undelimited. But for one who has attained Arahantship after developing this sixteen-based mindfulness of breathing, the limit of his life-span is definitely delimited. He [thinks], “So much of my life-formations (āyu-saṅkhāra) will now proceed, not [more]...”
284:
In the ሒĩkā:
Those breaths that arise together with the sixteenth consciousness and cease simultaneously with the death-consciousness (cuti-citta) are called the 'final breaths of death' (cuti-carimaka). In this context, these 'final breaths of death' are intended as the 'final breaths' (carimaka).

For a monk practicing this Ānāpānassati meditation, because the object of the breath is well-grasped, [the breaths are clear]. When contemplating the arising (uppāda) at the moment of the sixteenth consciousness before the death-consciousness, the arising of those breaths is clear. When contemplating the presence (ሒhiti), their presence is clear. When contemplating the dissolution (bhaṅga), their dissolution is clear.

A monk who reaches Arahatship by developing a meditation other than Ānāpānassati may or may not be able to determine the limit of his life. However, a monk who reaches Arahatship by developing this Ānāpānassati meditation with its sixteen bases is certainly able to determine the limit of his life.

Note:
Since all breaths associated with the three lower jhānas are intended as 'jhāna-carimaka', there is no benefit in specifically calling them 'jhāna-carimaka' in this sense. This point should also be considered.
1. The two phrases in parentheses are additions according to the ሒĩkā. Even without these additions, the meaning can be understood smoothly by connecting the preceding and following words.

Such a monk, knowing 'Now my life-formations (āyusaṅkhāra) will last only this long [284], and will not occur after this,' performs all his duties such as cleaning the body, dressing in the inner robe, and putting on the outer robe by his own will, and then closes his eyes. Like whom? Like Tissa Thera who lived at Koሒapabbata Monastery, like Mahātissa Thera who lived at Mahākarañjiya Monastery, like Tissa Thera the alms-gatherer in the great country of Devaputta, and like the two brother-elders who lived at Cittalapabbata Monastery.

Here is a story to illustrate this: Of the two brother-elders, one, after reciting the Pātimokkha on the full-moon Uposatha day, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, went to his dwelling place. Standing on the walkway (caṅkama) and looking at the moonlight, he investigated his life-formations and asked the Saṅgha: 'In what manner have you seen monks attaining Parinibbāna before?' Some replied, 'We have seen them attaining Parinibbāna while sitting in their seats.' Others said, 'We have seen them attaining Parinibbāna while sitting cross-legged in the air.' The Elder said, 'Now I will show you attaining Parinibbāna while walking on the walkway.' He then made a mark on the walkway and said, 'I will go from this end of the walkway to the other end, and upon returning, as soon as I reach this mark, I shall attain Parinibbāna.' He stepped onto the walkway, went to the other side, and upon returning, at the very moment his foot stepped on the mark, he attained Parinibbāna.

Therefore, a wise person endowed with vision and wisdom should always, day and night, diligently and truly practice this Ānāpānassati meditation, which is endowed with such manifold benefits. This is the exhortation.

The preceding discourse is a summary of the detailed explanation of Ānāpānassati meditation.

## (End of Ānāpānassati Meditation)

## 10. Explanation of the Development of Upasamānussati

239. Furthermore, a yogi who wishes to develop the recollection of peace (upasamānussati), which was mentioned immediately after Ānāpānassati, should go into seclusion, withdraw from external objects, and being well-composed [in meditation], should repeatedly reflect: 'Monks, whatever dhammas there are, whether conditioned (saṅkhata) or unconditioned (asaṅkhata), of those dhammas, dispassion (virāga) is said to be the foremost. That is to say, it is the crushing of pride (madanimmadana) because it is the fading away and removal of intoxication; it is the removal of thirst (pipāsavinaya) because it is the removal of all thirst; it is the uprooting of attachment (ālayasamugghāta) because it is the removal of all attachments and things attached to; it is the cutting off of the round (vaሒሒupaccheda) because it is the end of the round; it is the destruction of craving (taṇhakkhaya) because it is the end of craving; it is dispassion (virāga) because it is the fading away of defilements; it is cessation (nirodha) because it is the cessation of suffering; [it is Nibbāna because it is the departure] from craving called vāna...'

Note:
1. Connect 'being well-composed' with 'should be reflected upon repeatedly'.
2. Regarding the term 'madanimmadana', translating it as 'the fading away and removal of intoxication' is sufficient. However, for clarity in comparison with the upcoming commentary, the Pali name is also mentioned.
285:
The same method applies to the subsequent terms.

3. This translation is based on the commentary to the original Sutta in Aṅguttara Nikāya Commentary, Vol. 2, p. 296. The specific explanation in this Visuddhimagga will be found in the following paragraph. However, the meaning is the same.

4. This meaning is also based on the commentary to that original Sutta.

Because it has departed [from craving] (or: because it is the stilling of all heat¹), it is called Nibbāna.” In this way, as it has been taught, one should repeatedly recollect and contemplate the qualities of Nibbāna, which is called the stilling of all suffering.

In that passage beginning with "Yāvatā": "Yāvatā" means as far as (or as many as)². "Dhammā" means states (or phenomena)³. "Saṅkhatā vā asaṅkhatā vā" means whether they are formed by the meeting of causes and conditions, or not so formed⁴.

Notes:
1. The meaning in the parentheses is in accordance with the commentary to the original Sutta, which explains: "(Taṃ āgamma) sabbe pariḷāhā nibbāyanti."
2. Since this word "Yāvatā" has already been translated as "as far as" in the Burmese translation of the Sutta, it is not strictly necessary here, but it is translated again to complete the explanation in the Visuddhimagga.
3. This word "Dhammā" has also been translated above as "states."
4. Saṃ (together/meeting) + kata (made) = Saṅkhata (a state made by the meeting of causes). It is said to be "formed by the meeting of causes" when it arises when the relevant causes meet in harmony; for example, the sound produced when two sticks strike each other is called a "Saṅkhata-dhamma." A (not) + saṅkhata = Asaṅkhata (a state not made by the meeting of causes), or a state that exists without being made.

"Among those (all existing) states, dispassion (virāga) [285] is said to be the best" means that among those conditioned and unconditioned states, dispassion is praised as the most excellent. In this context, "dispassion" does not merely mean the absence of greed; rather, it refers to that unconditioned state which receives names such as "the crushing of intoxication (madanimmadana)... etc... Nibbāna." That unconditioned state should be understood as dispassion. Indeed, because all intoxications, such as the intoxication of pride and the intoxication of manhood, are intoxicated no more and are destroyed upon reaching that unconditioned state through the Noble Path, it is called "the crushing of intoxication" (madanimmadana). Because all thirst for sense pleasures (pipāsa) (or: all thirst such as the thirst for sense pleasures¹) is removed and ceases upon reaching that unconditioned state, it is called "the removal of thirst" (pipāsavinaya). Furthermore, because the five cords of sense desire, which are the things to which one clings (ālaya) (or: all types of clinging such as clinging to sense desires¹), are absolutely uprooted upon reaching that unconditioned state, it is called "the uprooting of attachment" (ālayasamugghāta). Furthermore, because the threefold round of rebirth included within the three realms is cut off upon reaching that unconditioned state, it is called "the cutting off of the round" (vaṭṭupaccheda). Furthermore, because upon reaching that

Notes:
1. In accordance with the Aṅguttara Commentary, Vol. 1, pp. 296-7, and the Itivuttaka Commentary, p. 272.

unconditioned state, craving (taṇhā) reaches total destruction, fades away, and ceases, it is called "the destruction of craving" (taṇhakkhaya), "dispassion" (virāga), and "cessation" (nirodha). Furthermore, craving is called "vāna" because it acts as a fastening, a binding, or a weaving for the sake of repeated existence in the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings; this state is called "Nibbāna" because it has departed from, is released from, and is disconnected from that craving called "vāna"¹. This is the explanation of the terms. In accordance with these explanations, one should repeatedly recollect and contemplate the peace called Nibbāna by way of these qualities, such as being the crushing of intoxication (madanimmadanatā).

Moreover, the Blessed One has also taught other qualities of peace in such Suttas as: "Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the unconditioned (asaṅkhata). And the truth (sacca). And the far shore (pāra). And the very hard to see (sududdasa). And the ageless (ajara). And the stable (dhuva). And the non-proliferated (nippapañca). And the deathless (amata). And the auspicious (siva). And the secure (khema). And the wonderful (abbhuta). And the

Notes:
1. Here, the definition of the word "vāna" is translated separately for easy understanding. "Nibbāna" is derived from "ni-vāna."

free from calamity (anītika). And the non-affliction (abyāpajjha). And the purity (visuddhi). And the island (dīpa) which is a support like an island in the middle of the water. And the shelter (tāṇa) which protects from all suffering. And the refuge (leṇa) where one hides for safety from all suffering." One should also repeatedly recollect by way of those qualities as well.
286:
As described, for the meditator who repeatedly recollects the qualities of the peaceful Nibbāna by way of such qualities as being the crushing of intoxication and the absence of intoxication, at that time his mind is not obsessed and oppressed by greed, his mind is not obsessed and oppressed by hate, and his mind is not obsessed and oppressed by delusion. At that time, his mind is indeed upright, taking the (peaceful quality of) Nibbāna as its object. In this way, by the same method described in the Recollection of the Buddha and so on, the jhāna factors arise in a single moment for the meditator whose hindrances have been suppressed. However, due to the profundity of the qualities of Nibbāna, or due to the mind being inclined toward recollecting many different qualities, the jhāna does not reach full absorption (appanā) but reaches only access concentration (upacāra) [286].

This jhāna that reaches access concentration is reckoned simply as "Recollection of Peace" (upasamānussati) because it occurs by way of repeatedly recollecting the qualities of Nibbāna, which is called peace (upasama).

To explain further: this recollection of peace, like the six recollections (such as the recollection of the Buddha), is fully accomplished only in a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka). Nevertheless, it should be attended to, ought to be attended to, and is good to be attended to even by a worldling (puthujjana) who values the peaceful Nibbāna. Indeed, even through the power of what has been heard (suta), the mind gains clarity and confidence in the peaceful Nibbāna. As for the benefits, the bhikkhu who is devoted to this meditation on the recollection of peace sleeps happily, wakes happily, has calm faculties, has a calm mind, is possessed of shame and fear of wrongdoing (hiri-ottappa), is inspiring, has a sublime inclination toward the noble Nibbāna, and is respected and held in high esteem by his fellow monks. Even if he does not penetrate or attain the higher states of the paths and fruits, he is bound for a happy destination (sugati).

Therefore, indeed, let the wise man,
Being diligent, develop this,
Recollection of the Noble Peace,
Which yields many such benefits.

This is the introduction to the detailed explanation of the Recollection of Peace.

Thus concludes the Eighth Chapter,
Named the Description of the Meditation Subject of Recollections,
In the Section on the Development of Concentration,
In the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga),
Composed for the Joy of Good People.
287:
Therefore, a person endowed with foresight and wisdom should truly develop mindfulness, without negligence, towards the noble and peaceful Nibbāna, which possesses such great benefits as mentioned. This is the exhortation.

This concludes the brief summary of the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the Recollection of Peace.

## (End of the Recollection of Peace).

This is the eighth chapter, titled 'The Exposition of the Meditation Subjects of Recollection' (Anussati-kammaṭṭhāna-niddesa), in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the purpose of gladdening good people, in the section on the development of concentration.

## (End of the Exposition of the Recollections).

## 9. Brahmavihāra-niddesa: Exposition of the Divine Abidings

## 1. Explanation of the Development of Loving-kindness

[287] 240. Furthermore, immediately after the meditation subjects of recollection, among the four Divine Abidings—(1) Loving-kindness (mettā), (2) Compassion (karuṇā), (3) Gladness (muditā), and (4) Equanimity (upekkhā)—which have been mentioned as brief headings, a beginner meditator (yogāvacara) who wishes to develop loving-kindness should first cut off impediments. Having learned the meditation subject from a teacher, and after finishing the meal and dispelling the drowsiness caused by it, he should sit comfortably in a well-prepared seat in a secluded place. Before developing the meditation, he should first contemplate the danger in anger and the benefit in patience.

Why? Because by this development of loving-kindness, anger is to be abandoned and patience is to be attained. It is not possible to abandon something whose danger is not yet seen, nor to attain something whose benefit is not yet known. Therefore:

'Friend, one who is corrupted by anger, overcome by anger, with a mind completely seized by it, kills even living beings.' By virtue of such suttas, the danger in anger should be seen.

'Patience is the highest austerity, the highest forbearance; the Buddhas say Nibbāna is supreme.'

'Him whose strength is patience, and who has strength as an army, I call a Brahmin.'

'There is no greater benefit than patience.' By virtue of such suttas, the benefit in patience should be known.

Thereafter, for the purpose of detaching the mind from anger, whose danger has been seen as described, and for the purpose of connecting the mind with patience, whose benefit is known, the development of loving-kindness should be undertaken. One who undertakes it should, from the very beginning, know the unsuitable persons: 'Loving-kindness should not be developed first towards these persons; it should never be developed towards these.'

Specifically, this loving-kindness should not be developed first towards these four types of persons: (1) an unpleasant person, (2) a very dear friend, (3) a neutral person, and (4) an enemy. It should not be developed specifically towards the opposite sex. It should never be developed towards the dead. For what reason should it not be developed first towards the unpleasant person and so on? The answer is: putting an unpleasant person in the place of a dear one is tiring. Putting a very dear friend in the place of a neutral one is tiring; indeed, if even a slight suffering arises for that very dear friend, one becomes as if in a state of weeping. [288] Putting a neutral person in the place of a respected or dear one is tiring. To one who remembers an enemy...
288:
If one considers that the distinction between persons—those towards whom loving-kindness should not be developed first and those towards whom it should not be developed at all—must be known, then the current text "puggalabhedo jānitabbo" (the distinction between persons should be known) is easily understood and appropriate.

Anger may arise [when remembering an enemy]. Therefore, one should not develop loving-kindness first towards a disliked person and so on.

However, for one who develops loving-kindness specifically towards a single person of the opposite sex, lust (rāga) may arise. It is said that a certain son of a minister asked a monk who was a regular visitor to his family, "Venerable sir, towards whom should loving-kindness be developed?" The Elder replied, "Towards a dear person." His own wife was dear to him. While developing loving-kindness towards her, he spent the whole night "fighting the wall" [trying to reach her]. Therefore, one should not develop loving-kindness specifically towards a person of the opposite sex.

Note 1: "Fighting the wall" means that after undertaking the Uposatha precepts, while sitting on his couch in a locked room and developing loving-kindness, lust—arising with loving-kindness as its precursor—blinded his vision. When he wanted to go to his wife, he could not find the doorway and, wishing to go even by breaking through the wall, he struck and beat against it. Thus, the Netti Commentary states, "Lust deceives by taking loving-kindness as its precursor." (Sub-commentary)

If one develops it towards a deceased person, one reaches neither absorption (appanā) nor access concentration (upacāra). It is said that a certain young monk began to practice loving-kindness towards his teacher. Loving-kindness did not arise in him. He went to a Great Elder and said, "Venerable sir, I am proficient in the attainment of loving-kindness jhāna, but I cannot enter that attainment now. What is the reason?" The Elder said, "Friend, look for the sign (the object)." While searching, he learned of his teacher's death. When he developed loving-kindness towards another person, he reached the attainment. Therefore, one should certainly not develop it towards a deceased person.

## How to Develop Loving-kindness

241. First of all, it should be developed towards oneself repeatedly in this way: "May I be happy and free from suffering," or "May I be free from enmity (avero homi), may I be free from mental suffering (abyāpajjho homi), may I be free from physical suffering (anīgho homi), and may I take care of myself happily (sukhī attānaṃ pariharāmi)."

Note 1: Connect "First of all... should be developed towards oneself."

If this is the case, does it contradict the words spoken in the Vibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma Piṭaka:

"How does a monk dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness? Just as he would develop loving-kindness upon seeing a single dear and pleasant person, so he pervades all beings with loving-kindness."

And the words spoken in the Paṭisambhidāmagga:

"In what five ways is the heart-deliverance of loving-kindness developed through unspecified pervasion? 'May all beings (sabbe sattā) be free from enmity, free from mental suffering, free from physical suffering, and may they take care of themselves happily.' 'May all breathing things (sabbe pāṇā)... all creatures (sabbe bhūtā)... all persons (sabbe puggalā)... all those who have reached the state of individuality (sabbe attabhāvapariyāpannā) be free from enmity,

Note 1: The indefinite and definite are translated together. The same applies to the following sentence.

free from mental suffering, and may they take care of themselves happily,' and so on."

[289] And the words spoken in the Mettā Sutta:

"May all beings be happy and secure; may they be happy-minded," and so on?
289:
If it is argued that in those three Pali passages, the development of loving-kindness towards oneself was not mentioned, (the answer is) those three passages do not contradict this. Why? Because those three passages were taught with the intention of meditation leading to absorption (appanā), whereas the instruction here in this Visuddhimagga to develop loving-kindness towards oneself is intended for the purpose of using oneself as a witness (sakkhibhāva).

Indeed, even if one develops loving-kindness towards oneself for a hundred or a thousand years in the way 'May I be happy,' absorption does not arise for him. However, for one who develops it as 'May I be happy,' the desire for the welfare and happiness of other beings arises by making oneself the witness (or by way of comparison): 'Just as I desire happiness, recoil from pain, wish to live and do not wish to die, so too do other beings.' The Blessed One also showed this method by saying:

'Having traversed all directions with the mind,
One finds no one anywhere dearer than oneself.
Since the self is so dear to others likewise,
Therefore one who loves himself should not harm others.'

242. Therefore, for the purpose of making oneself a witness, one should first pervade oneself with loving-kindness. Immediately after that, to facilitate the progression of happiness, one should reflect on the qualities of a person who is dear, pleasing, respected, and venerable—such as a teacher or one like a teacher, or a preceptor or one like a preceptor. One should recall the reasons for their being dear and pleasing, such as their generosity and kind speech, and the reasons for their being respected and venerable, such as their virtue (sīla) and learning (suta), and develop loving-kindness in this way: 'May this good person be happy and free from suffering.'

In such a person, absorption (appanā) can certainly be achieved. However, this monk, not being content with just that much and wishing to accomplish the breaking down of the barriers (sīmāsambheda), should next develop loving-kindness towards a very dear friend, then towards a neutral person, and then towards an enemy.
290:
When developing it in this way, one should make the mind soft and workable in each category and then extend it to the next.

[290] For a person who has no enemy, or who, due to being of the nature of a Great Man, does not even perceive an enemy even when others do him harm, he need not make the effort: 'My mind of loving-kindness has become workable towards a neutral person; now I shall extend it to an enemy.' Thus, the statement 'loving-kindness should be developed towards an enemy after a neutral person' is said with reference to a meditator who has an enemy.

243. Furthermore, if resentment (paṭigha) arises in that meditator as he extends his mind towards an enemy, due to remembering the wrongs committed by that person, then he should repeatedly enter into loving-kindness absorption towards any of the previous persons, and after emerging, dispel the resentment by repeatedly pervading that enemy person with loving-kindness. If, despite such effort, it does not subside, then he should strive repeatedly to abandon resentment by following the advice such as the Simile of the Saw (Kakacūpama Ovadā).

He should strive by admonishing himself in this manner: 'O angry man, has it not been said by the Blessed One:

"Monks, even if bandits were to savagely sever your limbs one by one with a double-handled saw, he who entertained hate in his heart on that account would not be one who carries out my teaching."

And:

"He who returns anger to an angry man is worse than the first. He who does not return anger to an angry man wins a battle that is hard to win."

"He practices for the welfare of both, his own and the other's, when, knowing the other is angry, he remains mindful and calm."

And:

"Monks, these seven things, which are pleasing to an enemy and bring about an enemy's purpose, come upon an angry woman or man. What seven? Here, monks, an enemy wishes thus for an enemy: 'O, may this person be ugly!' Why is that? Monks, an enemy does not delight in an enemy's beauty. Monks, this person, being overcome by anger and possessed by anger, even though he be well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, and clothed in white garments, yet he is ugly because he is overcome by anger. This is the first..."'
291:
Based on the explanation in the commentary, the word 'person' (puggala) can be taken to refer to both men and women. If 'man' and 'person' are taken as equivalent, then an angry woman should be considered as secondary.
2. Connect this reason (hetu) with the phrases 'being ugly' and so forth.
3. Note: Same as Note 2; it is stated again because the sentence is long.

... 'Monks, this is the first quality pleasing to an enemy, causing an enemy's satisfaction, which comes to an angry woman or man. (2) Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes for an enemy: "O, may this person sleep in pain!" ... "May he not be prosperous!" ... "May he not have wealth!" ... "May he not have fame!" ... "May he not have friends!" ... (7) Furthermore, monks, an enemy wishes for an enemy: "May he, after the breakup of the body, after death, not reach a happy destination, a heavenly world!" For what reason? Monks, an enemy does not rejoice in an enemy's going to a happy destination. Monks, this angry person, overcome and obsessed by anger, performs misconduct by body, speech, and mind. Having performed misconduct by body, speech, and mind, being overcome by anger, after the breakup of the body, after death, he reaches the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world (vinipāta), and hell. Monks, this is the seventh quality pleasing to an enemy, causing an enemy's satisfaction, which comes to an angry woman or man.' (AN 7.64).

'Monks, just as a log from a funeral pyre (chavālāta), burnt at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle, serves no purpose as timber in the village nor as timber in the forest; monks, I say this person is similar to that log.'

'Now you, being angry in this way, will not be a follower of the Blessed One's teaching. By being angry in return, you will be worse than the first angry person and will not win the battle that is hard to win. You will bring upon yourself those qualities that please an enemy, and you will become like that funeral pyre log (losing human prosperity and failing in the monk's duties).' (One should strive to abandon anger by admonishing oneself thus.)

244. If, while striving and exerting himself in this way, that resentment subsides, that is good. If it does not subside, then whatever quality of that person is peaceful and pure, which brings clarity and confidence when recollected, one should remove resentment by recollecting that specific quality.

To elaborate, in some people, only the bodily conduct (kāyasamācāra) is peaceful. His peaceful nature is known to all people through his performance of many duties and observances. But his verbal and mental conduct are not peaceful.
292:
Disregarding those unpeaceful verbal and mental conducts, one should only recollect the peace of his bodily conduct.

[292] In some people, only the verbal conduct (vacīsamācāra) is peaceful. The peaceful nature of his verbal conduct is known to all people. This is because he is naturally skilled in courteous greeting (paṭisanthāra), is polite, pleasant to talk to, amiable, and welcoming (not frowning or looking down). He is the first to greet others, recites the Dhamma with a sweet voice, and gives Dhamma talks with well-rounded words and phrases. However, his bodily and mental conduct are not peaceful. Disregarding those unpeaceful bodily and mental conducts, one should only recollect the peace of his verbal conduct.

In some people, only the mental conduct (manosamācāra) is peaceful. The peaceful nature of his mental conduct is evident to all people in such acts as paying homage to a shrine (cetiya). For a person whose mind is not peaceful, when paying homage to a shrine, a Bodhi tree, or Elders (Theras), he does not do so respectfully. In the Dhamma preaching hall, he sits with a distracted mind or nodding off. But a person with a peaceful mind pays homage with conviction. He listens to the Dhamma attentively, making it his purpose, and showing mental clarity through body and speech. Thus, in some people, only the mental conduct is peaceful, while bodily and verbal conduct are not. Disregarding those unpeaceful bodily and verbal conducts, one should only recollect the peace of his mental conduct.

In some people, not even one of these three qualities is peaceful. Toward such a person, one should arouse compassion (karuṇā), thinking: 'Although this person is now wandering in the human world, after a few days (before long), he will go to fill the eight great hells and the sixteen auxiliary hells (ussada-niraya).' Indeed, through compassion, resentment subsides.

In some people, all three of these qualities are peaceful. Regarding such a person, one can recollect whatever one wishes. Indeed, it is not difficult to develop loving-kindness (mettā) toward such a person.

To clarify this meaning, the Āghātapaṭivinaya Sutta from the Book of Fives in the Aṅguttara Nikāya should be explained in detail: 'Friends, there are these five ways of removing resentment. By means of these, a monk should entirely remove resentment that has arisen toward anyone.' (AN 5.162).

245. If, even while striving in this way, resentment and anger still arise in this yogi, then he should admonish himself as follows:
293:
“If an enemy has caused suffering to you in his own domain [your body], why do you wish to cause suffering in your own mind, which is not his domain?

Having abandoned the group of relatives who were of great help, even as they wept with tearful faces [to become a monk], why do you not abandon the enemy called anger, which causes great harm?

You protect the virtues (sīla); yet you cherish anger which cuts the very roots [of those virtues, such as shame, fear of wrongdoing, patience, loving-kindness, and compassion]. Who is as foolish as you?

You are angry because another has done an ignoble deed; why then do you yourself wish to do a similar deed?

If another, being an enemy, does something unpleasant because he wishes to provoke your anger, do you not fulfill that very enemy’s heart’s desire by giving way to anger?

Whether or not you can cause suffering to that enemy with whom you are angry, you are certainly torturing yourself right now with the suffering of anger.

If enemies, blinded by anger, have entered the harmful wrong path, why do you, by becoming angry, follow their example?

Cut off that very anger by which the enemy has done what is unpleasant to you; why be distressed by that person [who is merely a servant of anger]?

Because of the momentary nature of phenomena, those aggregates (khandhas) that did the unpleasant thing to you have already ceased. At whom, then, are you angry now?

If one causes suffering to another, who could he harm without that other [as a recipient]? Since you yourself are a cause of this suffering, why are you angry with the one who caused it?” (In this way, one should admonish oneself.)

246. If, however, the resentment of this yogi does not subside even as he admonishes himself in this way, he should then reflect on the fact that he and the other are owners of their kamma (kammassakatā). Therein, he should first reflect on his own kamma-ownership thus: “O yogi, what will you do by being angry with him? Will not this kamma rooted in anger lead to your own harm? For you are the owner of your kamma, heir to your kamma, born of your kamma, related to your kamma, and have your kamma as your refuge. Whatever kamma you do, of that you will be the heir. This kamma of yours is not...
294:
...capable of achieving Supreme Enlightenment, nor Paccekabuddhahood, nor the state of a disciple (sāvakabhūmi), nor any such prosperity as that of a Brahmā, a Sakka, a Universal Monarch, or a regional king. On the contrary, this kamma of yours will lead to your falling away from the Dispensation (Sāsana) and to such states as being an eater of scraps, and to the specific sufferings of hell and so forth. By doing this, you are like a man who, wanting to hit another, picks up glowing coals or excrement with both hands; you burn yourself first or make yourself stink.”

After reflecting on one’s own kamma-ownership, one should reflect on the other’s kamma-ownership: “What will your enemy do by being angry with you? Will it not lead to his own harm? For this venerable one is the owner of his kamma, heir to his kamma... whatever kamma he does, of that he will be the heir. This kamma of his is not capable of achieving Supreme Enlightenment... nor any such prosperity as that of a regional king and so forth. On the contrary, this kamma of his will lead to his falling away from the Dispensation and to such states as being an eater of scraps, and to the specific sufferings of hell and so forth. By doing this, he is like a man who, standing downwind, wants to throw dust at another; he only covers himself with it.” For the Blessed One said:

“Whoever harms a harmless person,
A pure man who is faultless,
The evil falls back on that fool,
Like fine dust thrown against the wind.”

247. If, however, the resentment of this yogi does not subside even as he reflects on kamma-ownership, he should then recollect the virtues of the Teacher’s (the Buddha’s) past conduct.

In that recollection, this is the method: “O monk, did not your Teacher, even while he was a Bodhisatta before his Enlightenment, during the four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), refrain from corrupting his mind even toward executioners and enemies in various births?” For instance, in the Sīlava Jātaka, when an enemy king, brought by a wicked minister who had offended against his own queen, was striving to seize his kingdom of three hundred leagues, [King Sīlava] did not allow his ministers, who had risen up to stop the enemy, even to touch a weapon.
295:
Furthermore, that Bodhisatta king, while being buried in a charnel ground up to his neck along with a thousand ministers, did not harbor even a slight mental ill-will toward the enemy king. Relying on the scratching of the earth by jackals who had come to eat the corpses (to escape from where he was buried), he exerted manly effort and regained his life. Having entered his royal bedchamber through the power of a yakkha and seeing the enemy king sleeping on the royal bed, he did not give way to anger. Instead, they made a mutual oath of non-harm, and he established the enemy king in the position of a friend, saying:

“A man should only hope; a wise man should not grow weary. I see myself now exactly as I had desired.” (Jā. 1.1.51)

In the Khantivādī Jātaka, the foolish King Kalābu of Kāsi asked, “O ascetic, what is your doctrine—what do you usually teach?” When he replied, “I am called Khantivādī because I teach patience,” the king had him beaten with whips fitted with iron thorns and had his hands and feet severed. Yet, the ascetic did not harbor even a trace of anger.

This patience of the Khantivādī ascetic is not yet so surprising. The reason is that an elderly person who has gone forth into the homeless life might be expected to practice such patience. What is even more remarkable is in the Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, where even as an infant who could only lie on his back:

“The arms of Dhammapāla, anointed with sandalwood paste, are being severed, O King! My life is coming to an end!”

While the Queen Mother was thus weeping and lamenting, the executioner, commanded by the father named King Mahāpatāpa, cut off the four limbs of the infant Dhammapāla like bamboo shoots. Not satisfied with even that, when the king ordered, “Cut off his head,” the infant made a firm resolution: “O Dhammapāla, now is the time to restrain your mind. Now, maintain an equal mind toward these four: the father who ordered the decapitation, the man who executes it, the mother who is lamenting, and yourself.” He did not show even a sign of ill-will.

Note: The sentences have been split or slightly modified from the literal Pali grammar to make them easier for the reader to understand, as they are narrative stories. Similar translations follow.

This patience of the infant Dhammapāla is also not yet so surprising,
296:
because a human being might be expected to act in this way. However, even as an animal, when he was the elephant named Chaddanta, though he was pierced in the navel by a poisoned arrow that penetrated through him, he did not corrupt his mind toward the hunter who caused such harm. As it is said in this verse:

[296] “The elephant, pierced by many arrows, spoke to the hunter with an uncorrupted mind: ‘For what purpose, or for what reason, friend, did you kill me? Whose instigation is this?’” (Jā. 1.16.124)
