When the hunter, in response to this question, said, “Venerable sir, I was sent for the sake of your tusks by the Queen of the King of Kāsi,” the elephant fulfilled her wish by cutting off and offering his own tusks, which were beautiful and radiant, emitting six-colored rays.

Furthermore, in the Mahākapi Jātaka, when he was a monkey of the langur species, a man whom he himself had rescued from a mountain precipice thought:

“This monkey is food for humans, just like other forest deer. What if I kill this monkey and eat him, for I am hungry?

Having eaten my fill, I will take the monkey meat as provisions and travel. It will be my travel food, and I will cross the wilderness with it.”

Thinking thus, the man lifted a stone and smashed the monkey’s head. Then the Bodhisatta monkey, looking at the man with eyes full of tears, said:

“O noble man, do not do this. You are my guest and worthy of honor. Yet you have done such a thing to me. You are a long-lived and wise person; you should rather prevent any other enemy from harming me.”

Having spoken, he did not corrupt his mind toward that malicious man, and without considering his own suffering, he led that very man to a safe area at the edge of the forest, the land of humans.

Furthermore, when he was the Naga King named Bhūridatta, while he was observing the Uposatha precepts and lying on top of an anthill, he was sprinkled all over his body with medicine like the fire of the end of an aeon. Even when he was put into a basket and made to perform throughout the whole of Jambudīpa, he did not harbor even a slight mental ill-will toward that Brahmin snake charmer. As it is said:

“Even when he puts me in a basket, even when he crushes me with his hand, I do not get angry with Alampāyana, for fear of breaking my virtue.” (Cariyā. 2.16)
297: “Even when massaged by hands to weaken me, or forcibly stuffed into a basket by treading with feet, I did not get angry at the snake charmer for fear that my virtue (sīla) would be broken”—this is the verse. [297] Even when he was the Nāga King Campeyya and was being oppressed by the snake charmer, the Bodhisatta did not allow even a slight thought of malice to arise. In accordance with this, it is said: “Even then, while I was practicing the Dhamma and observing the Uposatha, the snake charmer caught me and made me perform at the palace gate. Whatever color he thought of—blue, yellow, or red—following his mind, I became of that very color. I could turn land into water, and water into land. If I were to get angry with him, I could turn him into ashes in an instant. If I were to come under the power of my mind, I would fall away from virtue. For one who has fallen away from virtue, the supreme goal (Buddhahood) cannot be achieved.” (In the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka), having become the Nāga King Saṅkhapāla, he was pierced in eight places with sharp spears. Thorny creepers were inserted through the wounds, and a rope was firmly fixed through his nose. While being carried on a pole by sixteen sons of hunters, his body rubbing against the ground, he experienced great suffering. At that time, although he was capable of turning all the hunters into ashes just by looking at them in anger, he did not even open his eyes to show a sign of malice. In accordance with this, it is said: “O Āḷāra, the caravan leader, I constantly observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth and fifteenth days. Then sixteen sons of hunters came, bringing ropes and strong nooses. Having pierced my nose and pulled the rope tightly, those cruel hunters carried me away, binding me all around. I endured such suffering because I did not want to break my Uposatha.” [298] Not only were these wonders performed;
298: In the Mātuposaka Jātaka and others, many other wonders (of difficult endurance) were also performed. Now, for you who take refuge in and refer to that Blessed One, the Teacher, who has attained Omniscience and is endowed with the quality of patience (khanti) that is incomparable in the world including the devas, it is extremely improper and unbefitting to produce a mind of resentment. (One should reflect on the virtues practiced by the Teacher in his previous lives). 248. If, even while reflecting on the virtues of the Teacher’s past conduct in this way, the resentment of this yogi—who has been a slave to defilements for a long time—does not subside, then he should reflect on the Anamatagga Suttas. Indeed, it is said in those suttas: “Monks, it is not easy to find a being who has not been a mother in the past. It is not easy to find a being who has not been a father... a brother... a sister... a son... a daughter in the past.” Therefore, one should direct the mind toward that hostile person thus: “In the past, this person was my mother, carrying me in her womb for ten months. She removed urine, excrement, saliva, snot, etc., without loathing as if they were sandalwood. She made me dance on her breast (and sleep there [Note 1]), and nurtured me by carrying me on her limbs. Being my father, he traveled on goat-paths, stake-paths, etc. [Note 2], engaging in trade. For my sake, even risking his life, he entered battles with armies drawn up on both sides, crossed the great ocean by ship, and performed other difficult tasks. Thinking, ‘I will nurture my dear children,’ he gathered wealth by various means and nurtured me. Having been a brother, sister, son, or daughter, they performed such and such helpful deeds. Therefore, it is improper for me to harbor a malicious mind—to get angry—at this person.” 249. If, even while directing the mind in this way, he is still unable to extinguish the mind of anger, then this yogi should reflect on the benefits of loving-kindness (mettā) as follows: “O monk, was it not said by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, when the liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) is practiced, developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and well-undertaken, eleven benefits [299] are to be expected.’ What are the eleven? ...” (Note 1: Based on the variant reading nipajjāpente. Note 2: Ajapatha (goat-path), Saṅkupatha (stake-path). This refers to paths where one must go on all fours or use goats for transport in steep terrain.)
299:
It is stated in the Aṅguttara Commentary (Vol. 3, p. 36-7) that if 'mettā' is mentioned generally, it refers to preliminary loving-kindness; but if 'cetovimutti' (deliverance of mind) is mentioned, it refers specifically to the jhāna of loving-kindness. Mettā is called 'cetovimutti' because it is the deliverance from the hindrances of the mind, especially from ill-will (byāpāda).

Has it not been taught: '(1) One sleeps in comfort, (2) one wakes in comfort, (3) one sees no evil dreams, (4) one is dear to human beings, (5) one is dear to non-human beings, (6) deities protect one, (7) fire, poison, or weapons do not affect one, (8) the mind is easily concentrated, (9) the facial complexion is serene, (10) one dies unconfused, and (11) if one does not penetrate higher to the Path and Fruit, one is reborn in the Brahma world' (A. xi, 15)?

One should reflect: 'If you do not extinguish this mind of anger, you will be excluded from these benefits of loving-kindness and suffer loss.'

250. If, even after reflecting thus, the yogi is unable to extinguish it, he should perform the 'resolution into elements' (dhātu-vinibbhoga). How? 'O monk, when you are angry with that person, what are you angry with? Are you angry with the hair of the head, or the hair of the body, or the nails... or the urine? Or are you angry with the earth element in the hair, etc., or the water element, the fire element, or the air element? Or, among the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements, based on which this venerable one is called by such-and-such a name, are you angry with the aggregate of form, or the aggregate of feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness? Or are you angry with the eye-base, the object-base... the mind-base, or the mental-object base? Or are you angry with the eye-element, the object-element, the eye-consciousness element... the mind-element, the mental-object element, or the mind-consciousness element?' When he thus resolves into elements, there is no place for anger to establish itself, just as there is no place for a mustard seed on the point of an awl, or for a painting in the empty sky.

251. Furthermore, if he is unable to perform the resolution into elements, he should perform the 'sharing of gifts' (dāna-saṃvibhāga). He should give his own property to the other person, or accept the other's property. If the other person's livelihood is impure and his requisites are unfit for use, then he should only give his own property. When he acts thus, his resentment toward that person is surely appeased. And in the other person, even anger that has followed from past lives is appeased at that very moment. (How?) Just as the resentment was appeased in the Great Elder who received the bowl given by the Piṇḍapātika Elder at Cittalapabbata Monastery, who had been disturbed three times to give up his seat.

[300] 'Venerable sir, this bowl is worth eight kahāpaṇas. It was given to me by my mother, a lay devotee, as a gift rightfully obtained. Please perform a meritorious act for the great lay devotee...'
300:
...by accepting it.' Having said this, he gave the bowl, and it was like the Great Elder who received it (whose resentment was appeased). Such is the great power of giving. Thus it is said:

'Giving tames the untamed; giving accomplishes all goals.
Through giving and pleasant speech, they (the givers) rise and shine;
(The receivers) become soft, serene, and inclined to follow.'

252. When the resentment toward the enemy has been appeased in this way, the yogi's mind proceeds with loving-kindness toward that person, just as it does toward a dear person, a very dear friend, or a neutral person. Then, by repeatedly developing loving-kindness, he should achieve 'breaking down the barriers' (sīmā-sambheda) by making his mind equal toward these four persons: (1) oneself, (2) the dear person (piya), (3) the neutral person (majjhatta), and (4) the enemy (verī).

This is the characteristic of breaking down the barriers: Suppose this person practicing loving-kindness is sitting in a certain place with a dear person, a neutral person, and an enemy, himself being the fourth. Then bandits come and say, 'Venerable sir, give us one monk.' When asked 'For what purpose?', they reply, 'To kill him and take the blood from his throat for the purpose of making an offering.' If the monk thinks, 'Let them take this one or that one,' the breaking down of the barriers is not accomplished. Even if he thinks, 'Let them take me, but not these three,' the breaking down of the barriers is still not accomplished. Why? Because he wishes for the harm of whoever he wants them to take, and wishes for the welfare of the others only.

But when he does not see even one among the four persons who should be given to the bandits, and his mind proceeds with total equality toward himself and those three persons, then the breaking down of the barriers is accomplished. Therefore, the ancients said:

'When he sees no difference among the four—himself, the dear, the neutral, and the enemy—he is said to have a mind of welfare for all beings. He is not yet called "skilled" or "one who attains mettā at will" until the four barriers are broken by the monk. When he pervades the whole world, including the devas, equally with mettā, there is a great distinction from the former state, for his barriers are no longer known.'

[301] 253.
301:
At the very moment when the breaking down of the barriers (sīmāsambheda) is completed, this monk who develops loving-kindness acquires the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) and access concentration (upacāra). Furthermore, when the breaking down of the barriers has been effected, by repeating, developing, and cultivating that same sign of concentration (which arose through the breaking down of the barriers), he reaches absorption (appanā) without difficulty or hardship, following the method described under the earth kasiṇa.

By this much of the meditative sequence, this yogi has attained the first jhāna accompanied by loving-kindness, which is characterized by the abandoning of five factors, the possession of five factors, the three types of goodness, and the ten characteristics. Having attained that first jhāna, by repeating, developing, and cultivating that same sign of concentration, he successively reaches the second and third jhānas according to the fourfold method, and the second, third, and fourth jhānas according to the fivefold method.

The benefit is that this yogi (having attained the three or four jhānas of loving-kindness), by means of any one of the first jhāna and so on:

“He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, everywhere, and to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—abundant, exalted, immeasurable, without hostility, and without ill will.”

Indeed, this kind of “transformation” (vikubbanā)—the various and diverse manifestations of the jhāna—is accomplished only for a person whose mind has reached absorption through the first jhāna and so on.

254. To further explain: in the passage beginning with “mettāsahagatena”: Mettāsahagatena means “accompanied by (associated with) loving-kindness.” Cetasā means “with the mind.” Ekaṃ disaṃ (one direction)—this phrase is spoken in terms of pervading the beings included in one direction, starting with the group of beings first grasped in that single direction. Pharitvā (pervading) means “having touched” or “having made it an object.” Viharati (dwells) means “he maintains the dwelling in postures” firmly established and supported by the divine abode (brahmavihāra) of the mettā-jhāna. In the phrase tathā dutiyaṃ and so on, just as he dwells pervading any one direction among the East and so forth, so too, immediately after that, he pervades the second, the third, and the fourth; this is the meaning. By the words iti uddhaṃ, it is meant that he pervades the upper direction in this same manner. In adho tiriyaṃ, it means similarly for the lower direction and the intermediate directions. Therein, adho means “among the beings in the lower direction.” Tiriyaṃ means “among the beings in the intermediate directions.” In this way, in all ten directions, just as a horse is driven and turned back within a training ring, he sends forth and brings back the mind imbued with loving-kindness. This is the word-by-word commentary. Up to this point (the word tiriyaṃ), the sequence of words shows the “specified” (odhisa) pervasion of loving-kindness by grasping each direction individually.

The words beginning with sabbadhi, however, are spoken to show the “unspecified” (anodhisa) pervasion.
302:
In that passage, *sabbadhi* means in all (directions). *Sabbattatāya* means towards all (beings) such as the inferior, medium, superior, friends, enemies, and neutral persons, etc., as oneself [302]; it means by way of equality with oneself, without making a distinction such as "this is another being." Alternatively, by the word *sabbattatāya*, it means "with the whole mind, without letting it scatter outside even slightly." *Sabbāvantaṃ* means containing all beings, or associated with all beings; this is the meaning. *Lokaṃ* means the world of beings. To explain further, because of the presentation of synonymous terms such as *vipulena*, the term *mettasahagatena* is mentioned again in this passage which shows the pervasion of unspecified (*anodhisa*) loving-kindness. Or to explain in another way, just as in the case of showing the pervasion of specified (*odhisa*) loving-kindness, in showing this unspecified loving-kindness, the words *tathā* or *iti* are not repeated. Therefore, the phrase *mettasahagatena cetasā* is repeated. Or else, it is said by way of conclusion. In the term *vipulena*, its vastness should be understood by way of pervasion. By way of the fine-material sphere, this jhāna of loving-kindness is called "greatly-attained" (*mahaggata*). It is called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) by way of proficiency and by way of taking immeasurable beings as its object. It is called "free from enmity" (*avera*) because of the abandoning of the enemy, ill-will (*byāpāda*). It is called "free from affliction" (*abyāpajjha*) because of the abandoning of mental distress (*domanassa*); it means being without suffering. This is the meaning of the various ways of developing loving-kindness taught in the manner of "with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness," etc.

255. To explain further—just as this various development of loving-kindness is accomplished only for a person whose mind has reached absorption (*appanā*), so too:

"The liberation of mind through loving-kindness pervading without limit (*anodhisa*) occurs in five ways; the liberation of mind through loving-kindness pervading with limits (*odhisa*) occurs in seven ways; the liberation of mind through loving-kindness pervading the directions occurs in ten ways"—

this various development of loving-kindness taught in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* should also be understood as being accomplished only for a person whose mind has reached absorption.

Note 1: This "so too" connects with "this various development of loving-kindness taught in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*," etc.

In that *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: (1) May all beings (*sabbe sattā*) be free from enmity (*averā*), free from affliction (*abyāpajjhā*), free from suffering (*anīghā*), and may they maintain themselves in happiness (*sukhī attānaṃ pariharantu*). (2) May all breathing things (*sabbe pāṇā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (3) May all creatures (*sabbe bhūtā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (4) May all persons (*sabbe puggalā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (5) May all those who have reached a state of individuality (*sabbe attabhāvapariyāpannā*) be free from enmity, free from affliction, free from suffering, and may they maintain themselves in happiness—the liberation of mind through loving-kindness pervading without limit (*anodhisa*) in these five ways should be understood.

(2) May all men (*sabbe purisā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (3) May all noble ones (*sabbe ariyā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (4) May all ordinary people (*sabbe anariyā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (5) May all deities (*sabbe devā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (6) May all humans (*sabbe manussā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness. (7) May all those in states of deprivation (*sabbe vinipātikā*) be free from enmity... up to... maintain themselves in happiness—the liberation of mind through loving-kindness pervading with limits (*odhisa*) in these seven ways should be understood.

256. In that passage (beginning with 'sabbe sattā' which shows the method of developing loving-kindness), the word 'sabbe' (all) is a term of inclusive totality. Regarding 'sattā' (beings): they are called 'beings' because they are attached (sattā) and clung (visattā) to the aggregates such as form by desire and lust (chanda-rāga). For it was said by the Blessed One:

"Rādha, whatever desire, whatever lust, whatever delight, whatever craving there is for form—one is stuck there, one is attached there, therefore one is called a 'being' (satta)... for feeling... for perception... for mental formations... for consciousness, whatever desire... whatever craving there is, one is stuck there, one is attached there, therefore one is called a 'being' (satta)."

Furthermore, this term 'satta' (being) applies even to the Arahants who are free from lust, by way of established usage (ruḷhī), just as the term 'palm-leaf fan' (tālavaṇṭa) is used for a specific type of fan even when it is made of bamboo strips. Grammarians, however, without investigating the meaning, accept this as a mere name. Those who do investigate the meaning accept that they are called 'beings' (satta) because of their connection with the quality of 'sattva' (existence/vitality).

Note:
1. A name applied metaphorically due to similarity in form, etc., is called 'Āropita-ruḷhī' (metaphorical usage), just as a fan made of bamboo is called a 'palm-leaf fan'. Those with lust have the five aggregates, and Arahants who are free from lust also have the five aggregates; because of this similarity in having the five aggregates, Arahants are also called 'beings' by way of metaphorical usage. Furthermore, a name that has become established through common usage is called 'Pariṇata-ruḷhī' (customary usage). For example, one who teaches is called a 'teacher'; even when that person stops teaching, they are still called a 'teacher'. Similarly, because the term 'satta' was used while lust was present, it continues to be used for Arahants even after lust is gone; it is used by way of customary usage.
2. 'Because of connection with the quality of sattva'—here, 'sattva' refers to intelligence (buddhi), effort (vīriya), or the heat of vitality (usmā). Because of being endowed with these qualities, they are called 'sattā'. For example, a cloth is called 'blue' because it is endowed with the quality of the color blue. (Sub-commentary). In Sanskrit, it is 'sattva'.

They are called 'pāṇa' (breathing things) because they breathe; the meaning is that their existence is connected to inhalation and exhalation. They are called 'bhūta' (creatures) because they have become; the meaning is because of their well-arisen or newly manifested state. Hell is called 'pun'. They are called 'puggala' (persons) because they fall into (galanti) that hell; the meaning is they go there. 'Attabhāva' (personality) refers to the body, or the group of five aggregates, because it is the basis for the designation 'self' (atta). Why? Because it arises as a mere concept based on those five aggregates. They are called 'attabhāvapariyāpanna' because they are included (pariyāpanna) within that personality. 'Pariyāpanna' means delimited or contained within.

Note:
The name 'satta' in Pali and 'satta-wa' in Burmese have the same meaning. In this sense, it can be considered a figurative usage based on qualities (guṇūpacāra).
1. Pun (hell) + gala (going/falling) = puggala (one who goes to hell). Although this is the literal meaning, all beings are called 'puggala'. In the sub-commentary, grammarians say they are called 'puggala' because they fulfill (pūraṇa) and because they dissolve (galana).
304:
To explain further: 'Beings, when they are born in a new existence, are as if they fill up those various groups of beings. Because they fall and die at every moment, they drop away or pass away—this is the meaning of pūra + gala = puggala,' thus it is explained in another way. According to that intention, pūra (to fill) + gala (to drop away) = puggala (one who fills and drops away). This definition applies to all beings.

[304] To continue the explanation: Just like the word 'atta' (self), other words such as 'pāṇa' (breathing things) and so on should be understood as synonyms for all beings, applied by way of conventional usage (ruḷhī). Although there are other synonyms for all beings like 'jantu' (creatures) and 'jīva' (living souls), only these five terms are taken because of their prominence, and it is said: 'The liberation of mind through loving-kindness is pervaded in five ways without limitation (anodhiso).'

Those teachers who wish to distinguish the words 'satta', 'pāṇa', etc., not just by word but also by meaning, would find the unspecified pervasion (anodhiso) contradictory. (Note: If 'satta' is taken only as those with attachment (rāga), then Arahants who are free from attachment would be excluded. If 'pāṇa' is taken only as those who breathe, then Brahmas who do not breathe would be excluded. In this way, if the literal meanings are taken strictly, the pervasion would not reach all beings, and thus it would not be an 'unspecified' pervasion.) Therefore, without taking such distinctions in meaning, one should pervade unspecified loving-kindness by way of any one of these five ways.

## The Method of Counting the 528 Ways of Loving-kindness

257. In this pervasion, the thought 'May all beings be free from enmity' is one attainment (appanā). 'May they be free from ill-will' is one attainment. 'Free from ill-will' means free from the suffering of malice. 'May they be free from affliction' is one attainment. 'Free from affliction' means free from (physical) suffering. 'May they keep themselves happy' is one attainment. Therefore, among these four phrases, whichever is prominent, loving-kindness should be pervaded by way of that. Thus, in the five ways (all beings, etc.), by way of the four attainments (free from enmity, etc.), there are 20 attainments in the unspecified pervasion.

In the specified pervasion (odhiso), there are 28 attainments by way of the four qualities in the seven ways (all women, etc.). Furthermore, in this specified pervasion, 'women' and 'men' are stated by way of gender. 'Noble ones' and 'non-noble ones' are stated by way of being an ariya or a worldling (puthujjana). 'Deities', 'humans', and 'those in states of deprivation' (vinipātika) are stated by way of their mode of rebirth (upapatti).
305:
However, because it is shown in conjunction with the word 'abyāpajjha' (free from ill-will) which is pervaded to remove mental suffering, in this context, it should be taken as referring only to the remaining physical suffering.

In the directional pervasion, in the way beginning with 'In the eastern direction, may all beings...', there are 20 for each direction, totaling 200. In the way beginning with 'In the eastern direction, may all women...', there are 28 for each direction, totaling 280. Thus, there are 480 attainments. In this manner, all the attainments taught in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (20 unspecified + 28 specified + 480 directional) amount to 528. This concludes one part.

## The 11 Benefits of Loving-kindness

As just explained, by developing the liberation of mind through loving-kindness by way of any one of these 528 attainments, the practitioner (yogāvacara) gains the 11 benefits taught in the way beginning with 'He sleeps happily'.

[305] 258. Therein, 'He sleeps happily' means that while other people (who have not attained the liberation of mind through loving-kindness) sleep with difficulty, tossing and turning and snoring (making the sound 'gharu-gharu'), he sleeps happily without such difficulty. Even when fallen asleep, he is as if he has entered a meditative attainment. (1)

'He wakes happily' means that while others wake with difficulty, moaning, stretching, and tossing, he wakes happily without such difficulty, like a lotus flower blooming, without any bodily disturbance. (2)

'He sees no evil dreams' means that even if he dreams, he sees only auspicious dreams, as if he were worshipping a shrine, making an offering, or listening to the Dhamma. Unlike others who dream of being surrounded by thieves, harassed by wild beasts like tigers, or falling down a precipice, he does not see such evil dreams. (3)

'He is dear to humans' means he is loved and cherished by people, like a pearl necklace hanging on the chest or a flower garland worn on the head. (4)

'He is dear to non-humans' means he is dear to non-humans just as he is to humans, like the Elder Visākha.

That Elder Visākha, it is said, was a householder in the city of Pāṭaliputta (before ordaining). Living there, he heard: 'The island of Tambapaṇṇi is adorned with garlands of shrines and glows with yellow robes. There, in whatever place one desires, it is possible to sit or lie down. Everything is easily available there: suitable climate, suitable lodgings, suitable people, and the suitability for hearing the Dhamma.'

He handed over his wealth to his wife and children and left his home with only one kahāpaṇa tied in the hem of his garment. He stayed at the seacoast for one month waiting for a ship. Because of his skill in commerce, by buying goods in one place and selling them in another through righteous trade, he accumulated a thousand (kahāpaṇas) within that month. In due course, he arrived at the Mahāvihāra and requested ordination.
306:
While the householder Visākha was living in Pāṭaliputta, he heard the news: "The island of Sīhaḷadīpa is adorned with a succession of pagodas; it glows with the radiance of saffron robes. In that island of Sīhaḷadīpa, one can sit or lie down in any place one desires. All suitable conditions (sappāya)—the right climate, the right dwellings, the right persons, and the right hearing of the Dhamma—are easily found on that island."

The householder Visākha handed over his wealth to his wife and children and left home, carrying only a single bag of coins tied to the hem of his garment. Upon reaching the seaport, he had to wait a month for a ship. During that time, being skilled in trade, he bought goods from one place and sold them in another. Through righteous trade, he accumulated a thousand coins within that month. Thereafter, he proceeded to the Mahāvihāra monastery and requested ordination.

[306] When he was being led to the ordination hall (sīmā) to be ordained, the bag of a thousand coins fell from his waist. When asked, "What is this?" he replied, "It is a thousand coins, venerable sirs." The Saṅgha said, "Lay follower, from the time you become a monk, it will not be possible to manage this. Dispose of this money now." He said, "Let those who have come to the place of Visākha's ordination not go away empty-handed," and untying the bag, he scattered the coins on the ground within the precinct of the ordination hall (sīmā-māḷaka). Then he was ordained and attained the status of a bhikkhu.

After five years (vassa), having mastered the two Matikas (Dve Mātikā) and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, he took a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for himself. He then wandered about, staying for exactly four months at each monastery. While wandering in this manner—

The Elder Visākha, seeking his own virtues, stood in the midst of the forest and roared like a lion, uttering these words:
"Since the time I was ordained, and since the time I came into this forest, there has been no lapse in my conduct. Oh, Visākha, how great and noble are the gains and virtues you have attained!"

As the Elder Visākha was traveling to the Cittalapabbata monastery, he reached a fork in the road and stood there considering, "Is this the path to take, or is it that one?" Then, a deity residing on the mountain stretched out a hand and pointed, saying, "This is the path." The Elder Visākha went to the Cittalapabbata monastery and stayed there for four months. Thinking, "I will depart at dawn," he lay down. A tree deity residing in a Maṇila (rose-apple) tree at the head of the walkway sat on the step of the ladder and wept bitterly.

The Elder asked, "Who is this?" "I am the deity of the Maṇila tree, venerable sir," it replied. "Why are you weeping?" he asked. "Because of your departure, venerable sir," it replied. "What benefit do you gain by my staying here?" he asked. "Venerable sir, while you reside here, the non-humans (amanussa) treat each other with loving-kindness. Now, when you depart, they will quarrel and speak harsh and coarse words," it replied. The Elder Visākha said, "If my staying here allows you to live in comfort, then it is well," and he stayed there for another four months. Again, he planned to depart as before.
307:
The deity wept bitterly again in the same manner. In this way, the Elder Visākha remained in that very place and attained Parinibbāna there. As described, a monk who dwells in loving-kindness is dear to non-humans. (5)

Deities protect him—this means that deities protect him just as parents protect their child. (6)

[307] Fire, poison, or weapons cannot harm the body of one who develops loving-kindness—this means that fire does not burn or affect the body of one who dwells in loving-kindness, just as it did not burn the laywoman named Uttarā. Poison does not affect him, as in the case of the Elder Cūḷasiva, the reciter of the Saṃyutta Nikāya. Weapons do not harm him—they do not cut or penetrate—as in the case of the novice Saṅkicca. It means "they cannot destroy the body of one who develops loving-kindness." In this regard, they also tell the story of a mother cow with her calf. It is said that a certain mother cow stood giving milk to her calf. A hunter, intending to stab her, took aim and threw a long-handled spear with great force. The spear struck the cow's body but curled up like a palm leaf. This happened not by the power of access concentration (upacāra) or absorption concentration (appanā), but solely through the power of her strong love for her calf. Loving-kindness has such great power. (7)

The mind is quickly concentrated—this means that the mind of one who dwells in loving-kindness is concentrated very quickly. There is no sluggishness in that concentration. (8)

The facial expression is serene—this means that the face of one who develops loving-kindness has an exceptionally clear and bright complexion, like a ripe palm fruit that has just fallen from its stalk. (9)

He dies unconfused—this means that for one who dwells in loving-kindness, there is no such thing as a confused death. He dies without confusion, as if falling asleep. (10)

If he does not penetrate or attain the higher paths and fruits—this means that if he is unable to attain the fruit of Arahatship, which is higher than the attainment of loving-kindness (mettā-samāpatti), then upon passing away from this human life, he is reborn in the Brahma world, like one waking from sleep. (11) Here ends one section.

The preceding words are the detailed explanation of the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā).

## 2. Explanation of the Development of Compassion (Karuṇā-bhāvanā)

259. One who wishes to develop compassion should begin the development of compassion after reflecting on the danger of being heartless and the benefits of compassion. When beginning that development, one should not start with a dear person (piya-puggala) and so on. Indeed, a dear person remains in the position of a dear person;¹ a very dear friend remains in the position of a very dear friend; a neutral person remains in the position of a neutral person; an unpleasant person remains in the position of an unpleasant person; and an enemy remains in the position of an enemy. Those of a different gender and those who are deceased are not the proper objects. Rather:

"And how does a monk dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with compassion? Just as he would feel compassion upon seeing a person who is in distress and in a wretched condition, [308] so too..."

Note:
1. For one who strives to develop compassion for a dear person, the state of being a dear person cannot be avoided at the very beginning.
308:
If the state of being a beloved person is not absent, how can compassion (karuṇā) be developed? Therefore, the commentator states, "It stands only in the place of the beloved." (Ṭīkā) It is also indicated in that Ṭīkā that the same should be understood for the remaining individuals.

2. This is the meaning of 'durūpetaṃ'. Here, 'a bad or evil condition' refers to a visibly bad condition as well as evil unwholesome deeds. In the Ṭīkā, one who is endowed with bodily misconduct, etc., is explained as 'durūpeta'.

Because it is stated in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga, "In this way, one pervades all beings with compassion," one should first of all arouse compassion towards a person who has reached great suffering, who is of a nature deserving compassion (i.e., pitiable), who is destitute, and in an evil condition—such as a helpless, lonely man, deprived of food, sitting in a rest-house for the destitute with a begging bowl placed before him, seeing worms oozing from his leprous hands and feet, and groaning in intense pain—thinking, "Alas, this being has fallen into misery; if only he were free from this suffering!"

If such a person is not found, one should arouse compassion even for a happy person if they are an evildoer, by comparing them to a person about to be executed.

How? For example, by the king's command to "Kill him!", royal officers bind a thief caught with stolen goods and, beating him with hundreds of lashes at every crossroads, lead him to the place of execution. People give that thief snacks, food, flowers, perfumes, ointments, and betel. Although that thief goes along eating and enjoying those things as if endowed with wealth and enjoyment, no one thinks, "This man is happy and possesses great wealth." On the contrary, people feel compassion for that thief, reflecting, "This wretch is about to die now. With every step he takes, he draws closer and closer to death." In the same way, a monk practicing the meditation on compassion should arouse compassion even for a happy person who is an evildoer, reflecting, "This wretch, although now happy, well-dressed, and enjoying wealth, will soon experience much suffering and grief in the states of deprivation (apāya) because of the absence of any good deed performed through even one of the three doors (of action)."

Having thus developed compassion for that (pitiable) person, one should then proceed in the same manner towards a dear person, then towards a neutral person, and then towards an enemy, in that order. If, however, resentment (paṭigha) arises in this yogi towards the enemy in the manner previously mentioned, it should be subsided using the same method described in the section on loving-kindness (mettā). Furthermore, among these persons for whom compassion is developed, even if one has many performed merits, if one sees or hears that they are encountering one of the ruins (vyasana) such as ruin of relatives, ruin of health, or ruin of wealth—or even if they do not encounter such ruins, because they have not yet transcended the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha)—one should arouse compassion in every way, reflecting, "This person is indeed in suffering." Then, having broken the boundaries (sīmāsambheda) among the four persons—namely, oneself, the dear person, the neutral person, and the enemy—one should [309] cultivate and frequently practice that sign (nimitta) and develop absorption (appanā) through the power of the three and four jhanas, just as described in the section on loving-kindness.
309:
Having established the boundary-breaking, one who frequents, develops, and cultivates that sign should increase the absorption (appanā) by way of the three and four jhanas, just as described in the section on loving-kindness.

However, in the Aṅguttara Commentary, this sequence is stated: "First, compassion should be developed towards an enemy; having softened the mind towards that enemy, then towards a destitute person, then towards a dear person, and then towards oneself." This statement does not agree with the Vibhaṅga Pali, which says, "(as one would feel compassion upon seeing) a destitute person in an evil condition." Therefore, one should begin the meditation only in the manner already described, and after breaking the boundaries, increase the absorption.

Thereafter, the various ways of pervading compassion, such as "unspecified pervasion in five ways, specified pervasion in seven ways, and directional pervasion in ten ways," as well as the benefits such as "sleeping happily," etc., should be understood in the same way as described in the section on loving-kindness. This concludes this section.

This is the detailed explanation of the development of compassion (karuṇā-bhāvanā).

## 3. Explanation of the Development of Appreciative Joy (Muditā)

260. A person beginning the development of appreciative joy (muditā-bhāvanā) should also not start with a dear person and so on. Indeed, a dear person does not become the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) of appreciative joy merely by being dear; how much less so for a neutral person or an enemy. Those of the opposite sex or those who have passed away are not the field for appreciative joy at all.

Note: 1. Even if someone is a dear person, if they are not endowed with special qualities such as having a cheerful face, being the first to greet, speaking pleasantly, or speaking in a way that brings joy and harmony, or if they are not endowed with joyful circumstances such as prosperity, they do not become the proximate cause of muditā. If they are joyful and happy, being endowed with such special qualities, then muditā can be developed even for a dear person. This is a summary taken from the Ṭīkā.

A very dear friend, however, can be the proximate cause of muditā; such a friend is called a "boon companion" (soṇḍa-sahāya) in the Commentary. That very dear friend is indeed very joyful (or worthy of joy); he is one who laughs first and speaks later. Therefore, one should first pervade that very dear friend with muditā. Alternatively, seeing or hearing about a dear person being happy, well-prepared, and rejoicing, one should arouse appreciative joy (muditā), thinking, "How this being rejoices! Oh, how excellent! Oh, how good!"

Indeed, it is in reference to this very meaning that it is stated in the Abhidhamma Vibhaṅga: "How does a monk dwell pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by appreciative joy? Just as one would be joyful upon seeing a dear and pleasant person, in the same way, one pervades all beings with appreciative joy."

If this yogi's boon companion or dear person was happy in the past but is now destitute and in an evil condition, one should still arouse appreciative joy by recollecting their past happiness, thinking, "In the past, this person had such great wealth, a great following, and was always joyful," thus taking that aspect of joy. Or, (one may reflect) that in the future, they will again [attain] that prosperity...
310:
One should arouse appreciative joy (muditā) by reflecting only on that person’s past state of happiness, thinking: 'In the past, this person possessed such great wealth and a large retinue, and was always joyful,' thus taking up the aspect of their past joy. Furthermore, one should arouse appreciative joy by taking up the aspect of that person’s future joy, thinking: 'In the future, they will again obtain such wealth [311] and travel on the back of an elephant, the back of a horse, or in a golden palanquin.'

Having thus aroused appreciative joy towards a dear person, one should then proceed in order to a neutral person and then to an enemy. Absorption (appanā) should be developed. If, in the manner previously described, resentment arises towards an enemy, it should be subsided in the same way as described in the section on loving-kindness (mettā). Then, by making the mind equal towards the four persons—namely, oneself and these three—one should break down the barriers (sīmāsambheda). By repeating, developing, and cultivating that sign (nimitta), absorption should be developed through the three or four jhānas, just as described in the section on loving-kindness.

After that, the various ways of pervading—unspecified pervading in five ways, specified pervading in seven ways, and directional pervading in ten ways—as well as the benefits such as 'sleeping happily,' should be understood in the same way as described in the section on loving-kindness. This concludes the detailed explanation of the development of appreciative joy.

## The Development of Equanimity

261. One who wishes to develop the meditation on equanimity (upekkhā-bhāvanā) should first attain the three or four jhānas in loving-kindness and so on. Emerging from the proficient third jhāna [Note 1], one should see the disadvantages in the previous three meditations: because they are associated with the mental attention of cherishing beings in the manner of 'may they be happy,' etc.; because they are close to resentment and fawning [Note 2]; and because they are gross due to their association with joy (somanassa). Then, seeing the benefit of equanimity as being peaceful in nature, one should arouse equanimity by looking on with indifference at a person who is naturally neutral. Thereafter, towards a dear person and so on. For it is said:

'How does a monk dwell pervading one direction with a mind imbued with equanimity? Just as he would be equanimous upon seeing a person who is neither liked nor disliked, so he pervades all beings with equanimity.' (Vibhaṅga 673)

Therefore, having aroused equanimity towards a neutral person in the manner described, one should then do so towards a dear person, then a boon companion, and then an enemy. Thus, by breaking down the barriers through the mode of neutrality towards all—these three persons and oneself—one should repeat, develop, and cultivate that sign. For one who does so, the fourth jhāna arises in the same manner as described in the earth kasiṇa.

Notes:
1. Connect as: 'Emerging from the third jhāna... seeing the defects... seeing the benefits... one should arouse equanimity by looking on with indifference.'

Thereafter, the various ways of developing equanimity and the acquisition of benefits should be understood in the same way as described for loving-kindness. This concludes one part. This discourse is the detailed explanation of the development of equanimity.

## Miscellaneous Discussion

262. Having understood these Divine Abodes (Brahmavihāra) as taught by the Buddha, the Supreme Brahma, one should further understand this miscellaneous discussion regarding them.

## Etymological Definitions

Among these—loving-kindness (mettā), compassion (karuṇā), appreciative joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekkhā)—firstly, according to the meaning of the words: It is called mettā because it loves by way of desiring welfare (or desiring happiness). (Note: Derived from the root mid, to love, + suffix ta). Alternatively, it is called mettā because it occurs in a friend (mitta). Alternatively, this nature of desiring happiness is the state of occurring in a friend (mitta); therefore, it is called mettā.

When there is suffering of others, it causes the hearts of good people to tremble; thus it is called karuṇā. (Note: Derived from the root kar + suffix una, meaning compassion that makes the heart tremble). Alternatively, it is called karuṇā because it harasses or removes the suffering of others. (Note: Derived from the root kir + suffix una). Alternatively, it is called karuṇā because it is extended towards those in distress by way of pervading them.

Those endowed with muditā rejoice by means of it (with its help); because it is the cause of such rejoicing, it is called muditā. (Note: Derived from the root mud + suffix ta; only the virtuous can rejoice in others' prosperity). Alternatively, it is called muditā because it rejoices. Alternatively, muditā is merely the state of rejoicing.

It is called upekkhā because it looks on with equality, without taking sides, by abandoning concern such as 'May they be free from enmity' and by arriving at a neutral state.

## Characteristics and So Forth

263. Regarding these, loving-kindness (mettā) has the characteristic of occurring as the mode of promoting welfare. Its function (rasa) is to bring about welfare. It is manifested (paccupaṭṭhāna) as the removal of resentment. Its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is seeing the lovableness of beings. Its success is the subsiding of ill-will; its failure is the production of selfish affection.

Compassion (karuṇā) has the characteristic of occurring as the mode of removing the suffering of others. Its function is the inability to endure the suffering of others. It is manifested as non-cruelty (or the opposite of cruelty). Its proximate cause is seeing the helplessness of those overwhelmed by suffering. Its success is the subsiding of cruelty; its failure is the production of sorrow.

Appreciative joy (muditā) has the characteristic of rejoicing in the prosperity of others. Its function is the absence of envy. It is manifested as the removal of aversion (to others' success). Its proximate cause is seeing the prosperity of beings. Its success is the subsiding of aversion; its failure is the production of merry-making (frivolous joy).

Equanimity (upekkhā) has the characteristic of occurring as the mode of neutrality (Note: If the reading is majjhaṭṭhākāra, it is more appropriate, meaning 'the mode of standing in the middle'). Its function is seeing equality in beings. It is manifested as the subsiding of both resentment and approval. Its proximate cause is reflecting thus: 'Beings are owners of their kamma; [312] by whose will shall they become happy, or be released from suffering, or not decline from the prosperity they have reached?'

The subsiding of resentment and fawning towards beings is the success (sampatti) of that equanimity. ## Benefits

264. Furthermore, the happiness of insight (vipassanā-sukha) and the attainment of a fortunate rebirth (bhava-sampatti) are the common benefits of all four of these Divine Abidings (brahma-vihāra). The abandonment of ill-will and so forth, and the distancing from ill-will and so forth, are their specific (unshared) benefits. To elaborate: among these four, loving-kindness (mettā) has the benefit of distancing from ill-will (byāpāda) and anger (dosa). The other three have, respectively, the benefits of distancing from cruelty (vihiᅃsā), aversion (arati), and lust (rāga). Indeed, there is the following scriptural evidence:

‘Friends, that which is the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti) is the escape (nissaraᅃa) from ill-will. Friends, that which is the deliverance of mind through compassion (karuᅃā cetovimutti) is the escape from cruelty (vihesā). Friends, that which is the deliverance of mind through appreciative joy (muditā cetovimutti) is the escape from aversion (arati). Friends, that which is the deliverance of mind through equanimity (upekkhā cetovimutti) is the escape from lust (rāga).’

## Enemies

265. Among these four Divine Abidings, each has two enemies: a near enemy and a distant enemy. To elaborate: lust (rāga) is the near enemy of the Divine Abiding of loving-kindness (mettā) because it shares the quality of seeing virtues, like an enemy lurking near a person. That lust easily finds an opportunity to enter; therefore, loving-kindness must be well-guarded against that near enemy, lust. Ill-will (byāpāda) or anger (dosa) is the distant enemy, like an enemy of a person staying in a difficult place such as a mountain, because it is dissimilar to the similar nature [of lust] (or: because it has a nature dissimilar to mettā). Therefore, one should develop loving-kindness without fear of that distant enemy, ill-will. (The reason for not having to fear is that) it is impossible for one to develop loving-kindness and give way to anger at the same time.

Lust (rāga) and resentment (paṭigha) are the far enemies because they are dissimilar. Therefore, one should practice equanimity without fear of them. ## The Beginning, Middle, End, and the Expansion of the Object

266. For all these divine abodes, the beginning and root is the wholesome desire (chanda) to produce them. The middle is the suppression of the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) and so forth. The end is the attainment of absorption (appanā). The object is either a single being or many beings by way of the concept of beings (paññatti-dhamma). The expansion of the object occurs when reaching either access concentration (upacāra) or absorption (appanā).

Here is the order of expansion: Just as a skilled farmer marks out the area to be ploughed and then ploughs it, so too, at the very beginning, one should mark out a single dwelling and develop loving-kindness towards the beings in that dwelling, thinking, 'May the beings in this dwelling be free from enmity,' and so forth. Having made the mind soft and workable regarding the beings in that dwelling, one should then mark out two dwellings. Then, in succession, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten dwellings, then one street, half a village, a whole village, a district, a kingdom, one direction, and so on, until the entire universe or even beyond.
314:
Beyond that, or [specifically] towards beings existing in various directions [314], one should develop loving-kindness (metta). Likewise with compassion (karuṇā) and the others. This is the sequence for expanding the object in these divine abidings (brahmavihāras).

## The Resultant Benefit (Nissanda)

267. Furthermore, just as the formless attainments (āruppas) are the result issuing from the kasiṇa meditations, just as the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the result issuing from the concentration of the fine-material sphere and the lower formless concentrations, just as the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) is the result issuing from insight (vipassanā), and just as the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is the result issuing from serenity and insight (samatha-vipassanā), so too, among these four divine abidings, the divine abiding of equanimity (upekkhā) is the result issuing from the combination of the preceding three divine abidings. To illustrate with an analogy: just as it is impossible to set up the roof-peaks and rafters in the air without having erected the pillars and laid the beams, so too, it is impossible to develop the fourth divine abiding without the third jhāna obtained in the preceding three divine abidings. Here ends one part.

## Why They Are Called Divine Abidings, etc.

268. In this regard, the following questions may arise: Why are these—loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—called divine abidings (brahmavihāras)? Why are there only four? What is their sequence? And why are they called 'immeasurables' (appamaññā) in the Abhidhamma?

The answer is: Firstly, their status as divine abidings should be understood by way of their noble meaning and their faultlessness. To elaborate, these abidings (vihāras) are particularly praised and noble because they constitute the right and good practice towards beings. Furthermore, just as the Brahmas dwell with minds free from faults (such as the hindrances), so too, the meditators associated with these [qualities] dwell as equals to the Brahmas. Thus, they are called divine abidings because of their noble meaning and their faultlessness.

269. The answer to the question 'Why are there only four?' and so on, is as follows:

They are only four by way of the path of purification, etc.,
Their sequence is by way of the modes of welfare, etc.,
They occur in an immeasurable [object],
By which they are called 'immeasurables' in their range.

To elaborate: Among these, loving-kindness is the path of purification for one who is prone to ill-will (byāpāda) or anger. Compassion is the path of purification for one who is prone to cruelty (vihesā). Appreciative joy is the path of purification for one who is prone to discontent or envy (arati). Equanimity is the path of purification for one who is prone to lust (rāga). (Thus, they are only four because they are the four paths of purification for these four types of persons.) Furthermore, the mental attention towards beings is only fourfold by way of: bringing welfare, removing harm and misfortune, rejoicing in their success and prosperity, and not being biased (non-interference). (For this reason also, they are only four.) Moreover, just as a mother, among her four sons—namely, a young child, a sick child, an adolescent, and one busy with his own affairs—desires the growth of the young child, desires the removal of the illness of the sick child, desires the long-lasting youthfulness and prosperity of the adolescent, and does not worry about the one busy with his own affairs in any particular turn of events; so too, a monk who dwells in the immeasurables called the divine abidings should act towards all beings by way of developing loving-kindness and so on. Therefore, by way of this path of purification and so on, the immeasurables are only four.
315:
[315] (As for their sequence:) One who wishes to develop these four immeasurables should first practice towards beings with the intention of promoting their welfare; and loving-kindness (metta) has the characteristic of occurring as the mode of promoting welfare. Then, seeing, hearing, or considering the affliction of suffering in those beings for whom welfare was thus desired (such as in hell, etc.), one should practice with the intention of removing that suffering; and compassion (karuṇā) has the characteristic of occurring as the mode of removing suffering. Thereafter, seeing the success and prosperity of those beings whose welfare was desired and whose suffering has ceased as wished, one should practice with the intention of rejoicing in that success; and appreciative joy (muditā) has the characteristic of rejoicing. After that, because there is nothing further to be done, one should practice with the mode of neutrality known as looking on (or: staying in the middle without taking sides¹); and equanimity (upekkhā) has the characteristic of occurring as the mode of neutrality. Therefore, by way of these modes such as promoting welfare, loving-kindness is taught first among them. Then compassion, then appreciative joy, and then equanimity—this is how the sequence should be understood.

The reason for calling them 'immeasurables' (appamaññā) is that all these—loving-kindness, compassion, appreciative joy, and equanimity—occur towards an immeasurable object. Indeed, immeasurable beings are the objects of these [qualities]. Even for a single being, one does not limit it by saying 'loving-kindness, etc., should be developed only in this much of a portion,' but they occur only by way of pervading the whole [being]. (Therefore, they are called immeasurables.) Thus it was said:

'They are only four by way of the path of purification, etc.,
Their sequence is by way of the modes of welfare, etc.,
They occur in an immeasurable [object],
By which they are called "immeasurables" in their range.'

## The Attainable Jhānas

270. Although they have the single characteristic of having an immeasurable object as described, among these four immeasurables, the first three can only produce the group of the first three or four jhānas. Why? Because they are always associated with joy (somanassa). Why are these three associated with joy? Because they are the escape from—the removal of—ill-will, cruelty, and discontent, which are originated by grief (domanassa). The last one, equanimity, can only produce the remaining single jhāna (the fourth or fifth).

Why? Because it is associated with the feeling of equanimity (upekkhā-vedanā). Indeed, the divine abiding of equanimity, which occurs as the mode of neutrality towards beings, cannot occur without the feeling of equanimity. Here ends one part.

## Explanation to Avoid Misconception

271. 'In the Aṅguttara Nikāya, Book of the Eights, the Blessed One taught generally without distinction regarding the four immeasurables:

"Then, monk, you should develop this concentration with initial thought and sustained thought (savitakka savicāra); you should develop it without initial thought but with sustained thought only (avitakka vicāramatta); you should develop it without initial thought and without sustained thought (avitakka avicāra); you should develop it with rapture (sappītika); you should develop it without rapture (nippītika); you should develop it accompanied by pleasure (sāta-sahagata); you should develop it accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata)." [316]

Therefore, the four immeasurables can produce the group of the four or five jhānas'—if anyone were to say thus,
316:
One should tell that person, "Do not say such a thing." Indeed, if one were to take the general teaching as it is, the four foundations of mindfulness such as contemplation of the body would also result in the group of four or five jhanas. However, in the contemplation of feelings and so on, even the first jhana does not exist, let alone the second jhana and others. Therefore, do not misrepresent the Blessed One by merely grasping the shadow of the words (the literal sound). The word of the Buddha is indeed profound; that profound word of the Buddha should be grasped according to its intended meaning after approaching and attending upon teachers.

272. To elaborate further—this is the intended meaning of that word of the Buddha:

“Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief. It would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute.”

A certain monk requested the Blessed One to teach him the Dhamma in this way. It is said that this monk had previously made such a request and heard the Dhamma, but instead of going to the forest to practice the Dhamma of a recluse, he remained right there. Therefore, the Blessed One rebuked him, saying, “In this way, some vain men (mogha-purisa) only request me for the Dhamma, and when the Dhamma is spoken, they think they should only keep following me.” Then, seeing that the monk possessed the supporting conditions (upanissaya) for the attainment of Arahatship, the Blessed One advised him:

“Therefore, monk, you should train yourself thus: ‘My mind will be steady and well-settled internally (ajjhatta), and arisen evil unwholesome states will not remain overwhelming my mind.’ Thus, monk, you should train yourself.”

By this advice, “original concentration” (mūla-samādhi), which is mere one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā), is spoken of by way of one’s own internal states (niyakajjhatta).

Notes:
1. Ajjhatta—here means in the meditation object (gocarajjhatta). (Ṭīkā)
2. The mind will be steady—means it will be steady in the state of having a single object without wandering to external objects; therefore, it is well-settled. (Ṭīkā) To put it simply in Burmese, it means one should practice with the resolution: “It must be steady, it must be well-settled.”
3. Unwholesome states overwhelming the mind—this refers to the occurrence of only unwholesome consciousness together with unwholesome states, without the opportunity for wholesome consciousness to arise. Therefore, regarding (cittaṃ pariyādāya) “overwhelming the mind,” the commentaries explain it as “exhausting the wholesome mind”; this is the intended meaning.
4. In this context, there is the phrase “niyakajjhatta-vasena”—by way of one’s own internal states. Niyakajjhatta refers to the mental and physical phenomena within each individual.

This refers to the original concentration (mūla-samādhi) which is mere one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā) of that monk.

Notes:
According to that view, one must take the concentration that stands while contemplating the internal phenomena of one’s own body. However, in this context, all meditation objects, whether internal or external, should be taken. Therefore, in the Ṭīkā, the word ajjhatta is explained as the meditation object called gocarajjhatta. Then, it explains the text in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā) as saying “niyakajjhatta-vasena” because one-pointedness of mind is internal to one’s own continuity. However, since there is no one-pointedness of mind that is not niyakajjhatta, that explanation is also difficult to accept. Therefore, in the Visuddhimagga, the original text in this place might have been “gocarajjhatta-vasena.”

1. Cittekaggatā-matto—concentration which is mere one-pointedness of mind refers to the steadiness (samādhāna) that has just been attained by one who strives in meditation and has not yet been very well developed. It is called “original concentration” (mūla-samādhi) because it is the root cause for the specific types of concentration to be mentioned later. This concentration, which is mere one-pointedness, should be understood as momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi). (How is it so?) It is like in the teachings such as: “I make the mind well-settled, well-situated only internally (in the meditation object), I make it have the limit of a single steadiness, I keep it well.” To illustrate with an example: “Monks, my energy was exerted and did not slacken... etc... the mind was well-placed and one-pointed.”

Then, in order to show that “one should not be satisfied with just this much but should develop that same original concentration as follows”:

“Monk, when your mind is steady and well-settled internally (in the meditation object), and arisen evil unwholesome states do not remain overwhelming your mind; then, monk, you should train yourself: ‘My liberation of mind through loving-kindness (mettā cetovimutti) will be developed, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and well-perfected.’ Thus, monk, you should train yourself.” Having thus spoken of the development by way of loving-kindness, He again said: “Monk, when this concentration is thus developed and cultivated by you, then, monk, you should develop this original concentration with initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra)... etc... you should develop it accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā).”

The meaning is: Monk, when this original concentration has been thus developed by you by way of loving-kindness, then, without being satisfied with just that much, you [should develop] this...
317:
At that time, you should train yourself thus: 'The deliverance of mind through loving-kindness (mettā-cetovimutti) will be developed by me, cultivated, made much of, made a vehicle, made a basis, established, consolidated, and properly undertaken.' Thus, bhikkhu, you should train yourself." In this way, He taught the development of meditation (bhāvanā) to that bhikkhu by way of loving-kindness. Having taught thus:

"Bhikkhu, when this concentration (samādhi) has been thus developed and made much of by you..."

Note:
After saying, "I have had an object," He taught the words beginning with, "Quite secluded from sensual pleasures... [etc.] ...having reached and dwelling in the first jhāna." Therefore, just as in other teachings the initial one-pointedness of mind is known as momentary concentration (khaṇika-samādhi), so too in this teaching of instruction, the mere concentration of one-pointedness of mind taught as "my mind will be established" etc., should be known as momentary concentration. (Ṭīkā)

"At that time, you should develop this original concentration (mūla-samādhi) so that it is with initial thought and sustained thought... [etc.] ...and develop it so that it is accompanied by equanimity."

The intended meaning of that teaching is: "Bhikkhu, when this original concentration has been developed by you by way of loving-kindness as just described, at that time, not being satisfied with just that much—

[317] you should develop this original concentration even in other objects (such as the earth kasiṇa, etc.), bringing it to the group of four jhānas or five jhānas, so that it is with initial thought and sustained thought, and so on."

Furthermore, having taught thus, He again wished to show the bhikkhu the development by way of the group of four or five jhānas in other objects (such as the earth kasiṇa, etc.), preceded by the remaining three divine abodes (Brahmavihāra) such as compassion (karuṇā):

"Bhikkhu, when this concentration has been thus developed and made much of by you, then you should train yourself thus: 'The deliverance of mind through compassion (karuṇā-cetovimutti) will be developed by me...'"

Thus He taught, and so on.

Having thus shown the development by way of the group of four or five jhānas preceded by loving-kindness and so on, He again, in order to show the development preceded by the contemplation of the body (kāyānupassanā) and so on, said:

"Bhikkhu, when this concentration has been thus developed and made much of by you, then you should train yourself thus: 'I will dwell contemplating the body in the body...'"

Having taught thus, He said:

"Bhikkhu, when this concentration has been thus developed and well-developed by you, then, bhikkhu, wherever you go, you will go in comfort; wherever you stand, you will stand in comfort; wherever you sit, you will sit in comfort; wherever you lie down, you will lie down in comfort."

Thus, He concluded the teaching by culminating it in the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala). Therefore, it should be known that the first three divine abodes, such as loving-kindness, can only produce the group of three or four jhānas, while equanimity (upekkhā) can only produce the remaining single jhāna. Indeed, it is analyzed in that same way in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka.

## Subhaparamā and so on

273. In this way, the distinct and dissimilar powers of these four divine abodes, which stand in two ways—by the power of being able to produce the three or four jhānas, and by the power of being able to produce the remaining single jhāna—should be known by way of the deliverance of mind (cetovimutti) having the beautiful (subha) as its supreme, and so on. Indeed, in the Haliddavasana Sutta, these deliverances of mind through loving-kindness and so on are taught specifically as having the beautiful as the supreme, and so on. As it was said:

"Bhikkhus, I say that the deliverance of mind through loving-kindness has the beautiful (subhaparamā) as its supreme. Bhikkhus, I say that the deliverance of mind through compassion has the base of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-paramā) as its supreme. Bhikkhus, I say that the deliverance of mind through appreciative joy has the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana-paramā) as its supreme. Bhikkhus, I say that the deliverance of mind through equanimity has the base of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana-paramā) as its supreme."

[318] To explain further by raising a question: Why are these deliverances of mind taught in this way?

Note:
1. Connect with "the distinct powers of these four divine abodes."

Because they serve as the supporting condition (upanissaya) for those respective deliverances (such as the beautiful deliverance, etc.).
318:
To explain in detail—for one who habitually dwells in loving-kindness (mettā), beings are not repulsive but are lovable. When such a perception arises, because of the familiarity with non-repulsiveness, when directing the mind to the pure colors of blue, yellow, red, and white, the mind enters into those pure color kasinas easily, without difficulty or hardship. For this reason, loving-kindness is the proximate cause (upanissaya) for the beautiful liberation (subha-vimokkha), and not for anything beyond that. Therefore, it is said that it has the beautiful as its highest.

Furthermore, for one who habitually dwells in compassion (karuṇā), as they contemplate the suffering that can occur to beings—such as the physical suffering caused by being struck with a stick—the fault in materiality (rūpa) becomes very evident. When the fault in materiality is thus clearly known, having removed one of the material kasinas such as the earth kasina, and directing the mind to the concept of space (ākāsa-paññatti) which is the escape from materiality, the mind enters into that concept of space easily, without difficulty or hardship.
Note: According to the Ṭīkā, the reading 'satta-dukkhaṃ' is appropriate.
For this reason, compassion is the proximate cause for the attainment of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana), and not for anything beyond that. Therefore, it is said that it has the sphere of infinite space as its highest.

Furthermore, for one who habitually dwells in appreciative joy (muditā), as they contemplate the consciousness of beings who are joyful due to various causes of joy, the mind becomes familiar with grasping consciousness. When that happens, having passed the sphere of infinite space attained through the sequence of meditation, and directing the mind to the consciousness (of the sphere of infinite space) which has the concept of space as its object, the mind enters into that consciousness easily, without difficulty or hardship. For this reason, appreciative joy is the proximate cause for the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), and not for anything beyond that. Therefore, it is said that it has the sphere of infinite consciousness as its highest.

Furthermore, for one who habitually dwells in equanimity (upekkhā), because of the absence of the concern 'may beings be happy,' or 'may they be free from suffering,' or 'may they not be parted from the prosperity they have attained,' and because of the turning away from grasping ultimate reality (paramattha), the mind becomes skilled in grasping the concept (paññatti) that is not present (non-existent). When that happens, for one whose mind is familiar with turning away from grasping ultimate reality and whose mind is skilled in grasping what is not present in the ultimate sense, having passed the sphere of infinite consciousness attained through the sequence of meditation, and directing the mind to the non-existence (abhāva) of the consciousness that was an ultimate reality, the mind enters into that concept of non-existence easily, without difficulty or hardship. For this reason, equanimity is the proximate cause for the attainment of the sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), and not for anything beyond that. Therefore, it is said that it has the sphere of nothingness as its highest.
Note: The Burmese version of Visuddhimagga has 'sampatta-sukhato vā mā vimuccantu,' which should be translated as 'may they not be liberated from the prosperity they have attained.' The Siamese version has 'mā viyujjiṃsu' instead of 'mā vimuccantu.' This translation follows the sense of 'mā viyujjiṃsu.' This also indicates that the muditā passage 'yathāladdha-sampattito mā vigacchantu' is appropriate. The term 'skilled' (dakha) is based on the Sinhalese reading 'avijjamānaggahaṇe dakkhaṃ.'

## Fulfilling the Perfections and Other Qualities
274. Having thus understood the power of these divine abidings in terms of having the beautiful as the highest, etc., it should further be understood that all of these also fulfill all the good and noble qualities such as giving (dāna). [319] To explain in detail—through the desire for the welfare of beings,
319:
through the inability to endure the suffering of beings, through the desire for the long-lasting of the special prosperity attained by beings, and through the mind that proceeds impartially towards all beings, Great Beings (Bodhisattas) do not make distinctions such as 'this person should be given to, this person should not be given to,' and they give the gift (dāna) which is the root of happiness to all beings who come to them. Avoiding the harming of all those beings, they undertake virtue (sīla). To fulfill the perfection of virtue, they resort to renunciation (nekkhamma). For the sake of non-delusion regarding the welfare and harm of beings, they purify their wisdom (paññā). For the sake of the welfare and happiness of beings, they constantly arouse energy (viriya). Even when they have reached the state of heroism through the power of supreme energy, they endure (khanti) the various kinds of offenses committed by beings without retaliating. They do not fail in the promise (sacca) they have made, saying, 'We will give this to you, we will do this for you.' They have unwavering determination (adhiṭṭhāna) for the welfare and happiness of all those beings. They are the first to help those beings with unwavering loving-kindness (mettā). Through equanimity (upekkhā), they do not expect or desire anything in return. In this manner, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), they completely fulfill all the good and noble qualities, including the ten powers (dasabala), the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja), the six unshared knowledges (asādhāraṇa-ñāṇa), and the eighteen Buddha-qualities (buddhadhamma). Therefore, these divine abidings indeed fulfill all the good and noble qualities such as the perfection of giving. This concludes this section.

This is the Ninth Chapter, called the Exposition of the Divine Abidings (Brahmavihāra-niddesa), in the section on the Development of Concentration in the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga), composed for the purpose of gladdening good people.

## The Exposition of the Divine Abidings is Finished.

## 10. Āruppa-niddesa: Exposition of the Four Immaterial States
## 1. Explanation of the First Immaterial State: The Sphere of Infinite Space
[320] 275.
320:
## 10. Description of the Formless States (Āruppa-niddesa)
### Description of the First Formless State
275. Among the four formless states mentioned immediately after the Divine Abidings (Brahmavihāra), a person who wishes to develop the first one, the Base of Infinite Space (Ākāsānañcāyatana), reflects as follows: "It is because of the physical body (rūpa) that the taking up of sticks, the taking up of weapons, quarrels, strife, disputes, and accusations occur. None of these exist in the formless realm, which is entirely without form." Having reflected thus, as it is said: "He practices for the sake of disenchantment with, the fading away of, and the cessation of those very forms" (M. Ni. 2.103). Seeing the danger in this physical body (karaja-rūpa) through such things as the taking up of sticks and through the thousands of afflictions such as diseases of the eye and ear, and wishing to transcend it, he produces the fourth jhāna in any one of the nine kasinas, such as the earth kasina, excluding the limited-space kasina.

(Note 1: The sentence structure connects "the person who wishes... seeing the danger... produces the fourth jhāna in one of the kasinas.")
(Note 2: The term 'karaja-rūpa' literally means the body produced from semen and blood. However, the commentary explains it as the 'gross body' to show it as the basis for all aforementioned dangers. Thus, it is translated here as the physical or gross body for clarity.)

Although that meditator has already transcended the gross physical body by the power of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere, the kasina-form (kasiṇa-rūpa) is still similar to it. Therefore, he wishes to transcend that kasina-form as well. How? Just as a man who is afraid of snakes, being pursued by a snake in the forest, runs away swiftly; and in the place where he has fled and escaped, if he sees a palm leaf with painted lines, or a creeper, or a rope, or a crack in the parched earth, he is afraid and terrified, and does not wish even to look at it.

(Note 1: He has already transcended the gross physical body because he no longer directs his attention to it. One might ask why it is specified 'by the power of the fourth jhāna' when the first jhāna and others also do not attend to the gross body as they focus on the counterpart sign. While this is true, it is the fourth jhāna that reaches the state of imperturbability (āneñja) by abandoning gross factors, and thus it is said to have truly transcended it. - Commentary)

Or just as a man living in the same village with an enemy who does him harm, being oppressed by him through beating, binding, burning of his house, and so on, goes to live in another village; and there, if he sees a man with a similar appearance, voice, or behavior as that enemy, he is afraid and terrified, and does not wish even to look at him.
