Here is the application of these similes: The time when those men were oppressed by the snake or the enemy is like the time when the monk is associated with the physical body (karaja-rūpa) by way of the object. Their running away swiftly and going to another village is like the time when the monk transcends the physical body by the power of the fourth jhāna of the fine-material sphere. Their fear, terror, and desire not to look upon seeing the painted palm leaf, etc., in the place they fled to, or the man similar to the enemy in the other village, is like the monk’s desire to transcend even the kasina-form, having realized: "This [kasina-form] is similar to that [physical body]." Other similes such as a dog struck by a pig, or one who is afraid of ghosts, should also be understood in this context.
321:
One should also understand the similes such as the dog chased by a pig, the person afraid of ghosts, and so forth.

[321] 276. In this way, that yogi, desiring to depart from the material kasina which is the object of the fourth jhāna because of being weary of it, having mastered the five skills (vasī) and emerging from the proficient fourth rūpāvacara jhāna, sees the defects in that jhāna [Note 2] as: "This jhāna makes an object of the material kasina of which I am weary," and "It is close to the enemy of joy (somanassa)," and "It is gross compared to the peaceful liberation (vimokkha) of the formless states." However, there is no grossness in terms of the jhāna factors here; for just as this fourth rūpāvacara jhāna has two factors (equanimity and one-pointedness), so too do the formless (arūpa) jhānas have these same two factors.

Notes:
1. A dog, having once been chased by a pig in the forest, runs away. Later, in the twilight when it cannot see clearly, it sees a cooking pot from afar and, thinking it is a pig, runs away in fear. A person afraid of ghosts, seeing a palm tree with its top cut off in a place they have never visited at night, thinks it is a ghost and falls down in a faint from fear. This refers to such instances. (Ṭīkā)
2. Connect with: "sees the defects in that jhāna."

That yogi, seeing the defects in that fourth jhāna as described and ending his attachment to it, attends to the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana) as peaceful and infinite. He spreads the material kasina as far as the edge of the world system or as far as he desires, and then, attending to the space touched by that material kasina as "Space, space" (ākāsa, ākāsa) or "Infinite space" (ananto ākāso), he removes the kasina (kasiṇugghāṭana). In removing it, he does not roll it up like a mat, nor does he lift it out like a cake from a pan; rather, it is simply the non-attention, the not-bringing-to-mind, and the non-reviewing of that material kasina [Note 1]. By not attending, not bringing to mind, and not reviewing it, but instead attending to the space touched by it as "Space, space," he is said to "remove the kasina." The kasina being removed does not move upwards or peel away, nor does it sink down; [rather] it is said to be removed based solely on this yogi's non-attention [to the kasina] and his attention to "Space, space."

Note:
1. In these passages, the word "simply" (mya) is used as a substitute for the word "kēvalaṃ" (merely/only).

Only the space resulting from the removal of the kasina appears. Whether it is called "space resulting from the removal of the kasina" (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa) [Note 1], or "space touched by the kasina" (kasiṇaphuṭṭhokāsa), or "space secluded from the kasina" (kasiṇavivittokāsa), all these are the same.

That yogi repeatedly adverts to that sign of space resulting from the removal of the kasina as "Space, space," and subjects it to the striking of thought (takka) and applied thought (vitakka). To that yogi who thus repeatedly adverts and subjects it to the striking of thought and applied thought, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are suppressed, mindfulness (sati) is well-established, and the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration (upacāra samādhi). That yogi repeatedly practices, develops, and cultivates that sign. To that yogi who thus repeatedly reviews and attends, the mind of the Sphere of Infinite Space (ākāsānañcāyatana) reaches absorption (appanā) in the sign of space resulting from the removal of the kasina, just as the rūpāvacara mind does in the earth kasina and so forth.

Note:
1. The word-definition (vacanattha) corresponding to this meaning will be found in paragraph 280, page 566, note 1.

Indeed, here too, in the preliminary stage, three or four javanas are of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) and are associated only with the feeling of equanimity. The fourth or fifth javana is of the formless-sphere (arūpāvacara). The rest is the same as the method described in the section on the earth kasina.
322:
[322] The following explanation is specific: when the formless jhana consciousness has arisen in this way, that yogi bhikkhu [1]—to give an illustration—is like a man looking at the opening of a covered palanquin and the like, the mouth of a small door, or the mouth of a pot, which has been covered and bound with one of the cloths of blue, yellow, red, or white. If that covering cloth is removed by the force of the wind or by some other cause, he stands looking only at the sky. In the same way, having previously dwelt looking at the kasina mandala with the jhana-eye, when that sign is suddenly removed by this preliminary work of attention (parikamma-manasikāra) reflecting 'Space, space', he dwells looking only at the sign of space.

Note:
1. Connect as: 'That yogi bhikkhu... in the same way... having dwelt looking... if removed... dwells looking.'

To explain further: by this sequence of meditation, this yogi (or, regarding this yogi)—
'(Sabbaso rūpasaññānaṃ samatikkamā paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā nānattasaññānaṃ amanasikārā ananto ākāsoti ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati) With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the disappearance of perceptions of sensory reaction, with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [aware that] "space is infinite", he enters upon and dwells in the sphere of infinite space'—is thus said.

277. In that passage, 'sabbaso' (completely) means 'in every aspect' or 'entirely without remainder' [1]. Regarding 'perceptions of form' (rūpasaññānaṃ), this refers to the Rūpāvacara jhanas, which are spoken of using 'perception' as the head, as well as their objects. Indeed, the Rūpāvacara jhana is also called 'form' (rūpa) in such teachings as '(Rūpī rūpāni passati) One possessing form sees forms' [Note 1].

Note:
1. The term 'sabbaso' is explained in two ways. According to the first, it connects as 'surmounting in every aspect'; according to the second, it connects as 'all perceptions of form without remainder'.

(Or, one who has Rūpajhana) sees the kasina-forms. In such teachings as '(Bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni) He sees external forms, beautiful and ugly,' the object of that Rūpajhana, the kasina-form, is also called 'form' (rūpa) [Note 2]. Therefore, in this context, this name 'rūpasaññā' is a designation for the Rūpāvacara jhana, spoken of with perception as the head, defined as 'perception in form is rūpasaññā' [Note 3]. Furthermore, that object has the perception (name) 'form' (kasina-form); therefore, that object is called 'rūpasaññā'.

Note:
1. In the word 'rūpī', formed from 'rūpa' + suffix 'ī', the word 'jhāna' following 'rūpa' is elided. Thus, 'rūpa' expresses the meaning of 'rūpajhāna'. Therefore, 'rūpī' is translated as 'one who has rūpajhāna' or 'one who has attained rūpajhāna'.
2. Where it should say 'kasiṇarūpāni', 'kasiṇa' is elided and 'rūpāni' is said. Thus, 'rūpāni' is translated as 'kasina-forms'.
3. Where it should say 'rūpajhānasaññā', 'rūpasaññā' is said. Thus, 'rūpasaññā' is translated as 'perception in rūpajhāna'. Since it is spoken with perception as the primary head, the term 'rūpasaññā' refers to the rūpajhāna itself.

It means that the name of that object is 'form' (kasina-form). [If defined this way], the name 'rūpasaññā' is also the name of the object of that Rūpajhana, such as the earth kasina and so on [Note 1]. 'Samatikkamā' (through surmounting) means through fading away (virāga) and through cessation (nirodha). What is meant? It means that through the fading away and cessation of these fifteen perceptions of form known as jhanas—by way of wholesome, resultant, and functional—and of these nine perceptions of form known as objects—by way of the earth kasina and so on—in every aspect or entirely without remainder, he enters upon and dwells in the sphere of infinite space. Indeed, it is not possible for one who has not completely surmounted perceptions of form to enter upon and dwell in this sphere of infinite space. This is one explanation.

Note:
1. In the term 'rūpasaññā', taking 'saññā' to mean 'name', it shows that the kasina, which has the name 'form' or is associated with the name 'form', is also called 'rūpasaññā'. This is formed by a bahubbīhi compound definition; it is a matter for those proficient in Pali.

To explain further: in that passage (regarding reaching the sphere of infinite space through surmounting perceptions of form), for one who has not yet lost attachment to the object, the surmounting of perceptions is not possible. When perceptions are surmounted, the object is already surmounted. Therefore, without speaking of the surmounting of the object—
In that passage, 'What are perceptions of form?'
323:
The perception of a worldling (puthujjana) or a trainee (sekha) who enters a fine-material sphere attainment [1], or of a person born in the fine-material realm [2], or of an Arahant dwelling happily in the present life (through fine-material jhāna) [3], is the act of perceiving, the state of perceiving. These are called 'perceptions of form' (rūpasaññā). He has surmounted, overstepped, and completely transcended these perceptions of form. Therefore, it is said, 'with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form' (Vibh. 602).

Note:
1. This term indicates the person in whom wholesome fine-material sphere perceptions arise.
2. This term indicates the person in whom resultant fine-material sphere perceptions arise. In such a person, these resultant perceptions occur at the moments of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and death (cuti).
3. This term indicates the person in whom functional (kiriya) perceptions arise.

Thus, in the Vibhaṅga, the surmounting of perceptions alone is analyzed and taught. However, since these formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti) are to be reached only by surmounting the object—unlike the first jhāna etc., which are reached in a single object—it should be understood that this explanation is also made by the commentators in terms of surmounting the object.

278. Paṭighasaññānaṃ atthaṅgamā (With the disappearance of perceptions of resistance): Perceptions that arise from the impact (paṭighāta) between the bases such as the eye and the objects such as visible forms are called 'perceptions of resistance' (paṭighasaññā). This is a designation for the perception of visible forms and so on. As it is said:

'In that context, what are perceptions of resistance? Perception of visible forms, perception of sounds, perception of smells, perception of tastes, and perception of tangible objects—these are called perceptions of resistance' (Vibh. 603).

'With the disappearance' means by making them not arise, by abandoning, and by the non-occurrence of all ten of those perceptions of resistance, namely the five wholesome-resultants and the five unwholesome-resultants.

To explain further: It is true that these perceptions of resistance do not exist even for one who has attained the first jhāna and so on, because at that time consciousness does not proceed by way of the five doors. Nevertheless, just as pleasure and pain, which were abandoned elsewhere, are mentioned in the fourth jhāna, and just as personality-view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) etc., which were abandoned in other paths, are mentioned in the third path, it should be understood that the mention of the disappearance of these perceptions of resistance in the context of this formless jhāna is for the purpose of inspiring effort and by way of praising this jhāna.

Alternatively, although they do not exist even for one who has attained the fine-material sphere, they do not 'not exist' because of being abandoned. Why? Because fine-material sphere development does not lead to revulsion (virāga) towards form, and the occurrence of those perceptions is dependent on form. But this formless development leads to revulsion towards form. Therefore, it is appropriate to say that those perceptions of resistance are abandoned in this formless jhāna. Not only is it appropriate to say so, it is appropriate to definitely bear it in mind as such. Indeed, because those perceptions of resistance were not yet abandoned before this, the Blessed One said that sound is a 'thorn' (A.N. 10.72) to one who has attained the first jhāna. But because they are abandoned here, the imperturbability (āneñjata) (Vibh. 226) and the peaceful liberation (santa-vimokkha) (M.N. 1.66) of the formless attainments are stated. Furthermore, the ascetic Āḷāra Kālāma, while in a formless attainment, neither saw nor heard the sound of five hundred carts passing very close to him. This is one explanation.
324:
“Perception, the act of perceiving, the state of having perceived, of one who is associated with the mind-element or the mind-consciousness-element [who is not in attainment]—these are called ‘perceptions of diversity’ (nānattasaññā).” In this manner, it is analyzed and taught in the Vibhaṅga. In the context of these formless absorptions (arūpajhāna), it refers to those perceptions associated with the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element of one who is not in attainment, which occur in diverse objects of various natures such as forms, sounds, and so forth.

(Note 1: Nānattasaññā = perceptions occurring in objects of various/diverse natures. Note 2: Nānattasaññā = perceptions that are themselves of various/diverse natures.)

These perceptions occur in objects of various natures; therefore, they are called ‘perceptions of diversity.’ Furthermore, there are forty-four such perceptions: eight sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven sense-sphere wholesome resultant perceptions (Note: 1 receiving, 2 investigating, 8 great resultants), two unwholesome resultant perceptions (Note: receiving and investigating), and eleven sense-sphere functional perceptions. These forty-four perceptions are of diverse natures and are dissimilar to one another; therefore, they are called ‘perceptions of diversity.’ “By non-attention to those perceptions of diversity” means by not adverting, not attending, not bringing to mind, and not reflecting. It means that because one does not advert to, does not attend to, and does not reflect on those perceptions of diversity, they are said to be not attended to.

Furthermore, among these [three types of perceptions], the previously mentioned perceptions of form (rūpasaññā) and perceptions of impingement (paṭighasaññā) do not exist even in the formless existence (arūpabhava) produced by this absorption. It goes without saying that they do not exist at the time of entering and dwelling in this absorption in that existence. Therefore, their non-existence is stated in two ways: by “surmounting” (samatikkama) them and by their “disappearance” (atthaṅgama). However, among the forty-four perceptions of diversity, twenty-seven perceptions—namely, eight sense-sphere wholesome perceptions, nine sense-sphere functional perceptions (including the mind-door adverting), and ten unwholesome perceptions—do exist in the formless existence produced by this absorption. Therefore, it is said, “by non-attention to those perceptions of diversity.” Indeed, even in that formless existence, one who enters and dwells in this formless absorption does so only by not attending to those twenty-seven perceptions of diversity. If one attends to those twenty-seven perceptions of diversity, one is not in attainment. This is one explanation.

In brief, by the phrase “by surmounting perceptions of form,” the abandoning of all form-sphere (rūpāvacara) states is stated. By the two phrases “by the disappearance of perceptions of impingement” and “by non-attention to perceptions of diversity,” the abandoning of and non-attention to all sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness and mental factors are stated.

280. In the passage “Infinite is space” (ananto ākāso): “Infinite” means that its end in terms of arising or its end in terms of vanishing is not perceived or does not exist. Therefore, that space is called “infinite.” “Space” refers to the space disclosed by the removal of the kasina (kasiṇugghāṭimākāsa). Furthermore, infinity should be understood by the power of attention—that is, by attending to this space produced by the removal of the kasina as “infinite.”
325:
Therefore, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "He places the mind in that space, establishes it well, pervades it infinitely; therefore it is called infinite space" (Vibh. 605).

Note: This also relates to times outside of a Buddha's dispensation; since the arising and falling away of ultimate realities (paramattha) would not be known then, the meaning of 'infinite' according to worldly convention is also appropriate.

1. The kasina-object is removed by this space which is attended to. Because it is the cause for such removal, that space is called 'kasiṇuugghāṭa'. It is also called 'kasiṇuugghāṭima'. (Ṭīkā) According to this commentary, it should be translated precisely as 'that which causes the removal of the kasina-object'. However, because that meaning is difficult for those not proficient in Pali to understand, and because the definition 'kasiṇassa ugghāṭo' (the removal of the kasina is kasiṇuugghāṭa; the space accomplished by that removal of the kasina is kasiṇuugghāṭima) is also valid, it has been translated as above.

2. 'By way of attention' means: by taking only the absence or non-existence of the material form, and by not taking the limits (of arising and falling away), one pervades (attends) in the manner of 'infinite—without end or limit'. This is the power of the preliminary (parikamma) attention. (Ṭīkā)

He pervades (or touches/reaches) it by making it infinite. Therefore, He taught: "Infinite space—space that has no end or limit."

In the passage 'Ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati' (enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space), that space has no limit of arising or limit of falling away; therefore, it is called infinite (ananta). Infinite space is 'ākāsānanta'. 'Ākāsānanta' itself is 'ākāsānañca'. That 'ākāsānañca', which is the infinite space, is the 'āyatana' (base) in the sense of being the abode for this jhāna along with its associated mental states. How? Just as the abode of the devas is called 'devāyatana', so this is called 'ākāsānañcāyatana'.

'Upasampajja viharati' means having reached and produced that Ākāsānañcāyatana jhāna, one dwells with a posture and behavior suitable to that jhāna. This concludes one section.

This is the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the Sphere of Infinite Space.

## (End of the Explanation of the Sphere of Infinite Space)

Note: 1. In the Visuddhimagga, the meaning of the word 'āyatana' is explained as 'adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena' (in the sense of a base/support) to indicate it as an abode. Since it is translated here as 'the base which is the abode', that explanatory word is not needed and has been omitted.

## 2. Explanation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness

281. Furthermore, a meditator who wishes to develop the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, having achieved mastery in five ways over the attainment of the Sphere of Infinite Space, should see the disadvantage in the Sphere of Infinite Space, thinking: "This attainment is close to the enemy of the fine-material sphere jhānas, and it is not as peaceful as the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness." Having ended his attachment to that attainment and attending to the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness as peaceful, he should repeatedly advert to, attend to, and review the consciousness that occurred pervading that infinite space, noting "Consciousness, consciousness". He should strike it with thought and applied thought. He should not attend to it merely as "Infinite, infinite".

Note: 1. Since the later canonical evidence and its commentary contain the phrase 'anantaṃ viññāṇanti', it should also be 'anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ anantaṃ viññāṇanti' here. If so, it should be translated as "Infinite consciousness, infinite consciousness".

2. 'Anantaṃ anantaṃ' means one should not attend to or develop it merely as 'infinite, infinite'. However, one should attend to it as 'infinite consciousness, infinite consciousness' or simply as 'consciousness, consciousness'. (Ṭīkā)

As the meditator repeatedly directs the development-mind toward that object of consciousness, the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness (which has the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space as its object) is well-established, and the development-mind becomes concentrated through access concentration (upacāra samādhi). The meditator repeatedly frequents, develops, and cultivates that object-sign of the consciousness of the sphere of infinite space. As he does so, just as the Ākāsānañcāyatana jhāna mind occurs in the space (produced by the removal of the kasina), the Viññāṇañcāyatana jhāna mind attains absorption in the consciousness that pervaded the space. The method of absorption in this Sphere of Infinite Consciousness should be understood in the same way as mentioned for the first formless jhāna (or as mentioned in the section on the mindfulness of death).

To explain further—by this sequence of development, this meditator—

Note: Regarding the statement that one should not attend to it merely as 'infinite, infinite', it seems the original root text for the method of attention earlier might have been 'anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ anantaṃ viññāṇanti'.

1. This refers back to what was said in the last three lines of the third paragraph on page 321 of the Commentary, or alternatively, to what was shown in paragraph 117 in the section on mindfulness of death.

"(Sabbaso ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ samatikkamma anantaṃ viññāṇanti viññāṇañcāyatanaṃ upasampajja viharati) Completely transcending the sphere of infinite space in every way, attending 'consciousness is infinite', he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness."

282. In that passage, the word 'sabbaso' (completely) has the meaning already explained. In 'samatikkamma ākāsānañcāyatanaṃ' (transcending the sphere of infinite space), according to the method previously mentioned, the jhāna is called the sphere of infinite space, and the object is also [so called]. Indeed, the object is also [so called] by the same method previously mentioned.
326:
Alternatively, as for the method of attaining absorption (appanā): even in the case of an object that is a mental state, the method of attaining absorption in the immaterial jhānas should be understood by the method stated in the Maraṇassatiniddesa: "The immaterial jhāna reaches absorption through the power of meditation that transcends the object; for indeed, the mere transcending of the object of a lower jhāna by a jhāna that has already reached absorption is what occurs in the attainment of absorption in that higher immaterial jhāna." (Ṭīkā) In brief, this means that the attainment of absorption in a higher jhāna is merely the act of letting go of the object of the lower jhāna and entering into a new object.

(Ākāsānañca) It is infinite space; and because it is the object of the first immaterial jhāna, it is also an (āyatana) base in the sense of an abode, like the abode of the gods is called Devāyatana. For these two reasons, it is called Ākāsānañcāyatana. Likewise, it is Ākāsānañca; and because it is the cause of the arising of that jhāna, it is also an āyatana in the sense of a place of origin, as in such phrases as "Kamboja is the āyatana (source) of horses." For these two reasons as well, it is called Ākāsānañcāyatana. As has been stated, only after transcending both this jhāna and its object—that is, both aspects of the Ākāsānañcāyatana—by means of non-occurrence and non-attention, can one reach and abide in this Viññāṇañcāyatana jhāna. Therefore, taking both the jhāna and the object together, it should be understood that it was said: "By transcending the Sphere of Infinite Space."

Regarding the phrase "Anantaṃ viññāṇaṃ" (Infinite Consciousness): it means that one attends to that very consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space, which occurred by pervading [space] thus: "Infinite is space," by attending to it thus: "Infinite is consciousness." Alternatively, it is infinite by virtue of the attention. For that meditator, when attending without remainder to that consciousness which has space as its object, attends to it as "infinite."

As stated in the Vibhaṅga:
"(Anantaṃ viññāṇanti taṃyeva ākāsaṃ viññāṇena phuṭaṃ manasi karoti, anantaṃ pharati, tena vuccati anantaṃ viññāṇanti)
'Infinite consciousness' means: he pervades [space] by attending to it as infinite; he attends to the consciousness that has pervaded that very space which was pervaded as infinite; therefore it is called 'infinite consciousness'."

In that passage, the word "viññāṇena" (by consciousness) should be understood as the instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative (object). Indeed, the teachers of the Commentaries explain its meaning in this way: it means he pervades [space] as infinite and attends to the consciousness that has pervaded that space.

In the phrase "abides having reached the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness," that consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space has no (anta) end; therefore, it is "ananta" (infinite). "Ananta" itself is "ānañca." Instead of saying "viññāṇa-ānañca," it is said as "viññāṇañca." This is a conventional term (rūḷhī) that has arisen for the meaning of that word "viññāṇānañca." That "viññāṇañca," which is the infinite consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space, is the base (āyatana) in the sense of an abode for this second immaterial jhāna together with its associated states, just as the abode of the gods is called Devāyatana. Therefore, [this second immaterial jhāna] is called Viññāṇañcāyatana. The rest is the same as before. This concludes one section.

This is the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.

## (The explanation of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness is finished).

## 3. Explanation of the Sphere of Nothingness

283. Furthermore, a meditator who wishes to develop the Sphere of Nothingness, having achieved mastery in the attainment of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness in five ways, [sees that]: "This attainment is close to the enemy of the Sphere of Infinite Space, and it is not as peaceful as the Sphere of Nothingness."
327:
Having seen the danger in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, thinking, 'It is not as peaceful as the Sphere of Nothingness,' and having exhausted one's attachment to that attainment, one should attend to the Sphere of Nothingness as peaceful. One should attend to the non-existence (the concept of non-existence), the voidness, and the secluded aspect of that very consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space which was the object of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness. How? Without attending to that consciousness, one should repeatedly advert, attend, and reflect, 'There is nothing, there is nothing,' or 'Void, void,' or 'Secluded, secluded.' One should attend to it as if striking it with thought, or repeatedly striking it by revolving it with applied thought.

(Note: This Viññāṇañca is called Viññāṇañcāyatana because it is the objective support for the second immaterial jhāna.)

As he directs his mind towards that sign of the concept of non-existence (the non-existence of the consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space), the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is well-established, and the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration. The meditator repeatedly practices, develops, and cultivates that sign of the concept of non-existence. As he does so, just as the consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness arose in the sublime consciousness that pervaded space, the consciousness of the Sphere of Nothingness attains absorption in the non-existence, voidness, and seclusion of that very sublime consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space which had pervaded space. Here too, the method of absorption should be understood in the same way as previously described.

However, there is this distinction: when that absorption mind of the Sphere of Nothingness has arisen, that bhikkhu is like a man who, having seen a community of monks (Saṅgha) assembled for some business in a meeting hall and having gone elsewhere, returns when the monks have departed at the conclusion of their business. Standing at the door and looking again at that place, he sees it only as empty, he sees it only as secluded. It does not occur to him, 'So many monks have died' or 'They have departed to various directions'; rather, he sees only the non-existence, thinking, 'This place is empty, it is secluded.' In the same way, having previously dwelt seeing the consciousness that occurred in space with the jhāna-eye of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and now, when that consciousness has disappeared through the preliminary work of attention such as 'There is nothing, there is nothing,' he dwells seeing only its non-existence, which is its departure. To this extent, it is said: 'By completely surpassing the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, [perceiving] "there is nothing," he enters and dwells in the Sphere of Nothingness.'

284. Here too, the word 'completely' (sabbaso) has the same meaning as previously explained. In the term 'Sphere of Infinite Consciousness' (viññāṇañcāyatana), both the jhāna and the object are called 'Sphere of Infinite Consciousness' according to the method already stated. For the object is 'viññāṇañca' according to the previous method, and it is an 'āyatana' in the sense of a dwelling place, like the 'devāyatana' (abode of gods) is the dwelling of gods, because it is the objective support for the second immaterial jhāna.
328:
Similarly, it is called 'viññāṇañca'; and because that object is the cause for the arising of that very jhāna, it is also called 'āyatana' in the sense of a place of origin, as in such phrases as 'Kamboja is the āyatana (source) of horses.' For these two reasons, it is called 'viññāṇañcāyatana.' It should be understood that the statement 'surpassing the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness' is made by taking both the jhāna and the object together, since one can only enter and dwell in the Sphere of Nothingness after surpassing both by making them non-occurrent and by not attending to them.

Regarding 'there is nothing' (natthi kiñci), it means attending to it as 'there is nothing, there is nothing,' 'void, void,' 'secluded, secluded.' As it is said in the Vibhaṅga: '"There is nothing"—he makes that same consciousness (of the first immaterial state) non-existent, he makes it disappear, he makes it vanish, he sees that there is nothing; therefore it is said "there is nothing."' Although this is stated as if it were a comprehension of its cessation (bhaṅga), the meaning should be understood in this way: without adverting to, without attending to, and without reflecting on that consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space, but attending only to its non-existence, voidness, and seclusion, he is said to 'make it non-existent, make it disappear, make it vanish,' and not otherwise.

In the phrase 'enters and dwells in the Sphere of Nothingness,' 'nothingness' (akiñcana) means that not even a trace of that consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space remains; it means that not even the mere moment of its dissolution remains. The state of having nothing (akiñcana) is 'nothingness' (ākiñcañña); this is a designation for the departure or non-existence of the consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space. That nothingness is the 'āyatana' (abode) for this third immaterial jhāna in the sense of a dwelling place, like the 'devāyatana' is the abode of gods; thus it is the 'ākiñcaññāyatana.' The rest is the same as before.

This is the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the Sphere of Nothingness.

## (End of the Explanation of the Sphere of Nothingness)

## 4. Explanation of the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception

285. Furthermore, a meditator who wishes to develop the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, having achieved mastery in the five ways in the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness, sees the danger in the Sphere of Nothingness and the advantage in the higher state, thinking: 'This attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness is close to the enemy of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, and it is not as peaceful as the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception,' or 'Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart; this Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, which is free from gross perception but not devoid of subtle perception, is peaceful, it is sublime.' Having thus exhausted his attachment to the Sphere of Nothingness, he should attend to the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception as peaceful. He should repeatedly attend to, keep in mind, and reflect on that very attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness—which had occurred by taking the non-existence of the Sphere of Infinite Space as its object—as 'Peaceful, peaceful.'
329:
One should attend to it, bring it to mind, and reflect upon it repeatedly, making it as if struck by thought and struck by applied thought, with the thought: 'It is peaceful.'

To that meditator who repeatedly directs his mind towards that sign (the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness), the hindrances are suppressed, mindfulness is well-established, and the mind becomes concentrated through access concentration. He repeatedly associates with, develops, and cultivates that sign. As he does so, just as the consciousness of the Sphere of Nothingness arises in the concept of non-existence (the absence of the consciousness of the Sphere of Infinite Space), the consciousness of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception reaches absorption in the four aggregates known as the attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness. The method of absorption here should be understood in the same way as previously described. By this sequence of development, this meditator—

'Having completely transcended the Sphere of Nothingness, enters and dwells in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.'

286. In this text, the term 'completely' (sabbaso) has the same meaning as previously explained. Regarding the phrase 'having transcended the Sphere of Nothingness' (ākiñcaññāyatanaṃ samatikkamma), according to the method mentioned before, the 'Sphere of Nothingness' refers to both the jhāna and its object. Indeed, the object is called 'ākiñcañña' (nothingness) by the previous method; and because it is the object of the third immaterial jhāna, it is called 'āyatana' (base) in the sense of a dwelling place, like the 'devāyatana' (abode of the gods). Likewise, it is called 'ākiñcañña,' and because it is the cause for the arising of that same jhāna, it is called 'āyatana' in the sense of a place of origin, similar to phrases such as 'Kamboja is the origin (āyatana) of horses.' Thus, it should be understood that the statement 'having transcended the Sphere of Nothingness' is made by taking both the jhāna and the object together, transcending them by making them non-existent and by not attending to them, so that one may enter and dwell in this Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception.

Regarding the term 'Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception' (nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ), it is so called because of the existence of a perception of such a nature (extremely subtle). To first show what that perception is like for a meditator who has practiced in this way, the Vibhaṅga, having extracted the term 'neither percipient nor non-percipient' (nevasaññī-nāsaññī), states: 'He attends to that very attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness as peaceful; he develops the attainment with residual formations; therefore, it is called neither percipient nor non-percipient.' In that context, 'attends to it as peaceful' means he attends to it as 'peaceful' because it has a peaceful object, thinking: 'How peaceful indeed is this attainment, that it can remain even while making non-existence its object!'
330:
[330] If he attends to it as peaceful, how does transcendence occur? It occurs because of the absence of desire to attain it. To explain: although he attends to that attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness as peaceful, he does not have the adverting, bringing to mind, or attention (manasikāra) such as: 'I will advert to this attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness, I will attain it, I will resolve upon it, I will emerge from it, I will reflect upon it.' Why? Because the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception is more peaceful and more sublime than the Sphere of Nothingness.

To illustrate with an analogy: Suppose a king, possessing great royal majesty, riding on the back of a noble elephant and traveling through the city streets, sees ivory carvers and other craftsmen, firmly dressed in a single cloth, with their heads wrapped in a cloth, their bodies covered in ivory dust, performing various intricate ivory carvings and crafts. Seeing them, he is pleased with their skill, thinking: 'Oh, how clever these masters are, that they can perform such intricate crafts!' However, it does not occur to him: 'Oh, that I might give up my kingdom and become such a craftsman!' Why is that? Because of the great benefits of royal majesty. He passes by the craftsmen without any longing for their state. In the same way, although this meditator attends to that attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness as peaceful, he does not have the adverting, bringing to mind, or attention such as: 'I will advert to this attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness, I will attain it, I will resolve upon it, I will emerge from it, I will reflect upon it.'

Attending to that attainment of the Sphere of Nothingness as peaceful, he reaches that extremely subtle perception that has reached absorption by the method mentioned before, by which perception he is called 'neither percipient nor non-percipient,' and he is said to develop the 'attainment with residual formations.' 'Attainment with residual formations' (saṅkhārāvasesa-samāpatti) refers to the fourth immaterial attainment which has formations that have reached an extremely subtle state.

287. Now, to show the actual nature of that attainment which is called 'Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception' by virtue of the perception thus obtained: 

'The Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception refers to the states of consciousness and mental factors of one who has attained the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (a worldling or a trainee), or of one who is reborn there, or of an Arahant dwelling in happiness in this very life.'

Notes:
1. This refers to the person in whom the wholesome (kusala) jhāna arises.
2. This refers to the person in whom the resultant (vipāka) jhāna arises. This resultant jhāna occurs as rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and the decease consciousness.
3. This refers to the person in whom the functional (kiriya) jhāna arises.

Among these three types of states, what is intended here are the wholesome consciousness and mental factors of the person who has entered the attainment. The etymology of this term is: because of the absence of gross perception and the presence of subtle perception, this jhāna, together with its associated states, is called 'neither perception nor non-perception' (nevasaññānāsañña).
331:
The attainment called neither-perception-nor-non-perception [331] is also called a base (āyatana) because it is included within the mind-base (manāyatana) and the mental-object-base (dhammāyatana); thus it is 'nevasaññānāsaññāyatana'. Alternatively, the perception present in this fourth formless attainment is 'neither perception' (nevasaññā) because it is incapable of performing the distinct function of perception (namely, becoming an object of insight and producing revulsion); and it is 'not non-perception' (nāsaññā) because it exists in a subtle state as a remainder of formations (saṅkhāra) left over from gross formations. For these two reasons, it is called 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'. This 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' is also called a base (āyatana) in the sense of being the support for the remaining associated states; thus it is 'nevasaññānāsaññāyatana'.

To explain further: in this fourth formless attainment, it is not only perception that is of such a nature. In fact, feeling (vedanā) is also 'neither-feeling-nor-non-feeling'—it is not gross feeling but only subtle feeling. Consciousness (citta) is also 'neither-consciousness-nor-non-consciousness'—it is not gross consciousness but only subtle consciousness. Contact (phassa) is also 'neither-contact-nor-non-contact'—it is not gross contact but only subtle contact. The same applies to the remaining associated states. However, it should be understood that this teaching is given under the heading of perception (as 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'). Furthermore, this meaning should be illustrated by similes such as the oil for smearing a bowl.

It is said that a novice smeared a bowl with oil and set it aside. At the time for drinking gruel, the elder monk said, 'Bring the bowl.' The novice replied, 'Venerable sir, there is oil in the bowl.' Then, when the elder said, 'Novice, bring the oil, I will fill the oil-tube,' the novice replied, 'Venerable sir, there is no oil.' In that simile, because the oil had been kept inside [the monastery] overnight and was thus unallowable to be mixed with gruel, he said 'there is oil.' But in terms of filling an oil-tube, he said 'there is no oil.' In the same way, that perception is 'neither perception' because it is incapable of performing the distinct function of perception, and it is 'not non-perception' because it exists in a subtle state as a remainder of formations left over from gross formations.

What then is the function of perception here? It is the recognition of the object and the ability to produce revulsion (nibbidā) by becoming an object of insight (vipassanā). To explain: just as the fire element (tejo-dhātu) in cold water is unable to perform the function of burning, so too this perception of the fourth formless attainment is unable to make the function of recognition distinct. Furthermore, it is unable to produce the knowledge of revulsion by becoming an object of insight, unlike the perception in other attainments. Indeed, there is no monk who, without having previously practiced reflection and insight on other aggregates, is able to reach the knowledge of revulsion (nibbidā-ñāṇa) by contemplating the aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—not even the Venerable Sāriputta. However, a person who is a natural practitioner of insight (pakati-vipassaka) and possesses great wisdom like the Venerable Sāriputta might be able to do so. Even that Venerable Sāriputta could only do so by way of 'comprehension by groups' (kalāpasammasana), thinking, 'Thus, indeed, these states, having not been, come into being; having been, they disappear'; he could not do so by way of 'insight into states one by one' (anupadadhamma-vipassanā). Such is the subtlety reached by this attainment.
332:
This attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has reached such a degree of subtlety.

[332] Furthermore, just as it was illustrated by the simile of the oil for smearing the bowl, this meaning should also be illustrated by the simile of water on a journey. It is said that a novice walking ahead of an elder monk on a journey saw a little water and said, 'Venerable sir, there is water; please take off your sandals.' Then, when the elder said, 'If there is water, bring my bathing cloth, I will bathe,' the novice replied, 'Venerable sir, there is no water.' In that simile, because there was just enough to wet the sandals, he said 'there is water.' But in terms of the function of bathing, he said 'there is no water.' In the same way, that perception of the fourth formless attainment is 'neither perception' because it is incapable of performing the distinct function of perception, and it is 'not non-perception' because it exists in a subtle state as a remainder of formations left over from gross formations.

Not only by these, but this meaning should also be illustrated by other suitable similes. The phrase 'he dwells having attained it' (upasampajja viharati) is to be understood in the manner already described.

This is the detailed explanation of the meditation subject of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

## (The explanation of the meditation subject of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is finished.)

## Miscellaneous Discussion

288. The Lord, whose physical body is incomparable (possessing the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor marks, etc.), taught the fourfold formless attainments. Having understood those four formless attainments as described, one should also understand the miscellaneous discussion regarding them.

289. These four formless attainments occur by way of transcending the object (ārammaṇātikkama). Wise men do not wish for a transcendence of factors (aṅgātikkama) in these four.

To explain: among these formless attainments, the first occurs by transcending the sign of fine-material kasina. The second occurs by transcending the space (ākāsa) obtained by removing the kasina-material. The third occurs by transcending the first formless consciousness that occurred in that space. The fourth occurs by transcending the absence of the first formless consciousness that occurred in that space. Thus, it should be understood that all four of these formless attainments occur entirely by way of transcending the object. Wise men do not wish for a transcendence of factors in these, because there is no transcendence of factors here as there is in the fine-material sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti). Indeed, in all these formless attainments, there are only two jhana factors: equanimity (upekkhā) and one-pointedness of mind (cittekaggatā).

290. Even though there is no transcendence of factors—
In this context, the subsequent attainments are increasingly more excellent and refined.
333:
Regarding this superiority and excellence, the similes of the stories of a palace and the pieces of cloth should be understood.

[333] To explain in detail: Suppose on the lowest floor of a four-story palace, the five strands of sensual pleasure were present, exquisite in terms of divine dance, song, music, fragrant flowers, food, couches, and clothing. On the second floor, they would be more exquisite than that. On the third floor, more exquisite still. On the fourth floor, the most exquisite of all. In that palace, although all four are indeed palace floors and there is no difference between them as palace floors, yet, by the distinction of the abundance of the five strands of sensual pleasure, each higher floor is more exquisite than the one below it.

And just as there might be four pieces of cloth woven by a woman from coarse thread, fine thread, finer thread, and finest thread, weighing four palas, three palas, two palas, and one pala respectively,1 which are equal in length and breadth. In this simile, although those four cloths are equal in length and breadth and there is no difference in their dimensions, yet, in terms of pleasant touch, fineness, and great value, each subsequent cloth is more exquisite than the preceding one. In the same way, although in these four immaterial attainments there are only two factors, namely, equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, yet, through the distinction of development (bhāvanā), the factors of these attainments become more and more exquisite, and it should be understood that in this context, each subsequent attainment is more exquisite than the preceding one.

291. In this way, these four immaterial attainments, which are increasingly more exquisite in order—

"Attached to a pavilion in an impure place,
One stands there, and another leans on him;
Another stands outside without leaning,
And yet another leans on that one.

These four should be understood by the wise
In their respective order
According to their similarity to these four men."

Here is the connection of the meaning: It is said that there was a pavilion in an impure place. Then a man came, and being disgusted by that impurity, he stood as if attached to that pavilion, holding it with his hands. Then another man came and leaned on the man who was attached to the pavilion. Then another came and thought, "Both this one attached to the pavilion and the one leaning on him are poorly situated."

Footnote:
1. The weight of one pala is 4 kyat-tha. Therefore, a one-pala cloth weighs 4 kyat-tha, and a four-pala cloth weighs 16 kyat-tha.
334:
[334] "If the pavilion falls, they will surely fall down. Let me stand only outside." Having thought so, he stood only outside the pavilion, not leaning on the first man whom the second man leaned upon. Then another man came, and having considered the insecurity of the one attached to the pavilion and the one leaning on him, and seeing the one standing outside as well-situated, he stood leaning on that very person.

In this simile, the space (ākāsa) produced by the removal of the kasina should be regarded as the pavilion in the impure place. The sphere of boundless space (ākāsānañcāyatana), which has space as its object because of disgust for the material sign (rūpa-nimitta), should be regarded as the man attached to the pavilion because of disgust for the impurity. The sphere of boundless consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana), which proceeds by taking as its object the sphere of boundless space, should be regarded as the man leaning on the one attached to the pavilion. The sphere of nothingness (ākiñcaññāyatana), which does not take the sphere of boundless space as its object but takes the concept of non-existence (natthibhāva-paññatti) of that jhāna as its object, should be regarded as the man who stands outside the pavilion without leaning on the man attached to it, after considering the insecurity of both those men. The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), which proceeds by taking as its object the sphere of nothingness situated in the external area called the non-existence of the consciousness of boundless space, should be regarded as the man who stands leaning on the one outside, seeing him as well-situated after considering the insecurity of the one attached to the pavilion and the one leaning on him.

292. Furthermore—
This sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
Even though it sees the fault, it still makes that [sphere of nothingness] its object
Due to the absence of any other object;
Just as people, for the sake of livelihood, depend on a king whose faults they have seen.

Indeed, this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, even though it has seen the fault of that attainment, thinking, "This attainment is close to the enemy, the sphere of boundless consciousness," yet it still makes that sphere of nothingness its object due to the absence of any other object. How? Just as people depend on a king whose faults they have seen for the sake of livelihood. To explain: Even if people see the faults of a certain king who is the lord of all directions1 and who has coarse conduct of body, speech, and mind due to lack of restraint, thinking, "This king has coarse conduct," yet, not finding a livelihood elsewhere, they continue to depend on him for the sake of livelihood. In the same way, this sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, not finding another object, makes that sphere of nothingness its object even though it sees its faults.

293. And while making it the object—
As one who has climbed a long ladder
Leans on the ladder's rail,
Or as one who has climbed a mountain peak
Leans on the mountain top.

Footnote:
1. Sabbadisampati: Lord of all directions. This epithet is used to show that there is no other place for the people to go. (Sub-commentary)
335:
[335] "Or as one who has climbed a hill
Leans on his own knee;
Even so does this jhāna
Proceed by leaning [on that object]."

Thus far is one section completed.

In the Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) composed for the gladdening of good people, in the section on the development of concentration, this is the tenth chapter called the Description of the Immaterial States (Āruppa-niddesa).

## (The Detailed Description of the Immaterial States is finished.)

## 11. Description of Concentration (Samādhi-niddesa)

## 1. How to Develop the Perception of Repulsiveness in Nutriment

[336] 294. Now, the time has come to explain in detail the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā), which was briefly mentioned as "another perception" immediately after the immaterial states. In the term "āhāre paṭikūlasaññā," it is called "nutriment" (āhāra) because it brings [its own effects].
336: It is of four kinds: nutriment of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), nutriment of contact (phassāhāra), nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra), and nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra). Among these four, which nutriment brings what? The nutriment of edible food, which is swallowed, brings about—that is, causes to arise—materiality with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamaka-rūpa). [Note 1: 'Description of Concentration' (Samādhi-niddesa) is a general name for the eleven descriptions from the 'Description of Taking up a Meditation Subject' to the 'Description of Direct Knowledge'. Therefore, in the second volume of the Visuddhimagga, page 222, it is stated: 'These, which are called concentration under the heading of the mind, have been fully detailed in all their aspects in the Description of Concentration,' referring to the eight attainments along with access concentration. See also the Myanmar translation, volume 4, page 220. Although all these eleven descriptions are places where concentration is detailed, since other descriptions have specific names like 'Description of Taking up a Meditation Subject', etc., they are not individually called 'Description of Concentration'; only this part, which has no other name, is designated as the 'Description of Concentration'.] [Note 2: Kabaḷa (morsel of food) + ī (like) + kāra (made) = kabaḷīkāra. Though it may not be a literal morsel of rice, it is made like a morsel of rice.] The nutriment of edible food brings about materiality with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamaka-rūpa). [Note: Nutritive essence (ojā-rūpa) found in the morsel of food is called the nutriment of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra); only that nutritive essence causes the octad-materiality to arise.] The nutriment of contact, which is the meeting of the object and the mind, brings about the three feelings. The nutriment of mental volition, which is the urge of volition (manosañcetanā), brings about rebirth in the three realms of existence. The nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇa), which is the mind, brings about mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa) at the moment of rebirth. Among these four, in the nutriment of edible food (or because of it [Note 1: This causal meaning is shown in the Commentary; however, the meaning 'in' also seems smoother, so the translation is based on that.]), there is the danger of attachment (nikanti-bhaya), which is the craving for taste. In the nutriment of contact, there is the danger of approach. In the nutriment of mental volition, there is the danger of arriving and arising in a new existence. In the nutriment of consciousness, there is the danger of rebirth. Among these four nutriments which are accompanied by such fearsome dangers, the nutriment of edible food should be illustrated by the instruction containing the simile of the son's flesh [Note 2: See the Myanmar translation of the Saṃyutta Nikāya, Volume 1, page 309.]. The nutriment of contact should be illustrated by the instruction containing the simile of the flayed cow [Note 1-2: See the same Myanmar translation, page 310.]. The nutriment of mental volition should be illustrated by the instruction containing the simile of the pit of glowing embers. The nutriment of consciousness should be illustrated by the instruction containing the simile of the hundred spears [Note 3: See the same Myanmar translation, page 311.]. Among these four nutriments, only the nutriment of edible food, consisting of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, is intended as 'food' in this context. The perception that arises by way of grasping the aspect of repulsiveness in that edible food is called the 'perception of repulsiveness in food' (āhārepaṭikkūlasaññā). A meditator who wishes to develop that perception of repulsiveness in food, having learned the meditation subject and without deviating even a single word or part from the method learned, should go to a secluded place, withdraw from external objects, and being well-fixed [on the meditation subject], reflect on the repulsiveness of the nutriment of edible food—consisting of what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted—by way of ten aspects. They are: (1) gamanato—by way of going; (2) pariyesanato—by way of seeking; (3) paribhogato—by way of consuming; (4) āsayato—by way of the receptacle such as bile, etc.; (5) nidhānato—by way of the place of storage, the stomach; (6) aparipakkato—by way of the undigested; (7) paripakkato—by way of the digested; (8) phalato—by way of the fruit or result; (9) nissandato—by way of the outflow; and (10) sammakkhanato—by way of the smearing. ## (1) Reflection by way of going. 295. Therein, the reflection by way of going is as follows: A person who has become a good monk in this Dispensation of the Buddha, which possesses such great power, having spent the whole night either reciting the Buddha's words or performing the duties of a recluse, rises early, performs the duties at the courtyard of the stupa and the Bodhi tree, and prepares drinking water and water for use...
337:
sweeps the precinct (pariveṇa), cleanses his body, and having gone up to his seat and sat down, he reflects on the meditation subject for twenty or thirty rounds [1]. Then, rising from his seat, he takes his bowl and robes [2]. He leaves behind the forest groves (tapo-vana)—which are not crowded with people, are endowed with the bliss of seclusion, are well-supplied with shade and water, and are clean, cool, and delightful—and without regard for the noble joy of seclusion [1], he must go towards the village for the sake of food, like a jackal heading towards a cemetery.

Note: 1. 'For twenty or thirty rounds'—In this context, some teachers (Keci) say the number of times is known by the power of the continuity of the present (santati-paccuppanna). Other teachers (Apare) say it is known by sitting until one is warm. ... Reflection from 'going' to 'smearing' constitutes one round; in this way, one reflects on the meditation subject for twenty or thirty rounds. (Commentary)
2. Connect with: 'having taken... having left... without regard... he must go towards the village.'

Even while going thus, from the moment he descends from his couch or stool, he must tread upon the floor-coverings strewn with dust, geckos' droppings, and so on. Then, at times, he must see the front of the cell, which is more repulsive than the interior because it is fouled by the droppings of rats, bats, and the like. Then he sees the lower floor, which is more repulsive than the upper floor because it is smeared with the droppings of owls, pigeons, and the like. Then, from time to time, he sees the precinct ground, which is more repulsive than the lower floor because it is defiled by old grass and leaves blown by the wind, by the urine, excrement, spit, and snot of sick novices, and by mud and water in the rainy season. Then the monastery road must be seen as more repulsive than the precinct.

Note: 1. Connect with: 'having taken... having left... without regard... he must go towards the village.'

Then, having worshipped the Bodhi tree and the Stupa in due order, standing in the pavilion where one considers where to go for alms, he turns his back on such a delightful forest monastery—without looking back at the Stupa which is like a heap of pearls, the Bodhi tree which is as captivating as a peacock's tail, and the monastery which is as glorious as a celestial mansion—and sets out for the sake of food. Having departed, as he enters the road to the village, he must see the road with stumps and thorns, and the uneven road broken by the force of water.

Then, as if covering a sore, he puts on his inner robe; as if binding a wound-dressing, he ties his waist-band; as if covering a skeleton, he puts on his upper robe; and as if taking out a medicine pot, he takes his bowl from its bag. Upon reaching the vicinity of the village gate, he must see the carcasses of elephants, horses, oxen, buffaloes, humans, snakes, and dogs. Not only must they be seen, but he must also endure the stench of those carcasses as it strikes his nose. Then, standing at the village gate, he must look down the village streets to avoid dangers such as wild elephants and horses.
338: [338] As stated, from the floor-coverings to the various kinds of corpses, one must tread upon, see, and smell this collection of repulsive things for the sake of food. "Oh, how repulsive indeed is food!" Thus should the repulsiveness be reflected upon by way of going. (1) ## (2) Reflection by way of seeking. 296. How should it be reflected upon by way of seeking? As stated, even after enduring the collection of repulsive things by way of going, when entering the village, one must wander through the village streets house to house, wearing the outer robe with its seams and holding the bowl in hand, like a helpless beggar. In those village streets during the rainy season, at every step one takes, the feet sink into the mud and water even up to the calves; one must hold the bowl with one hand and lift the robe with the other. In the summer, one must wander with the body covered and smeared with dust and grass-bits raised by the force of the wind. Reaching the doors of various houses, one must see and even tread upon puddles mixed with the washings of fish, meat, and rice, spit, snot, dog dung, pig dung, and the like, which are teeming with various kinds of worms and swarming with bluebottles, as well as cesspools where filth and waste water are discarded. From those puddles and cesspools, those flies fly up and settle on the robe, on the bowl, and on the head. To the monk who has entered the house, some give and some do not. Even when they give, some give rice cooked the day before, or old snacks, or rotten wheat cakes and rice cakes. Among those who do not give, only some say, "Pass on, Bhante" (aticchatha). Some remain silent as if they do not see him. Some turn their faces the other way. Some address him with harsh words such as, "Go away, you shaveling!" In this manner, like a helpless beggar, one must wander and come out of the village for the sake of obtaining alms-food. As stated, from the time of entering the village until leaving it, one must tread upon, see, and endure the collection of repulsive things such as mud and water for the sake of food. "Oh, how repulsive indeed is food!" Thus should the repulsiveness be reflected upon by way of seeking. (2) ## (3) Reflection by way of consuming. 297. How should it be reflected upon by way of consuming? As stated, the monk who has sought food and is sitting comfortably in a suitable place outside the village, before he has yet lowered his hand into that food to eat—if he sees a monk of such nature [endowed with virtue, etc.] who is worthy of respect, or a modest and virtuous layperson, he is still able to invite them [to accept that food].
339: However, if one has to invite others, saying, 'Please accept this,' just as one puts one's hand into that food or touches it with the desire to eat, it becomes a matter of shame (because there might be suspicion that one is offering leftovers). For one who kneads the food with the hand, sweat trickles down from the five fingers and, following their course, moistens and softens even dry and hard food. Then, when that food, whose beauty is destroyed even by that mere kneading, is made into a morsel and placed in the mouth, the lower teeth perform the function of a mortar, the upper teeth the function of a pestle, and the tongue the function of a hand. There in the mouth, that morsel is like dog's food in a dog's bowl. Being pounded and crushed by the tooth-pestles and turned over by the tongue, it is smeared by the thin, clear saliva at the tip of the tongue, and from the middle of the tongue onwards, it is smeared by thick saliva. In places where the tooth-stick does not reach, it is smeared by the film of the teeth (tooth-filth). Thus crushed and smeared, that food immediately loses its distinction of color and smell and its prepared state; it reaches a state of extreme loathsomeness, like dog's vomit in a dog's bowl. Even though it is such, it must be swallowed because it has passed beyond the range of the eyes. Thus, its repulsiveness should be contemplated in terms of consumption. (3) ## (4) Contemplation by way of Abode (Āsaya) 298. How should it be contemplated by way of abode? When food that has been consumed in this way enters inside, even for Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or Universal Monarchs, there is one of the four abodes: bile, phlegm, pus, or blood. For those with little merit, however, all four abodes are present. Therefore, for one in whom the abode of bile is predominant, the food becomes extremely loathsome, like being smeared with thick honey and oil. For one in whom the abode of phlegm is predominant, it is like being smeared with the juice of Nāgabala leaves. For one in whom the abode of pus is predominant, it is like being smeared with rotten buttermilk. For one in whom the abode of blood is predominant, it is like being smeared with red dye. Thus, its repulsiveness should be contemplated by way of abode. (4) ## (5) Contemplation by way of Place of Deposit (Nidhāna) 299. How should it be contemplated by way of the place of deposit? That food, smeared by one of these four abodes, having entered the stomach, is not deposited in a golden vessel, nor in vessels of gems, silver, and so on. Indeed, if it is swallowed by a ten-year-old, it remains for ten years in a place resembling a cesspit that has not been washed. If it is swallowed by one who is twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, sixty, seventy, eighty, or ninety years old...
340:
If a person who lives for a hundred years eats and swallows, for those hundred years [340] it remains in a place resembling an unwashed cesspool—thus, it should be reflected upon as repulsive by way of its place of storage, the stomach. (5)

## (6) Reflection by way of the undigested

300. How is it to be reflected upon by way of the undigested? This food, having reached its place of storage in such a location (resembling a cesspool), as long as it remains undigested, stays in that very place described above—a place of utter darkness, permeated by various foul odors of corpses, a range for putrid winds, and disgusting with extremely foul smells. To give a comparison: just as when there is an unseasonable heavy rain in the summer, the grass, leaves, mats, and the rotting carcasses of snakes, dogs, and humans fallen into a pit at the gate of a Caṇḍāla village, heated by the sun's rays, remain covered with foam and bubbles; even so, the food swallowed on that day, the day before, and the days prior to that, all becoming one, covered by a film of phlegm, and seething with foam and bubbles produced by the heat of the bodily fire (tejo-dhātu), remains in a state of extreme loathsomeness—thus, it should be reflected upon as repulsive by way of the undigested. (6)

## (7) Reflection by way of the digested

301. How is it to be reflected upon by way of the digested? When that food, staying in the stomach, is digested by the intense bodily fire, it does not become like gold or silver ores turning into gold or silver. Instead, giving off foam and bubbles, it becomes like pale, fine clay ground on a stone and packed into a tube, turning into feces and filling the receptacle for digested food (pakkāsaya), and turning into urine and filling the bladder—thus, it should be reflected upon as repulsive by way of the digested. (7)

## (8) Reflection by way of the fruit

302. How is it to be reflected upon by way of the fruit? When this food is properly digested, it produces various foul parts such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, and so on. When it is not properly digested, it produces hundreds of diseases such as ringworm, itch, scabies, leprosy, vitiligo, chronic wasting disease (consumption), coughs, and dysentery. This is its fruit—thus, it should be reflected upon as repulsive by way of the fruit. (8)

## (9) Reflection by way of the secretion

303. How is it to be reflected upon by way of the secretion? This food, having entered through one opening (the mouth), when it flows out, it flows out from many openings in various ways, such as eye-wax from the eyes and ear-wax from the ears. Furthermore, at the time of swallowing, it is swallowed with a great retinue. But at the time of secretion, having turned into feces, urine, and so on, it is voided alone. [341] Moreover, on the first day, while eating that food, one may be very excited, joyful, and filled with rapture and happiness (pīti-somanassa); but on the second day, when it is secreted, one voids it with a grimacing face, feeling disgusted and dejected, while holding one's nose.
341:
Furthermore, on the first day, one may swallow it while being attached, greedy, bound, and infatuated by the craving for taste; but on the second day, after just one night has passed, one voids it without attachment, as if being oppressed, feeling distressed, ashamed, and disgusted. Therefore, the ancient teachers said these four verses:

Food, drink, snacks, and meals of great value,
Having entered through one door, flow out through nine.

Food, drink, snacks, and meals of great value,
One eats with a retinue, but voids in hiding.

Food, drink, snacks, and meals of great value,
One eats with delight, but voids with disgust.

Food, drink, snacks, and meals of great value,
After staying for just one night, all become putrid.

Thus, it should be reflected upon as repulsive by way of the secretion. (9)

## (10) Reflection by way of smearing

304. How is it to be reflected upon by way of smearing? Even at the time of consumption, this food smears the hands, lips, tongue, and palate. Because they are smeared by that food, those hands, lips, tongue, and palate become repulsive; even after they are washed, they must be washed again and again to remove the odor. When the food is consumed—to give a comparison: just as when rice is being cooked, the husks, fine bran, and broken grains boil up and smear the rim and lid of the pot; even so, being cooked and made to foam by the bodily fire that pervades the whole body, it boils up and smears the teeth in the form of tartar. It smears the tongue, palate, etc., in the form of saliva and phlegm. It smears the eyes, ears, nose, and lower orifices in the form of eye-wax, ear-wax, snot, urine, and feces. These orifices, such as the mouth, etc., which are smeared by these, are neither clean nor pleasant, even though they are washed daily. Among these orifices, after washing some, the hand must be washed again with water. After washing others, even if one washes them two or three times with cow-dung ash, or fine clay, or scented powder, the repulsiveness does not disappear—thus, it should be reflected upon as repulsive by way of smearing. (10)

## How concentration arises

[342] 305. For one who reflects on the repulsiveness in these ten ways as mentioned...
342:
(Sub-commentary)
3. Referring to the anus, it is again said to be "certain doors."
4. In some books, it is written "vigacchati" without "na"; this is incorrect. Only the reading "na vigacchati" is appropriate. Therefore, it is translated according to that reading.

As that yogi performs the preliminary work, striking it with thought and repeatedly striking it with applied thought, the nutriment taken as balls (kabaliṅkārāhāra) becomes manifest by way of its repulsive aspect. That yogi repeatedly resorts to, develops, and cultivates that sign of repulsiveness. As he does so, the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) are suppressed. Because of the profundity of the individual essence of nutriment as balls, the mind becomes concentrated with access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) that does not reach absorption (appanā). However, because the perception of the repulsive aspect is manifest in this meditation subject, this meditation subject is reckoned simply as "the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment" (āhāre paṭikkkūlasaññā).

## Benefits
The benefit is this: for the monk who applies himself to this meditation on the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment, the mind recoils, retreats, and turns away from craving for taste (rasataṇhā). Just as a person wishing to cross a difficult desert eats the flesh of his own son without intoxication, so too this yogi partakes of nutriment without intoxication, only for the sake of crossing over suffering. When he partakes in this way, for that yogi, through the gateway of fully understanding nutriment as balls, lust for the five cords of sensual pleasure (pañcakāmaguṇa) is easily and without difficulty brought to full understanding (i.e., it disappears). By way of fully understanding the five cords of sensual pleasure, he fully understands the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha). Furthermore, by way of the repulsive nature of undigested food and so on, the development of mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati) also reaches fulfillment for that yogi, and he is said to have practiced the way in conformity with the perception of foulness (asubhasaññā). Depending on this practice, if he does not attain the ultimate end, the Deathless Nibbāna, in this very life, he is destined for a happy state (sugati). Here ends one section.

The words just spoken are the detailed explanation of the development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment.

## (The development of the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment is finished.)

## 2. Development of the Definition of the Four Elements
306. Now, the turn has come to explain in detail the development of the definition of the four elements, which was briefly mentioned as "one definition" immediately after the perception of repulsiveness in nutriment. In that term, "definition" (vavatthāna) means the determination [by wisdom] by way of marking the individual essences of the four elements, such as hardness and so on. The determination of the four elements is called the "definition of the four elements" (catudhātuvavatthāna). Attention to the elements (dhātumanasikāra), the meditation subject of the elements (dhātukammaṭṭhāna), and the definition of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna)—these three are one in meaning. This definition of the four elements, which is the same in meaning, appears in two ways: in brief and in detail.

(Among them,) it appears in brief in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta. It appears in detail in the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, the Rāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma. To extract and expand upon it, that definition of the elements is:

"Bhikkhus, just as if a skilled butcher or a butcher's apprentice, having slaughtered a cow..."
343:
...having slaughtered a cow, were to sit at a crossroads after dividing it into portions; even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu reviews this very body, however it is placed, however it is disposed, by way of the elements: 'There are in this body the earth element (pathavīdhātu), the water element (āpodhātu), the fire element (tejodhātu), and the air element (vāyodhātu).'

In this way, it appears in brief in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta by way of one of sharp wisdom who takes the elements as a meditation subject.

The meaning of that teaching is: Just as a skilled butcher or his apprentice, who is maintained by his master's food and wages, having slaughtered a cow and pierced it through, were to sit at a crossroads—meaning the middle of the great roads going to the four quarters—after making it into portions; even so, a bhikkhu reviews this body by way of the elements, saying, "There is in this body the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the air element." It is said to be "however it is placed" because it is placed in any one of the four postures, and "however it is disposed" because it is placed as it is.

What is meant? It is this: Just as for the butcher, while he is rearing the cow, while he is leading it to the slaughterhouse, while he is tying it up there after leading it, while he is slaughtering it, and while he is looking at the slaughtered dead cow—until he has flayed it and divided it into portions—the perception "cow" does not disappear. But when he has divided it and is sitting there, the perception "cow" disappears and the perception "meat" arises. It does not occur to him, "I am selling a cow" or "These people are buying a cow." Rather, it occurs to him, "I am selling meat" and "These people are buying meat." Even so, for this yogi monk, in the past when he was an ignorant worldling, whether as a layman or as a monk, the perception "being," "man," or "person" does not disappear until he has analyzed this very body, however it is placed and however it is disposed, by breaking up the compactness and reviewing it by way of the elements. 

Note: 1. Connect with "the body however it is placed."

But when he reviews it by way of the elements, the perception "being" disappears, and the mind becomes well-established by way of the elements alone. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, just as if a skilled butcher... [as above] ...even so, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu... [as above] ...the air element."

307. In the Mahāhatthipadopama Sutta, however:
"And what, friends, is the internal earth element? Whatever is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, harsh, and clung to. And what is that? Namely: head hairs, body hairs, nails, teeth, skin, flesh, sinews, bones, bone marrow, kidneys, heart, liver, membranes, spleen, lungs..."
344:
...large intestines, small intestines, gorge, feces, (and) whatever else there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, hard, rough, and clung-to—this, friends, is called the internal earth element.

'And what, friends, is the internal water element? Whatever there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, liquid, of a liquid nature, and clung-to. What is that? Namely: bile, phlegm, pus, blood, sweat, fat, tears, grease, spittle, snot, oil of the joints, urine, (and) whatever else there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, liquid, of a liquid nature, and clung-to—this, friends, is called the internal water element.'
