'And what, friends, is the internal fire element? Whatever there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, fiery, of a fiery nature, and clung-to. What is that? Namely: that by which [the body] is warmed, that by which it ages, that by which it is consumed, and that by which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested, (and) whatever else there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, fiery, of a fiery nature, and clung-to—this, friends, is called the internal fire element.'

'And what, friends, is the internal air element? Whatever there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, airy, of an airy nature, and clung-to. What is that? Namely: up-going winds, down-going winds, winds in the belly, winds in the bowels, winds that circulate through the limbs, in-breath and out-breath—these six types of winds. (And) whatever else there is that is internal, belonging to oneself, airy, of an airy nature, and clung-to—this, friends, is called the internal air element.'

This detailed exposition is given for the sake of one who practices the meditation on the elements and whose wisdom is not very sharp. Similarly, [this detail] also appears in the Rāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga of the Abhidhamma.

Now follows the explanation of the terms that are not clear in that teaching. *Ajjhattaṃ* and *paccattaṃ*—both these terms are synonyms for *niyaka* (one's own). *Niyaka* means that which has arisen in oneself, that which is included in one's own continuity. Just as in the world (or in secular grammar), speech concerning women is called *adhitthi*, so too, because it occurs in oneself, it is called *ajjhatta*; and because it occurs dependent on oneself, it is called *paccatta*.

2. Connect "the collection of states..." with "is called *ajjhatta* and *paccatta*."
3. *Adhi + atta = adhyatta = ajjhatta*: states occurring in oneself.
4. *Pati pati + atta*: states occurring dependent on each individual self; states occurring separately in each individual.

*Kakkhaḷa* means *thaddha* (hard/rigid). *Kharigata* means *pharusa* (rough). Among these, the first term describes the characteristic (lakkhaṇa), and the second term describes the mode (ākāra). Indeed, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness (i.e., the earth element should be noted as hard); that earth element has a rough mode. Therefore, [345] it is taught as "*kakkhaḷaṃ kharigataṃ*" (hard and rough). *Upādinna* (clung-to) means firmly taken or grasped; it is firmly taken or grasped as "I" or "mine," or wrongly touched (misapprehended). This is the meaning of the word *upādinna*.

Notes:
1-2. Since these are already translated in the Burmese, these explanations are not very useful for the Burmese translation but are useful for the Pāḷi.
3. The characteristic of hardness is the intrinsic nature of the earth element; therefore, when a Vipassanā practitioner contemplates the earth element, it should be noted/contemplated as "hard" or "rigid."
4. As "I," as "a living being," or as "mine" (my eye, etc.).
345:
All internal phenomena of a living being that can be clung to—such as the eyes of a living being and so forth—are called *upādinna* (clung-to phenomena).

*Seyyathidaṃ* is an indeclinable particle; its meaning is: 'What is this nature?' (Note 1: Although the Visuddhimagga explains *taṃ* as 'that,' here it is translated as 'this nature' in consideration of *idaṃ* contained in the word *seyyathidaṃ*). Then, wishing to show the nature of the earth element in detail, he taught 'hair of the head, hair of the body,' and so forth. To clarify by removing potential objections: it should be understood that the earth element is explained in detail through twenty aspects, by adding the brain (*matthalunga*) to the nineteen aspects starting with head hair and body hair (Note 2: This refers to the method of counting by inclusion as shown on page 274, line 3, of the Burmese translation of the development of mindfulness occupied with the body). By the phrase 'or whatever else there may be,' the earth element present in the remaining three parts (water, fire, air) is included (Note 3: Alternatively, by this phrase 'or whatever else there may be,' the inclusion of the brain should be noted in the Pāḷi text according to the Ṭīkā).

It is called *āpo* (water) because it moves or reaches various places through the nature of flowing (Note 4: This explains the meaning of the word *āpa*). It is called *āpogata* (gone into water) because it enters into various types of water through the power of water produced by kamma and so on (Note 1: This explains the meaning of the word *āpogataṃ*). What is it? It is the characteristic of cohesion of the water element.

It is called *tejo* (fire/heat) by virtue of its sharpness (while being hot). In the same manner as mentioned, it is called *tejogata* because it enters into various types of heat. What is it? It is the characteristic of heat. 'By which it is heated' (*yena ca santappati*) means this body is heated by that disordered heat which has entered into the fire elements; it exists as heat in the form of a one-day fever and so on (Note 2: This passage refers to the heat of fever called *santappana-tejo*). 'By which it ages' (*yena ca jīrīyati*) means the heat by which this body ages, reaching the impairment of the faculties like the eyes, the exhaustion of strength, and states such as wrinkled skin and gray hair (Note 3: This refers to the natural heat that causes aging called *jīraṇa-tejo*). 'By which it is consumed by fever' (*yena ca paridayhati*) means this body suffers burning by that disordered and destructive heat.

That person, lamenting 'I am burning, I am burning,' yearns for the application of ghee washed a hundred times (or many times in cold water), *gosīsa* sandalwood, and so forth, as well as the fanning of a palm leaf (Note 1: This refers to the intense burning heat called *dāha-tejo*). 'By which what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested' means the heat by which the eaten rice etc., the drunk beverages etc., the chewed hard food etc., and the tasted or swallowed ripe mango, honey, molasses etc., reach proper digestion (Note 2: This refers to the digestive heat in the stomach called *pācaka-tejo*). It means they reach a state of separation into essence (*rasa*) and so forth (Note 3: 'Into essence etc.' means by way of essence, blood, flesh, fat, sinews, bones, bone marrow, and semen according to the Ṭīkā; Note 4: 'Reach a state of separation' (*vivekaṃ*) means becoming distinct, different, and separate from one another. Indeed, when the various types of nutriment eaten are digested, they become the essence (*rasa-dhātu*); the essence arises depending on that food. Similarly, when the essence is transformed, it becomes blood, and so on. All should be understood in this way according to the Ṭīkā). This is the intended meaning of the phrase 'reaches proper digestion.' Specifically, among these four types of fire element, the first three are produced by four causes: kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment. The last fire element is produced by kamma alone.

It is called *vāyo* (air) by virtue of moving or pushing (or by virtue of moving with momentum) (Note 1: This explains the meaning of the word *vāyo*. The air element means the nature of causing movement or pushing, the nature of moving with momentum). In the same manner as mentioned, it is called *vāyogata* because it enters into various types of air. What is it? It is the characteristic of supporting or distension (*vitthambhana*). Upward-going winds (*uddhaṅgamā vātā*) are those winds that ascend, causing belching, hiccups, and so forth. Downward-going winds (*adhogamā vātā*) are those winds that descend, expelling feces, urine, and so forth. Winds in the belly (*kucchisayā vātā*) are those winds situated in the abdomen outside the intestines. Winds in the bowels (*koṭṭhāsayā vātā*) are those winds situated inside the intestines. Winds that course through the limbs (*aṅgamaṅgānusārino vātā*) are those winds that spread through the major and minor limbs of the whole body by following the network of nerves, causing bending, stretching, and so forth.

In-breath (*assāsa*) is the nasal air that enters within (Note 1). Out-breath (*passāsa*) is the nasal air that exits outside (Note 2).
346:
Specifically, among these six types of air, the first five are produced by four causes: kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment. [346] In-breaths and out-breaths are produced by consciousness alone. In all detailed explanations of the water element and others, the phrase 'Yaṃ vā panaññampi kiñci' (or whatever else there may be) includes the remaining parts such as the water element in the other sections.

Thus, the earth element is detailed by twenty aspects, the water element by twelve aspects, the fire element by four aspects, and the air element by six aspects. Therefore, the four elements are detailed by forty-two aspects. This is the initial commentary on the Pali text regarding the definition of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna).

308. In the method of development (bhāvanānaya) for this definition of the four elements, for a monk of sharp wisdom, the detailed apprehension of elements such as 'hair is the earth element, body hair is the earth element' appears as a proliferation (papañca). Only when he attends to it as: 'That which has the characteristic of hardness is the earth element; that which has the characteristic of cohesion is the water element; that which has the characteristic of ripening is the fire element; that which has the characteristic of supporting is the air element,' does the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) become clear to him. However, for a monk who is not of sharp wisdom, attending to it in this [brief] way results in darkness and lack of clarity; the meditation subject becomes clear only when he attends to it in detail according to the previous method.

How? Just as when two monks are reciting a text containing many ellipses (peyyāla), the monk of sharp wisdom recites the full text of the ellipsis once or twice, and thereafter continues the recitation by way of the two ends [beginning and end]. Regarding this, the monk who is not of sharp wisdom might say: 'What kind of recitation is this? It does not even allow for the mere contact of the lips. If reciting in this way, when will the text be mastered?' He recites by expanding every ellipsis as it comes. The other monk says to him: 'What kind of recitation is this? It does not allow one to reach the end. If reciting in this way, when will the text reach its conclusion?'

In the same way, for a monk of sharp wisdom, the detailed apprehension of elements by way of hair, etc., appears as a proliferation. The meditation subject becomes clear only when he attends to it briefly in the manner: 'That which has the characteristic of hardness is the earth element,' and so on. For the other monk, attending to it in that [brief] way results in darkness and lack of clarity; it becomes clear only when he attends to it in detail by way of hair, etc.

Therefore, a monk of sharp wisdom who wishes to develop this meditation subject should go into seclusion, withdraw from external objects, and after contemplating his entire physical body (rūpakāya), [he should attend thus]: 'In this body, that which is the state of hardness or the state of roughness is the earth element.'

Note 1: By the term 'state of hardness,' the characteristic (lakkhaṇa) [of the earth element] is stated. Indeed, the earth element has the state of hardness as its characteristic. By the term 'state of roughness,' the mode that appears [to the meditative knowledge] is stated; the meaning is the mode to be grasped by knowledge. (Ṭīkā)
347:
For some individuals, [the elements] are grasped by way of performing their own functions (rasa). Among these two—characteristic (lakkhaṇa) and function (rasa)—this yogi who attends to the elements at the beginning of the practice grasps them (i.e., distinguishes them with wisdom) by their respective characteristics and functions. (Ṭīkā)

1. Connect with: "Concentration... arises." Here, the phrase "concentration is grasped by wisdom" means it is protected and supported by making the object clearly known and manifest.

2. Having grasped the elements as described: "In this body, there is the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), which is hardness or roughness."

Note:
"There is the water element (āpo-dhātu), which is liquidity or cohesion; there is the fire element (tejo-dhātu), which is heat or ripening; there is the air element (vāyo-dhātu), which is supporting, stiffness, or motion and causing motion." In this way, together with the characteristics and so forth, one should repeatedly reflect, attend to, and contemplate the elements even for a hundred or a thousand times. One should perform the act of attending repeatedly, as if striking with thought, or turning and striking with specialized thought. For that yogi monk who attends thus, whichever nature among the characteristics and so forth becomes clearly manifest, he should grasp only that nature, letting go of others, and cause the attention to arise as "earth element," "water element," and so forth, along with whichever characteristic is clearly manifest. A yogi who attends in this way also... etc... should appropriately fulfill these ten skills in attention (manasikāra-kosalla). (One should continue to show how the ten skills in attention arise here, following the method shown in paragraph 181 of the Burmese translation. Refer back to paragraph 181.) Thus, for the yogi who balances effort (vīriya) and concentration (samādhi) and brings about attention only to that manifest characteristic, when the faculties (indriya) such as faith (saddhā) become balanced and extremely pure and clear, they receive the support of the seven powers (bala) which are exceedingly potent due to the distancing of unwholesome states such as lack of faith (assaddhiya). Then the jhana factors such as initial application (vitakka) become particularly sharp and manifest. Because they are the direct opposites of those [jhana factors],

Alternatively, to show the non-sentient nature of the four great elements, the General of the Dhamma (Dhamma-senāpati) [Venerable Sāriputta] taught the four parts (koṭṭhāsa): "Depending on bone, depending on sinew, depending on flesh, and depending on skin, the enclosed space (ākāsa) is reckoned as 'form' (rūpa)." (M. Ni. 1.306). Having distinguished those four parts (such as bone and sinew) with the hand of wisdom that can follow into the intervals between them,

Note:
The hindrances (nīvaraṇa), along with the unwholesome states that share the same basis, are indeed distanced. By this much, this yogi has already attained access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) which has the characteristics of the elements as its object. Therefore, it is said: "One should repeatedly attend to them as mere elements, such as 'earth element, water element (fire element, air element)'... for that monk who strives in this way... concentration that is a mere access (upacāra) arises." (Ṭīkā)

Access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) should also be understood by the power of conventional usage (rūḷhī). Indeed, the concentration that occurs close to absorption (appanā) is called access concentration. In this meditation on the definition of the elements (dhātu-vavatthāna), there is no absorption. However, because it possesses characteristics similar to the characteristic (the absence of hindrances) of the [actual] access concentration that occurs close to absorption, it is called access concentration. (Ṭīkā, Vol. 1, p. 436, lines 5-8)

Distinguishing with the hand of wisdom, whatever hardness or roughness exists in these four parts (bone, sinew, flesh, skin), that is the earth element. Grasping the elements in this way by the previous method, one should repeatedly reflect, attend to, and contemplate them as mere elements, as non-sentient, and as non-living, as "earth element, water element (fire element, air element)." For that monk who strives in this way, before long, concentration that is a mere access arises, which does not reach absorption because its object is a natural state (sabhāva-dhamma) and it is grasped by wisdom that illuminates the distinction of the elements. This is the method of development for the definition of the four elements that comes in brief.

309. The method of development for the definition of the four elements that comes in detail should be understood as follows. A yogi monk whose wisdom is not very sharp and who wishes to develop this meditation subject, having learned the elements in detail through the forty-two aspects from a teacher, residing in a monastery endowed with the aforementioned qualities, having performed all duties, having gone to a secluded place and withdrawn from external objects,

being well-fixed [on the meditation subject], he should develop the meditation subject by way of these four modes: (1) Sasambhāra-saṅkhepa (Briefly with constituents), (2) Sasambhāra-vibhatti (Detailed with constituents), (3) Salakkhaṇa-saṅkhepa (Briefly with characteristics), and (4) Salakkhaṇa-vibhatti (Detailed with characteristics).

Note:
1. The sign (nimitta) by which the knowledge of "earth" and the name "earth" arise is called sambhāra. What is it? It is earth and so forth. Indeed, in the twenty parts such as hair, the knowledge and name "earth" arise depending on hardness; thus, earth is the cause of their arising. Therefore, in those twenty parts, earth is called the constituent (sambhāra). Because that hardness or earth is predominant in hair and so forth, those parts (hair, etc.) are called "sasambhāra" (with constituents). The same applies to the water parts and so forth. The brief (saṅkhepa) of hair and so forth which occur with their constituents like earth is called Sasambhāra-saṅkhepa. (Ṭīkā) According to this Ṭīkā, sambhāra refers to the four elements like earth. Taking hair and so forth, which occur with the constituent called earth element, as "sasambhāra," the brief observation of those hair and so forth should be taken as Sasambhāra-saṅkhepa. (This might not be the intention of the Commentator). In our [the translator's] view:

Note:
Just as the timber and bamboo of a house are called sambhāra (materials), it seems appropriate to take the collection of other material qualities (rūpa) contained in hair and so forth, other than the earth element, as sambhāra. If taken this way, when hair is called "earth element," it does not mean only the characteristic of hardness, but it is called earth element because it includes the constituents (sambhāra) of other elements and material qualities besides earth. Thus, the meaning that hair and so forth are called "sasambhāra-pathavī-dhātu" (earth element with its constituents) is very straightforward. Therefore, it should be taken that Sasambhāra-saṅkhepa means the brief observation of elements like earth together with (+sa) their constituents (sambhāra) which are the other material qualities.

2. Sasambhāra-vibhatti: The detailed (vibhatti) analysis of earth and so forth together with their constituents like hair. This is the meaning according to the Ṭīkā. In our view, it should be translated as the detailed analysis of earth and so forth including the constituents of other elements and material qualities.

3. Salakkhaṇa-saṅkhepa: The brief (saṅkhepa) of hair and so forth together with (+sa) their characteristics (lakkhaṇa) such as hardness.
348: 4. Detailed analysis of characteristics: Detailed analysis of hair, etc., along with their characteristics. ## (1) Contemplation by way of Brief Analysis of Components In this context, how should it be developed by way of brief analysis of components? In this Dispensation, a monk defines and views the hard characteristic in the twenty parts (from head-hair to brain) as the earth element. He defines and views the cohesive characteristic called water, which has reached the state of liquid, in the twelve parts (from bile to urine) as the water element. He defines and views the heat that causes ripening in the four parts (from that which heats, etc.) as the fire element. He defines and views the supporting and distending characteristic in the six parts (from up-going winds, etc.) as the air element. To that yogi monk who defines and views in this way, the elements become manifest. As he adverts to and brings to mind those elements again and again, access concentration (upacārasamādhi) arises in the manner already described. (1) ## (2) Contemplation by way of Detailed Analysis of Components 310. If, while developing it by way of brief analysis of components as described, the meditation subject is not yet successful or complete, that yogi monk should develop it by way of detailed analysis of components. How? That yogi monk should perform all the procedures mentioned in the explanation of the meditation subject of mindfulness occupied with the body, namely the seven kinds of skill in acquisition and the ten kinds of skill in attention, without omitting any of them regarding the thirty-two parts. Starting from the verbal recitation of the skin-pentad (taca-pañcaka), etc., in forward and backward order, all the methods mentioned there should be carried out. This is the only difference: there (in mindfulness occupied with the body), after bringing to mind hair, etc., by way of color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation, the mind should be established by way of repulsiveness; here (in the definition of the four elements), it should be established by way of the nature of the elements. Therefore, after bringing to mind hair, etc., in groups of five by way of color and so on, at the end, attention should be directed in the following manner. ## Contemplation of Head-hairs 311. These called head-hairs grow on the skin that covers the skull. Just as when kunda-grass grows on the top of an ant-hill, the top of the ant-hill does not know, 'Kunda-grass is growing on me,' nor does the kunda-grass know, 'We are growing on the top of an ant-hill'; even so, the skin covering the skull does not know, 'Head-hairs are growing on me,' nor do the head-hairs know, 'We are growing on the skin covering the skull.' These things (dhammas) are devoid of mutual concern and reviewing. Thus, head-hairs are a separate part in this body; they are non-sentient (acetana), indeterminate (abyākata) (or: they do not know an object), void (suñña), not a being (nissatta), and are the hard earth element (pathavīdhātu). ## Contemplation of Body-hairs 312. Body-hairs grow on the skin that covers the body. Just as when dabba-grass grows in the site of a deserted village, the site of the deserted village does not know, 'Dabba-grass is growing on me,' nor does the dabba-grass know, 'We are growing in the site of a deserted village'; even so, the skin covering the body does not know, 'Body-hairs are growing on me,' nor do the body-hairs know...
349:
Nor do the body hairs know 'we are growing on the skin covering the body.' These physical phenomena of body hairs and skin are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, body hairs are a separate part in this body; they are inanimate, indeterminate, void, not a living being, and are the hard earth element (pathavīdhātu). (Thus should one give attention.)

## Contemplation of Nails
313. Nails grow on the tips of the fingers and toes. Among those nails and the fingers and toes, just as when children play by piercing madhuka seeds with small sticks, the sticks do not know 'madhuka seeds are placed on us,' nor do the madhuka seeds know 'we are placed on sticks'; in the same way, the fingers and toes do not know 'nails grow on our tips,' nor do the nails know 'we grow on the tips of the fingers and toes.' These physical phenomena of nails and fingers/toes are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, nails are a separate part in this body... [they are inanimate, indeterminate, void, not a living being] and are the earth element (pathavīdhātu). (Thus should one give attention.)

## Contemplation of Teeth
314. Teeth grow in the jawbones. Among those teeth and the jawbones, just as when carpenters set posts in stone mortars by binding them with some kind of resin, the mortars do not know 'posts are standing in us,' nor do the posts know 'we are standing in mortars'; in the same way, the jawbones do not know 'teeth grow in us,' nor do the teeth know 'we grow in jawbones.' These physical phenomena of teeth and jawbones are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, teeth are a separate part in this body... etc. ...they are the earth element (pathavīdhātu). (Thus should one give attention.)

## Contemplation of Skin
315. The skin stands covering and enveloping the whole body. Among that skin and the body, just as when a large lute is covered with wet ox-hide, the large lute does not know 'I am covered with wet ox-hide,' nor does the wet ox-hide know 'I stand enveloping a large lute'; in the same way, the body does not know 'I am covered by skin,' nor does the skin know 'I stand enveloping the body.' These physical phenomena of skin and body are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, skin is a separate part in this body... etc. ...they are the earth element (pathavīdhātu). (Thus should one give attention.)

## Contemplation of Flesh
316. Flesh stands plastered over the skeleton of more than three hundred bones. Among that flesh and the bones, just as when a wall is plastered with thick clay, the wall does not know 'I am plastered with clay'
350:
[350] Just as a lump of fine clay does not know, "I am plastered and clinging to the wall," so too the skeleton does not know, "I am plastered with flesh consisting of nine hundred pieces." The flesh also does not know, "I am plastered and clinging to the skeleton." These phenomena, namely flesh and bones, are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called flesh is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element. (This should be reflected upon).

## Contemplating the Sinews
317. The sinews remain in the body binding the bones together. Among those sinews and bones, just as when wall timbers are bound with creepers, the wall timbers do not know, "We are bound by creepers," and the creepers do not know, "We are binding the wall timbers," so too the bones do not know, "We are bound by sinews," and the sinews do not know, "We are binding the bones." These phenomena, namely sinews and bones, are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called sinews is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element. (This should be reflected upon).

## Contemplating the Bones
318. Among the bones, the heel bone stands supporting the ankle bone; the ankle bone stands supporting the shin bone; the shin bone stands supporting the thigh bone; the thigh bone stands supporting the pelvis bone; the pelvis bone stands supporting the spinal column; the spinal column stands supporting the neck bone; the neck bone stands supporting the skull. The skull rests on the neck bone; the neck bone rests on the spinal column; the spinal column rests on the pelvis bone; the pelvis bone rests on the thigh bone; the thigh bone rests on the shin bone; the shin bone rests on the ankle bone; the ankle bone rests on the heel bone.

Among those bones, just as in stacks of bricks, wood, cow dung, etc., the lower bricks, etc., do not know, "We stand supporting the upper bricks, etc.," and the upper bricks, etc., do not know, "We rest upon the lower bricks, etc.," so too the heel bone does not know, "I stand supporting the ankle bone." The ankle bone does not know, "I stand supporting the shin bone." The shin bone does not know, "I stand supporting the thigh bone." The thigh bone does not know, "I stand supporting the pelvis bone." The pelvis bone does not know, "I stand supporting the spinal column." The spinal column does not know, "I stand supporting the neck bone." The neck bone does not know, "I stand supporting the skull." The skull does not know, "I rest upon the neck bone."
351:
The neck bone does not know, [351] "I rest upon the spinal column." The spinal column does not know, "I rest upon the pelvis bone." The pelvis bone does not know, "I rest upon the thigh bone." The thigh bone does not know, "I rest upon the shin bone." The shin bone does not know, "I rest upon the ankle bone." The ankle bone does not know, "I rest upon the heel bone." These phenomena, namely the upper bones and lower bones, are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called bone is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element. (This should be reflected upon).

## Contemplating the Bone Marrow
319. The bone marrow remains inside the various bones. Among that marrow and the bones, just as when blanched cane shoots, etc., are placed inside bamboo tubes, etc., the bamboo tubes do not know, "Cane shoots are placed within us," and the cane shoots do not know, "We remain within the bamboo tubes," so too the bones do not know, "Marrow remains within us," and the marrow does not know, "I remain within the bones." These phenomena, namely marrow and bones, are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called bone marrow is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element. (This should be reflected upon).

## Contemplating the Kidneys
320. The kidneys are bound by a large sinew that originates from the throat, travels a short distance, and divides into two; they remain surrounding the heart. Among those kidneys and the large sinew, just as in a cluster of two mangoes bound by a stalk, the stalk does not know, "I am binding a cluster of two mangoes," and the cluster of two mangoes does not know, "I am bound by a stalk," so too the large sinew does not know, "I am binding the kidneys," and the kidneys do not know, "I am bound by the large sinew." These phenomena, namely the kidneys and the large sinew, are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection. Thus, what is called kidneys is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element. (This should be reflected upon).

## Contemplating the Heart
321. The heart remains inside the body, depending on the center of the chest cavity. Among that heart and the chest cavity, just as when a piece of meat is placed depending on a worn-out palanquin frame, the interior of the palanquin frame does not know, "A piece of meat remains depending on me," and the piece of meat does not know, "I remain depending on a worn-out palanquin frame," so too the interior of the chest cavity does not know, "The heart remains depending on me," and the heart does not know, "I remain depending on the chest cavity." These phenomena, namely the heart and the chest cavity, are devoid of mutual advertence and reflection.
352:
[352] Therefore, what is called the heart is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).

## Contemplation of the Liver
322. The liver is situated inside the body, between the two breasts, leaning against the right side. Between that liver and the right side between the two breasts, for example, if a pair of meat lumps is attached to the side of a cooking pot, the side of the cooking pot does not know, "A pair of meat lumps is attached to me," nor do the meat lumps know, "We are attached to the side of a cooking pot." In the same way, the right side between the two breasts does not know, "The liver is situated depending on me," nor does the liver know, "I am situated depending on the right side between the two breasts." These phenomena, the liver and the right side between the two breasts, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Therefore, what is called the liver is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).

## Contemplation of the Membranes
323. Among the membranes, the concealed membrane is situated surrounding and covering the heart and the kidneys. The unconcealed membrane is situated under the skin throughout the whole body, covering the flesh. Between those membranes and the heart, etc., for example, if meat is wrapped in a coarse cloth, the meat does not know, "I am wrapped in a coarse cloth," nor does the coarse cloth know, "The meat is wrapped by me." In the same way, the kidneys, the heart, and the flesh of the whole body do not know, "I am covered by the membrane," nor does the membrane know, "The kidneys, the heart, and the flesh of the whole body are covered by me." These phenomena, the membrane, the heart, the kidneys, and the flesh, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Therefore, what is called the membrane is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).

## Contemplation of the Spleen
324. The spleen is situated on the left side of the heart, depending on the upper side of the stomach lining. Between that spleen and the stomach lining, for example, if a lump of cow dung is situated depending on the upper side of a granary, the upper side of the granary does not know, "A lump of cow dung is situated depending on me," nor does the lump of cow dung know, "I am situated depending on the upper side of a granary." In the same way, the upper side of the stomach lining does not know, "The spleen is situated depending on me," nor does the spleen know, "I am situated depending on the upper side of the stomach lining." These phenomena, the spleen and the upper side of the stomach lining, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Therefore, what is called the spleen is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).
353:
## Contemplation of the Lungs
[353] 325. The lungs are situated inside the body between the two breasts, hanging over and covering the heart and the liver. Between those lungs and the interior of the body, for example, if a bird's nest is hanging inside a decayed granary, the interior of the decayed granary does not know, "A bird's nest is hanging and situated in me," nor does the bird's nest know, "I am hanging and situated in the interior of a decayed granary." In the same way, the interior of that body does not know, "The lungs are hanging and situated in me," nor do the lungs know, "I am hanging and situated in such an interior of the body." These phenomena, the lungs and the interior of the body, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Therefore, what is called the lungs is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).

## Contemplation of the Large Intestine
326. The large intestine is situated inside the body, beginning from the throat and ending at the anus. Between that large intestine and the interior of the body, for example, if the body of a headless rat-snake¹ is coiled and placed in a trough filled with blood, the blood trough does not know, "The body of a rat-snake is situated in me," nor does the body of the rat-snake know, "I am situated in the blood trough." In the same way, the interior of the body does not know, "The large intestine is situated in me," nor does the large intestine know, "I am situated inside the body." These phenomena, the large intestine and the interior of the body, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Therefore, what is called the large intestine is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).

Note
1. Here, the meaning of "rat-snake" is the meaning of the word "dhammanī". In the Pyay Nissaya, it is translated as "grasshopper", but it should refer to that same rat-snake. In the Sinhalese Dictionary Nissaya, it is said to be translated as "house-snake". Since it has the same meaning as the word "gharasappa", only the meaning "rat-snake" is appropriate.

## Contemplation of the Small Intestine
327. The small intestine is situated between the coils of the large intestine, binding the twenty-one coils of the intestine. Between that small intestine and the large intestine, for example, if small ropes are sewing together a foot-wipe ring, the foot-wipe ring does not know, "Small ropes are sewing me together," nor do the small ropes know, "We are sewing together the foot-wipe ring." In the same way, the large intestine does not know, "The small intestine is binding me," nor does the small intestine know, "I am binding the large intestine." These phenomena, the small intestine and the large intestine, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Therefore, what is called the small intestine is a separate part in this body... (etc.) ...it is the earth element—thus (one should contemplate).

## Contemplation of Undigested Food
328. Undigested food is the food that has been eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, situated in the stomach. Between that food and the stomach, for example, where dog's vomit is situated in a dog's bowl, the dog's bowl does not know, "Dog's vomit is situated in me," nor does the dog's vomit know, "I am situated in the dog's bowl." In the same way, the stomach does not know, "Undigested food [354] is situated in me,"
354:
Undigested food also does not know, 'I am situated in the stomach.' These physical phenomena, undigested food and the stomach, are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called undigested food is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element (one should reflect).

## Contemplation of Feces
329. Feces, also known as excrement, is situated in the rectum, which is like an eight-finger-breadth bamboo joint at the end of the intestines. Between the feces and the rectum, for example, if fine pale clay is kneaded and stuffed into a bamboo joint, the bamboo joint does not know, 'Fine pale clay is situated in me,' nor does the fine pale clay know, 'I am situated in the bamboo joint.' In the same way, the rectum does not know, 'Feces is situated in me,' nor does the feces know, 'I am situated in the rectum.' These physical phenomena, feces and the rectum, are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called feces is a separate part in this body... it is the earth element (one should reflect).

## Contemplation of the Brain
330. The brain is situated inside the skull. Between the brain and the interior of the skull, for example, if a lump of dough is placed in an old gourd shell, the gourd shell does not know, 'A lump of dough is situated in me,' nor does the lump of dough know, 'I am situated in the gourd shell.' In the same way, the interior of the skull does not know, 'The brain is situated in me,' nor does the brain know, 'I am situated inside the skull.' These physical phenomena, the brain and the skull, are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called the brain is a separate part in this body; it is non-sentient, indeterminate (i.e., it does not know an object), void of self, not a living being, and is the rigid earth element (one should reflect).

## Contemplation of Bile
331. Among the two kinds of bile, free bile is connected with the life faculty and is spread throughout the whole body; local bile is situated in the gall-bladder. Between these two kinds of bile and their locations, for example, when oil is spread through a cake, the cake does not know, 'Oil is spread through me,' nor does the oil know, 'I am spread through the cake.' In the same way, the body does not know, 'Free bile is spread through me,' nor does the free bile know, 'I am spread through the body.' (As for the example of local bile:) If a luffa gourd shell is filled with rainwater, the luffa gourd shell does not know, 'Rainwater is situated in me,' nor does the rainwater know, 'I am situated in the luffa gourd shell.' In the same way, the gall-bladder does not know, 'Local bile is situated in me,' nor does the local bile know, 'I am situated in the gall-bladder.' These physical phenomena, these two kinds of bile and their locations, are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called bile is a separate part in this body...
355:
...it is non-sentient, indeterminate (i.e., it does not know an object), void of self, not a living being, liquid in nature, and has the characteristic of cohesion, which is the water element (one should reflect).

## Contemplation of Phlegm
332. Phlegm, in the amount of one pattha measure, is situated on the stomach lining. Between the phlegm and the stomach lining, for example, when a layer of froth forms on the surface of a cesspool, the cesspool does not know, 'A layer of froth is situated on me,' nor does the layer of froth know, 'I am situated on the cesspool.' In the same way, the stomach lining does not know, 'Phlegm is situated on me,' nor does the phlegm know, 'I am situated on the stomach lining.' These physical phenomena, phlegm and the stomach lining, are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called phlegm is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (one should reflect).

## Contemplation of Pus
333. Pus has no permanent location. Wherever the body is struck by a stump, a thorn, a weapon, a flame, etc., blood accumulates and matures there, or boils and carbuncles arise; pus is situated in those parts of the body. Between the pus and the body parts, for example, when resin oozes from a tree due to being cut by an axe, etc., the parts of the tree that were cut do not know, 'Resin is situated in us,' nor does the resin know, 'I am situated in the cut parts of the tree.' In the same way, the parts of the body struck by a stump, a thorn, etc., do not know, 'Pus is situated in us,' nor does the pus know, 'I am situated in those parts of the body.' These physical phenomena, pus and the struck body parts, are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called pus is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (one should reflect).

## Contemplation of Blood
334. Among the types of blood, circulating blood is spread throughout the whole body like free bile. Accumulated blood fills the lower part of the liver's location, in the amount of one pattha measure, and remains moistening the kidneys, heart, liver, and lungs. Between these two kinds of blood, the determination for circulating blood is the same as that for free bile. As for accumulated blood, it should be understood through this example: when an old potsherd is moistened by rainwater, and the water in the potsherd moistens the clods of earth, etc., underneath it, the clods of earth do not know, 'The water in the potsherd is moistening us'...
356:
Just as water in a pan does not know, "I am moistening the brickbats and so on," even so, the lower part of the liver and the kidneys and so on do not know, "Blood is situated in us," or "Blood is situated moistening us." Nor does the blood know, "I am situated filling the lower part of the liver and moistening the kidneys and so on." These physical phenomena of blood and its location are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called blood is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpo-dhātu). (Thus should one reflect.)

## Contemplation of Sweat
335. Sweat (seda) fills the pores of the hair and skin and both stays there and oozes out during times of heat from fire and so on. In that regard, between the sweat and the pores of the hair and skin, just as when bundles of lotus fibers, lotus stalks, and water-lily stalks are just pulled out of the water, the openings in the bundles of lotus fibers and so on do not know, "Water is oozing from us," nor does the water oozing from them know, "I am oozing from the openings of the lotus fibers and so on," even so, the pores of the hair and skin do not know, "Sweat is oozing from us." Nor does the sweat know, "I am oozing from the pores of the hair and skin." These physical phenomena of sweat and the pores of the hair and skin are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called sweat is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpo-dhātu). (Thus should one reflect.)

## Contemplation of Fat
336. Fat (meda) is the thick grease that pervades the whole body of a fat person and, in a thin person, stays relying on the flesh of the calves and so on. In that regard, between the fat and its location, just as when a heap of meat is covered with a yellow-dyed rag, the heap of meat does not know, "A yellow-dyed rag is situated relying on me," nor does the yellow-dyed rag know, "I am situated relying on a heap of meat," even so, the flesh in the whole body or in the calves and so on does not know, "Fat is situated relying on me." Nor does the fat know, "I am situated relying on the flesh in the whole body or in the calves and so on." These physical phenomena of fat and the flesh it relies on are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called fat is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpo-dhātu). (Thus should one reflect.)
357:
## Contemplation of Tears
337. When tears (assu) arise, they either fill the eye sockets or flow out. In that regard, between the tears and the eye sockets, just as when the cavities of young palm-nuts are filled with water, the cavities of the young palm-nuts do not know, "Water is situated in us," nor does the water situated in them know, "I am situated in the cavities of the young palm-nuts," even so, the eye sockets do not know, "Tears are situated in us." Nor do the tears know, "I am situated in the eye sockets." These physical phenomena of tears and eye sockets are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called tears is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpo-dhātu). (Thus should one reflect.)

## Contemplation of Skin-oil
338. Skin-oil (vasā) is the melted grease situated on the palms, the backs of the hands, the soles of the feet, the backs of the feet, the nostrils, the forehead, and the shoulder-points during times of heat from fire and so on. In that regard, between the skin-oil and its location, just as when oil is poured over a crust of rice, the crust of rice does not know, "Oil is situated overspreading me," nor does the oil know, "I am situated overspreading the crust of rice," even so, the area of the palms and so on does not know, "Skin-oil is situated overspreading me." Nor does the skin-oil know, "I am situated overspreading the area of the palms and so on." These physical phenomena of skin-oil and its location are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called skin-oil is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpo-dhātu). (Thus should one reflect.)

## Contemplation of Saliva
339. When there is a cause for the production of saliva (kheḷa), it descends from both sides of the cheeks and stays on the surface of the tongue. In that regard, between the saliva and the surface of the tongue, just as in a small hand-dug pit on a riverbank where water constantly seeps in, the surface of the pit does not know, "Water is staying in me," nor does the water know, "I am staying on the surface of the pit," even so, the surface of the tongue does not know, "Saliva, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, is staying on me." Nor does the saliva know, "I, having descended from both sides of the cheeks, am staying on the surface of the tongue." These physical phenomena of saliva and the tongue are devoid of mutual concern or reflection. Thus, what is called saliva is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpo-dhātu). (Thus should one reflect.)

## Contemplation of Snot
340.
358:
When snot is produced, it stays filling the nostrils or it trickles out. Among that snot and the nostrils, for example, if a shell (or mother-of-pearl) is filled with rotten curd, the shell does not know, "Rotten curd stays in me," nor does the rotten curd know, "I stay in the shell"; in the same way, the nostrils do not know, "Snot stays in us," nor does the snot know, "I stay in the nostrils." These material phenomena, snot and nostrils, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called snot is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpodhātu). (One should bring this to mind.)

## Contemplating Synovial Fluid
341. Synovial fluid stays in the one hundred and eighty joints, performing the function of lubricating the joints. Among that synovial fluid and the joints, for example, if an axle is lubricated with oil, the axle does not know, "The oil stays lubricating me," nor does the oil know, "I stay lubricating the axle"; in the same way, the one hundred and eighty joints do not know, "Synovial fluid stays lubricating us," nor does the synovial fluid know, "I stay lubricating the one hundred and eighty joints." These material phenomena, synovial fluid and joints, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called synovial fluid is a separate part in this body... it is the water element (āpodhātu). (One should bring this to mind.)

## Contemplating Urine
342. Urine stays inside the bladder. Among that urine and the bladder, for example, if a water-filter pot called a yavanaghaṭa, which has no opening for water to enter, is thrown into a cesspool, the yavanaghaṭa does not know, "Cesspool water stays in me," nor does the cesspool water know, "I stay in the yavanaghaṭa"; in the same way, the bladder does not know, "Urine stays in me," nor does the urine know, "I stay in the bladder." These material phenomena, urine and bladder, are devoid of mutual concern and reflection. Thus, what is called urine is a separate part in this body. It is insentient, an indeterminate state (avyākata) (i.e., a state that does not know an object), empty of self, not a living being; it is the water element (āpodhātu) which is liquid in nature and has the characteristic of binding. (One should bring this to mind.)

## Contemplating the Four Fire Elements
343. Having brought to mind the hair and so on in the manner already described, [one contemplates] that (heat) by which (the body) is burned; this heat is a separate part in this body, insentient, an indeterminate state (i.e., a state that does not know an object), empty of self, not a living being; it is the fire element (tejodhātu) which has the characteristic of maturing. (One should bring this to mind.) [One contemplates] that (heat) by which (the body) ages; (this heat is a separate part in this body... it is the fire element. One should bring this to mind.)
359:
[359] [One contemplates] that (heat) by which (the body) is intensely burned; (this heat is a separate part in this body... it is the fire element. One should bring this to mind.)
That (heat) by which the food that is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is well transformed and digested; this heat is a separate part in this body, insentient, an indeterminate state (i.e., a state that does not know an object), empty of self, not a living being; it is the fire element (tejodhātu) which has the characteristic of maturing. (One should bring this to mind.) In this way, one should bring to mind the parts of the fire element.

## Contemplating the Six Air Elements
344. Then, having grasped the up-going winds as up-going winds, the down-going winds as down-going winds, the winds in the belly as winds in the belly, the winds in the bowels as winds in the bowels, the winds pervading the limbs as winds pervading the limbs, and the in-breaths and out-breaths as in-breaths and out-breaths—what are called up-going winds are a separate part in this body, insentient, an indeterminate state (i.e., a state that does not know an object), empty of self, not a living being; it is the air element (vāyodhātu) which has the characteristic of supporting and distending. Likewise, what are called down-going winds..., what are called winds in the belly..., what are called winds in the bowels..., what are called winds pervading the limbs..., what are called in-breaths and out-breaths are a separate part in this body, insentient, an indeterminate state (i.e., a state that does not know an object), empty of self, not a living being; it is the air element (vāyodhātu) which has the characteristic of supporting and distending. In this way, one should bring to mind the parts of the air element. To that meditating monk who brings them to mind in this way, the elements become clear. To that meditating monk who adverts to and brings to mind those elements repeatedly, access concentration (upacāra samādhi) arises in the manner already described.

## (3) Contemplating by Brief Method of Characteristics
345. If, while developing [the meditation] in the way described (by the distribution of components), the meditation subject is not yet successful or complete, that meditating monk should develop it by the brief method of characteristics (salakkhaṇasaṅkhepa). How? In the twenty parts (such as hair, etc.), the characteristic of hardness should be defined as the earth element (pathavīdhātu). In those same twenty parts, the characteristic of binding should be defined as the water element (āpodhātu); the characteristic of maturing as the fire element (tejodhātu); and the characteristic of supporting and distending as the air element (vāyodhātu). (One should define and contemplate them.)
In the twelve parts (such as bile, etc.), the characteristic of binding should be defined as the water element (āpodhātu). In those same twelve parts, the characteristic of maturing as the fire element (tejodhātu); the characteristic of supporting and distending as the air element (vāyodhātu); and the characteristic of hardness as the earth element (pathavīdhātu). (One should define and contemplate them.)
In the four parts (such as the heat of fever, etc.), the characteristic of maturing should be defined as the fire element (tejodhātu). The characteristic of supporting and distending, which is inseparable from those four types of heat, should be defined as the air element (vāyodhātu); the characteristic of hardness as the earth element (pathavīdhātu); and the characteristic of binding as the water element (āpodhātu).
360:
The characteristic of cohesion should be defined as the water element.

[360] In the six parts (such as the up-going wind, etc.), the characteristic of distension and stiffness should be defined as the air element. In those same six parts, the characteristic of hardness should be defined as the earth element, the characteristic of cohesion as the water element, and the characteristic of ripening as the fire element. To the monk who defines them in this way, the elements become manifest. As he adverts to and attends to those elements repeatedly, access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) arises in the manner already described. (3)

## (4) Contemplation by Way of Analysis of Individual Characteristics

346. If the meditation subject is not successful or complete even when developed in the manner described (by brief individual characteristics), it should be developed by that monk by way of the analysis of individual characteristics (salakkhaṇavibhatti). How? Having grasped head hair and so on in the manner previously described, the characteristic of hardness in the hair should be defined as the earth element. In that same hair, the characteristic of cohesion should be defined as the water element, the characteristic of ripening as the fire element, and the characteristic of distension and stiffness as the air element. In this same way, in all other parts (koṭṭhāsa) such as body hair and so on, the four elements should be defined in each individual part. To the monk who defines them in this way, the elements become manifest. As he adverts to and attends to those elements repeatedly, access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) arises in the manner already described. (4)

Alternatively, the elements should also be attended to by way of these thirteen modes: (1) word meaning (vacanattha), (2) group (kalāpa), (3) powder (cuṇṇa), (4) characteristics, etc. (lakkhaṇādi), (5) origination (samuṭṭhāna), (6) diversity and unity (nānattekatta), (7) separation and non-separation (vinibbhogāvinibbhoga), (8) similarity and dissimilarity (sabhāgavisabhāga), (9) distinction between internal and external (ajjhattikabāhiravisesa), (10) inclusion (saṅgaha), (11) condition (paccaya), (12) non-attention (asamannāhāra), and (13) classification of conditions (paccayavibhāga).

## (1) Attention by Way of Word Meaning

347. Among those thirteen modes, for one attending by way of word meaning: it is 'earth' (pathavī) because it is spread out (patthaṭattā). It is 'water' (āpo) because it flows to various places, or because it is made to satisfy, or because it increases by moistening. It is 'fire' (tejo) because it burns with heat. It is 'air' (vāyo) because it moves or causes movement. In a general sense, they are called 'elements' (dhātu) because they bear their own characteristics, or because they arrange the suffering of the round of rebirths, or because they are the arrangement (or cause of arrangement) of suffering, or because they are the repository of suffering. Thus, they should be attended to by way of word meaning according to specific and general senses. (1)

## (2) Attention by Way of Group

348. As for attention by way of group: the earth element has been explained in detail by way of the twenty parts such as head hair, body hair, etc.; the water element has been explained in detail by way of the twelve parts such as bile, phlegm, etc. Among these thirty-two parts of the earth and water elements—

[361] The concept 'head hair' arises due to the harmonious combination of eight things: color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and the four elements. When these eight things are analyzed (by wisdom) individually, the concept 'head hair' no longer exists.

Therefore, head hair is merely a group of eight things; body hair and so on are likewise merely groups of eight things. To explain further: among these parts such as head hair, the part produced by kamma (kamma-samuṭṭhāna)...
361:
Note
1. I shall first present the original verse. (To be memorized if desired):

Color, odor, taste, and essence,
And the four elements as well;
From the combination of these eight things,
There is the conventional term 'hair'.
From the separation of these very things,
The conventional term 'hair' does not exist.

Color (vaṇṇa), odor (gandha), taste (rasa), nutritive essence (ojā), and the four great elements (cattāro mahābhūtā)—due to the harmonious combination of these eight things, the conventional term 'hair' (kesā) arises. When these same eight things are analyzed individually by wisdom, the conventional term 'hair' no longer exists.

2. The kamma-produced (kamma-samuṭṭhāna) part (koṭṭhāsa) refers to the root portion of the hair embedded within the skin; the same should be understood accordingly for body hair and so on. In these parts, there is also the group of nine factors (jīvita-navaka-kalāpa) including the digestive fire (pācaka-tejo). (Ṭīkā)

There is also a group of ten material factors (dasadhamma-kalāpa) together with the life faculty (jīvitindriya) and sex-determined materiality (bhāva-rūpa). However, due to the predominance of the qualities of earth and water (pathavī-satti, āpo-satti), they are reckoned and called the earth element and water element. In this way, they should be reflected upon by way of groups (kalāpa).

Note
1. This statement answers the question: why are they called the earth element and water element when they are actually groups of eight, nine, or ten material factors?

Here, I shall further present the method of counting the groups (kalāpa) and material factors as shown in the Ṭīkā.

Among these 42 parts (koṭṭhāsa), four—namely, undigested food, digested food, pus, and urine—are temperature-produced (utu-samuṭṭhāna) only. The digestive fire (pācaka-tejo) is kamma-produced (kamma-samuṭṭhāna) only. The in-breath and out-breath are mind-produced (citta-samuṭṭhāna) only. Thus, there are 6 parts that are single-originated (eka-samuṭṭhāna). Four parts—sweat, tears, saliva, and snot—are double-originated (dvi-samuṭṭhāna), being produced by temperature and mind. The remaining 32 parts are quadruple-originated (catu-samuṭṭhāna), being produced by the four causes: kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment.

Among those 42 parts, in the digestive fire part, only one jīvita-navaka-kalāpa is obtained. Among the other five single-originated parts, in the 4 temperature-produced parts, one utu-ja-aṭṭhaka-kalāpa is obtained for each. In the breath part, only one citta-ja-aṭṭhaka-kalāpa is obtained. (Total: 6 kalāpas, 49 material factors).

## (3) Reflection by Way of Particles (Cuṇṇa)

349. As for the reflection by way of particles: In this body, if one considers it in medium proportion, the earth element, which has reached the state of fine dust through the breaking down into atoms (paramāṇu), would be about one measure (doṇa). This earth element, being held together by the water element which is half its measure, protected by the fire element, and supported and stiffened by the air element, does not scatter or disintegrate. Because it does not scatter or disintegrate, it arrives at various conceptualizations such as the form of a woman or a man, and manifests states such as small, large, long, short, firm, and hard.

Note
In the 4 double-originated parts, 4 utu-ja-aṭṭhaka-kalāpas and 4 citta-ja-aṭṭhaka-kalāpas are obtained. (Total: 8 kalāpas, 64 material factors).

Among the quadruple-originated parts, in the temperature-born, mind-born, and nutriment-born parts, 3 aṭṭhaka-kalāpas are obtained for each. (Total: 96 kalāpas, 768 material factors). In the temperature-born and mind-born parts, 2 sadda-navaka-kalāpas are obtained (one utu-ja-sadda-navaka-kalāpa and one citta-ja-sadda-navaka-kalāpa; total: 2 kalāpas, 18 material factors). In the 8 kamma-born fire and air parts, 8 jīvita-navaka-kalāpas are obtained (Total: 72 material factors). In the remaining 24 kamma-born parts, 2 kalāpas each of kāya-dasaka and bhāva-dasaka are obtained (48 kalāpas, 480 material factors).

Furthermore, in this body, the water element, which is in the form of liquid and acts as the mode of cohesion, is established in the earth element, protected by fire, and supported and stiffened by air; thus it does not leak or flow out. Because it does not leak or flow out, it manifests the state of being moist and full.

Furthermore, in this body, the fire element, which has the characteristic of heat and acts as the mode of warmth that digests what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted, is established in the earth element, held together by water, and supported and stiffened by air; thus it matures this body and brings about the perfection of its complexion and beauty.

Note
In the 5 fleshy parts such as the eyes, 5 kalāpas are obtained: cakkhu-dasaka, sota-dasaka, ghāna-dasaka, jivhā-dasaka, and vatthu-dasaka (Total: 50 material factors). Thus, in a physical body complete with sense bases (āyatana), if one combines similar groups without analyzing the differences in types of material groups, there are 173 material groups (kalāpa) and 1501 material factors (rūpa). (Ṭīkā)

The summation is as follows: 6 kalāpas and 49 rūpas in single-originated; 8 kalāpas and 64 rūpas in double-originated; 96 kalāpas and 768 rūpas in triple-originated parts from the quadruple-originated; 2 sadda-navaka-kalāpas and 18 rūpas; 8 kalāpas and 72 rūpas in the 8 kamma-born fire-air parts; 48 kalāpas and 480 rūpas in the 24 kamma-born parts; 5 kalāpas and 50 rūpas in the eyes, etc. Adding these figures results in 173 kalāpas and 1501 rūpas.

Because that fire element matures it, this body can manifest the state of not rotting (i.e., it can remain without decaying).

Furthermore, in this body, the air element, which has the characteristic of moving, causing movement, and supporting-stiffening, and which pervades the major and minor limbs, is established in the earth element, held together by water, and protected by fire; thus it supports, stiffens, and strengthens this body. Because it is strengthened by that air element, this body does not fall over and can stand upright. Being struck by another kind of propelling air, it can manifest the bodily intimation (viññatti) that makes one's will known in the postures of walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; it can bend and stretch the hands and feet, and move them here and there. As described, this mechanical puppet of the four elements, which deceives the ignorant by appearing as a woman, man, etc., and is like a magical illusion, is constantly occurring (through walking, standing, etc.). Thus, it should be reflected upon by way of particles. (3)

## (4) Reflection by Way of Characteristics, etc.

[362] 350. As for the reflection by way of characteristics and so on: What is the characteristic of the earth element? What is its function? What is its manifestation? Having reflected on the four elements in this manner, the earth element has the characteristic of hardness (kakkhaḷatta-lakkhaṇa). It has the function (rasa) of being the foundation (patiṭṭhāna-rasa) for co-nascent states.
362:
[The earth element] has the manifestation of receiving co-nascent states. The water element has the characteristic of flowing (liquidity); its function is moistening and increasing; its manifestation is the cohesion (binding) of co-nascent states. The fire element has the characteristic of heat; its function is ripening; its manifestation is the supplying of softness to co-nascent states. The air element has the characteristic of supporting (distending or stiffness); its function is motion (moving); its manifestation is conveying (leading forward). Thus, it should be adverted to by way of characteristics, etc.

## (5) Attention by Way of Origin (Samuṭṭhāna)

351. Regarding attention by way of origin: The forty-two parts, such as the hair of the head, etc., have been shown in detail by way of the earth element and so on. Among these forty-two parts, these four parts—undigested food, feces, pus, and urine—are originated by temperature only (utu-samuṭṭhāna). These four parts—tears, sweat, saliva, and snot—are originated by temperature and mind (utu-citta-samuṭṭhāna). The digestive fire (pācakatejo) that ripens what is eaten, etc., is originated by kamma only (kamma-samuṭṭhāna). In-breaths and out-breaths are originated by mind only (citta-samuṭṭhāna). All the remaining thirty-two parts are originated by the four causes [kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment] (catu-samuṭṭhāna). Thus, it should be adverted to by way of origin.

## (6) Attention by Way of Diversity and Unity

352. Regarding attention by way of diversity and unity: All four elements are diverse from each other by way of their own characteristics, etc. Indeed, the characteristic, function, and manifestation of the earth element are one way; those of the water element, etc., are another. Although they are diverse by way of characteristics, etc., and by way of origin (kamma-originated, etc.), these four elements are unified by way of being matter (rūpa), great primaries (mahābhūta), elements (dhātu), phenomena (dhamma), impermanence (anicca), and so on. To explain: All four elements are called matter (rūpa) because they do not transcend the characteristic of being molested (ruppana). They are called great primaries (mahābhūta) because of reasons such as great manifestation (mahanta-pātubhāva).

Regarding "because of reasons such as great manifestation": These elements are called "Great Primaries" (mahābhūta) because of their great manifestation, their similarity to great beings (mahābhūta-sāmañña), their great maintenance (mahā-parihāra), their great change (mahā-vikāra), and because they are great and are elements (mahattā bhūtattā).

Therein, "because of great manifestation" means these elements are manifested greatly in both the non-clung-to (anupādinna) continuity and the clung-to (upādinna) continuity. Their great manifestation in the non-clung-to continuity is stated in the description of the Recollection of the Buddha (Buddhānussati-niddesa) in this way:

"Two hundred thousand and forty thousand (240,000) [yojanas] in thickness is this earth..."

and so on. In the clung-to (upādinna) continuity as well, they are manifested greatly by way of the bodies of fish, turtles, deities, dānava asuras, and so on. Indeed, He [the Buddha] said: "Monks, there are beings in the great ocean with bodies of a hundred yojanas..." and so on.
363:
(6-1)
Regarding the similarity to a magician (māyākāra): Just as a magician shows a piece of ice, which is not a gem, as a gem; or shows a brick, which is not gold, as gold; and just as he himself, though neither a demon (yakkha) nor a bird, displays the form of a demon or a bird; in the same way, these great elements (mahābhūta), though not blue themselves, display blue derived materiality (upādā-rūpa); though not yellow, red, or white, they display yellow, red, and white derived materiality. Thus, they are called 'great elements' (mahābhūta) because of their similarity to a magician.

Note 1: Mahā (great) + abhūta (unreal) magic = Mahābhūta (a great unreal magical feat). Alternatively, Mahā (great) + abbhūta (extraordinary/marvelous) = Mahābhūta (a great marvelous magical feat). The one who performs such magic is also called a mahābhūta. The four great elements are called mahābhūta because they are similar to that magical mahābhūta.

Alternatively, just as the great beings (mahābhūta) such as demons (yakkha) seize or possess a person, yet the location of those demons is found neither inside nor outside that possessed person, nor do they exist without depending on that person; in the same way, these great elements are not found existing inside or outside one another, nor do they exist without depending on one another. Because of their inconceivable (acinteyya) state of existence, they are called 'great elements' (mahābhūta) due to their similarity to great beings like demons. Furthermore, just as the great beings known as ogresses (yakkhinī) deceive beings by concealing their own terrifying nature with pleasing colors, shapes, and gestures; in the same way, these great elements deceive foolish people by concealing their own intrinsic nature, such as harshness, with the pleasing complexion of a woman's or man's body, with the pleasing shapes of limbs and extremities, and with pleasing gestures like the movement of hands, feet, fingers, and eyebrows. They do not allow their true nature to be seen. Because of this deceptiveness, they are called 'great elements' (mahābhūta) due to their similarity to the great beings known as ogresses. (6-2)

Regarding 'because of great maintenance' (mahā-parihāra): It means they are maintained by vast and great causes. To elaborate: these great elements persist because they are daily provided with great amounts of food, clothing, and so forth. Therefore, they are called 'great elements' (mahābhūta). Alternatively, they are called 'great elements' because they exist being maintained by many requisites. (6-3)

Note 1: This explanation is primarily useful in the original Pali text; in the Burmese translation, it is already clarified and thus less significant.
Note 2: Mahā (vast food, clothing, etc.) + bhūta (become/exist) = Mahābhūta (elements that exist through vast requisites).
Note 3: Mahā (many requisites) + parihāra (maintained) + bhūta (become/exist) = Mahābhūta (elements that exist only when maintained by many requisites). In this method, 'parihāra' is considered elided.

Regarding 'because of great transformation' (mahā-vikāra): These great elements, whether non-clung-to (anupādinna) or clung-to (upādinna), undergo great transformations. Among them, the greatness of transformation in non-clung-to elements becomes evident at the time of the destruction of the world-cycle (kappa). The transformation of clung-to elements becomes evident at the time of the disturbance of the elements (dhātu-kkhobha). As follows:

[364] When the world of space (okāsa-loka) is consumed by the world-destroying fire, the flames rise from the earth and reach up to the Brahma world.

When the world of space is destroyed by the transformation of water, then a single universe (cakkavāḷa) numbering a hundred thousand crores is crushed and destroyed.

When the world of space is destroyed by the transformation of wind, then a single universe numbering a hundred thousand crores is scattered and destroyed.

Through the disturbance of the earth element (pathavī-dhātu), it becomes like a 'wood-mouth' [snake]. Just as a body bitten by a 'wood-mouth' snake (kaṭṭhamukha), which has a mouth that makes things like wood, becomes stiff, hard, and rigid; in the same way, due to the disturbance of the earth element, the body becomes stiff, hard, and rigid. That body, with its disturbed earth element, is as if it has fallen into the mouth of a 'wood-mouth' snake (or as if bitten by one).

The body becomes putrid, or is bitten by a 'putrid-mouth' [snake]. Through the disturbance of the water element (āpo-dhātu), it becomes like a 'putrid-mouth' [snake]. Just as a body bitten by a 'putrid-mouth' snake (pūtimukha), which has a mouth that causes putrefaction, becomes putrid; in the same way, through the disturbance of the water element...
364:
(The body becomes putrid.) That body, with the disruption of the water element, is as if it has fallen into the mouth of a pūtimukha snake (or as if bitten by a pūtimukha snake).

"The body becomes scorched, as if bitten by an aggimukha snake.
With the provocation of the fire element, it becomes like an aggimukha."

The aggimukha snake, which has a mouth that causes heat like fire, bites. The body becomes intensely scorched. Similarly, due to the provocation of the fire element, (the body becomes intensely scorched). That body, with the disruption of the fire element, is as if it has fallen into the mouth of an aggimukha snake (or as if bitten by an aggimukha snake).

"The body becomes cut to pieces, as if bitten by a satthamukha snake.
With the provocation of the air element, it becomes like a satthamukha."

The satthamukha snake, which has a mouth that cuts like a weapon, bites. The body is cut into pieces in the sense of the tendons being severed. Similarly, due to the provocation of the air element, (the body is cut into pieces). That body, with the disruption of the air element, is as if it has fallen into the mouth of a satthamukha snake (or as if bitten by a satthamukha snake). [Note 1]

As described, because they are elements (bhūta) with great transformations, they are called "Great Essentials" (mahābhūta). (6-4)

In the sense of being great and manifest—in this regard, these Great Essentials are "great" (mahanta) because they must be grasped and discerned with great effort, and they are "elements" (bhūta) because they are manifest. Thus, because they are great and manifest, they are called mahābhūta. (6-5)

[Note 1: These verses and meanings are provided in full for those who wish to memorize them.]

As described, all these four elements are called mahābhūta for reasons such as their great manifestation (mahantapātubhāva).

Furthermore, because they bear their own individual characteristics, and because they bring about the suffering of the round of rebirth, or because they are the cause of producing suffering, or because they are the repository of suffering [Note 1], all four elements are called "elements" (dhātu) because they do not transcend the characteristic of an element. They are called "phenomena" (dhamma) because they bear their own characteristics and because they last according to their own moment (of mind and matter). They are "impermanent" (anicca) in the sense of perishing. They are "suffering" (dukkha) in the sense of being fearsome. They are "non-self" (anattā) in the sense of being coreless.

As described, the unity (sameness) of all four elements should be understood by way of their being matter, being great essentials, being elements, being phenomena, being impermanent, and so on. Thus, they should be attended to by way of diversity and unity. (6)

[Note 1: Refer back to the note on page 666, note 1.]

## (7) Attention by way of Resolution and Non-resolution

[365] 353. Regarding the method of attention by way of resolution and non-resolution: These four elements, which always arise simultaneously and together, cannot be resolved (separated) by location even in the smallest unit, such as a pure octad (suddhaṭṭhaka), etc. However, they are resolved (separated) by their individual characteristics. Thus, they should be attended to by way of resolution and non-resolution. (7)
365:
1. In this phrase, the restriction "only" shows that it does not mean the elements are separate from each other. Such separate elements can indeed be distinguished individually.
2. Here, the word "and so on" includes the jīvitanavaka-kalāpa (life-nonad group), which is the smallest unit among the kamma-born groups.
3. They cannot be distinguished by location, such as "this element is above, that element is below." In fact, wherever the earth element is present, the other three elements are also present; and wherever the other elements are present, the earth element is also present. Therefore, they cannot be distinguished by location.

## (8) Attention by way of Similarity and Dissimilarity
354. Attention by way of similarity and dissimilarity is as follows: Although they are inseparable as just described, among these four elements, the first two elements—earth and water—are similar in that they are heavy. Likewise, the latter two elements—fire and air—are similar in that they are light. The first two are dissimilar to the latter two, and the latter two are dissimilar to the first two. Thus, attention should be paid by way of similarity and dissimilarity. (8)

## (9) Attention by way of Internal and External Distinction
355. Attention by way of the distinction between internal and external elements is as follows: Internal (ajjhattika) elements are the support for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and heart-base, which are the bases for consciousness; for the media of communication (viññatti); and for the faculties (indriya) of femininity, masculinity, and life.

Note:
1. In the Atthasālinī, page 368, the earth element is analyzed using the terms: kakkhaḷaṃ (hard), mudukaṃ (soft), saṇhaṃ (smooth), pharuṃsaṃ (rough), garukaṃ (heavy), and lahukaṃ (light). In that context, the meaning of "light" should be understood either in comparison to something heavier or as being light by its own nature. Furthermore, according to the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) which is the basis for Note 1 to be mentioned on page 691,
they occur together with the four postures and are produced by the four causes: kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment. External (bāhira) elements are not the support for the bases, media of communication, or faculties; they do not occur together with the postures, and they are produced only by temperature. Thus, attention should be paid by way of the distinction between internal and external. (9)

## (10) Attention by way of Inclusion
356. Attention by way of inclusion or grouping is as follows: The earth element produced by kamma is included or grouped together with the other elements produced by kamma because there is no difference in their origin. Similarly, the earth element produced by mind, etc., is included or grouped together with the other elements produced by mind, etc. (The other three elements are likewise included or grouped with other elements of the same origin). Thus, attention should be paid by way of inclusion. (10)

## (11) Attention by way of Condition
357. Attention by way of condition or support is as follows: The earth element, being held together by the water element,

Note:
