It should also be understood that the water element is heavier than the earth element. Therefore, in this context, both earth and water elements are said to be heavy.

maintained by the fire element, and distended by the air element, acts as a condition by being the foundation for the other three great essentials. The water element, being founded on the earth element, maintained by the fire element, and distended by the air element, acts as a condition by being the cohesion for the other three great essentials. The fire element, being founded on the earth element, held together by the water element, and distended by the air element, acts as a condition by being the maturation for the other three great essentials. The air element, being founded on the earth element, held together by the water element, and matured by the fire element, acts as a condition by being the distension for the other three great essentials. Thus, attention should be paid by way of condition. (11)

## (12) Attention by way of Lack of Reflection
358. Attention by way of the lack of reflection or awareness is as follows: Among these four elements, the earth element does not know, "I am the earth element," or "I act as a condition by being the foundation for the three great essentials." The other three elements also do not know, "The earth element acts as a condition by being the foundation for us." This same principle applies to all the remaining three elements. Thus, attention should be paid by way of the lack of reflection. (12)

## (13) Attention by way of Analysis of Conditions
359. Attention by way of analyzing the specific conditions and specific powers is as follows: The conditions that support the four elements are fourfold: kamma, mind, temperature, and nutriment. Among them, for the elements produced by kamma, kamma alone is the condition.

Mind, temperature, and nutriment are not the causes [1]. For elements born of mind, temperature, and nutriment, only mind, temperature, and nutriment are the causes; others like kamma are not. Furthermore, kamma is the productive (janaka) cause of kamma-born elements; for the remaining elements, it is the strong dependence (upanissaya) cause by way of figurative expression [2]. Mind is the productive cause of mind-born elements;

However, because it is taught in the Suttanta discourses as 'depending on a person' or 'depending on a forest', it should be understood as the strong dependence condition by way of Suttanta figurative expression (pariyāya), meaning arising inseparably from a certain cause.

360. The benefit is this: the bhikkhu devoted to this meditation on the definition of the four elements plunges into emptiness and uproots the perception of a being (satta-saññā). Because the perception of a being has been uprooted, he does not fall into the conceptualization of wild beasts, yakkhas, or rakkhasas, and thus he is able to overcome fear and dread. ## Conclusion of the Discourse on Concentration

361. To conclude the discourse on concentration: with this much sequence of words on meditation, the detailed explanation of concentration and the method of its development [have been shown]. To show this, the questions were asked: "What is concentration? In what sense is it concentration?" and so forth.
368:
The explanation of the meaning of the question 'How should it be developed?'—which was presented through such methods as 'For what reason is it called concentration?'—is now complete in every respect. [368]

Indeed, only these two types of concentration, namely access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi), are intended here in the context of 'developing the mind' (cittaṃ bhāvayaṃ). Among these two, one-pointedness (ekaggatā) in the ten meditation subjects and in the states of mind preceding absorption is access concentration. One-pointedness of mind in the remaining thirty meditation subjects is absorption concentration. Both types of concentration are considered developed because those forty meditation subjects have been developed. Therefore, I said: 'The explanation of the meaning of the question "How should it be developed?" is complete in every respect.'

## The Benefits of Concentration

362. Regarding the question, 'What is the benefit of the development of concentration (samādhi-bhāvanā)?', there are five kinds of benefits of the development of concentration, beginning with 'pleasant abiding in the present life' (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra). To explain these five benefits in detail:

Arahants whose taints are destroyed develop concentration with the intention, 'Having entered into an attainment, we shall dwell happily for the whole day with a concentrated mind.' For these Arahants, the development of absorption concentration has the benefit of pleasant abiding in the present life. Thus, the Blessed One said: 'Cunda, these [jhanas] are not called "effacement" (sallekha) in the Discipline of the Noble One. These are called "pleasant abidings in the present life" (diṭṭhadhamma-sukhavihāra) in the Discipline of the Noble One.' (1)

For learners (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana) who develop it with the intention, 'Having emerged from the attainment, we shall practice insight with a concentrated mind,' the development of absorption concentration has the benefit of insight because it is the proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for insight. Likewise, the development of access concentration has the benefit of insight through the method of 'attaining an opportunity in a crowded place.' Thus, the Blessed One said: 'Develop concentration, monks. A monk who is concentrated, monks, understands things as they really are.' (2)

Note 1: This is the meaning of the phrase 'sambādhe okāsādhigamanayena'. In this regard, the sub-commentary states: 'Sambādhe' means in the round of rebirths, which is an extremely narrow and crowded place because it is burned and defiled by craving and other defilements. 'Okāsādhigamanayena' means by the method of obtaining the good opportunity called the 'ninth moment' (navama-khaṇa), which is suitable for attaining the fruit of the Path. Indeed, because that ninth moment is difficult to obtain, a person with a strong sense of urgency (saṃvega) does not wait to attain absorption jhāna but, established in access concentration alone, practices insight with the intention of swiftly escaping the suffering of the round of rebirths. Although this explanation seems smooth, it may not align with the intention of the Commentator. In the Mahākaccāna Sutta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya (Vol. 2, p. 277), it is stated: 'By that Blessed One... the attainment of opportunity in a crowded place was discovered for the purification of beings... for the realization of Nibbāna.' This sutta is also cited in the Visuddhimagga (p. 220). In the commentary to that sutta, 'crowded' (sambādha) is explained as the household life, which is crowded with the five cords of sensual pleasure. 'Attainment of opportunity' (okāsādhigama) is explained as obtaining the six recollections (anussati), such as the recollection of the Buddha. In that Kaccāna Sutta, it is taught how one can realize the Path, Fruit, and Nibbāna by practicing insight after attaining access concentration through the development of the six recollections. Similarly, by taking the method of 'attaining opportunity' from the Kaccāna Sutta, it should be understood that practicing insight while established in access concentration—attained through other meditation subjects as well—is what is meant by 'practicing insight by the method of attaining opportunity while living in the crowded household life.' This access concentration has the benefit of insight because it is a proximate cause for insight. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: 'Develop concentration, monks. A monk who is concentrated, monks, understands things as they really are.' (Note: The full Pali and translation are provided here for those who wish to memorize it.)

Those who, having produced the eight attainments and entered the jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge, emerge from that jhāna and produce direct knowledges—wishing for them according to the method described as 'being one, he becomes many' and so on—for them, the development of absorption concentration has the benefit of direct knowledge because it is the proximate cause for direct knowledge whenever the conditions are present. Thus, the Blessed One said: 'To whatever state to be realized by direct knowledge [369] he inclines his mind for realizing it by direct knowledge, he attains the ability to witness it for himself there, whenever the conditions are present.'
369:
(3)
Those worldlings who have not fallen away from the jhanas they have attained, whether they aspire to rebirth in the Brahma-world or not, their development of absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) brings about a special state of existence as its benefit. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
'Having developed the first jhana to a limited extent, where are they reborn? They are reborn in the company of the devas of the Brahma-pārisajja,' and so on.

Note 1: This is the meaning of the phrase 'sati sati āyatanne'. Here, the repetition 'sati sati' is a verbal distributive (vīcchā), similar to the phrase 'gacchante gacchante kāle' (as time goes on). By this distributive, it encompasses all the causes for obtaining the five supernormal powers (abhiññā). If there is a cause for obtaining only one supernormal power, it is the proximate cause for that one; if there are causes for two, three, or four, it is the proximate cause for those; if there are causes for all five, it is the proximate cause for all five. Therefore, to make this meaning clear, it is translated as 'to the extent that the conditions exist'. See also Note 1 on page 296.

The development of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) also brings about special states of existence in the happy destinations of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-sugati).

(4)
Furthermore, those noble ones (ariya) who, having produced the eight attainments and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), remain without consciousness for seven days, experiencing the bliss of Nibbāna—which is cessation—in this very life, develop concentration with that intention. For those noble ones, the development of absorption concentration has the attainment of cessation as its benefit. Therefore, it was said: 'The understanding which is mastery through sixteen kinds of knowledge-conduct and nine kinds of concentration-conduct is the knowledge of the attainment of cessation.'

Note 1: The phrase 'the peace which is cessation' is the literal grammatical meaning of the two words 'nirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ'. What ceases? According to the Pali text 'saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti', it should be understood that all mental phenomena (nāma-dhamma), including consciousness (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) characterized by perception (saññā) and feeling (vedanā), cease.

(5)
As just described, this fivefold benefit of the development of concentration, beginning with abiding in happiness in this very life, is the advantage of developing concentration.

'Therefore, in the practice of developing concentration, which has many benefits and cleanses the stains of defilements, the wise person should not be negligent.' This is the exhortation.

Note: When consciousness and mental factors cease, the mind-produced materiality (cittaja-rūpa) also ceases. When the knowing mind ceases, the suffering associated with materiality also becomes unapparent, so it can be said that all suffering ceases. Therefore, the Commentary states: 'To Nibbāna means to the cessation of the three kinds of suffering (suffering as pain, suffering in change, and suffering in formations). Indeed, although there is suffering in formations inherent in materiality, because there is no consciousness, it is as if it does not exist.'

[363] By this much, in this Path of Purification (Visuddhimagga) taught through the headings of virtue, concentration, and wisdom in the verse 'A man wise, established in virtue...', concentration has also been fully explained.

Thus, in the Path of Purification composed for the purpose of gladdening good people, the Eleventh Chapter, called the Exposition of Concentration (Samādhi-niddesa), is concluded.

## (The Exposition of Concentration is finished).
